# 2.3.2.1 Dithienosilole-Based D1-A-D2-A-D1-Type Molecular Donors

Bazan and coworkers took DTS as D2, pyridinethiadiazole (PT) or BT as A and bithiophene as D1 and obtained several SMDs through adjusting the position of the nitrogen of PT, which could obviously change the dipole moment and molecular stacking [106]. These SMDs showed broad and strong absorptions in the visible light region but due to the stronger electron-accepting ability of PT, the absorptions of $p { \mathrm { - D T S } } ( \mathrm { P T T h } _ { 2 } ) _ { 2 }$ $d \mathrm { - D T S } ( \mathrm { P T T h } _ { 2 } ) _ { 2 }$ , and SMD4 were red shifted compared with BT-based SMD5, and the shoulder peaks indicated the ordered stacking. With $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ as interlayer, SMD5-based device showed no obvious photovoltaic performance due to the poor crystallinity and phase separation, while the performance of PT-based SMDs was greatly related to the molecular symmetry. The PCEs of the devices based on symmetric $p { \mathrm { - D T S } } ( \mathrm { P T T h } _ { 2 } ) _ { 2 }$ and $d { \cdot } \mathrm { D T S } ( \mathrm { P T T h } _ { 2 } ) _ { 2 }$ were $6 . 7 0 \%$ and $5 . 5 6 \%$ , respectively, while asymmetric SMD4-based device only gave a PCE of $3 . 1 6 \%$ . The reason was that the long ordering range of blends based on symmetric SMDs was favorable for charge transport. However, the lone pairs of electrons in PT pyridyl nitrogen were sensitive to acid, leading to a decreased PCE when using poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrenesulfonicacid) (PEDOT:PSS) as interlayer. Therefore, Bazan and coworkers utilized fluorinated benzothiadiazole (FBT) to substitute PT to offer $p \mathrm { - D T S ( F B T T h } _ { 2 } ) _ { 2 }$ , which achieved a PCE of $7 . 0 \%$ with PEDOT:PSS as interlayer [107], and further optimization made the PCE promoted to $9 . 0 2 \%$ [108]. Extending the conjugation offered a series of SMDs, among which AT1 showed a bad planarity due to the steric hindrance, and little crystalline in the blends, leading to a poor PCE of $1 . 3 0 \%$ [109], while X1, X2, and F1-F3 all showed relatively large $\Delta \mu _ { \mathrm { g e } }$ , benefiting charge dissociation, and gave PCEs of approximately $6 \%$ [110]. By replacing the silicon of $p \mathrm { - D T S ( F B T T h _ { 2 } ) _ { 2 } }$ with germanium, $p \mathrm { - D T G ( F B T T h } _ { 2 } ) _ { 2 }$ was synthesized [111]. Good phase separation and well-connected domains were observed in the blend, and the PCE was comparable to that of $p \mathrm { - D T S ( F B T T h } _ { 2 } ) _ { 2 }$ -based device. Moreover, conjugation-extended $\mathrm { D T G } ( \mathrm { F B T } _ { 2 } \mathrm { T h } _ { 2 } ) _ { 2 }$ realized a promoted PCE of $9 . 1 0 \%$ [112]. The structures of the SMDs mentioned above were shown in Figure 2.9.

From Table 2.9, DTS-based D1-A-D2-A-D1-type SMDs usually show small $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } } \mathbf { s }$ which is conducive to light harvest; however, when blended with fullerene, $V _ { \mathrm { o c } } \mathrm { \mathbf { s } }$ were moderate with values of $0 . 7 0 { - } 0 . 8 0 \mathrm { V } _ { \mathrm { i } }$ showing room for improvement.

# 2.3.2.2 Benzodithiophene-Based D1-A-D2-A-D1-Type Molecular Donors

With triisopropylsilylethynyl (TIPS)-substituted BDT as D2, FBT-TIPSBDT showed a planar structure, leading to effective $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking and benefiting charge transport, and a PCE of $5 . 6 9 \%$ with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 4 \mathrm { V }$ was delivered [113]. Taking bithiophene as D1, pyridopyrazine (PP) as A, BDT as D2, SMDs with different side chains were reported [114]. Among these SMDs, SM3, and SM4 showed obvious self-assembly capabilities, but $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking of SM4 was denser. In blends, SM3-based one exhibited large phase separation, while SM4-based one showed bicontinuous interpenetrating networks, explaining the PCE difference $2 . 5 \%$ versus $6 . 5 \%$ ). Mullen and coworkers designed several SMDs and studied the effects of the conjugation length of the D1 and the length of its alkyl chains on the final performance [115]. With D1 changing from thiophene to $\mathrm { T } 3 2 b \mathrm { T }$ and to bithiophene, absorptions of M1, M2, and M3-C8 were red shifted with increased molar absorption coefficients, which was conducive to a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ . And the devices gave PCEs of $1 . 1 \%$ $3 . 7 \%$ , and $5 . 2 \%$ , respectively. With the alkyl chain on bithiophene changing from $n$ -octyl to $n$ -hexyl and to $n$ -butyl, molecular stacking became more ordered, facilitating charge transport, and the PCEs were promoted from $5 . 2 \%$ to $5 . 5 \%$ and to $6 . 0 \%$ . Zhan and coworkers introduced triphenylamine and $n$ -butyl-substituted benzene into D1 unit, and used diketopyrrolopyrrole (DPP) as A unit to offer DPA-diDPPBDT and $n$ -Bu-diDPPBDT [116]. They showed similar $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } } \mathbf { s }$ , but the stronger absorption of DPA-diDPPBDT and the favorable phase separation in the blend contributed to its higher PCE. Further replacing $n$ -butyl of $n$ -Bu-diDPPBDT with trifluoromethyl, BDTT $\left( \mathrm { D P P } \right) _ { 2 } – \mathrm { C F } _ { 3 }$ was obtained, which delivered a PCE of over $6 \%$ with simultaneously increased $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and FF [117]. The structures of the molecules mentioned above are shown in Figure 2.10.

# 2.3.2.3 Indacenodithiophene-Based D1-A-D2-A-D1-Type Molecular Donors

Indacenodithiophene (IDT) owns a large planar conjugated skeleton, which can form ordered stacking in the solid state and facilitate charge transport, making it a widely used central electron-donating block in the design of SMDs (Figure 2.11).

Hou and coworkers designed $\mathrm { I D T } ( \mathrm { B T T h } _ { 2 } ) _ { 2 }$ with IDT as D2 [118]. It showed a strong absorption in $5 0 0 { - } 7 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ and the device gave a PCE of $4 . 2 5 \%$ with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 3 \mathrm { V } _ { : }$ which was benefited from its deep HOMO energy level. Jen and coworkers took conjugation extended indacenodithienothiophene (IDTT) as D2 and reported four SMDs with increased dipole moment of D1-A group (IDTT-DFBT-BT, IDTT-FBT-TT, IDTT-FBT-BT, and IDTT-FBT-3T) [119]. A larger dipole moment could increase the self-assembly, enhance the order at the donor-acceptor interface, and increase the dielectric property that could lower the exciton binding energy and decrease charge recombination. Therefore, IDTT-FBT-3T achieved the best PCE of $6 . 5 4 \%$

BIT series reported by Wang and coworkers are representative examples. Compared with BIT, BIT-4F showed a lower-lying energy level due to the electron-withdrawing nature of difluorinated BT and a better planarity because of F-S or F-H interactions. By introducing a thiophene between D2 and A, BIT-4F-T showed a stronger absorption, higher $\pi$ -electron delocalization, and more ordered stacking, also, $\Delta \mu _ { \mathrm { g e } }$ of BIT-4F-T was increased, and these all contributed to the high PCE of $8 . 1 \%$ [120]. Based on BIT-4F-T, BIT6F, BIT8F, and BIT10F were reported by extending the conjugation length [121]. Conjugation expansion brought red-shifted absorption, increased molar absorption coefficient, up-shifted HOMO, and downshifted LUMO energy levels. These SMDs all showed face-on orientation, favoring charge transport. The devices based on BIT6F/BIT10F with centrosymmetric electron-rich IDT delivered higher PCEs than those of the devices based on BIT-4F-T/BIT8F with axisymmetric electron-deficient difluorinated BT. The highest PCE of $9 . 0 9 \%$ was achieved in BIT6F-based device.

From Table 2.11, this type of SMDs often show high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } } \mathrm { s }$ and FFs; however, their wide $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } } \mathbf { s }$ limit the maximum obtainable $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ . How to improve $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ without sacrificing $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and FF is urgent, which requires optimization both on molecule and device.

# 2.3.3 Porphyrin-Based Molecular Donors

Porphyrins (Por), which are widely used in low-bandgap donors, own unique characteristics: (i) large conjugated planar structure with $2 6 \pi$ -electrons can facilitate $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking, benefiting charge transport; (ii) wide absorption reaching NIR region and high extinction coefficient benefit light harvest and obtain a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ ;, and (ii) multiple modification sites make the molecular properties highly tunable. Herein, some high-performance Por-based SMDs (Figure 2.12) will be introduced.

The most representative structure of Por-type SMDs is A- $\pi$ Por $\pi$ -A. Regulating the side chain on Por, Peng and coworkers took zinc Por $( \mathrm { Z n P } )$ as central unit, acetylene as $\pi$ -linker, and DPP as terminal to offer DPPEZnP-based SMDs [122-124]. DPPEZnP-TEH, -TBO, and -THD all had broad absorptions from the ultraviolet (UV) to NIR region, attributed to the good conjugation planarity and the strong ICT effect. The devices achieved PCEs of $8 . 0 8 \%$ $9 . 0 6 \%$ , and $9 . 4 1 \%$ , respectively. Among them, DPPEZnP-TBO-based one achieved a respectable $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 9 . 5 8 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , while DPPEZnP-THD-based one realized a high FF of 0.70. By replacing the thienyl of the side chain of DPPEZnP-TBO with benzothienyl with a weaker electron-donating ability, DPPEZnP-BzTBO was obtained with a lower lying HOMO energy level [125]. And the final device provided a similar PCE but a higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 0 \mathrm { V } .$ Inserting another conjugated unit between acetylene and terminal moiety is also an effective strategy. With RD derivatives as A, PTTCNR with terthiophene insertion showed extended conjugation and polymorphic molecular stacking and realized a PCE of $8 . 2 1 \%$ [126]. Por-S with alkylthio-substituted phenyl insertion showed a good self-assemble ability and preferred to $J$ -aggregating in the blend, demonstrating a PCE of over $8 \%$ [127]. Utilizing CPDT and thienylenevinylenethiophene as insertion has also been reported with PCEs of approximately $8 \%$ [128, 129].

![](images/e1985b5f8ad9cc3f5b5fa9f0480d423f532d730e5adab216d4ac2a538e5e27af.jpg)  
Figure 2.12 Molecular structures of the Por-based SMDs. Source: Qihui Yue.

Medium-sized SMDs containing two Por units have also achieved excellent results. CS-DP with an A $\pi$ -Por- $\pi$ -Por- $\pi$ -A framework exhibited an ultra-narrow $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ of $1 . 2 6 \mathrm { e V }$ and delivered a PCE of $8 . 2 9 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 7 8 \mathrm { V } .$ It is worth noting that the energy loss $( E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } = E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \ \mathrm { o p t } } - q V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ where $q$ represents the elementary charge) was only $0 . 4 8 \mathrm { e V } ,$ much smaller compared with most fullerene-based SMSCs [130]. In addition, A- $\pi$ Por $\pi$ x $\pi$ Por $\pi$ -A framework has been reported, where X can be electron-donating or -accepting unit. With alkoxy-substituted benzene as the X, (DPP-ZnP-E)2-Ph delivered a PCE of $6 . 4 2 \%$ [131], and ZnP2BT-RH with BT as the X gave a record PCE of $1 0 . 0 2 \%$ [132]. Both SMDs exhibited small $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } } \mathbf { s }$ of approximately $1 . 4 0 \mathrm { e V }$ and high molar extinction coefficients, indicating the strong ICT effect.

Besides, there are some metal-free Por-based SMDs such as BP and CABP. They owned similar structures, and when they were mixed at a ratio of $0 . 7 5 \colon 0 . 2 5$ to form a solid solution, the PHJ device with fullerene as acceptor gave a PCE of $3 . 6 \%$ , higher than those of the devices using $1 0 0 \%$ BP or CABP. The proper energy levels of the solid solution could guarantee charge separation when matched with fullerene, and the partial disordering caused by the insertion of CABP into the BP crystal lattice could decrease the recombination, which both contributed to the performance enhancement [133].

As listed in Table 2.12, Por-based SMDs generally show narrow $E _ { \mathbf { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } } \mathbf { s }$ , favoring high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } } \mathbf { s }$ and are promising candidates for the rear cell of tandem devices [97]. However, the moderate $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 7 \mathrm { - } 0 . 8 \mathrm { V }$ and FF of 0.6-0.7 reveal room for further improvement.

# 2.3.4 Other Molecular Donors

Compared with D-A copolymers, D-A oligomers show wider $E _ { \mathbf { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } } \mathbf { s }$ , limiting the light harvest, but their high purity with defined structures and high crystallinity can facilitate charge transport (typical examples are shown in Figure 2.13). Wei and coworkers designed O-BDTdFBT by alternating BDT and difluorinated BT [134]. Compared with the polymer P-BDTdFBT, O-BDTdFBT exhibited a wider $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ of

$1 . 8 3 \mathrm { e V } ,$ but more obvious red-shifted absorption from the solution to the film indicated the more effective stacking. And the O-BDTdFBT-based blend showed higher crystallinity and proper phase separation, favoring exciton diffusion, charge separation, and transport, contributing to a higher PCE of $8 . 1 0 \%$ . Then, they reported O-1, O-2, M-1, and M-2 [135]. With the conjugation length increasing, red-shifted and stronger absorptions were observed. Compared with O-1 and O-2, M-1 and M-2 showed not only broadened absorptions and smaller $E _ { \mathbf { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } } \mathbf { s }$ but also more ordered stacking due to the better planarity. The devices gave PCEs of $1 . 0 6 \%$ $7 . 1 9 \%$ $9 . 2 5 \%$ and $8 . 9 1 \%$ , respectively, among which the poor performance of O-1-based one was due to the overmixed morphology.

In addition to the building blocks mentioned earlier, other units have showed good properties in SMDs (Figure 2.13). Nguyen and coworkers took DPP, thiophene, and benzofuran to construct $\mathrm { D P P } ( \mathrm { T B F u } ) _ { 2 }$ . It had matched both absorption and energy levels with $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ The optimized blend showed nanoscale phase separation and the device gave a PCE of $4 . 4 \%$ [136]. Sun and coworkers utilized POZ as the center, and linked BT, thiophene, and DCV on both sides of it in turn to offer POZ2, achieving a PCE of $7 . 4 4 \%$ [137]. Kido and coworkers regulated the side chain and the number of hydroxyl groups to offer squaraine (SQ) series SMDs, which well adjusted the photoelectronic properties and molecular stacking. Hydroxyl groups could downshift the HOMO energy level, while the linear side chain could improve the crystallinity. These SMDs showed different aggregation in the neat films, but they all $J$ -aggregated when matched with $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ , favoring a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ . And the SQ2-based device demonstrated a champion PCE of $4 . 0 \%$ [138].

The relevant performance parameters are listed in Table 2.13.

# 2.4 Current Progress on Small-Molecule Solar Cells with Nonfullerene Acceptors

To get high-performance SMsCs, material combination and morphology control are of great importance. For material combination, materials with different $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } } \mathbf { s }$ are needed, aiming to form complementary absorption to get a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ . Also, the energy-level alignment should be proper to get a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ meanwhile ensure the effective charge separation. Morphology control aims to form a balance between exciton dissociation and charge transport, and thus improve the performance. Fullerene-based SMSCs have achieved PCEs of over $1 0 \%$ as introduced [9-13]; however, fullerenes have some nonnegligible limitations such as synthetic difficulty, weak absorption, rigid energy levels, large $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ , and morphology instability. In contrast, small-molecule nonfullerene acceptors (SM-NFAs) exhibit highly tunable $E _ { \mathbf { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } } \mathbf { s }$ and energy levels, high absorption extinction coefficients, and high exciton diffusion coefficients; meanwhile, even a small driving force can drive efficient charge transfer in devices, and charges can transport through three-dimensional (3D) channels formed by strong $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking and intermolecular interactions [139-141], bringing great breakthroughs in the performance of SMSCs [5].

However, due to the lack of proper materials, the development of NFA-based VD-SMsCs is slow, only several examples were reported. For example, when $\alpha$ 6T was matched with SubPc and SubNc, compared with $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ -based device, the improved energy-level alignment and broadened absorption led to significantly increased $V _ { \mathrm { o c } } , J _ { \mathrm { s c } } .$ and thus PCEs ( $4 . 6 9 \%$ and $6 . 0 2 \%$ , respectively). Further depositing $\alpha$ 6T, SubNc, and SubPc sequentially, the PCE was promoted to $8 . 4 0 \%$ , attributed to the cascade-like energy levels that benefited exciton dissociation, and the energy transfer from SubPc to SubNc [142]. For SP-SMSCs, the choices of SM-NFAs are various. Through subtle molecular design, delicate morphology optimization, and device engineering, NFA-based SMSCs have achieved PCEs of over $1 5 \%$ [14-18].

Therefore, in this section, we mainly focus on the SP-SMsCs with NFAs, including binary and ternary devices.

# 2.4.1 Binary Solar Cells

Perylene diimide (PDI) derivatives have been introduced in SMSCs. However, due to the wide $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } } \mathbf { s }$ that limit light harvest, and rigid planar structures that tend to form large aggregates, when matched with SMDs, PDI-based SMSCs only show moderate performance [143]. Another type of SM-NFAs, fused-ring electron acceptors (FREAs), which often exhibit planar A-D-A structures, and highly tunable photoelectronic properties, have also been applied. Nowadays, combining a wide-bandgap SMD and a small-bandgap FREA has been proved to be effective in constructing high-performance SMsCs. Some instructive examples will be introduced as follows.

IDIC, derived from ITIC [144], is one of the most well-known NFAs used in SMSCs [145]. It shows a strong absorption in $5 0 0 { - } 8 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , which is complementary to the absorptions of most SMDs. Blending IDIC with DRTB-T delivered a high PCE of over $9 \%$ , attributed to the nanoscale phase separation and proper crystallinity [146]. Further pairing IDIC with various SMDs, such as H11, SM1, BDT(TVT-SR), P2TBR, could achieve PCEs of $9 \mathrm { - } 1 1 \%$ [147-150]. Fluorinating IDIC offered IDIC-4F, which is also popular in SMSCs. With OT-based D5T2F-P as donor, an impressive PCE of $9 . 3 6 \%$ was realized [151]. And with liquid-crystalline NDT-3T-R6 as donor, the PCE reached $1 0 . 7 \%$ with a high FF of over 0.70 [152]. Other ITIC derivatives, such as IT-4F and 6TIC, can also achieve excellent performance with PCEs of over $1 0 \%$ [153, 154], among which when 6TIC was matched with Por-based DPPEZnP-TBO, utilizing solvent additive and SVA could properly control crystallinity, improve phase separation and domain purity, contributing to an outstanding PCE of over $1 2 \%$ with a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of over $2 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and an FF of 0.74 [154].

Another popular NFA is Y6, which exhibits wide and strong absorption covering $6 0 0 { - } 9 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , and realized a record PCE of $1 5 . 7 \%$ in a PSC [155]. Then, various BDT-based SMDs have been applied to match with it. By modifying BTR with chlorine, BTR-Cl was obtained, which maintained liquid crystalline character, but showed enhanced molecular order with an edge-on orientation [156]. When matched with Y6 that preferred a face-on orientation, 3D charge pathways formed, and significant phase separation was observed. These contributed to a high PCE of $1 3 . 6 \%$ . Using BTEC-2F, BSFTR, SM1-F, as donors could also obtain comparable or slightly better performance [157-159]. Matching ZR1 based on a DTBDT core with Y6, the PCE reached $1 4 . 3 4 \%$ , attributed to the hierarchical morphology that was conducive to charge separation and transport [160]. Blending SMDs with some Y6-derived SM-NFAs also delivered encouraging results. Combinations of B1:BO-4Cl [15] and BT-2F:N3 [18] both demonstrated PCEs of over $1 5 \%$

SMSCs based on other SM-NFAs, such as DR3TBDTT:O-IDTBR, DRCN5T:F-2Cl, and BSFTR:NBDTP- $\cdot \mathrm { F _ { o u t } }$ , have also obtained inspiring PCEs [161-163].

# 2.4.2Ternary Solar Cells

Compared with binary SMsCs, the introduction of the third component to construct ternary SMSCs (t-SMsCs) can individually or simultaneously (i) enhance light harvest, (ii) facilitate charge transfer, (iii) regulate morphology, and (iv) strengthen morphology stability [164]. According to the composition of NFA-based t-SMSCs, they can be divided into three main categories: two SMDs/one SM-NFA, one SMD/two SM-NFAs, and one SMD/one fullerene/one SM-NFA, and the state-ofthe-art t-SMSCs have accomplished PCEs of over $1 5 \%$ and still show great potential [14, 16, 17].

The first category of t-SMsCs was seldom reported, which might be due to the difficulty in morphology control or the relatively low electron mobility of SM-NFAs. By adding DR3TBDTT-S-E into DCAO3TBDTT:IDIC system with a PCE of $9 . 4 9 \%$ , the PCE of the t-SMSC was improved to $1 0 . 0 4 \%$ with increased $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and FF. Such an enhancement was attributed to the fact that DR3TBDTT-S-E reduced the aggregations of the binary blend and established 3D charge transport pathways with mixed edge-on and face-on orientations [165]. For the second category, the two NFAs often exhibit similar structures with good compatibility. When adding $1 0 \%$ 4TIC into ZnP-TSEH:6TIC system, the crystallinity of the blend was effectively enhanced and proper multilength scale morphology formed, making the PCE promoted from $1 3 . 5 4 \%$ to $1 5 . 8 8 \%$ [16]. A small amount of Y7 can well modified the phase separation and molecular arrangement of B1:BO-4Cl-based system and thus promoted the PCE to a value of $1 6 . 2 8 \%$ [17].

From the perspectives of absorption complementarity, phase separation adjustment and electron transport ability, fullerene is a promising third component. In the BTR $\mathrm { \cdot P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and BTR:NITI binary SMSCs, PCEs of $9 . 3 0 \%$ and $6 . 8 2 \%$ were realized, respectively; however, the t-SMSC yielded significantly promoted performance with an average PCE of $1 3 . 2 0 \%$ [166]. Besides the absorption contribution from NITI and the cascade-like energy level alignment, the more important reason was the formation of hierarchical morphology: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ served as the framework, while BTR and NITI with good compatibility were filled in the vacancies of the framework, and SVA facilitated the phase separation between BTR and NITI, making NITI be extruded to the boundary of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ After charge separation, holes and electrons transported mainly through BTR and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ pathways. Such a morphology helped reduce the $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ , suppress recombination, and balance charge transport. This work manifested the indispensability of fullerene and NFAs, and this strategy has been proved to be effective in achieving high-performance t-SMsCs [14, 167-169]. For example, adding a small amount of fullerene into BTR-Cl:Y6 blend, the PCE was promoted from $1 3 . 6 \%$ to $1 5 . 3 4 \%$ with an enhanced FF, attributed to the reduced bimolecular recombination and the better mixed donor/acceptor phase with reasonable domain sizes [14].

# 2.5 Summary and Outlook

$p$ Type molecular photovoltaic materials are promising candidates for highly efficient OsCs. The molecular innovation is one of the important factors that promote the development of SMsCs, leading to great breakthroughs. In addition, when they are added into some PSC systems, impressive performance results have been obtained [170-172]. In this chapter, we mainly focus on their applications in SMSCs, and representative examples have been reviewed systematically. Regardless of the SMDs applied in VD- or SP-SMSCs, the molecular design includes backbone engineering (electron-donating and electron-accepting moieties) and accessional group optimization (side chain and $\pi$ -linker), which can affect not only photoelectronic properties but also morphology and thus performance. Nowadays, fullerene-based SMSCs have achieved PCEs of $1 0 \%$ in both VD- and SP-SMSCs, and NFA-based SMSCs have showed more excellent PCEs of over $1 5 \%$ . However, for the future of SMsCs, some challenges remain. Herein, we will discuss and provide some suggestions as follows.

For VD-SMsCs, how to achieve higher performance is the most challenging spot. Widely used $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ and $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ cannot take full advantages of the NIR light and often exhibit an large $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ . Taking into account of the merits of solution-processable SM-NFAs, designing vacuum-processable SM-NFAs is promising to promote the performance of VD-SMSCs, which needs to simultaneously consider molecular weight and thermal stability. Also, with the new materials, morphology control methods may be changed, which needs further investigation. Another topic is how to reduce cost. The materials that can be obtained with economical ingredients, high yields, and simple synthesis and purification process are preferred. For SP-SMSCs, the pursuit of higher performance is still one of the development directions, which requires the cooperation of material innovation and morphology optimization. For cost reduction, the requirements are the same as above. Also, the inevitable thickness variation during large-area fabrication and the expectation of sufficient light harvest indicate that thick film is particularly needed. Therefore, high mobility is necessary. In addition, from the perspective of environmental friendliness, the use of halogenated solvents or even some halogen-free solvents such as toluene and xylenes should be prudent.

Overall, we believe that continued development of materials including SMDs and SM-NFAs, together with morphology optimization, device engineering, and deep investigation on device physics, will contribute to the advance of SMSCs.

# Fullerene Acceptors

Zuo Xiao

National Center for Nanoscience and Technology, Center for Excellence in Nanoscience (CAs), Key Laboratory of Nanosystem and Hierarchical Fabrication (CAS), No.11 ZhongGuanCun BeiYiTiao, Beijing 100190, China

# 3.1 Introduction

In 1985, Kroto et al. observed the signal of $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ in mass spectrum when they tried to study the formation mechanism of long-chain carbon molecules in interstellar space and circumstellar shells [1]. This serendipity lead to the discovery of an important allotrope of carbon, the fullerenes. In 1990, Kratschmer et al. realized the macroscopic preparation of fullerenes [2]. From then on, fullerenes have attracted worldwide research interests, not only due to their fancy structures but also due to their unique physical and chemical properties. The past 35 years' research greatly expanded the knowledge on fullerenes. Fullerenes are cage-like molecules composed of 12 pentagons and a variable number of hexagons [3]. The $I _ { \mathrm { h } }$ symmetrical $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ and the $D _ { 5 \mathrm { h } }$ -symmetrical $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ are the two most abundant fullerenes in the crude fullerene soot (Figure 3.1a) [2]. Fullerenes with fewer than 60 carbon atoms are called "smaller fullerenes" [9], and those with more than 70 carbon atoms are called "higher fullerenes" [1o]. Although with low abundance, some smaller fullerenes and higher fullerenes were isolated and characterized in the experiment (Figure 3.1b) [4, 5, 11]. The cage of the fullerene molecules could be either empty or filled with atoms, molecules, or clusters. The latter are called endohedral fullerenes (Figure 3.1c) [6-8, 12]. The carbon atoms of fullerenes can also be replaced by heteroatoms (such as nitrogen and boron), affording so-called heterofullerenes [13]. Derivatives of azafullerenes (nitrogen-containing heterofullerenes) have been synthesized (Figure 3.1d) [14-16]. Fullerenes have abundant $\pi$ -electrons and curved conjugated $\pi$ system, which render them special chemical reactivity and optoelectronic properties. Fullerenes can undergo characteristic $\left[ 2 + n \right]$ cycloadditions at the 6,6-double bonds (Figure 3.1e) [17]. These reactions change the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 }$ -hybridized carbons into $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized ones and release the strain of fullerenes. Through these reactions, various functional groups can be introduced to fullerenes to make useful materials. Fullerene-based functional materials have been widely applied in optoelectronic devices and biological and medicinal fields [3, 18].

Due to the strong electron-affinity, low-lying lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) levels, and excellent electron transport capabilities, fullerenes and their derivatives have found important application as electron-accepting materials for organic solar cells (OsCs) [19, 20]. In 1992, Sariciftci et al. observed the ultrafast photoinduced electron transfer from a conjugated polymer MEH-PPV to the fullerene $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ , suggesting that fullerenes could be potential acceptors for organic photovoltaics [21]. In 1995, Heeger and coworkers invented bulk-heterojunction (BHJ) solar cells by blending the polymer donor MEH-PPV with a fullerene acceptor $\mathrm { \Delta C _ { 6 0 } }$ or $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M } ,$ [22]. In the active layer of a BHJ cell, the donor and acceptor undergo phase separation to form bicontinuous interpenetrating networks at the nanoscale. Such morphology generates sufficient interfaces between donor and acceptor, promotes exciton dissociation, and facilitates charge carrier transport. Under $4 3 0 \mathrm { n m }$ illumination, the MEH-PPV $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ solar cells showed ${ \sim } 9 0 \%$ internal quantum efficiency, which is much higher than that of pure conjugated polymer devices. The invention of BHJ solar cells opened a new avenue toward efficient and cost-effective solar cells, thus triggering extensive research [23]. One of the most popular directions is developing high-performance fullerene acceptor materials for OSCs. In the past 25 years, numerous fullerene acceptors have been designed and synthesized. In this section, representative fullerene acceptors for OSCs are summarized. These acceptors are categorized into five types: pristine fullerenes, fullerene monoadducts, fullerene bisadducts, fullerene multiadducts, and unconventional fullerenes. Molecular structural features, synthesis, material properties, and solar cells performance for different types of fullerene acceptors are introduced in detail.

# 3.2 Fullerene Acceptors for Organic Solar Cells

# 3.2.1 Pristine Fullerenes

Nowadays, bulk quantities of pristine fullerenes can be produced from either the vaporization of graphite or the controlled combustion of aromatic hydrocarbons. Kratschmer et al. first reported the macroscopic preparation of fullerenes from the soot of a vaporized graphite rod [2]. Smalley and coworkers improved this method by inventing a "contact arc" vaporization process and obtained $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ in gram quantities [24]. The content of fullerenes in the original soot reached $1 0 \%$ . Howard et al. reported an efficient combustion method for producing fullerenes [25]. By controlling the temperature, pressure, carbon/oxygen ratio, and residence time in the flame, they could obtain $_ { 3 \mathrm { g } }$ of fullerenes per kilogram of fuel carbon burned, with the $\mathrm { C _ { 7 0 } / C _ { 6 0 } }$ ratio varying from 0.26 to 5.7.

The above preparation methods make it possible to provide enough quantities of pristine fullerenes (predominantly $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ and $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ ) for solar cells application. Due to the low solubility of pristine fullerenes, they were mostly applied in vacuum-deposited OSCs (Table 3.1). In 2004, Forrest and coworkers fabricated vacuum-deposited solar cells by using $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ as the acceptor and the copper phthalocyanine (CuPc) as the donor [26]. The cells delivered a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of $3 . 5 \%$ at 1 sun, indicating the good potential of pristine fullerenes for vacuum-deposited all-small-molecule OSCs. In 2005, Forrest and coworkers improved the PCE of $\mathrm { C u P c : C _ { 6 0 } }$ cells to $5 . 0 \%$ by adopting a hybrid planar-mixed heterojunction device structure [27]. In 2009, Leo and coworkers reported vacuum-deposited BHJ cells based on a zinc phthalocyanine $\mathrm { ( Z n P c ) }$ donor and a $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ or $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ acceptor [28]. The $Z _ { \mathrm { n } } \mathrm { P c } { : } \mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ and $Z _ { \mathrm { { n P c : C _ { 7 0 } } } }$ cells delivered PCEs of $2 . 2 7 \%$ and $2 . 8 7 \%$ , respectively. The better performance of the $Z _ { \mathrm { { n P c : C _ { 7 0 } } } }$ cells is due to the higher short-circuit current density $( J _ { \mathrm { s c } } )$ , which is attributed to the stronger visible-light-absorption of $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ than $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ . The superior light-harvesting capability of $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ is due to its lower molecular symmetry, which relaxes the dipole selection rules of low-energy transitions and enhances the oscillator strength [42]. This work demonstrated the superiority of $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ for vacuum-deposited OSCs. Beside phthalocyanine donors, researchers also developed other small-molecule donors to match $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ or $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ . In 2011, Wong and coworkers designed a D--A small-molecule donor TPDCDTS [29]. The vacuum-deposited TPDCDT $\mathrm { \Delta S { : } C _ { 7 0 } }$ cells afforded a PCE of $3 . 8 2 \%$ , which is higher than that of the $\mathrm { T P D C D T S : C _ { 6 0 } }$ cells $( 2 . 6 9 \% )$ . Similar to Leo's results, the higher performance of the $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ cells came from the improved $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ . In the same year, Wurthner and coworkers reported a small-molecule donor based on a merocyanine dye HB194. The $\mathrm { H B 1 9 4 : C _ { 6 0 } }$ cells gave the highest PCE of $6 . 1 \%$ [30]. In 2012, Wong and coworkers designed a D-A-A type small-molecule donor DTDCTP [31]. The vacuum-deposited planar-mixed heterojunction solar cells based on DTDCTP and $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ afforded a high PCE of $6 . 4 \%$ . In 2013, Yokoyama and coworkers reported a polycyclic aromatic molecule tetraphenyldibenzoperiflanthene (DBP) working as the donor for vacuum-deposited cells [32]. The $\mathrm { D B P : C _ { 7 0 } }$ cells afforded a high PCE of $5 . 1 9 \%$ . By optimizing an electron filter buffer layer, Forrest and coworkers improved the PCE of $\mathrm { D B P : C _ { 7 0 } }$ cells to $8 . 1 \%$ [33]. In 2018, Forrest and coworkers developed a series of D-A-A' type small-molecule donors based on an asymmetric heterotetracene donor unit [34]. The alkyl chain on the donor unit shows significant influence to the device efficiency. Among the D-A-A' donors, the iBuBTDC with an isobutyl chain exhibited the best performance. The vacuum-deposited iBuBTDC $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ cells gave the highest PCE of $9 . 3 \%$

Besides being used in single-junction cells, pristine $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ and $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ were also applied in vacuum-deposited tandem cells and afforded higher efficiencies [43]. In 2010, Cheyns et al. reported $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ -based tandem solar cells with a high open-circuit voltage $( V _ { \mathrm { o c } } )$ of $1 . 9 2 \mathrm { V }$ and a PCE of $5 . 1 5 \%$ [35]. The tandem cells employed a chloroboron subnaphthalocyanine (SubNc) donor for the front cell and a chloroboron subphthalocyanine (SubPc) donor for the rear cell. In 2011, Riede et al. fabricated tandem cells with a fluorinated ZnPc donor F4-ZnPc and a $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ acceptor-based front cell and a sexithiophene-cored donor DCV6T and a $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ acceptor-based rear cell [36]. The tandem cells with a large effective area of $2 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ gave a certified PCE of $6 . 0 7 \%$ . In 2012, Forrest and coworkers reported tandem cells based on a $Z _ { \mathrm { { n P c : C _ { 7 0 } } } }$ front cell and a squaraine dye DPSQ and $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ -based rear cell [37]. A $6 . 6 \%$ PCE was achieved. In 2014, Leo and coworkers reported a triple-junction tandem cells based on a quinquethiophene-cored donor DCV5T-Me and a $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ acceptor [38]. The triple-junction cells afforded an extraordinary high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $2 . 7 9 \mathrm { V }$ and a PCE of $9 . 7 \%$ In 2018, Forrest and coworkers reported highly efficient tandem cells with a PCE of $1 5 . 4 \%$ [39]. The tandem cells adopted a vacuum-deposited $\mathrm { D T D C P B } { \colon } \mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ front cell and a solution-processed PCE-10:BT-CIC:TT-FIC nonfullerene ternary rear cell.

Although less reported, $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ and $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ can also be applied in solution-processed BHJ solar cells. In 2014, Lin et al. reported solution-processed BHJ cells based on D-A-A type small-molecule donors and $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ [40]. By using 1,2-dichlorobenzene as solvent, DTDCPB as the donor, and a $\mathrm { D } / \mathrm { A }$ ratio of $1 : 2 . 2$ , they could obtain homogeneous blend active layer via either spin-coating or bar-coating techniques.

The resulted $\mathrm { D T D C P B } { \colon } \mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ cells delivered PCEs up to $5 . 9 \%$ , which is ${ \sim } 9 0 \%$ of that of vacuum-deposited reference. In 2017, Muller and coworkers realized a high glass transition temperature of $2 2 4 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for a OSCs active layer by using a pristine fullerene acceptor alloy, $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 } { : } \mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 } \left( 1 { : } 1 \right)$ [41]. The $\mathrm { P T B 7 : C _ { 6 0 } : C _ { 7 0 } }$ (2 : 1 : 1) cells not only afforded a decent PCE of $5 . 3 \%$ but also showed excellent thermal stability.

# 3.2.2 Fullerene Monoadducts

To make fullerene acceptors more adaptable for solution-processed OsCs, it is necessary to introduce solubilizing side chains and functional groups on to fullerenes. Pristine fullerenes can only undergo addition reactions because there is no place on fullerene for substitution. The $\left[ 2 + n \right]$ cycloadditions and the 1,4-addition are the typical reactions making fullerene derivatives [44]. In this section, fullerene monoadduct acceptors developed via these addition reactions are introduced sequentially (Figure 3.2).

# 3.2.2.1 $[ 2 + 1 ]$ Addition Derivatives

The methanofullerene derivative $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ is the first and the most widely used fullerene acceptor in OSCs [22]. In 1995, Hummelen et al. reported the synthesis of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ via the reaction between $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ and an in-situ generated diazo compound [45]. The reaction mechanism includes several steps: $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ undergoes the 1,3-dipolar addition with the diazo species to give an pyrazole intermediate; with thermal extrusion of nitrogen, the intermediate turned into a pair of isomers, the [6,6]methanofullerene $( \mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M } )$ and the [5,6]fulleroid; the [5,6]fulleroid is not stable and undergoes isomerization to give the more stable isomer $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ . In 2003, Hummelen and coworkers synthesized $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ methanofullerene $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ , which has stronger visible absorption than $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ [46]. Different from $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ is a mixture of three regioisomers. Solar cells based on $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and a conjugated polymer donor MDMO-PPV afforded a PCE of $3 . 0 \%$ (Table 3.2). $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ show high electron mobility (OFET mobility ${ \sim } 0 . 1 0 \thinspace \mathrm { c m ^ { 2 } } \ \mathrm { V ^ { - 1 } } \ \mathrm { s ^ { - 1 } } )$ [77] and are well soluble in many kinds of organic solvents. Due to the suitable miscibility with many kinds of donor materials (conjugated polymers and small molecules), $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ become the benchmark acceptor materials for organic photovoltaic research. The performance for some representative PCBM-based solar cells is listed in Table 3.2 [47-56]. In 2016, Yan and coworkers reported highly efficient solar cells based on a conjugated polymer donor PffBT4T- $\mathrm { C } _ { 9 } \mathrm { C } _ { 1 3 }$ and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ [53]. The cells afforded a PCE of $1 1 . 7 \%$ , which is the highest efficiency achieved by polymer:fullerene solar cells to date.

The success of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ stimulated the development of PCBM-like fullerene acceptors. One direction is changing the aromatic part of the PCBM side chain. Troshin et al. developed $\mathrm { T h } { \mathrm { C } } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ by replacing the benzene moiety with a thienyl group [57]. Solar cells based on a donor polymer P3HT and $\mathrm { T h } { \mathrm { C } } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ gave a PCE of $3 . 7 \%$ . Jen and coworkers developed TPA-PCBM and MF-PCBM acceptors by replacing the benzene with the bulky aromatic groups triphenylamine (TPA) and 9,9-dimethylfluorene (MF), respectively [58]. TPA-PCBM and MF-PCBM showed comparable performance to $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ in the P3HT-based solar cells but offered the cells much improved thermal stability. This is due to the much higher glass-transition temperatures of TPA-PCBM and MF-PCBM than $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ . Another direction is modifying the aliphatic part of the PCBM side chain. Li and coworkers investigated the influence of the length of the middle alkyl chain to the performance of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ [59]. They found that FA1 with the dimethylene chain and FA2 with the pentamethylene chain show slightly better performance than $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ , delivering PCEs of $3 . 7 \%$ and $3 . 6 \%$ in P3HT-based solar cells, respectively. Cao and coworkers studied the effect of the ester alkyl chain to the performance of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ [60]. By using a butyl to replace the methyl group, they developed the acceptor PCBB.

PCBB showed higher performance than $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ in the MEH-PPV-based solar cells. The diaryl-substituted methanofullerenes are another type of PCBM-like acceptors. Garcia-Belmonte et al. reported a methanofullerene DPM-6 with two 4-hexyloxybenzenyl groups [61]. Although DPM-6 shows identical LUMO level as $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ , it delivered much higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ than $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ in P3HT-based solar cells due to the reduced crystallinity of DPM-6. Shibata and coworkers developed a series of asymmetrical diaryl-substituted methanofullerene acceptors [62]. The FA3 delivered higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and comparable efficiency to $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ in P3HT-based solar cells.

The aziridine-flanked $[ 2 + 1 ]$ monoadducts were also applied as acceptors for OSCs. In 2009, Wudl and coworkers synthesized the [6,6]APCBM and [5,6]APCBM by treating $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ with an azide compound [78]. These derivatives show good electron mobility up to $4 . 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 2 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ . Solar cells based on P3HT:[6,6]APCBM and P3HT:[5,6]APCBM gave PCEs of $2 . 3 \%$ and $2 . 8 \%$ ,respectively [63]. The [5,6]APCBM shows enhanced light absorption than [6,6]APCBM due to the lower molecular symmetry, thus contributing more photocurrent and offering high efficiency in solar cells. In 2012, Ding and coworkers developed a series of $N \mathrm { . }$ -alkylaziridino[60]fullerene (NNAF) acceptors via the reaction of $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ and primary alkylamines with the aid of hypervalent iodine reagents [64]. All synthesis could be done under ambient conditions. These facile prepared NNAFs showed good performance in OSCs. Among them, the NPEAF afforded the highest PCE of $2 . 9 2 \%$ in P3HT-based solar cells.

# 3.2.2.2 $[ 2 + 2 ]$ Addition Derivatives

In 2013, Swager and coworkers reported the synthesis of a series formal $[ 2 + 2 ]$ derivatives via the Diels-Alder reactions between $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ and the in situ generated tetraalkylcyclobutadienes [65]. The monoadduct TMCB-Mono delivered a PCE of $2 . 4 9 \%$ in P3HT-based solar cells. Compared with $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ , TMCB-Mono gave a higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ due to its higher LUMO level. In 2016, Ueda et al. reported a regio- and stereo-selective intermolecular $[ 2 + 2 ]$ cycloaddition of allenol esters with $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ [66]. With the aid of this new synthetic method, they obtained a cyclobutane-annulated fullerene acceptor FA4. Blending FA4 with the donor polymers P3HT and PTB7 delivered $3 . 0 0 \%$ and $3 . 7 8 \%$ PCEs in solar cells, respectively.

# 3.2.2.3 $[ 2 + 3 ]$ Addition Derivatives

The 1,3-dipolar $[ 2 + 3 ]$ addition of an azomethine ylide to fullerene is a classical functionalization method for fullerenes [79]. It is also called Prato reaction. The resulted fulleropyrrolidines can work as acceptors for OSCs. In 2010, Itoh and coworkers reported a series of fulleropyrrolidine acceptors [67]. The FA5 with a methoxyethoxyethyl and a 2-methoxyphenyl groups afforded the highest $3 . 4 4 \%$ PCE in P3HT-based solar cells, much better than that the reference $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ cells $( 2 . 5 3 \% )$ . The $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ for the fulleropyrrolidine-based cells are generally higher than that of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ cells due to the higher LUmO levels of the fulleropyrrolidine acceptors. In the same year, Lee and coworkers reported another fulleropyrrolidine acceptor $\mathrm { C _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { - T H - H x } }$ [68]. Solar cells based on $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ -TH-Hx and a low-bandgap polymer donor Si-PCPDTBT gave a PCE of $4 \%$ . In 2011, Chuang and coworkers reported a fulleroindoline derivative FA6 via the palladium-catalyzed $[ 2 + 3 ]$ annulation of anilide with $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ [69]. FA6 delivered a PCE of $0 . 6 \%$ in P3HT-based cells.

# 3.2.2.4 $[ 2 + 4 ]$ Addition Derivatives

The $[ 2 + 4 ]$ Diels-Alder cycloaddition is an efficient method for preparing fullerene acceptors. Li and coworkers reported the Diels-Alder reaction between $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ and indene [70]. The monoadduct $\mathrm { I C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { M A }$ delivered a PCE of $3 . 8 9 \%$ in P3HT-based solar cells, which is comparable to the reference $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ cells $( 3 . 8 8 \% )$ . Due to the higher LUMO of $\mathrm { I C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { M A }$ than $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ $\mathrm { I C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { M A }$ cells showed a $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { V }$ increase in $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ . Kim and coworkers synthesized a monoadduct OxCMA through the $[ 2 + 4 ]$ cycloaddition of an in situ generated $o$ xylylene to $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ [71]. OXCMA delivered a PCE of $3 . 6 0 \%$ in P3HT-based cells. Ding and coworkers reported a $[ 2 + 4 ]$ monoadduct mono-TOQC-H through the reaction of $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ and a ketone functionalized thieno-o-quinodimethane [72]. The P3HT:mono-TOQC-H cells gave a PCE of $3 . 9 \%$ , which is better than that of the $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 1 } B M }$ reference cells $( 3 . 6 \% )$ Frechet and coworkers reported an ester group functionalized dihydronaphthyl fullerene FA7 [73]. Solar cells based on FA7 and P3HT gave the best PCE of $4 . 2 \%$ which is slightly higher than that of P3HT $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ cells.

# 3.2.2.5 1,4-Addition Derivatives

Besides $\left[ 2 + n \right]$ cycloaddition, fullerenes can also undergo 1,4-addition to give functionalized derivatives. Nakamura and coworkers prepared the 1,4-adduct FA8 through the quenching of $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ dianion with 1-(bromomethyl)-4-butylbenzene [74]. Solar cells based on FA8 and P3HT afforded a PCE of $1 . 6 \%$ with a relatively high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 6 9 \mathrm { V } .$ Compared with the $\left[ 2 + n \right]$ derivatives, the 1,4-adducts possess higher LUMO levels, thus producing higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ for OsCs. Nakamura and coworkers also developed a series of 1,4-adducts through an efficient two-step synthesis strategy [80]. First, the 1,2-addition of Grignard reagents to $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ can afford the (organo)-(hydro)[60]fullerenes, $\mathrm { C _ { 6 0 } R _ { 1 } H }$ , in high yields with the aid of dimethylformamide. Then, deprotonation of the $\mathrm { C _ { 6 0 } R _ { 1 } H }$ followed by quenching the anion species $\mathrm { { C _ { 6 0 } } \mathrm { { R _ { 1 } } ^ { - } } }$ with alkyl halides $\mathbf { \Gamma } ( \mathbf { R } _ { 2 } \mathbf { X } )$ give the 1,4-adducts $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { R } _ { 1 } \mathrm { R } _ { 2 }$ in high yields. Among the synthesized $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { R } _ { 1 } \mathrm { R } _ { 2 }$ , the SIMEF acceptor shows the best photovoltaic performance. The solution processed p-i-n solar cells based on benzoporphyrin (BP) donor and SIMEF gave high PCEs up to $5 . 2 \%$ [75]. Wudl and coworkers also developed a series of 1,4-adducts with aryl functional groups [76]. The synthesis was accomplished by treating the 1,4-fullerenols with a variety of aromatic substrates in the presence of $p$ -toluene sulfonic acid. Among these derivatives, the PTPOB afforded the best PCE of $2 . 3 4 \%$ when blending with P3HT.

# 3.2.3 Fullerene Bisadducts

Although a large amount of fullerene monoadduct acceptors have been developed after the first report of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ , they could seldom challenge PCBM acceptors in OSCs. In this context, more and more researches have focused on the development of fullerene bisadduct acceptors (Figure 3.3). In 2008, Blom and coworkers first reported solar cells based on the bisadduct acceptor bis- $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ [81]. Compared with the monoadduct $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ , bis- $\mathrm { . P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ shows a ${ \sim } 0 . 1 \mathrm { e V }$ increase in the LUMO level, which can minimize the energy loss in the electron transfer from the donor to the acceptor. Consequently, the P3HT:bis- $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ cells gave a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of 0.73 V, which is $0 . 1 5 \mathrm { V }$ higher than the P3HT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ cells. Interestingly, the bis- $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ cells also showed similar $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and fill factor (FF) as the $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ cells, thus delivering a PCE of $4 . 5 \%$ , higher than that of the best $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ cells $( 3 . 8 \% )$ (Table 3.3). In 2009,

Blom and coworkers further reported bisadducts bis- $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and bis $- \mathrm { T h } { \mathrm { C } } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ which delivered PCEs of $2 . 3 \%$ and $2 . 5 \%$ in P3HT-based solar cells, respectively [82]. The development of indene $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ bisadducts $\mathrm { ( I C _ { 6 0 } B A ) }$ is an important milestone in the development of fullerene acceptors. In 2010, Li and coworkers reported $\mathrm { I C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B A }$ via the cycloaddition of two indenes on to $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ [70]. Compared with $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ $\mathrm { I C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B A }$ shows a $0 . 2 \mathrm { e V }$ increase in LUMO level. The ${ \mathrm { P } } 3 { \mathrm { H T } } { \mathrm { : I C } } _ { 6 0 } { \mathrm { B A } }$ cells delivered a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 4 \mathrm { V } ,$ which is $4 5 \%$ higher than that of $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 1 } B M }$ cells. With device optimization, the ${ \mathrm { P } } 3 { \mathrm { H T } } { \mathrm { : I C } } _ { 6 0 } { \mathrm { B A } }$ cells could afford the highest PCE of $6 . 4 8 \%$ , which is about twice that of $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 1 } B M }$ cells [83]. Li and coworkers also reported $\mathrm { I C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B A }$ [100]. Owing to the stronger light absorption, the best ${ \mathrm { P } } 3 { \mathrm { H T } } { \mathrm { : I C } } _ { 7 0 } { \mathrm { B A } }$ cells could give an excellent PCE of $7 . 4 \%$ [84]. The success of ICBA acceptors triggered a lot of following research in the development of fullerene bisadducts acceptors. At about the same time, three different groups reported the development of dihydronaphthyl-based $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ bisadducts $\mathrm { N C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B A }$ [71, 85, 86]. PCEs up to $5 . 3 7 \%$ were achieved by the $\mathrm { P 3 H T : N C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B A }$ solar cells. In 2012, Xie and coworkers developed a methoxy-functionalized $\mathrm { N C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B A }$ derivative, bis-MDNC [87]. Solar cells based on P3HT and bis-MDNC showed a PCE of $4 . 5 8 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 3 \mathrm { V } .$ In the same year, Wang and coworkers studied the alkyl chain length effect on the performance of dialkoxy-functionalized $\mathrm { N C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B A }$ acceptors [88]. They found that the C3-NCBA with a moderate-length propyl chain shows the best PCE of $4 . 1 \%$ in P3HT-based solar cells. Ding and coworkers reported a thiophene-functionalized fullerene bisadduct, bis-TOQC, by adding two thieno. $^ { \cdot 0 }$ -quinodimethane addends to $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ [72]. P3HT:bis-TOQC solar cells afforded a decent PCE of $5 . 1 \%$ Cheng et al. reported a series of diphenylmethano- $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ bisadduct acceptors [89]. The DPCBA and DMPCBA delivered $4 . 0 \%$ and $5 . 2 \%$ PCEs in P3HT-based solar cells, respectively. Meanwhile, due to the amorphous nature of DMPCBA, the P3HT:DMPCBA cells showed much improved thermal stability than the $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 1 } B M }$ reference cells.

Although bisadduct acceptors can offer higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ for solar cells, they generally deliver lower $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and FF as compared to the monoadduct acceptors. One reason is the increased steric hindrance from the addends, which inhibits the fullerene packing and lowers the electron mobility. In this regard, Li et al. used a very small 1,2-dihydromethano group $\left( \mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } \right)$ working as the addend to develop a bisadduct acceptor, methano $\mathrm { \ P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ [77]. The methano- $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ shows a high electron mobility of $0 . 0 1 4 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { \bf ~ V } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { \bf ~ s } ^ { - 1 }$ and delivered a $3 . 8 1 \%$ PCE in P3HT-based solar cells. Ding and coworkers synthesized OQMF and TOQMF by adding the in situ generated $o$ -quinodimethane and thieno-o-quinodimethane species to the methanofullerene $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { C H } _ { 2 }$ [90]. Decent PCEs of $5 . 7 4 \%$ and $5 . 5 1 \%$ were achieved for P3HT:OQMF and P3HT:TOQMF solar cells, respectively. Ding and coworkers also reported the $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ bisadduct OQMF70, which delivered an impressive PCE of $6 . 8 8 \%$ in P3HT-based solar cells [91]. Matsuo et al. reported efficient acceptors $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 } ( \mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } ) ( \mathrm { I n d } )$ and $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 } ( \mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } ) ( \mathrm { I n d } )$ by adding indene on to $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { C H } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { C H } _ { 2 }$ respectively [92]. $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 } ( \mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } ) ( \mathrm { I n d } )$ and $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 } ( \mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } ) ( \mathrm { I n d } )$ afforded decent PCEs of $5 . 9 \%$ and $6 . 4 \%$ , respectively, in P3HT-based solar cells.

Another factor leading to the low electron mobility of fullerene bisadducts is the isomeric mixture form of bisadducts, as the bis-functionalization on fullerenes is generally unselective. By using coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulation, Nelson and coworkers concluded that the "energetic disorder' brought from regioisomers of fullerene bisadducts is the major cause of reduction in electron mobility [101]. In this regard, considerable efforts have been paid to develop isomer-free bisadduct acceptors. An effective approach to obtain isomer-free bisadduct is employing high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) to separate the isomers. In 2014, Wang and coworkers reported the isolation of three isomers of $\mathrm { N C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B A }$ : trans-2 $\mathrm { \partial _ { \ z } N C _ { \ 6 0 } B A }$ , trans- $3 – \mathrm { N C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B A }$ , trans $4 – \mathrm { N C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B A }$ , and $e { \mathrm { - N C } } _ { 6 0 } { \mathrm { B A } }$ [93]. All isomerically pure isomers delivered higher efficiencies than the mixture $\mathrm { N C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B A }$ . The trans- $3 { \mathrm { - N C } } _ { 6 0 } { \mathrm { B A : P } } 3 { \mathrm { H T } }$ cells gave the best PCE of $6 . 3 \%$ In the same year, Wong and coworkers isolated a single isomer of $\mathrm { I C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B A }$ via multistep HPLC separation [94]. The structure of the isolated acceptor FA9 was confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis. FA9 delivered a PCE of $5 . 9 \%$ in solar cells, which is higher than that of the mixture. $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B A }$ -based cells $( 4 . 7 \% )$ . Xie and coworkers reported the isolation of two $\mathsf { b i s P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ stereomeric isomers, the trans-bisP $\mathrm { \Delta C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ and the cis-bisF $\mathrm { \Delta C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ [95]. The structures of both isomers were identified by single-crystal XRD analysis. Solar cells based on trans-bisP $\mathrm { \Delta C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ and cis-bisPC $_ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ afforded $1 . 8 4 \%$ and $1 . 7 2 \%$ PCEs, respectively. This work indicates that stereomeric factors can also influence the photovoltaic performance of fullerene acceptors. Another effective approach is the development of regioselective synthesis of isomer-free fullerene bisadducts. In 2011, Nakamura and coworkers synthesized the isomerically pure acceptor FA10 via an oxidative cyclopropanation reaction of silylmethylfullerene [74]. Solar cells based on FA10 and P3HT gave a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 2 \mathrm { V }$ and a PCE of $3 . 4 \%$ . In 2012, Nakamura and coworkers reported the isomer isomerically pure $6 6 \pi$ electron $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ derivatives via regioselective synthesis [96]. The acceptors FA11 and FA12 delivered $3 . 3 7 \%$ and $3 . 3 3 \%$ PCEs in BP-based solar cells. Tether-directed remote functionalization' is a useful strategy to obtain isomer-free fullerene multiadducts [102]. Using a molecular tether to carry two or more addition groups, multiaddition to fullerenes will present regioselectivity because the length, rigidity, and conformation of the tether can confine the reaction sites. In 2015, Imahori and coworkers reported an ethylene-tether-directed synthesis of an isomer-free indene- $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ bisadduct cis-2-BIEC [97]. Solar cells based on cis-2-BIEC and P3HT delivered a PCE of $2 . 8 \%$ In the same year, Wong and coworkers reported a one-pot selective synthesis of a bisadduct $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { P F }$ by directly using the side chain of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as the tether [98]. The isomer-free $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { P F }$ afforded a $3 . 3 \%$ PCE in P3HT-based solar cells. In 2016, Ding and coworkers developed another method for synthesizing isomer-free fullerene bisadducts, the "prebisaddition-confined bisfunctionalization (PCB)" approach [99]. The synthesis was highly selective for bisadducts with an e configuration. An isomer-free bisadduct $e$ -PPMF featuring a small $\mathrm { C H } _ { 2 }$ addend shows high electron mobility due to the eliminated energetic disorder from isomers and enhanced fullerene packing. $e$ -PPMF showed high performance not only in P3HT cells but also in other D-A copolymer cells. PCEs of $4 . 5 1 \%$ and $8 . 1 1 \%$ were achieved by P3HT: $e \mathrm { \cdot }$ PPMF and PPDT2FBT $e$ -PPMF solar cells, respectively. The $8 . 1 1 \%$ PCE is the highest efficiency achieved in fullerene-bisadduct-based solar cells to date.

# 3.2.4 Fullerene Multiadducts

The success of fullerene bisadduct acceptors stimulated the exploration and development of fullerene multiadduct acceptors (Figure 3.4). Blom and coworkers first reported the photovoltaic performance of a fullerene trisadduct tris- $\mathrm { . P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ [82]. However, tris- $\mathrm { \cdot P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ showed low electron mobility and only delivered a $0 . 2 1 \%$ PCE in P3HT-based cells (Table 3.4). In 2010, Fukuzumi and coworkers reported a trisadduct tris- $\mathrm { \cdot T h C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and a tetrakisadduct tetrakis. $\mathrm { \cdot T h C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ , which afforded 1ow PCEs of $0 . 3 4 \%$ and $0 . 0 9 \%$ in P3HT-based cells, respectively [103]. The indene $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ trisadduct $\mathrm { \Delta T C _ { 6 0 } T A ) }$ reported by Kim and coworkers showed a better PCE of $2 . 2 5 \%$ as compared to the PCBM-type trisadducts [104]. Since that the indene moieties are much smaller than the PCBM side chains, they should have less influence to the fullerene packing, thus rendering the trisadducts better electron-transporting capability and higher photovoltaic performance. Kim et al. also reported an o-xylylene $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ trisadduct (OxcTA), which delivered a higher PCE of $2 . 6 3 \%$ in P3HT-based solar cells [71]. Ding and coworkers synthesized an acceptor tris-TOQC through the trisaddition of thieno-o-quinodimethane to $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ [105]. The P3HT:tris-TOQC cells afforded a PCE of $1 . 1 2 \%$ . Considering that the steric hindrance of the addends has significant influence to the performance of multiadducts, Ding and coworkers developed a series of efficient multiadduct acceptors by using compact methano addend $\mathrm { C H } _ { 2 }$ . With one of the thieno-o-quinodimethane addends on tris-TOQC being replaced by a $\mathrm { C H } _ { 2 }$ , the resulted bis-TOQMF showed much improved performance in P3HT-based cells. The P3HT:bis-TOQMF cells afforded a PCE of $4 . 5 6 \%$ , much higher than that of P3HT:tris-TOQC cells. Similarly, a trisadduct bis-OQMF delivered a PCE of $4 . 2 3 \%$ in P3HT-based cells [106]. Further replacing one o-quinodimethane addend with the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 2 }$ , Ding and coworkers developed the trisadduct acceptor OQBMF [107]. Featuring two compact $\mathrm { C H } _ { 2 }$ groups, OQBMF exhibited outstanding performance in P3HT-based cells, offering a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 5 \mathrm { V }$ and a PCE of $6 . 4 3 \%$ . The $6 . 4 3 \%$ PCE is the highest efficiency achieved in fullerene-trisadduct-based solar cells to date. Ding and coworkers also synthesized a tetrakisadduct OQTMF featuring three $\mathrm { C H } _ { 2 }$ groups. The P3HT:OQTMF cells afforded a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 0 0 \mathrm { V }$ and a PCE of $2 . 9 8 \%$ . Isomer-free fullerene multiadducts were also developed for OsCs. Nakamura and coworkers discovered the highly selective and efficient pentaaddition of organocopper reagents to $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ [110]. The multiadduct FA13 synthesized via this reaction delivered a PCE of $1 . 0 8 \%$ in P3HT-based cells [108]. Xie and coworkers synthesized an isomer-free multiadduct $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 } ( \mathrm { O C H } _ { 3 } ) _ { 4 }$ -PCBM starting from $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { C l } _ { 6 }$ [109]. $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 } ( \mathrm { O C H } _ { 3 } ) _ { 4 }$ -PCBM gave a PCE of $2 . 2 4 \%$ in P3HT-based cells.

# 3.2.5 Unconventional Fullerenes

Unconventional fullerene acceptors were also developed and applied in OSCs (Figure 3.5). Martin and coworkers reported novel $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ and $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ homo- and heterodimers linked through 2-pyrazolino-pyrrolidino bridges [111]. Compared with the conventional $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ acceptor, the fullerene dimers show larger absorption coefficients. The dimers FA14, FA15, and FA16 afforded $0 . 9 1 \%$ $0 . 6 7 \%$ , and $0 . 9 1 \%$ PCEs in P3HT-based solar cells, respectively (Table 3.5). Open-cage fullerenes are novel fullerene derivatives generated via consecutive cleavage of $\sigma ^ { - }$ and $\pi$ carbon-carbon bonds on the fullerene cage [118]. The orifice on fullerene allows small atoms or molecules go inside the cavity to form interesting host-guest complexes. Open-cage fullerenes were also applied as acceptors for OSCs. In 2011, Murata et al. synthesized a series of open-cage fullerenes FA17, FA18, and FA19, which delivered $1 . 3 5 \%$ $2 . 4 9 \%$ , and $3 . 1 1 \%$ PCEs in P3HT-based solar cells, respectively [112]. In the same year, Chuang and coworkers reported a family of open-cage fullerene acceptors with various sizes of orifices [113]. The FA20, FA21, and FA22 afforded $2 . 9 \%$ $1 . 7 \%$ , and $1 . 2 \%$ PCEs in P3HT-based solar cells, respectively. In the above two studies, open-cage fullerenes with larger orifices generally show lower electron mobility and poorer performance in solar cells. The cage-opened structures lead to inefficient packing of fullerenes, thus reducing the electron mobility. Researchers also developed novel azafullerene acceptors for OsCs. In 2014, Ding and coworkers first reported an azafullerene acceptor $\mathrm { O Q T h C } _ { 5 9 } \mathrm { N }$ [114]. Possessing a relatively high LUMO level, $\mathrm { O Q T h C } _ { 5 9 } \mathrm { N }$ gives a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 7 8 \mathrm { V }$ and a PCE of $4 . 0 9 \%$ in fullerene:P3HT solar cells. In 2015, Viterisi and coworkers developed another azafullerene acceptor $\mathrm { D P C } _ { 5 9 } \mathrm { N }$ [115]. Compared with $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ $\mathrm { D P C } _ { 5 9 } \mathrm { N }$ shows stronger visible-light-absorbing capability and gave higher $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and external quantum efficiency in P3HT-based solar cells. A $2 . 2 4 \%$ PCE was achieved by $_ { \mathrm { P 3 H T : D P C } _ { 5 9 } \mathrm { N } }$ solar cells. Besides $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ and $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ derivatives, derivatives of higher fullerenes and endohedral fullerenes were also explored as acceptors for solar cells. In 2006, Hummelen and coworkers reported the PCBM-type acceptor $\mathrm { P C } _ { 8 5 } \mathrm { B M }$ based on $\mathrm { C } _ { 8 4 }$ [116]. Compared with $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ , the LUMO level of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 8 5 } \mathrm { B M }$ is $0 . 3 5 \mathrm { e V }$ lower, thus leading to a low $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 3 3 5 \mathrm { V }$ for the solar cells. The MDMO-PPV: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 8 5 } \mathrm { B M }$ only afforded a PCE of $0 . 2 5 \%$ . In 2009, Drees and coworkers reported a novel trimetallic nitride endohedral fullerene acceptor $\mathrm { L u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N @ C } _ { 8 0 }$ -PCBH [117]. The LUMO level of $\mathrm { L u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N @ C _ { 8 0 } }$ -PCBH is $0 . 2 6 \mathrm { V }$ higher than $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ . The $\mathrm { P 3 H T : L u } _ { 3 } \mathrm { N @ C _ { 8 0 } }$ -PCBH cells delivered a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 3 4 \mathrm { V }$ and an impressive PCE of $4 . 2 \%$

# 3.3 Summary

In this section, representative fullerene acceptors, including pristine fullerenes, fullerene monoadducts, fullerene bisadducts, fullerene multiadducts, and unconventional fullerenes, and their performance in OsCs are summarized:

(1) For pristine fullerene acceptors, $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ and $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ have shown excellent performance in vacuum-processed single-junction and tandem solar cells. The highest PCEs of $9 . 3 \%$ and $1 5 . 4 \%$ were achieved by pristine-fullerene-based single-junction and tandem solar cells, respectively. $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ and $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ are not favored in solution-processed solar cells due to their low solubility. Nevertheless, solution-processed cells based on pristine fullerenes afforded decent PCEs up to $5 . 9 \%$

(2) For fullerene monoadduct acceptors, $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ are still the most efficient and widely used acceptor in OSCs. Due to the good solubility and electron mobility, as well as suitable miscibility with many kinds of donor materials, $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ can generally guarantee decent performance of OSCs, thus being the benchmark acceptors for organic photovoltaic research. The highest PCE of $1 1 . 7 \%$ was achieved by $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ -based cells.

(3) For fullerene bisadduct acceptors, the mixture-formed bisadducts represented by $\mathrm { I C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B A }$ and $\mathrm { I C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B A }$ have demonstrated their success in P3HT-based solar cells. High $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and PCEs were achieved for these cells. However, due to the steric hindrance from the addends and the energetic disorder from the regioisomers, mixture-formed bisadduct acceptors show lower electron mobility than monoadduct acceptors. This limits their photovoltaic performance. In this context, isomer-free bisadduct acceptors were developed and showed high performance in OSCs. The highest PCE of $8 . 1 1 \%$ was achieved by an isomer-free bisadduct $e$ -PPMF, which was synthesized through a regioselective "PCB" method.

(4) For fullerene multiadduct acceptors, they generally show poor performance in solar cells due to the significantly decreased electron mobility caused by the bulky addends. By using the compact methano group $\mathrm { C H } _ { 2 }$ as the addend, Ding and coworkers developed a family of high-performance fullerene multiadduct acceptors. High $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ up to $1 . 0 0 \mathrm { V }$ and PCEs up to $6 . 4 3 \%$ were achieved by these $\mathrm { C H } _ { 2 }$ -containing fullerene multiadducts.

(5) For unconventional fullerene acceptors, a bunch of fullerene dimers, open-cage fullerenes, azafullerenes, higher fullerenes, and endohedral fullerenes have been applied in OSCs. These novel materials delivered PCEs up to $4 . 2 \%$ in P3HT-based solar cells.

Although significant progress has been made in fullerene acceptors in the past 25 years, the poor light-harvesting capability is the critical defect of fullerene acceptors and it limits the potential of fullerenes in solar cells. Recent years, the rise of strong-light-absorbing nonfullerene acceptors has greatly pushed the efficiency of OSCs into the $1 8 \%$ level [119]. However, fullerene acceptors still show their advantages like high electron mobility as compared to the nonfullerene acceptors. In this regard, combining the advantages of fullerene and nonfullerene acceptors to develop highly efficient multi-component solar cells [120] and thick-film solar cells [121] could be a promising direction in the future.
