# Non-fullerene Small-Molecule Acceptors for Organic Solar Cells

Wei Gao1, Jun Yuan?, Zhenghui Luo1, Jinru Cao3, Weihua Tang3, Yingping $Z o u ^ { 2 }$ and Chuluo Yang1

1 Shenzhen University, College of Materials Science and Engineering, Shenzhen Key Laboratory of Polymer   
Science and Technology, Shenzhen, 518060, P.R. China   
2Central South University, Collge of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Changsha, 410083, P.R. China   
3 Xiamen University, Department of Materials Science and Engineering, College of Materials, Xiamen,   
361005, PR. China

# 4.1 Molecular Design Principles

To overcome the shortcomings of fullerene derivatives, a potential non-fullerene small-molecule acceptor (SMA) should fulfill several fundamental require. ments [1-3]:

(i) Wide absorption range with intense molar extinction coefficient in the visible and near infrared (NIR) region: SMA possessing wide and strong light absorption ability in the visible and NIR region can make them an even stronger light absorber than polymers and achieve significant photocurrent generation through hole transfer to the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) of electron donor material after photoexcitation, which could significantly enhance the photocurrent as both channels (donor and acceptor) can contribute to free carrier generation;   
(ii) Matched energy levels with donor: The lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) and HOMO energy levels of SMA should be lower than those of electron donor in order to provide enough driving force for effective exciton separation. Typically, the energy offsets between HOMO of donor and HOMO of acceptor or LUMO of donor and LUMO of acceptor should be larger than $0 . 3 \mathrm { e V }$ in theory.   
(iii) High electron mobility: SMA should have high electron mobility that can match the high hole mobility of polymer to achieve balanced carriers transport, which is beneficial to reduce the charge recombination within devices.   
(iv) Good solubility and proper crystallization: SMA should possess good solubility in commonly used solvent, which is convenient for solution processing and

increases the miscibility with polymer to form uniform morphology. Moreover, the crystallization performance of SMA cannot be too strong or too weak. If the crystallinity of a SMA is too strong, it will induce a strong aggregation tendency that leads to excessively large domains with an inadequate interface between the donor and acceptor for efficient exciton dissociation. On the contrary, if the crystallinity of the SMAs is too weak, it is not conducive to ordered molecular packing and results in poor carrier transport performance.

In the past decades, the development of polymeric and small-molecule donor materials has constructed a large library of effective molecular structures and design strategies for organic photovoltaics (OPV) materials [4-6], which can be applied to the design of non-fullerene SMAs. In this chapter, we will mainly review perylene diimide (PDI)-based SMAs, acceptor-donor-acceptor (A-D-A)-type SMAs, and A-DA'D-A-type SMAs.

# 4.2 PDI-Based SMAs

Thanks to their exceptional optical and electronic properties, along with outstanding thermal/photo stability, low-cost synthesis and facile functionalization, PDIs-based organic semiconductor materials have been widely applied to organic field-effect transistors (OFETs), organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs), perovskite solar cells (PVSCs), and organic solar cells (OSCs) [1-3, 7-15]. The PDI monomers have a strong aggregation tendency to form oversized domain sizes due to their large conjugated planar structures, which is detrimental for exciton dissociation [16-22]. Therefore, developing twisted PDI-based SMAs is essential for suppressing aggregation propensity [23-26]. Functionalization of PDI on different positions $( \alpha , \beta$ positions, or the N position) is a main strategy of designing high-performance PDI-based SMAs (Figure 4.1). According to the number of PDI units, we can divide the PDI-based SMAs into PDI monomers, PDI dimers, PDI trimers, and PDI tetramers.

# 4.2.1 PDI Monomers

Limited by low power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) of related OSCs, monomeric PDIs were rarely studied, although PDI-based SMAs were tremendously utilized in the field. Nevertheless, there are some noteworthy works. In 2013, Bazan and coworkers blended $\mathrm { \ p { - } D T S { ( F B T T h _ { 2 } ) _ { 2 } } }$ with PDI (Figure 4.2) to fabricate all-small-molecule OSCs and yielded a PCE of $3 . 0 \%$ (Table 4.1) [27]. In the next year, Keivanidis's group achieved a PCE of $3 . 7 1 \%$ by combining PDI and PBDTTT-C-T, which is the highest values among PDI monomers functionalized only at N position [28].

To further reduce aggregation, substitutions at $\alpha$ or $\beta$ positions on PDI monomer were introduced. Patrick E. Hartnett et al. developed a slip-stacked acceptor of phenyl-PDI by introducing a phenyl group at each $\alpha$ position, and the PBTI3T:phenyl-PDI device gave a PCE up to $3 . 6 7 \%$ [29]. Apart from introducing phenyl groups at $\alpha$ position, adding benzene ring at $\beta$ region was also reported. The SMA of TP-PDI realized a PCE of $4 . 1 \%$ when mixed with PTB7-Th [30]. In a later report, the same group reported a SMA of TN-PDI by introducing a naphthalene ring at each $\alpha$ position, and TN-PDI delivered a PCE of $3 . 0 \%$ when matched with a wide bandgap polymer donor PDBT-T1 [31].

![](images/640f9e9dfa23d3b43d4c3fe786b16fd7d6e72b5bac69be4c31ee8fa7732d64d6.jpg)  
Figure 4.2 Chemical structures of monomeric PDIs. Source: Z. Luo and C. Yang.

Overall, the device performance of OSCs based on PDI monomers is not ideal, which is mainly related to the over-aggregation of PDI monomers. To alleviate the aggregation tendency, developing PDI dimers (or trimers or tetramers) is a good strategy.

# 4.2.2PDI Dimers

In addition to modifying PDI monomers, a direct way to reduce the molecular planarity is to connect two PDIs together by a single bond or functional groups such as spirofluorene, benzene, and thiophene (Figure 4.3). The first PDI dimer (Per 1) was reported by Narayan's research team in 2012, who connected two nitrogen atoms at each PDI's imide position through a single bond [32]. Compared with PDI monomer, Per 1 has reduced planarity and aggregation behavior, blending with PBDTTT-C-T achieved a PCE of $2 . 7 7 \%$ . Other than single bond, a non-conjugated 1,1-diphenylcyclohexane linker was introduced into PDI dimer through functionalization of N position, thereby a V-type PDI dimer of CP-V was developed, and OSCs-based PTB7-Th:CP-V delivered a PCE of $5 . 2 8 \%$ [33]. Just recently, Yang's research group reported that two PDI units were connected by $\beta$ and amine positions to develop two PDI oligomers. Among them, the device efficiency of PDI dimer T-PDI and PBDB-T combination reached $3 . 5 \%$ [34].

Figure 4.3 Chemical structures of selected PDI dimers. Source: Z. Luo and C. Yang.

As a matter of fact, the most researched are still $\beta$ position linked PDI SMAs. In 2014, Wang and coworkers developed a PDI dimer of s-diPBI by connecting the bay positions of two PDIs and blended it with polymer donor PBDTTT-C-T, successfully achieving a PCE of $3 . 6 3 \%$ [35]. In next two reports, they improved the device efficiency by changing the polymer donor and the optimizing the device process. Consequently, the highest efficiency reached $5 . 9 0 \%$ [36, 37]. Later, they reported two derivatives of s-diPBI, the $\beta$ positions at both ends of the dimer were capped with sulfur (SdiPBI-S) or selenium (SdiPBI-Se), which brought the PDI unit into a planar structure [38, 39]. Compared to s-diPBI, SdiPBI-S and SdiPBI-Se exhibit larger optical bandgaps and dihedral angles between the two PDI units. When combined with the medium-bandgap polymer PDBT-T1, SdiPBI-Se achieved a high PCE of $8 . 4 2 \%$ , while SdiPBI-S had a PCE of $7 . 1 6 \%$ , significantly higher than that of s-diPBI-based device. In addition to S and Se annulated PDIs, Hendsbee et al. synthesized a N-cyclized s-diPBI (N-PDI) at the gram level, requiring no column chromatography for purification [40]. The P3TEA:N-PDI-based device yielded a PCE of $7 . 5 5 \%$ . In the same year, Yang's group reported two thiophene ring-fused PDI dimers, namely SdiPBI-BT and diPBI-BT. The OSCs based on PDBT-T1:SdiPBI-BT exhibit a good PCE of $6 . 7 1 \%$ , which is higher than that of diPBI-BT-based devices $( 5 . 8 4 \% )$ [41]. In addition, Wang and coworkers employed mono-brominated PDI to synthesize two PDI dimers, NDP and SDP, using two different conditions in just one step (Figure 4.4) [42]. In comparison with the benzene-fused NDP, the spiro-fused SDP exhibits red-shifted absorption spectra due to the significant spiro-conjugation effect. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis indicates that SDP shows a three-dimensional (3D) cruciform configuration. When blending the two SMAs with PTB7-Th, the device efficiency was $5 . 1 8 \%$ for NDP-based device, and $6 . 4 3 \%$ for SDP-based device, respectively.

In addition to connecting two PDIs through a single bond, Zhao and coworkers studied the effect of spacer units on the aggregation and phase separation between PDI-based SMAs and polymer donor to further tune the morphology of active layers [43]. They inserted a series of spacer units including thiophene, benzene, bithiophene, and spirobifluorene between two PDI units and found that the planar dimer with benzene ring as the spacer unit has the largest domain size and worst photovoltaic performance $\mathrm { P C E } = 0 . 9 0 \%$ due to the strong intermolecular interaction. In contrast, $\mathrm { S F } { \cdot } \mathrm { P D I } _ { 2 }$ with spirobifluorene as the spacer unit has the best photovoltaic performance $\mathrm { ( P C E } = 2 . 3 5 \%$ , and the blend film with P3HT has a smaller domain size. In 2016, Yan and coworkers designed a new type of conjugated polymer P3TEA and combined it with $\mathrm { S F } { \cdot } \mathrm { P D I } _ { 2 }$ to fabricate OSC devices, eventually achieving an efficiency of $9 . 5 \%$ and an internal quantum efficiency of nearly $9 0 \%$ , along with high open-circuit voltage ( $\boldsymbol { V } _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of 1.11 V) and fill factor (FF of 0.64) [44]. The authors also calculated the energy loss (the difference between the bandgap of the donor material and the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the device), which was only 0.61 eV, indicating that non-fullerene OSCs have great potential for achieving low energy loss.

Ring-fusion strategy is an effective approach to enhance molecular packing, thereby improving charge carriers transport. In 2015, Jen's team developed a series of fused-ring PDI dimers bridged by furan, thiophene, and selenophene, namely FPDI-F, FPDI-T, and FPDI-Se [45]. Compared with the unfused dimer, the fused PDI dimers reduce the recombination energy and has an extended effective $\pi$ conjugation length, which is very conducive to exciton diffusion and charge transport. They found that the FPDI-T with a moderate torsion angle achieved a balance of various parameters, and thus delivering a highest PCE of $6 . 7 2 \%$

# 4.2.3PDI Trimers

In order to further investigate the twisting strategies and design non-fullerene materials that can form 3D or quasi 3D molecular structures, three PDI units can be introduced into one molecule. At present, the efficiency of solar cells based on PDI trimers as acceptors can reach as high as $1 1 . 0 1 \%$ [46].

Hou and coworkers elongated Perl to develop a PDI trimer of H-tri-PDI (Figure 4.5) [47]. When it is blended with an efficient narrow bandgap polymer donor PBDT-TS1, it achieves a PCE of $7 . 2 5 \%$ along with a high short-circuit current density $( J _ { \mathrm { s c } } )$ of $1 6 . 5 2 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ (Table 4.2). Employing a central core to exploit PDI trimers is the most common method. In 2014, Zhan and coworkers synthesized a PDI trimer called S(TPA-PDI), in which three PDI units are connected by triphenylamine units [48]. Due to the presence of $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ hybridized nitrogen atoms in the core, the whole molecule is quasi 3D and non-planar structure, which inhibits intermolecular interaction and aggregation. When blended with PBDTTT-C-T, the PCE of the device is $3 . 3 2 \%$ , and its electron mobility is only $2 . 3 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 } \thinspace \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ which explains the low FF $( 3 3 . 6 \% )$ . In the same year, Chen's research team directly connected three PDIs to the benzene ring to synthesize a novel PDI trimer of B(PDI)3, and the OSCs based on PTB7-Th:B(PDI)3 achieved a PCE of $5 . 6 5 \%$ [49]. Soon after, Peng's group reported a PDI trimer Ta-PDI with triazine as the central core. Compared with analog with benzene as the core, they found that the triazine-based trimer has a smaller twisted structure and a stronger tendency to aggregate, thus a higher electron mobility [50]. Using PTB7-Th as the polymer donor, the Ta-PDI-based OSC showed a PCE of $9 . 1 8 \%$ , with a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 7 . 1 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and a FF of $6 8 . 5 \%$ . In addition, they employed triphenylphosphine (TPP), triphenylphosphine monoxide (TPO), and triphenylphosphine sulfide as central core to develop three novel PDI trimmers, namely TPP-PDI, TPO-PDI, and TPS-PDI [46]. Compared with TPP-PDI and TPS-PDI, TPO-PDI shows the least twisted conformation due to the stronger electron-withdrawing ability of the oxygen atom, which improves the molecular packing of this SMA. Ultimately, OSCs based on PTTEA:TPO-PDI exhibit a PCE as high as $1 1 . 0 1 \%$ , significantly higher than those of device based on TPP-PDI $( 6 . 1 9 \% )$ and TPS-PDI $( 9 . 6 7 \% )$ . It is worth mentioning that the PCE of $1 1 . 0 1 \%$ is the highest value for PDI-based OSCs. In the same year, the same group developed two novel PDI trimers, ${ \sf A l q } _ { 3 }$ -PDI and $\mathrm { \bf A l q } _ { 3 } { \cdot } \mathrm { \bf P D I } 2$ , are synthesized by utilizing a 3D tri(8-hydroxyquinoline)aluminum(III) $( \mathsf { A l q } _ { 3 } )$ core, which can suppress the molecular aggregation properties [51]. In comparison with ${ \sf A l q } _ { 3 }$ -PDI, the extended $\pi$ -conjugation of ${ \sf A l q } _ { 3 }$ -PDI2 leads to enhanced molecular packing, which broadens the absorption spectra and improves the domain size of blend film. Thus, the OSCs based on PTTEA: ${ \sf A l q } _ { 3 }$ -PD12 yields higher $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and FF, thereby better device performance $( \mathrm { P C E } = 9 . 5 4 \% )$ $J _ { \mathrm { s c } } = 1 5 . 7 4 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ $\mathrm { F F } = 0 . 7 1 3$ relative to those of device based on ${ \sf A l q } _ { 3 }$ -PDI $( \mathrm { P C E } = 7 . 8 2 \%$ $J _ { \mathrm { s c } } = 1 3 . 5 6 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ $\mathrm { F F } = 0 . 6 6 3$

The fused-ring strategy can also be applied to develop PDI trimer-like PDI dimer. In 2015, Nuckolls and coworkers continued to extend NDP and developed a PDI trimer and a PDI tetramer, namely h-PDI3 and h-PDI4, and they achieved high PCEs in OSCs ( $7 . 9 \%$ for h-PDI3-based device and $8 . 3 \%$ for h-PDI4-based device), which were the highest values for non-fullerene bulk heterojunctions at that time [52]. In 2017, Chen and coworkers fused three PDI units into one benzotrithiophene, thus developing a fused-PDI trimer named Fused-TriPDI [53]. Compared with the non-fused precursor (TriPDI), Fused-TriPDI exhibits upshifted energy levels, better planarity, and enhanced electron mobility. As a result, the OSCs with PTB7-Th:Fused-TriPDI blend yielded higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } } , J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and FF relative to those of device based on TriPDI, thus promoted PCE. In the same year, Wang's research group developed TPH-Se by fusing three selenium-hybridized PDI units to a benzene ring [54]. In comparison with TPH without Se, the integration of

![](images/5f83ff405e3119b9634b4da6a7a653c284c96cd7691181941077e8ff9c4573b9.jpg)  
Figure 4.5 Chemical structures of selected PDI trimers. Source: Z. Luo and C. Yang.

Se to TPH endows TPH-Se higher LUMO energy level and enhanced absorption. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction results demonstrate that TPH-Se shows a more compact 3D network assembly and a more twisted propeller configuration relative to TPH, which can be ascribed to the Se. : -O interactions (Figure 4.6). Consequently, TPH and TPH-Se acceptor-based OSCs gave high PCE of $8 . 2 8 \%$ and $9 . 2 8 \%$ , respectively. The better PCE for TPH-Se-based device is mainly attributed to the upshift LUMO value, enhanced mobility and absorption of TPH-Se, and more favorable morphology.

# 4.2.4PDI Tetramers

In addition to the PDI trimers, we can also connect four PDI to the central cores to synthesize a PDI tetramers, which is beneficial to form 3D molecular structures, thereby facilitating to the charge transport.

In 2015, Yan and coworkers developed three PDI tetramers by connecting four PDI units with tetraphenylmethane, tetraphenylsilane, and tetraphenylgermane, namely TPC-PDI4, TPSi-PDI4, and TPGe-PDI4 (Figure 4.7), and they studied the effect of the central core on device performance and film morphology [55]. When blended them with the same polymer donor PffBT4T-2DT, it was found that devices based on TPC-PDI4 and TPSi-PDI4 exceeded $4 \%$ efficiency (Table 4.3), while the efficiency of the device based on TPGe-PDI4 is less than $2 \%$ . Other than the tetraphenylalkanes-like central core, spirobifluorene and spirocyclic dithiophene were used as central core to develop PDI tetramers, and the corresponding PDI tetramers are called SF-PDI4 and FSP [56, 57], respectively. The device efficiencies based on these two PDI tetramers as acceptors are $5 . 9 8 \%$ and $8 . 8 9 \%$ , respectively. Later, the PDI tetramer PBI-Por constructed with porphyrin as the core has a lower bandgap and weaker crystallinity than most PDI-based acceptors [58]. When mixing PBI-Por and the polymer PBDTBDD with complementary absorption, the device yields a PCE of $7 . 4 \%$ In addition to liking PDI unit at $\beta$ position, there is also a PDI tetramer of Me-PDI4 by connecting to the tetraphenyl carbon core unit through the imide region [59]. Combining it with the donor PBDTTT-C-T yielded a PCE of $2 . 3 5 \%$ . In 2017, Huang's team developed another PDI tetramer, P4N4, with 2,3,7,8-tetraphenylpyrazino[2,3-g]quinoxaline as the central core, using PDBT-T1 as the donor, the OSC with P4N4 as the acceptor achieved a PCE of $5 . 7 1 \%$ [60].

In 2015, Yan and coworkers developed a new PDI tetramer TPE-PDI4 (Figure 4.8) based on TPC-PDI4 by replacing carbon atoms with ethylene [61]. Because the tetrastyrene core has a four-leaf fan-like structure, its aggregation is weak. Blending with PffBT4T-2DT produces a suitable phase separation, and an efficiency of $5 . 5 3 \%$ was obtained. The following year, Yan and coworkers replaced the ethylene in TPE-PDI4 with pyrazine to synthesize the small-molecule TPPz-PDI4 [62]. The introduction of pyrazine reduced the torsion angle of the molecule, increased the electron mobility of the molecule, and further improved its efficiency $( 7 . 1 \% )$ From TPC-PDI4 to TPE-PDI4 to TPPz-PDI4, it is clear that reducing the degree of intramolecular distortion can improve electron mobility, fill factor, and device performance. Likewise, Yan and coworkers reported two PDI tetramers with fused and non-fused-ring structures based on tetrathienylbenzene as the core [63]. DFT calculations indicate that the fused FTTB-PDI4 shows a smaller twisted structure as compared with the non-fused PDI tetramer (TTB-PDI4), which leads to enhanced molecular packing and improved domain purity in the P3TEA:FTTB-PDI4 blend (Figure 4.9). Additionally, FTTB-PDI4 displays enhanced absorption capability, upshifted LUMO energy levels and blue-shifted absorption. Consequently, the P3TEA:FTTB-PDI4 devices achieve the a PCE as high as $1 0 . 5 8 \%$ along with a small energy loss of $0 . 5 3 \mathrm { V } ,$ which is the highest value of solar cells based on PDI as the acceptor at that time.

In 2016, Yu and coworkers used BDT as the core to construct the $\alpha$ substituted PDI tetramer of TPB [64]. Blending it with PTB7-Th achieved a PCE of $8 . 4 6 \%$ , along with a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ over $1 8 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . The next year, they employed the same central core to develop a $\beta$ substituted PDI tetramer of $\beta \mathrm { T P B } 6$ and developed TPB6-C (the fused $\beta \mathrm { T P B 6 } )$ [65]. In comparison with the unfused TPB6, TPB6-C exhibits enlarged conjugated skeleton, enhanced absorption, more rigid molecular structure, and shallower energy level. As a result, the inverted OsCs based on $\beta \mathrm { T P B 6 - C }$ and PTB7-Th exhibited a better efficiency of $7 . 6 9 \%$ than that of $\beta$ TPB6-based device.

Isomerization strategy plays a vital role in tuning absorption spectra, electronic structure, charge mobility, $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking, eventually determining the device performance [69-71]. For instance, Yang and coworkers developed two isomeric PDI tetramers, namely BPT-Se and BPT-Se1 [66]. In comparison with BPT-Se, BPT-Se1 exhibits a shallower energy level, enhanced absorption profile, and improved molecular packing. As a result, the OSCs based on BTP-Se and polymer PDBT-T1 as donor gave a PCE of $9 . 5 4 \%$ with an outstanding FF of 0.732, which are higher than those of the device based on BTP-Se $\mathrm { P C E } = 7 . 8 \%$ $\mathrm { F F } = 0 . 6 7 5$ ). In addition, Yan's group synthesized two isomeric PDI tetramers, a-FTTN-PDI4 and b-FTTN-PDI4, with different functionalization sites ( $\overset { \cdot } { \mathbf { \alpha } }$ and $\beta$ positions) on a naphthalene ring, respectively [67]. Photoluminescence spectra and GIWAXS results revel that a-FTTN-PDI4 showed better $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking than $\boldsymbol { \mathbf { b } }$ -FTTN-PDI4, thereby leading to enhanced electron mobility. Consequently, the P3TEA:a-FTTN-PDI4-based devices achieved a higher PCE of $8 . 6 \%$ than b-FTTN-PDI4-based ones. The next year, the same group synthesized two regio-isomeric PDI tetramers (oCP-FPDI4 and $p { \mathrm { C P F P D I 4 } } ,$ with a novel [2.2]paracyclophane central core [68]. Blending $p { \mathrm { C P } }$ -FPDI4 with polymer donor P3TEA realized a PCE of $9 . 0 6 \%$ , which is higher than that of oCP-FPDI4-based device $( 2 . 4 2 \% )$ due to the obviously reduced FF and $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ . The enhanced FF and $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ in $p { \mathrm { C P } }$ -FPDI4-based device are ascribed to the more suitable phase segregation, more effective charge dissociation, and balanced charge transport.

Although the device efficiency based on PDIs as acceptors is much lower than that of the A-D-A-type acceptors-based device, its intrinsic characteristics, including outstanding thermal/photo stability, low-cost synthesis, and facile functionalization, are still worthy of our attention. In addition, it can be used as an indoor photovoltaic or as a front cell for tandem devices. To further improve the device efficiency of PDI-based acceptors, some design guidelines are proposed: (i) the first and most important point is to broaden the absorption spectrum and enhance the light absorption capacity of PDIs; (ii) balancing the relationship between twisting angle and electron mobility plays an important role in producing suitable domain size/purity, thereby affecting the device performance; (ii) some commonly used molecular design strategies such as fusion strategy, isomeric strategy, and asymmetric strategy could be employed to optimize the molecular structure, thereby improving the physicochemical properties eventually increasing the device efficiency.

# 4.3 A-D-A-Type SMAs

In A-D-A-type SMA materials, A unit owns strong electron-withdrawing ability while D unit owns strong electron-donating ability. Such A-D-A configuration can produce strong intramolecular charge transfer (ICT) state between A and D units and endow SMAs with wide absorption range and low-lying HOMO and LUMO energy levels. Moreover, large $\pi$ -conjugated backbone with planar and rigid conformation of A-D-A-type SMAs can guarantee good intermolecular interaction and high electron mobility. Usually, the structure of A-D-A-type SMAs can be divided into three parts: electron-rich donor core (D unit), electron-deficient end group (A unit), and side chains linked to D unit, which makes the modifiable sites of such type of SMAs become very rich. Among them, A and D units show very critical roles in regulating bandgap, energy levels, and crystalline properties of SMAs, and side chains flanking on D unit is mainly to improve the solubility and fine-tune the crystalline properties of SMAs and thereby optimizing micromorphology of active layer [1-3].

In 2015, Zhan and coworkers first reported a novel A-D-A-type SMA, namely ITIC, by combining a ladder-type donor (indacenodithieno[3,2-b]thiophene, IDTT) with two 2-(3-oxo-2,3-dihydro- $. 1 H$ -inden-1-ylidene)malononitrile (INCN) terminal groups (Figure 4.10) [72]. Due to the strong push-pull electronic effect between IDTT and INCN units, ITIC shows a narrow bandgap of $1 . 5 9 \mathrm { e V }$ and meanwhile maintains deep-lying HOMO and LUMO energy levels of $- 5 . 4 8$ and $- 3 . 8 3 \mathrm { e V } ,$ respectively (Table 4.4). In addition, the planar and rigid backbone of ITIC promotes the good intermolecular $\pi { - } \pi$ stackings and thus obtains high electron mobility of up to $3 . 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ . As a result, ITIC blending with PTB7-Th achieved a $6 . 8 \%$ PCE multiplying from a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 1 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 4 . 2 1 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF of 0.591, which is comparable with that of PTB7-Th: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 }$ BM-based OSCs and creates a new record for fullerene-free OsCs. Later, Hou and coworkers selected a wide bandgap polymer PBDB-T in their laboratory to blend with ITIC, achieving an outstanding PCE of up to $1 1 . 2 \%$ (a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 9 9 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 6 . 8 1 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and a FF of 0.742) with excellent thermal stability. The significant PCE enhancement can be attributed to a more matched absorption spectrum and energy levels, and more compatible morphology in PBDB-T:ITIC blend than those in PTB7-Th:ITIC blend. Furthermore, an efficiency of $1 0 . 7 8 \%$ was certified based on PBDB-T:ITIC device with an area of $1 . 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ [87]. The excellent photovoltaic performance of ITIC shows the great potential of A-D-A-type SMAs, opening a new door for the development of highly-efficient non-fullerene acceptors (NFAs).

# 4.3.1  Side Chains Optimization

The role of side chains is multiple for achieving high-performance SMAs. On one hand, they provide SMAs with good solubility to support its synthesis and purification and meet the requirements of solution processing. On the other hand, side chain groups have great effects on the crystalline properties of SMAs and the miscibility between donor and acceptor, which directly affect the morphology, charge transport, and recombination within active layer. However, the influence of side chains is also very complicated due to the diversity of side chain types and different effects; therefore, side chains optimization is necessary and important in the development of SMAs.

![](images/807efef558d90e5305b803435f26e0419e2745caf815cd5c05fbee7c248b3b86.jpg)  
Figure 4.10 Chemical structures of non-fullerene SMAs with different side chains. Source: W. Gao and C. Yang.

In ITIC, four 4-hexylphenyl are linked to IDTT core via $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ hybridized carbon atoms with twisted phenyl groups not conjugated to backbone of SMAs, which leads to little effect on absorption and energy levels of SMAs but can inhibit excessive crystallization of molecules and regulate the morphology of active layer.

ITIC-Th was modified from ITIC by replacing 4-hexylphenyl with 5-hexylthiophen [73]. Compared to ITIC, the LUMO energy level of ITIC-Th has been reduced from $- 3 . 8 3$ to $- 3 . 9 3 \mathrm { e V }$ due to the influence of $\delta$ -induced effect between ladder-type core (IDTT) and thiophene groups, and the HOMO energy level dropped from $- 5 . 4 8$ to $- 5 . 6 6 \mathrm { e V } .$ The deeper HOMO and LUMO energy levels match more suitable with those of polymer donors and enlarge the HOMO-HOMO and LUMO-LUMO energy gaps between donor and acceptor, which provides greater driving force for more efficient exciton dissociation. ITIc-Th shows a high electron mobility of $6 . 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ due to better crystallization performance of ITIc-Th induced by sulfur-sulfur interaction between thiophene groups, which is found to be two times higher than that of ITIC pure film. As a result, OSCs based on PTB7-Th:ITIC-Th can achieve a $8 . 7 \%$ PCE, higher than that of PTB7-Th:ITIC-based OSCs.

Soon later, Li and coworkers changed the 4-hexylphenyl on ITIC into 3-hexylphenyl to synthesize $m$ -ITIC [69]. ITIC and $m$ -ITIC are isomers of each other with small difference lying in the relative positions of alkyl chains on phenyl. Compared with ITIC, $m$ -ITIC exhibits nearly same absorption spectrum and HOMO and LUMO energy levels but significantly enhanced $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking in neat film, and thus a higher electron mobility is achieved. As a result, OSCs based on J61:m-ITIC achieved a $1 1 . 7 7 \%$ PCE with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 1 2 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 8 . 3 1 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF of 0.706, which are all higher than those of J61:ITIC-based OSCs (a $1 0 . 5 7 \%$ PCE with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 9 8 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 7 . 9 7 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and FF of 0.655). More importantly, $m$ -ITIC-based OsCs show less thickness-dependent photovoltaic behavior than ITIC-based OSCs within film thickness range of $8 0 - 3 6 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , which is beneficial to the fabrication of large-area devices.

In 2016, Zhan and coworkers designed and synthesized another famous SMA IDIC based on an indaceno[1,2-b:5,6-b']dithiophene (IDT) core with $n$ -hexyl as side chains [74]. Due to the smaller steric hindrance effect of alkyl groups than aromatic phenyl groups, IDIC trends to become more planar, thus the intermolecular $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking effects of IDIC is remarkably improved with a high electron mobility of up to $1 . 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } \thinspace \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ in IDIC neat film. IDIC exhibits excellent photovoltaic performance that PDBT-T1:IDIC-based OSCs can achieve $8 . 7 1 \%$ PCE without any treatment and $1 0 . 3 7 \%$ PCE with $0 . 2 5 \%$ 1,8-diiodooctane (DIO) additive. When selecting fluorine-contained PM6 as polymer donor, OSCs based on PM6:IDIC can achieve $1 1 . 9 \%$ PCE without any treatment, which is a recorded value for as-cast OSCs at that time. Moreover, PM6:IDIC-based OSCs exhibit excellent thickness insensitivity property with over $1 1 \%$ PCE at film thickness of $2 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [88].

By introducing a phenyl group into the tail of the side chain of IDIC, Yang and coworkers designed and synthesized an excellent SMA IDIC-C4Ph [75]. Moderately weakened crystallinity is observed in IDIC-C4Ph neat film compared to that of IDIC neat film, which gains a subtle balance between the crystallinity and miscibility. OSCs based on PBDB-T:IDIC-C4Ph obtain a $1 1 . 5 \%$ PCE, which is significantly higher than $n$ -hexyl and 4-hexylphenyl substituted analogs-based OsCs. When changing polymer donor PBDB-T into PM6, as-cast OSCs based on PM6:IDIC-C4Ph achieved $1 3 . 2 3 \%$ PCE with a high FF of 0.760; moreover, a $1 4 \%$ PCE with a FF of 0.783 can be recorded after annealing. This side chain modification effectively regulates the crystallization of SMAs to synergistically improve morphology and molecular orientations of active layer.

In addition to SMAs with symmetrical side chains, Bo group designed and synthesized a IDIC analog, called IDT-OB, with asymmetric side chains on IDT core, that is, one $n$ -octyl and one 4-hexylphenyl are fixed on one substituted site [76]. This asymmetric alkyl substitution strategy achieves a fine tuning of crystalline properties of SMAs, leading to a better miscibility and phase separation between SMAs and polymer donors. OSCs based on PBDB-T:IDT-OB achieved a $1 0 . 1 2 \%$ PCE with a high and balanced carrier transport in active layer. In addition, IDT-OB also exhibits good film thickness insensitivity property and achieve a $9 . 1 7 \%$ PCE when the film thickness of OSCs based on PBDB-T:IDT-OB reaches $2 1 0 \mathrm { n m }$

# 4.3.2 End Groups Engineering

In A-D-A-type SMAs, A unit is a kind of active methylene compounds with very strong electron-withdrawing ability, we usually call them end group. Such types of end groups are relatively limited and mainly can be divided into two categories: 2-(3-oxo-2,3-dihydro- $. 1 H$ -inden-1-ylidene)malononitrile (INCN) and its derivatives, and 2-(6-oxo-5,6-dihydro-4H-cyclopenta[c]thiophen-4-ylidene)malononitrile (CPTCN) and its derivatives. The absorption, energy levels, and crystallization properties of SMAs can be effectively regulated by adjusting the type, number, and relative position of substituents on end group.

Hou and coworkers modified INCN end group by adding one or two methyl groups onto 5 or/and 6 position of INCN and synthesized two SMAs IT-M and IT-DM, respectively [77]. Methyl as a weak electron-donating unit slightly reduce the electron-withdrawing ability of INCN. As the number of methyl group increases, the LUMO energy levels of SMAs are gradually elevated with absorption spectra gradually blue-shifted from ITIC to IT-M then to IT-DM. As a result, PBDB-T:IT-Mand PBDB-T:IT-DM-based OSCs achieved $1 2 . 0 5 \%$ and $1 1 . 2 9 \%$ PCEs with high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } } \mathrm { s }$ of 0.94 and $0 . 9 7 \mathrm { V } ,$ respectively. Moreover, methyl-substituted end group improves the crystallization performance of SAMs, and monomethyl-substituted INCN enables IT-M with a more suitable crystallization property than ITIC and IT-DM. Therefore, the morphology of PBDB-T:IT-M blend film was optimized and obtained $7 4 \%$ high FF in devices (Figure 4.11).

After the success of methyl-substituted INCN, Hou and coworkers further modified the INCN with methoxy group due to the stronger electron-donating ability of oxygen atom than carbon atom and expected to obtain higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ in OSCs. Interestingly, four isomers of INCN derivatives substituted by single methoxy at different position of INCN can be completely separated, and corresponding isomers of four SMAs (IT-OM-1, IT-OM-2, IT-OM-3, and IT-OM-4) were obtained [78]. IT-OM-1, IT-OM-2, IT-OM-3, and IT-OM-4 show high but different LUMO energy levels, which are $- 3 . 7 6$ $- 3 . 8 6$ $- 3 . 8 0$ , and $- 3 . 8 1 \mathrm { e V } ,$ and achieved $6 . 3 \%$ $1 1 . 9 \%$ $1 0 . 8 \%$ , and $7 . 9 \%$ PCEs with $V _ { \mathrm { o c } } \mathrm { s }$ of 1.01, 0.93, 0.96, and $0 . 9 7 \mathrm { V }$ in devices, respectively, when blending with polymer donor PBDB-T. These results indicated that minor changes in the substitution position on INCN are demonstrated to not only influence the optoelectronic properties but also molecular packing of the isomers, leading to great difference in photovoltaic performance of four isomers-based OSCs.

Compared to adding electron-donating groups onto INCN, modifying INCN with electron-withdrawing units can enhance the electron-withdrawing ability of INCN. Li and coworkers substituted INCN with one fluorine (F), chlorine (Cl), bromine (Br), and iodine (I) atom onto 5 or 6 position of INCN and synthesized four SAMs F-ITIC, Cl-ITIC, Br-ITIC, and I-ITIC, respectively [79]. Compared to ITIC, halogen-substituted SMAs show red-shifted absorption spectra and dropped LUMO energy levels. As a result, OSCs based on wide bandgap polymer PTPDBDT and four SMAs achieved $8 . 8 { - } 9 . 5 \%$ PCE with significantly increased $J _ { \mathrm { s c } } \mathbf { s }$ but decreased $V _ { \mathrm { o c } } \mathrm { s }$ compared to PTPDBDT:ITIC-based OSCs, indicating single halogen substitution can effectively improve the photovoltaic performance of SMAs.

![](images/6f3edfcf8385b2556731c05884b812533cd887cd91de5f6b72131c8db355bcaf.jpg)  
Figure 4.11 Non-fullerene small-molecule acceptors with different end groups. Source: W. Gao and C. Yang.

The single halogen-substituted INCN has two isomers that are difficult to separate, which will result in three isomers of SAMs in the final product. Hou and coworkers developed F and Cl double-substituted end group on 5 and 6 position of INCN and synthesized IT-4F [80] and IT-4Cl [81]. F atom with strong electronegativity and small radius can form weak interactions with electron-rich sulfur atom via non-covalent bonds, which enhances the intermolecular $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking, thus promoting the carrier mobility in both neat and blend films. Though double fluorine-substituted INCN acting as end group significantly increase the $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of resultant SMAs-based OSCs, the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of OSCs also drops sharply. To compensate the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ loss, PBDB-T was optimized by adding sulfanyl chain and fluorine atom onto the thiophene side chains to obtain a polymer donor PBDB-T-SF with lower HOMO energy level. As a result, PBDB-T-SF:IT-4F-based OSCs achieved a recorded PCE of over $1 3 \%$ for the first time. Theoretical calculations have revealed that the carbon-chlorine (C-Cl) bond has a larger dipole moment than the carbon-fluorine (C-F) bond, indicating that Cl-substituted INCN shows a stronger electron-withdrawing ability than F-substituted one and leading to IT-4Cl, a reduced optical bandgap compared to IT-4F. As a result, OSCs based on PBDB-TF:IT-4Cl also achieved an over $1 3 \%$ PCE with a further increased $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ than that of PBDB-TF:IT-4F-based OSCs.

Three $\mathrm { F }$ atoms substituted INCN was first reported by Marks group, and corresponding six $\mathrm { F }$ atoms substituted SMA ITIC-6F was synthesized [82]. The bandgap of ITIC-6F can be further lowered to $1 . 5 1 \mathrm { e V }$ compared to IT-4F with a bandgap of $1 . 5 5 \mathrm { e V . }$ More importantly, the $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking effect between SMAs increases as the number of F atoms on SMA increases. ITIC-6F obtains a more intense $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking with a very short $d$ -spacing of $3 . 2 8 \mathring { \mathrm { A } }$ than that of IT-4F, which promotes the electron mobility of ITIC-6F film and enabled OSCs based on PBDB-TF:ITIC-6F to achieve an over $1 2 \%$ PCE.

Thiophene as an important building block in the construction of photoactive materials show many unique advantages than benzene, such as stronger electron-donating ability, more intense intermolecular interaction, and smaller steric hindrance effect. End groups contained thiophene unit will exhibit different property. Yang group developed an efficient end group called CPTCN by fusing cyclopentane-1,3-dione onto 3,4-position of thiophene for the first time and synthesized a novel SMA ITCPTC [83]. It was found that the absorption spectrum of ITCPTC is slightly red-shifted compared to ITIC but with a slight lower LUMO energy level. In addition, introducing thiophene into the end group of SMA is able to form S-S non-covalent bond interaction, leading to a better $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking and higher electron mobility of ITCPTC than those of ITIC in their neat films. As a result, PBT1-EH:ITCPTC-based OSCs achieved a PCE of $1 1 . 8 \%$ with a high FF of over $7 5 \%$ which are significantly higher than those of PBT1-EH:ITIC-based OSCs under same fabrication conditions, indicating the great potential of CPTCN as end group.

At the same time, Hou and coworkers developed an isomer of CPrcN by changing the fusion site between cyclopentane-1,3-dione and thiophene from 3,4-position to 2,3-position [84]. Such structure change significantly weakens the electron-withdrawing ability of end group, which leads to bandgap of ITCC significantly increasing from 1.58 to $1 . 6 7 \mathrm { e V }$ accompanied with LUMO energy level elevated from $- 3 . 9 6$ to $- 3 . 7 6 \mathrm { e V }$ in comparison with ITCPTC. As a result, OSCs based on PBDB-T:ITCC yielded an over $1 \mathrm { V } V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and a $1 1 . 4 \%$ PCE.

Subsequently, Yang group functionalized the CPTCN by adding one methyl group or one Cl atom onto the thiophene unit of CPTCN and synthesized two SMAs MeIC [85] and ITC-2Cl [86]. These two CPTCN derivatives show that no isomer with the dicyanomethyl group orientates inversely with methyl group or chlorine atom, which is different from single methyl or Cl-substituted INCN. Compared to ITCPTC, methylated MeIC show almost no blue shift in absorption spectrum but greatly elevated LUMO energy level, while the absorption spectrum of ITC-2Cl exhibits a remarkably red shift of over $5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ with LUMO energy level dropped. Methylated or chlorinated CPTcN both enhance the intermolecular $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking between SMAs and promotes the carrier mobility of neat and blend films. As a result, OSCs based on J71:MeIC achieved higher PCE and $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ than J71:ITCPTC-based OSCs, and PM6:ITC-2Cl-based OSCs achieved higher PCE and larger $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ than PM6:ITCPTC-based OSCs.

# 4.3.3 Core Units Engineering

# 4.3.3.1IDTT and Its Derivations

Compared with side chains and end groups, the electron-donating D cores are rich in type and variable in structure and play important roles in energy levels fine-tuning and backbone planarity manipulation. A library of novel D cores were thus developed via core structure innovations such as fused/non-fused cores, $\pi$ -bridge, and asymmetric strategies.

In view of the successfully explored ITIC-based system above, the IDTT core was considered a potential building block to design efficient fused ring electron acceptors (FREAs). IDTT is composed of middle benzene and thieno[3,2-b]thiophene (TT) at both ends fused by cyclopentadiene. As such, vast efforts were devoted to modulating modules in IDTT, and a library of novel derived FREAs has been developed.

It is widely accepted that the match between donor and acceptor is critical to device performance. In order to escape the limitation of matching wide optical bandgap $( E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } } )$ donor with narrow $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ acceptor, Zhu and coworkers designed a FREA called NIDBT [89] by replacing TT with benzothiophene. The introduced benzene weakens the electron-donating ability for the expected $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ of $1 . 8 4 \mathrm { e V } .$ As planned, narrow $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ donor PTB7-Th was blended with NIDBT, and the corresponding OSCs only exhibited a moderate PCE of $4 . 4 5 \%$ due to their almost overlapping absorption. On the contrary, flanking IDTT with another thiophene, the stronger electron-rich core 6,6,12,12 - tetrakis (4 -hexylphenyl) -indacenobis (dithieno. ${ } \cdot { } _ { 3 , 2 } - b ; 2 ^ { \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime } .$ d]thiophene) (IBDT) was obtained. To investigate the number and position of substituted fluorine atoms on the end groups on device properties, four novel FREAs (INIC, INIC1, INIC2, and INIC3, Figure 4.12) were synthesized [70]. All these four FREAs have strong absorption at $6 0 0 { - } 7 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ with high extinction coefficients of $2 . 1 0 { - } 2 . 5 0 \times 1 0 ^ { 5 } \mathrm { M ^ { - 1 } c m ^ { - 1 } }$ . Obviously, the fluorinated IC-based INIC1, INIC2, and INIC3 exhibited red-shifted absorption and deeper energy levels than these of INIC (without fluorine substitution). The resultant OSCs blending with FTAZ displayed the PCE of $7 . 7 0 \mathrm { - } 1 1 . 5 0 \%$ with small $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ $( 0 . 6 1 { - } 0 . 6 3 \mathrm { e V } )$ . In detailed, the device efficiency is gradually improved accompanied with the increased fluorine atoms in INIC series, and the highest PCE of $1 1 . 5 0 \%$ can be achieved in FTAZ:INIC3-based device due to fluorine-induced intermolecular interactions. Also, the FTAZ:INIC2-based OSCs presented a better property than FTAZ:INIC1, indicating the position of substituted fluorine significantly influences the device performance.

Coincidentally, through inserting pyrrole rings into IDTT, another electron-rich core named 5,5,12,12-tetrakis(4-hexylphenyl)-indacenobis(dithieno $[ 3 , 2 - b ; 2 ^ { \prime }$ $3 ^ { \prime }$ -d]pyrrol) (INP) [90] was developed by Tang and coworkers. The IC/IC-2F was end-capped for the synthesis of INPIC and INPIC-4F (structure shown in

![](images/da1e0e26556a9b0c49c990d53900a0ed208edb6069105f6727826ac14e519407.jpg)  
Figure 4.12Chemical structures of IDTT-based FREAs and its derivatives. Source:J. Cao and W. Tang.

Figure 4.12), respectively. Compared with INIC3 mentioned above, the composite INPIC-4F behaves a red-shifted absorption onset $( \lambda _ { \mathrm { o n s e t } } )$ of $8 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ (c. $2 4 \mathrm { n m } )$ with a narrower $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ of $1 . 3 9 \mathrm { e V } ,$ powerfully suggesting stronger electron-donating INP block than IDTT and IBDT. Molecular simulation results show that both INPIC and INPIC-4F have coplanar $\pi$ -conjugated frameworks. And the introduced fluorine endows INPIC-4F enhanced ICT effect, thereby facilitating charge transport for a high electron mobilites $\left( \mu _ { \mathrm { e } } \right)$ of $5 . 0 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ . Moreover, the PBDB-T:INPIC-4F blend dominated a stronger face-on $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking in out-of-plane (OOP) direction in comparison to PBDB-T:INPIC-based ones. The optimized PBDB-T:INPIC-4F devices afforded an outstanding PCE of $1 3 . 1 3 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 5 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 1 . 6 1 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF of 0.715, which is the highest value reported in literatures at that time (Table 4.5). The $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ was found to be as low as $0 . 5 6 \mathrm { e V } .$ Further crystallization dynamics study reveals that INPIC-4F tends to form polycrystalline due to its fast crystallization rate, causing large phase separation in corresponding blend films as well as affected device efficiency. Molecular engineering and device process were then implemented to manipulate the crystallinity of

INPIC or prolong the crystallization time during the spin coating for efficient/stable OSCs [106-108].

Unlike the above two examples modifying IDTT core to enhance electron-donating ability, Zhan's group directly fused thiophene on both sides of IDTT via cyclopentadiene (namely IU). The coupling of the as-developed IU with electron-withdrawing 2F-IC generated IUIC [91]. Due to the large $\pi$ -conjugation, IUIC exhibits strong absorption in NIR region $( 6 0 0 - 9 0 0 \mathrm { n m } )$ with an $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ of $1 . 4 1 \mathrm { e V } .$ In comparison with the IDTT-cored ITIC4 (IT-4F, $\mathrm { L U M O } = - 3 . 9 7 \mathrm { e V } )$ , IUIC shows the upshifted LUMO energy level of $- 3 . 8 7 \mathrm { e V } ,$ which is beneficial to the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the device. As a result, the as-cast OSCs blended with PTB7-Th achieved a PCE of $1 1 . 2 0 \%$ , much higher than that of ITIC4-based counterparts $( 8 . 1 8 \% )$ . More interestingly, its NIR absorption can retain most of the visible light, providing IUIC with the potential for semitransparent organic solar cells (ST-OSCs). The resulting ST-OSC based on PTB7-Th:IUIC afforded a PCE of over $1 0 . 2 0 \%$ with an average visible transmittance (AVT) of $3 1 \%$ without any extra treatment.

Apart from extending core size, heteroatom substitution is another strategy to enhance electron-donating ability. By replacing sulfur with selenium, Lin et al. [92] reported two FREAs, namely, SRID-4F and TRID-4F. Besides, the structure-property relationship induced by region-specific selenium substitution was systematically investigated. Compared with sulfur atom, the more polarized selenium atom is surrounded by looser electron cloud delocalization, which makes the stronger orbital overlap between selenium and the $\pi$ -conjugated system for narrower bandgap of selenium. Relative to IT-4F (1.51 eV), narrower $E _ { \mathbf { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } } \mathbf { s }$ were thus observed in SRID-4F and TRID-4F (1.44 and $1 . 4 8 \mathrm { e V } ,$ respectively), implying more efficient ICT effect occurred in these two selenium substituted FREAs. Morphology studies showed that SRID-4F exhibits smaller (010) $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking distance $( d _ { \pi - \pi } )$ of $3 . 4 \mathring \mathrm { A }$ than TRID-4F $( d _ { \pi - \pi } = 3 . 9 \mathring \mathrm { A } )$ with preferential face-on orientation. And more ordered nanostructure induced by large dipole moment and O-Se non-covalent interaction between selenium atom and the carbonyl group of indanone are beneficial to charge transport. The corresponding PM6:SRID-4F-based devices achieved a higher PCE of $1 3 . 0 5 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 5 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 0 . 2 1 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ than its isomer TRID-4F-based ones $( 1 2 . 3 3 \% )$ . The FFs of the devices are all over 0.750 (Table 4.5).

In A-D-A-type FREAs, the linkage between D cores and A end groups inevitably results in different steric isomers due to the rotatable single bond, whose uncertain impacts on device properties seriously hinder the development of novel FREAs. As depicted in Figure 4.13a, Tang's group [93] masterly attached hexyl chains into the both ends of D core, and a novel acceptor named ITC6-IC was explored (Figure 4.12). Molecular simulation calculation results (two rotamers TT-IC and TTC6-IC were selected as representatives of ITIC and ITC6-IC, respectively, Figure 4.13b) showed that the TT-IC has two dominant conformations at $0 ^ { \circ }$ and $1 8 0 ^ { \circ }$ , and their energy difference is only $4 . 3 5 \mathrm { k J } \mathrm { m o l } ^ { - 1 }$ , illustrating both conformations will possibly coexist. When the hexyl side chains were attached, the energy of TTC6-IC at $1 8 0 ^ { \circ }$ is increased to over $3 2 \mathrm { k J } \mathrm { m o l } ^ { - 1 }$ . The large energy effectively limits the appearance of other dominant conformations except for that at $0 ^ { \circ }$ , thus locking the conformation well. The as-developed ITC6-IC exhibited a slightly blue-shifted absorption but a higher maximum molar absorption coefficient of $2 . 6 4 \times 1 0 ^ { 5 } \mathrm { M ^ { - 1 } c m ^ { - 1 } }$ compared with that of ITIC $( 1 . 7 2 \times 1 0 ^ { 5 } \mathrm { M ^ { - 1 } c m ^ { - 1 } } ,$ . The steric hindrance of hexyl chains favors the formation of planar structure with uniform conformation and weakens the $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking in ITC6-IC. The resulting blend films using PBDB-T and ITC6-IC as active layer feature fibrous nano-interpenetrating network for efficient charge transport. The derived PBDB-T:ITC6-IC-based device displayed a PCE of $1 1 . 6 1 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 7 \mathrm { V } ,$ $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 6 . 4 1 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF of 0.730, higher than ITIC-based counterparts $3 1 . 6 1 \%$ PCE with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of 0.91 V). The higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 7 \mathrm { V }$ can be attributed to upshifted LUMO energy level of ITC6-IC. Further fluorinated end group strategy leads to lower LUMO energy level and narrower $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ for ITC6-4F [94]. Selecting PM7 with complementary absorption and deeper HOMO, the PCE of PM7:ITC6-4F control OSC was promoted to $1 4 . 4 7 \%$ (Table 4.5).

In spite of the modification on both ends of IDTT, the molecular engineering on the intermediate core is equally effective. Side chains are typically used to modify solubility, crystallinity as well as molecular aggregation behavior, occasionally accompanied with changes in absorption and energy level. Attaching substituted side chains on intermediate benzene, Tang and coworkers [95] reported two new FREAs, namely IM-4F (methyl-substituted) and IOM-4F (methoxy-substituted)(Figure 4.12). IM-4F exhibited upshifted HOMO/LUMO $( - 5 . 6 9 \mathrm { e V } / - 4 . 1 9 \mathrm { e V } )$ than IDTT-cored IT-4F, and the lowest $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ of $1 . 4 6 \mathrm { e V }$ can be also found. Induced by $\mathrm { p } { - } \pi$ conjugative effect and large electronegativity of oxygen atom, IOM-4F only showed an $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ of $1 . 4 8 \mathrm { e V } .$ Featuring tempered nanoflake morphology with clear phase boundaries, the PM6:IM-4F-based device yielded a champion PCE of $1 4 . 1 7 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 8 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 2 . 1 2 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF of 0.728. The following energy loss investigation suggested PM6:IM-4F cells behaved simultaneously reduced radiative/non-radiative recombination loss, thus a smallest $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ of $0 . 6 7 \mathrm { e V } ,$ which provide a broader outlook with reduced $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ via rational core modulation. Combining all three strategies of successfully developed acceptors ITC6-IC, ITC6-4F, and IM-4F above mentioned, a highly-efficient FREA called IMC6-4F [96] was designed and synthesized. As expected, the optimal PM6:IMC6-4F-based device contributed one of the record PCEs for binary OSCs of $1 5 . 5 7 \%$ (Table 4.5) with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 0 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 2 . 2 9 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF of 0.776, which is on a par with that of state-of-the-art acceptor Y6 [109]-based cells $1 5 . 7 0 \%$ PCE).

By replacing intermediate benzene with TT, Zhan and coworkers prepared a stronger electron-donating core, followed by the design of four FREAs (F6IC, F8IC, and F10IC, Figure 4.12) to systematically investigate structure-property relationship [97]. Increasing the core size from 6 to 10 fused rings upshifted the HOMO level from $- 5 . 6 6$ to $- 5 . 2 6 \mathrm { e V }$ and the LUMO level from $- 4 . 0 2$ to $- 3 . 9 6 \mathrm { e V } ,$ leading to a decrease of $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ from 1.36 to $1 . 2 5 \mathrm { e V } .$ Three PTB7-Th blended films showed small root-mean-square (RMS) roughness $( 0 . 9 4 \mathrm { - } 2 . 6 2 \mathrm { n m } )$ , and the smallest $d _ { \pi - \pi }$ of $3 . 4 1 \mathring { \mathrm { A } }$ can be found in PTB7-Th:F8IC-based blend, contributing to its high fullerene-like mobilities $( \mu _ { \mathrm { e } } = 1 . 6 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 } )$ . The resulting devices based on PTB7-Th:F8IC displayed a PCE of $1 0 . 9 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 6 4 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of

$2 5 . 1 2 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF ot 0.676, higher than that ot F6IC- and Floic-based counterparts ( $7 . 1 \%$ and $1 0 . 2 \%$ , respectively). After adding $3 0 \%$ of the third component $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ , double or triple peaks appeared in original position of lamellar and $\pi { - } \pi$ peaks, indicating preferentially face-on oriented PTB7-Th and F8IC domains co-exist in PTB7-Th:F8IC: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ -based ternary OSCs, which improved the PCE to $1 2 . 3 0 \%$ with simultaneously improved $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 6 7 \mathrm { V }$ and $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 5 . 6 1 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ However, similar absorption of F8IC and F10IC noted us extending core size has limited effect on performance promotion, and finding new alternative intermediate core is also an effective method. Then the acceptor named FPIC [98] was synthesized by the same group through replacing TT central core with pyrene, which features more planar structure and larger conjugation. Compared with the initial F8IC, weakened electron-donating core endows FPIC deeper HOMO of $- 5 . 7 5 \mathrm { e V }$ and upshifted LUMO of $- 3 . 9 7 \mathrm { e V } ,$ corresponding to a wider $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ of $1 . 6 3 \mathrm { e V } .$ The blue-shifted absorption resulted in the poor $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 5 . 3 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ thereby a moderate PCE of $8 . 4 5 \%$ when blended with common donor PTB7-Th. Considering complementary absorption of F8IC and FPIC (Figure 4.13c), FPIC was added into PTB7-Th:F8IC based binary OSCs as a third component. As expected, the $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ thus got a substantial increase to $2 6 . 3 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ with a champion PCE of $1 3 . 0 0 \%$ $3 6 \%$ improvement relative to that of F8IC-based devices $( 9 . 5 5 \% )$ (Table 4.5). The above design strategy does not enhance electron-donating ability of central core but just enlarges conjugation length, which limits the extraction of charge for poor device parameters. In this case, Wang and coworkers [99] took the place of two benzene in pyrene with thiophene units, and more electron-donating naphtho $1 , 2 \cdot b : 5 , 6 \cdot b ^ { \prime } \mathrm { ~ . ~ }$ |dithiophene (NDT) core was applied for FREAs design. Due to the reinforced ICT effect, the as-developed IDCIC (structure shown in Figure 4.12) presents broad absorption at $6 0 0 { - } 8 3 0 \mathrm { n m }$ with a narrow $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ of $1 . 4 5 \mathrm { e V } .$ Morphological study revealed that IDCIC tends to aggregate in DIO for poor solubility, while inhibited aggregation and excellent solubility with reduced domain size/purity can be found in chloronaphthalene (CN). Compromising the effect of the above two, binary additive of $0 . 2 5 \%$ CN&D1O was added and nanofiber structure with clear phase separation was observed in FTAZ:IDCIC-based blends for high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and FF. As a result, the OSCs achieved a maximum PCE of $1 3 . 5 8 \%$ with a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 1 . 9 8 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and a FF of 0.710 (Figure 4.13d). After that, another carbazole central core was employed by Tang's group, and two nonacyclic FREAs named CZTT-IC and CZTT-4F were synthesized [100]. CZTT-4F film exhibited broad absorption at $5 5 0 \mathrm { - } 8 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , c. $4 3 \mathrm { n m }$ red-shifted than CZTT-IC. Owning to fluorinated end groups, CZTT-4F has deeper HOMO/LUMO energy levels $( - 5 . 6 1 \mathrm { e V } / - 4 . 1 1 \mathrm { e V } )$ than CZTT-IC $( - 5 . 5 4 \mathrm { e V } / - 3 . 9 7 \mathrm { e V } )$ . In order to find a suitable donor for better device performance, two polymers (PBDB-T and PM6) were selected to match the acceptors. Contact angle result shows that CZTT-4F had a better miscibility with PM6 than that with PBDB-T, indicating the formation of excellent vertical phase separation for efficient charge transport. The derived OSCs delivered a PCE of $1 2 . 0 7 \%$ (Table 4.5), which is among the highest values for carbazole-based OSCs in the literature. On the contrary, the CZTT-IC blended well with PBDB-T and the corresponding devices obtained a $9 . 8 7 \%$ PCE with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of 0.97 V. Surprisingly, PM6:CZTT-4F-based device also showed enhanced thermal and light-soaking stability with $9 0 . 1 \% / 7 8 . 7 \%$ PCE retention after thermal annealing/light soaking for 100 hours.

In FREAs, cyclopentadiene is a very common structure used to condense the middle core and flanking units. However, this medium electron-donating C-bridged unit is adverse to design FREAs with stronger light-harvesting capability. As thus, Ding's group [101]attached electron-rich oxygen atoms into cyclopentadiene to construct carbon-oxygen-bridged (CO-bridged) ladder-type core, and two novel FREAs coupling with IC and IC-2F ( $\mathrm { C O } _ { i } 7 \mathrm { I C }$ and $\mathrm { C O } _ { i } 7 \mathrm { D F I C }$ , respectively, Figure 4.12) were reported. Both $\mathrm { C O } _ { i } 7 \mathrm { I C }$ and $\mathrm { C O } _ { i } 7 \mathrm { D F I C }$ have wider $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ $1 . 6 0 \mathrm { e V }$ and $1 . 5 5 \mathrm { e V } ,$ respectively) than their carbon-bridged IDTT-based counterparts. Besides, single-crystal analysis revealed that the $_ { 0 - S }$ non-covalent interaction exists between the carbonyl on the end group and the sulfur atom at both ends of the cores for conformation locking, and the introduced oxygen atoms caused the S-shaped backbone (Figure 4.13e). When blending with PTB7-Th, the $\mathrm { C O } _ { i }$ 7DFIC-based cells yielded a PCE of $8 . 3 2 \%$ with a decent FF of 0.719, higher than that of PTB7-Th:CO,7IC-based ones ( $6 . 3 6 \%$ PCE). Then the ${ \mathrm { C O } } _ { i } { 8 \mathrm { D F I C } }$ [102] was further developed via replacing the benzene with TT. The PCE was promoted to $1 2 . 1 6 \%$ with an impressive high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 6 . 1 2 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , which can be attributed to its strong light absorption at $6 0 0 { - } 1 0 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ $( E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \scriptsize ~ o p t } } = 1 . 2 6 \mathrm { e V } )$ . Different from Ding's strategy, Yan and coworkers [103] introduced oxygen atoms into flanked cyclopenta[2,1] $\cdot b ; 3 , 4 \cdot b ^ { \prime }$ dithiophene (CPDT) blocks, and the new building block called dithieno[3, $_ { 2 } \mathrm { - } b ; 2 ^ { \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime } .$ d]pyran (DTPR) was explored. For comparison, three IDTT-, CPDT-, and DTPR-based FREAs (IDTT-4Cl, CPDT-4Cl, and DTPR-4Cl, respectively) were synthesized by coupling with dichlorinated IC (IC-2Cl). The composite DTPR-4Cl behaved a $\lambda _ { \mathrm { o n s e t } }$ of $9 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ with a narrowest $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ of $1 . 3 0 \mathrm { e V } ,$ powerfully indicating stronger electron-donating ability of DTPR block than IDTT and CPDT. Morphology study suggested that the PTB7-Th:CPDT-4Cl showed the compromised $d _ { \pi - \pi }$ of $3 . 6 9 \mathring \mathrm { A }$ crystal coherence length (CCL) of $1 3 . 4 \mathring \mathrm { A }$ and Flory-Huggins parameter $( \chi )$ of 0.95, indicating suitable phase separation and domain sizes to suppress charge recombination for high FF (Figure 4.14). Consequently, the PTB7-Th:CPDT-4Cl-based devices achieved a champion PCE of $1 2 . 1 5 \%$ with a FF of ${ \sim } 0 . 7 0 0$ , outperforming that of IDTT-4Cl- and DTPR-4Cl-based cells $( 7 . 7 0 \%$ and $1 0 . 7 5 \%$ , respectively). Furthermore, by swapping the position of oxygen atom and carbon atom (alkyl connected) in DTPR-4Cl as well as extended alkyl chains, the NIR FREA called ITOT-4Cl was designed [104]. Compared with DTPR-4Cl, ITOT-4Cl exhibited a narrower $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ of $1 . 2 8 \mathrm { e V }$ and deeper HOMO/LUMO energy levels $( - 5 . 4 9 \mathrm { e V } / - 3 . 9 0 \mathrm { e V } )$ The OSCs choosing PBDB-T as donor displayed a PCE of $1 2 . 5 0 \%$ (Table 4.5). In order to further improve the performance of ITOT-4Cl-based device, the F-Br with strong crystalline was added into the binary active layer. Surprisingly, the additive of $\mathrm { F - B r }$ not significantly affected the CCL of PBDB-T:ITOT-4Cl-based blend $( 2 2 . 1 \mathring { \mathrm { A } }$ before and $2 2 . 4 \mathring \mathrm { A }$ after), indicating the preservation of order molecular packing. Consequently, the derived ternary OSCs with $4 0 \mathrm { w t } \%$ F-Br achieved enhanced $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 0 \mathrm { V } _ { : }$ $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 4 . 4 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and FF of 0.733, contributing to a record PCE of $1 4 . 2 9 \%$ among oxygen heterocycle containing NFAs-based devices.

Obviously, several strategies above such as extending the conjugation length of the D core and heteroatom substitution can effectively narrow $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ for more photons harvest, thus a satisfactory device performance. Nevertheless, unlimited horizontal conjugation extension undoubtedly poses a huge challenge to molecule synthesis and its solubility. Similarly, obtaining a heteroatom-substituted monomer often requires complicated steps. In this case, vertical expansion of the conjugate structure has become an effective alternative, and two-dimensional (2D)-conjugated side chain strategy was applied into FREA design. For example, Zhan and coworkers [105] introduced benzo[1,2-b:4,5-b']dithieno[3,2-b]thiophene (BDTT) building block as the central core, and two isomeric FREAs (FNIC1 and FNIC2, the structures shown in Figure 4.12) were developed to explore the effects of acceptors' isomerization on photoelectric properties. Both FREAs exhibited similar energy levels and broad absorption ranging from 600 to $9 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . A better-defined bilayer interpenetrated structure can be observed in PTB7-Th:FNIC2 with excellent vertical phase segregation for reduced bimolecular recombination. As a result, the PTB7-Th:FNIC2-based blend showed a $\mu _ { \mathrm { e } }$ of $1 . 4 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ $6 0 \%$ higher than that of PTB7-Th:FNIC1-based one. The as-cast OSCs fabricated with PTB7-Th:FNIC2 yielded a higher PCE of $1 3 . 0 0 \%$ with a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 3 . 9 3 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and FF of 0.734 than FNIC1-based device $( 1 0 . 3 0 \% )$ (Table 4.5). The corresponding PTB7-Th:FNIC2-based ST-OSCs achieved PCEs varying from $9 . 5 1 \%$ to $1 1 . 6 0 \%$ (AVTs from $2 0 . 3 \%$ to $1 3 . 6 \%$ , outperforming PTB7-Th:FNIC1-based counterparts.

# 4.3.3.2Spacer Unit Effects

FREAs generally feature high charge carrier mobility due to reduced reorganization energy induced by their rigid fused-ring-conjugated backbone. Besides, their energy levels and absorption can be fine-tuned via delicate molecular engineering. The modulation on fused-ring cores is one of the most common methods to develop diverse molecules, thus screening best-performing FREAs. However, modifying fused core including their core sizes and the increase or decrease of chemical groups also bring some defects such as complicated synthesis and difficult purification.

As thus, Zhan and coworkers [11o] firstly designed and synthesized a novel SMA named DC-IDT2T (the structure shown in Figure 4.15) by inserting thiophene between IDT core and end group ( $\overbar { \boldsymbol { \pi } }$ -bridge). The DC-IDT2T exhibits a strong absorption at $5 5 0 \mathrm { - } 7 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ with a medium $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ of $1 . 5 5 \mathrm { e V . }$ When blending with PBDTTT-C-T, the large difference $( 1 . 2 6 \mathrm { e V } )$ between DC-IDT2T's LUMO and PBDTTT-C-T's HOMO provides their corresponding device a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 0 \mathrm { V } .$ Disappointingly, the as-cast PBDTTT-C-T:DC-IDT2T-based OSCs only achieved a low PCE of $3 . 9 3 \%$ (Table 4.6). This terrible performance can be mainly attributed to low $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $8 . 3 3 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ caused by almost overlapping absorption of donor and acceptor. However, this work demonstrates $\pi$ -bridge is a potential strategy to develop novel acceptors. After that, the same group replaced thiophene $\pi$ -bridge with furan to generate DC-IDT2F [113]. The introduced furan weakened the electron-donating capability of core, leading to a $\mu _ { \mathrm { e } }$ of $4 . 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ in PBDTTT-C-T:DC-IDT2F-based blend $\left( 1 . 5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } \thinspace \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \thinspace \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 } \right.$ for PBDTTT-C-T:DC-IDT2T) for decreased $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ , thus a lower

PCE of $3 . 0 8 \%$ for its corresponding OsCs. Furthermore, Huang and coworkers continue to optimize molecular structure by adding nitrogen atom into thiophene bridge for the design of IDT-Tz [111]. The composite IDT-Tz shows a $\lambda _ { \mathrm { o n s e t } }$ of $8 0 8 \mathrm { n m }$ (c. 8nm red-shifted than DC-IDT2T [also called IDT-T]), corresponding to a narrower $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ of $1 . 5 3 \mathrm { e V . }$ The selected donor PTB7-Th has a complementary absorption with IDT-Tz, promoting the light harvest for high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ . In addition, the intramolecular nitrogen-sulfur (N-S) non-covalent interaction between the nitrogen atom of thiazole and the sulfur atom of IDT core can lock conformation, which improves the rigidity and planarity of the backbone for efficient charge transport. As a result, the device based on PTB7-Th:IDT-Tz delivered a PCE of $8 . 5 2 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 8 \mathrm { V } ,$ an enhanced $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 3 . 6 7 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and a FF of 0.708, much higher than that of PTB7-Th:IDT-T-based counterparts $( 4 . 0 8 \% )$

Side chain is widely accepted can manipulate the solubility and intermolecular aggregation behavior, and rational side chain modification can induce the formation of better blend morphology for high PCE. As thus, side chain engineering was conducted into thiophene bridge of DC-IDT2T (also called IEIC1 there), and three SMAs were synthesized by introducing $n$ -butyl (IEIC2), n-hexyl (IEIC3), and 2-ethyl-hexyl (IEIC), respectively (the structures shown in Figure 4.15) [112]. All three acceptors exhibited almost similar energy levels and absorption. However, due to the steric hindrance, different alkyl chain leads to diverse morphologies. The resonant soft

X-ray scattering (R-SoXS) study revealed that the mode domain size of corresponding blends has a parabolic trend accompanied the carbon numbers of alkyl side chains from 0 to 8. And the PTB7-Th:IEIC3 exhibited the smallest domain size with $1 8 \mathrm { n m }$ close to the exciton diffusion length (c. $1 0 \mathrm { n m } ,$ in organic materials, contributed to the high $\mu _ { \mathrm { e } }$ of $6 . 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } \thinspace \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ . The derived PTB7-Th:IEIC3-based OSCs afforded a champion PCE of $7 . 4 \%$ with a highest $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 2 . 8 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , outperforming the other three ones $( 3 . 9 \substack { - 6 . 0 \% } )$

On the basis of IEIC, Hou and coworkers [114] inserted oxygen atoms in the 2-ethylhexyl branch, and the star $\pi$ -bridged IEICO-4F was developed end capping with IC-2F (Figure 4.15). The O-S non-covalent interaction endows IEICO-4F good co-planarity and reduced reorganization energy, thus an ultra-narrow $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ of $1 . 2 4 \mathrm { e V }$ (the film absorption approaching $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { n m } ,$ for enhanced ICT effect. The clear phase separation can be observed in PBDTTT-EFT:IEICO-4F-based blend film with a RMS of $1 . 2 2 \mathrm { n m }$ . Consequently, an impressively high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 2 . 8 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 7 4 \mathrm { V }$ and a FF of 0.594 were obtained, contributed to a PCE of $1 0 . 0 0 \%$ for PBDTTT-EFT:IEICO-4F-based OSCs (Table 4.6). Moreover, benefiting from the donor evolvement and innovative device processes, the PCE of IEICO-4F-based binary OSCs has already been upgraded to $1 2 . 8 0 \%$ with a surprising $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 7 . 3 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ [127]. The stunning $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ also attracted us to adding IEICO-4F into binary system as a third component for highly-efficient ternary OsCs fabrication. Then utilizing sulfur to replace oxygen atoms, they further designed and synthesized IEICS-4F [115]. The IEICS-4F showed 0.11eV wider $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ than IEICO-4F and slightly upshifted HOMO/LUMO energy levels of $- 5 . 4 3 \mathrm { e V } / \mathrm { - } 4 . 0 8 \mathrm { e V } .$ To avoid spectral overlap, the PTB7-Th was selected as a matching donor. Morphological study revealed that sufficiently small domain size in PTB7-Th:IEICS-4F-based blend film induces the formation of highly crystalline domain, and this "near-optimum" morphology is beneficial to charge generation and minimized charge recombination. Besides, the preferential face-on orientation with high crystallinity of PTB7-Th:IEICS-4F boosts the charge transport. As a result, the PTB7-Th:IEICS-4F-based binary device displayed a PCE of $1 0 . 3 0 \%$ with enhanced FF of 0.670 (Table 4.6). The high AVT in visible range of IEICS-4F also contributed to the PCEs of $7 . 5 0 \%$ and $1 0 . 5 0 \%$ for binary ( $3 5 \%$ AVT in $3 7 0 { - } 7 4 0 \mathrm { n m }$ and tandem (AVT, $2 0 \%$ ) ST-OSCs, respectively (Figure 4.16a).

It can be found that several SMAs mentioned above showed the NIR absorption and high AVT in visible range, which foresees its stupendous application potential in ST-OSCs and as rear cell in tandem OSCs. However, a dilemma also should be noted that the UV-vis-NIR was utilized to harvest more photons for high device performance, which simultaneously results in the reduced device transparency. Therefore, novel SMA was further explored to balance the properties and transparency, and the ATT-2 (Figure 4.15) with low $E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { \mathrm { \ o p t } }$ of $1 . 3 2 \mathrm { e V }$ was designed by introducing ester-substituted thieno[3,4-b]thiophene $\pi$ -bridge [116]. The composite ATT-2 displays a strong absorption at $6 0 0 { - } 8 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , which well preserves a large part of the visible area. Combining with PTB7-Th, the optimal $2 \%$ CN treated OSCs afforded a
