The stability and cost issues are also important for commercial application of the OSCs. In the reduction of synthesis cost of the A-DA'D-A type SMAs, one way is the design and synthesis of molecules with more simple structure. Using the simple thiophene unit to replace the alkylated thieno[3,2-b]thiophene unit is the most intuitive approach to decrease the material cost of A-DA'D-A type molecules. Zou and coworkers reported six-membered-fused A-DA'D-A SMA Y21 by unidirectional replacement strategy to modify the $\mathrm { D A ^ { \prime } D }$ core [163]. The six-membered-fused molecule Y21 can also determinate a broad absorption ranges with an optical gap of $1 . 3 5 \mathrm { e V } .$ The OSCs based on Y21 blended with polymer donor PM6 exhibited a high PCE of $1 5 . 4 \%$ with a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 4 . 9 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 3 \mathrm { V } _ { ; }$ and a FF of 0.744. Another six-membered-fused asymmetric SMA Y22 can achieve the same result [164].

# 4.4.2 BT-Based A-DA'D-A SMAs

The breakthrough in the efficiency of SMA-based OSCs emerged in early 2019. Zou and coworkers introduced the benzo[c][1,2,5]thiadiazole (BT) unit in the middle of the central fused core, to form a new BT-core-based fused unit dithienothiophen[3,2-b]-pyrrolobenzothiadiazole (TPBT), then, a star SMA molecule Y6 based on the TPBT central unit was designed (Figure 4.24) [109]. The Y6 molecules stimulate the progress of OSCs with remarkable PCE of $1 5 { - } 1 8 \%$ , pushing the OSCs filed to new phase [145, 183]. The single crystal of the Y6 molecule confirm that there are two types of $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking between adjacent molecules, including the end group interactions and the central fused core interactions, as seen from the main view and side view of Figure 4.23 [184]. In addition, the specific molecular geometry (curve shape) of A-DA'D-A-type SMA Y6 could from a twisted 1D transport channel and slipped packing motif. Due to the dimerization in a crystal unit cell, the Y6 could form multi-transport channel, which is quite different from the ITIC-like molecules, resulting in a multi-dimension interpenetrating network and transport channels.

In recent years, significant efforts have been modified the molecular structure of Y6 to explore their photovoltaic applications and demonstrated their excellent morphological features, efficient charge generation, low voltage loss, and decent transport dynamic. The main optimizations of Y6 were focused on its end groups, central donor units, and side chains.

![](images/e47b9d7a6f54127d919e361e4905236b7befb31c1d1fee57db7d90496f509114.jpg)  
Figure 4.23 The single-crystal structure of Y6. Source: Zhu et al. [184]/Reproduced with permission of John Wiley & Sons.

The end groups play a vital role in determining their absorption, energy levels, and molecular packings, thus affecting the photovoltaic performance. The wide range of end groups developed for A-D-A-type SMAs provides useful guidelines for choosing the proper ending groups in the A-DA'D-A type SMAs. The current high-performance end groups applied in the A-DA'D-A type SMAs are featured with INCN and their similar structures. Since Zou and coworkers reported a SMA Y5 (composed of a DA'D core identical to Y6 and two INCN end groups, Figure 4.24) to achieve an impressive efficiency when blended with a common donor PBDB-T, the A-DA'D-A-type SMAs with different end groups (INCN derivatives) have sprung up for application in OSCs [165]. For instance, Hou and coworkers synthesized BTP-4Cl (Figure 4.24) containing the central core of Y6 and chlorinated INCN terminal that had a red-shifted absorption (c. $2 0 \mathrm { n m } ,$ and downshifted LUMO energy level (c. $1 0 0 \mathrm { m e V } )$ in comparison with Y6 [166]. The device based on PM6:BTP-4Cl showed a higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ than Y6-based device, which was attributed to the lower non-radiative recombination loss. The simultaneously improved $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ led to an improved PCE of $1 6 . 5 \%$ . He and coworkers introduced bromination to further promote the halogen-substituted in Y-series molecules (Figure 4.24). However, BTIC-4Br exhibited a poor solubility in chloroform solution. Thus, BTIC-2Br-m was designed and synthesized by modulating the numbers of bromine substituents, and the device-based PM6:BTIC-2Br-m showed a high PCE of $1 6 . 1 1 \%$ [167]. In parallel, the similar SMA with mono-brominated INCN as the end groups, namely TPT10 (Figure 4.24), was reported by Li and cowokers. In order to match the energy levels of TPT10, they developed a new polymer donor PTQ11 [168]. The devices-based PTQ11:TPT10 films showed a high PCE of $1 6 . 3 2 \%$ in spite of a zero energy offset between HOMO energy levels of donor and acceptor, which was important in understanding the charge transfer process. Beside the electron-withdrawing halogen group, Chen and coworkers introduced the electron-donating methyl group on the INCN terminal and synthesized BTP-M (Figure 4.24) with higher energy levels and blue-shifted absorption [169]. By blending with the common donor

![](images/df0ab79db9ea8109373d9c5bf8e11b981b1e248160b818e3f99d63d3542ee544.jpg)  
Figure 4.24Chemical structures of BT/Qx/Bse-based A-DA'D-A-type acceptors-. Source: J. Yuan and Y. Zou.

PBDB-T, the devices showed a low $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and FF, and then a low PCE of $4 . 2 6 \%$ , though the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ is as high as $0 . 9 7 5 \mathrm { V } .$ One possible reason leading to the low PCE is the photo-induced hole transfer from BTP-M to PM6 is insufficient, which is proved by the photoluminescence quenching experiments. However, BTP-M could form an alloy-like composite with Y6, which tunes the energy-level alignment and optimizes the blend morphology, and finally boosting the PCE to $1 7 . 0 3 \%$ for ternary OSCs based on PM6:Y6:BTP-M. In addition, Zou and coworkers employed a thienyl-fused indanone as end groups on the central core of Y6 and synthesized a new A-DA'D-A

SMA Y10 (Figure 4.24) [170]. Compared with Y6, Y10 presented an obviously elevated LUMO energy levels because of the introduction of the more easily polarized thiophene unit in terminal group, showing great potential in enhancement of $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ Meanwhile, Min and coworkers reported a SMA, called BTTr-2Cl by introducing the chlorine atom onto the thienyl-fused indanone terminal group (Figure 4.24) [171]. When combined with PM6, a decent PCE of $1 3 . 8 \%$ with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 9 \mathrm { V }$ was demonstrated. Beside these, conjugated extension is another strategy for modifying the terminal group. Chen and coworkers reported two novel terminals by extending the conjugation of INCN with one more thiophene or brominated thiophene, and two SMAs BTTPC and BTTPC-Br were synthesized (Figure 4.24) [172]. BTTPC and BTTPC-Br exhibited small HOMO energy offsets in combination with PBDB-T and thus showed a faster hole transfer feature than Y5. As a result, high PCEs of $1 4 . 5 1 \%$ and $1 5 . 2 2 \%$ were achieved for BTTPC and BTTPC-Br-based devices, greater than that of Y5-based device. Tandem OSCs can boost efficiency by using a wider range of the solar spectrum. However, one main limitation for the development of tandem OSCs comes from the lack of efficient NIR absorption materials for rear cells. To settle this issue, Li and coworkers designed a new low bandgap A-DA'D-A-type SMA BTPV-4F by inserting another ethylene double bond between the central core of Y6 (Figure 4.24) [173]. BTPV-4F showed a significantly red-shifted absorption to $1 0 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ (the optical bandgap near $1 . 2 1 \mathrm { e V } ,$ . As a result, the OSCs based on PTB7-Th:BTPV-4F demonstrated a PCE of $1 3 . 4 \%$ with a superior $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 8 . 9 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ .

Generally, the molecular packing and interaction of SMAs are important factors in determining the morphology of the blend film, which are closely related to their molecular structures. Hence, controlling the morphology of active layer is important to obtain high-efficiency OsCs. Understanding the molecular conjugated length and isomerization of fused central core are critical in controlling the electronic structure and aggregation behavior of SMAs. Regarding the backbone modification, developing the SMAs with different conjugated length or isomerization of fused central core has shown great potential in achieving different molecular packing, energy levels, dipole moment, and hence the device performance. For example, Zhang and coworkers reported a new SMA BP-4F by incorporating one thiophene into dithiophen[3,2-b]-pyrrolobenzothiadiazole or removing one thiophene from dithienothiophen[3,2-b]-pyrrolobenzothiadiazole (Figure 4.24). The result showed that the six-membered fused electron-deficient-core-based acceptor BP-4F exhibited relatively blue-shifted spectra in comparison to Y6 [174]. As a result, a PCE of $1 4 . 6 2 \%$ was obtained by using BP-4F in combination with PBDB-T-2Cl as the donor polymer with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 8 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 1 . 7 3 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF of $7 6 . 5 \%$ . Gao et al. systematically investigated the conformation effects of Y6 and its derivatives, and two SMAs (BP5T-4F and ABP4T-4F) with their end groups orientating toward different directions were designed and synthesized (Figure 4.24) [175]. Among them, ABP4T-4F is an asymmetric isomer from Y6 derivatives (with optimized side chains) by replacing two thieno[3,2 $^ { \cdot b }$ Ithiophene with one thiophene and one dithieno[3 ${ \therefore } 2 { \cdot } b { : } 2 ^ { \prime } { , } 3 ^ { \prime }$ d]thiophene. BP5T-4F extends the conjugated length of Y6 derivatives by fusing one more thiophene onto one side of the central core.

The result showed that extending conjugated length of core does not significantly affect the absorption; however, the conformation changes have big impact on aggregation-induced red-shift of absorption spectrum. In addition, asymmetric ABP4T-4F and BP5T-4F can significantly suppress non-radiative recombination. Therefore, the device based on PM6:ABP4T-4F exhibited a PCE of $1 5 . 2 \%$ with $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 2 \mathrm { V } ,$ and the PM6:BP5T-4F-based device showed a PCE of $1 6 . 7 \%$ with $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 8 \mathrm { V } .$

In previous reports, alkoxy chains have a significant influence on the electronic and morphological properties of organic-conjugated molecules. It is due to the electron-donating effect of alkoxy groups, meanwhile the intramolecular conformational locking effect in some molecular structures. Along these lines, Yan and coworkers introduced alkoxy side chains on the $\beta$ position of the central core and synthesized two new Y6 derivatives (Y6-1O and Y6-2O, Figure 4.24) [176]. However, Y6-2O exhibited a poor solubility $( 1 . 5 \mathrm { m g } \mathrm { m l ^ { - 1 } }$ in chloroform) and excessive aggregation property (due to the conformational locking effect of alkoxy group), resulting in low efficiency $\mathrm { ( P C E } = 6 . 6 \% $ . Interestingly, from the absorption spectra of Y6-1O and Y6-2O, all of them showed the relatively blue-shifted spectra in comparison to that of Y6. Compared to PM6:Y6-based devices, although PM6:Y6-1O exhibit a slightly lower $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 3 . 2 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , they can achieve an enhancement in $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 9 \mathrm { V }$ and FF of $7 8 . 3 \%$ , resulting in a high PCE of $1 6 . 1 \%$ Substitution of chalcogen species from sulfur to selenium in the $\pi$ -conjugation backbones can advantageously adjust both intrinsic optoelectronic properties and intermolecular interactions of the molecules. This is because the more polarizable selenium atom could produce stronger orbital overlap between selenium and the $\pi$ -conjugation system, leading to a higher quinoid resonance character. Therefore, a new selenium-substituted Y6 derivative (CH1007, Figure 4.24) was reported by Lin et al. [177]. From the crystallographic study, due to the $\mathtt { S - N }$ interaction between BT moieties, both of two molecules possess very unique central core interaction, which facilitates further development of molecular packing to construct 3D networks. However, compared with Y6, CH1007 exhibited a red-shifted absorption ( $\mathsf { c . 6 0 n m }$ resulting in an extraordinary of $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 7 . 4 8 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and a high PCE of $1 7 . 0 8 \%$ in $\mathrm { P M 6 { : } C H 1 0 0 7 { : } P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ ternary OSCs.

Side chains, as a solubilizing group, are the most widely used in OsCs. Carefully modulation of the side chains is the key to balance the processability, charge transport, and the aggregation behavior of blend films. In order to understand the influence of alkyl chains on the electronic and photonic properties of Y6, Yan and coworkers designed a series of Y6 derivatives, N3, N4, and N-C11 with alkyl chains of different size and branching position (Figure 4.24) [178]. N-C11, which is designed by swapping the position of $n$ -undecyl and 2-ethylhexyl alkyl chains on the Y6 molecule, exhibited a reduced PCE of $1 2 . 9 1 \%$ due to the decreased solubility and large over aggregated domains in the blend film. On the contrary, the other two acceptors N3 and N4 with 3rd-and 4th-position-branched alkyl chains showed a good solubility owing to the branched alkyl chains produced a twisted molecular backbone. Nonetheless, N4 exhibited excessive solubility, which also introduced undesirable large domains, lower domain purity, and edge-on orientation. Hou and coworkers adopted a simple alkyl chain modification strategy that changed 2-ethylhexyl (2-EH) on Y6 to 2-butyloctyl (2-BO) [179]. The obtained SMA, BTP-4F-12 (Figure 4.24), exhibited an enhanced crystallinity and electron mobility due to a better lamellar stacking in in-plane direction. More important, the enhanced solubility of BTP-4F-12 rendered a high PCE of $1 6 . 1 \%$ and $1 4 . 4 \%$ (active area of $1 . 0 7 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ ) for spin coating and blade coating, respectively, by using T1 as the donor and low-toxic tetrahydrofuran (THF) as the solvent. Huang and coworkers developed a SMA DTY6 with long-branched alkyl chains (2-decyltetradecyl, 2-DT) on the nitrogen atoms of the pyrrole motif of Y6 (Figure 4.24) [180]. The steric hindrance effect of long-branched alkyl chain could improve the solubility and, meanwhile, suppress the molecule-excessive aggregation. As expected, DTY6-based film exhibited a suitable domain size and, thus, ensured efficient charge transport, leading to an impressive efficiency of $1 6 . 3 \%$ when blended with PM6. Encouragingly, PM6:DTY6 blend showed an ideal candidate for a large-area module device owing to their good processability in non-halogen solvent such as $o$ -xylene (o-XY), toluene (TL), and 1,2,4-trimethyl-benzene (TMB). For the devices based on PM6:DTY6, a PCE of $1 6 . 1 \%$ was achieved under ambient fabrication conditions, after which modules with an area of $1 8 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ were fabricated. The best module gave an outstanding PCE of $1 4 . 4 \%$ (certified $1 3 . 9 8 \%$ ) with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $5 . 1 1 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $3 . 8 9 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF of 0.725.

# 4.4.3 BSe- and Qx-Based OSCs

As mentioned above, introducing the electron-deficient segment in the fused D unit of A-D-A-type molecules plays a key role in improvement of the performance of the OsCs. It is owing to the electronegative fused-ring core in $\mathbf { A } \mathbf { - } \mathbf { D } \mathbf { A } ^ { \prime } \mathbf { D - } \mathbf { A }$ type SMAs prefers quinoid resonance structures, resulting in low bandgap while maintaining deep energy levels matched well with high-performance polymer donors. However, limited by the synthetic difficulty of Cadogan reductive cyclization reaction, the main optimization performed for current $\mathsf { A } ^ { \prime }$ unit in A-DA'D-A-type SMAs were focused on BT, BTA, quinoxaline $\left( \mathbf { Q x } \right)$ , and 2,1,3-benzoselenadiazole (BSe). Although all of them can be employed as an electron-deficient $\mathbf { A ^ { \prime } }$ core in the $\mathrm { D A ^ { \prime } D }$ fused rings, their synthetic methods as well as electronic properties are different. In order to eliminate trade-off between the achievable $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and charge generation under small energy offset, Zhu and coworkers developed two types of Qx-based A-DA'D-A SMAs AQx-1 and AQx-2 for OSCs (Figure 4.24) [181]. By replacing the BT unit of Y6 with Qx unit, the corresponding quinoid resonance effect into heteroarene core could decrease the reorganization energy deriving from reduced free $\sigma$ -bonds in the Qx-based SMAs, facilitating electron transport and intermolecular packing. The device based on the PBDB-TF (PM6):AQx-2 blend exhibited a PCE of $1 6 . 6 4 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 6 \mathrm { e V } ,$ $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 5 . 3 8 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and FF of 0.763. Due to the high Urbach energies (c $2 5 { \mathrm { - } } 5 0 \mathrm { m e V } )$ in reported $\mathbf { A } \mathbf { - } \mathbf { D } \mathbf { A } ^ { \prime } \mathbf { D - } \mathbf { A }$ type molecules, Lin and coworkers introduced a facile method of selenium substitution to reduce the Urbach energy of A-DA'D-A-type molecules. The molecule structure of selenium substitution SMA (Y6Se) is shown in Figure 4.24 [182]. Compared to the sulfur-containing analog Y6, Y6Se showed a lower Urbach energy, broader absorption, and higher electron mobility. As a result, the device based on as-cast D18:Y6Se showed a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 7 . 9 8 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 4 \mathrm { e V } ,$ and FF of 0.753, resulting in a high PCE of $1 7 . 7 \%$ (average PCE for eight devices: $1 7 . 5 \%$

# Electron-Donating Ladder-Type Heteroacenes for Photovoltaic Applications: From Polymer Donor Materials to Small-Molecule Acceptor Materials

Qisheng Tu, Yunlong Ma\*, and Qingdong Zheng\*

Chinese Academy of Sciences, Fujian Institute of Research on the Structure of Matter, State Key Laboratory of Structural Chemistry, 155 Yangqiao West Road, Fuzhou, 350002, P.R. China

# 5.1 Introduction

Solution-processed polymer solar cells (PsCs) have become one of the promising low-cost solar energy harvesting technologies with their rapidly grown power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) from around $1 \%$ to over $1 7 \%$ in the past two decades [1-3]. Bulk heterojunction (BHJ) active layers with p-type semiconducting polymers as electron donors and n-type semiconductors (fullerene derivatives or nonfullerene molecules) as electron acceptors play a key role in determining the PCEs of PSCs. In the early years of research on PSCs, fullerene derivatives (such as $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } ,$ were the dominant acceptors and most semiconducting polymers were designed to match the energy levels as well as the absorption profiles of the fullerene derivatives [2, 4]. Because the absorption bands of most fullerene derivatives locate at the short-wavelength region $( 3 0 0 - 6 0 0 \mathrm { n m } )$ , many low bandgap (LBG) polymers with enhanced light absorption bands in the long wavelength region have been developed by which the best PCE of the fullerene-based PSCs has exceeded $1 1 \%$ [5]. Nonetheless, to further improve the PCEs of single-junction PSCs based on the LBG polymers and the fullerene derivatives to far beyond $1 1 \%$ becomes impossible considering the trade-off between their short-circuit current density $( J _ { \mathrm { s c } } )$ and open-circuit voltage $( V _ { \mathrm { o c } } )$ values. Therefore, nonfullerene acceptors (NFAs) are emerging to replace the traditional fullerene derivatives. Unless otherwise stated, NFAs in the review refer to the small-molecule acceptor materials. In contrast with the traditional fullerene acceptors with intense absorption bands in the short-wavelength region, the absorption bands of NFAs can be tuned from the visible region to near-infrared (NIR) region [6]. To achieve complementary absorption, donor materials with relatively wide bandgaps are needed to achieve high-performance nonfullerene PSCs [7]. In the past two decades, most breakthroughs are related to the inventions of novel donor or acceptor materials. Take the donor materials as examples, the inventions of copolymers with thieno[3,4-b]thiophene and benzodithiophene (BDT) alternating units (PTB7-Th, PTB7) led to PSCs with PCEs over $1 0 \%$ and the inventions of terthiophene-based LBG copolymers afforded one of the highest PCEs of $1 1 . 7 \%$ among all the fullerene-based PSCs [4, 5]. Similarly, the invention of the benchmark acceptor-donor-acceptor (A-D-A) type NFA (ITIC), which used indacenodithieno[3,2-b]thiophene (IDTT) as the electron-rich core, yielded an initial PCE of $6 . 8 \%$ for the nonfullerene PSCs [8]. Using these IDTT-like fused-ring cores with various side chains, many other A-D-A type NFAs have been developed with excellent PCEs over $1 2 \%$ [9]. More recently, Zou and coworkers reported a series of outstanding NFAs (such as Y6 and Y11) with initial PCEs over $1 5 \%$ , which incorporated electron-deficient benzothiadiazole (or benzotriazole)-fused core into the NFAs to form the $\mathrm { \Delta A { - } D { - } A ^ { \prime } { - } D { - } A }$ type configuration [10, 11]. This material innovation scenario indicates the importance of both donor and acceptor materials in determining the photovoltaic properties of PSCs.

For both donor and acceptor materials, the design of novel electron-donating units is essential. Among many electron-donating units, ladder-type heteroacenes, which consist of several "linearly overlapping" aromatic or heterocyclic subunits linked by sharing endocyclic carbon-carbon $\mathrm { C } { = } \mathrm { C } ,$ double bonds, stand out as ideal candidates due to their salient features of good thermal, mechanical, and chemical stabilities [12]. Ladder-type heteroacenes have extended conjugated frameworks, which can elongate the effective $\pi$ conjugation length and facilitate the charge carrier mobility. At the same time, various electron-donating aromatic building blocks such as thiophene, benzene, pyrrole, cyclopentadienyl moieties can be incorporated into the ladder-type frameworks to afford heteroacenes with tunable properties [4]. Furthermore, solubilizing alkyl chains can be introduced to the ladder-type heteroacenes to endow the target donor or acceptor materials with good solution processability. Therefore, the research of ladder-type heteroacenes has greatly boosted the development of PSCs.

There have been some reviews on the BDT-based copolymers (such as PTB7-Th, PBDB-T, and PM6), which are the most-researched donor materials for both fullerene and nonfullerene PSCs in the past decade [13]. In this chapter, we will mainly summarize the recent developments of heteroacene-based polymer donor materials developed in our research group in the past decade. However, some important breakthroughs in the heteroacene-based materials will also be covered to let readers have a whole story on the development of ladder-type heteroacene-based materials for PSCs. This chapter is organized as follows: in Section 5.2, we focus on discussing the structures and photovoltaic performances of new donor-acceptor (D-A) copolymers based on the various ladder-type heteroacenes. The ladder-type heteroacenes will be classified according to their ring numbers including pentacyclic, hexacyclic, heptacyclic, nonacyclic etc. In Section 5.3, we focus on discussing the structures and photovoltaic performances of new A-D-A type NFAs which were synthesized by using ladder-type heteroacenes as the central cores. Finally, we conclude with a summary of the challenges and future molecular design strategies for the heteroacene-based semiconducting materials in the PSC application.

# 5.2 D-A Copolymers Based on Ladder-Type Heteroacenes

To achieve an enhanced light-harvesting ability (LBG) as well as a large $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of a PSC device, one of the most potent approaches is to design alternating D-A copolymers, where the electron donor unit can be used to provide a deep-lying highest occupied molecular orbital (HOmO) level and the electron-deficient unit can be used to tune the electronic bandgap of the polymers [14]. For the D-A type copolymers based on heteroacenes, their bandgaps, energy levels, carrier mobilities etc. can be finely tuned by using heteroacenes with different molecular structures. At the same time, the selection of acceptor units as well as $\pi$ -bridges can also affect their optical, electrochemical, charge transport, and photovoltaic properties. Here, we mainly focus on the effect of the structure of the heteroacene core on the photovoltaic performance of the resulting D-A copolymers.

# 5.2.1 Pentacyclic and Hexacyclic Heteroacenes-Based D-A Copolymers

In 2010, Zheng et al. synthesized a D-A copolymer (PIFTBT6, Figure 5.1) based on the pentacyclic indenofluorene unit which contains two "linearly overlapping" fluorene segments [15]. As summarized in Table 5.1, despite a PCE of $0 . 9 7 \%$ for the PSCs based on PIFTBT6, a rather high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 8 \mathrm { V }$ was achieved due to the relatively deep-lying HOMO energy level of PIFTBT6. Subsequently, our group further used branched 2-ethylhexyl side chains to replace the hexyl side chains on the indenofluorene backbone thus affording an optimized D-A copolymer (PIFTBT8)

with an enhanced charge carrier mobility [16]. Therefore, the resulting PSCs based on PIFTBT8 showed a much higher PCE of $5 . 0 5 \%$ with a further increased $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 0 4 \mathrm { V } .$ These fluorene-derived units showed weak electron-donating nature thereby leading to the D-A copolymers with deep-lying HOMO energy levels. Compared to benzene, thiophene is more electron-rich; therefore, it can raise the HOmO energy level of the resulting material thereby leading to a reduced bandgap.

Replacing the phenyl groups at the ends of indenofluorene with thienyl groups affords another excellent example of ladder-type pentacyclic heteroacene, i.e. indacenodithiophene (IDT). The relatively strong electron-donating ability of IDT makes itself a good candidate for high-performance D-A copolymers with reduced bandgaps. Ting and coworkers synthesized an IDT-based D-A copolymer (a-PTPTBT) using benzothiadiazole as the acceptor unit. The copolymer (a-PTPTBT) showed an intriguing PCE of $6 . 4 1 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 5 \mathrm { V }$ and a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 1 . 2 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ [17]. Later, many IDT-based D-A copolymers were designed and synthesized by using different acceptor units for the copolymerization [4]. Nonetheless, none of these copolymers gave PCEs over $8 . 0 0 \%$ . In 2017, our group designed and synthesized an IDT-based copolymer (PIDTBTO-TT) using alkoxylated benzothiadiazole as the acceptor unit and thieno[3,2-b]thiophene as the $\pi$ -bridge [18]. With its increased conjugated backbone planarity, PIDTBTO-TT showed a reduced $\pi { - } \pi$ packing distance which is beneficial for more efficient charge transport. Thus, the single-junction device based on PIDTBTO-TT $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ exhibited a high PCE of $8 . 1 5 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 1 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 4 . 7 7 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF of $6 0 . 9 \%$ . When PIDTBTO$\mathrm { T T } { \mathrm { : P C } } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and PTB7-Th: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ were used as active layer materials in the bottom and top sub-cells in a tandem device, respectively, a high PCE of $1 1 . 1 5 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 7 0 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $9 . 6 8 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF of $6 7 . 8 \%$ was achieved. The efficiencies of $8 . 1 5 \%$ and $1 1 . 1 5 \%$ were the highest for the single-junction and tandem PSCs based on IDT-containing copolymers at that time, respectively. Substitution of the central phenyl group in IDT with naphthyl group leads to a hexacyclic dithienonaphthalene (DTN) building block, which contains two isomers, i.e. linear- and angular-shaped

DTNs. Using the linear- or angular-shaped DTN as a donor segment, and a benzothiadiazole derivative as an acceptor moiety, two isomeric DTN-based copolymers (PDTNTBT and PaDTNBTO) were synthesized in our group for the first time [19, 20]. The copolymer based on the angular-shape DTN (PaDTNBTO) showed a deeper-lying HOMO energy level and an improved charge transport compared to its linear-shaped analog. Thus, the PSCs based on PaDTNBTO: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ exhibited a higher PCE of $6 . 4 4 \%$ with a larger $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 2 \mathrm { V }$ in comparison with those of the PDTNTBT-based devices $( \mathrm { P C E } = 4 . 7 8 \%$ $V _ { \mathrm { o c } } = 0 . 8 6 \ : \mathrm { V } ,$ . These results suggested that the structural isomerization on the backbone of heteroacene plays a vital role on the energy levels, bandgaps, charge mobilities, and photovoltaic performances of the resulting copolymers.

It should be noted that all the above-mentioned D-A copolymers are of an amorphous nature due to four bulky substituents flanked on their $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized bridging atoms, which will restrain a closely intermolecular packing. Therefore, it was expected that the removal of one $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized bridging atom in the conjugated backbone of the donor unit would increase the molecular packing order (or crystallinity) of the resulting D-A copolymer. In 2016, for the first time, Wang et al. reported an indenothiophene-based copolymer (PITFBT) with a semicrystalline feature [22]. Due to the weak electron-donating ability of indenothiophene, PIFTBT exhibited a relatively deep-lying HOMO energy level of $- 5 . 5 0 \mathrm { e V }$ which is beneficial for achieving a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ for the resulting PSCs. More importantly, with the semicrystalline feature of PITFBT, the PITFBT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ blend with a proper solvent additive exhibited a widely distributed nanofibrillar structure which is favorable for efficient charge transport. As a result, the PITFBT-based PSC showed an impressive PCE of $9 . 1 4 \%$ with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 0 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 5 . 3 6 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF of $6 5 . 9 \%$

Dithienocarbazole (DTC), which is made by fusing two thiophenes on both sides of carbazole, was first developed by Geng and coworkers [21]. The copolymer of P(IID-DTC) was synthesized by the polymerization reaction between DTC and an isoindigo derivative [21]. P(IID-DTC) showed a low optical bandgap of $1 . 6 1 \mathrm { e V }$ with an up-shifted HOMO energy level of $- 5 . 2 2 \mathrm { e V } .$ The best-performance PSC based on $\mathrm { P ( I I D  – D T C ) { : } P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ blend exhibited an outstanding PCE of $8 . 2 0 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 7 8 \mathrm { V }$ and a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 5 . 2 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$

# 5.2.2 Heptacene-Based D-A Copolymers

Ladder-type tetra- $p$ -phenylene containing three "linearly overlapping" fluorene segments was used as a promising donor unit in high-performance D-A copolymers due to the extended $\pi$ -conjugation length. Compared to fluorene or indenofluorene, the ladder-type tetra- $p$ -phenylene derivative could broaden and strengthen the absorption band, thus resulting in an enhanced light-harvesting ability. Meanwhile, the relatively weak electron-donating feature of the ladder-type tetra. $p$ -phenylene building block will lead to deep-lying HOMO energy levels of the resulting copolymers. In 2010, Zheng et al. first reported a D-A copolymer (P3FTBT6 in Figure 5.2) based on the ladder-type tetra $p$ -phenylene, which was also the first example of ladder-type heptacene-based D-A copolymers [15]. P3FTBT6 displayed a relatively deep-lying HOMO energy level of $- 5 . 4 5 \mathrm { e V }$ (Table 5.2). Compared to the fluorene-based copolymer with the same acceptor segment, P3FTBT6 exhibited an enhanced and red-shifted absorption. When fabricated in ambient environment, the P3FTBT6 $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ -based device showed a PCE of $4 . 5 0 \%$ with a large $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 0 4 \mathrm { V } .$ These exciting results reveal that the ladder-type fused arenes with extended conjugation are promising building blocks for constructing high-performance D-A copolymers. Nonetheless, the six out-of-plane side chains on the three $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized bridging atoms in the conjugated backbone limit their charge carrier mobilities when blended with the fullerene derivatives. Subsequently, the central $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized bridging atom on the ladder-type tetra $p$ -phenylene segment was substituted with nitrogen in our group to afford a new heteroheptacene, i.e. diindenocarbazole (DIC). Using the DIC and a dithienylbenzothiadiazole derivative as the donor and acceptor moieties, respectively, a wide-bandgap copolymer (PC2)

with a deep-lying HOMO energy level of $- 5 . 4 3 \mathrm { e V }$ was synthesized. PSC based on PC2 presented an intriguing PCE of $7 . 2 6 \%$ with a large $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 3 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 4 . 2 2 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF of $5 4 . 7 \%$ [23]. Further side-chain engineering on the DIC core led to copolymer PC1BT6, which showed a slightly enhanced PCE of $7 . 3 4 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 5 \mathrm { V }$ and a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 4 . 0 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ [24]. By substituting the two phenyl ending groups in DIC core with thienyl units, Zheng et al. also developed a more electron-rich building block of heteroheptacene (DTCC), which could be used to synthesize LBG copolymers [33]. These heteroheptacene-based copolymers delivered bathochromic absorption bands and moderate charge carrier mobilities, which are in favor of fabricating efficient PsCs. At the same time, Cheng and coworkers also reported a DTCC-based copolymer of PCDCTBT which showed a decent PCE of $3 . 7 0 \%$ [25]. Furthermore, they developed a new heteroheptacene by replacing the nitrogen atom with the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized bridging atom in the central bridging atom to afford dithienocyclopentafluorene (DTCF) [25]. Through side-chain engineering in combination with device engineering, the DTCF-based copolymer (PFDCTBT-C8) showed an enhanced PCE of $7 . 0 0 \%$ [26]. When the other two $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized bridging carbon atoms of DTCC were replaced with silicon atoms in the PCDCTBT, the corresponding copolymer PDTSCBT exhibited an enhanced PCE of $5 . 2 0 \%$ in comparison with the PCE of $3 . 7 0 \%$ for PCDCTBT [27].

By replacing the central nitrogen atom in the DTCC with sulfur atom, a new ladder-type heteroheptacene building block, namely dithienocyclopentadibenzothiophene (DTCD), was reported by Zheng and coworkers [28]. The copolymer P2 based on DTCD and $2 { - } 2 ^ { \prime }$ -bithiophene afforded a decent PCE of $4 . 1 7 \%$ with a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of

$9 . 2 0 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 7 9 \mathrm { V } ,$ and a FF of $5 7 . 4 \%$ . To reduce the optical bandgap, electron-deficient benzothiadiazole derivative was utilized as an acceptor moiety to afford the D-A copolymer of PSBT which has a deeper-lying HOMO energy level of $- 5 . 4 0 \mathrm { e V }$ [29]. The optimal PSC based on $\mathrm { P S B T : P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ exhibited an increased PCE of $5 . 1 8 \%$ with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 4 \mathrm { V }$ in comparison to that of P2-based device. More recently, using the DTCD and a difluorobenzotriazole derivative as the electron-rich and electron-deficient moieties, respectively, our group further developed a D-A copolymer (PSS2) which presented a deep-lying HOMO energy level of $- 5 . 3 6 \mathrm { e V }$ and a wide optical bandgap of 2.01 eV [30]. When paired with a LBG NFA (EH-IDTBR), PSS2-based PSC afforded a PCE of $9 . 4 6 \%$ with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 0 3 \mathrm { V } ,$ $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 5 . 7 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF of $5 8 . 3 \%$ . It should be noted that the $9 . 4 6 \%$ PCE is the highest among all D-A copolymers based on these ladder-type heptacenes. In addition, after storage for 120 days, the optimal Pss2-based device exhibited good shelf-stability with a PCE of $9 . 0 3 \%$ , which is $9 5 \%$ of its initial value.

At the same time, Cheng and coworkers developed a heptacyclic benzodi (cyclopentadithiophene) (BDCPDT) building block, in which the thiophene is fastened on the two ends of BDT with $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized bridging atoms [31]. Using thieno[3,4-c]pyrrole-4,6-dione as the acceptor unit, the BDCPDT-based copolymer (PBDCPDT-TPD) afforded a decent PCE of $6 . 6 0 \%$ . Subsequently, Jen and coworkers extended the conjugation length of IDT unit with two additional thiophene rings on both ends of IDT to achieve a new heptacyclic heteroacene (IDTT), which later becomes a star building block for high-performance A-D-A NFAs [32]. A new D-A copolymer (PIDTT-DFBT) was synthesized by the copolymerization between the distannylated IDTT and a dibrominated benzothiadiazole derivative. Without any post-treatments, the PSC based on PIDTT-DFBT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ showed an intriguing PCE of $7 . 0 3 \%$ with a large $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 5 \mathrm { V } .$

# 5.2.3  D-A Copolymers Based on Heteroacenes with Nine or More Fused Rings

To further extend the conjugated length, Cheng et al. developed a ladder-type nonacyclic thienyl-phenylene-thienylene-phenylene-thienyl (TPTPT) building block which consists of alternating interfused benzene and thiophene segments [34]. The resulting D-A copolymer (PTPTPTBT in Figure 5.3) showed a relatively high hole mobility of $5 . 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ with HOMO/LUMO energy levels of $- 5 . 2 4 / - 3 . 3 8 \mathrm { e V } ,$ and an optical bandgap of $1 . 7 3 \mathrm { e V }$ (Table 5.3). The inverted PSC based on PTPTPTBT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ delivered a PCE of $5 . 9 0 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 7 6 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 2 . 1 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF of $6 4 . 0 \%$ . An undecyclic indacenodithiophenebiscyclopentadithiophene (IDTCPDT) with 11 aromatic rings in the conjugated backbone was developed by Jen and coworkers [35]. The IDTCPDT-based copolymer (PIDTCPDT-DFBT) showed a bathochromically shifted absorption band in comparison with the non-fused counterpart. It should be noted that PIDTCPDT-DFBT still exhibited suitable solubility despite its highly extended and rigid backbone. The best-performance field-effect transistor (FET) based on PIDTCPDT-DFBT showed an improved hole mobility of $2 . 4 \times 1 0 ^ { - 2 } \thinspace { \mathrm { c m } } ^ { 2 } \thinspace { \mathrm { V } } ^ { - 1 } \thinspace { \mathrm { s } } ^ { - 1 }$ compared to that based on the non-fused counterpart $( 1 . 6 \times 1 0 ^ { - 2 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 } )$ . When blended with $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ , the corresponding PSC showed a decent PCE of $6 . 4 6 \%$ which was lower than that of the counterpart with short conjugation length. The results suggest that the laddertype donor unit should have an optimal conjugated length to achieve D-A copolymers with enhanced performance. Since too long conjugation length will decrease the solubility of the resulting copolymers, researchers have usually introduced more bulky side chains on the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized bridging atoms which will inevitably lead to decreased charge mobilities.

# 5.3 A-D-A NFAs Based on Ladder-Type Heteroacenes

From 1995 to 2015, most efficient PSCs were fabricated by using a fullerene derivative as the electron acceptor material to blend with polymer donor or smallmolecule donor materials. However, the highest PCE of these fullerene-based PSCs can barely exceed $1 2 . 0 0 \%$ [2]. This PCE limitation of fullerene-based PSCs is mainly attributed to the fact that the absorption bands of the fullerene derivatives are located in the short wavelength region and their energy levels can be tuned in a very small range. Therefore, NFA materials are emerging as promising alternatives to replace the traditional fullerene derivatives with their easy synthesis accessibility. More importantly, these NFAs can provide tunable bandgaps and energy levels in much wider ranges thereby leading to well-matched absorption profiles and energy levels between the NFAs and the donor materials. Although there have been a number of design strategies for NFAs, the acceptors with an A-D-A structural motif have been the most extensively explored in recent years since the first report of ITIC acceptor by Zhan and coworkers in 2015 [8]. In the A-D-A-structured acceptors, the electron-donating ladder-type heteroacenes have a great effect on the photovoltaic performance of the resulting NFAs. Thus, in the following, we will discuss the influence of the chemical structures of ladder-type heteroacenes on the performance of NFAs. It should be noted that both ending groups and $\pi$ bridges of NFAs can also affect their photovoltaic performance.

# 5.3.1  A-D-A NFAs Based on Heteropentacenes and Heterohexacenes

As a coplanar and symmetric configuration, the pentacyclic IDT moiety is a promising electron-rich unit for designing efficient A-D-A NFAs. The first example of IDTbased NFAs is DC-IDT2T (Figure 5.4), which was synthesized by Zhan and coworkers by using 2-(3-oxo-2,3-dihydroinden-1-ylidene)malononitrile (INCN)

as the ending groups and thiophene as the $\pi$ -bridges [36]. DC-IDT2T has a LBG of $1 . 5 5 \mathrm { e V }$ with a relatively high-lying LUMO energy level. The PSC based on DC-IDT2T:PBDTTT-T-C showed a PCE of $3 . 9 3 \%$ (Table 5.4). Using a thieno[3,4-b]thiophene derivative as the $\pi$ -bridge to substitute the thiophene bridge in DC-IDT2T, Zhu and coworkers designed and synthesized another IDT-based NFA (ATT-2) with the same ending group of INCN [37]. ATT-2 showed a reduced optical bandgap of $1 . 3 2 \mathrm { e V }$ with a relatively deep-lying LUMO energy level of $- 3 . 9 0 \mathrm { e V } .$ Because of the complementary absorption and matched energy levels between PTB7-Th and ATT-2, the corresponding PSC delivered an excellent PCE of $9 . 5 8 \%$ with a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 0 . 7 5 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ despite its relatively low $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 7 3 \mathrm { V } .$ To further reduce the bandgaps of the IDT-based NFAs and enhance the light absorption in the NIR region, alkoxy side chains and fluorinated ending groups were simultaneously employed in the conjugated backbone of DC-IDT2T [38]. Because of the conformational lock and fluorination effects, the resulting NFA (IEICO-4F) showed a down-shifted LUMO energy of $- 4 . 1 9 \mathrm { e V } ,$ and a red-shifted absorption band with an absorption onset of $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , corresponding to a rather low optical bandgap of $1 . 2 4 \mathrm { e V } .$ A PCE of $1 0 . 0 0 \%$ with an impressive $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 2 . 8 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 7 4 \mathrm { V } ,$ and a FF of $5 9 . 4 \%$ was achieved for the PSC based on PTB7-Th:IEICO-4F. Through fine tuning the blend morphology, the best PCE of PTB7-Th:IEICO-4F-based PSCs was further improved to $1 2 . 8 0 \%$ with an enhanced $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 7 . 3 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ [45].

Using a heterohexacene-based building block developed for the D-A copolymers in our group, we further designed and synthesized a NFA (DTNIC8) with hexacyclic angular-shaped DTN as the electron-rich core and INCN as the ending groups [39]. DTNIC8 showed a deep-lying HOMO energy level of $- 5 . 9 1 \mathrm { e V }$ with a medium bandgap of $1 . 7 3 \mathrm { e V } .$ A well-defined phase separation morphology was observed in the blend film of PBDB-T:DTNIC8, yielding efficient exciton dissociation and transportation. Meanwhile, the hole and electron mobilities for the

PBDB-T:DTNIC8 blend were balanced with moderate values of $3 . 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }$ and $2 . 8 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ , respectively. The best-performance PSC based on DTNIC8 delivered a PCE of $9 . 0 3 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 6 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 2 . 9 2 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF of $7 2 . 8 \%$ . To further improve the photovoltaic performance, a new NFA (DTNR) was developed by using the ladder-type angular-shaped DTN flanked with the weak electron-deficient 3-ethylrhodanine moieties through benzothiadiazole-based bridging groups [40]. Compared to DTNIC8, DTNR showed an up-shifted LUMO energy level of $- 3 . 7 5 \mathrm { e V } ;$ which is beneficial to achieve a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and a decreased energy loss for the resulting PSC. When paired with the polymer donor of PTB7-Th, DTNR delivered an enhanced efficiency of $9 . 5 1 \%$ with an increased $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 0 8 \mathrm { V }$ as well as a rather low energy loss of $0 . 5 0 \mathrm { e V } .$ Additionally, the DTNR-based device showed a higher PCE and better storage stability in comparison with the $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ -based counterpart. At the same time, Chen and coworkers reported a NFA (NTIC) based on the linear-shaped DTN, which showed up-shifted HOMO/LUMO energy levels of $- 5 . 5 8 / - 3 . 7 6 \mathrm { e V }$ and a reduced optical bandgap of $1 . 6 7 \mathrm { e V }$ [41]. The best-performance PSC based on NTIC:PBDB-T showed a PCE of $8 . 6 3 \%$ which is lower than that of the device based on DTNIC8. Recently, Bo and coworkers also synthesized a naphthalene-based NFA (PDT-T), which has a LBG of $1 . 4 4 \mathrm { e V }$ [42]. When PDT-T was blended with a wide bandgap polymer of PBDB-T, the photo-current responses were extended to $9 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ for the PDT-T-based PSC. Therefore, a high PCE of $1 1 . 0 2 \%$ with a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 8 . 8 8 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ was obtained for the corresponding device. These results demonstrate that extending the conjugation length of ladder-type heteroacenes is helpful to improve the photovoltaic performance of NFAs. To strengthen the electron-donating ability of the central electron-rich core, thieno[3,2-b]thiophene was introduced to replace the naphthalene in DTN to afford a new NFA (IHIC) which has a reduced optical bandgap of $1 . 3 8 \mathrm { e V }$ in comparison with DTNIC8 [43]. The PTB7-Th:IHIC blend showed a high electron mobility of $1 . 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ which is favorable for obtaining a high PCE $( 9 . 7 7 \% )$ for the corresponding semi-transparent PSC. The same NFA was also reported in parallel and named as 4TIC by Jen and coworkers. The best-performance PSC based on PTB7-Th:4TIC delivered a PCE of $1 0 . 4 3 \%$ [46].

Using hexacyclic thiophene-phenylene-thieno[3,2-b]thiophene fused core, Sun and coworkers synthesized a new NFA (TPTT-IC) [44] which has a planar and asymmetric structure, and appropriate energy levels. When blended with a wide bandgap copolymer of PBT1-C, the resulting PSC based on TPTT-IC showed a high PCE of $1 0 . 5 0 \%$ , which is higher than that of the ITIC-based device under the same preparation conditions.

(%)</td><td>References</td></tr><tr><td>ITIC</td><td>1.59</td><td>PTB7-Th</td><td>5.48/3.83</td><td>0.81</td><td>14.21</td><td>59.1</td><td>6.80</td><td>[8]</td></tr><tr><td>IT-4F</td><td>1.51</td><td>PBDB-T-SF</td><td>5.66/-4.14</td><td>0.88</td><td>20.88</td><td>71.3</td><td>13.10</td><td>[47]</td></tr><tr><td>IT-4F</td><td>1.51</td><td>T1</td><td>5.66/-4.14</td><td>0.90</td><td>21.50</td><td>78.0</td><td>15.10</td><td>[48]</td></tr><tr><td>IT-4Cl</td><td>1.48</td><td>PM6</td><td>5.75/-4.27</td><td>0.79</td><td>22.67</td><td>75.2</td><td>13.45</td><td>[49]</td></tr><tr><td>ITCC</td><td>1.67</td><td>PBDB-T</td><td>5.47/3.76</td><td>1.01</td><td>15.90</td><td>71.0</td><td>11.40</td><td>[50]</td></tr><tr><td>CDTCN</td><td>1.48</td><td>PBDB-T</td><td>5.39/3.80</td><td>0.96</td><td>11.26</td><td>57.6</td><td>6.23</td><td>[51]</td></tr><tr><td>HCN-C8</td><td>1.67</td><td>J71</td><td>5.63/-3.54</td><td>1.01</td><td>6.24</td><td>37.8</td><td>2.38</td><td>[52]</td></tr><tr><td>HCN-C16</td><td>1.66</td><td>J71</td><td>5.63/-3.57</td><td>1.03</td><td>12.30</td><td>43.5</td><td>5.51</td><td>[52]</td></tr><tr><td>H2FCN-C16</td><td>1.59</td><td>J71</td><td>5.95/3.99</td><td>0.90</td><td>18.62</td><td>66.7</td><td>11.18</td><td>[52]</td></tr><tr><td>DTPC-DFIC</td><td>1.21</td><td>PTB7-Th</td><td>5.31/-4.10</td><td>0.76</td><td>21.92</td><td>61.3</td><td>10.21</td><td>[53]</td></tr><tr><td>FDICTF</td><td>1.63</td><td>PBDB-T</td><td>5.43/-3.71</td><td>0.94</td><td>15.81</td><td>66.0</td><td>9.81</td><td>[54]</td></tr><tr><td>DBTTC</td><td>1.64</td><td>PBDB-T</td><td>5.92/4.03</td><td>0.97</td><td>17.25</td><td>67.0</td><td>11.25</td><td>[55]</td></tr><tr><td>AT-4C1</td><td>1.60</td><td>PBDB-T</td><td>5.71/3.89</td><td>0.90</td><td>19.52</td><td>75.5</td><td>13.27</td><td>[56]</td></tr><tr><td>NFBDT</td><td>1.56</td><td>PBDB-T</td><td>5.40/3.83</td><td>0.87</td><td>17.85</td><td>67.2</td><td>10.42</td><td>[57]</td></tr><tr><td>ITIC5</td><td>1.53</td><td>J71</td><td>5.48/3.95</td><td>0.90</td><td>18.48</td><td>75.5</td><td>12.50</td><td>[58]</td></tr><tr><td>BT-IC</td><td>1.43</td><td>J71</td><td>5.32/3.85</td><td>0.90</td><td>17.75</td><td>65.7</td><td>10.46</td><td>[59]</td></tr><tr><td>BTTIC</td><td>1.47</td><td>PBDB-T</td><td>5.59/3.86</td><td>0.90</td><td>19.52</td><td>74.7</td><td>13.18</td><td>[60]</td></tr></table>

NFAs are summarized in Table 5.5. The benchmark NFA (ITIC) was first reported by Zhan and coworkers by using a ladder-type heptacyclic core (IDTT), which is formed by fusing two thiophene rings on the IDT unit [8]. The PSC based on PTB7-Th:ITIC only showed a modest PCE of $6 . 8 0 \%$ , which is mainly ascribed to the mismatched energy levels and overlapped absorption spectra between the LBG PTB7-Th donor and the LBG ITIC acceptor. When a wide bandgap polymer of PBDB-T was used to replace PTB7-Th, the resulting PSC showed a significantly enhanced PCE of $1 1 . 2 1 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 0 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 6 . 8 1 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF of $7 4 . 2 \%$ due to the more complementary absorption and well-matched energy levels [61]. Fluorine atom has strong electronegativity, and it is widely used in the modification of ending groups in NFAs. When fluorine atoms were introduced to the ending groups of ITIC, the resulting NFA (IT-4F) [47] showed a bathochromically shifted absorption band and deeper-lying energy levels than ITIC. At the same time, IT-4F delivered a higher electron mobility of $5 . 0 5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \thinspace \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ in comparison with ITIC, which is in favor of the enhanced charge transport in PSCs. When a wide bandgap polymer of PBDB-T-SF was used as the electron donor material, the resulting PSC showed a record-high PCE of $1 3 . 1 0 \%$ at that time with a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 0 . 8 8 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . The PCE of IT-4F-based device was further improved to $1 5 . 1 0 \%$ when a ternary conjugated D-A copolymer with a finely tuned HOMO level was used [48]. Hou and coworkers further introduced chlorine atoms into the ending groups of ITIC to obtain a chlorinated NFA (IT-4Cl) with red-shifted absorption compared to IT-4F [49]. The LUMO energy level of IT-4Cl was down-shifted to $- 4 . 2 7 \mathrm { e V } .$ Thus, a remarkable PCE of $1 3 . 4 5 \%$ with a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 2 . 6 7 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and a relatively low $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 7 9 \mathrm { V }$ was achieved for the PSC based on PM6:IT-4Cl. When the phenyl in the ending group of ITIC was replaced with the thienyl unit, the resulting NFA (ITCC) exhibited an up-shifted LUMO energy level of $- 3 . 7 6 \mathrm { e V }$ and an enhanced electron mobility of $9 . 2 6 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ [50]. Thus, a PCE of $1 1 . 4 0 \%$ with an improved $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 0 1 \mathrm { V }$ was obtained for the PSC based on PBDB-T:ITCC.

Compared to IDTT, DTCC shows relatively weak electron-donating ability. Our group first reported a NFA (CDTCN) by using DTCC as the central core and two thiophene units as $\pi$ -bridges [51]. With the strong intramolecular charge transfer (ICT) effect, CDTCN displayed a reduced bandgap of $1 . 4 8 \mathrm { e V }$ with a large absorption coefficient of $2 . 9 \times 1 0 ^ { 5 } \ \mathrm { M } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ . PSCs based on CDTCN:PBDB-T showed a decent PCE of $6 . 2 3 \%$ . At the same time, Sun and coworkers also reported a DTCC-cored NFA with a similar PCE of $6 . 0 0 \%$ [62]. Subsequently, our group further designed and synthesized three DTCC-based NFAs (HCN-C8, HCN-C16, and H2FCN-C16) to investigate the influences of side-chain and end-group fluorination on the optical, electrochemical, and photovoltaic properties of the NFAs [52]. Although the side chain on the central nitrogen bridging atom barely affects the energy levels and bandgaps, the substitution of $n$ -octyl with 2-hexyldecyl results in the molecular ordering change of the NAFs from crystalline (HCN-C8) to amorphous (HCN-C16), which can affect their miscibility with polymer donor materials. Furthermore, H2FCN-C16 with fluorinated ending groups (INCN2F) exhibited a reduced bandgap and deep-lying energy levels. The H2FCN-C16-based blend film exhibited a closer $\pi { - } \pi$ packing with improved crystallinity thereby resulting in its enhanced charge transport. The best-performance PSC based on H2FCN-C16:J71 yielded an impressive PCE of $1 1 . 1 8 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 0 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 8 . 6 2 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and a FF of $6 6 . 7 \%$ . However, the best-performance PSCs based on HCN-C8 and HCN-C16 showed PCEs of $2 . 3 8 \%$ and $5 . 5 1 \%$ ,respectively. These results suggest that the electron-rich DTcC is a promising building block for constructing high-performance NFAs. On the other hand, extending the $\pi$ conjugation of DTCC by substituting the central benzene units with naphthalene, a ladder-type dithienopicenocarbazole (DTPC) core was obtained. This two-dimensional conjugated DTPC with nitrogen bridging atom has a strong electron-donating ability, which could enhance the ICT effect and the intermolecular interaction of the resulting DTPC-derived NFAs. An ultra-narrow bandgap (1.21eV) NFA (DTPC-DFIC) based on DTPC was designed and synthesized by Jen and coworkers [53]. When combined with a spectral-complementary electron donor material of PTB7-Th, the DTPC-DFIC-based PSC exhibited an efficiency of $1 0 . 2 1 \%$ with a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 1 . 9 2 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ as well as a quite low energy loss of $0 . 4 5 \mathrm { e V } .$

Compared with DTCC, the DTCF unit contains an additional $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized bridging atom where two bulky side chains are attached in the conjugated backbone, which would impede the close intermolecular $\pi { - } \pi$ packing. Despite such deficiency, Chen and coworkers developed an excellent NFA (FDICTF) based on DTCF. PSCs based on FDICTF:PBDB-T displayed a PCE of $9 . 8 1 \%$ [54]. Using an electron-rich building block DTCD without the bulky side chain on the central bridging atom, our group designed and synthesized a new NFA (DBTTC) which is end-caped with 2-(6-oxo-5,6-dihydro- $4 H$ -cyclopenta[c]thiophen -4-ylidene)malononitrile [55]. DBTTC showed an optical bandgap of $1 . 6 4 \mathrm { e V }$ with a LUMO energy level of $- 4 . 0 3 \mathrm { e V } .$ The DBTTC:PBDB-T blend film exhibited clear phase separation with smooth surface, resulting in an improved charge transport. An impressive PCE of $1 1 . 2 5 \%$ with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 7 \mathrm { V }$ and a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 7 . 2 5 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ was obtained for the DBTTC-based PSC.

By replacing the naphthalene unit in linear-shaped DTN with the anthracene, Chen and coworkers designed and synthesized a new heteroheptacene (AT) with extended conjugation [56]. Using chlorinated INCN as the ending groups, a new NFA (AT-4Cl) was obtained which exhibited a decreased bandgap of $1 . 6 0 \mathrm { e V }$ and an increased electron mobility $1 . 8 5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \thinspace \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ . The PSC based on PM6:AT-4Cl afforded a high PCE of $1 3 . 2 7 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 0 \mathrm { V } _ { : }$ a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 9 . 5 2 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a FF of $7 5 . 5 \%$

With symmetrical configuration and high degree of coplanarity, the BDT unit is popular in constructing high-performance D-A copolymers. However, the BDT-based NFAs are rarely reported in comparison with a large number of BDT-based donor materials. Chen and coworkers synthesized a new NFA, namely NFBDT, based on a heptacyclic benzodi(cyclopentadithiophene) (FBDT) unit with a BDT-derived core [57]. The incorporation of BDT endows the target NFA (NFBDT) with a large conjugated backbone which would enhance the ICT effect. As a result, NFBDT showed a LBG of $1 . 5 6 \mathrm { e V }$ with a strong absorption band in the range of $6 0 0 { - } 8 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . Using the benchmark copolymer of PBDB-T as the donor material, the NFBDT-based PSC delivered an efficiency of $1 0 . 4 2 \%$ with a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 7 . 8 5 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 7 \mathrm { V } _ { : }$ and a relatively low FF of $6 7 . 2 \%$ . The result indicates that BDT is a promising candidate to design high-performance NFAs. To improve the photovoltaic property of FBDT-based NFAs, Zhan and coworkers replaced the phenyl of the INCN group in NFBDT with thienyl to obtain a new NFA (ITIC5) [58]. Compared to NFBDT, ITIC5 has a lower optical bandgap of $1 . 5 3 \mathrm { e V } .$ After thermal annealing, ITIC5-based blend film exhibited fine and continuous network with enhanced crystallinity, which efficiently facilitated charge dissociation and transport. The corresponding PSC showed an improved PCE of $1 2 . 5 0 \%$ with an increased FF of $7 5 . 5 \%$ , a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 0 \mathrm { V } ,$ and a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 8 . 4 8 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . Besides the terminal group optimization, ladder-type NFAs could also be modified to extend their absorption bands to NIR region by introducing electron-donating side chain on the backbone to strengthen the ICT effect. Liao and coworkers developed new NFA (BT-IC) based on the FBDT building block [59]. An electron-donating side chain, 2-ethylhexyloxy, was employed on the BDT segment to decrease the bandgap via elevating the HOMO energy level without reducing the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ . BT-IC showed a low optical bandgap of $1 . 4 3 \mathrm { e V }$ with an up-shifted HOMO energy level of $- 5 . 3 2 \mathrm { e V } .$ When paired with J71, the BT-IC-based PSC exhibited a PCE of $1 0 . 4 6 \%$ with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 0 \mathrm { V } .$ It should be noted that the HOMO driving force for this system is only around $0 . 1 \mathrm { e V }$ which is much less than the empirical value of $0 . 3 \mathrm { e V }$ to ensure the efficient charge dissociation. In combination with the modifications on ending group and side chain, Yang and coworkers reported a new FBDT-based NFA (BTTIC) with 2-(1-methyl-6-oxo-5, 6-dihydro-4H-cyclopenta[c]thiophen-4-ylidene)malononitrile as terminal groups [60]. Meanwhile, 2-D conjugated side chains, 2-ethylhexylthiophene, were anchored on the BDT unit. BTTIC showed a wide absorption band with an optical bandgap of $1 . 4 7 \mathrm { e V } .$ Benefiting from the favorable morphology of the PBDB-T:BTTIC blend, the corresponding device showed an impressive PCE of $1 3 . 1 8 \%$

# 5.3.2.2 NFAs Based on Heteroheptacenes Without $\mathsf { \pmb { s p } } ^ { 3 }$ -Hybridized Bridging Atoms

As previously reported, most ladder-type heteroheptacenes building blocks were usually fastened with $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized bridging atoms. However, the solubilizing side chains on the bridging atoms always stick out from the conjugated plane, which would increase the steric-hindrance effect and enlarge the intermolecular $\pi { - } \pi$ packing distance, leading to a decreased carrier transport for the resulting NFAs. Hence, it is urgently needed to explore new A-D-A-type NFAs without the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized bridging atoms in the ladder-type fused arenes core. Ma et al. developed two novel "M-series" LBG NFAs (M8 and M34 in Figure 5.6) based on ladder-type heteroheptacenes fastened with $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 }$ -hybridized nitrogen bridging atoms [63]. Both of them share the same side chains and ending groups, but they differ in the central electron-donating core. Replacing the benzodifuran with BDT in the heteroheptacene core resulted in a slightly blue-shifted absorption with a down-shifted HOMO energy level for M34. At the same time, a favorable morphology with a large portion of face-on orientation could be observed in the M34-based blend film. Therefore, PM6:M34 showed enhanced and more balanced charge transport with hole and electron mobilities of $6 . 2 5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 }$ and $2 . 6 5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \thinspace \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ , respectively. The corresponding PSC based on M34:PM6 exhibited an outstanding PCE of $1 5 . 2 4 \%$ (Table 5.6) with a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 3 . 6 3 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 1 \mathrm { V } ,$ and a FF of $7 0 . 7 \%$ which was much higher than the $4 . 2 1 \%$ efficiency for the M8-based device. The $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking distances and molecular orientations of the heteroheptacene-based NFAs can be effectively modulated by side-chain engineering to improve their photovoltaic performance. Therefore, the length of branched alkyl chain on the central benzo[1,2-b:4,5. $\mathbf { \nabla } \cdot  { b ^ { \prime } }$ ]bis(4-H-dithieno $3 , 2 \cdot b : 2 ^ { \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime } \cdot d ]$ pyrrole (BDTP) building block of M34 was systematically optimized [64]. The blend based on M36 with 2-butyloctyl side chains showed a dominated face-on molecular orientation with a closely $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking, leading to the best charge transport with hole/electron mobilities of $6 . 6 2 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } / 1 . 3 3 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ . However, enlarged $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking distances were obtained for the blends based on M2 with 2-ethylhexyl side chains and M38 with 2-decyltetradecyl side chains. Consequently, the PSC based on PM6:M36 achieved an outstanding PCE of $1 6 . 0 0 \%$ with a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 4 . 6 3 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 0 \mathrm { V } ,$ and a FF of $7 2 . 1 \%$ . Nevertheless, the PCEs were $1 1 . 1 6 \%$ and $8 . 8 9 \%$ for the PSCs based on M2 and M38, respectively. In addition to the length, the sizes and flanking positions of the alkyl chains were also systematically investigated, which later were shown to have a strong influence on the molecular orientation of "M-series"' acceptors [65]. It was found that with linear $n$ -dodecyl side chains on the nitrogen atoms, the resulting acceptor (M11) tends to adopt an "edge-on" orientation, thus leading to excellent horizontal charge transport with a FET mobility of $3 . 9 5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 2 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ . Interestingly, when the linear $n$ -dodecyl chains on the nitrogen atoms were replaced with 2-butyloctyl chains, the dominant crystallite textures of the resulting acceptors (M12 and M13) were changed from an "edge-on" manner to a "face-on" manner. Consequently, PSCs based on M12 and M13 showed much higher vertical electron transport, and therefore higher PCEs, than those based on M11. Further optimization of the M13-based devices yielded an outstanding efficiency of $1 5 . 6 3 \%$ [65]. By synergistic optimization of the ending groups and side chains on the backbone of M13, an acceptor named M3 was produced and devices based on this material obtained a prominent PCE of $1 6 . 6 6 \%$ [66]. To the best of our knowledge, the efficiency of $1 6 . 6 6 \%$ is the highest value for single-junction PSCs based on all the A-D-A-type NFAs reported to date and it is also comparable to those based on the A-D-A'-D-A-type Y6-derivated acceptors [1, 3, 10].

Very recently, our group developed three novel NFAs (MQ3, MQ5, and MQ6) by using asymmetric and symmetric ladder-type heteroheptacene cores which have one and two selenophene heterocycles, respectively, to study the influence of noncovalent intramolecular interaction and molecular symmetry on the photovoltaic properties of the "M-series" acceptors [67]. Although MQ3 and MQ5 have the same number of selenophene heterocycles, the heteroheptacene core of MQ5 is end-capped with selenophene rings, while that of MQ3 is end-capped with thiophene rings. Due to the enhanced noncovalent interaction of O. . .Se compared to O. . .S, MQ5 shows a bathochromically shifted absorption band and greatly enhanced charge transport thereby leading to a higher PCE of $1 5 . 6 4 \%$ compared to $1 3 . 5 1 \%$ for MQ3. Moreover, MQ6 with an asymmetric heteroheptacene core shows a further reduced $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking distance induced by the increased dipole moment thereby further improving the carrier transport of the resulting blend film. As a result, PSCs based on MQ6 exhibited the best performance among the three acceptors, with a maximum efficiency of $1 6 . 3 9 \%$

In addition to the above research, several other efforts, including end-group engineering and auxochromic group engineering, have also been devoted to the development of high-performance M-series NFAs and devices based on these acceptors have also achieved efficiencies over $1 5 \%$ [68-70]. All these results suggest that $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ carbon-free ladder-type skeletons with appropriate neighboring side chains are a promising class of building blocks to construct high-performance NFAs.

# 5.3.3 A-D-A NFAs Based on Heteroacenes with Eight or More Fused Rings

To extend the absorption band of NFAs, Ding and coworkers developed a carbonoxygen-bridged NFAs $\mathrm { \ C O } _ { i } 8 \mathrm { D F I C }$ , Figure 5.7) based on an octacyclic heteroacene core [71]. ${ \mathrm { C O } } _ { i } { 8 \mathrm { D F I C } }$ showed a rather low optical bandgap of $1 . 2 6 \mathrm { e V }$ with a strong absorption band located at $6 0 0 { - } 1 0 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . When blended with PTB7-Th, $\mathrm { C O } _ { i }$ 8DFIC-based PSC showed a PCE of $1 2 . 1 6 \%$ (Table 5.7) with a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 6 . 1 2 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and a relatively low $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 6 8 \mathrm { V } .$

In 2019, Tang and coworkers synthesized a nonacyclic DTCC-based heteroacene (CZTT) with an extended, rigid, and coplanar structure by fusing a thiophene on both flanks of DTCC [72]. Using fluorinated INCN as ending groups, CZTT-based NFA (CZTT-4F) exhibited a LBG of $1 . 4 8 \mathrm { e V } .$ Blended with PM6, CZTT-4F delivered a high PCE of $1 2 . 0 7 \%$ with a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 9 . 7 3 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . Compared to the fluorination in the ending groups, chlorination has also been proven to be effective to tune the photovoltaic performances of NFAs. Similar to CZTT, Hsu and coworkers developed a ladder-type nonacyclic heteroacene (DTTC) [73]. By using chlorinated ending groups, the NFA (DTTC-4Cl) exhibited red-shifted absorption [73]. The blend film based on DTTC-4Cl:PM6 showed a close $\pi { - } \pi$ packing distance thereby leading to a remarkable PCE of $1 5 . 4 2 \%$ with a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 2 . 6 4 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and a FF of $7 4 . 0 \%$ for the corresponding PSC. Tang and coworkers developed a nonacyclic core-based NFA (INPIC-4F) by inserting pyrrole in IDTT [74]. INPIC-4F showed a red-shifted absorption with a LBG of $1 . 3 9 \mathrm { e V } .$ Benefiting from the preferred crystallinity and morphology, PSC based on INPIC-4F:PBDB-T exhibited an intriguing PCE of $1 3 . 1 3 \%$ with a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 1 . 6 1 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and a relatively low $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 5 \mathrm { V } .$

An octacyclic heteroacene based on naphtho[1,2-b:5,6 $. b ^ { \prime }$ |dithiophene was developed by Zhan and coworkers, which was end-capped with INCN2F to get a NFA (IOIC2) [75]. IOIC2 exhibited a LBG of $1 . 5 5 \mathrm { e V }$ with HOMO/LUMO energy levels of $- 5 . 4 1 / - 3 . 7 8 \mathrm { e V } .$ The inverted PSCs based on FTAZ:IOIC2 blend gave a PCE of $1 2 . 3 0 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 0 \mathrm { V }$ and a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 9 . 7 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . Extending the effective conjugation length of central core in NFAs is a useful strategy to strengthen the ICT effect and $\pi { - } \pi$ interaction for reduced bandgaps and improved charge transport. Wang and coworkers extended the core of IOIC2 to decacyclclic heteroacene [76]. Thus, the corresponding NFA (IDCIC) showed a LBG of $1 . 4 5 \mathrm { e V }$ with an increased absorption coefficient of $3 . 3 \times 1 0 ^ { 5 } ~ \mathrm { M } ^ { - 1 } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ . Due to the extended conjugation, FTAZ:IDCIC blend film showed an improved charge transport with more balanced hole and electron mobilities in comparison with the IOIC2-based counterpart. The best-performance IDCIC-based PSC showed an improved PCE of $1 3 . 5 8 \%$ with an increased $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 1 . 9 8 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$

Zhan and coworkers further extended the core of IT-4F with undecyclic heteroacene to obtain a LBG NFA (IUIC) [77]. The strong electron-donating undecyclic heteroacene led to a broad absorption band up to $9 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ for IUIC. Because of the enhanced $\pi { - } \pi$ interaction, the electron mobility of IUIC was improved to $1 . 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ . And, the PSC based on PTB7-Th:IUIC blend delivered a decent PCE of $1 1 . 2 0 \%$

# 5.3.4Other NFAs

Another distinctive A-D-A NFAs were derived from noncovalently locked building blocks where 2,5-difluorobenzene (DFB) and 2,5-dialkoxybenzene (DOB) were usually incorporated as central cores to create intramolecular noncovalent reactions such as S...O, S...F, and H...F. Chen and coworkers synthesized a new NFA (DF-PCIC in Figure 5.8) containing a DFB core and two cyclopentadithiophene (CPD) segments [78]. A nearly planar structure is achieved by the F.. .H noncovalent interaction. The optimized PSC based on PBDB-T:DF-PCIC yielded a decent PCE of $1 0 . 1 4 \%$ (Table 5.8) with a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 5 . 6 6 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . Later, Bo and coworkers developed a noncovalently fused-ring NFA (DOC2C6-2F) based on the DOB core and the CPD groups, which was formed by a ladder-like donor unit locked with $\mathbf { 0 \cdot \cdot S }$ noncovalent interaction and flanked with two fluorinated ending groups [79]. Compared with DF-PCIC, DOC2C6-2F showed markedly broadened absorption with a lower optical bandgap of $1 . 4 2 \mathrm { e V } .$ The inverted PSC based on PBDB-T:DOC2C6-2F blend displayed an enhanced PCE of $1 3 . 2 4 \%$ with a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 1 . 3 5 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$

Besides the A-D-A type NFAs, A-D-A'-D-A-type NFAs are emerging recently since Zou and coworkers reported a new family of nitrogen-bridged small-molecule acceptors (Y-series, such as Y6) using an electron-deficient unit as the central core [1, 10, 11]. Y6 exhibited a broad absorption band in the range of $6 0 0 { - } 9 3 0 \mathrm { n m }$ with a low optical bandgap of $1 . 3 3 \mathrm { e V } .$ When paired with a wide bandgap polymer of PM6, the best-performance PSC based on Y6 showed an outstanding PCE of $1 5 . 7 \%$ . The discovery of these Y-series NFAs greatly promoted the advances of organic solar cells, and since then many research groups used these Y-series NFAs (especially Y6) to successfully achieve PSCs with PCEs over $1 6 . 0 0 \%$ [1, 80].

# 5.4 Conclusions and Outlook

In the past decade, a large number of ladder-type heteroacenes have been designed and synthesized for both donor and acceptor materials. Extension of the conjugated backbones usually resulted in decreased solubilities of the resulting materials. A good balance between the solubility and crystallinity should be maintained. The electron-donating abilities as well as the conjugated lengths of the ladder-type heteroacenes can affect the optical, electrochemical, and photovoltaic properties of the resulting acceptor materials. Similar to the electron-donating groups, the electronwithdrawing groups and $\pi$ bridges can also affect their optical, electrochemical, and photovoltaic properties. However, side chains mainly affect their crystallinity, molecular orientation as well as phase separation properties. So far, most ladder-type heteroacenes used bulky substituents flanked on their $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized bridging atoms to restrain the severe intermolecular aggregation induced by the extended planar $\pi$ -conjugated core. For NFAs, the bulky side chains on the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized bridging carbon atoms in the D unit will inevitably limit the efficient carrier transport of the resulting materials due to their decreased crystallinity. Therefore, it is in great need to explore novel A-D-A NFAs without the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized bridging atoms in D unit. So far, A-D-A NFAs without any $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized bridging atoms in the conjugated backbone are much less developed compared to those with the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized bridging atoms. Recently, our group developed a series of ladder-type heteroheptacene-based NFAs (M-series) which are all free of the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -hybridized bridging atoms. In our work, two pairs of neighboring side chains on the heteroheptacene core were used to suppress the immoderate intermolecular aggregation thereby leading to suitable phase separation with optimal domain sizes. As a result, the benchmark NFA (M3) developed in our laboratory showed an outstanding PCE of $1 6 . 6 6 \%$ . To the best of our knowledge, the PCE of $1 6 . 6 6 \%$ is the highest for PSCs based on all A-D-A type NFAs reported to date and it is also comparable to those based on the Y-series $\mathbf { \Delta A { - } D { - } A ^ { \prime } }$ -D-A-type) NFAs.

However, to achieve PSCs with PCEs over $2 0 \%$ , there are still some remaining issues to be resolved: (i) Reducing the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ loss via synergistic molecular designs on both the donor and acceptor materials; (ii) Developing novel infrared NFAs with high absorptivity and wide absorption range; (ii) Achieving NFAs with face-on orientation and efficient electron transport; and (iv) Designing of new structures in the D, A, and the $\pi$ -bridge which can be used to finely tune the properties of NFAs.
