# 7.2 The Device Structure and Basic Principles of All-PSCs

The typical all-PSCs device structure is presented in Figure 7.1a. The device basically consists of an ITO glass substrate, transport electrode, two interfacial layers (one is electron transporting layer and the other is hole transporting layer), the active layer of all-polymer D-A BHJ blend, and the metal contact top electrode. There are two mainstream device structures applied in all-PSC fabrication: the first one is conventional structure and presents the architecture of metal electrodes/electron transporting layer/active layer/hole transport layer/ITO glass substrate; and the other has the inverted structure compared with the conventional one. For efficient operation, the all-polymer photoactive blend should develop an interpenetrating network of donor and acceptor polymer domains to provide effective percolation pathways connecting the acceptor regions to the cathode and donor regions to the anode.

As shown in Figure 7.1b, the basics principles of all-PsCs are similar to conventional polymer-fullerene solar cells, which is the photoexcited state of an electron-hole pair bound together by the Coulomb attraction. In order to achieve photocurrent, these excited electron-hole pairs need to be dissociated into free charge carriers. In organic semiconductors, due to their relatively low dielectric constant, the photoexcited Frenkel excitons have a much stronger binding energy. A large driving force from the D-A energy level offset is needed for the exciton dissociation [24]. Conventional fullerene acceptors are spherically symmetric materials, which can have close contact with the donor polymers in arbitrary directions to achieve efficient charge transfer. Meanwhile, fullerene derivatives tend to form highly crystalline domains with large charge delocalization, which will lower the Coulomb barrier and hence improve exciton dissociation [14]. Likewise, proper packing orientation and degree of crystallinity in D-A polymers are helpful to efficiently dissociate electron-hole pairs into free charge carriers. Unfortunately, these all-polymer systems are anisotropic, to well control the orientation and crystallinity of both donor and acceptor crystals at the BHJ blend is a challenging task [25].

![](images/1a824c8bcbdce4ce9a79a663e54a816bef9f823d4a1c1d0dd4266563d6a8f216.jpg)  
Figure 7.2(a) $J - V$ curve under illumination and (b) EQE versus wavelength for a typical all-Psc. Source: Jianyu Yuan.

Figure 7.2a shows typical all-PSC current density (J) versus voltage (V) curve under illumination. Such plots are used to evaluate device performance parameters including: (i) the short-circuit current density $( J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ , the current flowing through an illuminated cell when there is no external resistance); (ii) the open-circuit voltage - $\boldsymbol { V } _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ , the cell voltage in sunlight when no current is flowing); (iii) the fill factor (FF; the ratio of maximum power output to theoretical power output); (iv) the PCE (the ratio of power output to power input). Figure $7 . 2 \mathrm { b }$ shows the external quantum efficiency (EQE) of a typical all-PSCs device. From the photocurrent spectrum, the ability of the solar cells to convert photons to electrons under irradiation at certain wavelengths and intensities can be obtained. In comparison with the conventional fullerene-based PSCs, the use of nonfullerene polymeric acceptor can further extend the photocurrent spectrum to near-infrared (NIR) region, potentially enhancing the $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of the PV device [2].

# 7.3 Materials Design Toward Efficient All-PSCs

# 7.3.1 Progress of N2200 and Its Derivative-Based All-PSCs

Aromatic diimide-based conjugated polymers are an important class of electron acceptor materials for all-PSCs [26]. For instant, the best-known NDI polymers have been regarded as the most efficient polymers. NDI groups have several advantages such as high electron affinity, electron-transporting capability, and excellent thermal and oxidative stability. Easy access to the functionalization of the NDI can be carried out at the carbon 2 and 6 positions for the preparation of regioselective dibrominated monomers and thus pure polymers [1]. In addition, side-chain engineering at the imide nitrogen position of NDI enables good solubility of polymers for solution processing and facile optimization of all-PSC blend morphology. For example, Guo and Watson pioneered the synthesis of NDI polymers by Stille coupling of regioisomerically pure dibromo-NDI monomer with various stannylated thiophene-based monomers. It is found that these polymers have low-lying LUMOs of c. $3 . 8 0 \mathrm { e V }$ and narrow bandgap of c. $1 . 4 5 \mathrm { e V } ,$ which are indicative of their promising n-type characteristics (Figure 7.3) [27]. Among them, an NDI- and bithiophene-based copolymer (a.k.a. the benchmark n-type polymer, N2200), which opened a new era of n-type polymer research due to its highly electron mobility (Figure 7.4a) [6]. Since then, a large variety of NDI polymers have been designed and synthesized during the past decent. The performance of NDI polymers in all-PsCs has been steadily improved by optimizing polymer molecular weight, side-chain engineering, backbone modification, random copolymer strategy, etc. [28]. The PCEs of all-PSCs employing NDI polymers have achieved remarkable progress from below $3 \%$ in 2014 to approaching $1 2 \%$ in 2020, which has surpassed the state-of-the-art performance of fullerene OsCs. Recently, some new aromatic diimide-based polymer acceptors with distinct electron properties from NDI polymers have been developed and showed promising performances. In this section, we focus on some typically NDI and PDI polymers as well as emerging BTI polymer acceptors that have produced important advances in all-PSC performance and present guidelines for the design of polymer acceptor materials based on aromatic diimide toward high-performance all-PSCs.

![](images/44d1a588ee8510ffa9414999913de461afdf1e651d073d3229403adfdf5385c3.jpg)  
Figure 7.3 Synthesis of NDI polymers. Source: Guo and Watson [27]/ Reproduced with permission of American Chemical Society.

# 7.3.1.1 Molecular Design Strategy for N2200 Derivatives

Our discussion begins from the N2200, which is still one of the best-performing polymer acceptors in all-PsCs. In most cases where the chemical structures of NDI polymer are derived from the N2200. In 2011, Loi and coworkers pioneered the fabrication of all-PSCs based on N2200 and P3HT, and an only PCE of ${ < } 1 \%$ was obtained because of the poor polymer blend morphology and mobility [29]. Afterward, this development of all-PsCs was triggered by the invention of efficient benzodithiophene (BDT) polymer donors. For example, PTB7, PTB7-Th, PBDB-T, and J51. [30]. Recently, Huang and coworkers tailored the polymer donor with a siloxane-terminated side chain, which yields a PCE over $1 0 \%$ for the first time for all-PSCs [31]. Despite this, N2200 has high crystallinity and a strong tendency to aggregate, which always leads to a poor miscibility with donors and forms large domain. In this regard, side-chain engineering, heteroatom substitution, molecular-weight optimization, and random terpolymerization were the most successful strategies for the optimization of the crystallinity of NDI polymers and the blend morphology with various polymer donors.

![](images/d02ece33cc19847ddbe1dfd23e21bc3fde3d43f2290d31e20c9e253799435d2f.jpg)  
Figure 7.4hml sttre of rntative amatic dimide-d conjtd yrs bsd nD), D), ad BT. Surce: Huiliang Sun

![](images/82708ee743db514e3124bb7d1bdeb37a5cf60fdfb7b4a4ea66661e23f7c9d328.jpg)  
Figure 7.4 (Continued)

Among them, side-chain engineering strategy is a simple but effective approach for tuning the crystallinity and blend morphology of all-PsCs without influencing on light absorption and energy levels. In 2016, Kim and coworkers investigated the effects of side-chain engineering of N220o. A series of NDI-bithiophene copolymers (NDI-2T) with different side chains of 2-hexyldecyl (2HD), 2-octyldodecyl (2OD), and 2-decyltetradecyl (2DT) is synthesized (Figure 7.4a) [32]. The results demonstrated that polymer equipped with the shortest side chain exhibited the highest electron mobility of $1 . 9 0 \mathsf { c m } ^ { 2 } \mathsf { V } ^ { - 1 } \mathsf { s } ^ { - 1 }$ and the PCE of $6 . 1 1 \%$ among the three polymers due to tighter molecule packing with a face-on orientation. A similar trend was observed in analogous series of NDI-monothiophene copolymers (NDI-T) (Figure 7.4a) [33]. In addition, the branching point of the side chains of polymer acceptors is another important factor effecting the performance of all-PsCs. For example, moving the branching point away from the NDI and its derivatives-based polymers was shown by Kim group and Zhou group to reduce steric hindrance around the polymer backbone and thus enhance intermolecular interactions, contributing to improved PCE (Figure 7.4a) [34]. The crystallinity of NDI polymers has also been tuned by using the asymmetry side chains. For example, asymmetry side chains with different lengths were incorporated into the NDI-T backbone to give the polymers, P(NDIEHDT-T) and P(NDIBOOD-T) (Figure 7.4a) [35]. Benefiting from the fine-tuning crystallinity of these copolymers and improved blend morphology, an all-PSC based on P-(NDIBOOD-T) yields a PCE of $6 . 8 9 \%$

Random terpolymerization is another effective approach to achieving a delicate balance between crystallinity and miscibility. The pioneering study was reported by Jenekhe and coworkers in 2015 [36]. A new series of random terpolymers composed of the NDI-biselenophene parent copolymer NDI-Se with bulky PDI as the third component were designed and synthesized to improve the blend compatibility enabled by the highly crystallinity of NDI polymers. As a result, the PCE of all-PSC based on 30PDI ( $3 0 \%$ PDI moiety, Figure 7.4a) was increased up to $6 . 3 \%$ from that $( 1 . 2 3 \% )$ of the parent copolymer. Recently, another bulky 2,6-diisopropyl-phenyl also incorporated into side chain of NDI terpolymer to tune aggregation and crystallinity by Bao and coworkers. An optimized blend morphology for the polymer PNDI0.5-based all-PSCs result in a significantly improved PCE from $5 . 1 \%$ to $8 . 5 \%$ (Figure 7.4a) [37]. A certain quantity of T2 in N2200 was replaced with T by Wang and coworkers, affording a series of random terpolymers. The increase of the amount of $\mathrm { T }$ in terpolymer led to disorder in the polymer backbone and greatly reduced crystallinity. Consequently, PNDI-T10 $1 0 \%$ NDI moiety, Figure 7.4a) yields the best all-PSC performance in those terpolymer acceptors due to the better miscibility with polymer donor, leading to a high PCE of $7 . 6 \%$ (Figure 7.4a) [38]. Recently, a selenophene analog of PNDI-T10, BBS10 (Figure 7.4a). The BSS10-based All-PSC shows a high internal quantum efficiency of $9 7 \%$ and a small energy loss $( E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } )$ of $0 . 5 9 \mathrm { e V } ,$ leading to a remarkable PCE of $1 0 . 1 \%$ [39].

The random terpolymerization has also been carried out to tune the crystallinity and packing structure of polymer acceptors by incorporating functional groups on the side chains. For example, Chen and coworkers designed and synthesized new the N2200-based terpolymer PNDI-Si25 (Figure 7.4a) by increasing the $\mathrm { m o l } \%$ of siloxane-terminated side chains, leading to a desirable face-on packing orientation of the polymer backbone [4o]. An impressive PCE of $7 . 4 \%$ was attained in PNDI-Si25-based all-PSCs, which is higher than that of N2200. Recently, Huang and coworkers replaced a certain amount of the 2OD chain in N2200 with oligoethylene oxide (OE) chain to tune polymer packing structure and blend morphology. A resulting high PCE of $8 . 1 \%$ and a remarkable FF of 0.75 were attained by the polymer NOE10 ( $1 0 \%$ OE moiety, Figure 7.4a) [41].

# 7.3.1.2 Molecular Design Strategy for PDI Polymers

PDI polymers have received much attention as they possess many properties in common with NDI polymers including in high electron affinity and decent electron transport ability. In 2007, Zhan et al. synthesized the first PDI polymer acceptor (PDI-TT) (Figure 7.4b) [42], which triggers the development of PDI polymers in all-PSCs. Despite this, the high-performance all-PSCs based on PDI polymers have rarely been reported compared with the NDI polymers due to the more twisted backbone $( 5 0 ^ { \circ } - 7 0 ^ { \circ } )$ enabled by severe steric hindrance in the PDI bay region. Therefore, molecular design strategy of PDI polymers for all-PSCs is highly consistent with that of NDI polymers. For example, Hou and coworkers designed and synthesized copolymer PPDIODT (Figure 7.4b) based on the PDI and the small T unit in the polymer backbone, yielding a high PCE of $6 . 5 8 \%$ in all-PSCs [43]. To further reduce the steric hindrance, Zhao and coworkers incorporated vinylene linkers into the PDI polymer and thus improved backbone planarity. Thus, polymer PDI-V (Figure 7.4b) showed a relatively high PCE of $7 . 5 7 \%$ in all-PSCs, which is much higher than those of the linker-free ones [43]. Where after, the same group synthesized fused PDI-V-based polymer NDP-V (Figure 7.4b) to further improve the efficiency of the PDI-V via decreasing conformational disorder due to the reduced number of rotatable C-C bonds in the backbone. Combing with higher absorption coefficient and more complementary absorption spectra with the polymer donor, the record PCE of $8 . 5 9 \%$ among the PDI polymers was achieved [44]. At the same time, Zhang and coworkers also developed a series of NDP-based polymers and achieved impressive PCEs [45]. To date, NDP-based polymer is the most successful PDI polymer.

# 7.3.1.3 Molecular Design Strategy for BTI Polymers

Despite the NDI and PDI polymers being the most successful in all-PSCs, they suffer from some disadvantages. For example, their absorption coefficient in the long-wavelength region is relatively low, and the absorption range is limited due to the high steric hindrance associated with NDI and PDI core and hence twisted polymer backbone. This limits the absorption of light absorption and thus photocurrent. In addition, low-lying LUMO energy level $_ { ( 3 . 9 0 \mathrm { e V } ) }$ of NDI and PDI polymers typically results in increased $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ in all-PSC. Therefore, developing polymer acceptors beyond NDI and PDI polymers to address the issues inherited in typically polymer acceptors may have a significantly impact in the advancement of all-PSCs [6]. Among these new polymer acceptors, BTI polymers have a different electronic structure from those of classical NDI and PDI polymers, showing tunable LUMO levels because of their delocalized FMO along polymer backbones. Such feature is highly desirable for improving $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ in OSCs by minimizing the energy offsets between the polymer donor and acceptor, resulting in reducing $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ . In addition, the open $\beta$ -positions of thiophene rings in BTI provide opportunities for backbone expansion and structural modification (Figure 7.5) [46].

Thus, polymer acceptors based on BTI and its derivatives (BTIn) yielded significantly improved PCEs in all-PSCs from ${ < } 1 \%$ in 2017 to ${ \sim } 1 4 \%$ in 2020 with high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } } \mathrm { s }$ For example, Guo and coworkers reported two new BTI polymer acceptors, s-BTI2-FT and f-BTI2-FT, based on a single bond connected BTI unit and fused BTI unit, respectively. Benefiting from extended $\pi$ -conjugation backbone and increased film crystallinity, f-BTI2-FT (Figure 7.4c) shows a much higher PCE of $6 . 8 5 \%$ compared with that $( 0 . 0 7 \% )$ of s-BTI2-FT (Figure 7.4c) in all-PSCs [47]. The same group also designed and synthesized a series of triimide-functionalized polymers, f-BT13-T and f-BTI3-FT (Figure 7.4c). Compared with BTI2 polymers, the BTI3 polymers show a larger $\pi$ -conjugation and narrower bandgaps as well as lower FMO levels. As a result, an increase PCE of $8 . 9 8 \%$ is achieved for the f-BTI3-T-based all-PSCs, which surpass the control device based on fullerene as electron acceptor $( 8 . 6 9 \% )$ [48].

Fluorination can be used to further optimize the FMO levels and improve the film morphology. Moreover, F atoms can trigger various non-covalent interactions, which can be beneficial for a self-planarized backbone and thus charge transport. However, incorporating F atoms into highly electron-deficient building block is greatly challenging due to the reduced chemical reactivity along with steric hindrance. Recently, Sun et al. devised an effective synthetic route to the dibrominated monomer s-FBT12-Br by introducing F atoms first and then forming the imide functionality later, here, a novel thiophene derivative FE-T (Figure 7.5a) was designed and synthesized by overcoming the synthetic barrier, featuring a monothiophene unit functionalized with both an electron-withdrawing F atom and an ester group [49].

Based on FE-T, the first fluorinated BTI building block, s-FBTI2, was developed and the corresponding polymer acceptor s-FBTI2-FT (Figure 7.6b) delivers a dramatically increased PCE of $6 . 5 \%$ compared with s-BTI2-FT-based cell $( 0 . 0 7 \% )$ . The PCE of all-PSCs based on f-FBTI2-T was further improved to $8 . 1 \%$ without using any additives via a synergistic strategy based on ring fusion and fluorination. Besides fluorination strategy (Figure 7.7) [50], Osaka and coworkers designed and synthesized a novel electron-deficient building block, TzBI, where the external thiophenes in f-BTI2 were replaced by thiazoles. The incorporation of TzBI into polymer enabled the resulting polymer PTzBITT (Figure 7.4c) with deep LUMO energy levels and high backbone planarity. All-PSCs with polymer PTzBITT as the electron acceptor yielded a PCE of $3 . 3 \%$ [51].

The terpolymerization strategy has successfully optimized the chemical structures of NDI and PDI polymers. However, very few all-PSCs with terpolymer acceptors can achieve PCEs ${ > } 7 \%$ because the key principle in the molecular design of NDI-based terpolymers is to introduce a third component to suppress their over aggregation and crystallinity, which can improve their compatibility with polymer donors. However, the irregular backbone of random terpolymers negatively influences the planarity and therefore inhibits charge transport. In order to minimize such effects and optimize all-polymer blend film morphology, posttreatments such as solvent vapor annealing and additives are usually required. These optimized approaches complicate device fabrication. Compared with the imide-functionalized NDI and PDI, the sulfur atom in the BTIn can promote intramolecular non-covalent interactions between (thienyl)S and (carbonyl)O or between S and other heteroatom on the neighboring unit, which not only promotes backbone coplanarity but also helps form more ideal blend morphology (Figure 7.8b). Recently, Guo and coworkers first incorporate the non-covalent interaction into polymer acceptor by the terpolymerization strategy (Figure 7.8b) [52], using thienopyrroledione (TPD) and f-BTI2 as the two acceptor units and 3,4-difluorothiophene (FT) as the donor co-unit. Thanks to the non-covalent $\mathrm { S } { \cdot } \cdot \mathrm { O }$ interactions triggered by the TPD, incorporating an optimal TPD content into the polymer backbone enables circumvent the disadvantages of molecular packing induced by the irregular sequence in the random polymer. More importantly, an optimal TPD context leads to increased face-on packing structure and improved miscibility with the donors. As a result, the best-performance terpolymer acceptor 30TPD shows a high PCE of $8 . 2 8 \%$ without any additive. $8 . 2 8 \%$ is the highest value among the additive-free all-PSCs based on a random polymer acceptor to date, which is much higher than those from the two-parent copolymer acceptor $4 . 4 \%$ for TPD polymer and BTI polymer, respectively).

# 7.3.1.4 BTI Polymers for High-Performance All-PSCs with Smal $\pmb { E } _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$

It was found that $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of All-PSC is typically lower than $_ { 0 . 9 \mathrm { V } }$ even for the most efficient ones based on NDI and PDI polymers. Large $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ is the main reason for limiting $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and efficiency of all-PsCs. To this end, Sun et al. designed and synthesized two new BTI polymer acceptors SPA1 and SPA2 by combing the terpolymerization with side-chain engineering strategy. Benefiting from tunable LUMOs of BTI polymers, the $E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } }$ offset between SPA1 and the polymer donor negligible to maximize the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ , resulting in All-PSCs with a remarkable $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 1 5 \mathrm { V } .$ However, the EQE was significantly limited because of a low degree of electron transfer and considerable charge recombination enabled by negligible $E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } }$ offset. In contrast, SPA2 with relatively low-lying LUMO shows a large $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 0 2 \mathrm { V }$ and a high EQE over $7 0 \%$ in all-PSCs, resulting in a high PCE of $9 . 2 1 \%$ (Figure 7.9) [53]. More importantly, both all-PSCs based on BTI polymers have relatively high EQE of electroluminescence $( 1 0 ^ { - 3 } )$ , which are much higher than that $( 1 0 ^ { - 7 } )$ of the NDI polymers, suggesting a greatly low nonradiative recombination loss $( E _ { \mathrm { l o s s , n r } } )$ of ${ < } 0 . 3 \mathrm { e V } .$ This is comparable to that of the perovskite solar cells and has rarely been achieved in all-PSCs.

![](images/5aac63175cfaa44d877b065a4e19dcc083c55d5e517d40e4f550f0e814935c70.jpg)  
Figure 7.8 ) Chemica stuctures f imide-untionlized ares and heterores; ) Bn-based terlymrs acetor inoporating intrmolecula non-covalent sulfur-oxygen interactions for additive-free all-PSCs. Source: Huiliang Sun.

Taking advantages of BTI for reducing $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s , n r } }$ , very recently, the incorporation of BTI into fused-ring electron acceptor (FREA)-based polymer leads to a new narrow-bandgap polymer acceptor L14 [7], featuring an acceptor-acceptor (A-A) type backbone. L14 not only shows a narrow bandgap and high absorption coefficient but also low-lying frontier molecular orbital levels, resulting in improved electron transfer characteristics, and unexpectedly, without sacrificing open-circuit voltage $( V _ { \mathrm { o c } } )$ , which is attributed to a small nonradiative recombination loss of $0 . 2 2 \mathrm { e V }$ enabled by high $\mathrm { E Q E } _ { \mathrm { E L } }$ of BTI polymer. As a result, a remarkable PCE of $1 4 . 3 \%$ is achieved, which is higher and its D-A analogue and also among the highest values for all-PSCs (Figure 7.10).

# 7.3.2 Progress of Polymer Acceptors Containing $\mathsf { \pmb { B } } \gets \mathsf { \pmb { N } }$ Unit

In this part, we summarize the progress of polymer acceptors containing $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ unit. At first, we introduce the principle of $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ to downshift LUMO/HOMO energy levels $( E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } } / E _ { \mathrm { H O M O } } )$ of conjugated polymers. Then we discuss the molecular design of electron-deficient building block based on $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ unit for polymer acceptors. Finally, we summarize how to tune the optoelectronic properties and optimize the phase separation morphology of polymer acceptors containing $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ unit toward high-performance all-PSCs.

# 7.3.2.1 Principle of $\mathsf { B } \gets \mathsf { N }$ Unit

Low-lying $E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } } / E _ { \mathrm { H O M O } }$ are key requirements for polymer acceptors of all-PSCs. The principle of $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ to downshift $E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } } / E _ { \mathrm { H O M O } }$ is shown in Figure 7.11. Boron atom has the vacant p-orbital and the nitrogen atom with the lone pair electrons. The lone pair of electrons of the nitrogen atom occupies the vacant p-orbital of the boron atom, thus forming boron-nitrogen coordination bond $\mathrm { ( B } { \gets } \mathrm { N } )$ . In $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ unit, the nitrogen atom shows cationic character (positive charge) and the boron atom shows anionic character (negative charge). When $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ unit is embedded in a $\pi$ -conjugated system, the positive charge of the nitrogen atom can increase the static potential of the whole $\pi$ -system, leading to enhanced electron-deficient nature of the $\pi$ system. Therefore, the $\pi$ system shows down-shifted $E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } }$ and $E _ { \mathrm { H O M O } }$ $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ unit can be used as an effective strategy to design polymer acceptors with low-lying $E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } }$ and EHOMO

# 7.3.2.2 Electron-Deficient Building Blocks Based on $\mathsf { B } \gets \mathsf { N }$ Unit

Electron-deficient building blocks based on either one $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ unit or two $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ units have both been reported. As shown in Figure 7.12, the $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ bridged thienylthiazole (BNTT) is an electron-deficient building block containing one $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ unit. Since the electron-deficient capability of BNTT is not adequately strong, BNTT needs to be copolymerized with another electron-deficient building block (such as TPD, isoindigo (IID)) to give A-A-type polymer acceptors [55]. The double BNBP and the double $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ bridged 2,5-di(thiophen-2-yl)pyrazine (BNIDT) (see Figure 7.12) are electron-deficient building blocks containing two $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ units [9, 12]. The two $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ units lead to dramatic downshift of the $E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } }$ of the building blocks themselves and endow them with superior strong electron-deficient capability. Therefore, BNBP and BNIDT can be copolymerized with typical electron-donating building blocks to afford donor-acceptor (D-A)-type polymer acceptors.

# 7.3.2.3Optimizing ELUMO

$E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } }$ is a key parameter for polymer acceptors, which can greatly affect their applications in all-PSCs. For the classic polymer acceptors based on NDI unit, their $E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } }$ are always low and could not be effectively tuned. This is because the LUMO is localized on the NDI units and that the $E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } }$ is mainly decided by the NDI unit.

![](images/ca783a8a91f75a22371c335b5e51f5b82b76575a9e367ade06fbe33824d50dc0.jpg)  
Figure 7.13 (a) $E _ { \mathsf { L U M O } }$ alignments of eight polymers based on BNBP unit. Source: Long et al. [56] / Reproduced with permission of American Chemical Society.; (b) chemical structures of P-BNBP-T and P-BNBP-Se; (c) $E _ { \mathsf { L U M O } } / E _ { \mathsf { H O M O } }$ alignment of P-BNBP-T and P-BNBP-Se. Source: Yingjian $\mathsf { Y } _ { \mathsf { U } }$ ; (d) chemical structure of P-BNBP-fBT and $J - V$ curve of the device based on the active layer of PTB7-Th:P-BNBP-fBT. Source: Long et al. [57]/ Reproduced with permission of John Wiley $\&$ Sons.

In comparison, polymer acceptors based on BNBP unit show delocalized LUMOs over the polymer backbones. Therefore, their $E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } }$ can be effectively tuned and optimized by changing the copolymerization units. Figure 7.13a shows eight D-A-type conjugated polymers with the same backbone but different substitutes on the A unit (BNBP unit) or the D unit (bithiophene unit). Their $E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } }$ are finely tuned within a wide range from $- 3 . 3 \mathrm { e V }$ to $- 3 . 7 \mathrm { e V }$ by changing the substitutes on the D units and the A units. The tunable $E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } }$ of polymer acceptors leads to open-circuit voltage as high as $1 . 0 { - } 1 . 3 \mathrm { V }$ in all-PSCs [56]. For example, P-BNBP-Se (Figure 7.13b), a copolymer of the BNBP unit and selenophene unit, exhibits the $E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } }$ of $- 3 . 6 6 \mathrm { e V } ,$ which is lower by $0 . 1 6 \mathrm { e V }$ than that of the copolymer of the BNBP unit and thiophene unit (P-BNBP-T). As a result, the energy levels of P-BNBP-Se match well with the widely used polymer donor PTB7-Th. The device of P-BNBP-Se shows a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of up to $1 . 0 3 \mathrm { V } .$ While the all-PSC device based on the

PTB7-Th:P-BNBP-T blend shows a PCE of $2 . 2 7 \%$ , the corresponding device with P-BNBP-Se as the acceptor exhibited an enhanced PCE of $4 . 2 6 \%$ [58].

An outstanding polymer acceptor is the copolymer of BNBP unit and $^ { 3 , 3 ^ { \prime } }$ -difluoro$^ { 2 , 2 ^ { \prime } }$ -bithiophene (fBT) unit (P-BNBP-fBT, see Figure 7.13d). The electron-deficient fluoro substitutes of the fBT unit can lower the $E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } }$ Of the polymer. As a result, all-PSCs with P-BNBP-fBT as the acceptor and PTB7-Th as the donor show $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of as high as $1 . 0 6 \mathrm { V } _ { : }$ PCE of $6 . 2 6 \%$ at the photon energy loss $( E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } )$ of only 0.51 eV [57].

# 7.3.2.4Tuning Absorption Spectra

Polymer acceptors should have small optical bandgaps and wide absorption spectra, which improve sunlight harvesting of all-PSCs. The absorption spectra of polymer acceptors based on $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ unit could be effectively tuned and optimized by changing the copolymerization units. Their bandgaps could be tuned in the wide range of $1 . 5 { \mathrm { - } } 1 . 9 { \mathrm { e V } } .$ For example, P-BNBP-T (Figure 7.14a), a copolymer of BNBP unit and thiophene unit, shows narrow absorption spectra with the absorption peak at $6 2 2 \mathrm { n m }$ and a medium bandgap of $1 . 9 2 \mathrm { e V } .$ When the copolymerization unit is substituted by the thiophene-flanked diketopyrrolopyrrole (DPP) unit, the bandgap of P-BNBP-DPP is decreased to $1 . 5 6 \mathrm { e V } .$ P-BNBP-DPP exhibits a broad absorption band from 500 to $8 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . The maximum absorption wavelength is $7 6 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , which is red shifted by c. $1 4 9 \mathrm { n m }$ compared with that of P-BNBP-T [59].

Indoor photovoltaic (IPV) cells have recently received great attention because of their promising applications as power sources for devices of the Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem. As shown in Figure 7.15b, the indoor artificial light sources, such as white light emitting diodes (LEDs) and fluorescent lamps (FLs), exhibit emission spectra mainly in the narrow wavelength region from 400 to $6 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . Medium bandgap is a basic requirement for polymer acceptors for IPV applications. According to the empirical prediction, the ideal bandgap of photoactive materials for IPVs is $1 . 9 { - } 2 . 0 \mathrm { e V } .$ PBN-10 shows a medium optical bandgap of $1 . 9 5 \mathrm { e V } ,$ which is ideal for IPV applications. The all-polymer photovoltaic device based on PBN-10 shows a high PCE of $2 7 . 4 \%$ at a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 1 6 \mathrm { V }$ under FL illumination of $2 0 0 0 \mathrm { { l x } }$ [11]. This result indicates that polymer acceptors based on $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ units are very suitable for IPV applications.

# 7.3.2.5 Enhancing Electron Mobility

For polymer acceptors, high electron mobilities $\left( \mu _ { \mathrm { e } } \right)$ are necessary for efficient electron transport and consequently for the all-PsC device performance. The all-PSC device performance of P-BN-TPD (Figure 7.16a) is very poor because of its very low electron mobility. This is attributed to the steric hindrance of the pendant bulky phenyl groups on the boron atom, which prevent close $\pi$ stacking of conjugated polymer backbones. The steric hindrance effect of the pendant phenyl groups can be alleviated by extending the length of the repeating units. IID unit is much longer than the TPD unit. As shown in Figure 7.16b, when using IID unit to replace TPD as the copolymerization unit, the length of the repeating unit increases from 1.24 to $1 . 9 5 \mathrm { n m }$ in DFT-optimized molecular configurations $( \mathrm { B } 3 \mathrm { L Y P } / 6 { - } 3 1 \mathrm { G } ^ { * } )$ . While P-BN-TPD shows the $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking distance $( d _ { \pi - \pi } )$ of the polymer backbones of $4 . 6 \mathring \mathrm { A }$ P-BN-IID exhibits decreased $d _ { \pi - \pi }$ of $3 . 8 \mathring \mathrm { A }$ indicating improved compact stacking of the polymer backbones. As a result, the $\mu _ { \mathrm { e } }$ is enhanced by nearly two orders of magnitude from $3 . 4 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 7 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ of P-BN-TPD to $2 . 8 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ (estimated with the SCLC method). The resulting PCE of the all-PSC devices is enhanced from $0 . 1 2 \%$ of P-BN-TPD to $5 . 0 4 \%$ of P-BN-IID [55].

![](images/dd74c3c26e5367ee7ae4e6f449a2f80747ce73208fa545c78e0bd76c159581f7.jpg)  
Figure 7.16 (a) Chemical structures of P-BN-TPD and P-BN-IID; (b) optimized molecular configurations of the repeating units of P-BN-TPD and P-BN-IID; (c) J-V curves of devices based on the active layers of PTB7-Th:P-BN-TPD and PTB7-Th:P-BN-IID. Source: Zhao et al. [55] / Reproduced with permission of John Wiley & Sons.

The "conjugated side chain' strategy, which is always used in molecular design of polymer donors, has also been used to enhance $\mu _ { \mathrm { e } }$ of polymer acceptors containing. $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ units. Figure 7.17 shows the chemical structures of P-BNBPp-T with conjugated alkyloxyphenyl side chain and the reference polymer P-BNBP-T with typical alkyl side chain. The $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking distance of P-BNBPP-T $( d _ { \pi - \pi } = 3 . 6 3 \mathring \mathrm { A } )$ with conjugated side chains was smaller than that of P-BNBP-T $( d _ { \pi - \pi } = 3 . 8 1 \mathring \mathrm { A } )$ . Because of the smaller $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking distance, the electron mobility of P-BNBPP-T $( \mu _ { \mathrm { e } } = 3 . 2 4 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 } )$ is higher than that of P-BNBP-T $( \mu _ { \mathrm { e } } = 7 . 1 6 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 } )$ by about five times. The enhancement of $\mu _ { \mathrm { e } }$ contributes to the PCE increase of the resulting all-PSC [60].

# 7.3.2.6 Optimizing Active Layer Morphology

For efficient charge separation and charge transporting, ideal active layer morphology of all-PsCs should be bicontinuous interpenetrating network with high phase purity and phase domain size of c. $2 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . Many factors influence active layer morphology of all-PsCs, such as crystallinity of polymers and aggregation tendency of polymer chains in solution. Figure 7.18 shows the chemical structures, two-dimensional (2D) grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (2D-GIWAXS) patterns of P1 and PBN-12. PBN-12 shows the (100) and (200) reflection peaks in the out-of-plane direction and a strong (010) $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking peak in both the in-plane and out-of-plane directions. However, P1 exhibits a (1o0) reflection peak in the out-of-plane direction and no obvious (010) $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking peak in both the in-plane and out-of-plane directions, suggesting that the crystallinity of PBN-12 film is much stronger than that of P1 film. In the film-forming process, the competition of crystallization of CD1 and PBN-12 leads to small-size phase separation and consequent excellent photovoltaic performance of the CD1:PBN-12 active layer [10].

![](images/7c7e441f4bb91adab22cdd47534a16a64f3b085b99a2baddd7664b95ce263720.jpg)  
Figure 7.18(a) Chemical structures of P1 and PBN-12; (b and c) 2D-GIWAXS patterns of P1 and PBN-12; (d and e) TEM images of CD1:P1 and CD1:PBN-12. Source: Zhao et al. [10] / Reproduced with permission of American Chemical Society.

It is difficult to manipulate active layer morphology of all-PsCs by conventional methods, such as thermal annealing, solvent annealing, and solvent additive. During all-PsC device fabrication, the regular method is to dissolve the polymer donor and the polymer acceptor together (DT method). Liu and coworkers reported an approach to improve active morphology of all-PSCs by dissolving polymer donor and polymer acceptor individually and then blending them immediately before spin-coating (DI method). The active layer with the DI method shows enhanced polymer ordering and higher domain purity than those with the DT method. This is due to the partially preserved polymer aggregates from solution. As the result, the PCE is enhanced from $5 . 3 6 \%$ to $7 . 0 9 \%$ [61]. Active layer morphology of all-PSCs based on CD1:PBN-12 blend can also be optimized by controlling the solution temperature for spin coating. With the solution temperature increasing from 30 to $9 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , the crystallinity of the polymer donor and the polymer acceptor in the active layer becomes stronger and the phase separation size becomes smaller. Consequently, the PCE of the all-PSC devices is enhanced from $7 . 7 8 \%$ to $1 0 . 0 4 \%$ Further increase of solution temperature to $1 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ leads to decreased device efficiency. The effect of solution temperature on the phase-separation morphology of all-PsCs can be explained by the increased diffusion rate of the polymer chains in the film-forming process and the disaggregation of polymer chains in solution at high temperature [62] (Figure 7.19).

![](images/40668e9f212052743f1f2d2868733caf5d3b2f121d844a821b7055176d086e6b.jpg)  
Figure 7.192D-GlWAXS patterns (top) and AFM height images (down) of CD1:PBN-12 blend films with different solution temperatures. Source: Wang et.al. [62] / Reproduced with permission of American Chemical Society.

Most of the all-PsC devices based on polymer acceptors containing $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ unit suffer from low FF. Recently, Huang and coworkers reported a new polymer acceptor, BN-2fT. All-PSC device based on BN-2fT as the acceptor and PBDB-T as the donor show an outstanding FF of $7 0 . 4 \%$ possibly due to the excellent active layer morphology [12].

# 7.3.3 Progress of Polymer Acceptors Bearing Cyano Groups

Cyano group is a very strong electron-withdrawing substituent and has been used to design polymer acceptors with excellent all-PSC device performance. As shown in Figure 7.20, Guo and coworkers reported a narrow-bandgap polymer acceptor DCNBT-IDT based on 5,6-dicyano-2,1,3-benzothiadiazole (DCNBT) building block. DCNBT-IDT shows the low $E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } }$ of $- 3 . 7 5 \mathrm { e V } ,$ a narrower bandgap of $1 . 4 3 \mathrm { e V } ,$ and a relatively high maximum absorption coefficient of $6 . 1 5 \times 1 0 ^ { 4 } \mathrm { { c m } ^ { - 1 } }$ . The all-PSC device with DCNBT-IDT as the polymer acceptor and PBDB-T as the polymer donor gave an outstanding PCE of $8 . 3 2 \%$ with a photoresponse of up to $8 7 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [63]. In order to further extend the photoresponse wavelength, Guo and coworkers modified the chemical structure of DCNBT-IDT to design DCNBT-TPIC with ultra-narrow bandgap. The indacenodithiophene (IDT) group in DCNBT-IDT is replaced by the more electron-donating carbon-oxygen-bridged ladder-type unit in DCNBT-TPIC. DCNBT-TPIC shows an optical bandgap of $1 . 2 8 \mathrm { e V }$ due to strong ICT character between the highly electron-deficient unit DCNBT and the highly electron-rich 5,5,11,11-tetraoctyl-5,11-dihydrothieno $[ 2 ^ { \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime } ; 5 , 6 ]$ pyrano[3,4-g]thieno-[3,2-c]isochromene (TPIC) unit. The all-PSC device based on DCNBT-TPIC exhibits a PCE of $1 0 . 2 2 \%$ with the short-circuit current density of up to $2 2 . 5 2 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and photoresponse of up to $9 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [64].

Another strategy to design polymer acceptors is to use small molecular electron acceptors (SMAs) as building blocks to construct conjugated polymers. Many SMAs, in which an electron-donating core unit is endcapped with two cyano-based groups, have been reported. Organic solar cells based on these SMAs show PCE of higher than $1 5 \% - 1 8 \%$ [65-68]. Li and coworkers firstly reported the approach to polymerize SMAs to synthesize polymer acceptors. The resulting polymer acceptors preserve the merits of the SMAs, such as proper energy levels, narrow bandgaps, high absorption coefficients, and high electron mobilities, and consequently exhibit excellent all-PSC device performance. As shown in Figure 7.21, Li and coworkers synthesized a polymer acceptor PZ1 with IDIC16 as the key building block and thiophene as the linking unit. PZ1 exhibits a broad absorption band with a narrow bandgap of $1 . 5 5 \mathrm { e V }$ and high absorption coefficient $( 1 . 3 \times 1 0 ^ { 5 } \mathrm { c m ^ { - 1 } } ,$ . Compared with its corresponding SMA, IDIC-C16, the absorption spectrum of PZ1 in thin film is red shifted by c. $5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . The $E _ { \mathrm { H O M O } }$ and the $E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } }$ of PZ1 are slightly up-shifted than those of IDIC-C16 by 0.08 and $0 . 0 4 \mathrm { e V } .$ respectively. The all-PSC device with PZ1 as acceptor and PBDB-T as donor achieved a high PCE of $9 . 1 9 \%$ [69]. By optimizing the polymer donors to match with PZ1, the PZ1-based all-PSC shows a PCE of as high as $1 1 . 2 \%$ which is among the highest values for the all-PSCs in 2019 [70].

Following the molecular design strategy of PZ1, a series of polymer acceptors have been developed. Yan and coworkers reported a polymer acceptor PFBDT-IDTIC by replacing the thiophene linker in PZ1 by BDT unit. PFBDT-IDTIC exhibits a high absorption coefficient of $2 . 7 4 \times 1 0 ^ { 5 } \mathrm { c m ^ { - 1 } }$ . All-PSCs based on PFBDT-IDTIC as the polymer acceptor and PM6 as the polymer donor gave a PCE of $1 0 . 3 \%$ [71]. As shown in Figure 7.20, Wang and coworkers reported a series of polymer acceptors PF2-DTC, PF2-DTSi, and PF2-DTGe with the same IDIC16 building block as acceptor unit but different central bridging atoms in donor units. Among the three polymers, PF2-DTSi exhibits the highest PCE of $1 0 . 7 7 \%$ due to its improved exciton dissociation, charge transport, and optimized morphology [72]. Wang and coworkers also reported a non-conjugated polymer acceptor PF1-TS4 (Figure 7.20) with the IDIC16 building block as acceptor unit and a thioalkyl segment as the donor unit. PF1-TS4 shows a narrow bandgap of $1 . 5 8 \mathrm { e V }$ and a high absorption coefficient of $1 . 2 5 \times 1 0 ^ { 5 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ . The PF1-TS4-based all-PSC device shows a PCE of $8 . 6 3 \%$ with excellent morphological stability under thermal annealing [73].

The development of Y6-type SMAs, which was initially reported by Zou and coworkers, leads to further enhancement of OSCs [74]. Y6-type SMAs have the great advantage of strong light absorption in the near-infrared region and small photon energy loss. To take advantage of Y6-type SMAs, several groups devoted to development of polymer acceptors based on Y6-type SMAs. As shown in Figure 7.22, Huang and coworkers reported a novel polymer acceptor PJ1 with a narrow bandgap of $1 . 4 \mathrm { e V }$ and a high absorption coefficient $( 1 . 3 9 \times 1 0 ^ { 5 } \mathrm { c m ^ { - 1 } } )$ at high molecular weight. PJ1 is an alternating copolymer of TTPBT-IC unit and thiophene unit. When PJ1 is blended with a polymer donor PBDB-T, the all-PSC device shows a high PCE as high as $1 4 . 4 \%$ . The authors found that the molecular weights of PJ1 play an important role in the optoelectronic properties, active layer morphology, and all-PSC device performance [75].

Guo and coworkers designed a new A-A-type polymer acceptor L14 (Figure 7.20) by copolymerizing brominated TTPBT-IC unit with another electron-deficient distannylated BTI (BTI-Tin) unit. L14 exhibits a narrow bandgap of $1 . 3 9 \mathrm { e V } _ { \mathrm { i } }$ a high absorption coefficient of $1 . 4 4 \times 1 0 ^ { 5 } \mathrm { c m ^ { - 1 } }$ , and a very small nonradiative recombination loss $( E _ { \mathrm { l o s s , n r } } )$ of $0 . 2 2 \mathrm { e V } .$ When L14 is blended with polymer donor PM6, all-PSC device with a high PCE of $1 4 . 3 \%$ is achieved [7].

# 7.4 Device Performance and Stability of All-PSCs

# 7.4.1 Morphology Optimization and Device Engineering

The BHJ morphology improvement of all-polymer blends is one of the core reasons for the recent success of all-PsCs. In general, there are two major challenges in controlling the all-polymer blend morphologies: (i) demixing of crystalline D-A polymer domains; (ii) tuning polymer packing orientation at D-A interfaces. The development of efficient p-type and n-type conjugated polymers demonstrated how changing the chemical structures of donor and acceptor polymer translates to desirable morphologies. However, it is necessary to gain insight into the correlation between processing conditions and BHJ morphologies of all-PSCs, which in turn will not only aid the further molecular design, but also establish general guidelines for fabricating desired all-polymer blends.

![](images/9cbdaba2589ec10d86f7edda68dd0abc7ce3ae58be34ebbee670feb2aa76bc74.jpg)  
Figure 7.23 Spin-coating process of all-polymer BHJ blend and further thermal treatment. Source: Jianyu Yuan.

For the polymer/fullerene system, optimizing the processing conditions of devices to achieve the desired active layer morphology is critical. A number of processing techniques, such as mixed solvents, additives, as well as thermal and solvent annealing, have been explored to control the bulk morphology to attain multiple structural requirements [76]. Among those reported processing approaches, thermal annealing and solvent additives are considered to be the most effective and versatile approaches as illustrated in Figure 7.23. In general, thermal annealing at temperatures beyond the glass-transition temperatures of donor or acceptor polymers will produce thermally induced morphology modifications and crystallizations in blend films as well as improvements of interfaces between active layers and electrodes [77]. Meanwhile, morphology control of the nanoscale structure of phase separation and polymer ordering in a blend film can be controlled through additive processing. Additives usually have a high boiling point and possess selective solubility to one of the active materials [16]. The addition of these additives can usually simultaneously enhance the light absorption and charge carrier mobility as well as suppress charge recombination, which contribute to higher $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and FF, ultimately enhancing the PCE. However, in all-PsCs, the morphology evolution after thermal annealing or use of additive is far less explored compared with that in polymer-fullerene solar cells. More importantly, the use of thermal annealing or additive process alone in general only allows for rudimentary morphology control.

The polymer acceptors with large planar structures such as NDI and PDI have stronger inter-chain interactions, which make their morphology more susceptible to posttreatment compared with the small molecules. In the system of N2200 based all-PsCs, we found that devices at the optimal annealing temperature of $1 6 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ exhibit over $3 0 \%$ enhanced PCE compared with those without any thermal treatment [78]. In addition, we also demonstrated widely adopted 1,8-di(R)octane $\mathrm { \Delta R = C l }$ , Br, and I) additives can be applied to multiple all-polymer devices with improved efficiency due to their general capability to increase the crystallinity and extend the effective time of film formation during deposition [17]. Interestingly, DBrO outperforms the widely used DIO in polymer-fullerene-based devices, obtaining a highest efficiency of $8 . 2 3 \%$ for the PTzBI/P(NDI2OD-T2)-based all-PSCs. In contrast, the addition of chloronaphthalene (CN) can alleviate the inter-chain interaction of polymers to prevent the formation of oversized domains, which make it especially efficient for systems using strongly aggregated polymers such as N2200. It is well known that BHJ morphology is superior to planar structure in organic solar cells. However, we first revealed that the P-i-N structure (planar heterojunction) can outperform the BHJ ones with a nearly $5 0 \%$ efficiency improvement in all-PSCs, reaching a PCE approaching $1 0 \%$ [22]. This planar structure can also provide an enhanced internal electric field and remarkably stable morphology under harsh thermal stress. We have further demonstrated generality of the P-i-N structure in several other all-polymer systems and revealed the improved charge generation in the P-i-N structured all-polymer blend [79]. Considering the adjustable polymer molecular weight and solubility, the P-i-N device structure can be more beneficial for all-polymer systems.

Researchers primarily focused on seeking an all-polymer pair that has desirable electrical properties and matched BHJ blend morphology. Engineering light absorption of all-polymer active layer (as shown in Figure 7.24) was relatively less explored in the early stages. Due to the intrinsically narrow absorption window of organic materials and the low thickness of all-polymer film, most binary all-PSCs utilize a relatively limited portion of sunlight. Therefore, ternary and tandem all-PSCs, which contain extra absorbing component, have been exploited as attractive approaches for broadening the absorption coverage of the active layers. The ternary approach, categorized into three classes: (i) two donors/one acceptor; (ii) one donor/two acceptors; and (iii) donor/acceptor/nonvolatile small-molecule additive, has similar simplicity in device fabrication, achieved by one-step solution processing [80, 81]. However, the introduction of the third component often has some effects on the carrier dynamics of all-PsCs, such as charge separation and transport, by altering the energy level alignment and morphology. Therefore, careful selection of the ternary components is critical for simultaneous optimization of all the photovoltaic parameters.

Tandem structure has been widely reported for enhancing the PCE in polymer-fullerene solar cells for better utilization of the solar spectrum. By using polymers with complementary absorption, tandem cell can extend the device absorption to the near-infrared region, covering significantly more solar spectrum. Meanwhile, the potential loss during photo-to-electron conversion process can be reduced by using tandem structure [82]. We reported an improved all-polymer tandem with a PCE of $8 . 3 \%$ [21], using complementary absorber layers for the first time in all-PSCs. A newly synthesized ternary conjugated polymer, PBFSF (bandgap of $1 . 5 5 \mathrm { e V } ,$ , was used as the donor and N2200 as the acceptor in the back cell. For the front cell, a pair of wide-bandgap polymers PTP8 (bandgap of $1 . 8 0 \mathrm { e V } )$ and P(NDI2HD-T) (bandgap of $1 . 8 5 \mathrm { e V } ,$ were used. Interestingly, homo tandem structures were also constructed to improve device absorption. Note that the optimal thickness of all-PSCs is usually around $1 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ since the carrier mobility of organic materials is relatively low, which thus limits the overall film absorption between $6 0 \%$ and $8 0 \%$ . Tandem structure with sub-cells using the same blend can equivalently double the film thickness. We reported a homo all-PsCs tandem structure using P2F-DO/N2200 blend. An improved PCE of $6 . 7 0 \%$ was achieved for the tandem device, which is over $4 3 \%$ higher than the $4 . 6 8 \%$ PCE of the optimized single cell [82]. In 2018, another homo tandem adopting PTzBI-Si as donor and N2200 as acceptor was reported. The tandem cell demonstrated an improved overall absorption according to the increased $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ , affording a PCE of $1 1 \%$ [31], while $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and FF were in agreement with the results of the single junction cell.

# 7.4.2 The Enhanced Stability of All-PSCs

The long-term stability of OPVs largely determines the prospect for future commercialization. In the past a few years, lots of efforts have been dedicated to improving stability of PSCs. And the stability of all-PSCs and polymer-PCBM systems has been compared. Through these investigations, as shown in Figure 7.25, it was found that the fullerene-based thin film exhibits thermal or photo-induced morphological instability due to the undesired endurance of environmental stress and fast molecular diffusion relative to the all-polymer blend [83]. In this section, we will discuss the long-term stability of all-PSCs under different situations such as thermal stress, ambient conditions, mechanical stress, and illumination (see Figure 7.4).

# 7.4.2.1 Thermal Stability

We first conducted a comparative study on two high-performance non-fullerene BHJ blends based on PBDBT:ITIC and PBDBT:N2200, with continuous heating at $8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in the $\Nu _ { 2 }$ glovebox without any encapsulation over 70 days [84]. It was found that the efficiency of PBDB-T:ITIC device deteriorated quickly to $7 6 \%$ of its initial value and further down to $5 4 \%$ . In contrast, the PBDB-T:N2200 all-PSCs showed significantly improved thermal stability with less than $1 0 \%$ PCE degradation after 1700 hours aging. More interestingly, we also reported that all-PsCs demonstrated high tolerance on $\mathrm { D } / \mathrm { A }$ blend ratios in comparison with the small molecular-based nonfullerene solar cells. These results indicate that the variation of blend composition has less effect on all-PsCs performance, which is ideal for large-area devices. Cao and coworkers first reported all-PSCs based on PTzBI-Si:N2200 with high efficiency over $1 0 \%$ . Meanwhile, the PTzBI-Si:N2200 all-polymer blend exhibits excellent thermal stability [31], the device retained over $9 5 \%$ of its initial efficiency after continuous exposure at $8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ In addition, by introducing PNDIT-F3N as an interfacial cathode layer, they reported homo tandem all-PsCs with a record PCE over $1 1 \%$ and remarkable stability, remaining $9 3 \%$ of the initial efficiency after thermally annealing at $8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 1o00hours. Quite recently, we reported efficient all-PsCs using a P-i-N planner structure, which still exhibited decent performance under continuous thermal stresses at a higher temperature of $1 6 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for nearly 1o00 hours, indicating exceptional stable morphology even under a harsh environment for these all-polymer blends [22]. The thermal stability originates from the innate properties of conjugated polymers, that is, low diffusion coefficients against aggregation. In contrast, heat promotes the fast diffusion and aggregation of small molecules, resulting in poor phase separation morphology.

# 7.4.2.2 Ambient Stability

Ambient stability of PsCs is desired for large-scale manufacturing of PV devices, considering the continuous exposure to ambient condition during printing process. In this regard, it was anticipated that the use of conjugated polymers would improve morphological stability under ambient condition due to their much more stable chemical structures. We reported superior ambient processability and stability of all-PSCs over fullerene-PSCs in 2019 [85], through a direct comparison of two N2200-based all-PSCs and fullerene-PSCs. In order to control the ambient humidity, we used an air glove box with controllable humidity. We chose two donors PBDB-T and PTzBI blended with PCBM or N2200. Different BHJ blends are tolerant of moisture to different extents. PCBM-based blends are effective under humidity from $0 \%$ to $2 0 \%$ , while all-polymer blends exhibit unprecedentedly stable performance (best PCE approaching $9 \%$ ) under humidity from $0 \%$ up to $8 0 \%$ . We also conducted a long-term air stability characterization of unencapsulated all-PSCs, which exhibited excellent stability aged at ambient condition ${ \sim } 2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ relative humidity: $2 0 \%$ These findings demonstrate that all-PsCs can achieve high device performance with ambient processing and show excellent long-term stability against oxygen and moisture, which situate them in an advantageous position for practical large-scale production of OSCs.

# 7.4.2.3 Mechanical Stability

To realize portable and wearable devices for real-life applications and endure various forms of mechanical stresses during the coating process such as roll-to-roll printing, mechanical integrity is an essential prerequisite of PSCs. In this regard, researchers have devoted significant efforts to examining the mechanical properties of photoactive materials for PSCs over the past decade. Unfortunately, the reported conventional fullerene-PSCs exhibited poor mechanical durability due to the stiffness of the

PCBM clusters. In 2015, Kim and coworkers first compared the mechanical properties between all-PSCs and fullerene-PSCs based on PBDTT-TPD:P(NDI2HD-T) and PBDTT-TPD:PCBM blends, respectively [86]. They investigated the tensile characteristics of the BHJ films through conducting a pseudo free-standing tensile test with a bar-shaped specimen, designed to exclude substrate effects and avoid complicated calculations. The elongation at break of the all-polymer blend $( 7 . 1 6 \% )$ was 60 times higher than that $( 0 . 1 2 \% )$ of the PCBM blend. The toughness of the all-polymer blend $( 5 6 8 . 7 \mathrm { J } \mathrm { m } ^ { - 3 } )$ was 470 times higher than that $( 1 . 2 \mathrm { J } \mathrm { m } ^ { - 3 } ) ,$ of the PCBM blend. These outstanding results obtained from the PBDTT-TPD:P(NDI2HD-T) blends originated from intrinsic ductility of the polymers, the presence of tie chains and entanglements to yield strengthened interfaces within the active layer films. Although the superior mechanical properties of all-polymer blends over fullerene-polymer blends have been clearly demonstrated, the mechanical properties of the real all-PsCs should be examined in the future. Until now, stretchable device fabrication without using prepatterned substrates is very limited due to the difficulty in integrating all the ductile components of the electrode, interlayer, and substrate into the device. In addition, Intrinsic properties of conjugated polymers, such as chemical structure (i.e. rigid backbones and flexible side chains), molecular weight, dispersity, and thin-film morphology (i.e. phase separation and molecular packing structure), must be correlated with the mechanical properties of the corresponding all-PSCs [87].

# 7.4.2.4 Photostability

Stability under long-term solar irradiation should be guaranteed in all kinds of solar cells since exposure to light is inevitable during the operation of these devices. Lots of previous reports have demonstrated that the photo-degradation mechanism of fullerene-PSCs is due to the chemical instability of fullerene derivatives under irradiation stress [88]. This feature would lead to the formation of energetic traps and thus cause the reduction of charge generation and carrier mobility. The superior chemical stability of the ND1/PDI building blocks is attributed to their low-lying LUMO energy levels and can enable the fabrication of photo-stable all-PsCs. A systematical study on P(ND12HD-T) and PCBM acceptors blending with the same polymer donor PBDTTPD was performed by Kim and coworkers [89], aiming to gain insight into their chemical stability under illumination in $\Nu _ { 2 }$ atmosphere. The two systems both exhibited similar initial PCE around $4 \%$ and pre-stored in high vacuum for more than 12 hours to maximally remove remaining solvents and additives to minimize their adverse effect on device stability. The encapsulated devices were exposed to 100 hours light irradiation under $\Nu _ { 2 }$ , as it was observed, the PCE of PBDTTPD:PCBM polymer-fullerene system decreased rapidly to $5 0 \%$ of the initial value for the first 12 hours and then slightly reduced for the next 80 hours. In contrast, the PBDTTPD:P(NDI2HD-T) system showed significantly improved photo-stability after 100 hours illumination, keeping $8 0 \%$ of its initial device PCE. The TAS and SCLC measurement showed that the polaron yield deceased significantly and then created trapped states near the $\mathrm { D } / \mathrm { A }$ interface in PCBM involved blend. While the P(ND12HD-T) remained stable nearly for 24 hours illumination, mainly benefitting from its superior endurance against photo-illumination. While these findings show case the potential of photo-stable all-PsCs, the photo-stability of only a few all-PSCs has been examined. Therefore, more assessments on different all-polymer blend systems are required to develop an in-depth understanding of the photo-degradation mechanism in all-PSCs.

# 7.5 Conclusion and Outlook

In conclusion, great progress with the PCE improved from ${ \sim } 5 \%$ to over $1 5 \%$ has been achieved through the invention and application of NDI, $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ and ITIC-based polymer acceptors for all-PSCs. To further enhance the PV performance to realize large-scale commercialization, continuous exploration of new classes of conjugated polymers is required [9o]. In particular, developing polymeric acceptors with suitable light absorption, superior charge-carrier mobility, and minimal voltage loss remains very important. Meanwhile, further optimizing the polymeric donor to match up with these acceptors is also critical. Along with materials development, the enhancement of the PV performance in all-PSCs is closely related to desirable active layer morphologies and defined device architecture. Relative to fullerene and small molecule-based solar cells, the construction of efficient P-i-N, ternary and tandem structure in all-PsCs is less explored, which is important for achieving higher PCEs. In addition to the enhancement of efficiency in all-PsCs, further exploration of the stability is urgent. In the past several years, lots of pioneering efforts have demonstrated that all-PsCs possess superior thermal, ambient, mechanical, and photo stabilities over fullerene or small molecule-based solar cells. In this regard, all-PsCs have been considered as a promising long-term source to power the mechanically robust electronic devices. In future research, the interplay between molecular structure and stability in all-PsCs should be extensively investigated to open new avenues for designing conjugated polymers that exhibit commercially viable stability. Last but not least, lab-to-market transition of all-PSCs should be promoted in the near future. All-PsCs now become a promising young candidate in all kinds of OPV technologies and gain worldwide interests due to their exceptional stability. Nonetheless, several challenges still remain, and collaborations between academia and industry will be increasingly necessary to eventually realize the application of all-PSCs.

# Organic Solar Cells with High Open-Circuit Voltage >1 V

Ailing Tang1, Yuze Lin?, and Erjun Zhou1

1National Center for Nanoscience and Technology, CAS Center for Excellence in Nanoscience, CAS Key Laboratory of Nanosystem and Hierarchical Fabrication, No. 11 Zhongguancun BeiYiTiao, Beijing, 100190, P.R. China 2 Institute of Chemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing National Laboratory for Molecular Sciences, CAS Key Laboratory of Organic Solids, No. 2 Zhongguancun North First Street, Beijing, 100190, PR. China

# 8.1 Introduction

Recently, the innovative development of photovoltaic materials has promoted rapid progress of the organic solar cells (OsCs), and now the power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) have reached over $1 8 \%$ [1-7]. As we know, the short-circuit current density $( J _ { \mathrm { s c } } )$ , the open-circuit voltage $( V _ { \mathrm { o c } } )$ , and the fill factor (FF) are the three main parameters that determine the PCEs of the photovoltaic devices. Till now, combined with the material design and device optimization, the internal quantum efficiencies approaching $1 0 0 \%$ , and the $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ above $2 6 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and the high FF near 0.80 have been achieved for the OSCs [8-14]. However, the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the state-of-the-art OSCs is still below $1 . 0 \mathrm { V } ,$ which restricts the PCE for a further breakthrough [15, 16]. The low $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ usually is attributed to the large energy loss $( E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } )$ . The $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ is defined as $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } = E _ { \mathrm { g } } - q V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ where $q$ is elementary charge and $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ is the optical bandgap of the organic semiconductor having the smaller bandgap within active layer of solar cells. $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ in OSCs is typically above $0 . 6 { \mathrm { e V } } _ { : }$ in contrast, it is usually around $0 . 4 \mathrm { e V }$ in Si-based solar cells or perovskite solar cells [17, 18]. There is a lot of room for improvement of the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of OSCs, because the $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ is much higher than the theoretical value predicted by Shockley-Queisser (SQ) theory [19]. Once the OsCs' energy loss is decreased, the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ will achieve a significant breakthrough and so will the device performance. Exploring the cause of the large $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ and seeking solutions are hot topics of current research in the field of OSCs.

Usually, $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ can also be expressed as the voltage loss ( $ { \left( V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } \right. } = E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } / q )$ [18]. According to the detailed balance analysis, the voltage loss in solar cells can be divided into three factors: $q V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } = \Delta E _ { 1 } + \Delta E _ { 2 } + \Delta E _ { 3 }$ [18, 20]. $\Delta E _ { 1 }$ is the radiative recombination loss due to the absorption above the bandgap. $\Delta E _ { 2 }$ is the radiative recombination loss originating from the absorption below the bandgap.

$\Delta E _ { 3 }$ is the non-radiative recombination loss, which can be quantified by the following formula: $\Delta E _ { 3 } = q \Delta V _ { \mathrm { o c } } ^ { \mathrm { n o n - r a d } } = - k T \mathrm { l n ( E Q E _ { \mathrm { E L } } ) }$ , where $k$ is the Boltzmann constant, $T$ is absolute temperature, and $\mathrm { E Q E _ { E L } }$ is radiative quantum efficiency of the solar cell tested in the dark [21]. Among them, $\Delta E _ { 1 }$ is unavoidable for all of the solar cells, while the radiative recombination of $\Delta E _ { 2 }$ comes from the formation of the charge transfer (CT) state in the OsCs. To decrease the value of $\Delta E _ { 2 }$ , it needs to reduce the energy offsets between the CT state and the singlet state of the donor or acceptor. $\Delta E _ { 3 }$ is a key loss channel in OSC devices, attributed to the low $\mathrm { E Q E } _ { \mathrm { E L } }$ $( \sim 1 0 ^ { - 6 } – 1 0 ^ { - 8 } )$ of the OsC devices [22, 23]. On the one hand, Benduhn et al. have found that the $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { o c } } ^ { \mathrm { n o n - r a d } }$ drastically increased as the energy of the CT state $( E _ { \mathrm { C T } } )$ decreases [24]. Recently, Eisner et al. proposed that $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { o c } } ^ { \mathrm { n o n - r a d } }$ could be reduced as the increase of the hybridization of the local excited (LE) and CT states based on their three-state model simulation [25]. When the energy of the LE and CT states is very close to each other, the oscillator strength from CT to ground state will increase due to the intensity borrowing mechanism, which will result in a considerable enhancement in $\mathrm { E Q E _ { E L } }$ [26], while the reduced energy offset between the LE and CT state may give rise to the slow and inefficient charge generation and further increase the overall radiative recombination rates, leading to the low FF and EQE. Thus, it is critical that fine-tuning the energy offsets at the $\mathrm { D } / \mathrm { A }$ interface.

Accompanied by the appearance of non-fullerene acceptors, there is a large space to control the energy offsets at the D/A interface. Compared with the fullerene-based OSCs, the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the non-fullerene-based OSCs has been significantly improved, and the value of $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ has increased to $1 . 3 \mathrm { V }$ for the single-junction OSCs [27]. At the same time, the number of high-efficiency OSCs with $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ above $1 . 0 \mathrm { V }$ is increasing (as shown in Figure 8.1). Though the highest PCE is still below $1 4 \%$ [28], these high-voltage systems will provide good candidates for future device mechanism research, which will guide material design for further improvements in device performance. Moreover, the ideal tandem solar cells need each sub-cell to have a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ because the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the tandem device equals the sum of $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of each sub-cell while the lower $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ value of the sub-cells determines the $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ [29-31]. The development of the high-efficiency OsCs with high voltage is critical to improve the tandem cells' device performance. More importantly, the rapid development of the Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem has promoted the research of indoor photovoltaics (iPV), which are expected to be a power supply source for the IoT systems [32-34]. The outdoor PV cell usually works under 1 sun illumination (AM 1.5G, $1 0 0 \mathrm { m W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ ). Simultaneously, the iPV can generate photoelectric conversion by harvesting artificial light, including fluorescent light (FL), white light-emitting diodes (LEDs), or the dim lighting environment [35]. Usually, the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the photovoltaic devices will decrease as the incident light density weakens [36]. iPVs need high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ values to offset the voltage drop under low light intensity. Besides, the active layer materials with medium bandgaps are also popular, which can match LEDs' emission and improve the light harvesting [37]. Thus, the studies of the high-efficiency OsCs with high voltage have important implications for future iPVs research.

![](images/890028a044a87d8873e481108fb9135ed8e1bfbe3383ed434c806e211f1676a1.jpg)  
Figure 8.1 PCE against $V _ { \mathrm { { o c } } }$ plots of the reported efficient organic solar cells with PCE above $5 \%$ and $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ above ${ 1 . 0 \lor } .$ Source: Ailing Tang, Yuze Lin, and Erjun Zhou.

Though significant progress has been achieved recently for the high-voltage OSCs, no review article focuses on them so far. Herein, we will summarize the recent development of the high-voltage OSCs, which mainly shows the PCEs above $8 \%$ with the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ higher than $1 . 0 \mathrm { V } .$ We will address how the molecular design of small-molecule acceptors (SMAs) and polymer acceptors (PAs) affects the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and performance of the device. These acceptors include the early reports of fullerene-based SMAs, non-fullerene SMAs containing perylene diimide (PDI) [18, 38], benzothiadiazole (BT) [39], benzotriazole (BTA) [40], 3,9-bis(2-methylene(3-(1,1-dicyanomethylene)-indanone)) (IC) and its derivatives etc. [41], and PAs composed of PDI [42], bithiophene imide (BTI) [43], double $\mathbf { B } { \gets } \mathbf { N }$ bridged bipyridyl [44], etc. Finally, we discuss the existing challenges and perspectives for the future development of high-voltage OSCs.

# 8.2 n-Type Small-Molecule Acceptors

# 8.2.1 Fullerene-Based SMAs

In 1995, soluble [6,6]-phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ , as shown in Figure 8.2) was used as an acceptor blending with polymer donors to construct polymer solar cells (PsCs) [45]. Since then, $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and its corresponding C70 derivative [6,6]-phenyl-C71-butyric acid methyl ester $\mathrm { ( P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M ) }$ have been widely applied to fabricate OSCs, and the PCEs of these OSCs have been increased to $1 1 \%$ now [46-51]. Owing to the low-lying lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) levels of the fullerene acceptors $( \sim - 4 . 1 3 \mathrm { e V } )$ , the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the OSCs is below $1 . 0 \mathrm { V }$ [51, 52]. Because of the difficulty of the structural modification for the fullerene acceptors, down-shifting the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) levels of the donors is the main pathway toward increasing the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the fullerene-based OSCs. Based on this, several types of high-voltage fullerene-based OsCs have been reported (Figure 8.2). The energy levels and device performances are illustrated in Table 8.1.

In 2018, poly(4,8-bist $5 ^ { \prime }$ ( $2 ^ { \prime \prime }$ -ethylhexyl)thio)- $\cdot 4 ^ { \prime }$ -fluorothiophen- $\cdot 2 ^ { \prime }$ -yl)benzo[1,2-b: $4 , 5 { \cdot } b ^ { \prime }$ dithiophene-2,6-diyl)-alt $\cdot 2 ^ { \prime }$ -ethylhexyl-3-fluorothieno[3,4 $^ b$ |thiophene-2-car boxylate (PBDTT-SF-TT) was designed by Yang and coworkers, which is composed of an alkylthiolated and fluorinated BDT motif and $2 ^ { \prime }$ -ethylhexyl-3-fluorothieno [3,4-b]thiophene-2-carboxylate (TT) unit. The $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ -based fullerene PSCs for PBDTT-SF-TT showed a PCE of $9 . 0 7 \%$ with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 0 0 \mathrm { V }$ and $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 4 . 7 9 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . The high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ is attributed to the low energy loss of $0 . 5 9 \mathrm { e V } .$ The results indicate the synergistic effect of fluorination and alkylthiolation on BDT moiety can achieve a good balance between high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and large $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ [53].

In 2016, Zheng et al. designed a novel wide-bandgap copolymer (PIT2FBT) by incorporating an asymmetric-indenothiophene donor and a difluorinated BT acceptor, yielding a deep-lying HOMO energy level of $- 5 . 5 4 \mathrm { e V } .$ PIT2FBT:PC, BM-based devices show a high PCE of $9 . 0 1 \%$ in combination with a large $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 0 \mathrm { V }$ [54]. In 2017, Chao and coworkers utilized dicyano-substituted bithiophene as an electron-donating unit and iso-indigo as an electron-accepting unit to synthesize a D-A copolymer, P4TIN. Benefiting from the deep HOMO level and the improved solubility, inverted solar cells fabricated with P4TIN: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ have achieved a very high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 0 6 \mathrm { V }$ and a high PCE of $8 . 3 6 \%$ [55].

Small molecules can serve as promising candidates for their polymer counterparts. In 2019, Beaujuge and coworkers reported new oligomer-like small molecules based on oligothiophenes by fluoridating the central thiophene, named 2F-DRCN5T. The fluorine substitution at the core unit could down-shift the HOmO levels, increase the energy of the CT state and reduce the non-radiative voltage loss. As a result, the solution-processed solar cells can yield a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 0 8 \mathrm { V } .$ After the thermal annealing and solvent-vapor annealing, the devices can achieve a high PCE of over $8 \%$ [56].

# 8.2.2 Non-fullerene SMAs

Over the past few years, compared with conventional fullerene acceptors, nonfullerene acceptors have received more and more attentions, benefitting from the enhanced photon harvesting, easily tunable molecular energy levels, and superior morphological stability. The careful energy level regulation of NFAs has promoted the fast development of high-voltage systems. According to the building blocks of the NFsMAs, we will divide them into six categories to review the recent progress of the high-voltage systems based on the NFSMAs.

# 8.2.2.1PDI-Based SMAs

PDI is a promising class of electron-deficient build blocks due to their high absorption coefficients and electron mobility. At the same time, PDI is easily modified by introducing alkyl or aryl substituents at the $N$ -positions and/or at the bay core positions. Some SMAs have been designed by linking with a wide variety of electron-donating units at the bay positions. The chemical structures of the PDI based SMAs are shown in Figure 8.3, and the energy levels and device properties are listed in Table 8.2.

In 2016, Yan and coworkers reported a PDI-based SMA named $\mathrm { S F } { \cdot } \mathrm { P D I } _ { 2 }$ , composed of two PDI units flanked with the central spirofluorene unit. Though the P3TEA:SF- $\cdot \mathrm { P D I } _ { 2 }$ -based OsC exhibits a negligible driving force, it could exhibit fast and efficient charge separation, leading to a high internal quantum efficiency (IQE) of near $9 0 \%$ and a promising PCE of $9 . 5 \%$ . In addition, the high $\mathrm { E Q E } _ { \mathrm { E L } }$ afforded the solar cells very low non-radiative recombination loss. As a result, the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of this blend is as high as 1.11 V [18]. They used the combination of P3TEA and $\mathrm { S F } { \cdot } \mathrm { P D I } _ { 2 }$ to construct a homo-tandem SMA OSC. The homo-tandem SMA OSCs exhibit a promising PCE of $1 0 . 8 \%$ , with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ over $2 . 1 \mathrm { V }$ [70]. They synthesized two novel PDI tetramers with fused and nonfused structures based on a tetrathienylbenzene (TTB) core and PDI terminals. For nonfused PDI-tetramer, TTB-PDI4, thiophene is linked with TTB and four PDI units, while for the fused PDI-tetramer, FTTB-PDI4, thiophene rings are fused with PDI units. Compared with the single bonds of nonfused PDI-tetramer, the ring fusion can decrease the rotational freedom between the thiophene and PDI units, up-shift the LUMO level, and enhance light absorption. FTTB-PDI4 exhibits a "double-decker" geometry containing two pairs of mostly parallel PDI units. Consequently, the P3TEA:FTTB-PDI4 devices achieve the highest PCE of $1 0 . 5 8 \%$ with an improved $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of 1.13 V, $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 3 . 8 9 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and FF of
