# 9.2.2Block Copolymers

BCPs have been widely studied due to their unique characteristics to obtain multifunction through self-assembly. As shown in Figures 9.5 and 9.6, BCPs with the intramolecular $\mathrm { D } { - } \mathbf { A }$ structures were used as the light-sensitive layer in the scOsCs. Besides, the morphologies have been meticulously investigated, and an encouraging SCOSC performance based on BCPs was achieved, exceeding $6 \%$ in the state-of-the-art study. Figure 9.5 presents the BCPs applied in the SCOSCs, which contain oligothiophenes or $n$ -PVs as the donor blocks.

One of the first examples of D-A block polymers was reported in 2000 by Janssen and coworkers [44]. Two BCPs (BCP1, BCP2) with the $n$ -PV blocks as the donor segment and PBI as the acceptor segment were prepared via the Pd-catalyzed Suzuki cross-coupling reaction. Further spectroscopic studies demonstrated that fast photo-induced charge transfer (CT) was obtained in the two systems both in solution and as-cast films while serious recombination also existed, especially in solution. The SCOSCs with the configuration of ITO/PEDOT:PSS/AL/LiF/Al gave $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $0 . 0 0 8 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ (BCP1) and $0 . 0 1 2 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ (BCP2), respectively. Another similar BCP (BCP3) was reported by Mikroyannidis et al. through the Heck coupling reaction [45]. Unfortunately, the photovoltaic properties of BCP3 analyzed in SCOSCs only showed a PCE of $0 . 0 2 \%$ . Briefly, in the D-A copolymers present above, the alkyl linkages were used to connect the $n$ -PVs and PBI macrosegments, leading to unappropriated microphase-separated nanostructures and poor performance.

A full-conjugated copolymer (BCP4) combining oligothiophenes as donor block and PDPP3T oligomers as acceptor block was developed by B.C. Thompson and coworkers [46]. For the first time, the donor and acceptor macrosegments of the block copolymer present two independent domains in the film state, indicating that this molecular design principle can be efficient to achieve high PCEs in BCP-based SCOsCs. This result also demonstrated that well-ordered molecule orientation and appropriate phase separation can be realized through rational structural designs.

Under the same guidelines, R. Verduzco and coworkers reported the synthesis of the all-conjugated block copolymer BCP5 as the active material for SCOSCs [47]. BCP5 was prepared through the GRIM (Grignard metathesis), in which a bromo end-functionalized P3HT macroreagent was synthesized and then Suzuki-Miyaura polycondensation was used to prepare the polymers. The morphology of BCP5 films was further investigated by the X-ray scattering, in which the in-plane lamellar morphologies of alternating D and A domains with a diameter of $9 \mathrm { n m }$ were obtained in the thin film. The photovoltaic performance was found to significantly depend on the thermal annealing (TA) treatment. The PCE increased from $1 . 5 \%$ after annealed for 20 minutes at $1 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ to $2 . 7 \%$ for 10 minutes at $1 6 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , and the best device gave $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $5 . 2 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and a PCE of $3 . 1 0 \%$ , which is among the highest PCEs for SCOSCs based on diblock copolymers in that period. Interestingly, all these devices present high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ (open-circuit voltage) values in the range of $1 . 1 0 { - } 1 . 2 0 \mathrm { V } .$

A library of copolymers BCP6 with various substituents on the fluorene and thiophene units were also developed by Verduzco and coworkers to analyze the effects on the solubility and packing of the polymers [48]. Despite a large number of copolymers, the added alkyl side units on the thiophene units corrupted the photovoltaic properties and the PCEs were inferior to $0 . 1 0 \%$ , indicating that the introduction of solubilizing alkyl chains on the thiophene rings has a detrimental effect on phase segregation.

![](images/783e85e68f449e6864d91e87c46349543dd38e727fc76d70f00e308e0c927ff9.jpg)  
Figure 9.5  Chemical structures of block conjugated copolymers for SCOsCs (Part 1).

![](images/a1a15bde6f09a58f24c22e6e74f9533f9b07c83a57e8bc3b1d5d97e04ee471d7.jpg)  
Figure 9.6 Chemical structures of block conjugated copolymers for SCOsCs (Part 2).

Further studies on the effect of linkage between the D and A blocks were investigated by Verduzco's group and Gomez's group [49, 50]. A new copolymer (BCP7) in which the P3HT donor block and the dithienyl benzothiadiazole acceptor block were connected by a fluorene segment was compared with the same alkyl-substituted poly(3-hexylthiophene-2,5-diyl)-block-poly((9,9-dioctylfluorene)-2,7-diyl-alt-[4,7- bis(thiophen-5-yl)-2,1,3-benzothiadiazole]- $^ { 2 ^ { \prime } , 2 ^ { \prime \prime } }$ -diyl) (P3HT-FTBTF) (BCP6). Although BCP6 exhibited lower molecular weight and higher P3HT content, both copolymers present rather similar absorption spectra. In the solar cell tests, the insertion of the fluorene bridge was reported to produce a large increase of PCEs from $0 . 0 5 \%$ for BCP6 to $2 . 2 4 \%$ for BCP7, due to more efficient charge separation in the fluorene-bridged copolymer.

In another study, M. Sommer and coworkers described the synthesis of a new type of copolymer BCP8 including the semifluorinated octyl-substituted dithienyl benzothiadiazole as the acceptor block and P3HT macroreagent as the donor block [51]. Compared with the alkyl-substituted copolymers, the introduction of partially fluorinated alkyl chains increased the Flory-Huggins interaction parameters between the donor and acceptor blocks, which led to almost full recrystallization of the P3HT block in the copolymers. SCOSCs with the configuration of ITO/PEDOT:PSS/active layers/Al were fabricated, and the BCP8-based device gave a higher PCE of $0 . 9 5 \%$

A recent study investigated by Gomez and coworkers presented the point that the electron transfer in the acceptor block can be the key parameter that limited the performance of SCOsCs. It was also emphasized that both donor and acceptor blocks should be carefully designed to achieve ambipolar charge transport and maximize the output power of photovoltaic cells. Under this principle, several D-A BCPs contained naphthalene diimide (NDI), or PBI groups were reported to enhance electron transport property as well as the nanophase separation.

In 2012, Nakabayashi et al. reported pioneering research in which "D-A-D" type BCPs (BCP9) with the end-functional P3HT as donor part and naphthalimidedithiophene as acceptor part were prepared. A wide photoresponse ranging from 350 to $8 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ was obtained in the as-cast BCp9 films, and the onset of absorption was enhanced to $8 9 0 \mathrm { n m }$ after thermal annealing, suggesting an optimized self-aggregation in the post-processing condition. This work provided a fundamental example for the NDI-based copolymers and showed its potentiality for applications in SCOSCs.

Choi and coworkers demonstrated a new series of D-A BCPs without olig. othiophenes as the donor blocks. Two types of copolymers composed of quinoxaline-thiophene and naphthalene diimide-selenophene blocks were synthesized, in which the donor and acceptor blocks are connected by flexible alkyl spacers (BCP11) or directly connected (BCP10) [52]. Besides, both the polymers contained a 1:1 ratio of donor and acceptor blocks measured by gas-phase chromatography. Photovoltaic cells with copolymers were fabricated in the inverted architecture $\mathrm { I T O / Z n O / A L / M o O _ { 3 } / A l }$ SCOSCs based on BCP10 presented discouraging photovoltaic properties with $J _ { \mathrm { s c } } = 1 . 3 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ $\mathrm { F F } = 0 . 3 5$ , and $\mathrm { P C E } = 0 . 3 6 \%$ while an enhanced performance with $J _ { \mathrm { s c } } = 4 . 0 4 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and $\mathrm { P C E } = 1 . 5 4 \%$ in the BCP11-based devices. Further studies indicated that the insertion of a flexible linkage between D and A blocks in BCP11 inhibited the charge recombination in the copolymer.

![](images/4b2b51bee3b5ade03cefa262abc1912eb63d35c056e7592bd896b2d899c07b9d.jpg)  
Scheme 9.4The synthetic route of block copolymer BCP12. (i) ${ \mathsf { P d } } _ { 2 } ( { \mathsf { d b } } { \mathsf { a } } ) _ { 3 }$ $P ( o { \cdot } \mathrm { t o } \mathrm { l y } \mathrm { l } ) _ { 3 }$ toluene, and chlorobenzene under microwave irradiation at ${ 1 8 0 } ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C } ;$ (ii) $\mathsf { P d } ( \mathsf { P P h } _ { 3 } ) _ { 4 }$ in toluene at $1 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$ , and (ii) ${ \mathsf { P d } } _ { 2 } ( { \mathsf { d b } } { \mathsf { a } } ) _ { 3 }$ and $P ( o { \cdot } \mathrm { t o } \lfloor \mathsf { y } \mathsf { l } ) _ { 3 }$ and toluene at $1 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf { C }$

To obtain a complementary absorption and simplify the synthesis process, Choi and coworkers reported another example of conjugated BCP (BCP12) [53], in which a wide-bandgap donor block of DT-BDT-thiophenecarboxylate is connected to a narrow-bandgap acceptor block of naphthalene diimide-selenophene, and the detailed synthetic route was illustrated in Scheme 9.4. The copolymer was synthesized by Stille coupling of carefully prepared end-functional oligomeric D and A blocks. The $M _ { n }$ of D and A macroreagent and D-A copolymer clarified by the gel permeation chromatography (GPC) were 6.84, 10.7, and $1 8 . 1 \mathrm { k D a }$ , respectively, with PDI (Polymer Dispersion Index) of 1.53, 2.16, and 2.31. Interestingly, the absorption of BCP12 in the solution consisted of the features of D and A blocks. sCOsCs prepared with the configuration of $\mathrm { I T O / Z n O / B C P 1 2 / M o O _ { 3 } / A g }$ delivered $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $8 . 3 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 3 \mathrm { V } ,$ FF of 0.50, and the PCE close to $4 . 0 \%$ , while the cell based on the mixture of D and A oligomeric materials gave a suppressed performance with a lower PCE of $1 . 1 4 \%$ and decreased characteristics of $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ , and FF. The device stability based on BCP12 in ambient conditions was also investigated, and the results indicated that SCOSCs prepared with BCP12 still contained $8 0 \%$ of the original performance after 2o00 hours of storage. The main-chain engineering was further studied by the same group.

With the aim to increase the crystallinity of the donor block and optimize the nanoscale morphology, an extra thiophene segment was introduced in the donor block of DT-BDT-thiophenecarboxylate, giving a new block copolymer BCP13 [54]. The solar cells based on BCP13 gave an enhanced $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 0 . 7 7 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , FF of 0.63, and a PCE of $5 . 2 8 \%$ compared with the SCOsCs based on BCP12. Furthermore, selenophene units in the acceptor block were replaced by the bithiophene, and a new copolymer BCP14 was obtained [55]. Due to the long $\pi$ -conjugated backbone both in D and A blocks, SCOSCs based on the block copolymer BCP14 provided a PCE of $6 . 4 3 \%$ , which is the best result among the reported SCOSCs based on BCPs so far.

Besides the outstanding works of NDI-based BCPs, Huang and coworkers synthesized block copolymers BCP15 combining macrosegments of P3HT and PBI [56]. To remove the excess P3HT and reduce the polydispersity, preparative GPC was prepared to get several individual fractions of these copolymers. The research indicated that the optical and electrochemical properties strongly depend on the ratio of the P3HT and PBI blocks. The best results were obtained with a copolymer of the lowest PDI (1.23) containing $4 3 \%$ of P3HT, the PCE was increased from $0 . 0 6 \%$ to $1 . 0 0 \%$ after annealing at $1 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ Recently, Sivula and coworkers developed a new type of fully conjugated "A-D-A" copolymer BCP16 via the Heck-Mizoroki coupling [57]. Despite the relatively poor device performance with a PCE of $1 . 5 1 \%$ , the preparation of BCP16 was carefully studied and the chemical structures of functional macrosegments poly{ $( E )$ -1,2-ethene-alt-5,12-dibromo-2,9-di(tridecan-7-yl)anthra[2,1,9-def:6,5,10- d'e'f]diisoquinoline-1,3,8,10(2H,9H)-tetraone} (pPDIV)-(H/V) and polyy $^ { 2 , 6 ^ { \prime } }$ -4,8- di(5-ethylhexylthienyl)benzo[1,2-b;3,4-b]dithiophene-alt-5-dibutyloctyl-3,6-bis(5- bromothiophen-2-yl)pyrrolo[3,4-c]pyrrole-1,4-dione} (pBDTTDPP)-- $\left( \mathrm { B r / B r } \right)$ were verified through the matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI)-time-offlight (TOF) mass spectra, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and GPC measurements, which was contributed to the good air stability of pPDIV-(H/V) compared with the tributylstannyl-contained conjugated segments.

# 9.2.3 Double-Cable Conjugated Polymers

Double-cable conjugated polymer is one of the most important conjugated materials in SCOsCs. In 1996, Benincori et al. reported the first photovoltaic application of double-cable conjugated polymer DCP1 via electrochemical polymerization (ECP) [58]. The $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ was directly grafted into the bridging carbon of cyclopentadithiophene to get the monomer m1, which was suitable for ECP. Ferraris et al. synthesized a new double-cable polymer DCP2 via ECP, in which poly-bithiophene was used as the backbone and connected with pendant $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ as side unit via flexible alkyl chain spacer, as shown in Scheme 9.5 [59]. Both DCP1 and DCP2 exhibited photoelectrochemical and electrochemical properties of the conjugated backbones and the pendant fullerenes. However, poor solubility in common solvents makes them inappropriate materials in solution-processed OSCs. So, it is important to develop soluble double-cable conjugated polymers.

In 2o01, the first solution-processed scOsc based on double-cable polymer (DCP3) was reported by Janssen and coworkers through a Sonogashira coupling reaction (Scheme 9.6) [60]. Photovoltaic devices were fabricated, using spin-coated DCP3 films as the active layer, ITO/PEDOT:PSS, and Al as electrodes. Under white-light illumination $\mathrm { 1 0 0 m W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , air mass (AM) 1.5), a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $0 . 4 2 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$

![](images/c9878d5e23710ef766a36634aea037dee6cc84520616ecd106749a0e79c87198.jpg)  
Scheme 9.5 Synthetic routes and chemical structures of DCP1 and DCP2.

$V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 3 \mathrm { V } ,$ and FF of 0.29 were obtained. Although the PCE is only $0 . 1 \%$ , the result indicated a new type of material that can be used in SCOsCs. In the same year, Zhang et al. reported two double-cable conjugated polymers DCP4 and DCP5, using poly-thiophene as the main chain and fullerene moiety as side groups, in which the content of fullerene is 7 and $1 4 \mathrm { m o l } \%$ respectively, as shown in Scheme 9.6 [61]. Both DCP4 and DCP5 showed good solubility in chloroform, so that the polymer films could be prepared by spin coating from chloroform solution. The as-cast films showed an orange phase and then turned to dark blue after thermal annealing or solvent-vapor annealing (SVA) treatment. Absorption spectra showed that the onset of the two polymer films had red-shift (about $1 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ ) to $7 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ after the annealing treatment, which is similar to the related polymers without $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ moiety, indicating that the small content of fullerene repeating unit has a negligible effect on the self-assembly of the poly-thiophene backbone. They prepared photodiodes by spin coating the film of DCP4 or DCP5 $\mathrm { 7 0 n m } )$ onto the top of ITO/PEDOT:PSS electrodes and Al electrodes $\left( 6 0 \mathrm { n m } \right)$ were evaporated on the top of the polymer layer. The EQE spectra showed that DCP5-based devices had doubled response intensity. After treating the copolymer films with chloroform vapor, the EQE at long wavelengths was significantly enhanced due to the ordered state of the copolymers. The diode under the illumination of monochromatic light at 505 nm $( 0 . 1 \mathrm { m W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } )$ showed a PCE of $0 . 6 \%$ , an FF of 0.25, and a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 7 5 \mathrm { V } .$ The $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ was decreased to $0 . 4 5 \mathrm { V }$ after the treatment by chloroform vapor, which indicated a reflection of the diminished energy separation of the double-cable conjugated polymer.

In 2007, Li and coworkers designed and synthesized a new double-cable polymer (DCP6) with higher fullerene content and good solubility, as shown in Scheme 9.7 [62]. They selected polythiophene as the electron-donating backbone and fullerene as electron-accepting moiety, with an attached alkyl-phenylene group to ensure the solubility. They firstly synthesized the precursor polymer DCP6-k and then used two steps to graft the acceptor $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ . The content of the fullerene repeating unit was detected by elemental analysis of the content of carbon in the polymer, and the result showed that almost each repeated unit of backbone was substituted by one $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ molecule. With such a high content of $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ , DCP6 was applied into SCOSCs with a configuration of ITO/PEDOT:PSS/DCP6/Ca/Al. Under the illumination of AM 1.5G, $1 0 0 \mathrm { m W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , the device showed a PCE of $0 . 5 2 \%$ , with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 7 5 \mathrm { V }$ and a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 . 4 1 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , which was among the best performance of double-cable polymer-based SCOsCs at that time and was more than five times higher than that of the related BHJ devices. Since then, this synthetic method of "grafting fullerene on electron-donating polymers" was widely used in the synthesis of double-cable conjugated polymers.

![](images/91e4994681a92b991403dc4c4f437993e61fa8b79e5c666ed3d107c0f3180be9.jpg)  
Scheme 9.6Chemical structures and synthetic routes of DCP3-DCP5.

![](images/48137102dec5fbfa55a9321ffe29904695775fcf46fc5a0add74badd9abd6dd8.jpg)  
Scheme 9.7Synthetic routes and chemical structures of DCP6-10.

In 2010, Hashimoto and coworkers [63] synthesized two new double-cable polymers, including diblock polymer (DCP7) and random copolymer (DCP8), with poly(3-alkylthiophene) as backbone and PCBM as pendant unit, through a series of synthetic routes, including GRIM, Ni-catalyzed quasi-living polymerization, and the "click" cycloaddition reaction. The ratio of the fullerene attached thiophene unit was estimated by $^ 1 \mathrm { H }$ NMR spectra as $1 1 \%$ and $1 3 \%$ for the DCP7 and DCP8, respectively, corresponding to the contents of fullerene in polymers of 38 and $4 1 \mathrm { w t } \%$ SCOSCs were fabricated with the normal configuration (ITO/PEDOT:PSS/Polymer/Al). Under the illumination of simulated sunlight (AM 1.5G, $1 0 0 \mathrm { m W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ ), the device based on DCP7 showed a PCE of $1 . 7 0 \%$ with $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 5 4 \mathrm { V } , J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $6 . 1 5 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and FF of 0.51, which was the best performance of SCOsCs at that time, much better than that based on DCP8 (PCE of $0 . 4 8 \%$ with $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of 0.76 V, $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 . 8 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and FF of 0.35). The thermal stability of DCP7 devices and the related BHJ devices of P3HT with PCBM were studied and showed a striking contrast under thermal annealing at $1 3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ The SCOSC based on DCP7 showed only a slight decrease of PCE from $1 . 5 9 \%$ to $1 . 5 0 \%$ after 80 hours, while the BHJ device was decreased by almost $8 0 \%$ due to the PCBM aggregation. In 2012, the same group reported a higher PCE $( 2 . 5 \%$ , with FF of 0.63) of DCP7-based photovoltaic devices through controlling the synthesis method and optimizing the annealing condition of the devices. These results suggest that the application of single fullerene-attached diblock double-cable conjugated polymer could be an effective way to achieve efficient and stable SCosCs. Five years later, Chen et al. introduced selenophene into the backbone of the P3HT and used similar methods to synthesize a new BCP with pendant PCBM (DCP9), and P3HT-based polymer (DCP10) was also synthesized for comparison [64]. Thermal annealing of the double-cable polymer films induced the microphase separation of approximately $3 0 \mathrm { n m }$ SCOSCs were fabricated using a reversed structure of $\scriptstyle \mathrm { I T O } / Z \mathrm { n O } ,$ /active layer/ $\mathrm { { ' M o O } } _ { 3 } / \mathrm { { A g } }$ . Under the irradiation of simulated solar light (AM 1.5G, $1 0 0 \mathrm { m W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ ), the devices based on the as-cast films showed negligible performance for the two polymers. After thermal annealing, both polymers showed the same trend of the decrease of $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and increase of FF, $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ , and PCE without a large difference. The device fabricated from the film of DCP9 annealed at $2 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ showed the best PCE of $1 . 5 2 \%$ with $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 5 1 \mathrm { V } , J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $5 . 0 2 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and FF of 0.59.

As shown in Scheme 9.8, in 2017, Pierini et al. synthesized a new double-cable polymer poly[3-dodecylthiophene-co-3-(6-fullerenylhexyl)thiophene] (DCP11) based on polythiophene with pendant fullerene, using a strategy of "grafting after polymerization" [65]. According to the $^ 1 \mathrm { H }$ NMR spectrum, DCP11 had a high content of the fullerene-grafted thiophene moiety $4 2 \%$ in molar ratio). More importantly, nanofibers of the double-cable polymer were produced by the technique of electrospinning and successfully integrated into SCOsCs. An optimized supramolecular and nanoscale structure of the active layer provided a high PCE of $5 . 5 8 \%$ . The dodecyl linker between the conjugated chain and fullerene reduced the charge recombination. The well-packed polymer chains with proper orientation generated the high performance of the devices. Two years later, the same group synthesized two new double-cable polymers (DCP12, DCP13), bearing different content of $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ -fullerene moieties and photo cross-linkable bromine groups at the end of a hexamethylenic side chain, from two homo-polymeric precursors with similar molecular weights but different regioregularity degrees, as shown in Scheme 9.8. When employed as active material in SCOSCs (ITO/PEDOT:PSS/active layer/Al), the polymer DCP13 with higher regioregularity degree and lower content of fullerene showed better performance, giving a PCE of $5 . 2 1 \%$ , higher than $3 . 5 5 \%$ of the DCP12-based devices. Introduction of an Au nanoparticle thin layer between PEDOT:PSS and polymer layer further enhanced the performance of the devices and the PCE increased to $5 . 6 8 \%$ . Furthermore, the end group of bromines in these polymers can be cross-linked by the photochemical cleavage of $\mathrm { C - B r }$ bonds under ultraviolet (Uv) light. Consequently, the UV-exposed devices showed better stability than the uncross-linked counterparts, after 80 hours of annealing at $1 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ . These results represent the highest performance of SCOsCs based on fullerene-grafted double-cable polymers, which is comparable to most reported P3HT-based BHJ solar cells [66-69].

![](images/806f1b35ad141b7b9a3c77556b076332970ade8b0c0a60103bbbd69a06a5650a.jpg)  
Scheme 9.8The chemical structures and synthetic routes of DCP11-13.

In addition to the above double-cable polymers grafted with fullerene derivatives, aromatic di-imide containing electron acceptors, such as NDI [70, 71], PBI [70, 72-81], and their derivatives [82], were also applied as pendant units in double-cable polymers for SCOsCs. Thelakkat and coworkers [69, 83] reported a DCP DCP14, as shown in Figure 9.7, with a poly(vinyltriphenylamine) segment as the electron donor for hole transport and a polyacrylate segment bearing PBI side groups as the electron acceptor for electron transport. The film of DCP14 with a thickness of $2 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ was used as the active layer in a photovoltaic device with ITO/PEDOT:PSS and Al as electrodes. Under the irradiation of a white-light source (AM 1.5G, $7 7 \mathrm { m W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ ), the device gave a PCE of $0 . 0 7 \%$ , which was 10 times higher than that of the related BHJ devices. To improve the polymer's electrochemical stability, hole-carrier mobility, and to vary its highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) values, Thelakkat and coworkers [73] used bis(4-methoxyphenyl) phenylamine and $N , N ^ { \prime }$ -bis(4-methoxyphenyl) $\cdot N , N ^ { \prime }$ -diphenyl-( $_ { \mathrm { ( 1 , 1 ^ { \prime } } }$ -biphenyl)- $^ { \cdot 4 , 4 ^ { \prime } }$ diamine as the hole-conducting moieties to take the place of bisphenyl-4-vinylphenylamine in DCP14 and synthesized two new polymers DCP15 and DCP16. The PCEs of the SCOSCs with DCP15 and DCP16 got fourfold to fivefold improvement, up to $0 . 2 6 \%$ and $0 . 3 2 \%$ , compared with DCP14. In the next year, the same group reported a new polymer DCP17 with P3HT as the donor block and the same type of poly(perylene bisimide acrylate) as acceptor block to improve the crystalline of the donor part to give rise to rich phase behavior and improve the charge-carrier mobility. Russell and coworkers [84] used the same strategy to prepare a new polymer DCP18, which was used in SCOSCs and got a PCE of $0 . 4 9 \%$ . The unit of DPP with imide groups has a strong electron-withdrawing ability, which can reduce the bandgap of conjugated block. Koyuncu et al. [75] reported a new polymer DCP19 by using DPP-introduced oligothiophene as low-bandgap donor moiety and the same poly(perylene bisimide acrylate) of DCP18 as acceptor moiety. The polymer provided a strong and broad optical absorption, from 300 to $7 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , with compatible HOMO-lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) levels to DCP18. Through solvent annealing in dichloromethane, microphase separation can be found in the polymer film, resulting in an optimized PCE of $0 . 8 9 \%$ in SCOSC.

![](images/ba445f8cf9454257f454fb735391a4ee2cfc742e77ee2298c1bc2ad6d45ff7d9.jpg)  
Figure 9.7 Chemical structures of the double-cable polymers DCP14-DCP23.

ECP is an efficient method to synthesize carbazole-contained polymers. Koyuncu et al. [85] synthesized a new double-cable polymer DCP20 with a PBI-linked carbazole moiety by ECP. Remarkable fluorescence quenching can be detected in the films caused by the intramolecular charge transfer from the donor backbone of carbazole to the acceptor of pendant PBIs. However, the PCE of DCP20-based SCOSC was only $0 . 1 \%$ . In 2011, Mohamad et al. [86] reported the polymer DCP21, a new double-cable polymer with alternating 2,7-linked carbazole and dithienyl units as the backbone, PBI as pendant acceptor, and hexyl chain as the attached linker. They also found evidence about electron transfer from the conjugated backbone to the pendant PBI units, resulting in weak fluorescence and highly efficient quenching of excitons in both solutions and thin films. The study of steady-state photo-induced absorption spectroscopy confirmed the existence of long-lived polaronic states due to exciton dissociation on DCP21. However, these results did not provide an efficient SCOSC. The devices based on DCP21 only showed a low EQE of around $0 . 4 3 \%$ at $4 1 0 \mathrm { n m }$

In 2018, Ledwon and coworkers reported two new double-cable polymers DCP22-23 containing NDI and PBI as acceptor side groups [70]. Both polymers used poly[3,6-carbazole-alt-5,5- $( 4 ^ { \prime } , 7 ^ { \prime }$ -di-2-thienyl- $^ { 2 ^ { \prime } , 1 ^ { \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime } }$ -benzothiadiazole)]as the conjugated backbone. The introduction of benzothiadiazole to the backbone resulted in a broader absorption of polymers, covering the spectrum from 300 to $7 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . Photovoltaic properties of the two polymers-based SCOsCs with the configuration of ITO/PEDOT:PSS/Polymer/Al showed a disappointing PCE of $0 . 0 3 \%$

Since 2017, Li and coworkers reported a series of double-cable polymers with PBI or its derivative, as shown in Figure 9.8 [76-82, 87-89]. They firstly synthesized three polymers DCP24-26, which used DPP and BDT as conjugated backbone and PBI as side unit with different length of alkyl chain as linkers. The DPP-contained backbone gave the polymers a narrow bandgap with wide absorption from 300 to $9 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . The crystalline properties of the polymers were systematically studied. The results showed that longer alkyl (dodecyl) linkers can improve the crystallinity of the polymers compared with the shorter alkyl (hexyl) linkers, which could be further optimized by introducing sulfur atoms into the alkylthiophene side groups. As a result, the polymer DCP26 was found to show better nanophase separation and get the best PCE of $2 . 7 4 \%$ in the SCOSCs, while DCP24 and DCP25-based SCOSCs only provided low PCEs of $0 . 5 1 \%$ and $1 . 6 4 \%$ [76]. From this work, the authors were inspired to design new double-cable polymers with strong crystalline conjugated backbones to balance the contradictory crystallinity and phase separation requirements for charge generation and charge transport in the SCOsCs. Therefore, they brought out a new strategy of using linear conjugated backbone to adjust the phase separation of the double-cable polymers and reported other three new polymers DCP27-29 [77]. They used linear conjugated backbone poly(benzodithiophene) (PBDTT) as the donor for hole transport, pendant PBI units as the acceptor for electron transport, and a dodecyl linker as the connected part. To further tune the energy levels and crystallinity, they also introduced sulfur and fluorine substituents to the donor parts of the polymers. From the grazing-incidence wide-angle/small-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS/GISAXS) results of the polymer films, the double-cable polymers showed a "face-on" orientation of both the BDT backbone and the pendant PBI units, which was favorable for charge transport in OSCs. Nanophase separation of the backbone and PBI side units was pointed out by the X-ray diffraction (XRD) and microscopy data, which is important to dissociate the excitons and transfer the resulting free charges to the electrodes. These advantages resulted in high quantum efficiency of EQEs up to 0.65 and internal quantum efficiencies (IQEs) up to 0.80 and high PCEs up to $4 . 1 8 \%$ , which is one of the highest performances in SCOsCs at that time. However, there is a significant drawback for the three polymers, in which the wide bandgap of the

![](images/2404f48e1b90eb9706d87006d050566da9b292d432d82cc2bb78894aa3568fb2.jpg)  
Figure 9.8 Chemical structures of the double-cable polymers DCP24-DCP29.

PBDTT backbone gives a small range of absorption of the polymer films, which limited the utilization range of sunlight.

Then, Li and coworkers selected other electron-deficient units based conjugated backbones to tune the bandgap of the PBI-based double-cable polymers, such as isoindigo (DCP30) [79], thieno[3,4-c]pyrrole-4,6-dione (TPD, DCP31-33) [87], and another DPP-based polymer (DCP34) [88] was simultaneously investigated. They successfully developed multiple double-cable polymers with narrow bandgap, and the onset of their absorption varied from 700 to $9 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . However, they failed to get high quantum efficiency in the SCOSCs with these polymers as single active layer and most of the PCEs were below $3 \%$ . Besides, the influence of different content of the acceptor PBI in the double-cable polymers was also investigated; they synthesized two series of polymers using DPP, TPD, and BDT as the backbone and tuned the ratio of the pendant PBIs, as shown in Figure 9.9. Their studies suggested that the pendant PBI units can not only influence the energy level and the absorption spectrum but also improve the polymers' crystallinity and then alter the phase separation of the backbone and the side acceptors in the polymer films. Interestingly, these multifunctional double-cable polymers can act as electron donor or acceptor in BHJ solar cells or as the single active material in SCOsCs [78, 87].

In 2019, Li and coworkers found a new way to improve the PCE of SCOSCs through thermal-driven D/A lamellar phase separation. As shown in Figure 9.10, they designed a new double-cable polymer DCP35 containing a strongly crystalline conjugated backbone (based on two-dimensional BDT alternating with 5,7-bis(2-ethylhexyl)benzo[1,2-c:4,5- $c ^ { \prime }$ Jdithiophene-4,8-dione) as donor and PBI as the pendant acceptor. According to the results of thermal gravimetric analysis and differential scanning calorimeter, the polymer films were annealed at different temperatures for several minutes. After thermal stress, both the crystalline backbones and PBI side units tended to self-organize to form a well-ordered $\mathrm { D } / \mathrm { A }$ lamellar nanostructure, especially at a high temperature of $2 3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , leading to highly efficient charge transport and low charge recombination. Therefore, a high PCE of $6 . 3 \%$ in SCOsCs can be obtained [80]. In the same year, they designed two new double-cable polymers with the same conjugated backbone and PBI side units, in which PBIs were positioned at one side (DCP36) and two sides symmetrically (DCP37) along the conjugated backbones. After thermal annealing, both PBI side units and conjugated backbones in DCP37 tended to self-organize to ordered nanostructures, resulting in good crystalline cooperativity, and the DCP37-based SCOSCs showed a higher PCE of $3 . 4 3 \%$ , while PBI units in DCP36 hampered the crystallization of conjugated backbones resulting in poor crystalline cooperativity, and the DCP36-based SCOSCs only provided a PCE of $2 . 4 2 \%$ [81].

![](images/c8c2c8d4f77bb28140963a34a3d2a2130b0c54b8a03bd14bc088f3eb0835b7b0.jpg)  
Figure 9.9 Chemical structures of the double-cable polymers DCP30-DCP34.

![](images/35fca154f2fd4a4095ecf1eb480dbe2c82cc1db169eb123d08f3b0de7a87a625.jpg)  
Figure 9.10  Chemical structures of the double-cable polymers DCP35-DCP40.

From DCP24 to DCP37, they found that all the double-cable polymers have the same side pendant PBI units. In 2019, they designed a new polymer DCP38 by choosing a new acceptor unit benzo[ghi]-perylene triimide (BPTI) to replace the PBI unit in DCP29 to improve the electron transport efficiency in the polymer films. Consequently, they found the pendant units BPTI dominated the crystallinity of the conjugated backbone and enhanced the acceptors' contact region with each other. This could improve the electron transport of the new double-cable polymer DCP38 in the thin film, as confirmed by space-charge limited current measurement. Therefore, the DCP38-based SCOSCs could provide a PCE of $4 . 3 4 \%$ , compared with $1 . 9 2 \%$ based on DCP29 [82]. More recently, they brought out a new strategy to improve the exciton dissociation efficiency by controlling miscibility between conjugated backbones and aromatic side units in double-cable polymers. They designed two new polymers DCP39, DCP40 with the same NDI side units and two almost identical conjugated backbones with extra Cl atoms on the different positions of the conjugated backbones. The polymer DCP39 with Cl atoms positioned at the main chains formed the twist backbones, could get better miscibility between the backbones and NDI side units, which could contribute to the efficient exciton diffusion and charge separation. Consequently, DCP39-based SCOSCs gave a high PCE of $8 . 4 0 \%$ , with high EQEs up to 0.75 and FFs close to 0.70, which is also the highest PCE in SCOSCs until now [71].

According to the above paragraphs, Li and coworkers devoted themselves to developing SCOsCs by designing new double-cable polymers with different backbones, side units, and linkers since 2017. Several different strategies were under consideration to tune the energy levels, extend the absorption spectrum of the polymers, and adjust the nanophase separation of the polymer films. Finally, high quantum efficiencies were achieved in SCOsCs. These results will intrigue new conceptions about SCOSCs toward high PCEs and further application.

# 9.3 Morphological Studies of the Photo-Active Layers in the SCOSCs

The photovoltaic performances of OsCs are determined by several factors, such as microstructures of the active layer, charge carrier mobilities of the related materials, and the interface between the active layer and electrodes. Especially, the microstructures related to the surface morphologies and micro-phase separation of the photo-active layers predominate over the others. The relative studies of morphological control have been widely studied in the BHJOsCs that require biphasic films in which D and A domains should form two independent continuous networks as well as sufficient miscible regions. Besides, some feasible methods, including solvent additives, TA, and SVA, have been proven to be beneficial to form appropriate morphologies. Although the D-A heterojunction concept was also introduced to construct the photosensitive materials in the SCOsCs, which is the so-called \*intramolecular heterojunction," the morphological formation in the single-component system has unique properties.

In the single-component system, chemical structures of photo-active materials have been restricted by the fully conjugated chemical structures or length-limited alkyl linkage between the D and A groups. Hence, the formation of suitable morphology was the synergistic crystallization of the donor, acceptor, and linkage. This unique characteristic needs to be carefully considered to obtain appropriate morphologies, the size of the D and A domains, which are closely related to the crystallinity and miscibility of the materials, should dimension commensurate with the exciton diffusion length while providing percolation pathways for the photogenerated charges. In this regard, the perfect morphology should well balance the crys. tallinity, the phase mixing, and the phase separation.

# 9.3.1  Morphological Studies of the Molecular Dyads in ScosCs

Molecular dyads with fullerene or PBI as the electron acceptor have been widely used as the photovoltaic conversion medium in the SCOsCs, and the molecule aggregation in the photo-active films shows a significant correlation with the type of acceptor units, which means that fullerene-based dyads exhibit distinct characteristics in the nanoscale morphological separation compared with PBI-based systems. Therefore, a detailed discussion of the morphology control of the molecular dyads in SCOSCs was present depending on the classes of the acceptor.

In the fullerene-based \*in-chain' scOsC systems, the morphologies of the optimized SM14 films were systemically studied through the 2D-GIXRD (grazing X-ray diffraction) (Figure 9.11d), atomic force microscope (AFM, Figure 9.11a-b), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Figure 9.11c). As shown in Figure 9.11d, the XRD diffractogram of SM14 films shows peaks at $2 q = 5 . 0 7 ^ { \circ }$ and $4 . 3 7 ^ { \circ }$ , indicating an inter-plane spacing of 1.74 and $2 . 0 2 \mathrm { n m }$ , which is similar to the aggregation in the blended DPP:PCBM films. And the disappearance of the diffraction peak at $2 q = 2 4 ^ { \circ }$ revealed that the SM14 films existed the edge-on orientation in the casting films. Furthermore, the crystalline size of SM14 in the solid film is 24.4 and $4 1 . 5 \mathrm { n m }$ for interplane and in-plane directions, respectively, and the large sheet structures were also observed in the AFM and TEM measurements. In the manuscript, the authors also emphasized that these long-range ordering microstructures are beneficial for high-performance OSCs.

As for the fullerene-based "side-chain" system, materials developed by Nguyen et al. (SM33) and Min and coworkers (SM34) were selected as the representatives. As shown in Figure 9.12, the as-cast SM33 (also named BDTRh-PCBM) films showed a homogeneous and flat surface with a root-mean-square (RMS) roughness of $0 . 4 1 \mathrm { n m }$ while the BDTRh:PCBM (BHJOSCs as control) blends exhibited severe phase separation with the relatively high RMS of $1 6 . 7 \mathrm { n m }$ . The results indicated that the self-aggregation tendency to form large molecular domains was suppressed when donor and acceptor parts were covalently connected.

![](images/46714025fc5a52f5fb7d889470c12485cfc503d619afb994bc10d883c3e67c58.jpg)  
Figure 9.11 (a) AFM height and (b) phase images and (c) TEM images of the SM14 based device, (d) 2D-GIXRD pattern of SM14. Lower inset: intermolecular and intramolecular distances, upper inset: crystalline size. Source: Narayanaswamy et al. [27]/Reproduced with permission of John Wiley $\&$ Sons.

Furthermore, the intermolecular packing and orientation of SM33 in the SCOSC by comparison with BDTRh:PCBM blends in the BHJOSCs were also investigated through the GIWAXS measurements. Firstly, the pristine BDTRh films were prepared, and the results demonstrated a trend of aggregation with strong (100) out-of-plane interlamellar scattering peaks and (010) $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking peaks in both in-plane and out-of-plane directions. When blended with PCBM, a hump-shape scattering peak appears due to aggregation of PCBM while the scattering features of neat BDTRh were also observed, which means the donor and acceptor still held their crystal domains associated with the large phase separation as shown in the AFM measurements. In the SM33 film, a weak and broad (100) interlamellar packing similar to the BDTRh:PCBM blends were obtained while the crystalline structure BDTRh was significantly hindered. The same phenomena were observed in the single-component molecular material SM34 developed by Min et al.

![](images/a070430fb5fb8a946cf87e8d417cdcbe7f53642ddfca479b43774f6ecb42be36.jpg)  
Figure 9.122D-GIWAXS images of (a) BDTRh, (b) BDTRh:PCBM, and (c) BDTRh-PCBM (SM33) films. Corresponding line-cuts in (d) in-plane and (e) out-of-plane directions. Source: Nguyen et al. [38]/Reproduced with permission of John Wiley & Sons.

However, another kind of scenery in microscopic phase separation in SCOsCs can be observed in the PBI-based dyads. Figure 9.13 shows the morphological studies investigated by Geng and coworkers.

To achieve appropriated micro-phase separation, the linear molecular dyads (SM35-37) with the liquid crystalline property oligo(fluorene-alt-bithiophene)s (OFbTs) as the donor and PBI units as the acceptor were prepared. The OFbTs were connected to the PBIs through a carbon-nitrogen bond and the strong $\pi { - } \pi$ interactions qualify OFbTs and PBIs as the potential blocks for molecular self-assembly architectures. Through the TEM measurements, dark-bright stripes appeared in the films for all three co-oligomers after thermal annealing at $2 1 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for two minutes while the ordered structure can be only observed in the SM37 system. However, the molecular orientation in the annealed materials is still relatively weak.

To enhance the nanoscale self-aggregation, SVA is a promising method. Herein, the order degree of co-oligomers was increased with the $\mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { C l } _ { 2 }$ vapor annealing. As shown in Figure 9.13d-f, the persistent lengths of the lamellae increase from 50 to $1 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ for thermally annealed films to $1 0 0 { - } 4 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ for solvent-vapor annealed films, and the crystalline sizes of the lamellae are 5.6, 7.4, and $8 . 9 \mathrm { n m }$ for SM35, SM36, and SM37, respectively.

In a further study, flexible linkages with different lengths were introduced to connect the OFbTs and PBI segments, and the effect of the varied periods on the micro-phase formation was also investigated by the same group. As shown in Figure 9.14, the ordered structures within the powders of these co-oligomers were investigated by X-ray scattering and diffraction. A new diffraction peak appeared at $2 \theta = 0 . 5 7 ^ { \circ }$ $0 . 6 5 ^ { \circ }$ , and $0 . 5 4 ^ { \circ }$ for SM41, SM42, and SM43, respectively, indicating the formation of lamellar nanostructures with a period of $1 5 . 5 \mathrm { n m }$ for SM41, $1 3 . 6 \mathrm { n m }$ for SM42, and $1 6 . 3 \mathrm { n m }$ for SM43. Compared with the SM37 (without alkyl linker between the donor and acceptor segments), the introduction of flexible spacers yielded a more regular microstructure. And the length of spacers also showed a significant effect on the molecular self-assembly. After thermal annealing at $1 6 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 10 minutes, the well-prepared films of the co-oligomers were studied by TEM. The dark-bright stripes are clearly present in the films with the periods of $1 4 . 2 \pm 0 . 4$ $1 5 . 0 \pm 1 . 0$ , and $1 4 . 6 \pm 0 . 7 \mathrm { n m }$ for SM41, SM42, and SM43, respectively. Besides, the SM42 showed multi-diffraction rings in the SAED patterns (selected area electron diffraction), and two of them with the $d$ -spacings of 3.5 and $4 . 4 \mathring \mathrm { A }$ are attributed to the $\ " \pi \mathrm { - } \pi \mathrm { \Omega } ^ { \ast }$ stacking distances of the adjacent PDI units and donor segments, respectively. The tendency to form ordered structures was predominated by the PBI in the shorter linkage system SM42, and the aggregation properties of the donor segment were enhanced when the $\mathrm { C } _ { 2 }$ -alkyl was replaced by $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 }$ -alkyl. Combining all the above observations, appropriate nanostructures with the highest intermolecular packing order can be obtained in the SM42.

# 9.3.2 Morphological Studies of the Block Copolymers in ScOSCs

It has been reported that BCPs could form well-ordered nanophase separation that is beneficial for charge separation via rationally controlling the crystallinity between donor and acceptor segments. The representative work was developed by Choi and coworkers, in which the formation of the appropriate morphologies in high-performance BCPs (BCP12-14) with the donor and acceptor blocks (DBs and ABs) as control was studied.

Figure 9.15 illustrated the study of morphologies and micro-separation within the BCPs developed by D.H. Choi and coworkers. The surface morphologies were measured by the AFM measurement, in which a smooth morphology that was rarely affected by the additive was obtained in the as-cast and optimized BCP12 films, while larger surface domains can be observed in the DBs/ABs blended films. Furthermore, TEM was used to investigate the internal morphologies of the films in two different systems (BCP12 film-based SCOSCs and DBs/ABs blend film-based BHJ OSCs), as shown in Figure 9.15c,f. The results indicated that the BCP12 exhibited a uniform and homogeneous morphology, which is beneficial to efficient exciton diffusion and charge transport.

![](images/cb21e3ed87ad942ab659c3d6da95cef78548509380c31d09c56a212e9bbe7127.jpg)  
Figure 9.15 AFM images (scale bar $= 1 \mu \mathrm { m } )$ of the active layer in PSC devices fabricated with $1 . 0 \mathrm { v o l } \%$ CN: topography of (a) BCP12 and (d) DBs/ABs blend films and phase images of films fabricated with (b) BCP12 and (e) DBs/ABs blend. TEM images (scale bar $= 2 0 0 \mathsf { n m }$ of the active layer in PSC devices fabricated with $1 . 0 \mathrm { v o l } \%$ CN: (c) BCP12 and (f) DBs/ABs blend films. Source: Lee et al. [53]/with permission of American Chemical Society.

In the subsequent research, the additional thiophene unit was introduced to expand the conjugated system of the donor segment and the enlarged donor block can promote profound effects on the micro-phase separation. The crystallinity and orientation of the polymer chains were investigated through GIwAXS measurement, as shown in Figure 9.16. A high-intensity (010) diffraction peak appeared in the as-cast films and the corresponding $d$ spacing is $3 . 7 8 \mathring \mathrm { A }$ , indicating that the copolymer chains exhibited the face-on orientation. And the more uniform crystalline-crystalline phase of donor blocks and acceptor blocks can be formed after post-processing treatment of 10minutes TA at $1 8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , revealed by the significantly enhanced (100) and (200) diffraction peaks in the $\mathbf { q } _ { z }$ direction and the narrower full width at half maximum of (010) peak in ${ \sf q } _ { x y }$ direction. The same phenomena were also observed in the Kelvin probe force microscope (KPFM) test. Annealed polymer film also possessed highly continuous CPD (contact potential difference) bright/dark images with high contrast. The results demonstrated that the dispersed donor- and acceptor-rich domains were induced after annealing.

# 9.3.3 Morphological Studies of the Double-Cable Polymers in SCOsCs

Generally, the double-cable polymer is formed by three segments: the conjugated backbone, the pendant side units, and the covalent linkers. Compared with the block copolymers, it is very difficult to control the morphology of the double-cable polymers, as both the main chain of conjugated backbones and the acceptor side units have strong crystallinity and aggregation tendency, which restrict each other, making it difficult to form a regular nanophase separation structure.

Li and coworkers have done a series of studies on tuning the nanophase separation of the double-cable polymers and made significant progress. For the polymer DCP24-26, as shown in Figures 9.8 and 9.17, the GIWAXS patterns revealed a clear enhanced crystallinity and face-on orientation from DCP 24 to DCP 26 by using longer alkyl (dodecyl) linkers and alkylthiothiophene side groups. Such changes are consistent with both enhanced planarity and rigidity of the $\pi$ -conjugated backbone and stronger $\pi$ stacking interactions, which were beneficial for the charge transport efficiency and were reflected in the enhanced FF and PCE of the single-component photovoltaic devices of these polymers with an order of $\mathbf { D C P 2 6 } > \mathbf { D C P 2 5 } > \mathbf { D C P 2 4 }$ [76].

The study of DCP27-29 revealed another strategy of using a linear conjugated backbone to improve the crystalline and adjust the phase separation of the double-cable polymers. Meanwhile, S and $\mathrm { F }$ atoms were also introduced into the alkylthiophene side groups. As shown in Figure 9.18, the AFM phase images showed small contrast with $1 0 { - } 2 0 \mathrm { n m }$ surface morphology characteristics. The GIwAxs showed that the polymers had preferentially "face-on' orientation with the characteristic distance of about $5 { - } 6 \mathrm { n m }$ from the peak (1o0) in the in-plane direction. And the GISAXS showed a $d$ spacing of about $5 \mathrm { n m }$ , which was about twofold $d$ spacing of the distance between the backbone and acceptor units, as confirmed by the TEM images. Then they illustrated the nanophase separation of the polymers, as schematically shown in Figure 9.18e, which could ensure efficient exciton dissociation into free charge carriers and provide percolating pathways for both electrons and holes.

To get better nanophase separation, they designed a new polymer DCP35 with a strongly crystalline backbone. After annealing at a high temperature, both the backbone and the pendant acceptor units could self-aggregate into ordered nanostructures. As shown in Figure $_ { 9 . 1 9 \mathrm { a } , \mathrm { b } }$ , from the grazing-incidence medium-angle X-ray scattering (GIMAXS) profiles, four scattering peaks that can be observed in the thin film annealed at $2 8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , which is a typical scattering feature of lamellar structures with an alternating arrangement of donor and acceptor segments. And a $6 . 9 \mathrm { n m }$ of $d$ spacing can be obtained from the peak q1, which should be the distance of the lamellar stacking between two backbones, as shown in Figure 9.19c. However, the peak q1 is obscure when the polymer thin films were annealed at low temperatures, especially those in the as-cast films indicated a highly amorphous and disordered nanostructure. After thermal annealing at high temperature, taking the GIWAXS results into consideration, they inferred that the degree of crystallization in the polymer film was enhanced by increasing the annealing temperature. Therefore, the nanophase separation was optimized, resulting in high charge transport efficiency, low charge recombination, and an excellent PCE of $6 . 3 \%$ in SCOSCs [80]. Li and coworkers also reported polymers DCP36-37 and raised a new term of crystalline cooperativity in double-cable polymers. DCP37 is a derivative of DCP35, from which Cl atoms on the alkyl-thiophene side groups were cleared away. As shown in Figure 9.20, the films of DCP37 showed the same crystalline properties as DCP35, with good crystalline cooperativity between the conjugated backbones and the side units. However, DCP36 presented completely different crystalline characteristics as its acceptor PBI units are on the same side of the backbones.

From the AFM height images, thin films of DCP37 showed fibrous structures with a smooth surface and the RMS roughness values were small, only from 0.81 to $1 . 0 9 \mathrm { n m }$ , even annealed at $2 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ However, the films of DCP36 presented notable granular crystals with a rough surface when annealed at high temperatures. For the GIwAxs, the coherence lengths (CLs) of (010) diffraction peaks in DCP36 and DC37 increased with the rising annealing temperature, while CLs of (o0) diffraction peak in their related donor polymer poly[(2,6-(4,8-bis(5-(2-ethylhexyl)thiophen-2-yl)-benzo[1,2-b:4,5-b']dithiophene))- alt-(5,5- $_ { 1 ^ { \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime } }$ -di-2-thienyl- $^ { 5 ^ { \prime } , 7 ^ { \prime } }$ -bis(2-ethylhexyl)benzo $[ 1 ^ { \prime } , 2 ^ { \prime } { \cdot } \mathrm { c } { : } 4 ^ { \prime } , 5 ^ { \prime } { \cdot } \mathrm { c } ^ { \prime } ]$ dithiophene4,8-dione)] (PBDB-T) remained constant. This inferred that the enhanced CLs of (010) peaks were driven by the enhanced crystallinity of PBIs at high temperatures. Otherwise, when increasing annealing temperature, the $d$ spacings of (ho0) peaks in DCP36 are significantly enhanced, which may be caused by the large crystalline domain of PBIs, while they were almost unchanged in DCP37. In consideration of the absorption, mobility, and the results of AFM and GIWAXS, the PBIs in DCP36 showed a strong tendency of crystallization and enhanced the crystallization of conjugated backbones, inducing poor crystalline cooperativity. This caused bad nanophase separation in DCP36 thin films but large phase separation in DCP37 thin films, so that they had completely different charge generation and recombination processes, resulting in different performances in their SCOSCs.

When they used NDI to replace the PBI side units in DCP35 and synthesized two new double-cable polymers (DCP39, DCP40) with isomeric structures, they studied the influence of the miscibility of the donor and acceptor segments. The GIWAxS showed that the two polymers had similar crystallinity in the crystal region, as shown in Figure 9.21a-c. However, from the study of differential scanning calorimetry (DsC) and contact angle, they got the Flory-Huggins interaction parameter $( \chi )$ which could reflect the mixability between donor and acceptor segments in the amorphous region of the double-cable polymers. As a result,

DCP39 had a higher x (1.02), which is almost twofold of the x in DCP40, indicating that the conjugated backbones and NDIs in DCP40 had better miscibility to create more interface to promote the exciton dissociation (Figure 9.21d). Consequently, DCP40-based SCOSCs could provide a record PCE of $8 . 4 \%$ with the highest EQE over 0.75, much better than the performance of DCP39.

Above all, these auspicious results provided several methods to tune the nanophase separation or miscibility in double-cable polymers and suggested promising guidelines to design high-performance SCOSCs.

# 9.4  Perspective and Challenges of ScosCs

Although new materials with exhilarating photovoltaic performance have been already applied in the SCOsC field, there are still two essential challenges:

(1) Charge generation process in SCOSC system, including the exciton diffusion, charge separation, and transports. Only a few studies revealed that efficient charge separation could be obtained in some BCPs [53, 90, 91]. Despite the limited studies, some interesting results could also be obtained in double-cable polymers, in which the IQEs over 0.80 and FFs over 0.65 could be realized, suggesting highly efficient transport of charge carriers in the SC active layers [80]. However, the charge generation process in SCOSCs is far to be understood, such as how to balance the exciton separation/charge transport in nanoscale, how to define the interface of donor/acceptor (as face-on or edge-on) [92], the charge recombination mechanism, etc.   
(2) $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ , defined as the difference between $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and optical bandgap of the active layer, was found to be high, ${ \sim } 0 . 7 0 \mathrm { V } ,$ for the SCOsCs. For high-performance BHJOSCs, $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ is often in the range of $0 . 4 \mathrm { - } 0 . 5 \mathrm { V } .$ In general, $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ can be divided into three parts, which are the charge transfer (CT) voltage losses $( \Delta V _ { \mathrm { C T } } )$ , i.e. losses associated with the driving force needed for efficient charge transfer from the exciton state to CT state; radiative recombination voltage losses $( \Delta V _ { \mathrm { r a d } } )$ , related to radiative recombination of charge carriers, and nonradiative voltage losses $( \Delta V _ { \mathrm { n o n - r a d } } )$ . All of these losses in BHJOsCs are reduced thanks to the development of fused-ring non-fullerene electron acceptors. However, these acceptors are yet to be incorporated into SC polymers, and the intrinsic mechanism of $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ in SCOSCs has been rarely studied.

Nevertheless, in this "dawn of SCOsCs"' [17], more efforts should be provided to further enhance the performance of SCOsCs. The efforts included: (i) developing better designed SC conjugated materials, for instance, via introducing electron acceptors with the absorption spectra in the NIR region, (ii) understanding the evolution of microstructures in these materials by using new techniques, such as Raman and IR spectroscopy, Fourier transformed pump-probe spectroscopy in the fs regime, (ii) studying the charge generation process in SCOsCs, especially compared with that in BHJOSCs, (iv) stability and mechanical properties, and the study in large-area flexible SCOsCs should be paid special attention. Success in these areas will make SCOSCs more attractive and contribute more to the development of the field of OSCs.

# Tandem Organic Solar Cells: Recent Progress and Challenge

Lingxian Meng, Xiangjian Wan, and Yongsheng Chen

Nankai University, The Centre of Nanoscale Science and Technology and Key Laboratory of Functional Polymer Materials, College of Chemistry, 94 Weijin Road, Tianjin, 300071, P.R. China

# 10.1 Introduction

Organic solar cells (OsCs) have drawn great attentions with the advantages of low cost, flexibility, lightweight, and large-area printing [1-8]. In the past few years, benefiting from the new active layer materials design, mechanism understanding, and device optimization, OSCs have witnessed rapid development in power conversion efficiencies (PCEs), reaching over $1 7 \%$ for single-junction and tandem solar cells [9-11]. Although with great success, the PCEs of OSCs are still far behind than those of inorganic material-based solar cells such as silicon and recently developed perovskite solar cells [12-14]. For single-junction photovoltaic devices, the maximum theoretical PCE is defined by the Shockley-Queisser limit [15], which is independent on the particular type of materials. For OsCs, some intrinsic and special properties of organic semiconductor materials are responsible for the less efficiencies of OSCs. For example, the low charge mobilities and narrow absorption windows of most organic materials make OSC devices have only limited thickness of the active layers and low current in many cases [16, 17]. However, organic materials have their own intrinsic advantages. Unlike inorganic materials, organic materials have great varieties and their optical and physical properties could be tuned effectively from the molecule design [3, 18-20]. In principle, organic materials with any bandgaps could be designed and synthesized. Most importantly, organic materials could be solution processed using the existing industrial printing techniques such as screen printing and roll-to-roll printing in large scale. Therefore, how to take the advantages of organic materials and get high efficiencies have been extensively explored in OSC community. To this end, one of the effective strategies is to develop tandem cells with stacking two or more cells with complementary absorption spectra in series or parallel connection, which could harvest photons at the highest possible potential and simultaneously conquer thermalization losses for single-junction solar cells (Figure 10.1) [21-24]. The varieties and tunable bandgaps of organic materials make them ideal candidates for use in tandem cells. Since the physical connection of the subcells in parallel architectures is challenging and hard to compatible with future solution-processed production of OSCs, the vast majority of tandem OSCs are series connection, in which the active layers are stacked in series through interconnection layers (ICLs) (Figure 10.1c,d). Note that the tandem OSCs in this chapter all refer to the series-connection devices, i.e. 2-terminal tandem devices without special note.

Source: Di Carlo Rasi and Jonssen [21]. Reproduced with permission of John Wiley & Sons. (c) The device structure of tandem OSCs with series connection and (d) parallel connection. Source: Lingxian Meng, Xiangjian Wan, Yongsheng Chen.

To obtain high PCEs for the series-connection tandem devices, there are several factors that need to be considered simultaneously. Firstly, the subcells should have complementary and wide absorptions and thus well-balanced and high short-circuit current density $( J _ { \mathrm { s c } } )$ of the tandem devices are expected. Secondly, the subcells should have minimal energy loss $( E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } )$ and high open-circuit voltage $( V _ { \mathrm { o c } } )$ since the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the series-connection tandem device equals to the sum of the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ values of each subcells if there is no potential loss in the ICLs. Thirdly, it is critical to have efficient and well-designed ICLs that can form ohmic contact with subcell active layers to ensure efficient charge extractions. In addition, the ICLs should be highly transparent and robust enough to protect underlying layers in the device fabrication process [22, 23].

![](images/d6cbab4fd06d5db1e22e66fc0230e13ed310fec079647cfb9519bf06f78b14f9.jpg)  
Figure 10.2 Fullerene acceptors used in tandem OSCs.

In the past decade, great efforts have been devoted to tandem OSCs and the photovoltaic performance has reached $1 7 \%$ [11]. And some excellent and comprehensive reviews have been reported on this topic [21, 22, 25-30]. In this chapter, we will review the recent progress of tandem OsCs in the views of chemists. Firstly, we will review the recent progress of solution-processed tandem OsCs focusing on the subcell active layer materials. Secondly, the development and progress of ICLs will be discussed. Thirdly, the efficiency prediction for tandem OSCs will be discussed through a semi-empirical analysis model we reported earlier. Lastly, a summary and outlook with challenge analysis will be given.

# 10.2 Active Layer Materials in Tandem OsCs

Similar to the single-junction OsCs, active layer materials play the fundamental roles in the development of tandem OSCs. To exploit the full potential of the tandem OSCs, great efforts have been devoted to the subcell active layers, mainly focusing on the active materials design with different bandgaps to fulfill the requirement of complementary absorption range of tandem cells. With isotropic electron transfer capabilities and high electron mobilities, fullerene derivatives had been the standard acceptors since the invention of BHJ device in 1995 [31]. Thus, many wideand low-bandgap donor materials have been designed and screened as front and rear active layers donors with fullerene derivative acceptors for fabricating tandem devices. And the PCEs increased from $6 . 5 \%$ in 2007 to $1 2 . 7 \%$ in 2017 for the tandem devices using fullerene derivatives as acceptors [2, 32]. However, some intrinsic properties of fullerene derivatives such as weak absorptions and hardly tunable energy levels significantly limit the further improvement performance of OSCs including the single-junction and tandem devices. To address the above issues, in recent years, various non-fullerene acceptors (NFAs) have been designed and made great success for single-junction and tandem devices [9, 19, 20, 30, 33-40].

To date, a high PCE of $1 7 . 3 \%$ has been achieved for the tandem device [11]. In this section, we will review the progress of tandem OSCs in the past decades, which is roughly divided into two parts based on the acceptors, i.e. fullerene acceptors and NFAs utilized in the tandem cells. The chemical structures, bandgap, and photovoltaic parameters of the representative materials used in tandem OsCs are listed in Table 10.1, 10.2, and Figure 10.2-10.5.

# 10.2.1Tandem OSCs Based on Fullerene Acceptors

In the early years, the tandem OSCs were fabricated with the vacuum-deposited approach [22, 23, 28]. The first all solution-processed (except the top evaporated electrode) tandem OSC was reported by Kim et al. [2]. In the tandem device, PCPDTBT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ were used as the front cell and rear cell, respectively. The complementary absorptions of PCPDTBT and P3HT made the whole cell covering the spectra range from 400 to nearly $9 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ and a PCE of $6 . 5 \%$ was achieved. This work demonstrated the great potential of the solution-processed tandem OsCs. However, in the following three years, little progress has been made on tandem OSCs, mainly limited by few active layer materials with suitable bandgaps, especially narrow bandgap materials. In 2010, Janssen and coworkers proposed a methodology by analyzing the optical absorption and electrical characteristics of individual single-junction subcells to identify the optimum device layout of the corresponding tandem device and could provide predicted optimal film thickness of the front and rear cells to obtain the better $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ [41]. Guided by this methodology, a tandem device, comprising a wide-bandgap polymer PFTBT with a bandgap of $1 . 9 5 \mathrm { e V }$ and a low-bandgap one (pBBTDPP2) with a bandgap of $1 . 4 0 \mathrm { e V }$ mixed with $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as the electron acceptor, was fabricated, and eventually a PCE of $4 . 9 \%$ was achieved. In 2012, Yang and coworkers reported a low-bandgap polymer, PBDTT-DPP, with an optical bandgap of $1 . 4 4 \mathrm { e V }$ and absorption onset of $8 5 8 \mathrm { n m }$ [42]. The single-junction device of PBDTT-DPP: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ gave a PCE over $6 \%$ P3HT and the indene-C60 bisadduct $\mathrm { ( I C _ { 6 0 } B A ) }$ were selected as front cell materials owing to the high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the single-junction cell. Finally, a tandem OsC with inverted structure using ${ \mathrm { P } } 3 { \mathrm { H T } } { \mathrm { : I C } } _ { 6 0 } { \mathrm { B A } }$ as the front cell materials and PBDTT-DPP $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as the rear cell materials was fabricated and a certified PCE of $8 . 6 2 \%$ from NREL was achieved. Subsequently, they designed three polymers with low bandgap of $1 . 4 { \mathrm { - } } 1 . 5 { \mathrm { e V } }$ based on benzodithiophene (BDT) and diketopyrrolopyrrole (DPP) units [43]. The low bandgap and high performance of these polymer-based single-junction devices enabled them to be suitable as rear cells in tandem OSCs. With these polymers mixed with $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as the rear cells and ${ \mathrm { P } } 3 { \mathrm { H T } } { \mathrm { : I C } } _ { 6 0 } { \mathrm { B A } }$ as the front cell, PCEs of tandem OSCs close to $9 \%$ were achieved. Subsequently, Janssen and coworkers reported a low-bandgap $\left( 1 . 4 6 \mathrm { e V } \right)$ polymer of DPP derivative, PDPP5T, and used it as rear cell donor materials in tandem OSCs [44]. Despite with efficient PCE of $5 . 3 \%$ PDPP5T: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 }$ BM-based single-junction device only yielded a lower $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 5 8 \mathrm { V } .$ To ensure a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the tandem device, they used PCDTBT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as the front cell with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 0 \mathrm { V } .$ A PCE of $7 . 0 \%$ was achieved with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of 1.44 V, $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $9 . 0 \mathrm { m A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and fill factor (FF) of 0.54 for the tandem device.
