on, Jen et al. reported a fluoro-containing low-bandgap polymer PCPDTFBT and used it as rear cell donor material for constructing semitransparent solar cells and tandem solar cells with ${ \mathrm { P } } 3 { \mathrm { H T } } { \mathrm { : I C } } _ { 6 0 } { \mathrm { B A } }$ as the front cell materials to give PCEs of $5 . 0 \%$ and $8 . 2 \%$ , respectively [45]. The above work demonstrated that the design of efficient rear cell donor materials with low bandgap is an effective strategy and also the prerequisite for constructing high-performance tandem OsCs. In 2013, Yang and coworkers designed a new polymer PDTP-DFBT with a low bandgap of $1 . 3 8 \mathrm { e V }$ [46]. The single-junction device of PDTP-DFBT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ showed a PCE of $7 . 9 \%$ with high external quantum efficiency (EQE) over $6 0 \%$ and spectral response that extended to $9 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . The tandem solar cell with PDTP-DFBT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as the rear cell and P3HT:ICBA as the front cell gave a certified and high PCE of $1 0 . 6 \%$ . In their following work, a homo-tandem device using PDTP-DFBT $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as the front and rear cells was constructed [47]. The homo-tandem device could harvest more efficient light compared with the single-junction device with maximum absorption increasing from $7 0 \%$ to $9 0 \%$ in visible region. A PCE of $1 0 . 2 \%$ was achieved for the homo-tandem device, indicating that the homo-tandem strategy is also an effective alternative strategy in enhancing the PCE for the corresponding single-junction device. In 2015, Heeger and coworkers reported a homo-tandem device based on PTB7-Th (also named PCE10) $\mathrm { \cdot P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ active layer using a novel ICL [48]. After careful optimization, a best PCE of $1 1 . 3 \%$ was achieved. In 2016, Hou and coworkers reported a new low-bandgap polymer named PDPP4T-2F, which showed an absorption onset at $9 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , corresponding to an optical bandgap of $1 . 3 7 \mathrm { e V }$ [49]. PDPP4T-2I $\mathrm { \mathrm { \Omega } ^ { \mathrm { \Omega } } } : \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ -based device showed a PCE of $7 . 5 8 \%$ and a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 7 8 \mathrm { V }$ owing to the deep highest occupied molecular orbital (HOmO) of the polymer. Then, using a wide-bandgap polymer PBDD4T-2F accompanied with $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as the front cell and $\mathrm { P D P P 4 T : P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ as the rear cell, a tandem device was fabricated and demonstrated an outstanding PCE of $1 1 . 6 2 \%$

Although ${ \mathrm { P } } 3 { \mathrm { H T } } { \mathrm { : I C } } _ { 6 0 } { \mathrm { B A } }$ had showed decent single-junction device performance and achieved initial success as front cell in several high efficiency tandem devices as discussed above, its low $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ limit the further device improvement of the tandem OSCs using them as front cell. So, designing wide-bandgap and efficient donor materials is as important as that of low-bandgap polymers. Peng and coworkers designed a wide-bandgap (1.81eV) polymer PBDTFBZS consisting of dialkylthiol-substituted benzo[1,2-b:4,5. $\cdot b ^ { \prime }$ ldithiophene donor block and monofluorinated benzotriazole acceptor block [50]. The PBDTFBZS: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ -based single-junction device showed good performance with a PCE of $6 . 1 8 \%$ and a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 8 \mathrm { V } .$ Tandem device using PBDTFBZS $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as front cell and PNDTDPP: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as rear cell afforded a PCE of $9 . 4 \%$ . Hwang and coworkers designed and synthesized two D-A copolymers, PTIPSBDTDTQX and PTIPSBDT-DFDTQX, based on the donor unit TIPS substituted benzodithiophene (TIPSBDT) and the acceptor quinoxaline-based units with or without fluorine substitution [51]. The introduction of F atoms on the quinoxaline unit is effective in lowering both the HOMO and lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) energy levels of PTIPSBDTDFDTQX to get a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 1 \mathrm { V }$ and a PCE of $5 . 2 5 \%$ for the single-junction device. Finally, a PCE of $7 . 2 \%$ was achieved for the tandem device using PTIPSBDTDFDTQX $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as the front cell and PBPT ${ \cdot 8 { : } \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } } \mathrm { B M }$ as the rear cell. Later on, Hou and coworkers reported a polythiophene derivative named PDCBT [52]. The device based on PDCBT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ showed a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 0 \mathrm { V }$ and high EQE values in the range $4 0 0 { - } 6 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . A tandem device using $\mathrm { P D C B T : P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ as front cell and PBDT-TS1: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as rear cell was fabricated. Although these two polymers PDCBT and PBDT-TS1 show some overlapping absorption in the range from 550 to $6 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , symmetric current densities could still be realized by careful optimization of the thickness of the active layers. Finally, a PCE of $1 0 . 1 6 \%$ for the tandem device was obtained. Subsequently, other low bandgap polymers such as PDTBTBz- $2 \mathrm { F _ { a n t i } }$ with a remarkably high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 7 \mathrm { V }$ and PTZ1 with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 4 \mathrm { V }$ were designed and used as front cell donor materials for constructing tandem devices and PCEs over $1 0 \%$ were achieved [53, 54]. In 2017, Zheng and coworkers reported a polymer, PIDTBTO-TT, with a bandgap of $1 . 8 7 \mathrm { e V }$ and successfully applied it into the tandem OSCs [55]. By selecting PTB7-Th: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as the rear cell and PIDTBTO-TT mixed with $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as the front cell, a high PCE of $1 1 . 1 5 \%$ for the tandem device was obtained. In the same year, Kim and coworkers reported two side chain fluorinated wide-bandgap P1 (2F) and P2 (4F) which had deep HOMO and thus high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of 0.91V and $1 . 0 0 \mathrm { V }$ respectively [56]. Using the two polymers and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as front cell materials with PTB $7 – \mathrm { T h } { : } \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as rear cells, the optimized tandem devices gave PCEs of $1 1 . 4 2 \%$ and $1 0 . 0 5 \%$ , with high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of 1.64 and $1 . 7 2 \mathrm { V } ,$ respectively. These results demonstrated the excellent examples for new wide band gap materials design approaches to advance the field of tandem OSCs.

It is clear that the progress of tandem OsCs is intimately connected with the active layer materials. The above results for solution-processed tandem OSCs are all based on polymer donors. As the counterpart of polymers, solution-processed small molecules have shown great potentials with advantages of no batch to batch, high mobility, and generally high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ , which enable them to be excellent alternative in tandem devices. In the past decade, various solution-processed small molecule donors have been designed and synthesized. Among them, molecules with the acceptor-donor-acceptor (A-D-A) architecture developed by our group have showed the best device performance and demonstrated completely comparable device performance in contrast to that of polymers [3, 20]. In recent years, we have reported series of solution-processed high efficiency small molecule donors and acceptors with the A-D-A type architecture. Some small molecule donors such as DRCN7T [76], DRCN5T [77], DR3TBDT [78], DR3TBDTT [79], and DR3TSBDT [80] designed and synthesized by our group have become the representative molecules and widely used in the OsC community. In view of their suitable absorption range, high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and good FF of the single junction devices, these A-D-A molecules would be ideal alternatives to substitute the widely-used P3HT as front cell materials to fabricate high-efficiency tandem OSCs. Thus, we selected three small molecules DR3TSBDT, DR3TBDTT, and DRBDT-TT as the front cell donor materials with $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as acceptor to fabricate tandem devices. And PTB7- $\mathrm { T h } { \cdot } \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ was utilized as the rear cell owing to the materials availability and high device repeat properties for the single-junction device [57]. Using an all solution-processed procedure except the back Al electrode, three tandem devices with the inverted structures were fabricated. Among them, the device based on DR3TSBDT showed a PCE of $1 1 . 4 7 \%$ , with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 6 8 9 \mathrm { V }$ $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 0 . 5 1 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and FF of $6 4 . 6 \%$ , which was among the highest values reported for tandem cells in 2016. The tandem OSCs based on DR3TBDTT and DRBDT-TT also showed high PCEs of $1 0 . 7 3 \%$ and $1 0 . 4 3 \%$ Yang and coworkers also designed a small molecule SMPV1 and used it to fabricate homo-tandem device to afford a PCE of $1 0 . 1 \%$ with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 8 2 \mathrm { V }$ and good FF of $7 2 \%$ [58]. In 2016, Huang and coworkers employed a porphyrin derivative molecule DPPZnP-THE as the rear cell donor material to fabricate tandem device. DPPZnP-THE covered a broad range from 300 to $9 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ with a low bandgap of $1 . 3 7 \mathrm { e V }$ [59]. Selecting PThBDTP: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as the front cell, a PCE of $1 1 . 3 5 \%$ was achieved. The above results demonstrated the great potential of small molecule active layers for high performance solution-processed tandem OsCs.

In order to obtain higher efficiency, it is important for the subcells to have complementary absorptions and generate high and balanced (matched) currents. This requires a rather challenging effort to design and select suitable active materials for use in the subcells. In 2017, we and collaborators reported a high performance solution-processed tandem solar cell based on two small molecules DR3TsBDT and DPPEZnP-TBO, which offered efficient and complementary absorption when being used as electron donor materials in the front and rear subcells, respectively [32]. Through delicated film thickness adjustment, the $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of the tandem device reached $1 2 . 2 9 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . Eventually, an all small molecule tandem device with a PCE of $1 2 . 5 0 \%$ (verified $1 2 . 7 0 \%$ ) was achieved, representing a new level of capability for solution-processed OsCs.

# 10.2.2 Tandem OsCs Based on Non-fullerene Acceptors

Although much progress has been made in fullerene derivative-based OSCs including single-junction and tandem OsCs, the intrinsic properties of fullerene derivatives such as weak absorptions and hardly tunable energy levels significantly limit the device performance. To address these issues, great efforts have been devoted to NFAs and substantial progress have been made in the OSC community [19, 30, 33]. Various types of NFAs including small molecules and polymers have been designed and evaluated. Among them, molecules with A-D-A architecture which have borrowed the design rationale from the A-D-A donor molecules have achieved big success. Detailed properties on the A-D-A architecture molecules can be seen in our recent review paper [20]. To date, the vast majority of single-junction devices using NFAs with high PCEs are fabricated using A-D-A type acceptors [19, 30, 33]. Compared with fullerene-based acceptors, NFAs, especially A-D-A type acceptors, exhibit excellent more merits and greater potential for constructing high-performance tandem OSCs, for example, (i) NFAs-based single-junction devices generally show low $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ , which makes them obtain higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ in the tandem devices, (ii) the easiness of bandgap tunability of NFAs presents more room to design subcells and thus high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of the corresponding tandem OsCs are highly expected. With these advantages, many studies have been conducted on the NFA-based tandem OSCs and great progress has been made in recent years.

In 2016, Chen and coworkers demonstrated the first efficient non-fullerene tandem OSC by utilizing two NFA systems as the front and rear cells via solution processing [60]. Benefiting from the high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of 1.11 V for the ${ \mathrm { P } } 3 { \mathrm { H T } } { \mathrm { : S F } } ( { \mathrm { D P P B } } ) _ { 4 }$ -based front cell and $0 . 9 5 \mathrm { V }$ for the PTB7-Th:IEIC-based rear cell, the tandem OSC showed a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 9 7 \mathrm { V }$ and a PCE of $8 . 4 8 \%$ . With the high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ , the tandem device was used for the solar-cell-driven water splitting tests, indicating the great potential of high-voltage tandem cells. However, the overlap absorption and inferior FF of the front and rear cell impeded the further improvement of photovoltaic performance. Later on, Yan and coworkers reported a homo-tandem device with an impressively high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ over $2 . 1 \mathrm { V }$ [61]. They used P3TEA as the donor and $\mathrm { S F } { \cdot } \mathrm { P D I } _ { 2 }$ as the acceptor in the front and rear cell to construct the homo-tandem device. With device optimization, a PCE of $1 0 . 8 \%$ was achieved accompanied with the outstanding $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $2 . 1 3 \mathrm { V } .$ In 2017, Peng and coworkers designed and synthesized a wide-bandgap copolymer PBDTS-TDZ. When accompanied with ITIC as the acceptor, a PCE of $1 2 . 8 0 \%$ was achieved with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 1 \mathrm { V }$ [62]. A homo-tandem device was also fabricated. Finally, an outstanding PCE of $1 3 . 3 5 \%$ was achieved through optimizing the thickness of the front and rear cells with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $2 . 1 3 \mathrm { V } .$ The above results gave more confidence for the researchers in the OsC field to fabricate higher efficiency tandem devices. Subsequently, the study on tandem OsCs mainly focuses on the design and synthesis of NFAs, especially those A-D-A type small molecule acceptors with complementary absorptions. The wide bandgap materials can provide high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and the low bandgap materials facilitate to increase $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of the tandem devices. And thus, high efficiency tandem devices can be expected.

In 2017, a low-bandgap acceptor 4TIC with absorption onset around $9 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ was designed and synthesized by Jen and coworkers [63]. The single-junction device with PTB7-Th as the donor material gave a PCE of $1 0 . 4 3 \%$ with $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 8 . 7 5 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , FF of 0.72, and $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 7 8 \mathrm { V } .$ The high efficiency together with its small voltage loss made PTB7-Th:4TIC a suitable rear subcell for tandem solar cells. They fabricated a series- connection tandem OSCs incorporating this rear cell and PBDB-T:ITIC as front cell, and obtained a promising PCE of $1 2 . 6 2 \%$ . In their next work, they designed an acceptor, 6TBA. With PTB7-Th as donor material, 6TBA-based device exhibited a higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 8 \mathrm { V }$ and lower voltage loss of $0 . 5 4 \mathrm { V }$ than that of PBDB-T:ITIC [64]. A tandem device was then fabricated using PTB7-Th:6TBA as the front cell and PTB7-Th:4TIC as the rear cell delivered a high PCE of $1 3 . 2 0 \%$ In order to balance the tradeoff between the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ in the tandem device, Yang and coworkers reported two NFAs named FOIC and F8IC based on the terthieno [3,2-b]thiophen (6T) core with one or two $\mathrm { F }$ atoms substituent on the end groups and used the ternary system PTB7-Th:FO1C:F81C as rear cell materials for tandem cell [65]. The $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the rear cells could be tuned in a wide range $( 0 . 6 7 – 0 . 7 5 \mathrm { V } )$ by changing the ratio of the two acceptors. Finally, employing PBDB-T:IT-M as the front cell, a tandem device with a PCE of $1 3 . 3 \%$ was obtained.

Hou and coworkers reported a tandem device based on two A-D-A type acceptors and delivered an outstanding PCE of $1 3 . 8 \%$ , a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 7 9 \mathrm { V } ,$ a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 2 . 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and an FF of 0.641 [66]. Firstly, an acceptor ITCC-M was designed based on the well-known acceptor ITIC through replacing the phenyl group in the end groups by $\alpha$ -methylthiophene groups. Compared with ITIC, the $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ of ITCC-M was enlarged by around $0 . 1 1 \mathrm { e V }$ with the half-peak-height position in the long-wavelength direction shifting from $7 5 0 ~ \mathrm { n m }$ to $7 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . Blending with PBDB-T as the donor material, ITCC-M-based device showed a PCE of $9 \%$ with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ over 1 V. Next, they selected a near-infrared absorption acceptor, IEICO and a polymer donor PBDTTT-E-T as the rear cell. Finally, the tandem device was fabricated using a ZnO/PCP-Na as the ICL and gave an impressive efficiency of $1 3 . 8 \%$ . The moderate EQE response and range of the rear cell together with the low FF limited the device performance. So, in their following work [67], to extend the absorption range and enable well complementary absorption of the subcells, IEICO-4F with absorption onset around $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ was selected to replace IEICO as the rear cell acceptor. Meanwhile, an acceptor IT-M with a bandgap of $1 . 6 \mathrm { e V }$ and a wide-bandgap polymer J52-F were selected as the front cell. The much more complementary absorption of the subcells contributed to the improved $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 3 . 3 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and thus enhanced PCE of $1 4 . 9 \%$ In 2019, Huang and coworkers reported a NFA TfiF-4FIC with $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ of $1 . 6 1 \mathrm { e V }$ [68]. The single-junction device based on PM6:TfiF-4FIC delivered a PCE of $1 3 . 1 \%$ with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 8 \mathrm { V }$ and a notable FF of $7 6 \%$ . The excellent photovoltaic parameters, together with the wide bandgap, enable PM6:TfIF-4FIC a good candidate as the front cell for fabricating tandem OsCs. A ternary combination PCE10:PCDTBT:IEICO-4F was optimized as the rear cell materials to ensure a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 5 . 3 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . Finally, the tandem device afforded a PCE of $1 5 . 0 \%$ . In 2021, Huang and coworkers developed an efficient ICL of ZnO NPs:PEI/PEI/PEDOT:PSS [69]. They used PM7:TfiF-4Cl as the front cell and $\mathrm { P C E 1 0 : C O } _ { i } \mathrm { 8 D F I C : P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ as the rear cell to construct the tandem device. In order to suppress the charge recombination of the front cell with the increased thickness of the active layer to get higher FF, they increase the proportion of the TfiF-4Cl in the front cell to manipulate the optical field distribution and then increase the $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ . With this stragety, the tandem device could simultaneously achieve higher $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and FF. Finally, a PCE of $1 8 . 7 1 \%$ was obtained. Recently, Anthopoulos and coworkers also synthesized a wide-bandgap acceptor, IDTTA. Using PBDB-T as the donor, the single-junction device of IDTTA exhibited a PCE of $1 0 . 8 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 8 \mathrm { V }$ [70]. Employing PBDB-T:IDTTA as the front cell and PTB7-Th:IEICO-4F as the rear cell, the tandem device was fabricated to realize a PCE of $1 5 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 6 6 \mathrm { V }$ and $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 3 . 6 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$

Benzo[1,2-b:4,5 $. b ^ { \prime }$ Jdithiophene (BDT) is a widely used building block in the OSC community. Numerous donor materials including polymers and small molecules incorporating the BDT unit have been synthesized. In 2017, our group reported the first BDT-based acceptor NFBDT with a heptacyclic benzodi(cyclopentadithiophene) (FBDT) unit as the central unit, where the BDT core unit is covalently rigidified at its 3,7-positions with two external fused thiophene (T) units by the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ -carbon bridges [81]. And PCE over $1 0 \%$ was achieved for the single-junction device based on PBDB-T:NFBDT. To meet the demands of rear cell in tandem device, we designed a new BDT core-based acceptor NOBDT through modifying the acceptor NFBDT by introducing $\mathrm { F }$ substituted end groups and BDT core incorporating oxygen alkyl chains [71]. NOBDT showed a near-infrared absorption with absorption onset around $9 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . The single-junction device of

PTB7-Th:NOBDT demonstrated a PCE $1 0 . 5 5 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 7 7 \mathrm { V }$ and energy loss $0 . 6 2 \mathrm { e V } ,$ indicating great potential in tandem OsCs. Meanwhile, we designed an acceptor F-M with absorption onset of $7 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ and the single-junction device based on PBDB-T:F-M exhibited a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ around $1 \mathrm { V } .$ By systematically optimizing the thickness of subcell active layers under the guidance of optical simulation, a high PCE of $1 4 . 1 1 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of 1.71 V, a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 1 . 7 2 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and a satisfactory FF of 0.70 was achieved. In the following work, to balance the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of the tandem device, we reported a tandem device employing two subcells with the same donor PBDB-T and two acceptors F-M and NNBDT with complementary absorptions. An efficient tandem OSC with an optimized PCE of $1 4 . 5 2 \%$ was achieved with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 8 2 \mathrm { V } ,$ a notable FF of $7 4 . 7 \%$ , and a $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 0 . 6 8 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ [72]. This work demonstrates a promising strategy for fabricating high efficiency tandem OSCs through careful selection of the subcell active layer materials and tradeoff of the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of the tandem cells. The results also demonstrated that the BDT unit-based acceptors are indeed good candidates for fabricating high efficiency tandem devices, which is proved by the work reported by Forrest and coworkers [73]. Using a near infrared absorption acceptor BT-ClC blending with PCE-10 as the rear cell, and visible absorption vacuum deposited DTDCPB:C70 as the front cell, a tandem device was fabricated and delivered a PCE of $1 4 . 3 \%$ for $2 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ device and a maximum PCE of $1 5 \%$ was afforded. In their following work, in order to improve the $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and efficiency of the tandem device, a low bandgap acceptor TT-FIC was added in the above rear cell PCE10:BT-ClC binary system [74]. Using the same front cell of DTDCPB $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ , a tandem device was constructed and gave an improved PCE of $1 5 . 4 \%$

Despite that NFA-based tandem OSCs have made much progress, the overall efficiencies were still unsatisfactory. It is essential to synergistically design and screen the front and rear cell materials from the perspective of energy losses, absorption ranges, and the photovoltaic parameters such as FF and EQE of the subcell. In 2018, we have proposed a semi-empirical analysis for the possible but realistic PCE limit of two terminal monolithic tandem OSCs, which will be discussed in details in the following part. Under the guidance of the model analysis, one can not only get the possible PCEs for the defined subcells but also rationally design subcell active layers. Based on the model analyzed above, we constructed a tandem device using two A-D-A acceptors-based subcells with complementary absorptions covering a wide range from 300 to $1 0 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [11]. According to the semi-empirical model, firstly, a low bandgap A-D-A small molecule acceptor O6T-4F was selected as the rear cell acceptor material as it has an infrared absorption onset of ${ \sim } 1 0 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ (optical bandgap $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ $1 . 2 0 \mathrm { e V } )$ and the single-junction device based on it with PTB7-Th as donor and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as the secondary acceptor exhibited a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ with EQE response value over $7 0 \%$ in the infrared absorption range, an FF of $6 9 . 7 \%$ , and a low $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ of 0.51 eV. Next, PBDB-T:F-M was selected as front cell as the combination exhibits not only absorption onset close to the ideal absorption onset of $7 2 0 \mathrm { n m }$ but also with optimal current $\sim 1 6 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and high EQE response (average $\sim 7 0 \%$ in the range of $3 0 0 { - } 7 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , FF $( 6 9 . 8 \% )$ . Using an all solution-processed procedure except the back electrode, a tandem device was constructed and achieved a record PCE of $1 7 . 3 \%$ . In 2021, in order to extend the absorption range of the rear cell, Li and coworkers designed and synthesized a low-bandgap acceptor BTPV-4F by inserting a double bond between the central core and end groups of the acceptor Y6 [75]. Benefiting from its extended conjugation length, the optical bandgap of the BTPV-4F is only $1 . 2 1 \mathrm { e V }$ with an absorption onset of $1 0 2 1 \mathrm { n m }$ When blending with PTB7-Th and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ , BTPV-4F based single-junction device demonstrated a higher $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $2 8 . 9 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ with a notable FF of $6 9 . 3 \%$ . Meanwhile, a wide-bandgap acceptor $m$ -DTC-2F was synthesized with a bandgap of $1 . 6 1 \mathrm { e V }$ as the front cell. PM6:m-DTC-2F-based device exhibits a PCE of $1 2 . 1 \%$ with a higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 9 9 \mathrm { V } .$ Finally, the tandem device with PM6:m-DTC-2F as the front cell and PTB7-Th:BTPV-4F $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as the rear cell achieved a promising PCE of $1 6 . 4 \%$ with a high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 4 . 5 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . The high efficiency and the semi-empirical analysis model indicate that OSC has much more potential than previously thought if using tandem cell. And $\mathrm { P C E } > 2 5 \%$ could be achieved through careful active layer material design under the guidance of above semi-empirical analysis together with device optimization, including subcell active layer morphology control, thickness optimization and interconnecting layer engineering.

# 10.3 Interconnecting Layer Materials

In the tandem photovoltaic devices, the subcells are connected by the ICL materials, which extract charge carriers from the front and rear subcells and meanwhile provide a recombination region for the collected carriers. Thus, ICL materials are the critical components for realizing high performance for tandem OSCs [22, 23, 82]. For efficient ICLs, they should form ohmic contact with subcell active layers to ensure efficient charge extractions. And they should be highly transparent and robust enough to protect underlying layer during subsequent fabrication process. ICL is generally composed of a p-type hole transporting layer (HTL) and an n-type electron transporting layer (ETL). ICLs in tandem cells could be roughly divided into two major configurations: ETL-conducting layer-HTL (e-c-h-type) and ETL-HTL (e-h-type) in the conventional structure or h-c-e-type and h-e-type in the inverted structure [25, 83]. In fact, the ETL and HTL materials used in single-junction OSCs can be combined and used as ICL materials in tandem OSCs. For the e-c-h-type or h-c-e configuration, a conductive layer, generally very thin metal, is sandwiched between the ETL and HTL. The ETL and HTL are used to collect the electron and hole from the subcells, respectively, where the conductive layer is served as charge recombination center. At present, thin-film metals (i.e. Au, Ag, Al) are usually applied as conductive layer materials for most of e-c-h (or h-c-e) type ICLs. And the combination can satisfy the requirements for the ICLs, such as high transparency, minimized voltage losses, and functioned as an optical spacer to match the current between the subcells. In recent years, many e-c-h-type (or h-c-e-type) ICLs have been designed for tandem OSCs, such as $\mathrm { T i O _ { 2 } / A l / P E D O T { : } P S S }$ [84], $\mathrm { M o O } _ { 3 } / \mathrm { A l } / \mathrm { Z n O }$ [85], PEDOT:PSS/AgNW/ZnO [86], $\mathrm { M o O } _ { 3 } / \mathrm { A g } /$ PFN [87, 88], ZnO/M-PEDOT:PSS/PMA or PMA:M-PEDOT:PSS/ZnO [89], $\bf M _ { 0 } O _ { 3 } / M$ -PEDOT:PSS/ZnO [65, 90], BPhen $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 } / \mathrm { A g }$ NP/PEDOT:PSS [74], $\mathrm { M o O _ { 3 } / A g / Z n O / P F N  – B r }$ [64].

However, complicated evaporation steps and possible optical losses induced by the metal layer are often encountered for the h-c-e-type (or e-c-h-type) ICLs. Thus, many attentions have been drawn on the h-e-type (or e-h-type) ICLs, which can realize all solution process and demonstrate much advantages than the h-c-e-type (or e-c-h-type) ICLs. For the h-e-type (or e-h-type) ICLs, the hole and electron of the subcells are collected by the HTL and ETL, respectively, and the charge recombination occurs and completes at the ETL-HTL contact interface. Thus, a separate conductive layer is not needed. Currently, most of the HTL materials in the h-e-type (or e-h-type) ICLs are PEDOT:PSS or its modified products. PEDOT:PSS accompanied with ETL, especially n-type metal oxide, are the most popularly used h-e-type (or e-h) type ICL materials for tandem OSCs, such as PEDOT:PSS/ZnO [61, 91, 92], PEDOT:PSS/ZnO/CPE [93], PEDOT:PSS] $\mathrm { S n O } _ { 2 }$ [94], PEDOT:PSS/NPE [95], PEDOT:PSS/PEIE [96], M-PEDOT/CDQ PEI [97], $\mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { x } } \mathrm { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /PEDOT:PSS/ZnO NPs [98], $\mathrm { T i O } _ { 2 } / \mathrm { M }$ -PDEOT [99], ZnO/N-PEDOT:PSS [71], PNDIT-EHP-F3N:PEI/PEDOT:PSS [100]. Other combinations without PEDOT:PSS were also reported, such as $\mathrm { P O M / Z n O }$ [101], ZnO/CPE-K [48, 102], ZnO/PCP-Na [66], and $\mathrm { M o O } _ { x } / \mathrm { S n O } _ { \mathrm { x } }$ [103]. Device parameters of some representative tandem OSCs using various ICLs are also summarized in Tables 10.1 and 10.2.

# 10.4 The Semi-Empirical Analysis of Tandem OSCs

There are some theoretical calculations predicting the maximum efficiency of tandem OSCs. For example, as early as in 2008, Brabec and coworkers conducted a calculation that tandem devices based on PCBM derivatives as acceptors could gave efficiencies up to $1 5 \%$ [82]. In 2018, we proposed a semi-empirical model to direct the design and selection of subcell materials for tandem devices. With the guidance of this semi-empirical model, a record PCE of $1 7 . 3 \%$ has been achieved for tandem device, which is a new level for solution-processed OSCs [11]. The semi-empirical analysis was conducted on a 2-terminal monolithic tandem device with two subcells in series. Of course, it can be extended to be used in single-junction and multijunction series connected device. The details can be found in references [11, 104]. The following is the main content.

Based on some assumptions, the three photovoltaic parameters $V _ { \mathrm { o c } } , J _ { \mathrm { s c } , }$ and FF of a 2-terminal monolithic tandem device are obtained as follows:

(1) For a rear cell with absorption onset $\lambda _ { 1 }$ , the $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of the tandem cell could be obtained from Eq. (10.1).

$$
J _ { \mathrm { s c , t a n d e m } } = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \cdot \int _ { 3 0 0 } ^ { \lambda _ { 1 } } { \frac { q \lambda } { h c } } \cdot E ( \lambda ) \cdot \operatorname { E Q E } ( \lambda ) \cdot \mathrm { d } \lambda = \int _ { 3 0 0 } ^ { \lambda _ { 2 } } { \frac { q \lambda } { h c } } \cdot E ( \lambda ) \cdot \operatorname { E Q E } ( \lambda ) \cdot \mathrm { d } \lambda
$$

where $E ( \lambda )$ is the spectral irradiance in AM 1.5G, $\lambda _ { 1 }$ and $\lambda _ { 2 }$ are the absorption onset of rear and front cell, $h$ is Planck's constant, $c$ is the speed of light, and $q$ is the elementary charge.

The absorption onset $( \lambda _ { 2 } )$ of a matched front cell could be determined from Eq. (10.2) under AM 1.5G light illumination.

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle { \cal J } _ { \mathrm { s c , f r o n t } } = { \cal J } _ { \mathrm { s c , r e a r } } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \cdot \int _ { 3 0 0 } ^ { \lambda _ { 1 } } \frac { q \lambda } { h c } } \cdot E ( \lambda ) { \displaystyle \cdot \mathrm { E Q E } ( \lambda ) } { \displaystyle \cdot \mathrm { d } \lambda } }  \\ { { \displaystyle ~ = \int _ { 3 0 0 } ^ { \lambda _ { 2 } } \frac { q \lambda } { h c } } { \displaystyle \cdot \mathrm { E } ( \lambda ) } { \displaystyle \cdot \mathrm { E Q E } ( \lambda ) } { \displaystyle \cdot \mathrm { d } \lambda } }  \end{array}
$$

(2) The $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the subcells is determined by the following equations:

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { V _ { \mathrm { o c , f r o n t } } = \displaystyle \frac { 1 } { q } ( E _ { \mathrm { g } } - E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } ) = \displaystyle \frac { 1 } { q } \left( \frac { 1 2 4 0 } { \lambda _ { \mathrm { 2 } } } - E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } \right) } } \\ { { V _ { \mathrm { o c , r e a r } } = \displaystyle \frac { 1 } { q } ( E _ { \mathrm { g } } - E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } ) = \displaystyle \frac { 1 } { q } \left( \frac { 1 2 4 0 } { \lambda _ { \mathrm { 1 } } } - E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } \right) } } \end{array}
$$

Herein, the front and rear cell are considered to have the same $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ for the calculation simplification. The $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ is assumed to be $0 . 4 \mathrm { - } 0 . 8 \mathrm { e V } .$ The $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the tandem cell is given by

$$
V _ { \mathrm { o c , t a n d e m } } = V _ { \mathrm { o c , f r o n t } } + V _ { \mathrm { o c , r e a r } } = { \frac { 1 } { q } } \left( { \frac { 1 2 4 0 } { \lambda _ { 2 } } } + { \frac { 1 2 4 0 } { \lambda _ { 1 } } } - 2 E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } \right)
$$

So for the tandem solar cells, the PCE can be calculated from Eq. (10.6).

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } {  { \operatorname { P C E } ( \mathcal { A } _ { o } ) = V _ { \mathrm { o c } } . J _ { \mathrm { s c , t a n d e m } } \cdot \operatorname { F F } / P _ { \mathrm { i n } } } } \\ & { } & { = \frac { 1 } { q } [ ( \frac { 1 2 4 0 } { \lambda _ { 1 } } - E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } ) + ( \frac { 1 2 4 0 } { \lambda _ { 2 } } - E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } ) ] } \\ & { } & { \cdot \frac { 1 } { 2 } \cdot \int _ { 3 0 0 } ^ { \lambda _ { 1 } } \frac { q \lambda } { h c } \cdot E ( \lambda ) \cdot \operatorname { E Q E } ( \lambda ) \cdot \mathrm { d } \lambda \cdot \operatorname { F F } / P _ { \mathrm { i n } } } \end{array}
$$

According to the above assumptions, Figure 10.6a shows the achievable PCEs $( 1 4 \small { - } 2 8 \% )$ of the 2T tandem cells (double junctions) versus $\lambda _ { \mathrm { o n s e t } }$ (corresponding to $E _ { \mathrm { g } } )$ of rear cell active layer, $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ , EQE, at a fixed FF of 0.75. Furthermore, as shown in Figure 10.6b, if the $\lambda _ { \mathrm { o n s e t , r e a r c e l l } }$ is up to $1 1 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ with an average EQE of $7 5 \%$ , FF being 0.75 and a typical $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ of $0 . 6 { \mathrm { e V } } ,$ a PCE of ${ \sim } 2 0 \%$ can be reached. Note that $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ plays a great impact on the PCEs from the modeling results as shown in Figure 10.6c,d. For example, with the fixed FF of 0.75 and EQE of $7 5 \%$ when $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ equals to $0 . 5 \mathrm { e V } ,$ a $\mathrm { P C E } _ { \operatorname* { m a x } }$ of ${ \sim } 2 2 . 6 \%$ was obtained with the $\lambda _ { \mathrm { o n s e t , r e a r c e l l } } = 1 0 6 0 \mathrm { - } 1 1 2 5 \mathrm { n m }$ when the $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ .5 $0 . 6 { \mathrm { e V } } ,$ $2 0 . 2 \%$ $\mathrm { P C E } _ { \operatorname* { m a x } }$ was obtained with $\lambda _ { \mathrm { o n s e t , r e a r c e l l } } = 1 0 3 0 \mathrm { - } 1 1 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ ; however, when the $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ is as large as $0 . 7 \mathrm { e V } ,$ the $\mathrm { P C E } _ { \operatorname* { m a x } }$ % $1 7 . 8 \%$ was obtained at a large range for $\lambda _ { \mathrm { o n s e t , r e a r c e l l } } = 9 0 0 \mathrm { - } 1 1 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ These modeling results also indicate that the optimum $\lambda _ { \mathrm { o n s e t , r e a r c e l l } }$ , i.e. the $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ of the rear sub cell active layer, is somewhat smaller than the optimum one in the SQ limit studies (of ${ \sim } 1 1 2 7 \mathrm { n m }$ ) [105], probably due to the large $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ of OSCs [106]. According to the model analysis, to get a high PCE of the tandem cell, each subcell should have high EQE response, small $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ and high FF, and the absorption of them should be complementary and sufficiently broad.

# 10.5 Conclusion and Outlook

In this chapter, we have summarized the recent progress of tandem OSCs mainly focusing on the active layer materials. Presently, the tandem OsCs have attained great progress with higher PCE over $1 7 \%$ . It should be noted that the PCEs of single-junction OsCs have also reached $1 7 \%$ and some even $1 8 \%$ in recent years, thanks to the active layer materials design and device optimization engineering. The results have demonstrated not only challenge but also opportunity for tandem OSCs. In the era of fullerene acceptor-based OSCs, tandem devices did not demonstrate higher efficiency than that of single-junction devices until suitable subcell materials with complementary absorption had been designed and screened. The history will repeat in the era of NFAs for tandem OSCs. It is strongly believed that higher efficiencies of tandem cells can be achieved through delicate active layer material design and screening together with the device optimization. Although triple and multiple junction cells can give higher efficiency in principle, it is more feasible to develop double junction tandem devices if considering the balance between device efficiency and device fabrication complexity. According to the semi-empirical model analysis discussed above, PCEs ${ > } 2 5 \%$ are predicted for double junction tandem OsCs. Better subcell active layer materials are believed to be the key to realize the efficiency target. The present success of various donor and acceptor materials, especially new A-D-A molecules, will definitely give very valuable insights in designing better active layer materials.

Firstly, efficient rear cell with infrared absorption onset up to $1 0 5 0 \mathrm { - } 1 1 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ is the prerequisite to get high performance tandem OsCs. However, currently, there are no rear cell active materials that can meet all the requirements such as absorption range, $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ and EQE discussed in the above model analysis. Therefore, it is urgent to design rear cell materials with onset up to $1 0 5 0 \mathrm { - } 1 1 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ and good photovoltaic performance with low $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ and high EQE. Secondly, the front cell should have a complimentary absorption with an onset of around $7 2 0 \mathrm { n m }$ in order to have maximized matched $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ with the rear cell according to the above model analysis. Meanwhile, the two subcells should have minimal $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ to have high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and thus ensure high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ for the tandem devices. Besides, EQE and the FF of the subcells should be carefully considered for selecting the materials. Thirdly, it is also a tough task to develop efficient ICLs without incorporating PEDOT:PSS since the acidic and hydrophilic nature of PEDOT:PSS is not favorable for the stability of tandem devices.

According to the model analysis, assuming an $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ of $0 . 4 \mathrm { e V } ,$ average EQE of $8 0 \%$ and FF of $8 0 \%$ , the absorption onsets of 1100 and $7 2 0 \mathrm { n m }$ for the rear and front cells, respectively, a PCE of $2 8 . 6 0 \%$ can be obtained for a 2T tandem device. It seems to be a greatly challenging PCE value. It is strongly believed that it can be realized since the single parameters such as $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ , EQE, and FF have already been realized in the reported device. If they can be realized combinedly, the seemly impossible PCEs can come into reality for tandem OSCs.

# Large-Area Flexible Organic Solar Cells

Shaorong Huang1\*, Yufei Wang2\*, Lintao Hou2\*\*, and Lie Chen1\*\*

# 11.1 Introduction

Organic solar cells (OsCs), as a sustainable energy technology, have the characteristics of lightweight, low-cost, and flexibility and have unique advantages to manufacture large-area flexible devices via solution processing methods [1, 2]. Moreover, stability tests have shown that it is possible for OSCs to have a life span of up to 10 years, which shows their potential for practical application [3]. Therefore, OSCs have attracted much attention from both the academia and the industry recent years. However, compared with small-area OSCs, large-area devices exhibit much lower performance, especially the ones fabricated on large-area flexible substrates. Material requirements, fabrication methods, efficiency loss change drastically as the trend shifts from small-area to large-area OSCs.

OSCs generally are fabricated by spin coating in the laboratory [4], but such process is inappropriate for large-scale and flexible production. The experience gained by spin coating process has limited values for large-area preparation technology. Currently, the most potential mass production process for large-area OSCs has been proven to the roll-to-roll (R2R) technology. A various of film-forming methods, mainly including blade coating, slot-die coating, inkjet printing, spray coating, screen printing, relief printing and gravure printing, can be integrated into the R2R process to form a complete system. In addition, material requirements and efficiency loss of the large-area productions are quite different from those of the small-area ones. Therefore, a comprehensive consideration of these processes is highly required for large-area devices. This chapter focuses on large-area flexible organic solar cells (FOsCs), including material requirements, flexible electrode and substrates, large-area flexible device fabrication, and efficiency loss in large-area devices and modules. Finally, we make a conclusion on the prospects and challenges of the development of large-area FOSCs.

# 11.2 Material Requirements for Large-Area Flexible Organic Solar Cells

The material requirements for large-area FOSCs are more complicated than those for small-area OsCs on glass substrate. Besides possessing excellent photovoltaic property, the materials need to be of good stretchable property and compatible to printing process. Due to the strong entanglement of the macromolecular chain, the films of polymer-based active layer often show good stretchability, which is a good property for flexible device. The power conversion efficiency (PCE) is observed to be very sensitive to the thickness of the active layer. For small-area OsCs, the thickness of the active layer prepared by spin coating is normally about $1 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , an optimal result of comprehensive consideration of light absorption, morphology, charge transport and recombination, and other possible photophysical processes to achieve the best device performance. However, for the large-area devices, the thickness of active layers generally should be much greater than that of small-area devices due to the requirement of large-area coating and printing technology. Therefore, large-area manufacture process put forward new requirements for materials, that is, materials for large-area devices should work well in a thick film. The low charge mobility and high charge recombination in the bulk heterojunction (BHJ) films are found to be the key limitations to form a high-performance thick film.

In the past few years, many efforts have been made to develop high-quality films with good thickness tolerance. In this section, we mainly focus on the active layer materials for large-area FOsCs and will introduce four type systems for thick-film active layer: fullerene-based binary system, non-fullerene-based binary system, ternary system, and all-polymer system. At last, the design strategies of the materials for large-scale devices will be discussed.

# 11.2.1 Fullerene-Based Binary System

The fullerene-based binary system based on the fullerene and its derivatives $( \mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ [5], indene-C60 bisadduct [ICBA], etc.) as acceptors with high efficiency and thick active layer has been reported in the past early years. Fullerene-based binary system can be divided into two types: polymer: fullerene system and small molecule: fullerene system. The structures and the device parameters are shown in Figure 11.1 and Table 11.1, respectively. The initial stage of the research on devices with thick-film polymer: fullerene binary started from the P3HT:PCBM system. P3HT has the characteristics of low price and simple synthesis, presenting the most potential for practical application. In addition, the regular chain structure of P3HT also can facilitate their self-organization into two-dimensional sheets by means of inter-chain stacking, promoting charge transport. Combined with the ultrafast three-dimensional charge transfer channel of fullerene, P3HT:PCBM system possesses high charge mobility and favorable morphology of the blend film upon various optimal treatments, leading to a high thick-film performance. Yang and coworkers reported highly efficient polymer solar cells (PSCs) based on $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 1 } B M }$ by controlling the active layer growth rate to increase hole mobility, balance charge transport, and improve absorption.

An outstanding PCE of $4 . 4 \%$ with a $2 1 0 \sim 2 3 0 \mathrm { n m }$ thickness of active layer was achieved [6]. However, the poor light harvesting and high HOmO energy level of P3HT limit the further improvement in the device performance.

To expand the absorption range and down-shift the HOMO energy level, the design concept of narrow bandgap donor-acceptor (D-A) has been employed in developing efficient polymer donors for fullerene-based binary devices. Internal regulation of molecular structure and external morphological optimization of the film are often performed to improve the charge mobility and film morphology for thick film application. Internal regulation of molecular structure is aimed to improve the planarity of the backbone for efficient charge transport, such as incorporation of the planar building blocks, side chain engineering, $\pi$ -bridge engineering, quinoidal units. External optimal treatments of the films are conducting extra pretreatment or posttreatment to induce a favorable growth of the active layer. These extra treatments mainly include thermal annealing, solvent annealing, additives, etc.

It has demonstrated that temperature-dependent aggregation effect is a key feature for donor polymers to develop favorable morphology and form thick active layers. A polymer with temperature-dependent aggregation property can dissolve in a certain solvent at high temperature and then gradually aggregate during the cooling process. Generally, temperature-dependent aggregation characteristic is the unique behavior of highly crystalline polymers. Regulating the transition between aggregation and disaggregation by solution temperature and concentration can readily fine-tune crystallinity and domain size, which is beneficial to form a high-quality thick film. In 2014, Yan and coworkers [7] reported three polymer donors (PffBT4T-2OD, PBTff4T-2OD, and PNT4T-2OD) based on polymultithiophene chain. These polymers have strong temperature-dependent aggregation properties, and the morphology can be well controlled by such temperature-dependent aggregation behavior. As a result, the PCE of over $1 0 \%$ with a fill factor (FF) of over $7 0 \%$ has been achieved by PffBT4T-2OD blended with $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ . The devices also worked well with $3 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ -thick active layer. In 2017, the same group synthesized a new polymer PffBT4T-C9C11 [8] by changing the blanched alkyl chain in PffBT4T-2OD. Side chain engineering was demonstrated to further optimize the morphology of the active layer, and a breakthrough PCE of $1 1 . 7 \%$ with nearly $3 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ -thick active layer has been achieved. They also declared that the position of the alkyl chain and the fluorine atom in the polymer backbone was the main factor affecting the temperature-dependent aggregation of the materials.

The devices based on PffBT4T-2OD with different fullerene derivatives obtained high PCE, but the strong aggregation property of PffBT4T-2OD often leads to large and unsuitable domains during the room-temperature process. To ensure the solution spin-coating process, the active layer solution and indium tin oxide (ITO) substrate are both preheated to ${ 7 0 } \sim 1 1 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ before coating, which is detrimental for large-area device process. In 2017, Chen's group firstly reported that random copolymerization was a facile and effective method to regulate the aggregation of polymer PffBT4T-2OD. They synthesized new terpolymer donors (PffBT-2TPF4) [9, 18] by introducing tetrafluorinated benzene (PF4) as the third unit into polymer PffBT4T-2OD through random copolymerization. The aperiodic sequence distribution caused by random copolymerization effectively reduced the aggregation of the polymers, enabling a room-temperature process of the active layer. On the other hand, due to the self-assembly of the PF4 and careful control on the loading of PF4 into the backbone, the developed terpolymers still exhibited obviously temperature-dependent aggregation properties, beneficial for the formation of the well-defined film-state packing. Eventually, the room temperature processed terpolymers obtained a comparable performance to the high temperature processed PffBT4T-2OD. In 2019, they further introduced a self-assembly third unit of dimethyl $^ { 2 , 2 ^ { \prime } }$ -(thieno[3,2-b]thiophene-2,5-diyl)bis(thiophene-3-carboxylate) (4T2C) into the PffBT4T-2OD matrix. Regulation of the loadings of the 4T2C unit, the morphology of active layer (PffBT4T-4T2C-9 $/ 1 { : } \mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M } ,$ can be well-tuned to form a homogeneous fibril-like bicontinuous interpenetrating network with a preferred face-on orientation. As a result, the terpolymer-based device achieved a remarkable FF near $8 0 \%$ , which is the highest value of the fullerene-based solar cells without any treatment at that time. Moreover, an impressive PCE over $9 . 0 \%$ was obtained when the thickness of active layer over $3 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [10]. Siloxane-terminated side chain of the polymers has been reported to have the ability to affect orientation of the molecules. In 2017, Chen and coworkers synthesized a terpolymer PFBT4T-C5Si- $2 5 \%$ [11] by introducing siloxane-terminated side chains through random copolymerization. PFBT4T-C5Si- $2 5 \%$ showed better molecular $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking and enhanced vertical carrier transport than PffBT4T-2OD. PFBT4T-C5Si $2 5 \% { : } \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ displayed low film surface roughness, balanced charge transport, and small phase separation. High PCEs of $1 1 . 0 9 \%$ and $1 0 . 1 5 \%$ were obtained for the active layer with a thickness of 420 and $6 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , respectively.

In addition to the PffBT4T-2OD family, fused ring moieties are also good building blocks to construct polymer donors for active layer with good thickness tolerance. In 2014, Huang and coworkers prepared the devices based on PBDT-DTNT $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ with thick films. Incorporation of naphthalene unit was found to endow the PBDT-DTNT with a high mobility. The PBDT-DTNT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ obtained a PCE of $8 . 6 2 \%$ for a $2 8 0 \mathrm { n m }$ thick film and $7 . 2 4 \%$ for a nearly $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ thick film [12]. In 2016, they also introduced naphthalene unit into polymer NT812 [13]. A face-on orientation was detected in polymer NT812 film. When blended with $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ , a PCE of $1 0 . 3 3 \%$ for a $3 2 0 \mathrm { n m }$ thick film and a PCE of $8 . 3 5 \%$ for a $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ -thick film were achieved. In 2017, they synthesized a new polymer donor BDTffBX-DT with naked BDT unit. Non-halogenated solvent processed active layer based on BDTffBX-DT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ demonstrated a face-on orientation with a suitable phase separation. With a film thickness of $2 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , BDTffBX-DT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ obtained a PCE of $9 . 4 \%$ [14]. The same group also successfully used naphthalene unit to improve the performance of PffBT4T-2OD family with thick film. They created a polymer donor PNTT with deep HOMO energy levels and high hole mobility [15]. The device based on the PNTT. $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ obtained the best efficiency of $1 1 . 3 \%$ at a film thickness of $2 8 0 \mathrm { n m }$ and a decent PCE of $9 \%$ at a film thickness of $1 0 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$

Small-molecule semiconductors are also used as donor materials for thick-film fullerene-based OSCs. Wei and coworkers reported thick-film OSCs based on $\mathrm { N D T P - C N C O O : P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ [16]. Due to the ordered stacking between molecules and favorable film morphology, the efficiency of $7 . 2 0 \%$ was obtained with a $3 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ -thick active layer. Wong and coworkers reported a small-molecule donor BTR with rigid and flat backbone and numerous flexible side chains. A PCE of $9 . 3 \%$ and $8 . 0 \%$ was achieved at a thickness of 250 and $4 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , respectively [17]. Later, Kim and coworkers reported R2R slot-die coating device modules based on $\mathrm { B T R : P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ obtaining a PCE of $7 . 4 6 \%$ and $4 . 8 3 \%$ for single cells and modules with an active area of $1 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ , respectively [19].

# 11.2.2 Non-fullerene-Based Binary System

Compared with the fullerene acceptor with narrow absorption and fixed energy levels, non-fullerene acceptors have been rapidly developed in recent years. Non-fullerene acceptors are normally referred to the conjugated small molecules with high electron affinity. They have the advantages of low cost, adjustable energy levels, and good light absorption making them promising alternatives to replace fullerene acceptors for OsCs. Zhan and coworkers have made important contributions to the design and synthesis of non-fullerene acceptors. In 2015, they designed the first non-fullerene acceptor ITIC with the absorption expanding to near-infrared light. Using polymer PTB7-Th with narrow bandgap as donor, a PCE of $6 . 8 \%$ was obtained [20]. In 2016, Hou and coworkers developed a wide-bandgap polymer PBDB-T and processed a non-fullerene-based device with PBDB-T:ITIC. A notable PCE of $1 1 . 2 1 \%$ was obtained [21], which is the first report that the efficiency of non-fullerene-based device exceeded that of fullerene-based one. The high performance of the non-fullerene-based device was ascribed to complementary absorption of donor and acceptor, appropriate energy level alignment, and favorable phase-separation morphology.

Similar to fullerene systems, for obtaining high-performance thick-film active layer, non-fullerene-based systems also should have high charge carrier mobility, wide light absorption, appropriate phase separation morphology, low bimolecular recombination, and so on. With the rapid development of the non-fullerene acceptors, the polymer donors with complimentary absorption have been also reported. The molecular structures and device parameters are shown in Figure 11.2 and Table 11.2. Huang and coworkers prepared thick-film devices based on a blend of wide-bandgap conjugated polymer PTzBI and ITIC. A PCE of $7 . 0 9 \%$ with a film thickness of $3 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ was achieved [22]. Similarly, Zhang and coworkers synthesized a wide-bandgap polymer PTZ1 based on thiazolothiazole unit. By optimizing the morphology of the active layer upon thermal annealing, the device with PTZ1:IDIC delivered the best performance of $9 . 5 \%$ at a film thickness of $2 1 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [23]. It has been reported that the functional atoms, F and Cl atoms, not only have the ability of down-shifting HOMO energy level to boost the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ , but also can improve the crystallinity of the materials for efficient charge transport [33-35]. Hou and coworkers reported a polymer donor PBDB-T-SF with low energy levels, in which fluorine and sulfur atoms were introduced into the side chains of PBDB-T. When blended with non-fullerene acceptor IT-4F, the PBDB-T-SF:IT-4F-based devices exhibited a PCE of over $1 2 \%$ with a wide thickness range of $1 0 0 { - } 2 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [24]. Zhang and coworkers synthesized two efficient polymer donors, PM6 and PM7. PM6 and PM7 have the same skeleton to the polymer PBDB-T, but only replace the H atom on thiophene side chain by F atom and Cl atom, respectively. Due to the improved inter-chain interaction and down-shifted HOMO levels favored by F and Cl atom, both PM6 and PM7 have a higher crystallinity, enhanced absorption, higher carrier mobility , and higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the devices than PBDB-T. The device based on PM6:IDIC obtained a PCE of $1 1 \%$ at the active layer thickness of $2 5 5 \mathrm { n m }$ [25]. The PM6:IT-4F blends achieved an excellent PCE of $1 2 . 2 \%$ with a $2 8 5 \mathrm { n m }$ -thick film [26]. As for the PM7:IT-4F-based device, a PCE of $1 2 . 0 \%$ was obtained at a $2 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ -thick active layer [27].

Small molecular donors have also been employed for preparation of thick-film non-fullerene OsCs. In 2018, Hou and coworkers reported a highly efficient non-fullerene OSCs based on small molecular donors (DRTB-T-C2, DRTB-T-C4, DRTB-T-C6, DRTB-T-C8) and IT-4F acceptor. By prolonging the length of the end alkyl chain of the donors, the active layer preferred to form a face-on orientation. The devices based on DRTB-T-C4:IT-4F retained a high PCE of $1 0 \%$ with the active layer thickness up to $3 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [28].

Although non-fullerene materials have many advantages, the lower charge mobility of non-fullerene materials than fullerene materials is a major problem when they are applied as thick film. Non-fullerene acceptor with a preferential face-on orientation is very conductive to charge transport. Bo and coworkers synthesized a new non-fullerene electron acceptor IDT-OB with asymmetric side chains. The IDT-OB exhibited a face-on orientation, thereby leading to a high charge mobility. A notable PCE of $9 . 1 7 \%$ was obtained when the thickness of the active layer was $2 1 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [29]. Luo et al. synthesized a new small molecule acceptor (IDTPC), which exhibited more ordered face-on $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking and higher electron mobility when compared with its similar molecule IDTCN. The PTQi0:IDTPC-based device delivered a PCE of $1 0 . 0 \%$ at active layer thickness of $4 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [30]. In addition, the design concept of halogenated polymers has also been regarded as a highly effective strategy for designing non-fullerene acceptors with improved charge mobility. A series of efficient non-fullerene acceptors with F and Cl endcap were synthesized, such as IT-4F, Y6, BTP-4Cl. In 2019, Zou and coworkers designed and synthesized a new small-molecule non-fullerene acceptor Y6, which has multiple electronic push and pull effects, high carrier mobility, and broadened absorption. The devices based on PM6:Y6 achieved a remarkable PCE of over $1 5 \%$ with a thin active layer of ${ \sim } 1 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ and $1 4 . 3 \%$ with a thickness of $2 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [31]. In 2020, Hou and coworkers processed $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ thick-film devices employing PM6 as polymer donor and Cl-functionalized small-molecule BTP-4Cl as acceptor. The BTP-4Cl-based thick-film device was demonstrated to display low trap-assist recombination and appropriate phase separation morphology. PM6:BTP-4Cl-based device with $4 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ area exhibited a PCE of $1 0 . 1 \%$ with an active layer thickness of $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [32]. Thereby, these materials show great potential for manufacturing large-scale FOSCs.

# 11.2.3Ternary System

The ternary blending strategy of incorporating a third component into the active layer of binary OsCs is a facile and effective method to improve the device performance. The role of the third component in the ternary blending can be donor or acceptor to adjust the energy levels, broaden the absorption, and optimize the phase morphology. Working mechanism of ternary OSC includes charge transfer mechanism, energy transfer mechanism, parallel linkage mechanism, alloy model mechanism, etc. [36-39] Highly crystalline conjugated polymers or small molecules as the third component are in favor of improving the charge mobility and thickness tolerability. Molecules for the ternary system with thick films are shown in Figure 11.3, and Table 11.3 displays the corresponding performance for these systems.

Some ternary OsCs based on non-fullerene acceptors have performed with thick active layers. For example, Baran et al. reported P3HT:IDTBR:IDFBR-based devices, which exhibited a high PCE of $5 . 7 \%$ with a film thickness of $3 2 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [40].

In fact, taking advantage of the fullerene derivatives and non-fullerene molecules and using both as acceptors for constructing a thick-film ternary device is very meaningful. Wei and coworkers synthesized a molecule $p \mathrm { - D T S } ( \mathrm { F B T T H } _ { 2 } ) _ { 2 }$ for ternary devices with thick film. Addition of small molecule was found to improve the crystallinity and face-on orientation of the active layer. The PTB7-Th: $p$ -DTS( $\mathrm { F B T T H } _ { 2 } ) _ { 2 }$ $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ -based ternary device achieved a PCE of $1 0 . 7 8 \%$ with active layer thickness of $2 7 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [41]. Ameri and coworkers processed ternary devices by adding a polymer PBTZT-STAT-BDTT-8 to the PTB7-th: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ system. A PCE of $1 1 . 0 3 \%$ with active layer thickness of $3 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ was obtained [42]. In addition, nonradiative Forster resonance energy transfer from the PBTZT-STAT-BDTT-8 to PTB7-Th polymer bandgap polymer PTB7-Th was detected in the blend, contributing to the improvement of device performance. Zhang et al. added a liquid crystalline small-molecule donor BTR to the $\mathrm { P T B 7 - T h } { \mathrm { : P C } } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ system. The morphology of active layer was optimized, as revealed by the increased coherence length and domain purity with addition of BTR. As a result, a PCE $1 1 . 4 \%$ was obtained for the device with an active layer thickness of $2 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [43]. Zhu and coworkers also prepared ternary devices with thick active layer by adopting BTR as donor, a small-molecule NITI and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as acceptors. For the BTR:NITI-based binary device, a PCE of $8 . 6 6 \%$ with a film thickness of $2 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ was obtained. After incorporation of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ into the blend, the morphology of the active layer showed more appropriate phase separation. As a result, the BTR:NITI: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 }$ BM-based ternary device yielded a PCE of $1 3 . 6 \%$ with a film thickness of $3 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [44]. In 2020, Zhang and coworkers processed a ternary device based on $\mathrm { P M 7 : Y 6 : P C _ { 6 1 } B M }$ Addition of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ into the active layer was observed to improve charge mobilities and reduce charge recombination, leading to an improved efficiency of $1 4 . 3 \%$ with a film thickness of $3 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [45].

Controlling the morphology of large-area BHJ devices is still a tricky problem. To solve this issue, Chen and coworkers [46] adopted a pseudo-planar heterojunction (PPHJ) method to fabricate a large-area ternary with the fullerene derivative ICBA as the third component to enhance the PCE of the device with PM6:IT-4F. It can be found that ICBA promoted the vertical phase separation and the formation of PPHJ structure. Furthermore, the addition of ICBA also improved the crystallinity of PM6, thus accelerating the exciton dissociation and charge transfer. Consequently, $1 . 0 5 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ PPHJ device based on PM6:ICBA:IT-4F with a ratio of $1 : 0 . 1 : 0 . 9$ fabricated by blade-coating achieved a notable PCE of $1 4 . 2 5 \%$ , which was superior than both of the corresponding BHJ devices $( 1 3 . 7 3 \% )$ and the binary OSC $( 1 3 . 1 9 \% )$

# 11.2.4 All-Polymer-Based System

All-PsCs have excellent thermal stability, flexibility, and mechanical stability features. Relative to small molecules, high-viscosity polymers are more conducive to large-scale manufacturing [47]. The typical molecular structures for all-PSCs with thick film are shown in Figure 11.4, and Table 11.4 displays their corresponding performance. N2200 acceptor is widely used in all-PSCs, which was first synthesized by Yan et al. [51]. Huang and coworkers reported a thick film all-PSC based on PTzBI:N2200 [48]. Manipulating the molecular weight of N2200 was found to effectively adjust the exciton generation, charge transfer, and recombination. An optimal PCE of $9 . 1 6 \%$ was obtained with a film thickness of $1 2 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . When the film thickness increased to $2 3 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , a PCE of $6 . 3 7 \%$ was obtained, together with a good thermal and mechanical stability. Later on, to further tailor the properties of the polymer PTzBI, they introduced a siloxane-terminated side chain into PTzBI and obtained a new donor PTzBI-Si. PTzBI-Si has high crystallinity with a face-on orientation, leading to high and balanced charge mobility. Consequently, by using the green solvent 2-methyltetrahydrofuran, a PCE of $1 0 . 0 5 \%$ was obtained for the active layer with a film thickness of $1 4 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , while a PCE of $8 . 8 1 \%$ was obtained with the thickness of $1 8 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [49]. In 2018, they further processed a ternary device based on PBTA-Si:PTzBI-Si:N2200 with PBTA-Si as the third component. Under a thickness of 350 and $4 2 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , a high PCE of $9 . 1 7 \%$ and $8 . 3 4 \%$ was obtained, respectively [50]. Compared with the binary OSCs based on PTzBI-Si:N2200 blends, ternary all-polymer system has higher thickness tolerance.
