# 11.2.5 Design Strategies of the Materials for Large-Area Devices

Considerable efforts and progress have been made on thick-film devices. It demonstrates that high charge carrier mobility, low bimolecular recombination, and favorable morphology with appropriate domain size and high phase purity are extraordinarily favorable to meet the requirements of large-scale device fabrication. Therefore, besides improving light harvesting, developing high-mobility materials is the most important to obtain high-performance thick flms for large-scale application. Many design strategies, such enhancing molecular planarity of the backbone, improving crystallinity and inter-chain interaction by functional atoms effect (e.g. fluorine, chlorine, siloxane, and sulfur atoms) and weak non-covalent bonds, introducing the quinoidal units, are proven to be very effective for developing high-mobility materials. On the other hand, the optimization of BHJ morphology is also very important. Developing film morphology with ordered and preferential face-on orientation can guarantee high charge transport in a thick active layer. Moreover, external optimal treatments are also attractive methods to further optimize the morphology of the active layer.

As for the donor materials, small-molecule donors are more pure and lead to better batch-to-batch reproduction than polymer donors, while polymer donors are more flexible, easier to synthesis, and with better film-forming property, which makes them more attractive for large-area FOsCs. As for acceptor materials, fullerene and its derivatives have some fatal disadvantages, such as high cost, poor absorption, and limited ability to control the energy levels; thereby, they would not be ideal and extensively used acceptors for practical application. High-performance non-fullerene acceptors are more appealing than fullerene and its derivatives. On the other hand, fullerene has the characteristics of low reorganization energy and high reduction potential, which can accelerate the transfer of photo-induced charge and avoid the return of electrons simultaneously. Taking advantage of the fullerene and non-fullerene molecules to fabricate thick-film ternary devices is very promising. Furthermore, the state-of-the-art devices are based on the active layers that at least one component is a small molecule. In fact, compared with the device with small molecules, all-PsCs have superior thermal and mechanical stability, therefore they are more suitable for large-scale manufacturing, if their efficiency can be substantially improved.

# 11.3 Flexible Electrodes and Substrates

As one of the emerging solar cells, FOsCs have become a powerful rival to the traditional silicon solar cells owing to the advantages of light weight, flexible fabrication, and semitransparency. In order to achieve good mechanical property and high efficiency, it is essential to prepare highly transparent ultra-flexible electrodes and substrates to match high-performance photoactive layers.

# 11.3.1 Flexible Substrates

To maximize the absorption of the incidence sunlight in the active layers, the substrates used for the preparation of FOsCs should have good flexibility, transparency, and durability. Meanwhile, the ideal substrate must be compatible with the device structures, electrode types, and printing methods, which is favorable to achieve stable and long-life FOSCs. In addition, the substrate for FOSCs must possess a smooth surface in the nanoscale range to prevent spikes and irregularities of ultrathin films from penetrating through the device. Likewise, the influence of the substrate on the preparation process and stability of device must be considered, such as casting solvents intermiscibility, water/UV resistance, thermal stability, and shrinkage and dimensional stability. Generally, the commonly used substrates for FOsCs are mainly divided into plastics and metal foils.

The metal foil substrate is suitable for FOSCs with high-temperature process, and it can maintain good stability in the air (barrier to water and oxygen) [52-55]. In addition, the unique high conductivity of the metal foil can simultaneously act as the bottom electrode. Especially, stainless steel can withstand a high temperature up to $1 0 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and its excellent high corrosion resistance and chemical stability are favored for FOsCs. However, metal foil substrates also have some drawbacks of non-transparency, poor flexibility, and large surface roughness, which can produce a great obstacle to achieving high-efficiency and ultra-flexible FOsCs. Actually, the surface roughness of the metal foil substrates can be solved by polishing or using an additional planarization layer [53]. But, a bad result could be produced when the conducting substrates as the back contact are completely isolated from the photovoltaic device through the thick additional planarization layer.

The transparent plastic substrate is mainly based on polymers and can be well applied in the process of R2R production due to its high flexibility. Common polymer substrates mainly include polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polyethylene naphthalate (PEN), polyethersulfone (PES), polyimide (PI) [56-62]. Except PI that can absorb part of visible light, other polymer substrates have high transmittance in the range of visible light, which is suitable for most FOsCs. Remarkably, the thermal resistance of PI to high temperatures up to $3 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ gives the ability of FOSCs bearing rigorous fabrication processing and working at high temperature.

There are some disadvantages existing in plastic devices, of course, such as the unstable dimensions during high-temperature processing and poor water and oxygen isolation. Therefore, an additional barrier coating is required for plastic devices to reduce deformation of plastic substrate and permeation of water and oxygen. Moreover, it improves the interlayer adhesion and the device resistance to chemicals. At present, the most mainstream plastic device substrates designed for large-area production of FOSCs are PET and PEN with PI substrates as supplement in a few cases. PET possesses the advantages of low cost and smooth surface, while PEN has good thermal stability [63]. PET was first introduced into FOSCs as substrate by Siegfried Bauer and coworkers, who designed high flexibility and lightweight

OSCs with thickness up to $1 . 4 \mu \mathrm { m }$ (thinnest plastic substrate was $1 2 5 \mu \mathrm { m }$ at that time) [64]. After Siegfried Bauer, the FOSCs with using PET substrates began to spread gradually.

# 11.3.2 Flexible Transparent Electrode Designs

The realization of high-performance FOsCs mainly depends on good transparency and high conductivity of flexible electrodes. In addition to these requirements, the flexible transparent electrodes (FTEs) should also have the properties of low cost, easy-to-use in large-area, excellent bending, and low-temperature preparation with energy-saving and time-saving. The traditional flexible transparent electrode for OSCs is ITO; however, ITO electrode for FOSCs is easy to be broken, and its conductivity will drop sharply when the number of bending increases, which leads to a poor device performance. Therefore, a series of candidates for the ITO electrode have emerged to enhance the mechanical properties and prolong device lifetime, which are mainly divided into conducting polymers, carbon nanotubes, graphene, metal nanowires, and hybrid films.

# 11.3.2.1 Conducting Polymers

Different from ITO film (forming on the plastic), which is brittle and expensive, conductive polymers have excellent flexibility and are solution-processable. Among them, the most representative conductive polymer of poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrenesulfonate) (PEDOT:PSS) has been widely used as the electrode material and the electrode interface layer for low-cost large-area ultrathin organic electronics owing to the advantages of high transparency, thermal stability, and good solubility in water or polar solvents. The possibility of PEDOT:PSS as anode instead of ITO for FOSCs was evaluated by Zhang et al. in 2002, which indicated that highly transparent PEDOT:PSS has a great potential and prospect on fabricating plastic OSCs [65]. Since then, the investigation about transparent PEDOT:PSS electrode of the large-area FOsCs is not rare.

Na et al. [66] used PEDOT:PSS doped with dimethyl sulfoxide (DMsO) as an anode to prepare FOSCs based on P3HT:PCBM with plastic substrates (PET) and glass substrates considering the poor conductivity of PEDOT:PSS (Figure 11.5). Compared with ITO-based OSCs (glass $3 . 6 6 \%$ and flexible $2 . 9 9 \%$ , a comparable PCE (glass $3 . 2 7 \%$ and flexible $2 . 8 \%$ ) was obtained in OSCs with PEDOT (doping with $5 \%$ DMsO) as the anode. Through further flexibility measurement, the PCE of FOSCs based on ITO electrode almost reaches 0 after 75 bending cycles, while the PCE of FOSCs with PEDOT anodes can still achieve $2 . 7 3 \%$ . This result showed that the FOSCs with PEDOT anode have excellent mechanical flexibility compared with ITO-based FOsCs. In addition, different from the fragile and expensive ITO, all ITO-free flexible devices show that low-cost PEDOT:PSS will be a promising anode or cathode material used for FOSCs, especially in the preparation of R2R flexible devices.

Similarly, the PEDOT:PSS anode with $\mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 }$ treatment was reported by Zhou and coworkers [67] who achieved a good result in all-plastic OSCs based on PES substrate (Figure 11.6). After PEDOT was treated with $\mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 }$ , the conductivity was significantly improved to $1 4 6 0 { \mathrm { S c m } } ^ { - 1 }$ . In addition, the PEDOT:PSS film with $\mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 }$ treatment could achieve a higher transmittance and a lower sheet resistance than the traditional $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ treatment. More importantly, the toxicity of $\mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 }$ is far less than $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ , which was more suitable for large-area OSCs based on flexible substrates. The FOSCs with $\mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 }$ coated PES as a transparent bottom electrode were fabricated with excellent performance parameters in P3HT:ICBA including an open-circuit voltage of $0 . 8 4 \mathrm { V } ,$ a good FF of $6 0 \%$ , an optimal PCE of $3 . 3 \%$ . The result showed that ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 3 } { \mathrm { P O } } _ { 4 }$ treatment can become an effective way to improve the performance of FOSCs based on PEDOT anodes.

![](images/bcc7f1829f77b6a00a1234de4bfd83e2781b2ae75ffe4f20c586eff04defbc3b.jpg)  
Figure 11.5 (a) Architecture of ITO-free based OSCs and its TEM cross-sectional image on the ${ 1 0 0 } \mathsf { n m }$ scale bar. Curves of (b) efficiency and (c) relative resistance with bending numbers based on ITO and ITO-free FOSCs. Source: Na et al. [66]. Reproduced with permission of John Wiley $\&$ Sons.

It is undeniable that the conductivity of PEDOT:PSS increases sharply after strong acid treatment $\mathrm { ( H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } \mathrm { ) }$ , but the presence of residual strong acid may damage the device structure and lead to a poor stability. Yan and coworkers [68] developed a transfer-printing technique using mild acid to weaken the influence of strong acid on FOSCs (Figure 11.7). The conductivity, transmittance, and stability of transferred PEDOT:PSS film after two-step mild acid processing $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 3 }$ dipping and ${ \mathrm { H } } _ { 3 } { \mathrm { P O } } _ { 4 }$ soaking) were greatly improved. Finally, the fabricated FOSCs based on PDMS/transferred PEDOT:PSS/PBDTT- $\mathrm { S - T T : P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M / C a / A l }$ exhibited a significant improvement on the performance and air stability. This study showed that the two-step weak acid treatment method could further improve the stability of FOSCs while maintaining high conductivity property of PEDOT:PSS.

![](images/9a6e3e6ad11a8a2dbc910c1b3cc5c75ccb05b710a322d829da7ae3383dc75d90.jpg)  
Figure 11.6(a) Device structure of all-plastic OsCs, J - V characteristics of (b) representative solar cell and (c) reference cell in the dark and under $1 0 0 \mathsf { m W } / \mathsf { c m } ^ { 2 }$ white light illumination in linear and semilog scale. Source: Meng et al. [67]. Reproduced with permission of American Chemical Society.

Since the formation of metal oxide requires high temperature and high vacuum sputtering conditions, the use of transparent metal oxide electrodes in FOsCs undoubtedly increases the manufacturing cost. Ge and coworkers [69] reported a low-temperature all-solution-processed FOsC (Figure 11.8), which exhibited an excellent performance. After using the PEDOT:PSS film with $\mathrm { C H } _ { 4 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 3 }$ treatment as the transparent anode, the PCE of FOsCs based on PET/PEDOT:PSS(FTE)/PEDOT:PSS(buffer layer)/PBDB-T:IT-M/PDINO/Al structure reached $1 0 . 1 2 \%$ and the FF exceeded $7 0 \%$ . The performance improvement of FOSCs was attributed to the suitable work function formed on the transparent anode after PEDOT:PSS treatment with gentle acid under room temperature, which also endowed a better interface contact and hole transport ability. In particular, the fabricated FOSCs exhibited a good mechanical flexibility. The PCE of flexible devices still could maintain $9 4 \%$ of original PCE after 1000 bending measurement. The application of gentle acid on the PEDOT:PSS makes the fabrication of FOSCs possible at room temperature and can effectively facilitate the development of large-area fabrication methods.

![](images/dfb9255b8bf534b7e6832aeb01150a42c306ccddb94301f5052dbca5e50fbb3f.jpg)  
Figure 11.7 (a) Transfer-printing technique, (b) transmittance spectra of transferred PEDOT:PSS under different temperatures, (c) the stability measurement of FOSCs with different acids. Source: Fan et al. [68]. Reproduced with permission of American Chemical Society.

Although PEDOT:PSS as the transparent electrode has been successfully applied in FOSCs, the PEDOT:PSS has the probability of diffusion in device due to the acidic and hygroscopicity nature, which tends to destroy the structure and decrease the stability of devices. In addition, the conductivity of PEDOT:PSS film is relatively poor, which leads to a high interface contact resistance. Chen et al. reported a scalable and highly conductive PEDOT:PSS:CNTs transparent electrode which presents a high conductivity of $3 2 6 4 . 2 7 \mathrm { S c m ^ { - 1 } }$ with a high transmittance over $8 5 \%$ The device (PBDTTT- $\mathsf { z } { \cdot } \mathrm { T } { \mathrm { : P C } } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } ,$ based on PEDOT:PSS:CNTs electrode achieves a high efficiency of $7 . 4 7 \%$ . Although the above problems can be solved with acid treatment (strong acid and mild acid), more or less acid residues still existed in PEDOT:PSS films after acid treatment, which may affect device performance. Moreover, the improvement space of the transmittance and conductivity for PEDOT:PSS is limited by itself. Thus, it is generally not the preferred transparent electrode material for high-efficiency FOSCs.

# 11.3.2.2 Carbon Nanotubes

Carbon nanotubes have received extensive attention owing to the advantages of low resistance and super transmittance in the wavelength range of visible and infrared light, highly mechanical flexibility, and low-temperature deposition. In particular, single-walled carbon nanotubes (swcNTs) possess a dominant position of large-area fabrication, easy synthesis, and suitable deposition on flexible substrates. Thus, SwCNTs can become an alternative to ITO bottom electrode which contains precious metal indium.

SwCNTs transparent electrode formed through printing method on the plastic PET substrate was reported by McGehee and coworkers (Figure 11.9) [70]. The fabricated swcNTs film via the printing method exhibited a relatively smooth surface and uniform morphology with a high transmittance of $8 5 \%$ at the wavelength of $5 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . Meanwhile, the flexible devices with PET/SwCNTs/ PEDOT:PSS/P3HT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ /Al structure were fabricated with a high PCE of $2 . 5 \%$ at that time. The photovoltaic performance of flexible device was close to that of ITO glass substrate $( 3 \% )$ , which proved that SwCNTs have a potential application as the transparent electrode material in FOsCs. In addition, flexible devices based on SWCNTs exhibited a superior mechanical flexibility than the plastic substrate with ITO.

![](images/46001eff5ca72d526aa3379dca468c507b6500e73cdbcdb7aa4a8251eb046a53.jpg)  
Figure 11.9The AFM images of SWCNT film (a) before and (b) after PEDOT:PSS deposition, the corresponding the roughness values are 7 and $3 . 5 \mathsf { n m }$ , respectively, (c) transmittance spectra of SWCNTs flm and ITO, (d) current density-voltage curves of glass/ITO-based devices and PET/SwCNT-based devices. Source: Rowell et al. [70]. Reproduced with permission of AIP Publishing LLC.

Furthermore, Zarbin and coworkers [71] reported a highly conductive and transparent film based on carbon nanotube (Figure 11.10). By combining optimal concentration CNTs with high conductivity polyaniline (PANI) for secondary doping, the composite film (PANI/CNTs) has a superior transmittance of $8 9 \%$ at $5 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ and a sheet resistance of $2 9 5 \Omega / \bigtriangledown .$ In particular, the presence of CNT increased the chemical resistance of the film. Meanwhile, the composite electrode film could be easily fabricated on a flexible substrate and could maintain a good mechanical flexibility. Additionally, the conductivity and transmittance of PANI/CNTs film can be better maintained after bending test. Finally, the flexible device using the composite film electrode as the transparent bottom electrode achieved a better interface contact and a larger active area caused by regular rough surface of PANI/CNTs film. Thus, a better photovoltaic performance of device was obtained than the traditional ITO devices.

![](images/0c3035d8559fafbb5200ba2810cb710da75d4c91bbf1b7631ed297441df0f191.jpg)  
Figure 11.10 (a) Schematic diagram of polymerization in carbon nanotube dispersion, (b) the relationship between sheet resistance and transmittance at $5 5 0 \mathsf { n m }$ for different PANI/CNTs films and (c) the configuration of flexible devices. Source: Salvatierra et al. [71]. Reproduced with permission of John Wiley $\&$ Sons.

Matsuo and coworkers fabricated SwcNT films with the direct drying deposition method, which exhibited better electrical property than CNT films prepared by other methods and regular ITO on flexible substrates (Figure 11.11) [72]. After the SwCNT film was doped with molybdenum trioxide by thermal annealing at $3 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , the transmittance of films was superior to the pristine SwCNTs film, and the color of film was changed from green to deep-blue. The SwCNT film doped with $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ as a transparent bottom electrode was firstly proposed in the narrow-band donor polymer PTB7 flexible OsC. Since the high short-circuit current density and the high shunt resistance were obtained compared with the devices with pristine SwCNTs films, the PCEs of $3 . 4 3 \%$ and $3 . 9 1 \%$ for flexible devices based on PI and PET were obtained, respectively. Especially, the PCE could still reach $3 . 8 2 \%$ for PET-based substrate devices after 10 bending tests as $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ -doped SwCNTs exhibited both high flexibility and high conductivity. This work confirmed that high-performance flexible devices based on carbon nanotubes could be achieved via a simple and stable method.

Although the CNT materials as transparent electrode for FOSCs have many advantages such as low absorption and high conductivity, there is a fundamental limitation existing in CNTs. Generally, a better conducting percolation network can be formed unless the density of CNTs satisfied certain threshold. Principally the high-density CNT films possess not only a low sheet resistance but a low transmittance. And most of the carbon nanotube films are limited by the synthesis methods and have a large rough surface, which is incompatible with the large-area fabrication of highly efficient FOSCs.

# 11.3.2.3 Graphene

Two-dimension carbon nanomaterials, also known as graphene, possess super chemical and physical property like low contact resistance, high conductivity, good thermal stability and high flexibility, which offers a strong possibility of its application into FOsCs as the transparent electrode. The synthesis methods of graphene applied in FOsCs are majorly divided into chemical vapor deposition and reduction of graphite oxide.

Zhang and coworkers prepared a reduced graphene oxide film through chemical method and transferred it to the flexible PET substrates surface as the transparent bottom electrode. The performance of flexible devices was dependent on the efficiency of charge transport that determined by sheet resistance of reduced graphene oxide film when the optical transmittance of reduced graphene oxide film is above $6 5 \%$ . However, the flexible device performance was greatly related to the transmission of reduced graphene oxide film when it is below $6 5 \%$ . Especially, the performance of flexible devices based on the reduced graphene oxide film still sustains $2 . 9 \%$ after 1o0o times of bending test, which demonstrated the high possibility of constructing FOsCs based on chemically reduced graphene oxide thin films (Figure 11.12) [73].

![](images/17e7a8d844e895592dda6df6200a871a507e846a4ee9d19582779a88012c5666.jpg)

Source: Yin et al. [73]. Reproduced with permission of American Chemical Society.

Considering the formation of transparent electrode based on thin metals and ITO requires high vacuum and abundant time, the new type of visibly-transparent flexible (including plastic substrate and paper substrate) OsCs with all-graphene electrode was proposed by Kong and coworkers (Figure 11.13) [74]. The top electrode based on graphene was formed by using dry-transfer method at room temperature. The high optical transmission of $6 9 \%$ was reached at the wavelength of $5 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ by combining organic polymer with graphene electrode. The fabricated FOSCs with all-graphene electrode achieved the transmission of $5 4 \sim 6 1 \%$ in the visible light range with PCEs of $2 . 8 8 \sim 3 . 8 \%$ . Besides, the flexible devices with superior all-graphene electrode are mechanically robust, and the performance of the devices is hardly changed after bending of 100 times.

![](images/792eb885878f29342406e7cd432b3876695161fd2f287755c1362e3627bf4255.jpg)  
Figure 11.13 (a) The optimal device structure, (b) energy level diagram, (c) the photographs of substrates (PEN, paper, Kapton tape) before and after fabrication, (d) the relationship between normalized PCE and bending cycle number. Source: Song et al. [74] Reproduced with permission of John Wiley & Sons.

R2R slot-die printing method with use of shear force and one-step reducing posttreatment was developed by Chen and coworkers to fabricate transparent PEDOT:PSS:reduced graphene oxide (RGO) composite electrode for flexible devices. The transmission and conductivity of PEDOT:PSS:RGO film after hydroiodic acid (HI) treatment were significantly improved to $8 2 \%$ and $1 9 4 9 \mathrm { S c m ^ { - 1 } }$ , as HI can simultaneously remove insulating PSS content and reduce GO. Furthermore, a super mechanical flexibility was found in the flexible composite electrode of PEDOT:PSS:RGO under various curvature radius conditions. In addition, the price of PEDOT:PSS:RGO electrode is much lower about $2 . 8 \mathrm { ~ \$ ~ } \$ 8$ for per square meter than the traditional commercial ITO electrode. Ultimately, a higher PCE of $8 . 3 2 \%$ was achieved in large-area $( 1 . 0 1 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ effective area) flexible devices with using PEDOT:PSS:RGO electrode and $\mathrm { P T B 7 - T h } { \mathrm { : P C } } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ active layer than the flexible device based on the ITO electrode (Figure 11.14) [75].

Despite graphene materials being successfully applied on the electrode flexible device, the result is modestly undesirable. The good stability and high conductivity of graphene material are urgently required to the application of high-efficiency flexible devices based on non-fullerene acceptors. Besides, most of graphene fabrication methods such as chemical vapor deposition are expensive, which is another key issue for the production of large-scale FOSCs.

# 11.3.2.4 Metallic Nanowires

The transparent bottom electrodes based on metallic materials have always occupied a large proportion in market owing to the super conductivity. The metallic materials as transparent electrodes are mainly divided into metal nanowire (NW), metallic mesh [76], metal grid [77], and ultrathin metal film [78]. Metallic nanowires that possess the structure of percolation network have exhibited promising electrical property and optical transparency, including copper, gold, cupronickel, and sliver [79-82]. After a random dispersed silver was firstly synthesized by P. Peumans and coworkers under low temperature condition [76], silver (Ag) nanowire has become the current mainstream of transparent electrodes used in the flexible OsCs owing to the advantages of high transmittance, low sheet resistance, and good mechanical flexibility.

Kang and coworkers proposed a high-efficiency flexible solar device with solution-processable Ag nanowire transparent bottom electrode (Figure 11.15) [83]. The Ag NWs/PET film exhibited a better performance such as the conductivity (sheet resistance\~13 $\Omega \thinspace \mathrm { s q } ^ { - 1 } .$ ) and transparency (diffusive transmittance ${ \approx } 9 3 . 5 \%$ at $5 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ and mechanical flexibility $( \Delta \Omega \Omega _ { 0 } ^ { \mathrm { ~ - 1 } } \approx 1 . 1 \pm 1 \%$ under the bending radius ${ \approx } 2 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ than the ITO/PET film (sheet resistance ${ \approx } 4 6 \Omega \mathrm { s q } ^ { - 1 }$ , diffusive transmittance ${ \approx } 9 1 . 2 \%$ ${ \Delta \Omega \Omega _ { 0 } } ^ { - 1 } { \approx } 6 4 . 6 \pm 2 4 \%$ under the bending radius of $2 0 0 \mu \mathrm { m } \dot { }$ ). Furthermore, the flexible device with $\mathbf { A g N W }$ electrodes based on the PTB7-F20 $\mathrm { \Omega } \mathrm { \cdot } \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ active layer achieved a commensurate efficiency with the ITO/glass devices ( $5 . 0 2 \%$ versus $6 . 6 7 \%$ ) and the Ag NWs/glass device $( \mathrm { P C E } \approx 5 . 8 0 \%$ . Remarkably, the comparative value of PCE acquired from Ag NWs/PET flexible devices could still remain the initial value of $9 5 \%$ after undergoing the bending test for 1o00 times, which was much higher than the flexible devices with ITO/PET structure ( $6 3 \%$ of initial efficiency after identical bending condition).

![](images/49950e96fa9db94aa9c7b7e690e1697d5e8936477bfb18efb5855b05d10079f8.jpg)  
Figure 11.15  (a) Diagram of OSCs and cross-section SEM images with the structure of substrate/Ag NW/PEDOT:PSS/PBDTTT- $\mathsf { C } \mathsf { \cdot P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathsf { B M } _ { \ell }$ LiF/Al, (b) specular transmittances of various substrates with different electrodes, (c) the relationship between resistance change and bending number under bending radius of $1 . 5 \mathsf { m m }$ (d) $J - V$ curves of flexible devices based on PBT7- $\mathsf { F } 2 0 { : } \mathsf { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathsf { B M }$ with different electrodes. Source: Song et al. [83]. Reproduced with permission of John Wiley $\&$ Sons.

Since the challenge existed in the formation of large uniform interconnected network of Ag nanowire electrode, Seo and coworkers developed a cold isostatic-pressured (CIP) method to produce an interconnected network by forming the intimate contact between Ag nanowires (Figure 11.16) [84]. Thus, the performance of Ag nanowire fabricated through CIP method, such as conductivity, surface roughness, and flexibility, was extraordinarily improved. Likewise, a lower sheet resistance and a higher figure of merit were manifested for the Ag nanowire using CIP method than the regular Ag nanowire electrode. In addition, a larger FF of $6 3 . 5 \%$ was realized in FOSCs with CIP than regular FOSCs $( 5 3 \% )$ since the smooth surface roughness of Ag electrode by CIP generated a large short-circuit current density. Furthermore, the smoother surface of Ag nanowire electrode by CIP method realized a higher reproducibility of $1 0 0 \%$ than FOSCs with annealed Ag NW electrodes $(7 5 \% )$ . Besides, the PCE of prepared flexible devices with CIP could retain $9 5 \%$ of initial performance after bending cycle of 1o00 times under extremely small radius of $4 . 8 \mathrm { m m }$

![](images/ac3d9307cac3f968e24fdf633883eae60cdfcd9db67d7d394fafaecda2295fef.jpg)  
Figure 11.16 (a) Diagram of fabricated Ag NWs with CIP method, and the SEM images of Ag NWs (b) before and (c) after CIP treatment, (d) structure of flexible device, (e) the relationship between the performance parameters $( V _ { \mathrm { o c } } , J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ , FF, PCE) of flexible devices and bending radius. Source: Seo et al. [84]. Reproduced with permission of John Wiley & Sons.

Recently, a method using water to construct the Ag nanowire was reported by Chen and coworkers with the realization of a grid-like, smooth, flexible Ag nanowire electrode [85]. The new method that used water suspension of Ag NWs and polyelectrolyte (PssNa) to fabricate flexible transparent electrode, is simple, and does not need any extra treatment. The fabricated Ag nanowire electrode possesses a superior performance such as transmission $( 9 2 \% )$ , sheet resistance $( 1 0 ~ \Omega ~ \Omega ^ { - 1 } )$ , surface roughness, and flexibility, which was extremely embodied in the flexible devices. Therefore, a superior performance was determined in the single-junction $( 1 3 . 1 \% )$ and tandem $( 1 6 . 5 \% )$ flexible (PET) devices, which was comparable to commercial ITO-based glass devices. An excellent durability was realized in the flexible devices with use of water-processed Ag nanowire. Especially, a low value of performance degradation was obtained under different bending radiuses and bending times. In addition, the Ag nanowire electrode that possesses high performance offered a great possibility of the application in organic light-emitting diodes and transistors. Meanwhile, it could also be used as a reference for study of other dispersions and flexible electrode materials.

The flexible transparent electrode based on Ag nanowire has been extensively applied on the flexible devices and exhibits a promising future comparing with other electrode materials (PEDOT:PSS, carbon nanotube, graphene) and becomes the current mainstream in flexible electrodes. The issues still existed in the length control, stability, and reproducibility of Ag nanowire, which should be considered and addressed.

# 11.3.2.5Hybrid Films

Although transparent electrode materials such as conducting polymer (PEDOT:PsS), carbon nanotubes, graphene, metal nanowire (Ag nanowire) have their own unique fascination, all of them have modest shortcoming when used in high-efficiency flexible OSCs. To better utilize these transparent electrode materials in FOSCs, current researchers have combined some complementary electrode materials to achieve the aim as much as possible that the performance reaches or surpasses the level of traditional ITO glass device with identical active layer system.

Ge and coworkers combined the advantages of Ag nanowire electrode and graphene electrode to conceal the defects of Ag network and reported a graphene and Ag NWs composite electrode for FOSCs (Figure 11.17) [86]. The composite electrode possessed a high transmission in the whole optical wavelength and a good conductivity. Meanwhile, the surface roughness and conductivity of graphene and Ag NWs composite electrode were further improved by spin-coating PH1000 film. In addition, the inappropriate work function between composite electrode and PEDOT:PSS was also ameliorated by PH1000 film. Thus, the fabricated flexible devices with graphene and Ag NWs/PH1o00 electrode achieved a more excellent photovoltaic performance $( 1 3 . 4 4 \% )$ with the help of suitable energy level, uniform interface layer, and good ohmic contact. As the composite electrodes were resistant to bending, a super mechanical flexibility was realized in the prepared flexible device, and the photovoltaic performance could reach $8 4 . 6 \%$ of original efficiency after bending of over 1o0o times (radius $= 2 \mathrm { m m }$ , which was favorable for larger-scale flexible devices used in commercial market.

PEDOT ${ \tt P S S ^ { 1 } }$ and PEDOT ${ \tt P S S } ^ { 2 }$ are single and double interface layer, respectively. Source: Zhang et al. [86]. ![](images/739ec71c81fc83d398cc5c93ec1329d31da40c26f4e60b71945fd5aae967eaaa.jpg)

Recently, Li and coworkers proposed a concept of "welding" to develop a flexible OSC with intimate binding of transparent bottom electrode and substrate (Figure 11.18) [87]. To solve the mismatch issue between transmittance/absorption spectra of bottom electrode and active layer based on non-fullerene system, a welding bottom electrode with the Em-Ag/Ag NWs:AZO-SG structure was designed for flexible devices. The composite electrode exhibited a super optical and electrical performance with smooth surface and good flexibility. A comparable result is achieved for the flexible devices compared with the ITO glass devices using identical active layer. In particular, two high PCE records were achieved in the FOSCs based on small-area $( 1 5 . 2 1 \% )$ and large-area $( 1 2 . 2 8 \% )$ single-junction system. Moreover, super mechanical robustness was found in the flexible devices with welding composite electrode structure, which provided an excellent reference for developing new-type transparent bottom electrodes and promoted the development of large-area flexible devices.

To achieve the optimal film performance in flexibility and electricity as well as optics, leaf-like biomimetic electrodes (PPZA) that possess efficient light capture and glossy surface were proposed by Tang and coworkers (Figure 11.19) [88]. The biomimetic electrodes were fabricated by mimicking the internal anatomy of the leaf using the contact film transfer technique, which effectively improved the efficiency and mechanical robustness of flexible OsCs. Through the synergistic effect of these components (including conductive Ag NWs, transparent ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ protecting layer, light-scattering PS spheres, and ultrathin flexible PI substrate), the prepared composite electrode PPZA exhibited a high optical transparency $( 8 8 . 2 \% )$ uniform surface $( 2 . 4 \mathrm { n m } )$ , good conductivity $\left( 2 3 . 4 \Omega \mathrm { s q } ^ { - 1 } \right) ,$ , and superior bendability. Furthermore, the flexible devices based on $\mathrm { P M } 6 { : } \mathrm { N } 3 { : } \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ system with PPZA as the bottom electrode achieved an excellent photovoltaic performance (a record PCE value of $1 6 . 1 \%$ and a good reproducibility and resistance to flexural strain. In addition, a super-high flexibility characteristic was embodied in these devices. The PCE of flexible OSCs could reserve $8 5 \%$ of pristine value after the 500o times bending.

![](images/1c4250caed7a24694ab95857db47013e36b0752bb14d5d453a14368060582250.jpg)  
Figure 11.19 (a) Diagram of leaf internal structure, (b) fabrication route of the biomimetic electrode, (c) flexible device architecture, (d) $J - V$ curves of flexible devices. Source: Qu et al. [88]. Reproduced with permission of John Wiley $\&$ Sons.

This kind of composite electrodes with complementary advantages have been suc. cessfully explored for flexible OSCs and have pushed PCE exceeding $1 6 \%$ . Currently, the simplification and exploitation of the preparation method to improve the reproducibility of composite electrodes are still the main goals. The final prospect is to achieve high-performance flexible devices, which can catch up with ITO glass-based devices using the same active layer, and then to realize the goal of replacing ITO with low-cost flexible electrodes.

# 11.4 Large-Area Flexible Device Fabrication

Commercial large-area flexible OsCs should be able to be manufactured through scale-up methods. Spin coating is the most commonly used method for active layer preparation of organic solar cells. In addition, the electrodes and most buffer layers of the state-of-the-art OsCs are fabricated under high vacuum condition in an inert atmosphere. The laboratory fabrication method is not suitable for low-cost and mass production, especially for the large-area devices on flexible substrates. R2R technology is the most prospective for manifesting high-performance large-area FOSCs. In R2R process, a flexible transparent plastic is used as a "web," which is usually unrolled to apply the coating, and then rolled again. Figure 11.20 shows the comparison of the conventional spin coating and R2R process [89].

![](images/64fd90eb561a4640bcd74e9dc29c75b4f9766fb4ba2b5252c7d9a6b8ac3df227.jpg)  
Conventionl device on glass study   
Figure 11.20  Comparison between conventional spin coating process on glass and large-area roll-to-roll process on flexible substrates of organic solar cells. Source: Alstrup et al. [89]. Reproduced with permission of American Chemical Society.

# 11.4.1 Coating and Printing Methods

High-quality film of each layer in a device is a key factor for high-efficiency OSCs. For large-scale R2R process, either the printing methods or the coating methods are usually employed to form a wet film. These methods are blade coating, slot-die coating, spray coating, inkjet printing, relief printing, gravure printing, screen printing, etc. However, dry film is used in OsCs, which is obtained by various other methods (such as drying or curing). The quality of the films processed by abovementioned methods is strongly related to the processing speed, the viscosity of the ink, processing temperature, solvent evaporation rate, etc.

![](images/042497a791f57aad0790aad08e5ba0e5f0fb5cd7b917d6780d9de0b11c2e6bbf.jpg)  
Figure 11.21 Schematic illustration of blade coating.

# 11.4.1.1 Blade Coating

Unlike spin coating, blade coating exhibits excellent compatibility to large-area R2R technology. Figure 11.21 shows schematic illustration of blade coating. When preparing the active layer, the ink is dropped in front of the blade, and then the blade moves parallel to substrate with a constant speed to form a thin film. The area can be easily scaled up, and the material usage is almost $1 0 0 \%$ with zero wastage in blade coating. The film thickness processed by blade coating is determined by the ink concentration and viscosity, the gap between blade and substrate, the blade speed, blade shape, the surface roughness of substrate, the meniscus formed between the wet film and the blade, and solvent evaporation rate. The film thickness of the final dry film can be calculated by the following equation, commonly in a wide range from nanometer to micrometer scale.

$$
d = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \left( g { \frac { c } { \rho } } \right)
$$

where ' $\dot { \boldsymbol { d } } ^ { \flat }$ is film thickness, $" g '$ is the distance between blade and substrate, "c' is ink concentration, $^ { \ast } \rho ^ { \ast }$ is film density. In addition, the film morphology developed by such method is also different from that prepared by spin coating, because spin coating depends on centrifugal force by different direction to form the thin films, but blade coating has the same direction centrifugal force during film process. The same direction centrifugal force can induce alignment of film along the blade moving direction. On the other hand, the slow solvent evaporation in the wet film by blade coating also can improve the crystallinity and optimize the morphology of active layer. In the past 10 years, the blade coating method has become a commonly used method for preparing large-area OSCs in the laboratory.

Initially, blade coating method was performed on fullerene-based active layer. In 2008, Mens et al. [90] fabricated a BHJ blend of MDMO-PPV: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ by the blade coating. They observed that $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ showed higher crystallinity in blade-coated film than in spin-coated film. The slower solvent evaporation in blade coating than in spin coating resulted in the stronger aggregation of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ Soon later, Meng and coworkers also used blade coating to prepare $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 1 } B M }$ devices. They used the toluene with lower boiling point as processing solvent to replace high-boiling-point chlorobenzene (CB) or dichlorobenzene. Desired donor-acceptor self-organization was achieved without the slow drying process and high-boiling-point solvent. A PCE of $3 . 8 \%$ was obtained by blade coating, much higher than the $2 . 6 \%$ obtained by spin coating in toluene solution [91]. Meng and coworkers further processed large-area OSCs by accelerated blade coating. To obtain uniform film, the ink was blade-coated on a hot substrate with an acceleration of the blade motion to compensate the decrease in the wet film thickness because of the depletion of the solution. After the blade motion formed a wet film, hot air from the dryer was immediately directed from above to enhance drying and uniformity. In 2016, Yan and coworkers boosted the PCE of the fullerene-based OSCs up to $9 . 5 \%$ processed by blade coating [92].

With the emergence of non-fullerene acceptors, blade coating method has attracted great attention to be employed in large-area non-fullerene-based devices. Hou and coworkers reported blade-coated non-fullerene OsCs based on PBTA-TF:IT-M with environmentally friendly solvents, tetrahydrofuran/isopropyl alcohol (THF/IPA), a PCE of $1 0 . 6 \%$ with the device area of $1 . 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ was obtained [93]. Zhao et al. also prepared PBTA-TF:IT-M-based device by blade coating method using environmentally friendly solvents that achieved a PCE of $1 1 . 7 \%$ . Ma and coworkers prepared PBDB-T:ITIC-based OSCs by blade coating method [94]. The device achieved a PCE of $1 0 . 0 3 \%$ , higher than the spin coating processed one. They also found that only $0 . 2 5 \%$ DIO additive was required for the blade-coated device, which is much lower than that for spin-coated one ( $1 \%$ DIO additive). The less imported additives in the film are beneficial for device stability. Ma's group also conducted blade coating to fabricate ternary device based on PBDB-T:PTB7-Th:FOIC. An excellent PCE of $1 2 . 0 2 \%$ was obtained, ascribing to the synergistic effect in optimizing morphology by the combination of blade coating and ternary strategy [95]. Recently, they reported PM6:IT-4F-based devices and found that substrate temperature affected IT-4F molecular stacking, the device obtained a PCE of $1 0 . 2 2 \%$ at film thickness of $4 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [96].

Apart from producing BHJ films, blade coating also satisfies the needs of planar heterjunction (PHJ) OSCs using layer-by-layer method. In 2020, Min and coworkers reported PHJ OSCs with PM6 as polymer donor and Y6 as acceptor by layer-by-layer blade coating [97]. Due to suitable vertical phase separation for charge transport, the device obtained a PCE of $1 6 . 3 5 \%$ , higher than BHJ device $( 1 5 . 3 7 \% )$ . They also adopted layer-by-layer method to process $1 1 . 5 2 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ module, which obtained a record efficiency of $1 1 . 8 6 \%$ with a geometric fill factor (GFF) of over $9 0 \%$ . In 2020, Ma and coworkers reported double BHJ films PBDB-T:IT-M/PBDB-T:FOIC fabricated by sequential-blade coating. Because of the strong crystallinity of FOIC [98], the PBDB-T:FOIC film displayed a large phase separation, resulting in poor efficiency of the device. In sequential-blade coating system, the bottom film PBDB-T:IT-M with film thickness of $1 5 \mathrm { n m }$ produces crystal nuclei for the top film PBDB-T:FOIC with film thickness $1 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . Thereby, the balanced crystallize rate between PBDB-T and FOIC was obtained. Ultimately, PBDB-T:IT-M/PBDB-T:FOIC sequential-blade coating device achieved a PCE of $1 1 . 8 6 \%$ . In 2020, Huang and coworkers designed a small molecule acceptor DTY6 to apply in OSC module devices using non-halogen solvent o-xylene. By blade coating, the PM6:DTY6-based OSCs with an active layer area of $1 8 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ achieved a PCE of $1 4 . 4 \%$ [99].

Blade coating shows great potential in the large-area fabrication of highly efficient OsCs. Film thickness and morphology control during blade-coating process is the most important issue that should be concerned to obtain high device performance. For example, during the blade coating process, the solvent evaporation is not as effective as the spin coating method; therefore, the improved crystallinity of film can facilitate the charge transport. However, for the highly crystalline materials, blade coating always leads to the excessive aggregation, unfavorable morphology, and unbalanced charge transport of the film, which also often happens in other large-scale coating and printing processes. In addition to regulating the key factors, which determine the thickness and morphology of films mentioned above, some assistant methods, e.g. preheating blade and substrate, fixing the blade and moving substrate, changing the ink supplementary pattern, have also been employed as effective approaches to improve the film quality.

# 11.4.1.2 Slot-Die Coating

Figure 11.22 shows the schematic illustration of slot-die coating. The coating motion of slot-die coating is similar to that of blade coating. Commonly used blade coating has a constant amount of solution beneath the blade gap, whereas slot-die coating can provide continuous supply of ink, which can be regarded as an upgrade blade coating in a certain sense. The slot-die head, the most important part in this process, has a gap formed by two blades, which is placed over the web. On the slot-die head, there is an ink container connecting to a piston pump or a pressure tank, which directly feeds the ink to the coating head. During the device process, a striped pattern can be printed by attaching a mask to the slot-die head. The thickness of dry film processed by slot-die coating can be evaluated by the following equation:

$$
d = \frac { f } { S w } \times \frac { c } { \rho }
$$

Where ' $\dot { a } ^ { \dag }$ is thickness, $\ " f \ "$ is the flow rate, $^ { 6 } S ^ { \prime }$ is web speed, "w' is the coated width, $\cdot \boldsymbol { c } ^ { \prime \prime }$ is the ink concentration, and ' $\cdot \rho ^ { \dag }$ is the film density. From the equation we can see that the coating thickness strongly depends on the ink velocity and concentration, flow rate, the slot-die gap, web speed, etc. Additional steps are often required to control the meniscus and print a fine pattern. For example, the slot-die head can be kept at high temperature to control the viscosity and solubility of the ink. These coating parameters also exert great influence on the film morphology, similar to the case of blade coating.

![](images/b2a74cb331d2a00abfc500832a0eefb62d53002e00ebd39018501a28d51b4925.jpg)  
Figure 11.22 Schematic illustration of slot-die coating.

Zimmermann et al. processed P3HT:PCBM-based device modules using the slot-die method and the active layers processed in ambient atmosphere. An FF of $6 4 \%$ was achieved by PET foil as substrate, which was close to the results on glass substrate [100]. Schrodner et al. also coated PEDOT:PSS and P3HT:PCBM layers by slot-die method on PET foils and compared device performance of different solvents processed active layers [101]. Brabec and coworkers reported slot-die coated active layers for solar cells processed from non-halogenated solvents, obtaining a PCE of $3 \%$ on flexible substrates [102]. Krebs and coworkers reported a slot-die coated PDTSTTz:PCBM solar cell with a PCE of $3 . 5 \%$ . The active layer thickness is optimized by controlling substrate speed [103]. They also established a completely ITO and vacuum-free R2R process, which allows the processing of all layers of the device without moving the substrate to different equipment.

For the non-fullerene-based system, Min and coworkers reported PBDB-T-SF:IT4F-based devices by slot-die coating method, delivering a PCE of $1 2 . 9 \%$ [104]. Equipping the large-scale device module to a water splitting system yielded a solar-to-hydrogen efficiency of $6 . 1 5 \%$ . Moon and coworkers prepared a flexible device module based on a SMD2:ITIC. A PCE of $5 . 2 5 \%$ was obtained with an active area of $8 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ [105]. Chen and coworkers applied the shear impulse to control the film morphology. The efficiency of flexible devices via slot-die printing achieves $9 . 1 0 \%$ for PTB7-Th:PC71BM and $9 . 7 7 \%$ for PBDB-T:ITIC based on $1 . 0 4 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ . Furthermore, $1 5 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ flexible modules with effective efficiency up to $7 . 5 8 \%$ (PTB7-Th:PC71BM) and $8 . 9 0 \%$ (PBDB-T:ITIC) are demonstrated with satisfying mechanical flexibility and operating stability [106]. Recently, Ma and coworkers reported PM6:Y6-based device using halogenated (chlorobenzene [CB]) and hydrocarbon solvents 1,2,4-trimethylbenzene (TMB) and ortho-xylene (o-XY)) to fabricate photoactive devices. By controlling solution and substrate temperatures to obtain similar morphology of active layers, notable efficiency of $1 5 . 2 \%$ $1 5 . 4 \%$ and $1 5 . 6 \%$ was achieved for CB, TMB, and $o$ -XY solvents, respectively [107]. Huang and coworkers reported a slot-die coated all-PSC based on PTzBI:N2200, a PCE of $9 . 1 0 \%$ was obtained [108].

Slot-die coating has been regarded as the greatest prospect toward the R2R production of solar panels. Nevertheless, due to the requirement of high-precision control over various coating parameters, slot-die coating is expensive at present. Additionally, a good pattern is normally required at a low speed of the web, preventing a rapid drying of multilayer structures in high-throughput continuous processing. Thereby, more efforts should further explore and understand operating parameters of slot-die coating, for minimization of efficiency loss during the transition from small-area devices to large-scale printed modules.

![](images/fbd310e4af55a1dd52a8c51ae5b7794bb9ab60f9dd3788abd0a787769bf530e7.jpg)  
Figure 11.23 Schematic illustration of the inkjet printing process.

# 11.4.1.3 Inkjet Printing

Inkjet printing technology is widely used in daily life, and the use of printers is a good example. In recent years, inkjet printing has been applied in the field of OSCs. The most common inkjet printing methods are continuous inkjet printing and drop-on-demand inkjet printing. Drop-on-demand inkjet printing has higher material efficiency, which has proven to be more relevant to the electronics industry. As shown in Figure 11.23, it is a drop-on-demand inkjet printer. The film formation is composed of the droplet formation, ejection, positioning, spreading and coalescence on the substrate, and the final solidification. The printer head is mounted on the substrate, and either the substrate or the printer head is movable. The printer head is connected to a continuous solution supply pump. The pressure pulse controls the rate of droplet ejection from the printer head. The mechanical force of the piezoelectric transducer on the solution container generates the pulse. Generally, inkjet printing has a high demand on ink, and a low viscosity $( 4 { - } 3 0 \mathrm { c P } )$ and high surface tension (typically ${ > } 3 5 \mathrm { m N m ^ { - 1 } }$ ) are required for the operation. The film thickness is determined by four parameters: the droplet volume $( V _ { \mathrm { d } } )$ , the ink concentration $( c )$ the number of droplets per unit area $( N _ { \mathrm { d } } )$ , and the density of the material $( \rho )$

$$
d = N _ { \mathrm { d } } V _ { \mathrm { d } } \times \frac { c } { \rho }
$$

Eom et al. studied the effect of additives on the efficiency of inkjet-printed devices, and the results showed that the surface morphology and charge collection were improved by adding various additives [109]. In 2014, an all inkjet-printed, all-air-processed OSC has been fabricated with a PCE of $5 \%$ [110]. Similarly, in 2015, Eggenhuisen et al. reported the use of environmentally friendly solvents to produce an all-inkjet-printed large-area $( > 1 \thinspace \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } ) ,$ OSCs in air atmosphere. The device was fabricated using industrial-scale (512 nozzles) print heads, compatible with R2R technology and attained a PCE of $4 . 1 \%$ [111]. In 2019, Corzo et al. reported P3HT:O-IDTBR-based devices fabricated by the inkjet printing method. They studied the deposition temperature and drop spacing parameters. Finally, the PCEs of 6.47 and $6 \%$ were achieved for the 0.1 and $2 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ OSCs. Furthermore, large-area marine-like devices were fabricated with a PCE of $4 . 7 6 \%$ [112].

The advantage of inkjet printing is a noncontact processing that effectively utilizes materials and has great flexibility in printing shape and thickness. However, it is difficult to retain these advantages in the case of high throughput. It is necessary to use a solution with appropriate dynamic viscosity, density, and surface tension to print normally in the printer head. For the surface of the substrate, the solution needs to be adjusted to avoid surface interactions, for example, to dewetting or drying (coffee rings). Since it is difficult to form an ideal ink for inkjet printing, this printing technology still has great challenges in mass production in the future.

![](images/0daf266931653885b610edda3b3b66e0113bf5a85766030fd030e0ed9339c3d0.jpg)  
Figure 11.24 Schematic illustration of the spray coating process.

# 11.4.1.4 Spray Coating

Spray coating is a solution-based deposition technique that has been widely used in building painting and a number of industrial applications. It also has the advantages of low material waste, touch-free, and fast, compatible to the R2R process. Figure 11.24 shows an ultrasonic spray coater. The work mechanism of the spray coating is somewhat similar to that of inkjet coating, just the aerosol droplet instead of liquid droplet for film forming. The ink is forced through an airbrush nozzle to generate aerosol, then depositing on the substrate to form a film. Distance between the airbrush nozzle and substrate can be $1 0 { - } 3 0 \mathrm { c m }$ , much longer than those of blade coating and slot-die coating. This method is universal, being capable of solution coating every layer of an OSC device, and a wide viscosity range for the ink is acceptable. The film thickness and morphology strongly depend on the ink concentration, ink viscosity, the choice of solvents, and the distance between the airbrush nozzle and substrate, etc.

Previous work on deposition of active layers by spray coating method mainly focused on P3HT:PCBM blends [113-118]. A device efficiency of lower than $3 . 0 \%$ was reported for P3HT:PCBM solar cells when the active layer was spray cast from a solution of two-solvent system. When the film was casted from a two-solvent system of orthodichlorobenzene (oDCB) as the primary solvent and mesitylene as the secondary solvent, a booted PCE of $3 . 7 5 \%$ has been reported. This is because the secondary solvent with a lower boiling point and lower surface tension has been shown to promote the wettability and uniformity of the P3HT:PCBM film [114, 117]. Using a solvent mixture of DCB and CB, a PCE of $4 . 1 \%$ was achieved in P3HT:PCBM solar cells by airbrush spray coating [119]. In 2013, Wang et al. reported a spray-cast device based on a fullerene system, obtaining a PCE of $5 . 0 \%$ [120]. In 2015, Vak et al. deposited the active layer of ${ \mathrm { P } } 3 { \mathrm { H T } } { \mathrm { : I C } } _ { 6 0 } { \mathrm { B A } }$ by spraying method and achieved PCE of $4 . 2 \%$ . Besides, they used an LED-photodiode couple as an optical thickness monitor, and the spray deposition process operates in a manner analogous to a vacuum deposition process [121].

Spray coating not only can deposit the active layers, but also can deposit electrodes and buffer layers. There are some reports on successful deposition of the PEDOT:PSS transparent electrodes [122] and ZnO electron transporting layers [123, 124] by spray coating method. Even though the OSCs can indeed be processed by spray coating, obtaining a smooth and uniform film is still a big challenge. In the touch-free coating, the aerosol has to fly the long distance between nozzle and substrate before coating on the surface of the substrate, so the transition process from aerosol to film is difficult to be precisely control, leading to a great impact on the film morphology.

# 11.4.1.5 Screen Printing, Relief Printing, and Gravure Printing

When printing a defined area or pattern, the industry usually chooses screen printing, gravure printing, and relief printing technology. As shown in Figure 11.25a-c, engrave the image to be printed onto the image carrier, and then transfer it to the substrate. For screen printing technology, the image carrier is the mesh with printed pattern. In gravure printing, the printed image is engraved in the printing cylinder, and the ink to be printed is filled into the groove. The image of relief printing is also engraved on the cylinder, but it is a relief structure. Theoretically, screen printing, relief printing, and gravure printing can be used to fabricate any layer of a device if the materials can be processed by solution, and there are indeed some reported instances for printed active layers, buffer layers, and electrodes. At present, screen printing is mainly used to print large-scale electrodes of OsCs.

Figure 11.25a shows the screen printing method. Screen printing is conducted with a woven screen made of steel mesh or synthetic fiber. The pre-patterned screen is filled with the coating ink. A rigid squeegee brings the screen into a close contact with the substrate, then the squeegee moves across the screen to transfer the pattern onto the substrate. The film thickness is related to the ink concentration, viscosity, and theoretical paste volume of the screen. In 2011, Krebs et al. reported three different types of silver based screen-printable metal inks, including organic solvent-based, UV-curable, and water-based silver inks. Compared with the UV-curable ink and the water-based ink, the organic solvent-based ink had negative effect on the performance of the devices [125]. In addition, screen-printed silver grids have been embedded in the substrate to make electrodes for OPV devices [126-128]. Screen printing was also reported for coating active layers [129]. Therefore, screen printing has been proven to be one of the important printing technologies for large-scale device modules [130].

![](images/876a84052fcdb2ea0d19835f3f90f2fbd6055e8e177f589a1c834ed8357fca0e.jpg)  
Figure 11.25 (a) Schematic illustration of screen printing, (b) gravure printing, (c) and relief printing.

Figure 11.25c shows the relief printing method. The working process of relief printing is that the image is reproduced in relief, and then the printing cylinder transfers the ink to the substrate. In 2013, Hosel et al. used relief printing in anode printing silver bottom electrodes for device modules. The authors declared that relief printing was the best technique for process silver electrode, as it has a high production speed and consumes less ink [131]. In 2018, Alem et al. demonstrated a solar cell with the electron transport layer (ZnO) and the active layer $( \mathrm { P C D T B T : P C _ { 7 1 } B M } )$ deposited by relief printing. The photovoltaic cells of $1 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ with the active layer processed by relief printing showed an efficiency of up to $3 . 5 \%$ which is comparable to those of other printing/coating techniques [132]. In 2019, Hart et al. successfully printed the anode (Ag) by relief printing [133].

Figure 11.25b shows the gravure printing method. The main difference between the gravure printing process and relief printing is that, in gravure printing, the transfer of ink is done through cavities, which is opposite to the relief. Using gravure printing to print transparents has also been reported. In 2015, Montanino et al. processed highly conductive and transparent films based on PEDOT:PSS doped with DMSO onto a flexible substrate PEN, by gravure printing method. The corresponding device based on PTB7:PCBM with the printed anode yielded a PCE value around $2 \%$ [134]. In 2018, Huang and Zhu reported that by tailoring the ink properties, printing conditions, and post-printing treatment, gravure printing enabled the printing of high-resolution, highly conductive $\mathbf { A g } \mathbf { N W }$ patterns in large area. The printed Ag NW patterns on the flexible substrate showed excellent flexibility under repeated bending [135]. In 2020, Wang and coworkers prepared uniformly printed Ag NW films. Owing to the good uniformity of the gravure-printed $\mathrm { A g \ N W }$ electrode, the highest PCE of $1 3 . 6 1 \%$ was achieved for $1 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ PSCs based on the gravure-printed flexible transparent electrodes [136]. Chen and coworkers reported a scalable and highly conductive PEDOT:PSS:CNTs transparent electrode by gravure printing. A large-area flexible electrode with a sheet resistance of $1 7 \Omega \mathrm { s q } ^ { - 1 }$ and a light transmittance of $8 0 . 7 \%$ was obtained by using the R2R technique [137].

# 11.4.2 R2R Methodology

R2R methodology is the best choice to be employed for high-performance large-area FOSCs. Figure 11.20 shows a small R2R process for OSCs, and Figure 11.26 shows

![](images/70ed6077223971695a6c5e4eb1f6c916eddd4cf426728fc90b7af376552d403e.jpg)  
Figure 11.26  R2R printing and coating machine for organic solar cell. (a) Appearance of the whole instrument, (b) an enlarged view of a part of the instrument.

R2R machine for large-scale devices. In R2R technique, a "web" is used. The web includes PET, PEN, polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), and so on. PET is most commonly used in R2R manufacturing of OSCs. In the manufacturing process, the web is first unwound from the roll and then further processed by a printing/coating machine. After processing the pattern/ink to the web, it rolls up again. Apart from the printing/coating of the pattern/ink, other procedures (cleaning, speed control, surface treatments, heating, drying, UV curing, etc.) are also needed to obtain a complete OSC.

Coating steps can be divided into two categories. One is a discrete strategy: each step has a separate unwinder and rewinder. The other is the integrated strategy: all steps are integrated with each other in a single unwinding and rewinding process. In the case of high automation, the raw materials enter the machine at one end, and the completed solar cells can be output at the other end. Such an integration process will not only greatly reduce processing costs, but also help to obtain better product output. This is indeed an ideal process for the preparation of industrial large-scale OSCs. In actual production, the integrated system is very complicated, because each step requires different processing parameters. Therefore, it is best to use discrete methods to process such large-area OSCs, because each layer can be processed separately and after coating/printing, and the web can be moved to the next machine for processing.

The printing/coating process is carried out on a motor-driven roller or freely rotating due to the action of the web, guiding the web through the printing/coating unit. Methods such as blade coating, slot-die coating, inkjet printing, spray coating, and screen printing include at least one roller. Complex techniques such as relief printing and gravure printing involve at least two rollers, one roller containing the pattern and the web supported by another coating roller. Depending upon the system, more rolls can be utilized.

Krebs et al. established a complete manufacturing process of the devices and reported a detailed work on mass production from the lab to the fab [138]. Moreover, they also analyzed some neglected aspects during industrial production, such as labor, materials, and electricity costs. Therefore, a comprehensive consideration of material, modules, coating methods and cost is highly required for commercialization of the large-area devices method. Many efforts have been made in fabrication of the upscale devices, and some encouraged progresses have been achieved in the coating fabrication of active layers. Compared with that of spin-coated devices, the morphology of slot-die coating device is more difficult to modulate because of the complex processing parameters such as striping speed, inking speed, processing temperature, etc. Recently, Ma and coworkers realized an impressive PCE of $1 5 . 6 \%$ for PM6:Y6-based device by slot-die coating. Such high performance is almost equal to that fabricated by spin coating [107]. Slot-die coating method exhibits great compatibility with R2R setting and has been considered to be the most potential for industrial-scale manufacturing. However, high-performance large-area flexible devices and modules processed by all R2R technique are rarely reported, so there are still big challenges in a fundamental understanding of a complete manufacturing process.

# 11.5 Efficiency Loss in Large-Area Devices and Modules

Although the high-efficiency photovoltaic device has been explored in laboratory environment (refer to small-area devices), the route from large-area devices to module pattern is yet not easy. Herein, there is a broad cognition that PCE inevitably and significantly decreases with the increase of device area since the large-area electrode has large resistance (particular in modular solar cells). The importance of drying process conditions from small-area to large area R2R production was demonstrated by Krebs and coworkers, who also proposed the essentiality of the sacrificial solvent system and some basic problems such as uncontrolled electric energy in the later installation of OsCs [139]. As the connection part of each solar cell in module has no contribution to photovoltaic performance, a concept of GFF is proposed for evaluating the PCE loss from the geometric patterns, which is defined as the ratio between photoactive layer area and total area [140]. In addition, the regular processing solvents in high-efficiency OsCs are halogen solvents including chlorobenzene, $o$ -dichlorobenzene, and chloroform, which harm the environment and deviate from the idea of green chemistry. Therefore, these processing solvents are often replaced by non-halogen solvents without sacrificing too much PCE.

Thereby, the PCE loss from small-area devices to module solar cells is mainly divided into electrical loss, geometric loss, optical loss, and additional loss. The electrical loss, geometric loss, and optical loss are mainly manifested in the reduction of $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and FF, while the additional loss resulted from the use of non-halogen solvents [19, 100, 141-144].

# 11.5.1 Electrical Loss

The electrical loss from small-area devices to modules can be reflected in the elec. trode resistance $( R _ { \mathrm { s } } )$ and inter-contact resistance $( R _ { \mathrm { i n t } } )$ between single cells. The cells between modules are commonly connected in series to acquire the vast voltage, but resulting in a higher internal resistance $( R _ { \mathrm { i } } )$ in modules. Apart from above, the $R _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ that existed in module also possesses a large proportion in electrical loss, as displayed in Figure 11.27.

The sheet resistances $( R _ { \mathrm { s } } )$ of top electrodes and bottom electrodes can be obtained through Eq. (11.1). Meanwhile, the $R _ { \mathrm { i } }$ produced from module was acquired by Eq. (11.2). Herein, $\rho$ refers to the resistivity, $" d "$ is the thickness of active layer in single cell. "w" denotes the width of single OSCs, $^ { \ast } L ^ { \prime \prime }$ and $^ { 6 6 } I ^ { 5 9 }$ stand for the length of active layer and inter-contact parts. Besides, an interior proportional relationship between $R _ { \mathrm { s } }$ and $R _ { \mathrm { i } }$ was existed in Eq. (11.3). Undoubtedly, the improvement of devices in area must correspond to the rise of electrode areas, including top and bottom electrodes. Specially, the value of $R _ { \mathrm { s } }$ was increased drastically with the introduction of flexible substrates, which is much higher than the substrate based on ITO glass. Therefore, a higher internal resistance $R _ { \mathrm { i } }$ in modules was achieved than devices based on small area. The $R _ { \mathrm { i } }$ of OSCs also exhibits an intimate influence on the photovoltaic parameters ( $\boldsymbol { J } _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and FF), and the ultimate effects are presented on the values of PCE.

![](images/dc55ae0e5eb99e70d27fbe4777aae4a0d9fe36a1696d6ebe9e25c7b9b41e9ba3.jpg)  
Figure 11.27 Cross section and the equivalent circuit diagram of OSC modules. "w" denotes the width of OSCs, "L" and $" r "$ stand for the length of active layer and inter-contact parts. Source: Lucera et al. [144]. Reproduced with permission of John Wiley $\&$ Sons.

$$
\begin{array} { l } { \displaystyle R _ { \mathrm { s } } = \frac { \rho } { d } } \\ { \displaystyle R _ { \mathrm { i } } = \frac { \rho } { d } \times \frac { L } { W } } \\ { \displaystyle R _ { \mathrm { i } } = R _ { \mathrm { s } } \times \frac { L } { W } } \end{array}
$$

The $R _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ is introduced by the incomplete contact between adjacent cells in modules, which also brings a large "dead region' defined as the inactive part. Exactly, the $R _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ formed by ohmic contact between bottom and top electrodes (as shown in Figure 11.27) is determined by electrode materials, normal stress, and surface environment. Besides, the contact carrier at the interface is also affected by the work functions of bottom and top electrodes and the condition of contact surface. Generally, the smooth interface contact with homogeneous and high conductivity trans. parent electrodes is beneficial to obtaining the low values of $R _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ . A high PCE of module could be achieved by decreasing $R _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ [69].

# 11.5.2Geometric Loss

The "dead area' between the neighboring cells (displayed in Figure 11.28) is originated from the inter-connect part among top and bottom electrodes and active layer, which does not have the ability to generate photocurrent. Thus, the geometric loss is proposed. Moreover, the GFF is defined as the ratio of effective active area to the total device area (refers modules):

$$
{ \mathrm { G F F } } = { \frac { \mathrm { e f f e c t i v e ~ a c t i v e ~ a r e a } } { \mathrm { t o t a l ~ a r e a } } } = { \frac { n \times w \times L } { n \times w \times ( L + l ) } } = { \frac { L } { L + l } }
$$

Here, $w$ represents the width of single OSCs, $n$ is the number of OSCs, $L$ and $l$ refer to the length of effective active layer and dead area between inter-contact parts, respectively. The PCEs of module and cells satisfy the following relationship equation:

$$
\mathrm { P C E } _ { \mathrm { m o d u l e } } = \mathrm { P C E } _ { \mathrm { c e l l } } \times \mathrm { G F F }
$$

Therefore, the realization of low geometric loss, corresponding to a high GFF, always is critical for high-efficiency modules. Intrinsically, the small length of dead area possesses an essential role on the efficiency of module, because the small dead area denotes a high value of GFF [144].

![](images/31f351d736c91129041e582c46687ef3726b8eb6f57fbaa2439c3c796b652eff.jpg)  
Figure 11.28 Cross-sectional diagram of module formed through single solar cells in series, where l and L are the length of dead area and effective active layer area. Source: Wang et al. [145]. Reproduced with permission of John Wiley $\&$ Sons.

# 11.5.3  Optical Loss

The optical loss is another key parameter influencing the module efficiency, because the transparency of large-area flexible electrode is lower than these rigid devices based on ITO glass. The optical loss is caused by the inadequate incident light (below $1 0 0 \%$ , which is the result of reflection and low transparency of flexible electrode in flexible module. Furthermore, compared with the small-area ITO devices, the adoption of large-area bottom electrodes also accompanies the large optical loss due to the strong absorption and reflection of incident light in thick functional-layer films of modules. The optical loss can be analyzed by the transfer matrix formalism, which can give the systematic and precise results [146-148].

# 11.5.4 Additional Loss

In addition to the abovementioned main loss in the module cells, there is the additional loss remaining that can be easily neglected in the transform process from small-area to large-area devices. The additional loss in large-area films comes from more defects than small-area devices, which can lead to a large current leakage in module consisting of multiple monolithic interconnecting cells in series and parallel. Hence, reducing defects of active layer by using the thick film is favorable for promoting the PCE loss. Meanwhile, it is a powerful way to diminish current leakage in modules. Apart from above loss, the introduction of free halogen is a key role in decreasing the toxicity of solvent (such as chlorobenzene, $o$ -dichlorobenzene, etc.) in the large-area fabrication route [101]. The difference of $1 0 \% \sim 2 0 \%$ still existed when replacing the conventional toxic solvents to free-halogen solvents (such as xylene, toluene, and tetrahydronaphthalene, etc.). Thus, the decline of the performance from the alternative green solvent should be premeditated into the PCE loss.

# 11.5.5 Modular Designs

To minimize the PCE loss, the high-transparency and high-conductivity electrodes are used in module. And the active layer materials for modules should possess the good retention characteristics of photovoltaic performance when using the thick film and green solvent. Meanwhile, the design of large-area modules should be carefully considered and selected for achieving low internal resistance (affected by the width and length of monolithic cell) and small length of dead area (directly determined by the length of interconnected part), corresponding to the low electrical loss and high GFF. Indeed, the dead area in module has no contribution on photocurrent, and the interconnected part should be reduced as much as possible. Further. more, the modular design owns a pretty decisive factor affecting the PCE loss. The high-efficiency solar module commonly has the intimate relation with optimal modular design.

# 11.6 Conclusion and Outlook

Different from small-area devices by spin coating, large-area flexible devices have a rigorous demand on the active layer materials, fabrication method, bottom electrode, and modular design. Roughly, the active layer materials for large-area need possess some certain tolerance to thickness; meanwhile, the mechanical and photovoltaic performances of FOsCs are also limited by flexibility and transparency of flexible electrodes.

Pursuing high-efficiency FOSCs is persistent and continuing. To better satisfy the diverse requirements of people, the distinctive advantages of ultrahigh flexibility and semitransparency of large-area FOsCs in the future should be positively developed. Moreover, the researchers who mainly focused on the photovoltaic performance are transforming their interests into the practical application of wearable device and smart windows. Through continuous innovation and development, the ultra-FOSCs will be widely used in the world.

# Organic Photovoltaics for Indoor Applications

Zhan'ao Tan1, Yinglong Bai?, and Shan Jiang?
