# 12.1 Introduction

Since the industrial revolution, more and more carbon dioxide has been released into the atmosphere, leading to a rise in global temperatures, much of which can be traced to energy production and the burning of fossil fuels [1-6]. Energy production and consumption have always been an important part of social development. The solution to the global energy crisis is to find clean energy to transform the supply of traditional energy [7]. At present, solar energy is an important clean energy with the advantages of low cost, abundant resources, renewable, and no environmental pollution [8]. There are many ways to utilize solar energy, among which, photovoltaic (PV) technology is considered as one of the most effective strategies to convert light energy into electric energy [9]. As a technology of light energy collection and utilization, PV cell is used worldwide as a single or matching power source in different energy consumption fields, which has taken center stage as a more desirable alternative [10-12]. At present, scientists have been trying to find efficient and low-cost PV technology. PV utilization technology can be divided into three generations, the first generation is based on chip solar cells, mainly crystalline silicon (c-Si) solar cells. The second generation is thin-film solar cells, such as those made of amor. phous silicon (a-Si), CdTe and $\mathrm { C u I n G a S e } _ { 2 }$ (CIGS), and other different inorganic film composed of III-V compound (GaAs) solar cells. The third generation of emerging solar cells includes dye-sensitized solar cells, perovskite solar cells, and organic solar cells [13, 14]. c-Si solar cells account for over $9 0 \%$ of the market, and thin-film solar cells account for the rest. Although currently emerging solar cells cannot compete with c-Si and thin-film solar cells in terms of efficiency, they are expected to achieve other applications that were not covered by the previous two generations of solar cells such as semi-transparent, ultra-flexible. This is also an important reason why the third-generation solar cell has always been a research hotspot.

Due to the inferior stability of third-generation solar cells, it seems more feasible to use them in mild indoor environments than in standard outdoor sunlight, compared with commercialized c-Si panels. The development of PV technology for low light intensity and indoor environment applications has a broad application prospect in the field of household and building management systems. In recent years, flexible wearable devices, Internet of Things (IoTs), and other portable electronic devices have rapidly penetrated into our daily life [15, 16]. There is optimism that IoT technology will benefit our daily life in all sorts of smart ways. The success of IoT technologies will depend to a large extent on the capabilities and number of terminal nodes (sensors and actuators) that detects the state of the environment or equipment and communicate wirelessly with each other or connect to gateways. By 2020, the IoTs terminal node usage is expected to reach tens of billions. Figure 12.1a shows the comparison of the number of articles on IoTs and indoor photovoltaics (IPVs) on the Web of Science from 2005 to 2020 [20, 21]. These devices will be integrated with wireless devices and communication systems, although they are designed to operate periodically and consume little power (from microwatts to milliwatts, Figure 12.1b). Maintaining a stable power supply over the long term independent of the power grid is also a fairly challenging task. Therefore, the self-powered system of these electronic devices is a key factor in the success of IoT technology [22]. How to solve the power supply is undoubtedly an urgent problem to be solved. Due to the unique requirements of the IoTs, many people have accepted the scheme of using PV technology for energy collection under low light intensity or indoor conditions [23]. Efficient IPVs will be an excellent and friendly solution to provide sustainable energy to drive these devices by capturing ambient light energy from indoor lighting. The use of IPV can greatly reduce the maintenance cost of indoor installation for electronic equipments. Third-generation PV cells have great potential to meet the energy requirements of most indoor electronics, making them very promising power candidates. Figure 12.1c shows a typical wireless sensor network with organic photovoltaic (OPV) energy collection modules and the cross-section schematic diagram of OPV modules [17, 24]. As a result, IPV is increasingly becoming an important technology for the IoTs, the home, and a variety of electronic applications [25-27].

In the past few decades, OPV technology has made significant progresses. By synthesizing novel photoactive donor and acceptor materials (especially developing non-fullerene acceptors), engineering device structures, and optimizing blended layer phase-separation morphology, the power conversion efficiency (PCE) of single-junction solar cells has reached over $1 8 \%$ under air mass (AM) $1 . 5 6 \ 1$ sun irradiation [28]. At the same time, OPVs can be used as portable power sources to charge low-power electronic devices in indoor environments. Today, buildings with lights on 24hours a day (hospitals, shops, airports, offices, and factories) are common, and artificial lighting is a common source of light [29, 30]. Indoor ambient lighting sources, such as white light-emitting diodes (LEDs), fluorescent lamps (FLs), and halogen lamps, can provide sufficient energy for most small and low-power indoor electronic devices. At present, primary/secondary batteries are the most widely available power supply option for these indoor electronic devices, but battery power systems require regular replacement and maintenance, which adds to human and material costs [31]. Therefore, it is imperative to choose a semi-permanent indoor energy collection system, which can convert indoor light energy into electric energy and make low-power indoor electronic device work normally [32, 33]. In general, the PV performance of OPV devices is not as good as that of inorganic counterparts under sunlight. However, studies have shown that OPVs can convert indoor light into electricity more efficiently than other inorganic PVs (Figure 12.1d). For PV devices, efficient light collection is always the most important. Different from the wide spectrum of AM $1 . 5 6$ sunlight from ultraviolet-visible (UV-Vis) spectroscopy to infrared, indoor light is in the visible range, leading to the optimization of IPV without the pursuit of narrow bandgap photoactive materials. Freunek et al. have shown that when comparing different light sources, it is the spectral range of the light source, rather than the intensity of the light source, that determines the device PCE [34]. In addition, the maximum PCE available for PV devices depends on the structure of device and the bandgap of the photoactive layer. The active layer with a lower bandgap will produce a larger PCE under outdoor sun lighting, while the active layer with a higher bandgap will produce a larger PCE under indoor lighting. It can be predicted that the active layer bandgap for devices suitable for indoor lighting sources should be about 1.9-2.1 eV.

Organic materials have high absorption coefficient and adjustable absorption range, and the leakage current is small under dim lighting conditions, which makes the light absorption and power conversion of indoor lighting environment more effective. In addition, its lightweight and mechanical flexibility make it an ideal power source for indoor IoTs of wireless sensor networks [35, 36]. Therefore, OPVs have great potential in collecting environmental energy, which cannot be achieved with silicon-based inorganic PV. Based on this, OPVs is developing rapidly as an ideal indoor energy supply solution.

# 12.2 The Characteristics of Indoor Lighting Sources

At present, indoor lighting equipments mainly focus on FL and LED lighting sources. Figure 12.2a shows physical image of FL and LED. They have unique spectral characteristics and luminescence principles. Traditional FL, namely low pressure mercury lamp, is to use the mercury vapor at low pressure after the release of ultraviolet light, so that the phosphor gives off visible light luminescence, so it belongs to low pressure arc discharge light source. The electric energy consumed by FL in gas discharge is mainly converted into electromagnetic radiation in the ultraviolet range. About $3 \%$ of the energy is directly converted into visible light in the discharge, and the main wavelengths are $4 0 5 \mathrm { n m }$ (blue-violet), $4 3 6 \mathrm { n m }$ (blue), $4 5 6 \mathrm { n m }$ (green), and $5 7 7 \mathrm { n m }$ (yellow).

The color temperature range of FL for lighting is between 2700 and $6 5 0 0 \mathrm { K }$ , which can be divided into warm color light, warm white color light, and cool color light according to the different color temperature. The color temperature of warm color light is below 3300 K. Warm color light is similar to incandescent lamp, and red light has more components, which can give people a warm, healthy, and comfortable feeling, suitable for family, residence, dormitory, hotel and other places with low temperature. Warm white light also calls neutral color, with a color temperature between 3300 and 5300 K, because the light is downy, which makes people feel happy, comfortable and serene, suitable for shops, hospitals, offices, restaurants, waiting rooms, and other places. The color temperature of cool color light is above $5 3 0 0 \mathrm { K }$ , illuminant is close to natural light, having bright feeling, suitable for office, conference room, classroom, drawing room, design room, library reading room, exhibition window, and other places [18, 38].

The LEDs used for indoor lighting are white LEDs, which represent white light source with different color temperature. Generally speaking, indoor lighting sources have three color temperatures: warm white (2700-3000 K), natural white (4000-4500K), and cold white (5000-6500K). The higher the color temperature, the more blue light emitted in the white light. There are generally two ways to make white LEDs. For the most widely used phosphor LED, light is generated by the combined emission of GaN blue LED and yellow phosphor. In the blue region, there is a peak broadband spectrum. The color temperature of white LED can be adjusted by adjusting the thickness of phosphor coating. In addition, white light can be generated by red (R), green (G), and blue (B) LEDs, where three different red, green, and blue (RGB) colored LEDs are integrated into a module to generate white light by adding colors [18].

Interior lighting is a visual design, since the brightness of indoor light source is affected by human visual perception. When the human eyes observe a radiator from a certain direction, the intensity of human eyes vision depends not only on the radiation intensity of the radiator in that direction but also on the wavelength of the radiation. Human eyes can only see the electromagnetic radiation with a wavelength of $4 0 0 { - } 7 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ called visible light. Even within the range of visible light, human eyes have different visual sensitivity to different wavelengths of light. They are most sensitive to yellow and green light but less sensitive to red and purple light. They have no visual response to infrared and ultraviolet light other than visible light. In photometry, a function ${ \mathrm { V } } ( \lambda )$ , called the "visual function' or "spectral optical efficiency," is defined to show the difference in the sensitivity of the human eyes to different wavelengths of radiation, as shown in Figure 12.2b. To the human eyes, the most sensitive wavelength located at $5 5 5 \mathrm { n m }$ and the visibility function value is 1 $( V ( \lambda @ 5 5 5 ) = 1 )$ Therefore, brightness is quantified using illuminance, which is measured by the spectral sensitivity of the human eyes [18]. For indoor light sources, the illuminance (light flux per unit area) is used as the unit of measurement after taking into account the different reactions of human eyes to light at different wavelengths, and the International System of Unit (SI) lux (lx) is adopted. The illumination of indoor lighting ranges from 200 to 1000 lx, which is 100-500 times lower than the standard AM 1.5 G illumination (Figure 12.2c,d) [19].

# 12.3 Testing System and Parameters for Indoor OPVs

For standard PV cells, the most direct evaluation of their performance is their PCE, which is measured by the short-circuit current density $( J _ { \mathrm { s c } } )$ , open-circuit voltage $( V _ { \mathrm { o c } } )$ , and filling factor (FF) under light conditions, concerning the accuracy of the AM 1.5G standard irradiance spectrum, the irradiance spectrum of the solar simulator, the spectral responsivity of the reference cell, and the spectral responsivity of the test devices. Obviously, solar simulators play an equivalent role with reference cells in the accurate measurements of PCEs. According to the IEC 60904-9 and ASTM E927-10 standards, spectral mismatch, irradiance spatial non-uniformity, and temporal instability are three important parameters to define a solar simulator. Therefore, the best way to accurately evaluate PCEs of OPVs is by choosing a combination of a spectral matched reference cell and a Class AAA solar simulator [39].

So far, there is no standard operating procedures for OPV test under indoor light conditions. In order to accurately evaluate PCE of a PV cells under a certain non-standard illumination condition, the incident light power must be carefully measured. The incident light power was usually evaluated by a lux meter, but this method is not suitable for PV measurement. The illuminance of a light source $( E _ { V }$ in the unit of lux) can be calculated through the exact emission power spectrum as expressed by the following equation [23]:

$$
E _ { V } = K _ { \mathrm { m } } \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } E _ { \lambda } ( \lambda ) \cdot V ( \lambda ) d _ { \lambda }
$$

where the coefficient $K _ { \mathrm { m } }$ is equal to $6 8 3 \mathrm { l m } \mathrm { \mathrm { W } ^ { - 1 } }$ , and $E _ { \lambda }$ corresponds to emission spectra. $V ( \lambda )$ is spectral luminosity factor for human photopic vision (Figure 12.2c). A low-precision lux meter does not have the ability to accurately measure the emission power spectrum and the illuminance from the lux meter is only a rough result. Furthermore, the commercially available lux meters are equipped with spherical probes, which are very different to the planar PV cells and thus not suitable for evaluating the incident light power. Therefore, it is particularly urgent to develop a standardized indoor light condition PV cell testing system.

IPV test and characterization system can simulate a variety of indoor light color, light intensity, and spectrum, along with large illumination area. Traceable to light intensity calibrated devices is key for accurately evaluating the indoor PV conversion efficiency [40]. Figure 12.3a,b demonstrates the schematic diagram with LED white light source and sectional view of the IPV cell testing system, respectively. Light intensity range can cover $2 0 0 \sim 1 0 0 0 0 \mathrm { l x } . I \mathrm { - } V$ characteristic curve measurement can be automatically conducted by source measure units, and the parameters of $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ , FF, and PCE can be derived according to the target light intensity. As shown

# 12.4 Research Progresses

In order to widely applicate OPV devices in indoor environment, enhancement of the PCE is very important. Considering the intensity of indoor light source is lower and the spectrum is narrower than that of AM 1.5G standard sunlight, the optimization strategies for indoor OPV devices are different to the outdoor countparts. Firstly, the absorption band of the photoactive layer should match the spectrum of the indoor light source within $3 8 0 { - } 7 8 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , and the external quantum efficiency (EQE) should be as high as possible to improve the efficiency of converting incident light into current. Secondly, since lower incident light intensity leads to lower carrier density, the trap assisted charge recombination must be effectively suppressed, which will increase the $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and FF of OPVs. Thirdly, considering the additional voltage loss (about 0.2 V) due to the significantly reduced light intensity, wide-bandgap materials should be selected as far as possible so that a higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ can still be remained under indoor lighting [40]. At present, the research on OPVs for indoor applications mainly focuses on the following aspects. Figure 12.4a-c presents the molecular structures of the donor, fullerene acceptor, and non-fullerene acceptor mentioned in this chapter, and the PV performance of the devices is summarized in Table 12.1.

# 12.4.1 Fullerene-Based OPVs for Indoor Application

The decrease of $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ under indoor lighting is the main limiting factor affecting the device efficiency under indoor lighting conditions. Increasing the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of OPVs and matching the spectrum to improve $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ are the key factors to maximize the performance of devices under indoor conditions. $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ is directly related to the energy level difference between the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOmO) of the donor and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) of the acceptor.

In 2016, Lee et al. compared the device performance with P3HT, poly[N- $. 9 ^ { \prime }$ heptadecanyl-2,7-carbazole-alt-5,5- $( 4 ^ { \prime } , 7 ^ { \prime }$ di-2-thienyl- $^ { 2 ^ { \prime } , 1 ^ { \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime } }$ -benzothiadiazole)] (PCDTBT), and PTB7 as donor and fullerene derivative $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as acceptor under indoor lighting conditions [41]. Among them, $\mathrm { P C D T B T : P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ -based device demonstrates the best performance, $P _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ of $1 3 . 9 \mu \mathrm { W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , PCE of $1 6 . 6 \%$ and $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 7 2 \mathrm { V }$ under the FL illumination $( 3 0 0 \mathrm { { l x } ) }$ . Although the PCE of PTB7: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ -based device is higher than that of PCDTBT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 }$ BM-based device under AM $1 . 5 6$ standard sunlight illumination, the PCE of the device under FL is lower due to the narrow bandgap of PTB7. Notably, the bandgap of PCDTBT is $1 . 9 \mathrm { e V } ,$ which matches well with the emission spectrum of FL [41]. In 2019, You et al. compared the IPV properties of PDTBTBz $2 \mathrm { F _ { a n t i } }$ , P3HT, poly[(2,6-(4,8-bis(5-(2-ethylhexyl)thiophen-2-yl)-benzo[1,2-b:4,5. $\cdot b ^ { \prime }$ |dithiophene))- alt-(5,5- $^ { 1 ^ { \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime } }$ -di-2-thienyl- $5 ^ { \prime } , 7 ^ { \prime }$ -bis(2-ethylhexyl)benzo| $_ { 1 ^ { \prime } , 2 ^ { \prime } - c : 4 ^ { \prime } , 5 ^ { \prime } - c ^ { \prime } }$ |dithiophene4,8-dione)] (PBDB-T), and PTB7, four donor polymers with different interband energies, emphasizing the importance of matching absorption spectrum of photoactive materials with the indoor light source spectrum. Figure 12.5a shows the device structure and thickness of each layer of a typical polymer:fullerene bulk heterojunction (BHJ) cell, and the energy level structures of four different donor polymers PDTBTBz-2Fanti, P3HT, PBDB-T, and PTB7 combined with fullerene acceptor $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ are displayed in Figure 12.5b [42]. Among these polymers, the absorption of PDTBTBz $2 \mathrm { F _ { a n t i } }$ in the $2 \mathrm { e V }$ wide-bandgap matchs well with the irradiation spectra of LEDs (Figure 12.5c). This spectral matching results in a high PCE of $2 3 . 1 \%$ for PDTBTBz- $2 \mathrm { F _ { a n t i } }$ $\mathrm { \cdot P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ based devices under LED $( 1 0 0 0 \mathrm { { l x } ) }$ illumination (Figure 12.5d) [42]. Chen et al. reported a series of small molecular donors with finely regulated energy levels and bandgaps [43]. In the four molecules, the bandgap of 7-(4-(di-p-tolylamino)phenyl)benzo[c][1,2,5]thiadiazole-4-carbonitrile (DTCPB) is $2 . 0 4 \mathrm { e V } ,$ and the PCE is $6 . 5 5 \%$ under AM 1.5G 1 sun irradiation. Under FLs $( 1 2 0 0 \mathrm { { l x } ) }$ , DTCPB based devices can significantly increase the PCE to $1 6 \%$ due to efficiently enhanced harvesting light at visible wavelengths [43]. These results indicate that widegap materials $( E _ { \mathrm { g } } = { \sim } 2 \mathsf { e V } )$ are beneficial to achieve high PCE under indoor conditions.

(b) Energy levels of four different donor polymers PDTBTBz- $\cdot 2 \mathsf { F } _ { \mathsf { a n t i } }$ , P3HT, PBDB-T, and PTB7 combined with fullerene acceptor $\mathsf { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathsf { B M }$ (c) Film absorption spectra of four donor polymers blended with fullerene acceptor $\mathsf { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathsf { B M }$ (d) $J - V$ curves of corresponding devices under $1 0 0 0 \mathsf { l x }$ LED illumination. Source: You et al. [42]/Reproduced with permission of John Wiley $\&$ Sons.

In order to get a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ , the HOMO of the donor must be deep enough. Singh et al. designed benzothiophene with alkyl $\left( \mathrm { W F } _ { 3 } \right)$ , alkyl sulfide $( \mathrm { W F } _ { 3 } \mathrm { S } )$ , and fluorothiophene $( \mathrm { W F } _ { 3 } \mathrm { F } )$ , demonstrating different HOMO levels [44]. The optical bandgaps of all three polymers range from 1.73 to $1 . 7 8 \mathrm { e V } .$ Due to the electronegative substituent of fluorine, the HOMO of $\mathrm { W F } _ { 3 } \mathrm { F }$ is reduced to $- 5 . 6 2 \mathrm { e V . }$ Thus, the PCE of the device under AM 1.5 G 1 sun and LED $( 5 0 0 \mathrm { l x } )$ illumination reaches $9 . 4 4 \%$ and $1 7 . 3 \%$ A with $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of 0.88 and $0 . 6 9 \mathrm { V } ,$ respectively [44]. Yin et al. designed a porphyrin-based A-D-A donor material P1, which has a wide and strong absorption from visible light to near-infrared region, thus achieving a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $_ { 0 . 9 \mathrm { V } }$ under 1 sun lighting condition. $\mathrm { P 1 } { : } \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and PCDTBT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 }$ BM-based devices reach a PCE of $1 9 . 2 \%$ and $1 8 . 7 \%$ under LED lighting condition, with $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of 0.76 and $0 . 7 4 \mathrm { V } ,$ respectively [45].

Using acceptors with high LUMO levels is another way to increase $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ P3HT:indene-C60bisadduct (ICBA)-based device demonstrates higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 9 \mathrm { V }$ than that of $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 1 } B M }$ -based device with $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 6 1 \mathrm { V }$ under AM 1.5G 1 sun illumination, due to the higher LUMO level of ICBA $( - 3 . 7 4 \mathrm { e V } )$ than that of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ $_ { ( - 3 . 9 0 \mathrm { e V } ) }$ [46]. Therefore, under TL5 FL $( 5 0 0 \mathrm { { l x } ) }$ illumination conditions, the PCE of P3HT:ICBA-based device reaches $1 3 . 8 \%$ with a $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 7 3 \mathrm { V } ,$ significantly higher than $\mathrm { P 3 H T : P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { { l } }$ BM-based device with a PCE of $9 . 5 9 \%$ with

$V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 4 3 \mathrm { V } .$ Although the $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of the P3HT:ICBA-based device $( 5 0 \mu \mathrm { A c m } ^ { - 2 } .$ ) is lower than that of the $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 1 } B M }$ device $( 6 2 \mu \mathrm { A c m } ^ { - 2 } ,$ , a higher power output $( P _ { \mathrm { o u t } } )$ of $2 2 . 5 7 \mu \mathrm { W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ is achieved due to the higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ [46]. Arai et al. reported two small molecular donors BDT-2T-ID and BDT-1T-ID, with a deep HOMO of $- 5 . 1 3$ and $- 5 . 2 3 \mathrm { e V } ,$ respectively, and large $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ being $1 . 7 { - } 1 . 8 \mathrm { e V }$ [14]. Compared with PTB7-based devices $\mathrm { ( P C E = 6 . 7 \% ) }$ under standard 1 sun illumination, BDT-2T-ID and BDT-1T-IDB-based devices show inferior PCE of $6 . 1 \%$ and $3 . 9 \%$ respectively. However, their $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ (around 1V) is much higher than PTB7-based device (0.77 V) due to their deeper HOMO levels. Under LED illumination, the PCE of BDT-2T-ID and BDT-1T-ID-based devices significantly increases to $1 6 . 2 \%$ and $1 2 . 9 \%$ , respectively, three times higher than that of PTB7-based devices, because of their deep HOMO level results in a larger $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ under LED illumination [14]. They also synthesized small-molecule light absorbers, 1DTP-ID and 2DTP-ID, and evaluated their OPV performances using a binary BHJ system with fullerene acceptor - $\mathrm { . } \mathrm { ~ } N$ -phenyl-2-phenyl[60]fulleropyrrolidine [PNP]) under LED illumination with different illuminances $( 2 0 0 - 1 0 0 0 0 \mathrm { l x } )$ and color temperatures (2900-7500 K) [47]. The 1DTP-ID-based OPVs, tailored for indoor applications demonstrate notably high power outputs of $1 1 . 3 \mu \mathrm { W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ with PCE of $1 9 . 5 \%$ at $2 0 0 \mathrm { { l x } }$ and $6 4 . 7 \mu \mathrm { W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ with PCE of $2 2 . 4 \%$ at $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { { l x } }$ [47]. Lee et al. reported that BTR $\mathrm { \cdot P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ -based device demonstrated a PCE of $2 8 . 1 \%$ under the FL $( 1 0 0 0 \mathrm { { k } ) }$ illumination and the $P _ { \mathrm { o u t } }$ value reached $7 8 . 2 \mu \mathrm { W } \tau \mathrm { m } ^ { - 2 }$ , which is possible to charge a button-sized battery [48].

# 12.4.2 Non-fullerene-Based OPVs for Indoor Application

Compared to fullerene-based OPVs, non-fullerene-based OPVs have many advantages in further improving the PCE in indoor lighting condition. Fullerene derivatives have poor absorption in visible band, which can lead to loss of photocurrent. The tunability of their electronic structure is also very limited, which is hard to achieve high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the device. In contrast, non-fullerene acceptors can endow molecules with strong light absorption in the visible region through molecular design, and the energy levels can be easily adjusted to maximize $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ , so many research groups have studied their indoor PV properties.

In 2019, Dayneko et al. fabricated PV devices with the donor polymer PPDT2FBT and four different acceptors, $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ 3,9-bis(2-methylene-(3-(1,1-dicyano methylene)- 5-methylindanone)-- 5,5,11,11-tetrakis(4-hexylphenyl)-dithieno[2,3- ${ \bf { d } } { : } 2 ^ { \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime } { \bf { - d } } ^ { \prime } ]$ s-indaceno| $[ 1 , 2 - \mathbf { b } ; 5 , 6 - \mathbf { b } ^ { \prime } ]$ -dithiophene (ITIC-M), 3,9-bis(2-methylene-(3- (1,1-dicyanomethylene)-6,7-difluoro)-indanone))-5,5,11,11-tetrakis(4-hexylphenyl)- dithieno $[ 2 , 3 \mathrm { - } \mathrm { d } ; 2 ^ { \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime } \mathrm { - } \mathrm { d } ^ { \prime } ]$ -s-indaceno[] $\lvert , 2 \cdot \mathrm { b } ; 5 , 6 \cdot \mathrm { b } ^ { \prime } \rvert$ dithiophene (ITIC-F), and $\mathrm { t P D I } _ { 2 } \mathrm { N } .$ EH using a halogen-free ink formulation and spin-cast or slot-die coating methods. Under a standard illumination condition (AM 1.5G, 1 sun), devices with slot-die coated active layers produce PCE values from 6 to $9 \%$ , while the perylene diimide-based acceptor, $\mathrm { t P D I } _ { 2 } \mathrm { N } { \cdot } \mathrm { E H }$ .exhibits $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ above 1V. Under varied indoor LED illumination conditions (2800 and $5 6 0 0 \mathrm { K }$ $1 0 0 0 0 { - } 3 0 0 \mathrm { l x } )$ a Si reference cell and devices using the PPDT2FBT:ITIC-F blend show large PCE drop with a decrease illumination intensity owing to poor spectral overlap.

PPDT2FBT:ITIC-M-based devices show less of a PCE drop owing to the ITIC-M acceptor having stronger absorption in the visible region. Both PPDT2FBT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and PPDT2FBT: $\mathrm { t P D I } _ { 2 } \mathrm { N } .$ -EH-based devices have minor PCE drop with decreasing the light intensity [49]. Ding et al. demonstrated all-polymer IPVs using a blend of polymer donor (CD1) and polymer acceptor (PBN-10) as the active layer. Owing to the medium bandgap $( E _ { \mathrm { g } } = 1 . 9 3 \mathrm { e V } )$ and proper energy level alignment of the two polymers, the all-polymer IPV cell shows a high PCE of $2 7 . 4 \%$ with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 1 6 \mathrm { V }$ under 1000 lx FL illumination (Figure 12.6a) [37]. The large bandgaps of CD1 $( 1 . 9 3 \mathrm { e V } )$ and PBN-10 $( 1 . 9 5 \mathrm { e V } )$ provide absorption matching the emission spectrum of the indoor lighting source (Figure 12.6c). The HOMO and LUMO levels of CD1 and PBN-10 were $- 5 . 8 1$ and $- 3 . 4 2 \mathrm { e V } ,$ respectively. A large energy shift between the LUMO of the acceptor and the HOMO of the donor is expected to increase the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the device (Figure 12.6b) [37].

Cui et al. used the wide-bandgap materials consisting of polymer donor poly[1-(5-(4,8-bis(5-(2-ethylhexyl)-4-fluorothiophen-2-yl)-6-methylbenzo[1,2-b:4,5- ${ \mathfrak { b } } ^ { \prime }$ dithiophen-2-yl) thiophen-2-yl)-5,7-bis(2-ethylhexyl)-3-(5-methylthiophen-2-yl)- 4H,8H-benzo[1,2-c:4,5-c']dithiophene-4,8-dione] (PBDB-TF) and non-fullerene acceptor  3,9-bis(4-(1,1-dicyanomethylene)-3-methylene-2-oxo-cyclopenta[b]thiophen)-5,5,11,11-tetrakis(4-hexylphenyl)-dithieno $[ 2 , 3 \mathrm { - d } ^ { \prime } { : } 2 , 3 \mathrm { - d } ^ { \prime } ]$ -s-indaceno[1,2-b:5, $6 { - } \mathbf { b } ^ { \prime } ]$ -dithiophene (ITCC) to absorb the indoor light. They also drilled the applications of fullerene derivative acceptor $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and the low-bandgap non-fullerene acceptor IT-4F in the indoor applications, which aims to compare with the performance of non-fullerene-based OPV devices. As seen from Figure 12.6d, the PBDB-TF has absorbance range from 300 to $6 8 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , which matches well with the LED radiative spectrum. Figure 12.6e shows the energy levels of donors and receptors containing PBDB-TF, $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ , ITCC, IT-4F. The higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of indoor OPV devices may benefit from the low-lying ionization potential of ITcC, but a low $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and a large $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ loss in the $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ -based OPV device may be caused by the relatively large electron affinity of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ . The PBDB-TF delivers more prominent performance when combined with both fullerene and non-fullerene acceptors. To evaluate the IPV performance based on non-fullerene acceptor under ambient indoor light conditions, they constructed inverted OPV devices with structure of indium tin oxide (ITO)  substrate/poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrenesulfonate) (PEDOT:PSS)/active layer/poly[(9,9-bis) $3 ^ { \prime }$ $( N , N$ dimethyl)- $. N$ ethylammonium)- propyl)-2,7-fluorene)-alt-2,7-(9,9-dioctylfluorene)] (PFN-Br)/Al, where the active layers are PBI $\mathrm { \Delta ) B { - } T F { : } P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ , PBDB-TF:ITCC, PBDB-TF:IT-4F, respectively. As a result, thanks to the higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ , the PBDB-TF:ITCC-based OPV cells showed superior PV performance than the PBDB-TF:IT-4F-based devices at the same illumination conditions, and the PBDB-TF:ITCC-based device shows the maximum PCE of $2 2 . 0 \%$ under indoor light source of $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { { l x } }$ (Figure 12.6f). At the same time, the OPV device based on PBDB-TF:IT-4F also realizes a PCE of over $2 0 \%$ which is also higher than the device based on fullerene acceptor of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ with PCE of $1 8 . 1 \%$ . High performance of non-fullerene acceptor-based devices mainly benefits from the matching absorption spectrum, low $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ loss, and low charge recombination [50].

# 12.4.3 Multiple Blend OPVs for Indoor Application

In the binary OPs, limited absorption mainly limits $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ . In order to overcome this limitation, the ternary device structure has been applied to IPVs. The third component in the active layer can not only increase $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ through complementary light absorption but also improve the FF value by adjusting the mixture morphology of BHJ. Singh et al. employed different non-fullerene acceptors which contain amorphous PDI4 and (4,4,9,9-tetrakis(4-hexylphenyl)-4,9-dihydro-s-indaceno [1,b:5,6-b']dithiophene-2,7-bis(methanylylidene))bis(1,3-diethyl-2-thioxodihydropyrimidine-4,6(1H, 5H)-dione) (IDT), and the 5,5,11,11-tetrakis(4-hexylphenyl)-5,11- dihydro-s-indaceno $[ 1 , 2 \cdot \mathbf { b } ; 5 , 6 \cdot \mathbf { b } ^ { \prime } ]$ |dithiophene-3, 9-bis(methanylylidene))bis (1,3-diethyl-2-thioxodihydropyrimidine-4,6(1H, 5H)-dione) (IDDT) as a crystalline modulators used in ternary-blend indoor OPV devices. Figure 12.7a shows the normalized absorption spectra of the materials used in photoactive layers containing poly [(5,6-difluoro-2,1,3-benzothiadiazol-4,7-diyl)-alt- $^ { \prime 3 , 3 ^ { \prime \prime \prime } }$ -di(2-octyldodecyl) $^ { \cdot 2 , 2 ^ { \prime } }$ $5 ^ { \prime } , 2 ^ { \prime \prime } , 5 ^ { \prime \prime } , 2 ^ { \prime \prime \prime }$ -quaterthiophen- $^ { 5 , 5 ^ { \prime \prime \prime } }$ -diyl)] (OD), $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ , PDI2, PDI4, IDT, and IDDT. Benefitting from the addition of non-fullerene acceptors, the OPV device realizes the efficient charge separation and transport, reduced energetic disorder, and the suppression of non-geminate recombination, which is originating from the formation of flatten film surface and smaller $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking distance. To evaluate the IPV performance based on ternary blend films under ambient indoor light conditions, they constructed inverted OPV devices. As a result, the OPV devices with ternary blend films of $\mathrm { O D } { : } \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } { : } \mathrm { P D I } 2$ $\mathrm { O D } { : } \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } { : } \mathrm { P D I } 4$ $\mathrm { O D } { : } \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } { : } \mathrm { I D T }$ and $\mathrm { O D : P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ IDDT, showed PCEs of $2 0 . 5 \%$ $1 8 . 2 7 \%$ $2 1 . 1 3 \%$ and $1 9 . 0 5 \%$ , respectively, higher than the device with binary-blend absorb layer showing PCE of $1 4 . 1 5 \%$ , testing under indoor light source ( $\scriptstyle \mathbf { 1 0 0 0 } \ln \mathbf { x }$ LED lamp) (Figure 12.7b) [51].

Recently, we used wide-bandgap photoactive materials, including the benzotriazole-based polymer donor (J52-F), chlorinated polymer donor (PM7), and A2-A1-D-A1-A2-structured acceptor (BTA3), to construct ternary OPVs for indoor light applications (Figure 12.7c) [40]. Benefitting from the introduction of PM7 as the third component in J52-F:BTA3-based blend, an enhanced PCE of $2 0 . 0 4 \%$ with a high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $1 . 0 0 \mathrm { V }$ can be obtained under the test conditions with an illumination of $3 0 0 \mathrm { l x }$ from a LED lighting source with a color temperature of $3 0 0 0 \mathrm { K }$ (Figure 12.7d). The excellent device performance is inseparable from the matched spectrum, enhanced light absorption, and the reduced $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ . Meanwhile, the improved charge transport capability and suppressed carrier recombination also play an indelible role [40].

In order to further optimize the absorption of indoor light intensity, the quaternary bulk heterojunction (Q-BHJ) device is also proposed. This structure uses two donors and two acceptors to form the active layer. Nam et al. successfully fabricated Q-BHJ devices with wide absorption range and improved charge transfer performance [52]. Figure 12.7e shows the absorption spectra of PBDB-T, ITIC-Th, PTB7-Th, and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ films. Under AM 1.5G 1 sun illumination, the PCE of the PBDB-T $\mathrm { \langle P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ -based device is $7 . 3 8 \%$ , and the PCE of the PTB7-Th:ITIC-Th-based device is $7 . 5 0 \%$ . However, the PCE of the quaternary PTB7-Th:PBDB-T:ITIC-Th: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ device is significantly improved to $9 . 4 6 \%$ with $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 1 \mathrm { V } , J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 9 . 4 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ , and FF of $6 0 . 3 \%$ . The Q-BHJ device also shows better stability, and the encapsulated Q-BHJ device maintains $8 7 . 7 \%$ of the initial PCE after heating at $6 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 1020 minutes, while the PCE of PTB7-Th:ITIC-Th-based device decreases to $5 4 . 5 \%$ of the initial value. Q-BHJ devices obtained the best PCE of $1 4 . 2 9 \%$ at 1000lx LED illumination (Figure 12.7f), showing great potential to achieve high PCE while improving device stability. In addition, they also demonstrated a semi-transparent device with high transparency and high PCE of $1 5 . 4 6 \%$ under LED lighting conditions $( 1 0 0 0 \mathrm { { k } ) }$ [52].

# 12.4.4 Interface Engineering of OPVs for Indoor Application

The interfaces between the electrodes and the photoactive layer significantly influence the efficiency and stability of OPVs. By choosing suitable interfacial materials, the energetic barrier height at the interface could be reduced to form an ohmic contact with less series resistance, inducing high charge collection efficiency of the corresponding electrodes for holes or electrons [56]. The conventional BHJ OPVs are composed of a photoactive layer sandwiched between an ITO/PEDOT:PSS positive electrode and a $\mathrm { C a } / \mathrm { A l }$ low-work-function negative electrode. However, both the PEDOT:PSS layer and the low-work-function metal electrode are known to degrade the device lifetime, since the low-work-function metal is susceptible to degradation by oxygen and water vapor, and the PEDOT:PSS layer is acidic and corrosive to the ITO electrode. To enhance the device stability, inverted device structure is proposed, where the ITO electrode is modified with low-work-function buffer layer and high-work-function stable interface layer is inserted between the stable metal electrode and photoactive layer [57]. The choice of electrode modification layer is mainly based on the electron energy level and charge transfer characteristics of the material. At the same time, the modified layer can adjust the roughness of the substrate, prevent the top electrode from diffusing to the active layer, and even block the invasion of oxygen and water. As the thickness of different active layers varies, the interface layer also has an important influence on the performance of the device, because it is directly related to $R _ { \mathrm { s } }$ and $R _ { \mathrm { s h } }$ in the device. Therefore, for IPV, the choice of appropriate interface modification layer plays a crucial role in improving the performance of devices.

Kyaw et al. studied the effect of calcium thickness on the performance of $\mathrm { p D T S ( F B T T h } _ { 2 } ) _ { 2 } \mathrm { : P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ devices under different light intensities [58]. The FF is sensitive to the thickness of a calcium layer between the BHJ layer and the Al cathode, and the highest FF is $7 3 \%$ for $2 0 \mathrm { n m \ C a }$ thickness. Analysis of the $J { - } V$ characteristics at various light intensities provides information on the different recombination mechanisms in the BHJ solar cells with different thicknesses of the Ca layer, finding that the $J { - } V$ curves are dominated by first-order recombination from the short-circuit condition to the maximum power point and evolve to bimolecular recombination in the range of voltage from the maximum power point to the open-circuit condition in the optimized device with a Ca thickness of $2 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [58].

Lechene et al. reported optimizing the performance of the PCDTBT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 }$ BM-based IPV device by varying the thickness of the electron transport ethoxylated polyethylene imide (polyethylenimine ethoxylated [PEIE]) layer. Figure $1 2 . 8 \mathsf { a - c }$ shows the $J { - } V$ , FF, and PCE curves of OPVs with three different PEIE thicknesses. PEIE thickness has little effect on device performance under AM 1.5G 1 sun condition, while it has significant effect on device performance under indoor lighting condition. With thick PEIE, the PCE of device is $7 . 6 \%$ under indoor lighting condition with high $R _ { \mathrm { s h } }$ of $5 0 0 \mathrm { K } \Omega$ while the device with thin PEIE gives poor PCE of $0 . 7 \%$ due to significant leakage current [59]. Owing to the reduced current generation at low light intensity, possessing a sufficiently large shunt resistance associated with a low leakage current is of utmost importance for performance maximization. Goo and colleagues also reported optimizing P3HT:ICBA-based device performance by changing PEIE thickness [61]. The PV properties under different lighting condition were optimized by controlling the thickness of the PEIE layers, and the electrical, optical, and surface properties of the PEIE-modified ITO were investigated. Inverted OPVs based on P3HT:ICBA with an $8 . 5 \mathrm { - n m }$ -thick PEIE layer yielded a maximum PCE of $1 3 . 9 \%$ under an LED light with a luminance of $5 0 0 \mathrm { l x }$ Meanwhile, the same device showed poor performance with a PCE of $3 . 1 \%$ under 1 sun illumination owing to the insulating nature of PEIE [61]. Shin et al. conducted an in-depth study on electron-collecting layers comprising PEIE modification, ZnO nanoparticles (NPs), or a combination of the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ NPs and PEIE modification [62]. While poor PV behavior was observed for P3HT:ICBA-based OPVs with the ZnO NPs owing to the relatively high work function of the electron collection layer (ECL) under LED light in the absence of UV light, outstanding indoor performance with PCE of $1 4 . 1 \%$ under 1000-lx LED lamp was achieved by OPVs with PEIE modification as the PEIE contributed to work function reduction of the ECL [62].

Saeed et al. demonstrated the IPV performance of P3HT:ICBA-based flexible OPVs with PEDOT:PSS-based electrodes in comparison with reference OPVs with ITO electrodes [63]. The OPV with PEDOT:PSS (PH 1000) electrode produced an average PCE of $1 1 . 1 \%$ , whereas the reference device with the ITO electrode exhibited a PCE of $8 . 8 \%$ under a 500-lx LED illumination. The flexible OPVs also exhibited superior flexibility over reference OPVs by retaining their PCE up to $8 5 \%$ even after 500 bending cycles in air, whereas the reference OPVs declined to $8 0 \%$ of their PCE under the same bending conditions [63]. Lee et al. reported the indoor performance of flexible OPVs utilizing quasi-amorphous $\mathrm { Z n O / A g / Z n O }$ as the transparent conducting electrode [64]. A $\mathrm { Z n O / A g / Z n O }$ electrode with specific thickness values of $4 0 / 9 / 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ provides excellent transparent conducting electrode properties with transmittances up to $9 2 \%$ in the visible region, a sheet resistance of $4 . 8 \Omega$ per square, and a root-mean squared surface roughness value of $2 . 1 \mathrm { n m }$ . In addition, the micro-cavity effect and quasi-amorphous structural properties of the $\mathrm { Z n O / A g / Z n O }$ electrode allow further enhanced light absorption and mechanical stability, respectively. P3HT:ICBA-based inverted OPVs with the $\mathrm { Z n O / A g / Z n O }$ $( 4 0 / 9 / 5 0 \mathrm { n m } )$ electrode yield an averaged PCE of $1 2 . 3 \%$ under a LED lamp with a luminance of $5 0 0 \mathrm { l x }$ , which is $2 0 \%$ greater than the PCE value of the reference device with ITO electrode [64]. Ma et al. studied the effect of ECLs on OPV performance under the indoor low-light intensity [60]. Perylene-3,4:9,10-bis(dicarboximide) (PDI)-NO and PFN were selected as the electron transport layer (ETLs) and used in the two non-fullerene systems, P3TEA:FTTB-PDI4 and PM6:Y6-O. Under AM 1.5G 1-sun conditions, the device based on PM-6:Y6-O with perylene diimides with amino N-oxide as the terminal substituent (PDI-NO) and PFN exhibits very similar performances. However, under low-light intensity, however, the PFN-based devices suffer from much reduced performance, whereas PDI-NO can still maintain high efficiencies (Figure 12.8d). Devices based on PDI-NO and PM6:Y6-O can achieve high PCEs up to $3 1 \%$ under indoor lighting conditions. Further analysis shows that PDI-NO with a deep HOMO-based devices exhibits significantly lower leakage current and trap-assisted recombination under low-light intensity range (Figure 12.8e) [60].

# 12.4.5 Thick Film OPVs for Indoor Application

Because organic semiconductors have lower carrier mobility and shorter exciton diffusion length than inorganic semiconductors, the thicker active layer of $3 0 0 { - } 1 0 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ often hinders the improvement of device PCE. Therefore, most of the previously reported high PCE results were obtained in active layers of $1 0 0 { - } 2 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ thickness. Although the absorption coefficient of organic semiconductors is much higher than that of inorganic semiconductors, and the active layer about $1 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ thick can absorb most of the incident light for OPVs, it is still challenge to fabricate such thin film with good uniformity by printing technology to ensure high manufacturing yields. Small et al. reported that space charge accumulation is one of the main reasons for the PCE reduction for polydithienogermole-thienopyrrolodione (PDTGTPD): $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ -based devices with thickness ${ > } 2 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [65]. Vincent et al. proposed the OPV optimization design rule based on P3HT:ICBA, which realized the efficient absorption of indoor lighting sources [66]. P3HT:ICBA was chosen as the active layer because of its high overlap with the LED lighting source spectrum. In their experiments, they observed that the thickness of the optimal active layer varies with the light intensity. Under AM $1 . 5 6$ illumination, the device with a $1 3 0 \mathrm { n m }$ thick active layer has a PCE of $4 . 2 \%$ , and under $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { { l x } }$ LED illumination, a device with a $2 3 0 \mathrm { n m }$ thick active layer has a PCE of $5 . 4 \%$ . As the thickness of the active layer increases from 80 to $4 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , the leakage current of the device decreases [66].

Shin and colleagues studied the PV characteristics of PPDT2FBT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ blended devices under indoor lights with varying photoactive layer thickness $\left( 1 2 0 - 8 7 0 \mathrm { n m } \right)$ [67]. The well-matched absorption of photoactive layer and irradiance spectrum of indoor LED light substantially improved the indoor light harvesting (Figure 12.9a). As shown in Figure 12.9b, the PPDT2FBT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ device showed the best PCE of $1 6 \%$ and the maximum power of $4 4 . 8 \mu \mathrm { W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ under $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { { l x } }$ LED light, and the device with an $8 7 0 – \mathrm { n m }$ -thick photoactive layer still exhibited an excellent performance with a $1 2 . 5 \%$ PCE [67]. The indoor devices showed the noticeably enhanced thickness tolerance in the $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and FF values due to much lower series resistance/ parallel resistance $( R _ { \mathrm { s } } / R _ { \mathrm { p } } )$ ratio with a thick photoactive layer under the LED condition. These results indicate that the well-matched absorption with the irradiance spectrum and the large $R _ { \mathrm { p } }$ associated with thick photoactive layer are prerequisite for achieving efficient indoor OPVs with high $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and FF values [67].

Liu et al. systematically studied the effect of $R _ { \mathrm { s } }$ on the PBDB-TF:3,9-bis(2-methy lene-(3-(1,1-dicyanomethylene) 5-methylindanone)-- 5,5,11,11-tetrakis(4-hexylphenyl)-dithieno $[ 2 , 3 \mathrm { - } \mathrm { d } ; 2 ^ { \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime } \mathrm { - } \mathrm { d } ^ { \prime } ]$ -s-indaceno[1,2-b:5,6-b']-dithiophene (IT-M)-based device by introducing external $R _ { \mathrm { s } }$ and tuning active layer thickness from $1 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ to $1 \mu \mathrm { m }$ [53]. Compared with the AM 1.5G condition, the efficiencies were observably improved under low light, regardless of enlarging external $R _ { \mathrm { s } }$ or increasing active layer thickness as shown in Figure 12.9c, indicating that the OPV cells under low light show dramatical restrained recombination processes, impressive exciton dissociation probability, and longer carrier lifetime differing with $\mathrm { A M } \ 1 . 5 \mathrm { G }$ condition. The optical modeling of the energy distribution for OPV cells with varied PBDB-TF:IT-M thicknesses was carried out, and the main signals are within $2 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ near the PEDOT:PSS side for $1 \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick OPV cell (Figure 12.9d), indicating that photons are completely absorbed within $2 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [53].

# 12.4.6 Large-Area OPVs for Indoor Application

Upscaling of OPV cell has been a concern for outdoor applications due to the high $R _ { \mathrm { s } }$ from large-area modules causing lower FF. However, for indoor applications, $R _ { \mathrm { s } }$ is less critical. Instead $R _ { \mathrm { p } }$ is more critical to the device performance. Via optimizing the active layers to have a good match with the indoor light source, $1 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ OPV cells were fabricated and a top PCE of $2 2 \%$ under $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { { l x } }$ LED (2700 K) illumination was demonstrated by Cui et al. [54]. The best device showed very good stability under continuous illumination after 500 hours with over $9 5 \%$ of the original PCE maintained. They also fabricated PBDB-TF:IO-4Cl based OPV devices, and the PCE of the devices with area of $1 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ (spin coating) and $4 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ (squeegee coating) reached $2 6 . 1 \%$ and $2 3 . 9 \%$ , respectively, under 2800 K 1000 lx LED illumination [54]. The device also showed good stability under continuous indoor lighting condition, and maintained its PCE even after 1000 hours.

The series resistance is increased compared with that of the small-area devices due to longer ITO pathway throughout the 8-pixel. Although the active area is much big. ger than the small-area device, the FF does not drop much [41]. Arai et al. fabricated OPV energy-harvesting modules utilizing the BDT-2T-ID:PNP photoactive layer, with a total active area of $9 . 5 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ by connecting in series six subcells each with an area of $\sim 1 . 6 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ , as shown in Figure 12.10b [14]. The OPV modules were prepared using both a rigid glass substrate and a flexible polyethylene naphthalate (PEN) substrate, by adopting the same structure used for the small-area devices. $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of both OPV modules scaled ideally with the number of the series-connected cells, achieving high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $4 . 2 \mathrm { - } 4 . 3 \mathrm { V }$ at $2 0 0 \mathrm { { l x } }$ The average $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ for each subcell can be estimated as $0 . 7 0 { - } 0 . 7 2 \mathrm { V } ,$ indicative of a low degree of current leakage in these indoor OPV modules. The upscaling from $6 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ for the small-area cells to $9 . 5 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ for the practical modules caused only a negligible variation in FF from $6 7 \%$ to $6 6 \% - 6 9 \%$ , resulting in considerably high maximum power outputs of up to $1 1 1 \mu \mathrm { W }$ $( \mathrm { P C E } \approx 1 5 \% )$ at $2 0 0 \mathrm { { l x } }$ [14]. # 12.5 Summary and Prospective

In conclusion, among various potential applications of OPVs, it seems more feasible to use them in mild indoor environments as power generation because of superior PCE and stability over outdoor AM $1 . 5 \mathrm { G } 1$ sun conditions. Commonly used indoor light sources (FLs and LEDs) have narrower emission spectra $( 4 0 0 - 7 0 0 \mathrm { n m } )$ ) with lower intensity $( 2 0 0 { - } 1 0 0 0 \mathrm { l x } )$ as compared to the solar spectrum. Highly tunable bandgaps and energy levels, high absorption coefficients, and small leakage currents under dim light make OPVs promising candidates for indoor applications. The future large demand of sustainable energy source for low-power consumption applications due to the rapid growth of the IoTs will greatly stimulate the growth of IPV technologies. To commercialize the OPVs for indoor application, the key issues of efficiency, stability, and cost should be carefully considered.

For further improving the efficiency of organic IPVs, the molecular structures and the bandgaps of donor and acceptor materials should be finely tuned to be well matched with specific indoor light sources, especially for LEDs, which are more cost-effective and energy-saving than FL sources. Simultaneously, the energy level offsets between the donor and acceptor materials to ensure high $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and minimal energy loss as well as formation of appropriate interpenetrating network with suitable domain sizes in active layer should also be considered during material design. Fullerene-based acceptors are dominant in IPV applications due to their unique features of well-matched absorption and superior transport properties. However, the emergence of non-fullerenes acceptors may blaze a trail for promoting PCE of IPVs. Besides, ternary and multiple compositions are also helpful to finely optimize the morphology of blend film for further improving the performance. Furthermore, from viewpoint of indoor OPV devices, a high $R _ { \mathrm { p } }$ is essential for high performance. Increasing the thickness of the photoactive layer and interface engineering with introducing the charge transport layer are effective strategies to enhance $R _ { \mathrm { p } }$ with suppressed leakage currents [54]. In addition, because the $R _ { \mathrm { s } }$ effect is not significant in indoor OPVs, it is easy to scale up for modules with high efficiency. By careful optimization, an over $4 0 \%$ PCE can be expected for organic IPVs, assuming EQE reaches $9 0 \%$ above the gap in the emission spectrum of the indoor light with energy loss of $0 . 5 0 \mathrm { e V }$ [54].

Stability of the organic IPVs is another critical factor for commercialization, although the stability of organic IPVs should be better theoretically due to lower light intensity and mild working environment absence of UV light [55]. The target market of organic IPV is the replacement of small batteries powering IoT sensors to greatly reduce the maintenance of these wireless nodes. Therefore, more than 10 years lifetime with at least $8 0 \%$ of the initial efficiency is required for organic IPV devices to replace the battery market for the IoTs. Furthermore, the power output of the device should be around $3 0 \mu \mathrm { W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ under radiance of 500lx with PCE above $2 0 \%$ for the targeted applications [17]. Many approaches, such as introducing photo-stable photoactive materials, constructing inverted device structure, using stable interfacial layers and metal electrodes, controlling phase-separated morphology, and involving physical encapsulation, have been proven to be useful for improving the stability of the OPVs [68].

Steady reductions in the production costs of individual cells or modules will speed up the commercialization process of organic IPVs. The overall cost of an OPV module mainly includes materials, capital, and labor, and the overall costs depend primarily on the materials cost, especially on the cost of photoactive materials [69, 70]. Therefore, the synthetic accessibility of photoactive materials should be as low as possible for cost cutting with less synthetic steps and scalable purification processes.

# Interfacial Design for Efficient Organic Solar Cells

Yao Liu1, Menglan Lv2, and Shengjian Liu3

1Beijing University of Chemical Technology, Beijing Advanced Innovation Center for Soft Matter Science and Engineering, State Key Laboratory of Chemical Resource Engineering, Beijing, 100029, P.R. China 2Guizhou Institute of Technology, School of Chemical Engineering, Guiyang, 55o003, P.R. China 3South China Normal University, School of Chemistry, Guangzhou, 510006, P.R. China

# 13.1 Introduction

Organic solar cells (OsCs) open another door for capturing solar energy as a sustainable and clean replacement of fossil fuel. This emerging photovoltaic technology has been the focus of academic and industrial community for decades, due to the great advantages in fabricating lightweight, flexible devices through inexpensive large area solution processing [1-5]. The last two decades have seen dramatic increases of power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) from $1 \%$ to ${ > } 1 8 \%$ in single-junction solar cell devices due to tremendous efforts in device engineering and the synthetic tailoring on the chemical structure of organic semiconductors [6, 7]. Tang first proposed the fabrication of bilayer OsCs composed of vacuum-evaporated p-type and n-type organic semiconductors in 1986 [8]. Later, following the discovery of ultrafast electron transfer from poly[2-methoxy-5-(2-ethylhexyloxy)]-1,4-phenylenevinylene (MEH-PPV) to fullerene $\left( \mathbf { C } _ { 6 0 } \right)$ in 1992, Heeger and coworkers pioneered the study of conjugated polymers as electron donors and fullerenes as electron acceptors in OSCs [9, 10]. Following this, Yu et al. and Halls et al. found that the use of bulk heterojunction (BHJ) in OSCs could improve exciton (tightly bound electron and hole pair) diffusion length in the active layer [11, 12]. Since then, the concept of BHJ OsCs has become a benchmark for efficient device design and optimization, ushering OsCs to rapidly advance the pace of third-generation photovoltaic research.

Generally, the fabrication of BHJ OSCs is realized by sandwiching a bicontinuous interpenetrating network of donor and acceptor between two charge-extracting electrodes [13, 14]. Charge extraction and transport are crucial for the contact between metal electrodes and organic semiconductors [15, 16]. The energy level mismatch at such contact usually impedes charge transport and collection due to additional energy barriers at the device interface [17-19]. For example, non-ohmic interfacial contact suppresses charge transport efficiency between metal electrodes and active layers, leading to additional charge carrier recombination at such interfaces and a resultant inferior device performance [2o]. To overcome this undesirable effect, interface engineering, i.e. development of interlayer materials and their integration into devices, has emerged as an effective strategy to improve the efficiencies of solar cells [21]. Theoretically, during OSCs operation, when excitons dissociate into free holes and electrons, the anode will collect holes while electrons are extracted at the cathode, owing to the existence of built-in electrostatic field $( V _ { \mathrm { b i } } )$ as induced by the asymmetric metal electrodes with different work-function (WF) [22]. In general, larger $V _ { \mathrm { b i } }$ in solar cell devices is beneficial for more efficient extraction of photo-generated charges. The integration of interlayer materials in OSCs tunes the work-functions of metal electrodes, aiming to increase the $V _ { \mathrm { b i } }$ of the devices and suppress charge recombination loss, to the benefit of increasing the open-circuit voltage $( V _ { \mathrm { o c } } )$ , short-circuit current density $( J _ { \mathrm { s c } } )$ , and fill factor (FF) of the solar cells [23, 24].

Solution-processed interlayer materials have recently come into the focus of fundamental research, and practical development efforts, since they allow for synthetic tailoring of their properties, are compatible with such device fabrication approaches as slot-die coating, ink-jet printing, spray-coating, etc., enabling all-organic device architectures [25, 26]. Thus, significant efforts have been devoted to exploring novel solution-processed interfacial materials to realize all-solution-processed multilayer solar cells. Such interlayer materials usually have orthogonal solubility relative to the photoactive layer materials and hold the potential as multifunctional interfacial layers to manipulate the mechanical and electrical contact in solar cell devices [27, 28].

In this chapter, we first introduce the mechanism and effect of interfacial design on device performance. Following this, we will review some representative cathode and anode interlayer materials, such as organic/polymer electrolytes, organic-inorganic hybrids, graphene oxides (GOs), transition metal oxides (TMOs), and self-assembled functional materials and their integration into efficient OsCs. We intend to describe our current understanding based on recent progress and outstanding issues of interlayer materials in OSCs and propose future directions and opportunities.

# 13.2 The Mechanism and Effect of Interfacial Design

# 13.2.1 The Role of Electrode Work-Function Difference

In a typical BHJ OSCs, the donor-acceptor active layer is loaded in-between the high work-function $( \phi _ { \mathrm { A n } } )$ anode and low work-function $( \pmb { \phi } _ { \mathrm { C a t h } } )$ cathode (Figure 13.1a). The anode-cathode work-function difference $( \delta \Phi _ { \mathrm { A C } } )$ dictates the magnitude of built-in electrostatic field $( V _ { \mathrm { b i } } )$ , impacting the open-circuit voltage $( V _ { \mathrm { o c } } )$ , short-circuit current density $( J _ { \mathrm { s c } } )$ , and FF. At zero applied voltage bias, the internal electric field shows the largest magnitude. Under illumination, the drift of photo-generated electrons and holes toward the corresponding electrodes is fast, producing the maximum current density (Figure 13.1b). With the increasing of applied voltage in forward direction, the external electric field partially compensates the internal one, i.e. the net electric field decreases (Figure 13.1c). The charge extraction process gradually changes to a slower diffusion process due to the charge concentration gradient, changing from a large concentration at the donor-acceptor interface to a small concentration at the active layer/electrode interface for selective electrodes. Since it takes longer time for the charges to be removed, recombination may compete with extraction, and as a result, $J _ { \mathrm { s c } } , F F$ , and $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ will decrease. Monomolecular recombination dominates the charge losses in the short-circuit regime, while bimolecular recombination tends to play a critical role when approaching the open-circuit point [29]. The larger values of $\delta \phi _ { \mathrm { A C } }$ afford faster charge extraction at short-circuit regime, which may reduce the recombination losses and increase $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ when extraction and recombination time constants are comparable. When efficient charge extraction takes place, the range of external voltage biases is also extended toward the larger positive voltage biases, leading to higher $F F$ values. Yet, the effect of $\delta \phi _ { \mathrm { A C } }$ on $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ is more intricate. For a relatively small $\delta \phi _ { \mathrm { A C } }$ , one can correlate the magnitudes of $\delta \phi _ { \mathrm { A C } }$ with $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ directly [30]. In another case, suppose the $\delta \phi _ { \mathrm { A C } }$ is significantly larger than the difference between the energy levels of the highest occupied molecular orbital of donor $\mathrm { ( H O M O _ { D } ) } ,$ and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital of acceptor $\mathrm { ( L U M O _ { A } . }$ ), the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the devices can be evaluated by the following empirical relation [31].

![](images/5df709ac2f905b01e52d31c29e2edb998e6d8fd56979d832147fd16ccacdbdde.jpg)  
Figure 13.1  Schematic energy band diagrams: (a) anode, donor, acceptor, and cathode materials separately; OSCs in different regimes of device operation at (b) zero and (c) forward/positive $( + V _ { \mathsf { a p p l i e d } } )$ Voltage biases. Source: Yao Liu.

$$
V _ { o c } = \left| \mathrm { H O M O _ { D } } \right| - \left| \mathrm { L U M O _ { A } } \right| - 0 . 3 \mathrm { e V }
$$

The origin of the factor $0 . 3 \mathrm { e V }$ has been in the focus of many studies since its reduction offers a possibility for improving device performance [32]. This factor has been attributed to the generation of charge transfer (CT) state at the donor-acceptor interface. The difference between the quasi-Fermi levels in donor and acceptor components under a certain illumination level has been suggested to directly determine $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ . Furthermore, the work-function offset between cathode and anode may directly affect the position of the quasi-Fermi level in the device active layer. Thus, the enhancement of $V _ { \mathrm { b i } }$ in solar cell devices through interfacial design is crucial for achieving better device performance, especially for a higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ [33].

# 13.2.2 The Interaction Between Metal Electrode and Interlayers

Energy level alignment at the contact between interlayers and metal electrodes has been the focus of tremendous research. The interfacial electronic structures at such contact are very complicated, and several semiempirical models were developed to describe such interfaces [34-38]. However, none of them can perfectly explain the experimental results of such interfacial contact. Thus, we will generally take some widely investigated materials as examples and highlight some important experimental results. Conjugated polyelectrolytes (CPEs) have been widely investigated as surface modification materials in organic electronics, which show thickness dependent effects on metal work-function modification. Specifically, when coating a thin layer of CPEs on metal surface $\scriptstyle \left( < 1 0 \mathrm { n m } \right)$ , the interaction of charge moieties with metal electrode can generate interfacial dipoles, showing the power of tuning the work-function of metal electrodes (Figure 13.2a,b). However, since CPEs contain ionic side chains and mobile counter ions, one should consider the influence of mobile counter ions and ionic chain reorientation, when coating a relative thick CPE interlayer on metal surface (i.e. an interlayer thickness over the quantum mechanical tunneling limit $[ \sim 1 0 \mathrm { n m } ] ;$ . According to the molecular reorientation model (Figure 13.2c), when applied an external electrical field on the devices, the counter ions of CPEs hold the potential to drift to the corresponding electrodes while the ionic side chains of CPEs prefer reorganize to have more adjacent contact with metal electrodes. As a result, the mobile counter ions with CPEs are crucial for interfacial modification in organic electronics [39]. Additionally, the ionic species in CPEs play a critical role on interfacial dipole generation and orientation, affording various degrees and directions of vacuum energy level shifting. Thus, the polyelectrolyte interlayers generally tune metal work-function through the generation of interfacial dipole at the contact of interlayer/electrode [40]. As another important example demonstrated by Kippelen and coworkers, the modification of numerous metal electrodes can be realized by coating an ultrathin $\left( < 1 0 \mathrm { n m } \right)$ layer of insulating ethoxylated polyethyleneimine (PEIE) or branched polyethyleneimine (PEI) [41]. The effect of this material system on interfacial modification can be mainly attributed to both (i) the orientation of the internal molecular dipole, induced by the lone pair of the nitrogen atom, and (ii) an interfacial dipole, due to partial charge transfer from the amine groups after physical adsorption onto the metal electrode surface. Interestingly, Emrick and coworkers also found that the combination of amine functionalities and electroactive molecules, such as fullerenes, affords the resultant interlayer materials with work-function pinning effect on metal surface, enabling work-function reduction of numerous metal electrodes to the same level. As a result, the amine functionalized interlayer materials have some universal capability to modulate the work-function of metal electrodes. This unique and interesting property most likely attributes to the nitrogen lone pair of the amine groups, which are capable to induce interfacial dipoles through partial charge transfer [42].

![](images/ca7fd0ba46b9ac33ae5627abf5f6fb821d13f66f7b92a3d598ecd24048d34fc5.jpg)

Source: Lee et al. [39]/Reproduced with permission of John Wiley & Sons.

Zwitterions are charge neutral with dipole moments that influence the surroundings. This unique structure affords a good platform to study the impact of dipole orientation on interfacial modification [23] (Figure 13.3a). For example, Lee et al. calculated the permanent dipole moment of sulfobetaine (SB) zwitterions, which shows a value up to 15.2 Debye with the negative charge predominantly onto $- S 0 _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ group and positive charge onto the $- \mathbf { N } ^ { + }$ group [44]. Duzhko and coworkers proposed a classical electrostatic model of dipole-image dipole interaction to explain the impact of zwitterions on metal surface [43]. In this model, suppose an electrostatic dipole $\mathbf { p _ { o } }$ near the metal surface at a distance r. One can describe the surface polarization of such dipole by an image charge model [45](Figure 13.3b). Ideally, the positive and negative sides of the dipole are mirrored across the plane of the metal surface by charges of the same value but opposite sign, inducing an image dipole $\pmb { p _ { i } }$ Taking SB-functionalized polymers as example, the negative charges of the sulfonic group can be considered to locate further away from the polymer backbone when comparing with the positive charges on the nitrogen. As a result, the negative side of the dipole is more likely to reorient when applying electric field, while the positive side of the dipole can be regarded as relatively anchored (Figure 13.3a). In principle, suppose the dipole is anchored at a point of positive charge, the torque $\mathbf { \rho } ( \tau )$ will drive the rotation of the original dipole. There are two possible quasi-stable orientations that are normal to the surface at $\theta = 0$ or $\theta = \pi$ , i.e. the dipole is pointing away from or toward the surface (Figure 13.3c). Yet, the orientation away from the surface has a shorter distance, which is more energetically favorable than the opposite orientation due to the potential interaction energy. Thus, in the interfacial dipole model, the self-induced torque of the dipole moment and energy minimization tend to drive the negative charges of sulfonic groups toward the metal surface. Such a net charge orientation generates an interfacial dipole $\left( \Delta \right)$ at the contact of metal electrode with zwitterions, which impacts the work-function of metal electrodes to the benefit of aligning interfacial energy levels in organic electronic devices [26] (Figure 13.3d).
