# 13.2.3 Doping Effect on Energy Level Alignment

Interfacial doping is an efficient strategy to align the energy levels at the interface between electrodes and organic semiconductors (i.e. the hard-soft materials interface) to improve charge injection and extraction efficiency [46-55]. For example, contact doping at the organic/electrode interface has been developed to improve the electrical contact in solar cell devices as demonstrated by Gomez and coworkers [56]. A sulfonated poly(phenyl sulfone) (SPs) has been found to work as a strong polymeric acid, inducing interfacial doping of polymer donor in BHJ active layer. Such contact doping can efficiently overcome interfacial energy barrier to promote charge collection at the device interface. Although the SPS can perform as efficiently as poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene)-poly(styrene sulfonate) (PEDOT:pss) in solar cell devices, the intrinsically insulating property of SPS

Hakes ns plocessg iess auuacuve wne cunpaieu wiu r EDU1.r33. specnicanly, one has to optimize the degree of sulfonation on SPS and its thickness $( < 3 \mathrm { n m } )$ to achieve optimal device performance. Yet, these results demonstrate the great potential of interfacial doping for making efficient solar cell devices. Kippelen and coworkers reported a solution-based method for electrical p-doping of conjugated organic semiconductors with a limited doping depth on their thin flm surface. They achieved relatively controllable doping depth by simply immersing organic semiconductor thin films into a polyoxometalate solution (phosphomolybdic acid, PMA) in nitromethane [57]. This method can be used to numerous organic semiconductors, which increases their surface electrical conductivity and work-function and improves their photo-oxidative stability in air. This interfacial doping approach is applicable to various organic electronic devices, such as thin film photovoltaics and transistors, improving hole injection or collection at device interface. Ho and coworkers found a general strategy to realize solution-processed doped films over a wide range of work-functions $( 3 . 0 { - } 5 . 8 \mathrm { e V } )$ , by charge doping of CPEs and then internal ion exchange to generate self-compensated heavily doped polymers. This strategy can generate solution-processed ohmic contacts for high-performance organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs), solar cells, photodiodes, and transistors, showing great power for aligning energy levels in organic electronic devices [47]. Self-doping interlayer materials were also designed and synthesized for solar cell applications [58]. Wu et al. developed n-type water/alcohol-soluble conjugated polymers (wscPs) containing naphthalene diimides (NDIs) moieties. These NDI-based polymer interlayers show self-doping property, which are suitable for device fabrication and working as efficient electron transporting layers (ETLs) to generate doped interface between active layers and metal electrodes, affording high-performance solar cell devices with a broad interlayer thickness range (from 5 to $1 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [59]. Hu et al. designed and synthesized perylene diimides (PDIs)-based polyelectrolytes as interlayers in OSCs. These polymer interlayers show self-doping property, which is due to the doping effect of counter ions on PDI units. Thus, the superior electrical property of these interlayers affords the device interface with excellent electron-transporting properties in a wide interlayer thickness range. Interestingly, the counter ions play a critical role on the doping behavior, optoelectronic, and morphological properties of the resulting polyelectrolytes [60]. Emrick group covalently integrated planar electronically active PDI-based units into polyelectrolyte dopants. Impressively, the doping level of the target polymer can be tuned by varying the PDI-to-cation ratio, allowing chemical synthesis to optimize the doping efficiency of the resultant polymers. Thus, these PDI-based ionene polymer interlayers enable organic electronic devices with controllable interfacial doping and energy level alignment at the active layer/electrode interface through readily achieved solution processing method [46, 58]. A further study showed that some self-doping organic semiconductors (e.g. fullerene derivatives, CPEs) have the potential to improve the stability of lead halide perovskite solar cells [61-63]. Wang et al. reported that self-doped PDI derivatives show some kind of electron transfer process in solution. These self-doped PDI derivatives with stable n-type doping capability and facile solution processability can be used as electron transport layers in OsCs, affording high performance devices and showing great potential in organic electronics [64]. Sun et al. observed that the interface between the n-type interlayer and the donor polymers produces an extra contact surface for exciton dissociation. This interfacial contact also aligned energy levels between the n-type interlayer and the acceptor in the BHJ active layers, affording efficient electron extraction from the BHJ, which further improves the efficiencies of the solar cells [65].

# 13.2.4 Interface on BHJ Morphology and Device Stability

The morphology of BHJ active layer plays an important role on device performance [66, 67]. Several groups have demonstrated that the surface energy of the interfacial materials significantly impacts the morphology evolution and vertical phase separation of the BHJ active layers [68, 69]. As a result, the appropriate selection of interfacial materials holds the promise to improve their compatibility with the BHJ active layers and optimize the atop-BHJ active layer morphology, which is beneficial for the resultant charge dissociation and transport in solar cell devices. Fang and coworkers developed two hydrophilic small molecules and used them as cathode interlayers in inverted OSCs. They compared the effect of the conjugated units of underlying interlayer materials on the evolution of BHJ morphology. The more hydrophobic surface of the interlayer leads to the generation of better morphology upon the organic photoactive layer deposition, which is beneficial for the enhancement of $V _ { \mathrm { o c } } , J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ , and $F F$ of inverted OsCs. Thus, the rational optimization of cathode interlayer could improve the bulk film morphology of the active layer to the benefit of achieving high-performance devices [7o]. Wang and coworkers synthesized a novel polymer as underlying interlayer on PEDOT:PSS to optimize the morphology of the BHJ active layer in polymer solar cells. This novel polymer contains polar phosphonate moieties in the side chains, affording the PEDOT:PSS with more compatible surface energy with the active layer, which drives the donor polymer in the active layer to accumulate at the anode side and improve its crystallization. These interesting interfacial self-assembly results are beneficial for charge separation and transport, contributing to $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and PCE improvement of the solar cell devices [71]. To simply device fabrication, one blended poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) derivatives into the active layer solutions to prepare in situ self-assembled PEG-based interlayers during the formation of BHJ active layer. It is due to the spontaneous migration of PEG-based derivatives to the surface of the active layers [72-76]. Additional functions of interlayer materials are their promise to improve device stability and durability. For example, some interlayers have the ability to work as additional protecting layers for the photoactive layers to prevent the penetration of oxygen and water. In addition, some interlayers hold the power to enhance the adhesion between the photoactive layers and the electrodes, affording a better device performance for flexible OSCs [77-79]. Thus, interface engineering is an efficient strategy to optimize the efficiency and stability of the solar cell devices.

# 13.2.5 Interfacial Morphology Characterizations

The morphology of solution processed interlayers is also an interesting topic in OSC research [8o]. Numerous studies have reported that the surface feature of the interlayer is an important factor that impacts solar cell performance, especially when polyelectrolytes were used for surface modifications [14, 24, 43, 44, 81, 82]. Several experimental techniques, such as scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and atomic force microscopy (AFM), are the most common characterizations to provide surface morphology and roughness information at high resolution. In near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure (NEXAFS) measurements, polarized soft X-ray is used to investigate the orientation of covalent bond. NEXAFS has emerged as an important technique to reveal the chain orientation of organic molecules used for interfacial modification [14]. It is a technique for specific elements because the K-shell absorption edges of different elements have different energies. Specifically, the NEXAFS information can be revealed in Auger electron yield mode $\left( \sim 1 \mathrm { n m } \right)$ or total electron yield $( \sim 1 0 \mathrm { n m } )$ , which provides structure information of different sample thicknesses. This technique is currently the most powerful measurement to show the molecular orientation at different sample depths near the surface. For example, the NEXAFS characterization was used to probe the aromatic backbone orientation of conjugated polymer zwitterions. In the NEXAFS spectra, the peak at $2 8 5 . 5 \mathrm { e V }$ is characteristic of the thiophene carbon-carbon (double bond) $\pi ^ { * }$ absorption. By varying the incidence angle of X-ray and combining with the change of signal intensity, the orientation of conjugated backbone can be analyzed [43].

Another example is the characterization of interfacial dipole. Generally, molecular structure and its arrangement at the interface dictate the interfacial electric dipole moment. The characterization of the interfacial dipole is important for understanding and exploring its influence on device interface engineering [80]. Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPs) is a highly surface-sensitive characterization because of the shallow probe depth of ultraviolet (UV) light. In UPS measurement, when coating a thin film of dipole layer on metal surface, one can extract the dipole moment from the shift of the secondary electron cutoff $( E _ { \mathrm { S E C } } )$ in the high binding (low kinetic) energy region [83]. The dipole orientation plays a critical role on interfacial modification. For example, perpendicular alignment of sulfobetaine side chains to Au and indium tin oxide (ITO) surfaces was probed by the carbon K-edge NEXAFS measurements (Figure 13.4a,b). Note that the partial electron yield mode of NEXAFS that was used provides a surface-weighted signal, which is dominated by the outermost $( 2 \mathrm { - } 4 \mathrm { n m } )$ portion of the film. Hence, the degree of alignment was averaged in a $4 \mathrm { n m }$ -thick film, and a top layer away from the underlying metal substrate was measured. Consistent with the UPS measurements that show no effect beyond the $3 { - } 4 \mathrm { n m }$ , the degree of alignment was found to be significantly better in thinner film. The orientation of molecular dipole moments (toward or away from the metal surface) was also revealed by vibrationally resonant sum frequency generation spectroscopy (VR-SFG) (Figure 13.4c). It has been shown that ${ \mathrm { S O } } _ { 3 } { } ^ { - }$ groups point toward the Au surface, i.e. the dipoles point away. Partial alignment of side chains that was concluded from both the NEXAFS and VR-SFG is consistent with the fact that both techniques probe the average orientation in the films. Similarly, for ITO surface, VR-SFG indicates that molecular dipole moments of fullerene derivatives are pointing away from the ITO surface, creating a net dipole moment that reduces the ITO work-function [44, 81].

# 13.3 Anode Interlayer Materials

# 13.3.1PEDOT:PSS

PEDOT:PSS is the most widely used polymer hole transport layer (HTL) in both OSCs and OLEDs due to its unique solution processing property. Generally, PEDOT:PSS is made up of PEDOT and PSS, in which PEDOT acts as conductive polymer and PSS acts as a dispersing agent. PSS is attached to PEDOT by an oxidative polymerization of ethylenedioxythiophene (EDOT). In OSCs, the water solubility of PEDOT: PSS provides many advantages when it is employed as an HTL, such as: (i) sequential solution process of HTL and active layer could be realized due to the different solubility; (ii) water as a solvent for processing PEDOT:PSS is very environmentally friendly and beneficial for future applications; (ii) the conductivity of PEDOT:PSS could be easily adjusted by varying the ratio of PEDOT to PSS, which could satisfy various application conditions; (iv) the PEDOT:PSS possess high transparency via the near-infrared to visible light range, which could minimize the absorption loss in OSCs; (v) PEDOT:PSS has a work-function of $5 . 1 \mathrm { e V }$ [20], which could not only match with HOMO levels of most donor materials, but also can form ohmic contact with ITO [84, 85].

Despite the extraordinary advantages as we mentioned above, some shortcomings of PEDOT:PSS still deserve attentions for further application in broader areas. Here are some issues that need to be addressed: (i) the acidity of PEDOT:PSS due to the styrene sulfonic acid constituents could corrode anodes such as ITO, which will lead to decreasing longtime stability of OSCs [86-88]; (ii) moisture and oxygen in the air could easily contaminate and diffuse into PEDOT:PSS since PEDOT:PSS is a water-soluble material, which could aggravate the degradation of OSCs [89, 90]; (ii) the relatively low conductivity still limits the application of PEDOT:PSS in large-scale fabrication process; (iv) the work-function of PEDOT:PSS should be deeper since more and more high-performance donor materials have been developed. Therefore, many ingenious works focused on the above issues have been conducted and achieved great progress.

As a polymer material, PEDOT:PSS (Scheme 13.1) is noted for its high conductivity. In OSCs, a highly conductive HTL guarantees minimum inner resistance and suppressed voltage drop in the interlayer, and an optimal internal field of the photoactive layer, therefore, results in enhanced exciton dissociation and charge extraction. However, the optimum thickness of PEDOT:PSS processed via spin coating in laboratory is about ${ \sim } 4 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , and device performance fluctuations could happen when PEDOT:PSS thickness changes [91]. Also it is difficult to realize precise control of PEDOT:PSS thickness when using industrial fabrication process such as roll-to-roll (R2R) printing, blade coating, inkjet printing, and so on. To ensure a better applicability of PEDOT:PSS in large-scale OSCs, improving the conductivity is the most straightforward way.

![](images/0f7c4c085a1cf69cebccc0d0fd303e6024eb2e48042897e49f179ad4b5cafef6.jpg)  
Scheme 13.1Chemical structure of PEDOT: PSS.

Generally, the film morphology, chemical and physical characteristics, which could be modified through a variety of posttreatments, determine the electrical properties of PEDOT:PSs. For example, it has been demonstrated that thermal treatment [92], which now is common knowledge in research community, is an effective way to enhance the conductivity of PEDOT:PSS. Besides, in some reports, effects of light treatment on PEDOT:PSS also have been investigated and found that the number of charge trapping defects could be reduced by UV or UV-ozone [93]. There are several other methods that are reported to enhance the conductivity of PEDOT:Pss, such as the addition of organic compounds such as ethylene glycol (EG), dimethyl sulfate, or ionic liquid into PEDOT:PSS solution and the surface treatment of PEDOr:PSs films with polar organic solution of salt, inorganic acid, or cosolvent. In 2002, Joo and coworkers [94] found that using dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), N,N-dimethyl formamide (DMF), and tetrahydrofuran (THF) separately as solvent additives could increase the PEDOT:PSS film conductivity. It is found that about two-order enhancement of conductivity was obtained when DMsO was added. From then on, adding polar organic solvents into PEDOT:PSS solution for improving the conductivity has gained great attention, and conductivity ranging from 0.61 to $6 7 7 \mathrm { S c m ^ { - 1 } }$ could be realized by employing various kinds of polar organic solvents as additives [95]. Ouyang et al. achieved more than two orders of magnitude enhancement of conductivity through adding solvents such as ethylene glycol (EG), meso-erythritol and 2-nitroethanol into the PEDOT:PSS aqueous solution [96].

Solvent mixture and surface posttreatment with polar solvent are the most common ways to enhance the conductivity of PEDOT:PSS. For example, in 2011, Kim et al. observed a high conductivity of $1 4 1 8 \mathrm { S c m ^ { - 1 } }$ for PEDOT:PSS films by using solvent additive and solvent posttreatment. The posttreatment induced PEDOT:PSS showed lower PSS to PEDOT ratio, which contributes to the higher conductivity. Furthermore, ITO-free OSCs were realized using modified PEDOT:PSS as transparent electrode [97]. Other posttreatments with fluoro compound such as hexafluoroacetone (HFA) [98] were also reported to enhance the conductivity of PEDOT:PSS by simply dropping HFA aqueous solution onto PEDOT:PSS films; as a result, a conductivity of $1 3 2 5 \mathrm { S c m ^ { - 1 } }$ was obtained. Eom et al. found that when mixing glycerol with PEDOT:PSS solution, glycerol could promote the aggregation of PEDOT phase, and an increase of conductivity from 0.782 to $1 5 2 \mathrm { S c m } ^ { - 1 }$ could be obtained [99]. When the other common solvent 2-propanol was used, the resultant PEDOT:PSS films could also get an enhanced conductivity [100].

Adding materials with high conductivity into PEDOT:PSS has also been proved to be effective to increase the conductivity of PEDOT:PSS. As an example, multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MwCNTs) are exploited as additives, and researchers found that a net-like structured conductive channels could be formed via self-assembly of MWCNTs. Wang et al. processed PEDOT:PSS/MWCNTs films by the polymerization of EDOT with MwcNTs and PSS solution [101]. The resultant

PEDOT:PSS/MwCNTs films exhibited special structure characteristics in which MWCNTs act as the core wrapped with PEDOT:PSS. The conductivity could be dramatically enhanced by the $\pi { - } \pi$ conjugation conducted by the chains of MWCNTs and PEDOT:PSS. Yet, the material preparation of PEDOT:PSS/MWCNTs is more suitable for supercapacitors or thermoelectric electronic other than OSCs. Fortunately, with the development of two-dimensional (2D) materials such as $\mathrm { W S } _ { 2 }$ or $\mathbf { M o S } _ { 2 }$ , exfoliation and functionalization of 2D nanosheets or nanoflakes are exploited and investigated in PEDOT:PSS-based composite materials for hole transporting in OSCs. In 2017, Huang and coworkers [102] proposed a facial and scalable protocol method for efficient exfoliation of bulk transition metal dichalcogenides (TMD) and graphite assisted with PEDOT:PSS solution, for preparing single- and few-layer nanosheets. It is worth noting that single crystalline characteristic of bulk materials could be retained by these TMD nanosheets, which is essential for application in OSCs. Consequently, the conductivity of PEDOT:PSS/ $\mathrm { W S } _ { 2 }$ up to $1 . 4 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } \mathrm { S c m ^ { - 1 } }$ was obtained, which is higher than that of pristine PEDOT:PSS. Furthermore, solar cell devices based on PEDOT:PSS/ $\mathrm { w s } _ { \scriptscriptstyle 2 }$ showed more superior $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and PCE than those with bare PEDOT:PSS. Also, the PEDOT:PSS/ $\mathrm { w s } _ { 2 }$ HTL fabrication is simply realized by processing hybrid PEDOT:PSS/ $\mathrm { w s } _ { 2 }$ ink prepared by a simple centrifugation.

The corrosivity and hygroscopicity of PEDOT:PSS could accelerate device degradation. Therefore, it is of great importance to reduce or eliminate the negative impact of the corrosivity and hygroscopicity of PEDOT:PSS. Zhang and coworkers [103] demonstrated a protocol for fabrication of $\mathrm { P E D O T : P S S / M o O } _ { 3 }$ composite films by in situ formation of $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ in aqueous PEDOT:PSS solutions. Through the combination of high conductivity of PEDOT:PSS and the ambient stability of $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ high-performance HTL based on $\mathrm { P E D O T : P S S / M o O } _ { 3 }$ with smooth surface and considerably reduced hygroscopicity was obtained. Due to the low hygroscopicity of PEDOT:PSS/ $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ films, the longtime stability of the solar cell devices is greatly improved. In 2018, Zhou and coworkers [104] reported a facile and effective method for developing high-performance PEDOT:PSS/ $\mathrm { w o } _ { x }$ composite HTLs by simply mixing $\mathrm { W O } _ { x }$ nanoparticles with PEDOT:PSS solution. The authors provided sufficient evidence to prove that besides effective charge extraction properties, finely tuned active layer morphology could also be obtained by the surface free energy difference between PEDOT:PSS and $\mathrm { W O } _ { x }$ . The high FF of the optimal devices with PEDOT:PSS/ $\mathrm { w o } _ { x }$ as HTL is mainly attributed to the superior carrier extraction along with longer carrier lifetime. Choi and coworkers [105] incorporated photo-cross-linking agent into PEDOT:PSS by a fast photo-polymerization process. As a result, hydrophobic PEDOT:PSS film, a water-resistant HTL, was obtained. The resultant PEDOT:PSs films were employed in both perovskite and polymer solar cells. The PCEs and stability of the devices are simultaneously improved. Since the hydrophilic characteristics of PEDOT:PSS were suppressed and the modified one showed water-resistant property, the penetration of water into PEDOT:PSS was reduced. As a result, devices with hydrophobic PEDOT:PSS retained $6 0 \%$ of original PCEs after 570hours of storage. Besides, the MeOH treatment could remove the Pss content and improve the surface conductivity as many early literatures have reported. Chen's group [106] introduced an evaporated $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ layer to form a $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /PEDOT:PSS bilayer for protecting the ITO anode. The ultrathin $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ interlayer combined with PEDOT:PSS also plays an important role in enhancing the light intensity and charge generation in the photoactive layer. Greatly improved device stability was realized due to the reduced moisture and oxygen adsorption of the modified PEDOT:PSS.

Although various methods were used to reduce the negative impacts of the acid characteristics of PEDOT:PSS, new HTL materials are still in demand since the corrosion of ITO in OSCs is inevitable with the existence of PSS. Thus, the redundant sulfonic acid group of PEDOT:PSS is an alternative method. With the basic cognition that the high acidity of PEDOT:PSS is from the anionic dispersant PSS, in 2016, Li and Zeng [107] successfully developed a water-soluble sulfobutylated phenol formaldehyde resin (BsPF) with flexible alkyl sulfonic acid groups. Water-soluble PEDOT:BSPF was obtained by using BSPF as dopant. Notably, when using PEDOT:BSPF as HTL to modify ITO in OSCs, the device performance was improved significantly. The authors demonstrated that BSPF may be of promising potential as dopant of polymer semiconductors, especially for PEDOT-based organic electronics. In 2019, another dopant was developed and applied to dope PEDOT to obtain new conductive polymer by Li's group [108]. In this work, the authors continued their study on investigating the charge extraction property of PEDOT:PSS via the regulation of structure homogeneity. To enhance the structural homogeneity of PEDOT derivatives, the authors applied a doping process to PEDOT with a conductive dispersant poly(diphenylamine-4-sulfonic acid) (PDAS), a new HTL material PEDOT:PDAS was obtained. It is worth noting that in comparison to PEDOT:PSS, PEDOT:PDAS exhibits a much higher work-function $\left( 5 . 3 8 \mathrm { e V } \right)$ and a lower acidity $\mathrm { ( p H } \sim 7 )$ along with outstanding film formation and structural homogeneity. Moreover, the conductivity of PEDOT:PDAS was much higher than that of PEDOT:PSS-4083 although with a low PEDOT ratio in PEDOT:PDAS. For solar cell applications, PEDOT:PDAS exhibited comparable charge extraction ability with the PEDOT:PSS control films, resulting in comparable device performance. More interestingly, the synthesis method of the dispersant PDAS is very simple, and the raw materials are cheap and readily available, making PEDOT:PDAS a very promising HTL material.

Huang's group [109] focused on reducing the acid group of PEDOT:PSS by performing a facile doping of PEDOT:PSS with dopamine hydrochloride (DA-HCl) (Figure 13.5). PEDOT:PSS-DA was obtained after the reaction between DA-HCl and the sulfonic acid of PSS. Compared with PEDOT:PSS, the PEDOT:PSS-DA possesses higher work-function and superior conductivity. Consequently, when using PEDOT:PSS-DA as HTL, OSCs based on different photoactive layers observed an enhanced PCEs, indicating that doping strategy for PEDOT:PSS with amino derivatives is of great potential to develop novel HTLs. Very recently, the same group [110] proposed a secondary doping protocol by employing novel oxoammonium salts $\mathrm { ( T E M P O ^ { + } X ^ { - } }$ , 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxoammonium, $\mathbf { X } = \left( \mathbf { B } \mathbf { r } ^ { - } \right.$ $\mathrm { B F 4 ^ { - } }$ OTf-, $\mathrm { T F S I ^ { - } }$ ) as efficient, facile p-type dopants. Increased carrier density along with enhanced conductivity was achieved when $\mathrm { T E M P O ^ { + } X ^ { - } }$ salts were introduced into PEDOT:PSS. Moreover, the surface energy and work-function of the resultant HTL were finely tuned with the evolution of the counter ions of $\mathrm { T E M P O ^ { + } X ^ { - } }$ , resulting in better energy level alignment and improved charge collection. The authors also demonstrated the universality of this doping strategy via applying this method to other conjugated polymers. The improved conductivity and tunable work-function could be similarly realized.

![](images/ef2ffe490490e2922284e522da3a99581d81dbad0ca72d35c15708499a4245ba.jpg)  
Figure 13.5The schematic self-assembly process of PEDOT:PSS-DA film after the doping of dopamine hydrochloride in PEDOT:PSS. Source: Zeng et al. [109]/Reproduced with permission of John Wiley & Sons.

# 13.3.2 Conjugated Polyelectrolytes

CPEs (Scheme 13.2) as another substitute for PEDOT:PSS have attracted widespread attention. Ke et al. prepared a new solution-processable self-doped sulfonic acid ring-substituted polyaniline (SPAN) as the HTL material in inverted OSCs. SPAN shows higher conductivity and better film quality when compared with PEDOT:PSS [111]. Lacher et al. developed a novel polymer HTL material (EDOT-SuNa) based on conductive EDOT with the property of tunable work-function and hydrophobicity. Therefore, the devices with the EDOT-based polymer HTL exhibited a higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ when compared with the devices containing regular PEDOT:PSS [112]. Li et al. synthesized carboxyl-functionalized polythiophene (P3CPenT), which was used as HTL in OSCs. P3CPenT exhibited several ideal properties as an HTL, including suitable solubility in some polar solvents and better energy level alignment with the active layer [113]. Bazan and coworkers reported a series of pH neutral CPEs(CPE-K, CPE-Na, and CPE-TBA) as HTL materials in OSCs, and the CPE-K showed excellent film formation and solution processing property. The low contact resistance and improved FF of OsCs attribute to the self-doping effect between the side chains of CPE-K and conjugated backbone. Self-doping effect eliminates the inhomogeneity of the charge transport, and the device containing CPE-K exhibited an excellent performance [114-116]. Meanwhile, Cui et al. reported another pH-neutral CPE with wide bandgap (PCP-Na), which exhibited an electrical conductivity of $1 . 6 6 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } \mathrm { S c m ^ { - 1 } }$ The PCP-Na modified ITO exhibited a work-function of $5 . 2 2 \mathrm { e V } ,$ which is beneficial for hole collection in OSCs [117]. Cai et al. demonstrated the efficient hole transport ability of PEDOT-S as HTL in OSCs. Therefore, PEDOT-S showed high conductivity and optical transparency in OSCs. With a UV-Ozone treatment, the work-function of PEDOT-S can increase from 4.9 to $5 . 2 \mathrm { e V } ,$ which enables its efficient hole extraction ability for devices. The experimental results show that PEDOT-S as HTL can operate well in a wide range of thicknesses, which is beneficial for the printing production [118]. Jo et al. prepared a series of self-doped CPEs (PhNa-1T, PhNa-2T, and PhNa-3T). Those self-doped polymers show high conductivity and excellent hole transport property in the vertical direction of their films. Meanwhile, PhNa-1T has a low roughness surface, which shows a good contact with the active layer [119].

Scheme 13.2 The chemical structure of some typical CPEs.

# 13.3.3 Cross-Linkable Polymers

Cross-linkable polymers represent another class of promising HTL materials (Scheme 13.3), which can be thermally or photochemically cross-linked to form HTLs. The cross-linked HTL materials are sufficiently solvent resistance, which is benefit for the fabrication of multilayer OsCs through solution processing technology. Hains and coworker reported a cross-linkable polymer material (TPDSi2:TFB) as HTL. TPDSi2:TFB showed strong electron-blocking ability, good hole-transporting characteristics, and high transmittance. The solar cell devices with TPDSi2:TFB HTL exhibited high PCE and superior thermal stability compared with the devices using regular PEDOT:PSS as HTL [120]. Subsequently, the same group investigated the design, synthesis, characterization of a novel cross-linkable HTL material, PABTSi2:TFB. This cross-linkable material exhibited a higher HOMO level than TPDSi2:TFB [121]. Sun et al. also reported a solution-processed cross-linkable HTL material, TPD-BVB. The solar cell devices using TPD-BVB as HTL showed comparable efficiency and superior long-term air stability when compared with the devices fabricated with PEDOT:PSS [122]. Xu et al. reported a cross-linked D-A copolymer (PBDTTT-Br25) as an additional hole collection layer, which was inserted between a PEDOT:PSS layer and the photoactive layer. Inserting the PBDTTT-Br25 layer can provide an additional donor/acceptor interface, which facilitates hole transport, thereby reducing the possibility of charge carrier recombination [123]. Tsai et al. developed a styryl-functionalized triaryl-amine-based material (DVTPD), which can be thermally cross-linked at $1 8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 30 minutes to form a solvent-resistant thin film. The film exhibited good coverage onto the substrate in the fabrication of multilayer OsCs. Meanwhile, the hole mobility of DVTPD can be significantly enhanced by incorporating an ionic dopant (DPITPFB) [124]. Sun et al. reported a hole transport and electron-blocking material containing triphenylamine, polyperfluorocyclobutane (TPA-PFCB), which was inserted between a PEDOT:PSS layer and the ITO anode. The solar cell devices containing TPA-PFCB showed a higher PCE compared with the control devices made from regular PEDOT:PSS [125]. Sun et al. studied the optical, electrical, and electrochemical properties of a new class of thermally cross-linkable hole transport materials. The conductivity and optical transparency of these HTL materials were improved by P-doping. The bilayer hybrid HTL structure with one neutral layer on the bottom of the doped layer has been used to provide both efficient hole-transporting and electron-blocking properties in the devices [126].

![](images/e0fafe0ec3ef0c042b6e3a0dc22271d457e4640a2f0f1e6bfa24cdbe44bf69b0.jpg)  
Scheme 13.3 The chemical structure of cross-linkable hole transporting materials.

# 13.3.4Graphene Oxides (GOs)

GO as another promising type of HTL material for OSCs can be simply processed in solution and has excellent light transparency. Also, its work-function is comparable to PEDOT:PSS. Li et al. reported that the PCEs of solar cell devices containing $2 \mathrm { n m }$ GO HTLs are comparable to those with PEDOT:PSS as HTLs [127]. Kim et al. investigated the influence of the concentrations of GO dispersion on device performance. When using $0 . 1 5 \mathrm { w t } \%$ GO dispersion, they can get nearly complete coverage of GO on the substrates. Meanwhile, incorporating a more conductive material, single-walled carbon nanotubes (SwCNTs) in GO could improve the vertical conductivity of the HTL [128]. Smith and colleagues presented large-area solar cell devices using GO as the HTLs [129]. However, GO is insulating, which will increase the internal resistance of the devices with the increase of the GO film thickness, leading to a rapid PCE decline, which is unfavorable for the printing production. In GO, because most of carbon atoms are $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 3 }$ hybridized, which were bonded with oxygen, it destroys the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 }$ conjugation. Hence, the substantial oxygen groups in GO make it an insulating material. The chemical reaction can partially reduce the GO, which will decrease the number of the oxygen groups bonded with carbon atoms and increase the $\mathsf { s p } ^ { 2 }$ hybrid of GO. Therefore, this strategy has been an effective method to improve the conductivity of GO martial. Yang et al. demonstrated that GO treated with $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ plasma showing a high work-function of $5 . 2 \mathrm { e V }$ and the solar cell device performance was improved [130]. Li et al. reported that GO with precise oxidation (pr-GO) showed adjustable work-function, large interfacial dipole, and excellent film-forming properties. Meanwhile, the pr-GO exhibited excellent hole extraction capability, which can enhance device efficiency [131]. Kim et al. found a simple method to reduce GO and introduced fluorine group in GO. The functionalization of graphene oxide (FrGO) was performed by one-step reduction. The FrGO showed ideal properties as HTL in OSCs, such as high work-function and good conductivity $( 3 . 5 \mathrm { S } \mathrm { m } ^ { - 1 } ) ,$ [132]. Ding et al. demonstrated that a few-layered graphene quantum dots (F-GQDs) can be used as HTL for OSCs. The 4 nm F-GQDs with a high content of periphery COOH groups have a high work-function $( 5 . 2 6 \mathrm { e V } )$ and excellent film-forming property. The solar cells using F-GQD as the HTLs exhibited a higher PCE than its counterparts based on the GO or PEDOT:PSS HTL. These results showed the great potential of F-GQD as HTL for OSCs [133]. Liu et al. designed and prepared sulfated GO- $\mathrm { \mathrm { O S O } } _ { 3 } \mathrm { H }$ Owing to the high work-function, ${ \mathrm { G O - O S O } } _ { 3 } { \mathrm { H } }$ exhibited an excellent performance as a HTL in solar cell devices [134]. Zhao et al. prepared a 2D $\pi$ -conjugated material $\mathrm { G } { \cdot } \mathrm { S O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { H }$ by introducing sulfonic acid to graphene scaffold $\left( \mathrm { G } { \cdot } \mathrm { S } \mathrm { O } _ { 3 } \mathrm { H } \right)$ and obtained a work-function of $4 . 8 \mathrm { e V } ,$ which matches well with the HOMO of the donor polymer in active layer [135]. Stratakis et al. showed a photochemical method for partial reduction and doping of GO films. They can tailor the work-function of the GO-Cl from 4.9 to $5 . 2 3 \mathrm { e V }$ by controlling the reaction time to match the HOMO of polymer donors [136]. Xia et al. reported a method to partially reduce GO by direct UV-ozone treatment. Since the ozone molecules can oxidize GO into $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ and generate highly conductive graphene particles, the UV-ozone treatment can improve the conductivity of GO HTLs. The $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ , FF, and PCE of the solar cells were significantly improved by using the modified GO HTLs. However, chemical reduction method is inadequate for mass production because of the toxicity of reductant. The other method to produce GO is thermal method, which is a green method without using reductant [137] By thermal annealing treatment of GO, Jeon et al. prepared a re-GO with a conductivity of $1 . 8 \mathrm { S c m ^ { - 1 } }$ , which worked well as HTLs in solar cells [138].

# 13.3.5 Metal Oxides (MOs)

TMOs have tunability in terms of their electronic properties and inherent stability of oxidation, which are considered as promising HTL materials in OSCs. Kim et al. reported the use of a solution-processed molybdenum oxide nanoparticle layer $( \mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 } )$ as an HTL in OSCs. The $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ nanoparticles can reduce the charge recombination and resistance of OsCs [139]. Zhang et al. proposed a double-layer anode buffer layer composed of PTFE and $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ . The PTFE/ $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ double layer can form an interfacial dipole that increases the work-function of ITO anode and thus facilitates hole extraction [140]. Cheng et al. prepared solution-processed $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ $\left( \mathbf { s } { \mathrm { - } } \mathbf { M } \mathbf { o } \mathbf { O } _ { 3 } \right)$ ) as a HTL in solar cell devices. The $\mathbf { s } { \mathrm { - } } \mathbf { M } \mathbf { o } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 3 }$ ultrathin films treated with UV annealing showed better transmittance, surface morphology, and film quality [141]. Ji et al. sprayed the molybdenum oxide $\left( \mathrm { M o O } _ { 3 } \right)$ ) microarray on the active layer by ultrasonic spraying at a very low temperature of $8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ . Compared with devices without $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ , the solution-processed $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ microarray improved the charge carrier transport and the PCE of the devices [142]. Kim et al. reported the use of low-temperature solution-processed vanadium oxide (s-VOx) and poly(4-styrene sulfonic acid) (PSS) composite material as HTLs. The s-VOx:PSS showed a work-function of $5 . 0 \sim 5 . 3 \mathrm { e V } ,$ affording an enhanced charge injection/extraction process at the interface due to the reduction of the energy barrier between the HTL and the organic active layer. Compared with the original s-VOx film, the s-VOx:PSS-based solar cells showed significantly improved performance [143]. Bao et al. reported a simple $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ plasma treatment method for preparing vanadium oxide $( \mathrm { V } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 5 } )$ anode buffer layer on ITO. Compared with the traditional PEDOT:PSS HTL, solar cells using the ${ \bf V } _ { 2 } { \bf O } _ { 5 }$ $\mathrm { \mathrm { ~  ~ \cal ~ O ~ } } _ { 2 }$ plasma) anode buffer layer produced higher efficiencies [144]. Jiang et al. reported the application of $\mathrm { V } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 5 } { \cdot } n \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ film as HTL in OSCs. The $\mathrm { V } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 5 } { \cdot } n \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ layer was prepared directly from the vanadium oxide powder via the fusion quenching sol-gel method. When using $\mathrm { V } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 5 } { \cdot } n \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ as HTL, the PCEs of the solar cells increased significantly [145]. Xu et al. proposed a method using a solution-treated vanadium oxide $\left( \mathsf { s } { \mathrm { - } } \mathsf { V } \mathbf { O } _ { \mathrm { X } } \right)$ as HTLs in OSCs. The devices with s-VOx as HTLs were more efficient and showed better storage stability than the OSCs with PEDOT:PSS layer [146]. Irwin et al. did comprehensive studies on the electrical properties, microstructure, electronic structure, and optical properties of nickel oxide (NiO) thin films. The NiO can form a nearly transparent interlayer on the ITO substrate, showing a smooth, crystalline, and oriented morphology [147]. Xue et al. developed an indium-free transparent electrode with a $\mathrm { N i O / A g / N i O }$ structure. This indium-free transparent electrode not only has excellent optical and electrical properties but also has suitable surface morphology, good thermal, humidity, and environmental stability [148]. Yang et al. prepared $\mathrm { N i O } _ { x }$ films at room temperature from aqueous solution, which were used as the anode buffer layers in OSCs [149]. Yu et al. fabricated $\mathrm { C u O } _ { x }$ anode buffer layer from copper acetylacetonate precursor aqueous solution at room temperature. Compared with OSCs with PEDOT:PSS anode buffer layer, the PCE of the devices with $\mathrm { { C u O } _ { x } }$ anode buffer layers reached a much higher value [150].

# 13.4 Cathode Interlayer Materials

# 13.4.1 Organic Small Molecules

Various organic small molecules have been developed as cathode interlayers, including neutral or charged and conjugated or non-conjugated materials. To improve the efficiency and stability of OsCs, efficient small molecule-based cathode interlayer materials were designed by tailoring molecular structure and preparation method (Scheme 13.4). Wudl and coworkers demonstrated that $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } Q H S O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ can work efficiently as cathode interlayers in OSCs, which mainly improved FF and PCE of the devices. Compared with the devices without $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } Q H S O _ { 3 } } ^ { - }$ interlayer, the electron mobility of the optimal device was increased by two times [151]. Su and coworkers developed a unique set of star-like interlayer materials based on fluorene with neutral phosphonate pendent chains (3TPA-FEP) and triphenylamine (TPA) core. The molecule tends to aggregate due to the integration of polar phosphonate groups, resulting in a rough surface morphology. The $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of the devices was improved because the rough interlayer increased the contact area with metal cathode [152]. Later Zhang et al. reported small-molecule interlayers (PDIN and PDINO) based on n-type PDI derivative with amino terminal substituent. PDIN showed superior electrical conductivity of $8 . 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 6 } \mathrm { S c m ^ { - 1 } }$ , three orders of magnitude higher than PFN of $6 . 9 \times 1 0 ^ { - 9 } \mathrm { S c m ^ { - 1 } }$ . Due to the $\pi$ stacks enhanced by self-organizing, the devices with PDIN showed significantly improved PCEs. Furthermore, the device performance was insensitive to the metal cathode, and high efficiencies were obtained in devices with Al, Ag, or Au cathodes [153]. Hou and coworkers reported NDIO based on NDI as cathode interlayer. The solar cell efficiency has been increased by $8 0 \%$ compared with the devices without interlayer [154]. Kim and coworkers demonstrated efficient cathode interlayer materials based on fluorene and phenothiazine trimer backbones with quaternary ammonium bromide pendant groups. These interlayers can efficiently improve the performance of the solar cell devices [155, 156]. Fang and coworkers designed two different conjugated small molecules with polar $N , N \mathrm { \Omega }$ -dimethyl amino end group, benzo[c][1,2,5]thiadiazole (FBF-N) and bisthiophenyl-benzo[c][1,2,5]thiadiazole (FTBTF-N), for use in inverted OsCs. Polar amine groups are beneficial to decrease ITO workfunction and increase $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the solar cells [7o]. Su and coworkers demonstrated a star-shaped small molecule based on a triazine core (TzPyBr) for use in OSCs as cathode interlayers [81]. It is proposed that the deep HOMO of TzPyBr effectively blocked hole transport toward the cathode, thus suppressing the interface recombination [157] Ouyang et al. designed a small-molecule electrolyte (MSAPBS) with an LUMO level of $- 2 . 3 1 \mathrm { e V }$ and a high electron mobility of $1 . 1 8 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ , which allowed optimal photon capture and provided excellent photo-generated charge carrier collection in OsCs [158]. Yang and coworkers also developed a series of star-like small molecules based on triazine core (Tn1) or hexakis(fluoren-2-yl)benzene (HFB) (T1-OH). Taking T1-OH as an example, the diethanolamine groups in this molecule reduced the work-function of the cathode electrode to enhance electron collection. Also, these functional groups made T1-OH soluble in polar solvents (methanol or water), which was required for solution-processed OsCs [159, 160]. Huang and coworkers synthesized amino-functionalized organic platinum (II) complex (Pt-N) for solar cell interlayer applications. The wide bandgap of Pt-N also acts as an exciton blocker and inhibits the quenching of excitons at the cathode interface. In addition, metal-metal supramolecular interactions forming a highly conductive electron transport channel can increase the strong $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking in organic platinum (II) complex (Pt-N) films [161]. Later, Huang and coauthors reported that two fluorene units were connected to the porphyrin nuclei by acetylene bond to form a planar-structured interlayer material (FNEZnP-OE). The fine coplanarity of the molecule significantly enhanced the electron mobility of the interlayer material, affording high-performance solar cell devices [162]. In addition to above methods of increasing molecular interactions, Li and coauthors applied aggregation-induced emission units into cathode interlayer materials. The $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and FF of the devices were dramatically improved, leading to a much higher PCE [163]. Ge and coworkers designed and synthesized a series of small-molecule interlayer materials with benzophenone (BP) unit as a core bonding different polar group, including hydroxyl (BPOH), neutral amino (BPN), amino N-oxide (BPO), and sulfobetaine (BPS) ions. OSCs containing BPN, BPO, BPS, and PFN interlayers showed enhanced PCEs [164]. Very recently, Zhang et al. reported a self n-doped hydrogen-bonding interlayer material, aliphatic amine-functionalized perylene-diimide (PDINN), which simultaneously down-shifts the work-function of the air-stable cathodes (silver and copper) and maintains good interfacial contact with the active layer through hydrogen bonding with CF bond. The OSCs based on PDINN engineered silver cathode demonstrate a high efficiency of $1 7 . 2 3 \%$ $\mathrm { \Delta ( V _ { o c } = 0 . 8 4 7 V , } J _ { \mathrm { s c } } = 2 5 . 8 9 \mathrm { m A c m ^ { - 2 } }$ $\mathrm { F F } = 7 8 . 5 9 \% )$ [165].

![](images/54ae7a43c33cbd870697bb5cf4e1b616ca459cd9a93911d68ed39f66ae034e98.jpg)  
Scheme 13.4 Molecular structure of small-molecule interlayer materials.

Fullerene derivatives as another kind of efficient interlayer materials are based on fullerene acceptor moiety, and they can be dissolved in a range of polar solvents. Fullerene derivatives have been the most widely used electron acceptor in OSCs for several decades, due to their superior electronic and processing properties. Fullerene derivatives have similar energy levels and charge transport capabilities with the acceptors of active layers in OsCs, which would be promising and efficient interlayer materials for OsCs (Scheme 13.5). Jen and coauthors reported the use of solution-processed self n-doped fulleropyrrolidinium iodide (FPI) and FPI-doped PCBM with high conductivity as interlayers in OSCs. It was proposed that when the iodides on the FPI and the buckyballs undergo electron transfer, effective n-doping and high conductivity are obtained. They further proposed that tetrabutylammonium salts (TBAX, $\mathbf { X } ^ { - } = \mathbf { F } ^ { - }$ $\mathrm { B r ^ { - } , \ I ^ { - } }$ can also effectively dope fullerenes by electron transfer between the anions of TBAX and the buckyball. Thus, the anions of these alkyl ammonium-based surfactants also hold promise for doping the electron acceptor when in contact with the active layer to optimize interfacial contact and improve solar cell efficiency [166]. Chen and coauthors reported two kinds of PCBM derivatives (PCBDAN and PCBDANI) and used them as cathode buffer layer materials in OSCs. In comparison with the traditional low work-function active metal Ca cathode, both PCBDAN and PCBDANI cathode buffer layers demonstrated identical or slightly improved photovoltaic performance in PsCs. Meanwhile, they presented a strategy to fabricate polymer solar cells in inverted geometry, where PCBDAN was used as an additive in active layer and worked as cathode interlayers by self-organization. Furthermore, PCBDAN could be used both as acceptor and cathode interlayer in similar inverted OsCs [167-170]. In 2014, Emrick and coworkers used amine-functionalized fullerene $\mathrm { ( C _ { 6 0 } - N ) }$ and sulfobetaine-substituted zwitterionic fullerene $\left( \mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }  – \mathrm { S B } \right)$ as cathode-independent buffer layer in conventional solar cell devices. Specifically, when coating a thin layer of $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { - N }$ , the work-function of common metal electrodes, such as Ag, Cu, and Au, can be significantly reduced to $3 . 6 5 \mathrm { e V } .$ The integration of $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { - N }$ into solar cell devices can result in excellent ohmic contact for electron injection and a large built-in potential for efficient charge extraction. Later, the same group further reported that $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ -SB can modify the work-function of ITO from 4.5 to $4 . 0 \mathrm { e V }$ and act as an electron transport layer in inverted OsCs to improve device performance [42, 171]. Chen and coworkers synthesized $Z _ { \mathrm { n O - C _ { 6 0 } } }$ as a cathode interlayer material by the reaction of hydroxyl containing fullerene derivative, PCBE-OH, with zinc. The $Z _ { \mathrm { n O - C _ { 6 0 } } }$ interlayers enhanced the function of electron collection in the devices, produced a fullerene-rich cathode surface, and promoted compatibility of the BHJ layer at the interface [172]. Siao and coworkers reported that an azide-cross-linked fullerene interlayer (C-PCBN3) can significantly improve the $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ , and $F F$ of the devices compared with those with a $\mathrm { T i O } _ { 2 }$ interlayer or no interlayer [173]. Liu et al. reported fullerene polymer ionenes that involved dibromo-alkanes and $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ -diamine. The resulting cationic polymer interlayer $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ -ionene can support the utilization of a variety of high work-function metals such as Ag, Cu, and Au as the cathode for high performance OsCs [174].

![](images/749da19af4d749f049261b0a63e1765dc776a7989a059ff71e4b2e38b4ae3d1e.jpg)  
Scheme 13.5 Molecular structure of some typical fullerene interlayer materials.

# 13.4.2 Polymer Cathode Interlayer Materials

Over the past decades, water/alcohol-soluble conjugated polymers (wscPs) have achieved great success as cathode interlayer materials for various organic electronic devices (Scheme 13.6). By taking advantage of the difference in solubility between wsCPs interlayer materials and traditional organic semiconductors, multilayered devices can be prepared by solution processing. These WsCPs can effectively reduce the work-function of the metal cathode and improve the electron transport in the devices by forming interfacial dipole at the interface between active layer and metal electrode.

In 2009, Cao and coworkers first demonstrated the use of wscPs as cathode interlayer in OSCs. They found that the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and PCE of the devices were improved remarkably after incorporating a thin layer of poly[(9,9-bis(3-(N,N-dimethylamino) propyl)-2,7-fluorene)-alt-2,7-(9,9-dioctylfluorene)] (PFN). The observed enhancement of $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ was ascribed to the improved built-in field due to the interfacial dipole generated by the interlayer [175]. Later, they reported that the PFN interlayer could simultaneously enhance $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ , and $F F$ of solar cells, leading to a high efficiency of both conventional and inverted device. The presence of interfacial dipoles enhances the intrinsic potential of the whole device, improves the electron transport characteristics, eliminates the accumulation of space charge, and reduces the energy loss due to the increase in the intrinsic field and carrier mobility [24, 176]. The work-function of cathode can also be regulated by non-CPEs with charged ionic groups in the structure. In 2012, Kippelen and coauthors successfully used non-CPEs PEI and PEIE as neutral surface modifiers and found that these materials are of great significance in single-junction and tandem photovoltaic devices. These materials successfully adjust the work-functions of the metal electrodes, increase build-in potential, and reduce the interfacial energy barrier [41, 177]. Except for the amino-containing groups, Cao and coworkers reported a novel conjugated polymer, PCP-EP, in which the hydrophilic phosphate ester side chain could not only effectively improve the solubility of polycarbazole materials but also effectively regulate the work-function of ITO electrode by forming an interface dipole. Thus, it can improve the electron transport and PCEs of photovoltaic devices [178]. In 2013, Liu et al. reported a novel cathode interlayer material, $\mathrm { H g }$ containing derivative of amino-functionalized polymer (PFEN-Hg). This interlayer material showed excellent performance in a wide range of thicknesses window, due to the existence of $\mathrm { H g \mathrm { - } H g }$ interactions and the improved $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking. Further investigation indicated that PFEN-Hg showed some attractive properties, such as good film formation, effective work-function adjustment, low optical absorption, and excellent electron collection [179]. Lv et al. reported a hyperbranched soluble polymer HBPFN by one-pot $^ { * } \mathrm { A } 2 + \mathrm { B } 3 ^ { , , }$ Suzuki polymerization and used it as a cathode interlayer in OsCs. This work demonstrated that the structure ordering of the conjugated polymer main chains is not necessary for the interfacial materials to perform effectively [180]. Zhang and coauthors reported an n-type conjugated polymer containing dibenzothiophene-S,S-dioxide (FsO), bispyridinium, and fluorene scaffolds in the backbone (PFsOPyCl) and used this polymer as cathode interlayer in OsCs. The solar cell devices exhibited simultaneous enhancement in $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ , and $F F$ relative to the device with bare Al electrodes [181]. Recently, Huang and coauthors developed self $\mathbf { n }$ -doped wSCPs. Two n-type WSCPs were reported, and both contain an NDI-based conjugated main chain, with highly polar amino- or ammonium-functionalized side chains, respectively. OsCs based on these self-doped wsCP ETLs exhibit significantly improved device performance, especially they can be processed with a broad thickness range of $5 { - } 1 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [59]. Sun et al. reported that using $n$ -type PFN-2TNDI as cathode interlayer in conventional fullerene-free solar cells resulted in much higher efficiency. The results show that the contact between the n-type cathode interlayers and the donor in the active layer provided an additional interface for charge dissociation, and the energy level matching between the interlayer and the acceptor in the active layer can be effectively optimized, enhancing electron extraction from the BHJ active layer at the interface. Compared with PFN, the PFN-2TNDI layer enhanced the photocurrent generation due to the appropriate energy level offset between the donor layer and the cathode interlayer, and it is suitable for exciton dissociation [65]. Many groups found n-doping behavior between non-conjugated polymer interlayer materials bearing polar moieties and a typical acceptor. This intermolecular n-doping effect may be a general phenomenon and could play an important role for those polymer cathode interlayer materials to work effectively in solar cell devices [182, 183].

Scheme 13.6 Molecular structure of some typical polymer cathode interlayer materials.

# 13.4.3 Graphene Derivatives and Other Emerging Alternatives

Graphene and its derivatives have a high specific surface area, remarkable thermal/electrical properties, high charge carrier mobility, transparency, mechanical flexibility, and compatibility with solution processability, and hence they have been used in electronic devices. In addition, the semi-metallic band structure of graphene affords widely variable work-functions based on its continuously tunable Fermi energy. Dai and coworkers demonstrated an excellent electron-transporting cesium-neutralized GO(GO-Cs) layer, and the periphery -COOH groups in GO are replaced by -CO0Cs groups [184, 185]. Conventional and inverted OSCs with the GO-Cs cathode interlayer exhibited the same performance compared with those that used the most advanced cathode interlayer materials. Then Heeger and coworkers discovered a method of dealing with GO. Graphene was stamped and subsequently oxidized with $\mathrm { H N O } _ { 3 }$ , and a transferable GO layer was obtained with a work-function of $4 . 3 \mathrm { e V }$ [186]. Because this GO cathode interlayer material can make electron extraction/transport from the BHJ active layer to the Al cathode more efficient, the $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ was improved and the series resistance was reduced. Yang and coauthors reported that a new graphene-fullerene composite (reduced graphene oxide (rGO)-pyrene-PCBM) was attached onto rGO via the noncovalent functionalization approach. The pyrene-PCBM moiety was synthesized via a facile esterification reaction, and pyrene was used as an anchoring bridge to link rGO and PCBM. rGO-pyrene-PCBM was successfully applied as electron extraction layer for solar cell devices [187]. Lv and coauthors developed a solution-processable n-doped graphene cathode interlayer material PDINO-G for OSCs by adding graphene to the classic alcohol/water-soluble interlayer material PDINO. The n-doped graphene-PDINO composite (PDINO-G) interlayer possessed increased conductivity, lower work-function, reduced charge recombination, and increased charge extraction rate. Previously, n-doped graphene was prepared only on the surface of chemical vapor-deposited (CVD) graphene films without solution processability. The effect of this cathode interlayer on photovoltaic performance of OSCs was studied by selecting the photovoltaic model system. The solar cell efficiency was significantly enhanced in comparison with that of the devices without graphene modification on the PDINO. The universality of the high-performance PDINO-G interlayer was verified in two other photovoltaic systems [188]. Later they reported that two three-dimensional (3D) interlayer materials, POssFN and ADMAFN, are excellent surfactants for dispersing graphene in ethanol. The two 3D-surfactant-based graphene composites (POsSFN-G and ADMAFN-G) can work as high-performance cathode interlayers in OSCs [189].

# 13.5 Conclusion and Outlook

We summarized recent progress on interfacial design in OsCs, mainly focusing on the mechanism of interfacial modification, the strategies of performing device engineering, and the typical interlayer materials that have been developed for device optimization. Despite the great progress on the design of efficient interlayer materials and the understanding of the mechanism on interfacial design, much more study still lies ahead to get a comprehensive description of their multiple functionalities, resolve outstanding problems, and propose a view of future directions.

(1) Due to the diverse design on interlayer materials, it is challenging to draw a clear picture to understand the role of interlayers on device operation. Many models were developed to describe the energy level alignment at the contact between interlayer and metal electrode. However, since now, no one model can explain all the experiment results. Thus, one has to develop more powerful characterizations to probe the correlation of interfacial morphology and electronic structures at the device interface, including molecular packing, dipole orientation, and their influence on energy level alignment at the interface.

(2) The developed organic interlayer materials generally contain some unique func. tionalities (amine, zwitterions, electrolytes...). Some of them have the potential to degrade the organic semiconductors in the active layers. For example, Zhou and coworkers found that the recently developed non-fullerene acceptors can react with amine groups in PEIE, leading to device degradation [190]. Thus, the community has to give more emphasis on the chemical stability at the device interface.

(3) The morphology stability of the interlayer plays a critical role on the durability of device operation. Some small molecular interlayer materials hold the potential to diffuse into the active layer, degrading themselves as well as the active layer. On the other hand, most of the efficient interlayers to date are generally hydrophilic, while the active layers are just the opposite. Thus, the long-term stability of the devices is quite challenging due to the potential de-wetting effect of the interlayers on the active layers.

# 14.1 Introduction

Modern organic solar cells (OsCs) are based on a sandwiched structure with a bulk-heterojunction (BHJ) active layer consisting of a mixture of electron donor and electron acceptor [1, 2]. At the heart of OSC, BHJ active layer plays a significant role in the power conversion process, which associates with light-harvesting, exciton dissociation, charge transport and charge collection. During this process, both electron donor and electron acceptor in the active layer could absorb photons and create excitons and the produced excitons can then dissociate into holes and electrons when they diffuse to the interfaces of electron-donor and electron-acceptor domains. However, due to the low dielectric permittivity of $\pi$ -conjugated organic semiconductors, the excitons are tightly bounded by Coulombic force and only show a short diffusion length of around $5 { - } 1 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [3]. Hence, the domain sizes of donor and acceptor should be confined in $1 0 { - } 2 0 \mathrm { n m }$ to ensure excitons having rich donor-acceptor interfaces for exciton dissociation. On the other hand, after excitons dissociating into holes and electrons, a bi-continuous interpenetrating donor/acceptor network with high domain purity is required for efficient charge transport [4]. On top of that, exploring the nanoscale morphology of BHJ active layers while understanding the correlation between morphology and performance is a significant driving force for advancing OSCs.

The general way to fabricate the BHJ active layers of OSCs is solution processing; herein, conjugated electron donors and acceptors are first dissolved in a solution and then cast into a blend film. During the film-forming process, the donor and acceptor materials will partially demix to lower the free energy of the system and cause phase separation, finally forming a series of heterojunctions throughout the active layer. The donor and acceptor materials used here are p-type and n-type semiconductors, respectively, e.g. conjugated polymer, conjugated small molecule, and fullerene derivatives. With different chemical structures, these semiconducting materials can form various structural orders ranging from micron-scale to nanoscale in the BHJ active layer. It is also evident that this nanoscale morphology can be adjusted by film-processing methods, such as the choice of solvents, post-deposition treatments, and casting environments. Consequently, the morphological metrics within OsCs deliver a rich area to study, allowing researchers to explore and optimize the structural order, miscibility, and phase purity of blend components, as well as component distribution in the direction normal to the film. In this chapter, we first introduce a range of morphology characterization techniques including microscopic, scattering, and depth profiling methods (see Figure 14.1). We then discuss typical methods for morphology manipulation and address the correlation between domain size, miscibility, domain purity with $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ , FF, and $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of an OSC. Finally, we compare the traditional fullerene and the novel non-fullerene acceptors on the basis of morphology and discuss the existing challenges and future prospects in morphology characterization and manipulation in OsCs toward high performance.

# 14.2 Morphological Characterization of Organic Solar Cells

# 14.2.1 Microscopic Methods

Microscopic method is the most intuitive method to examine the morphology of OSCs from nanometer to micrometer scales. There are three mainstream microscopic techniques: optical microscopy, scanning probe microscopy (SPM), and electron microscopy. As optical microscopes use lenses and visible light to magnify the sample, their resolution is limited to approximately $0 . 2 \mu \mathrm { m }$ and not suitable for characterizing the nanoscale morphology of OsCs. In this section, we will focus on the SPM and electron microscopy techniques.

SPM was founded in as early as 1980s. It is a surface-sensitive technique that can investigate the surface information by scanning the sample with a physical tip. By applying different tips toward different interactions between tip and sample, the surface morphology, conductivity, potential, stiffness, elastic modulus, and thermal properties of the sample can be determined. Among SPM, atomic force microscopy (AFM) is the most commonly used technique in OSCs. As shown in Figure 14.2a, AFM consists of a sharp tip, a laser beam deflection system, and a position-sensitive detector. During operation, the tip can raster scan the sample through the van der Waals interaction between sample and tip, whilst the laser deflection can be used in a feedback loop to control force and tip position for imaging and measuring. As the crystalline and amorphous domains in organic films exhibit distinct contrast in topology and elastic modulus, topography is the most widely used information in OSCs. For example, Sun [8] group employed tapping mode AFM to study the surface morphology of a high crystalline polymer PBT1-S film (Figure 14.2b,c). Herein, the height and phase images in AFM are related to the difference of topology and material stiffness. It can be found that fibril-like crystals of PBT1-S are clearly resolved in both height and phase images across the entire area. For BHJ blend films, AFM topography provides information on the phase-separated domain size on the film surface, which sometimes cannot be simply applied to the bulk, especially when there is a surface wetting layer formed [10-13].

In addition, AFM can be extended to conducting atomic force microscopy (c-AFM), which is capable of probing the properties of the film beyond the top surface. As shown in Figure 14.2d, c-AFM works in conjunction with an external voltage source and probes the sample with a conductive tip. When c-AFM is scanning, the voltage source applies a potential difference between the tip and the conductive substrate, while the conductive tip can examine current and record the topography and current images simultaneously at the same location of the photoactive layer. As c-AFM represents the local electrical properties of the blend film, the dark current images at positive and negative tip can reflect hole and electron transports [14]. Under forward bias (conductive substrate is positively biased), electrons are injected from the sharp tip to the sample and the bright region in c-AFM images is related to the electron injection which represents the electron-acceptor domain. Similarly, under reverse bias (conductive tip is positively biased), the c-AFM images thus show hole transport and the bright region is related to donor domain [15]. However, it should be noted that due to the different geometries of c-AFM and the planar device in mobility measurement, the traditional Mott-Gurney law is not suitable for c-AFM to quantify the carrier mobility. Herein, a semiempirical modified law (Eq. (14.1) with the consideration of tip-sample geometry was proposed by Ginger group [16] to estimate the carrier mobilities in c-AFM:

$$
J = { \frac { 9 } { 8 } } \varepsilon \varepsilon _ { 0 } \mu _ { 0 } e ^ { 0 . 8 9 \gamma \left( { \frac { V } { L } } \right) ^ { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } { \frac { V ^ { 2 } } { L ^ { 3 } } } \delta \left( { \frac { L } { d } } \right) ^ { 1 . 6 \pm 0 . 1 }
$$

where $J$ and $V$ are the average current density and applied voltage of the AFM tip, respectively, $\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon _ { 0 }$ are the relative dielectric constant of active layer and permittivity of free space, respectively, $\mu _ { 0 }$ is the charge carrier mobility, $\gamma$ is the charge density dependence of the mobility, $L$ is the thickness of the active layer, $d$ is the diameter of the contact area between the tip and the active layer, and $\delta$ is the empirical dimensionless parameter of the offset between c-AFM calculations and the planar device data which is $7 . 8 { \pm } 1$

c-AFM can be further extended into photoconductive atomic force microscopy (pc-AFM) when it is performed in conjunction with an external light source. As shown in Figure 14.2e, a diffraction-limited laser beam illuminates the sample from the bottom, while a conductive tip can measure electrical properties simultaneously. Compared to AFM and c-AFM, pc-AFM can provide local photocurrents and illustrate how the individual nanostructures contribute to the device performance in OSCs. For example, Nguyen group applied a white light to illuminate the PM6:Y6 film while measuring the photocurrent. As shown in Figure 14.2f [9], the PM6:Y6 film with $1 \%$ low molecular weight fraction (LMwF) PM6 exhibits a continuous interpenetrating network of hole- (PM6, bright area) and electron (Y6, dark area)-rich domains with high photocurrent. However, the hole- and electron-rich domains are not continuously separated in the $5 2 \%$ LMWF PM6:Y6 film and only obtained a low photocurrent (Figure $1 4 . 2 \mathrm { g }$ , consistent with their device performance. Furthermore, although c-AFM and pc-AFM have been widely used and provided valuable information for the solar cell community, two concerns should be noted. First, performing c-AFM or pc-AFM with high bias could induce local oxidation or reduction in the blend film, which means they should be carried out in vacuum or inert atmospheres. Second, electrical currents only follow the path of the active layer with the lowest resistance, which can also straight down through the film, implying that the map of electrical conductance is not just simply correlated with the surface morphology and but should also be analyzed with caution.

In addition, combining AFM with a tunable infrared laser (IR-AFM) to produce a chemical contrast has also been studied to characterize morphology of the BHJ active layers. To conduct IR-AFM, the IR laser focuses on the interaction region between the AFM tip and sample. After the sample absorbed IR photons, an electric dipole can be generated from the vibrational motion of the IR-resonant bonds of the sample, enabling an attractive force between the AFM tip and sample molecules. For example, PII-2T-PS and PPDI-T possess different characteristic peaks at 1453 and $1 7 0 6 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ in their FTIR spectra, respectively. By activating the PII-2T-PS:PPDI-T blend film at 1453 and $1 7 0 6 \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 }$ , IR-AFM is able to spatially map the donor and acceptor domains with a resolution of about $1 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [17].

Compared to the traditional optical microscopy, electron microscopy applies electrons for imaging, enabling superior spatial resolution to magnify the sample. Among electron microscopy techniques, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) is the most widely used method for organic semiconductor films. TEM is often operated in a bright-field (BF) imaging mode, where a cluster of electron beam goes through the thin film and run into the atoms in the sample, the collided electrons can then scattered into different angular and form bright and dark parts in the image with the mass, density, and thickness variations of the sample. In general, the contrast of a TEM image in OSCs is related to the crystallinity or the aggre. gation of components in the film. For example, as shown in Figure 14.3a, when $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ molecules aggregated strongly in the film, a dark ball-like domain with a domain size of $2 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ can be found due to the higher electron density of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ aggregation [18]. Similarly, in Figure 14.3b, ${ \mathrm { C O } } _ { i } { 8 \mathrm { D F I C } }$ molecules obtained higher crystallinity than PTB7-Th after solvent annealing, which allows us to observe ${ \mathrm { C O } } _ { i } { 8 \mathrm { D F I C } }$ lamellar crystals with the size of about $2 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ in the film [19].

One extension to the traditional bright-field TEM is combining a series of 2D TEM to construct 3D TEM image. As shown in Figure 14.3c,d, 3D-TEM can be realized by taking a series of 2D-TEM projections at different angles by tilting the sample (specimen) with respect to the electron beam and subsequently reconstructing to the 3D image on the basis of computerized tomography. Figure 14.3e [5] shows a reconstructed 3D nanoscale polymer network of a $\mathrm { P F 1 0 T B { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ film. It can be found that the bright region belongs to PFioTB domain, which demonstrates an interconnected polymer-rich strand forming a truly three-dimensional network.

Since the commonly used donor and acceptor materials in OsCs are $\pi$ -conjugated, organic semiconducting materials, it is not easy to obtain decent contrast for TEM if the donor and acceptor possess similar chemical structure. Hence, researchers have combined electron energy-loss spectroscopy with TEM (EF-TEM) to probe the organic films at different energy windows to enhance contrast of the components in the BHJ active layer [22]. For example, Rechberger et al. [20] have successfully applied EF-TEM to resolve the morphology of a ternary PIDTTQ:Si-PCPDTBT $\mathrm { \cdot P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ BHJ film. Herein, the zero-loss filtered image is the same to the regular bright-field TEM, and the contrast in the film is only attributed to their local density differences. While probing the film at $3 0 \pm 4 \mathrm { e V }$ could maximize the contrast between polymers (PIDTTQ:Si-PCPDTBT) and fullerene $\mathrm { ( P C _ { 7 0 } B M ) }$ , probing the film at an energy loss of $2 6 7 \mathrm { e V }$ with an energy window of $3 0 \mathrm { e V }$ could maximize the structure-sensitive contrast between PIDTTQ and Si-PCPDTBT. Overall, a RGB color can be established on top of the above two views to visualize the nanomorphology of PIDTTQ, Si-PCPDTBT, and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ in the film (Figure 14.3f).
