Scanning transmission X-ray microscopy (STXM) is a powerful synchrotron-based technique, which can utilize a variable-energy focused X-ray to measure the sample and quantitatively map the chemical composition of organic films at a wavelength with high contrast. In addition to the regular morphological metrics such as shape and domain size, STxM can also provide information on miscibility and domain purities. In 2009, Watts et al. [23] successfully applied STXM to reveal quantitative information about the residual weight fraction of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ in P3HT matrix and first discovered the limited purity in BHJ active layer. Later, as shown in Figure $1 4 . 3 \mathrm { g } .$ Collins et al. [21] further studied the composition profiles of $\mathrm { P T B 7 : P C _ { 7 0 } B M }$ films cast from CB or CB:DIO solution and demonstrated the effect of domain purity on device performance in solar cells.

# 14.2.2 Scattering Methods

Although traditional microscopic techniques can provide the information of domain sizes, shapes, and purities, due to the less-ordered structure and similar electron density of donor and acceptor in organic semiconductor films, it is still difficult to get sufficient spatial resolution and thus not capable of fully examining molecular packing and domain purity in a BHJ film. Therefore, scattering techniques based on X-ray or neutron are often used as a complementary technique to comprehensively characterize the nanoscale morphology of the BHJ active layer at multiple length scales. Scattering is a reciprocal space technique, which can probe the structure of the sample by utilizing scattering effect to generate patterns that can be correlated with nanoscale morphology. To enhance interactions between X-ray/neutrons and the thin BHJ active layers, scattering techniques are always carried out with synchrotron radiation to enable high flux and collimated X-ray or neutron photons to enhance intensity. Figure 14.4 shows a typical schematic view of scattering measurements processed in three different geometries:

(1) Grazing incidence scattering geometry: Grazing incidence scattering geometry is the most commonly used geometry for film samples. Here, a collimated X-ray or neuron impinges on the sample under a grazing angle $k _ { \mathrm { i } }$ to minimize the background signal while enhancing the scattering intensity. The scattering beam can be then collected by a 2D charge-coupled device (CCD) and simply interpreted by the Bragg equation $n \lambda = 2 d \mathrm { s i n } \theta$ . From Figure 14.4a, it is clear to see that the scattering angle $k _ { \mathrm { f } }$ is inversely proportional to the distance $( d )$ between the sample and the CCD. Therefore, depending on the distance between the sample and the CCD, the related experiments can be typically referred to wide-angle scattering (WAS) or small-angle scattering (SAS) which could reflect the morphology information associated with large or small $k _ { \mathrm { f } } .$ It should be noted that WAS and

![](images/377a052bacfaabcc182ab5ee12f4ccd95109151a69e62c4ffbbab2619a3d5b65.jpg)  
Figure 14.4  Schematic view of the typical (a) grazing incidence, (b) transmission, and (c) reflection geometry for X-ray and neutron scattering measurements.

SAS measurements are also suitable for the transmission and reflectance scattering geometries.

(2) Transmission scattering geometry: In transmission geometry, the X-ray or neuron impinges the sample and goes through directly under an incident angle of $k _ { \mathrm { i } }$ , while the scattering signal can be collected by a CCD (Figure 14.4b). Compared to the grazing incidence scattering geometry, the thickness of the sample used here should be thin enough for the X-ray or neuron to penetrate and form decent scattering intensity on CCD.

(3) Reflectance geometry: In contrast to the grazing incidence geometry where the specular reflection is blocked and only the diffuse scattering being detected, reflectance geometry only measures the specular reflection at $q _ { z }$ direction and the scattering at $q _ { y }$ direction is null. Therefore, reflectance geometry scattering is often used for detecting the depth information of films. Here, by changing the perpendicular wavevector transfer of the incident angle $( k _ { \mathrm { i } } )$ , the resulting scattering intensity can reveal information at different depths (Figure 14.4c). For $k _ { \mathrm { i } } < k _ { \mathrm { c } }$ (critical angle), highly sensitive surface information can be achieved within several nanometers. For $k _ { \mathrm { i } } > k _ { \mathrm { c } }$ , the scattering intensity reflects the averaged information of the film.

Grazing incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIwAxs) can be understood as wide-angle X-ray scattering (with the scattering 0 large than $2 ^ { \circ }$ ) in a grazing incidence geometry. According to the Bragg equation, it can be found that the scattering signal obtained in GIwAxs is associated with the sub-nanometer structure $( 0 . 5 { - } 2 \mathrm { n m } )$ , which reflects the information of the molecular packing and crystallinity of the active layer [24]. Figure $1 4 . 5 \mathrm { a - d }$ summarizes four typical scenarios of GiwAxs patterns in organic semiconducting flms. Here, the $q _ { x y }$ direction in 2D GIwAxs patterns only reflect the in-plane information (lateral morphology parallel to the film) of the film, while the $q _ { z }$ direction in 2D GIWAXS patterns relates to the out-of-plane information (vertical morphology normal to the film) of the film. As shown in Figure 14.5a, when there is a highly crystalline film (crystal spacing: $d$ ) with an orientation normal to the substrate, scattering peaks will appear along the vertical $q _ { z }$ direction (out-of-plane). In Figure 14.5b, scattering peaks could emerge along both horizontal $q _ { x y }$ (in-plane) and vertical $q _ { z }$ (out-of-plane) directions if there are two highly crystalline domains with an orientation parallel and perpendicular to the substrate. Besides, when the film is more textured and the domains inside are oriented with an angular distribution around the out-of-plane, scattering peaks in out-of-plane will be broadened (Figure 14.5c). In the case of a film with isotropic crystals, diffraction peaks will smear out into Debye-Scherrer-like rings (Figure 14.5d).

![](images/137fea269fd3850bb97c4162362fee0c55e621fcdd52e02315033b21b063fdac.jpg)

[11]/ Reproduced with permission from John Wiley and Sons. (h) The crystalline structure of a widely studied conjugated polymer (i.e. P3HT). (i) Aggregation of fullerenes in the film.

To ensure strong $\pi { - } \pi$ ordering and good solubility, organic semiconducting materials always feature a larger planar conjugated structure and alkyl side chains in their chemical structures [25]. Herein, we will start with two commonly used high efficiency materials PffBT4T-2OD and PTB7-Th to examine the crystalline structure of polymer donors. Figure 14.5e shows the 2D GIwAXS pattern of a pure PffBT4T-2OD film cast from CB; it can be found that its GIWAXS pattern exhibits a strong crescent pattern at $q _ { z } = 0 . 3 0 \mathring \mathrm { A } ^ { - 1 }$ , which is attributed to the (100) lamellar packing of PffBT4T-2OD. A lamellar spacing $d = 2 . 1 \mathrm { n m }$ ) of PffBT4T-2OD can also be calculated by $d = 2 \pi / q$ . Meanwhile, in the $q _ { z } = 0 . 6$ and $0 . 9 \mathring \mathrm { A } ^ { - 1 }$ , two relatively weak crescent patterns can also be observed, which are attributed to the second(200) and third- (300) diffraction peaks of the lamellar packing of PffBT4T-2OD. Moreover, in the in-plane direction, a peak can be observed at $q = 1 . 7 5 \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 }$ , which is ascribed to the $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking of PffBT4T-2OD with the spacing of $0 . 3 6 \mathrm { n m }$ . Overall, we can conclude that the side chains and backbone of PffBT4T-2OD are perpendicular to the substrate orderly, indicating that PffBT4T-2OD molecules mainly exhibit the so-called "edge-on' crystalline structure in the film (Figure 14.5h, note that the chemical structure here is a scheme only). On the contrary, as shown in Figure 14.5f, the 2D GIWAXS pattern of PTB7-Th film exhibits (100) diffraction peak in in-plane, while the (010) $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking diffraction peak in out-of-plane, indicating that the conjugated backbone of PTB7-Th is parallel to the substrate. As depicted in Figure $1 4 . 5 \mathrm { h }$ , this crystalline structure has been defined as "face-on" molecular packing. "Edge-on" and "face-on' are the most common molecular orientation in polymer donor materials. It has been widely accepted that "face-on' molecular order is more favorable for OSCs as holes and electrons can transfer more efficiently through $\pi { - } \pi$ stacks along the out-of-plane, while "edge-on" molecular order is more favorable for transistor device because holes and electrons are transported in in-plane [26]. In addition, "flat-on" molecular order with ordered backbone in out-of-plane also exists in organic films (Figure 14.5h). However, due to the unstable structure of this crystalline structure, it is not commonly observed.

Fullerene electron acceptors possess a ball-like geometry structure, as shown in Figure 14.5i, which does not have complicated molecular orientations like conjugated polymers and always pack isotopically in the film. Figure $1 4 . 5 \mathrm { g }$ shows a 2D GIWAXS image of the PffBT4T ${ \cdot 2 } \mathrm { O D } { : } \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ blend film, in addition to the "edge-on" crystalline structure of PffBT4T-2OD, a Debye-Scherrer-like ring locating at $1 . 4 \mathring \mathrm { A } ^ { - 1 }$ can also be found and relates to the aggregation of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ This Debye-Scherrer-like ring shows the same intensity in either in-place or out-of-plane, suggesting that $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ exists in the film isotopically with domain spacing of $2 \mathrm { n m }$ . Due to the isotopic feature of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ , the charge generation in polymer:fullerene system is relatively simple. As shown in Figure 14.6a,b, the charge generation efficiency mainly depends on the aggregation state of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ attempting to suppress $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ aggregation to provide more donor:acceptor interfaces in BHJ active layer has been accepted as an efficient routine to improve charge generation. In contrast to fullerene acceptor, the geometry structure of the modern non-fullerene acceptors is more complicated, which consists of three parts, alkyl chains, an electron-donating backbone core, and two electron-accepting end-groups. Non-fullerene acceptors can exhibit "face-on," "edge-on," and "flat-on" molecular orientations in a film, sometimes simultaneously. This leads to much complicated morphological geometry for charge generation [27]. As shown in Figure 14.6c, when both polymer donor and non-fullerene acceptors exhibit face-on orientation, charges can be generated at the interfaces between the conjugated $\pi { - } \pi$ backbones of polymer donor and non-fullerene acceptors, which has been proved to be an efficient process [19]. However, when polymer donor and non-fullerene acceptors exhibit edge-on and face-on molecular packing respectively, charge generation might occur between the alky chain of polymer and $\pi { - } \pi$ backbone of non-fullerenes and cause different charge generation fundamentals [28] (Figure 14.6d). In addition to molecular order, GiwAxS can also be used to calculate the crystalline correlation lengths (crystalline size) of the crystals in the BHJ active layer by the Scherrer equation:

![](images/d3f6eb6285cbab80c00c585a7e772931fbfd802fbaa620b326209a17691fc0f0.jpg)  
Figure 14.6 Schemes of the polymer: fullerene films with (a) strong and (b) weak fullerene aggregation. Schemes of the polymer:non-fullerene films with (c) both polymer and non-fullerene acceptor exhibiting face-on molecular orientation and (d) polymer showing edge-on but non-fullerene acceptor displaying face-on molecular orientation.

$$
D _ { h k l } = 2 \pi K / \Delta q _ { h k l }
$$

where $D _ { h k l }$ could be roughly translated as the mean size of the crystalline domains which is smaller or equal to the grain size, $K$ is the shape factor of the related crystals in the film, a typical value of about 0.9 is commonly used for organic materials, and $\Delta q _ { h k l }$ is half of the maximum intensity of the diffraction peak in 1D GIWAXS profile.

In contrast to GIwAXS that possesses a relatively short sample-detector distance (centimeters) to collect scattering signal at large angle region $\left( 2 \theta > 5 ^ { \circ } \right) ,$ , grazing incidence small-angle X-ray scattering(GISAXS) has a much longer sample-detector distance (several meters) and collects scattering signal at small scattering angle region $\left( 2 \theta < 5 ^ { \circ } \right)$ . Accordingly, all the pixels on the detector collect signal from a small angular range, and GISAXS can be easily regarded as zooming in the GIwAXS pattern in the small angle regime. Due to the small scattering angle in GISAXS, GISAXS is usually used to investigate the size scale from 10 to $5 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ The scattering signal of GISAXS is from the variations of the mean electronic density and the mean electron scattering length of the components in the film. In OSCs, GISAXS could reflect the information of size, shape, phase separation, and uniformity of the distributions of donor and acceptor components. Since the GISAXS experiments are based on the intensity of the Fourier transform of the electron density, the received 2D GISAXS data must be interpreted to yield relevant morphological information. However, due to the complicated scattering process in the BHJ layers, there is no versatile formula to model all BHJ layers and it is difficult to assign a scattering pattern to a specific morphology. Therefore, multiple form factors and structure factors are often used to interpret the morphological information. Consequently, GISAXS is often used as a supplemental tool to fully characterize morphology in conjunction with electron microscopy.

Figure 14.7a shows a typical 2D GISAXS pattern of a BHJ film. The most distinct feature in GISAXS pattern is the horizontal scattering strip in the region about $q _ { z } = 0 . 0 3 \mathring \mathrm { A } ^ { - 1 }$ , which is often used to model the lateral morphological structure. Wu et al. [29] applied GISAXS to reveal the domain size of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ . Figure 14.7b shows the 1D profiles of a $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ film during the heating process to $1 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ ; it can be found that the as-cast $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ film does not show any Bragg diffraction peaks but exhibits a weak broad scattering peak in the range from 0.o04 to $0 . 1 \mathring \mathrm { A } ^ { - 1 }$ This broad peak becomes more pronounced with the increased annealing temperature, which is attributed to the aggregation of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ particles during annealing. Hence, a conventional polydisperse spherical model with Schultz size distributions was applied to model the domain size of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ particles. As a result, they found that the average size of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ clusters increased from 10 to $1 7 . 5 \mathrm { n m }$ when the temperature increased from 30 to $1 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and become stable after prolonging the thermal annealing (TA) at $1 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (Figure 14.7c).

In addition, Su and coworkers [30] also established a GISAXS model to study the domain size, shape, and aggregation in a PCPDTBT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ film. They found that the GISAXS intensity in its 1D profile can be divided into two regions which mainly come from different phase: (i) an upturn in the low. $q$ region $( < 0 . 0 1 \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 } )$ following power-law behavior, which is associated with the polymer domain and can be fitted by the Debye-Anderson-Brumberger (DAB) model; (ii) a shoulder in the middle. $q$ region $( 0 . 0 1 { - } 0 . 0 3 \mathring \mathrm { A } ^ { - 1 } ) ,$ which can be fitted by the fractal model and its signal mainly come from the aggregation of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ phase (Figure 14.7d). Overall, the GISAXS data can be well fitted by the DAB-Fractal model:

$$
\begin{array} { l } { \displaystyle \mathrm { I } ( \boldsymbol { q } ) = \frac { A _ { 1 } } { \left[ 1 + \left( q \xi \right) ^ { 2 } \right] ^ { 2 } } + A _ { 2 } \langle P ( \boldsymbol { q } , R ) \rangle S ( \boldsymbol { q } , R , \eta , \mathrm { D } ) + B } \\ { \displaystyle S ( \boldsymbol { q } ) = 1 + \frac { \sin \left[ \left( D - 1 \right) \tan ^ { - 1 } { ( q \eta ) } \right] b \pm \sqrt { b ^ { 2 } - 4 a c } } { \left( q R \right) ^ { D } } \frac { D \Gamma \left( D - 1 \right) } { \left[ 1 + \frac { 1 } { \left( q \eta \right) ^ { 2 } } \right] ^ { ( D - 1 ) / 2 } } } \end{array}
$$

where the first item represents the amorphous $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ dispersed PCPDTBT phase, $A _ { 1 }$ is an independent fitting parameter, and $\xi$ is the average correlation length of the polymer domain. The second item $S ( q )$ represents the contribution from fractal-like aggregations of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ , where $P ( q , R )$ and $S ( q , R , \eta , D )$ are the form and structure factor of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ $R$ is the mean spherical radius of primary $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ molecules, and $D$ is the dimensionality of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ which describes the interaction between primary particles in this fractal-like aggregation system. The average domain size of the $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ domain can be then roughly characterized by the Guinier radius $( R _ { \mathrm { g } } )$ of the network:

![](images/ebb1a94add787b2de9f6892d95d90daba5b3e967506f02e9f8820c2cad179fca.jpg)  
Figure 14.7(a) A typical 2D GISAXS pattern of the BHJ active layer film. (b) 1D GISAXS profiles of $\mathsf { P 3 H T : P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathsf { B M }$ film extracted from the corresponding 2D patterns. $\mathsf { P 3 H T : P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathsf { B M }$ film was first thermal annealed at 30, 60, 100, 130, and $1 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf C$ while their related GISAXS data are recorded. Under the temperature of $1 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathsf C ,$ the GISAXS data were recorded at intervals of 10s. (d) GISAXS intensity calculated by model fitting constituted of the intensities determined by Debye-Bueche model (blue line) and Fractal aggregation model (green line), Source: Liao et al. [30]/Reproduced with permission of Royal Society of Chemistry. (e) The schematic illustration of PffBT4T-2OD $\mathsf { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathsf { B M }$ film with different fullerene aggregation. Source: Li et al. [31]/Reproduced with permission of Elsevier.

$$
R _ { g } = \sqrt { \left( \frac { D ( D + 1 ) } { 2 } \right) } \eta
$$

Furthermore, Wang group [31] further applied this model to fit a highly crystalline PffBT4T-2OD $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ system. As shown in Figure 14.7e, they found that when an amorphous polymer PCDTBT8 was introduced into the highly crystalline PffBT4T-2OD: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ blend, the dimensionality of the $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ aggregation can decrease from 3 to 2.7, delivering a loose aggregation to $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ and providing more PffBT4T-2OD: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ interfaces for charge generation. In addition to the above polydisperse spherical and DAB-Fractal model for GISAXS modeling, other methods such as distorted-wave Born approximation (DwBA) model [32], Guinier approximation [33], polydisperse ellipsoid with hard sphere [34], and Porod approximation [35] including different form and structure factors have also been employed to characterize the morphology of fullerene- and non-fullerene-based OSCs.

In addition, GIsAxs can be transferred into grazing incidence small-angle neutron scattering (GISANS) when X-ray is replaced by a neutron source. Different to GISAXS probing matter through the electron, GISAXS interacts with the sample through nuclear interactions, which enable higher penetration toward most of the elements and results in a better signal-to-noise ratio in detection. Hence, compared to GISAXS, GISANS could probe nanostructure possessing low or non-contrast for X-rays, and the possibility to study vertical composition and even buried structure [36, 37]. For example, Muller-Buschbaum group [38] applied a time of flight (TOF) mode of GISANS to investigate the structure of the $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ film. Since the critical angle for GIsANS depends on the wavelength of neutron, applying GISANS at different neutron wavelengths under a fixed incident allows probing the scattering information of different depths. At small wavelength, the scattering intensity is relating to information of the bulk film. At large wavelength, the incident angle is smaller than the critical angle and therefore is related to structure information at the near surface region. Figure $1 4 . 8 \mathrm { a - d }$ shows the TOF-GISANS image of $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ film measured at the neutron wavelength of 3.7, 4.5, 6.7, and $9 . 9 \mathring \mathrm { A }$ . Here, three main features of a specular reflection peak, a Yoneda peak, and transmitted signal hidden by the beam stop can be observed. Normally, the intensity in the Yoneda region along the $q _ { y }$ is used to interpret the inner nanostructures of the sample. With the increased neutron wavelength, it can be found that the intensity side maxima at the Yoneda peak position first expand to a high- $\cdot q _ { \mathrm { y } }$ range and then disappeared at long neutron wavelengths $( 9 . 2 5 \mathring \mathrm { A } )$ suggesting that the average domain size on the film surface is bigger than that of the inner film. However, it should be noted that performing neutron scattering requires neutron-scattering facilities, which is not easily accessible for users, and neutron scattering always feature low flux, which requires longer measurement time compared to X-ray scattering.

As organic semiconductors always show energy dependence in their optical constants, applying the different energy dependence of the donor and acceptor in the BHJ active layer can also be used to enhance the scattering contrast in a scattering experiment. Resonant soft X-ray scattering (RSoXS) can measure the sample at specific resonant energies and enhances the scattering intensity by several orders of magnitude. Like GISAXS, RSoXS is also processed at small scattering angles. Differently, RSoXS is usually operated in a transmission geometry under vacuum, which is difficult to realize in situ measurements like GISAXs. More importantly, in addition to measuring the multiple length scales of a BHJ film, the best advantage of RSoXS is that it allows measuring the domain purity of components. Figure 14.8e [4] shows a typical 2D RSoXS pattern of a BHJ film. Here, a line cut is extracted from the 2D pattern and used for modeling, and the total scattering intensity (TSI) of the film can be described by the equation below:

$$
\mathrm { T S I } = \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } I ( q ) q ^ { 2 } \mathrm { d } q = 2 \pi ^ { 2 } \Delta \rho _ { 1 2 } ^ { 2 } \phi _ { 1 } \phi _ { 2 } \mathrm { V }
$$

![](images/117318ea9cb0c0ab73055625f1bdc852a2abfa8ab1b61e4b97746a5b88eb82b3.jpg)  
Figure 14.8TOF-GISANS patterns of $\mathsf { P 3 H T : P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathsf { B M }$ film measured at different wavelength of (a) 3.7, (b) 4.5, (c) 6.7, (d) $9 . 9 \mathbb { A } .$ Source: Guo et al. [38]/Reproduced with permission of American Chemical Society. (e) Typical 2D RSoXS image of a BHJ film. Source: Jiao and Ade [4]/Reproduced with permission of John Wiley $\&$ Sons. (f) Integrated scattering profiles and the domain purity of PTB7 $\mathsf { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathsf { B M }$ films cast from CB and CB:DIO solutions. Source: Collins et al. [21]/Reproduced with permission of John Wiley $\&$ Sons.

where the $\Delta \rho _ { 1 2 }$ is the contrast of the electron density between acceptor and donor, $V$ is the total volume of the film being illuminated during scattering, and $\phi _ { 1 }$ and $\phi _ { 2 }$ are the volume fraction of donor and acceptor domains. By considering the straightforward relation between $\phi _ { 1 }$ and $\phi _ { 2 }$ , the normalized total integrated scattering intensity (TSI) values can be calculated to evaluate the average domain purity over all length scales for blends. It should note that the average domain purity received here is not the absolute domain purity. A specimen with the highest TSI is defined as domain purity of 1, while the domain purity of other specimens can be calculated by the difference of TSI. As shown in Figure 14.8f [21], the $\mathrm { P T B 7 : P C _ { 7 0 } B M }$ films formed with or without 1-8-diiodooctane (DIO) additive obtained average domain purity of 1.0 and 0.8, indicating that more mixed region and diffuse interfaces existing in the $\mathrm { P T B 7 : P C _ { 7 0 } B M }$ film processed with DIO.

# 14.2.3 Depth Profile

Since the architecture of OsCs features stacks consisting of multiple functional layers, surfaces and interfaces in OsCs play an important role in the device performance. Consequently, characterizing the vertical stratifications of electron donors and acceptors in a BHJ active layer is also significant for further optimizing morphology and obtaining higher PCE.

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPs) is a spectroscopic technique that can quantify the elements, identify the chemical state and the electronic structure of the film surface by the photoelectric effect, which has widely been used in surface characterization in OsCs. In polymer:fullerene solar cells, as polymer donors often contain sulfur and carbon elements whilst fullerene acceptor only contains carbon element, the sulfur signal S (2p) can be used to represent the content of polymer donors; therefore, the S $( 2 \mathsf { p } ) / \mathsf { C }$ (1s) signal can be applied to deduce the polymer/fullerene ratio in the film. For example, Franky group found that the S $( { 2 \mathrm { p } } ) / \mathrm { C }$ (1s) peak-area ratio in the bottom surface is much large than that in the top surface, implying that there is a PDTs-BTD-rich layer in the bottom surface but a $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ -rich layer in the top surface. Besides, due to the limited inelastic-free path of electrons, the regular XPS can only measure the depth of the surface ${ < } 1 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . To fully characterize vertical morphology, Wang group [39] employed XPS with etching technique to probe the whole vertical morphology information of a PBDB-T:ITIC film. During their measurements, they first cast PBDB-T:ITIC blend film on the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ substrate and then etched the blend film while conducting XPS to measure the distribution of elements at different thickness. Figure 14.9a shows the N (1s), O (1s), S (2p), and Zn (2p) ratio of the PBDB-T:ITIC film at different etching steps. As all $\mathbf { N }$ atoms are from ITIC and most of the S atoms are from PBDB-T, it can be concluded that there is a PBDB-T rich layer at the first $1 0 \mathrm { n m }$ of the film and the PBDB-T:ITIC ratio becomes stable and uniform in the rest of the thickness.

In addition to XPS, secondary-ion mass spectrometry (SIMs) can also probe the surface information of a film by sputtering the film with a focused primary ion beam $( \mathrm { A r } _ { + } )$ while collecting the ejected secondary ions for mass spectrometry analysis. As early as 2004, Janssen group [42] has applied TOF-SIMS to study the depth information of a MDMO-PPV: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ device, indicating the possibility of achieving good resolution in layer-to-layer depth profiling. Later, since the $ { { } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { H } ^ { - } }$ secondary ion is not subject to interference from $^ { 3 2 } \mathrm { S } ^ { - }$ and $^ { 1 6 } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 2 } -$ that has similar mass, more researchers [43] used deuterated acceptors to replace the regular acceptors to enhance the contrast of SIMS and have revealed the vertical morphology of fullerene and non-fullerene systems more accurately. Besides XPS and SIMS, other surface-sensitive techniques such as Auger electron spectroscopy (AES), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and ultraviolet photo-electron spectroscopy (UPS) can also quantify the distribution of elements in a film and have been proved to be efficient methods for characterizing the depth profiles of OSCs.

Near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure (NEXAFS) can measure the transition between the core states to unoccupied orbitals of molecules, which can provide quantification of the mass composition at the surfaces and the buried interface of thin films. In a typical NEXAFS measurement, an X-ray beam will bombard the surface of the film and can be then absorbed when $\mathbf { X }$ -ray radiation is polarized in the direction of the transition dipole moment (TDM) of the electron orbitals of a molecule. As materials possessing different compositions give different spectra,

Figure 14.9(a) Depth profile of PBDB-T:ITIC film measured by XPS with etching technique. (b) Carbon K-edge NEXAF spectra of $\mathsf { P 3 H T : P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathsf { B M }$ films treated with pre-annealing and post-annealing. Source: Chen et al. [40]/Reproduced with permission of American Chemical Society. (c) Neutron scattering reflectivity and (d) scattering length density profiles of $\mathsf { P 1 } \mathrm { { : } P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathsf { B M }$ and $\mathsf { P 2 } { \cdot } \mathsf { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathsf { B M }$ films. Source: Wang et al. [41]/Reproduced with permission of John Wiley $\&$ Sons.

NEXAFS is a good method to study the chain orientation of polymer molecules and the composition near a film surface. Figure 14.9b [40] shows the NEXAFS spectra of $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ pre-annealed and post-annealed films measured in Auger (AEY) and total (TEY) electron yields. Here, two peaks located at 285.0 and $2 8 6 . 4 6 \mathrm { e V }$ are from the $\mathrm { C } { = } \mathrm { C } \pi ^ { * }$ resonances of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ , and the peak at $2 8 5 . 8 5 \mathrm { e V }$ is from the $\mathrm { C } { = } \mathrm { C }$ $\pi ^ { * }$ resonance of P3HT. In the pre-annealed film, it is clear that the $\mathrm { C } { = } \mathrm { C }$ $\pi ^ { * }$ resonances from P3HT exhibit stronger intensity than the one from $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ in the pre-annealed film and become reverse in the post-annealed film, suggesting that there is a P3HT-rich layer in the top surface $\left( 1 0 \mathrm { n m } \right)$ of pre-annealed $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ film but a $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ rich layer in the top surface of the post-annealed P3HT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ film. Furthermore, as AEY and TEY probe the film at the first 1 and $1 0 \mathrm { n m }$ respectively, it allows analyzing the depth information. By comparing the AEY and TEY spectra of the post-annealed film, we can also conclude that the average $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M } / \mathrm { P } 3 \mathrm { H T }$ ratio in the first $1 0 \mathrm { n m }$ is higher than that in the first $1 \mathrm { n m }$

Unlike XPS or DSIMS that can quantify the elements components of the film at different depths, X-ray reflectivity (XRR) and neutron reflectivity (NR) techniques can utilize the difference of electron densities of the components in the film to provide depth information, which allows us to get the depth profile with sub-nanoscale resolution. In a typical NR measurement, neutrons impinge on a sample and are collected by the CCD in a reflection geometry. During the measurement, the ratio of the elastically scattered to incident neutrons is measured as the function of the momentum transfer vector, while the specular reflection could be used for the investigation of the vertical morphology. Unlike XPS or DSIMS that can quantify the elements directly, XRR and NR need further modeling and analysis of the original data. Generally, in the NR modeling, the scattering length densities (SLDs) of the components in the film as well as the substrate should be obtained before fitting, and the film will be fitted into multiple layers with each layer being assigned a thickness, a roughness, and an SLD. The resulting SLD profile is essentially the chemical/density distribution profile as a function of depth perpendicular to the sample surface, and the volume fraction of one component at a particular depth can be easily converted from the fitted SLD value. Wang et al. [41] have studied the vertical morphology of I $\mathrm { \Delta \Omega } ) 1 { : } \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ and $\mathrm { P 2 } { \mathrm { : P C } } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ films by NR. Figure 14.9c,d shows the 1D NR profile, and it can be found that the NR profile of both $\mathrm { P 1 : P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ and $\mathrm { P 2 } { \mathrm { : P C } } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ films is well fitted by a slab model that consists of multiple thin recursive layers. Here, the high SLD of $\mathrm { S i O } _ { x }$ is evidenced by a distinct peak located between the PEDOT:PSS and Si layers, and the location of the $\mathrm { S i } / \mathrm { S i O } _ { x }$ , PEDOT:PSS, and PCDTBT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ interfaces can also be easily identified. In addition, compared to the NR measurements, XRR possesses higher incident energy which only requires a short measurement time. However, XRR also features low contrast of the components; hence, deuterated acceptor or donor materials are always utilized in XRR measurement.

Ellipsometry is a non-destructive characterization technique that can provide the information of optical constants by measuring the changes in the polarization state of the light upon reflection from a thin film. As different components in the BHJ layer always have different optical constants, ellipsometry could be used to measure the vertical-component distribution in the film with further analysis. In 2008, Nelson group [44] used variable-angle spectroscopic ellipsometry (VASE) to study the concentration-depth profiles of as-cast and solvent-annealed $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ blend films. They first obtained the optical constants of the neat P3HT and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ films and then applied an effective medium approximation (EMA) to build the sub-layers whilst simulate the vertical-component distributions of P3HT and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ It should also be noted that the accuracy of the VASE technique for depth profile is highly dependent on the used model. Hence, multi-sample and multi-angle measurements are recommended, together with other complementary characterizations to eliminate the deviation.

In addition, Lu group [7] recently introduced a plasma-etching method to probe the film-depth-dependent light absorption and has successfully resolved the distribution of the vertical components in a polymer:non-fullerene PBDB-T:ITIC film. They applied a low-pressure oxygen plasma to remove the surface layer of the film without damaging the underneath nanomorphology, while measuring the absorption of the blend with different etching degree. As shown in Figure 14.10, PBDB-T and ITIC possess different absorption range; the absorption spectra of each sublayer at different depths can be deduced from the changes of the absorption spectra during step etching.

# 14.3 Morphological Manipulation of Organic Solar Cells

# 14.3.1 Thermal Annealing

As thermal energy is a basic driving force for the molecule movement and morphological rearrangement in a film, heating the BHJ active layer is an effective method for morphology manipulation and has been widely studied. Figure 14.11a shows a typical process of heating the active layer-putting the as-cast active layer film on a hotplate under certain temperature for a certain time, which is also named TA. As early as 2003, Padinger et al. [47] have observed a PCE improvement from $1 \%$ to $3 . 5 \%$ after placing the $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ device on a hotplate with a temperature of $7 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 30 minutes. Later, Heeger group [48] further increased the TA temperature to $1 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and obtained a PCE approaching $5 \%$ in $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ device with improved FF and $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ . They also found that the improvement of the device performance can be attributed to the enhanced crystallinity of P3HT, which leads to prominent phase separation and therefore facilitating charge transport in OsCs. Afterward, TA has been utilized to improve the performance of various high crystalline polymer:fullerene $\left( \mathrm { P f f B T 4 T - 2 O D : P C _ { 7 0 } B M } \right)$ [12], small-molecule-donor:fullerene $\mathrm { \left( B Q R : P C _ { 7 0 } B M \right) }$ [49] systems. It is widely accepted that TA can further encourage molecular alignment and improve phase separation between donors and acceptors toward favorable charge transport and enhanced PCE. On the other hand, it is worth noting that TA could be detrimental to the device performance for some amorphous systems. For instance, Wang et al [50] found that the $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking coherence length of PCDTBT is reduced upon TA even at low temperatures, which leads to a decreased hole mobility and device performance. Samuel group [51] also observed that TA PTB7-Th: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ film at $1 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ could not affect the crystallinity and orientation of PTB7-Th but could induce strong aggregation of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ in the blend film which results in excessive phase separation and reduced exciton dissociation in the device.

In non-fullerene systems, TA has also been demonstrated to be an effective method to optimize the BHJ morphology and improve the efficiencies in some state-of-the-art non-fullerene OSCs including PBDB-T:ITIC, PBDB-T-2F:IT-4F, and PM6:Y6. Compared to the fullerene systems, TA not only could adjust the crystalline structure of the electron donor but can also rearrange the molecular packing of non-fullerene acceptors. For example [45] (Figure 14.11b,c), when PBDB-T:IT-M film is upon TA, not only the $( h O O )$ alkyl chain stacking of PBDB-T is improved but the $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking of IT-M at $1 . 7 \mathring \mathrm { A } ^ { - 1 }$ also exhibits a significant enhancement. With the enhanced $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking of IT-M, absorbance is enhanced and contributes to achieving higher $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ . Furthermore, the effects of TA on the recent high efficiency PM6:Y6 OSCs has been studied by Liu [46] group and Marks [52] group. Liu et al. found that Y6 exhibits a unique 2D packing structure with a polymer-like conjugated backbone oriented normal to the substrate (Figure 14.11d), which is favorable for vertical charge transport. When the PM6:Y6 film is thermally annealed at temperatures of 60 and $8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , the crystal size and diffraction peak area of Y6 are increased, together with enhanced mobility and therefore improved $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and FF of OSCs. However, further increased TA temperature to $1 1 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ is detrimental to the crystalline structure of Y6 and results in reduced device performance (Figure 14.11e). In addition, in Marks's work, although they did not observe any change in the crystalline structure of PM6:Y6 films upon TA, they found that Y6 could migrate to the top surface of the BHJ film and facilitate a favorable vertical structure in the inverted PM6:Y6 devices. As a result, thermal-annealed OSCs obtained effective carrier mobility, leading to improved FF and PCE.

![](images/b304f4d3b88208d98841a149b918bc230c0c2753ce51de915e5fb8ba8448dbee.jpg)

(c) The absorbance of as-cast and thermal-annealed PBDB-T:IT-M films. Source: Liu et al. [45]/Reproduced with permission of Royal Society of Chemistry. It should be emphasized that the TA temperature for different systems could be different due to the unique glass transition temperature $( T _ { \mathrm { g } } )$ of each BHJ active layer. For instance, the optimized TA temperature for the traditional $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ is around $1 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ ; however, it ranges from 80 to $1 1 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for some non-fullerene OSCs. Furthermore, in addition to TA, other methods such as microwave annealing [53] and pulsed laser heating [54] can also deliver thermal energy to the BHJ layer and have been proved to promote the crystallization as well as device performance.

# 14.3.2 Solvent Vapor Annealing

In addition to TA, solvent vapor annealing (SVA) is another method to enhance crys. tallinity of the BHJ active layer. As its name implies, SVA relates to keeping a film in a solvent atmosphere, allowing the rearrangement of molecules toward an equilibrium state (Figure 14.12a). In 2005, Yang group first reported utilizing SVA to control the growth rate of the $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ active layer to enhance the device performance. They found that SVA could encourage P3HT to form a highly ordered $\pi$ -conjugated structure in the film, which not only resulted in facilitated charge transport but also enhanced aggregation of P3HT and consequently improved absorption at long wavelength. The effect of SVA on the morphology of fullerene acceptors has been investigated by Tang et al. [57] They found that solvent annealing of the $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ film with tetrahydrofuran (THF) could increase the domain size of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ clusters to $3 0 \mathrm { n m }$ ; however, it can be reduced to $2 0 \mathrm { n m }$ after SVA with carbon disulfide $( \mathrm { C S } _ { 2 } )$ . This can be explained by the better solubility of $\mathrm { C S } _ { 2 }$ to $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ which partially dissolves the $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ clusters and leads to reduced aggregation. In addition to the polymer:fullerene system, Jones group [58] recently reported that SVA can tune the molecular orientation of a small-molecule donor and fullerene system $\mathrm { ( B T R : P C _ { 7 0 } B M ) }$ , delivering more face-on molecular orientation of BQR in the film and leading to enhanced charge mobility and suppressed recombination in OSCs.

For non-fullerene acceptors, Gurney et al. [55] systemically investigated the effect of solvents used for SVA on the morphology of PTB7-Th:ITIC films. In their work, a range of solvents including Acetone, ${ \mathrm { C S } } _ { 2 }$ , and CB were applied with the same SVA procedure. As shown in Figure 14.12b-d, they found that by exposing the PTB7-Th:ITIC film to $\mathrm { C S } _ { 2 }$ for 60seconds after casting, the film obtained a big increase in the lamellar stacking of PTB7-Th in the in-plane as well as the $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking in both PTB7-Th and ITIC in the out-of-plane direction. However, when acetone, a solvent with high vapor pressure but poor solubility was used for solvent annealing, the PTB7-Th:ITIC film shows a reduction in molecular ordering alongside with less change in the domain size and spacing. As a result, they concluded that the solvent for SVA should possess good solubility and high vapor pressure, to penetrate the active layer and promote molecular ordering. Very recently, Ding group [6] also applied SVA to a high-efficiency D18:Y6 system. As shown in Figure 14.12e,f upon SVA, the high crystalline D18 polymer donor exhibits improved crystallinity and increased crystal size, leading to an unprecedented PCE of $1 8 . 2 \%$

In addition to the regular SVA, Cao group [59] has combined TA and SVA for a BIT6F $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ polymer:fullerene film and has successfully improved the efficiency from $7 \%$ to $9 \%$ with an excellent FF of $7 7 \%$ . They found that SVA could promote the nucleation and growth of BIT-6F crystals in the as-cast film, while the further TA treatment could be beneficial in driving better continuous morphology and maintain small phase separation in the film. Furthermore, Zhang et al. [60] developed an in situ SVA method to solvent-anneal the film during the spin-coating process (SC-SVA). Compared to the regular SVA, SC-SVA can control the aggregation of ITIC small molecules more effectively, avoid the formation of large-scale phase separation in the active layer, and make the device obtain higher exciton dissociation efficiency, resulting in enhanced charge transport and device performance (with the PCE from $6 . 2 5 \%$ to $7 . 2 1 \%$ ). In addition, it should be noted that SVA could be detrimental for some high crystalline fullerene and non-fullerene acceptors. For example, Yang group [61] found that when the SVA time increases to more than one minute, P3HT will crystalize excessively and leads to large phase separation and inefficient exciton dissociation. Besides, Figure $1 4 . 1 2 \mathrm { g } , \mathrm { h }$ shows the optical microscopy images of the as-cast and solvent-annealed PBDB-T:INPIC-4F films [56]. It can be found that SVA promotes the formation of INPIC-4F spherulites and causes large phase separation in the film, leading to reduced device performance.

# 14.3.3 Solvent

During the film-coating process of the BHJ active layers, the surface energy of the solution system will gradually decrease and the evaporation of the solvent will make the solid phase separates from the solution. Consequently, the final morphology of the film is highly dependent on the solvent evaporation rate, viscosity, surface tension, and miscibility of donor and acceptor in a solution system. In 2001, Hummelen et al [62] first studied the effect of solvents on the morphology and performance of MDMO-PPV: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ OSCs. They found that the film cast by toluene exhibits a large phase separation and coarse surface, while the film cast by chlorobenzene shows a homogeneous film and smooth surface, which is attributed to the better solubility of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ in chlorobenzene. Lee et al. [63] found that P3HT tends to form edge-on molecular orientation in the film when casting from the CF solvent but inclined to form face-on molecular orientation when casting from the DCB solvent (Figure 14.13a,b). This is due to the different boiling points of the solvent; DCB possesses a higher boiling point and leads to a slow film-drying process, which allows the alkyl chain of P3HT to orderly organize in the out-of-plane. However, CF has a lower boiling point and enables fast-drying process only to allow the backbone of P3HT to organize in the out-of-plane. Very recently, the effect of the solvent on the morphology of Y6 has also been studied by Liu group [46]. As shown in Figure 14.13c,d, Y6 film cast from CF exhibits a lamellar stacking peak at $0 . 2 7 \mathring { \mathrm { A } } ^ { - 1 }$ in in-plane and a strong $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking peak at $1 . 7 5 \mathring \mathrm { A } ^ { - 1 }$ in out-of-plane, indicating that Y6 molecules take a face-on molecular orientation in the film. However, when CB was used to cast the film, the $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking of Y6 shows a significantly reduced intensity, whilst a strong dispersive diffraction peak can be observed at $1 . 2 \mathring \mathrm { A } ^ { - 1 }$ which is related to the isotropic amorphous Y6. As a result, the PM6:Y6 device fabricated by CF obtained superior efficiency $( 1 6 . 5 \% )$ than that from CB.

![](images/6aae742e9a190cb5df65a731002982373472f9817539658c31886debf0a2e437.jpg)

(e) Schematic illustration of Hansen space which can be used to determine the solubility between a solvent and a solute.

In addition, employing mixed solvent to optimize the morphology and enhance the performance of OsCs has also been studied. For example, Ye et al. [64] designed an efficient ternary mixed solvent for $\mathrm { P D P P 3 T : P C _ { 7 0 } B M }$ OSCs by introducing CF and DIO into the host DCB solvent. In their work, $\mathrm { P D P P 3 T : P C _ { 7 0 } B M }$ film cast from neat DCB solvent possesses large phase separation and rougher interfaces between PDPP3T donor and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ acceptor, resulting in inferior exciton dissociation efficiency and low $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ in OSCs. When CF is combined with DCB, the film obtained improved domain purity. Although it enabled enhanced FF, the $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ is still low due to the relatively large domain size and sharp interfaces. Moreover, when DCB, CF, and DIO are used as mixed solvents simultaneously, the $\mathrm { P D P P 3 T : P C _ { 7 0 } B M }$ film obtained relatively fuzzy donor-acceptor interfaces with small phase separation between PDPP3T and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ , consequently to both enhanced FF and $J _ { \mathrm { s c . } }$ Recently, Wang group [65] also applied a binary solvents approach to optimize the morphology of a polymer:non-fullerene PBDB-T:INPIC-4F system and obtained an improved efficiency from $8 . 1 \%$ to $1 3 . 1 \%$ . They found that casting film with different solvents possessing different boiling points enables the regulation of molecular ordering and phase-separated nanoscale morphology. When the film is cast using CB, the relatively high boiling point of CB could allow INPIC-4F molecules to have enough time to grow up and finally forms large spherulites, resulting in poor exciton dissociation and low $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of solar cells. In contrast, casting film from the low boiling point solvent CF leads to relatively low crystallinity and inferior charge transport, resulting in reduced FF. Encouragingly, when combining CB and CF as a mixed solvent (CB:CF $[ 1 . 5 : 1 , \mathrm { v } / \mathrm { v } ] )$ , small phase separation for charge dissociation and continuous network for charge transport can be realized.

Toxic halogenated solvents such as CB, DCB, and CF can dissolve most of the organic semiconducting materials and deliver favorable morphology in OSCs, which are the most commonly used solvents for BHJ deposition. However, when it comes to the commercialization of OsCs, "halogen-free" green solvents are more attractive as they are environmentally friendly and compatible with sustainable and mass industrial manufacturing. In an attempt to rationally select an alternative solvent to substitute halogenated solvents, Hansen solubility parameters (HSPs) have been utilized to predict and calculate the quality of a solvent. As shown in Figure 14.13e [66], HSP describes the total cohesion energy of the solvent, which is consisting of three parts: dispersion $( \delta _ { \mathrm { d } , } )$ polarity $( \delta _ { \mathfrak { p } } )$ , and hydrogen bonding $( \delta _ { \mathrm { h } } )$ . With the calculation of these three parameters, the miscibility, solubility, and tendency of phase separation between solute and solvent can be examined by:

$$
R _ { \mathrm { a } } ^ { 2 } = 4 \big ( \Delta \delta _ { \mathrm { d } } \big ) ^ { 2 } + \big ( \Delta \delta _ { \mathrm { p } } \big ) ^ { 2 } + \big ( \Delta \delta _ { \mathrm { h } } \big ) ^ { 2 }
$$

where $R _ { \mathrm { a } }$ is the Euclidean distance which can define a 3D Hansen space, and $R _ { 0 }$ is the interaction radius of the dissolvability measured experimentally. $R _ { \mathrm { a } } > R _ { 0 }$ means the solute could dissolve in the solvent, while $R _ { \mathrm { a } } < R _ { 0 }$ suggests the solvent and solute are unlike to mix. Although HSP could not interpret factors such as crystal structures or $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking, it can be used as an instruction to narrow down the selection range of processing solvents. For example, DCB is a good solvent for $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ system, an environmentally friendly solvent system consisting of acetophenone (AP) and mesitylene (MS) can be used to mimic the solubility and similar volatility of DCB based on HSPs and achieve comparable device efficiency. In addition, Yan group [67] also developed a hydrocarbon solvent system 1,2,4-trimethylbenzene (TMB) and 1-phenylnaphthalene (PN) to substitute the traditional CB and DIO solvent system in a temperature-dependent aggregation polymer:fullerene PffBT4T $\mathrm { \cdot } \mathrm { C _ { 9 } C _ { 1 3 } } \mathrm { : P C _ { 7 0 } B M }$ system and obtained a favorable morphology as well as enhanced device efficiency.

In non-fullerene OsCs, Hou group [68] also demonstrated two environmentally friendly solvent mixtures, o-xylene/PN and THF/IPA which can replace the CB:DIO solvent system and exhibit promising prospects for spin-coating and blade-coating-based PBTA-TF:IT-M OSCs.

# 14.3.4 Solvent Additive

Besides using mixed solvents for adjusting the morphology of BHJ active layer in OSCs, incorporating a few percentages of secondary solvent as the additive to the primary host solvent has also been found effective for morphology optimization. DIO is the most widely used solvent additive and has made significant contributions to the OSC field. As early as 2007, Peet et al. [69] reported that introducing $2 \%$ of DIO in the host CB solvent allows PCPDTBT to obtain optimal alky chain conformations in the PCPDTBT: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ blend film during the film-drying process, leading to enhanced aggregation and absorbance of PCPDTBT and improved device efficiency from $2 . 8 \%$ to $5 . 5 \%$ . Later, $\mathrm { Y u }$ group [70] further achieved a record efficiency of $7 . 4 \%$ with the assistance of DIO in the $\mathrm { P T B 7 : P C _ { 7 0 } B M }$ system and found that the improved performance is due to the selective dissolvability of DIO to fullerene, which can reduce the fullerene aggregation in the BHJ active layer (Figure 14.14a,b). Since then, with the utilization of GIWAXS, GISAXS, and TEM, more and more researchers revealed that with a small amount of DIO in the host solvent (e.g. CB, DCB), DIO could increase the crystallinity of the polymer whilst decrease the domain size of fullerene aggregation, which could improve the exciton dissociation efficiency and charge transport ability simultaneously. After that, DIO has been a primary solvent additive for optimizing morphology in polymer:fullerene OSCs (e.g. PTB7-Th: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ $\mathrm { P f f B T 4 T - 2 O D : P C _ { 7 0 } B M }$ PBDB- $\mathrm { T } { : } \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M } ,$ . In polymer:non-fullerene systems, DIO has also been proved to be effective for morphology optimization in a variety of systems (e.g. PBDB-T:ITIC, PTB7-Th:ITIC, PM6:IT-4F, PTB7-Th:IEICO-4F). For example, Ye et al. [71] have demonstrated that DIO can enhance the $\pi { - } \pi$ coherence length of IT-M small molecular acceptor whilst improving the domain purity in PBDB-T:IT-M OSCs, resulting in facilitated charge transport (Figure 14.14c,d). Wang group [73] reported that DIO can promote the $J$ -aggregation of ${ \mathrm { C O } } _ { i } { 8 \mathrm { D F I C } }$ in PTB7-Th:CO,8DFIC blend film, leading to a significant red-shift of absorbance and improved $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and PCE.

Due to the success of DIO, researchers developed a variety of alkanes, mercaptans, and naphthalene solvent additives to assist the micro-nanomorphology optimization in OSCs (Figure 14.14e). In general, there are three guidelines for selecting the additive and host solvent: (i) Host solvent has high solubility to both donor and acceptor, but the solvent additive has selective solubility to one component only. (ii) The host solvent has a lower boiling point, but the solvent additive possesses a higher boiling point. (iii) The solvent additive only accounts for the $0 . 2 { - } 5 \mathrm { v o l } \%$ in the solvent system. On top of these features, host solvent and additives could have different vaporizing speed, allowing donor and acceptor molecules to have different organization manner during the film-drying process. Besides, it is worth noting that the role of solvent additive can be varied depending on their interactions with donor or acceptor materials. For example, octanedithiol additive can increase the crystallinity in the $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ system but could reduce the crystallinity in ${ \mathrm { P } } 3 { \mathrm { H T } } { \mathrm { : I C } } _ { 7 0 } { \mathrm { B A } }$ system [74, 75]. Baran group [76] observed that DIO has a contrasting effect on the microstructure and device performance of $\mathrm { P T B 7 - T h : P C _ { 7 0 } B M }$ and PTB7-Th:ITIC OSCs. Despite the positive impact of DIO (with $3 \mathrm { v o l } \%$ in CB) in $\mathrm { P T B 7 - T h } { \mathrm { : P C } } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ to weak fullerene aggregation, DIO can increase the phase separation between PTB7-Th and ITIC resulting in unfavorable exciton dissociation. Furthermore, the content of the additive to the host solvent is crucial, with slight change could lead to contrasting morphology and device performance. For example, Bazan group noticed that incorporating $0 . 5 \%$ or $1 \%$ of DIO in CF host solvent could reduce the fullerene aggregation and encourage small phase separation in the PSFSiF: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ film, but with the incorporation of $5 \%$ DIO could allow a slower crystallization of the active layer and result in large phase separation.

Furthermore, employing multiple additives to optimize the morphology and device performance has also been studied. Ma and coworkers [72] have combined ODT and DIO as a binary additive to work with CB host solvent. By applying in situ GIWAXS, TEM, and R-SoXS measurements, they found that ODT tends to work at the beginning of the film-forming process which could control the nucleation of the crystals, while DIO works throughout the whole film-forming process which can control the crystal growth. They received an active layer that could not only maintain the small domain size like as-cast film but also get enhanced crystallinity (Figure 14.14f). In addition to the morphology optimization, solvent additive has been reported to enhance the morphology stability in OsCs. For example, Zhan's group [77] has applied a solvent additive $^ { 4 , 4 ^ { \prime } }$ bisphenol (BPO) in a variety of fluoropolymer:fullerene systems. They found that BPO not only can improve the crystallinity of fluoropolymer whilst enhancing its light absorption ability and carrier transport ability but could also form hydrogen bonds between fluoropolymer polymers and fullerene. The formation of hydrogen bonds could lock the polymer donor and fullerene acceptor in the active layer and prevent them to aggregate, leading to improved morphology stability. As a result, the $\mathrm { P T B 7 - T h : P C _ { 7 0 } B M }$ device fabricated with BPO could maintain $8 0 \%$ PCE after heat treatment at $1 3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ exhibiting superior morphology stability than the device fabricated without BPO - $5 0 \%$ drop in PCE).

# 14.3.5 Solid Additive

Although solvent additives are very effective for morphology optimization and have been widely used in the current high-performance solar cells, they could be trapped in the BHJ layer due to their high boiling points and have adverse effects on the device stability and reproducibility in large-scale production [78, 79]. Consequently, solid additive has been studied to adjust the morphology of OsCs. As early as 2014, Moon et al. [80] designed a small-molecule 2,2,3,3,4,4,4-heptafluoro $. N$ -phenyl-butyr-amide (F-ADD) as solid additive to tune the vertical morphology of the $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ film. They found that F-ADD is not immiscible with P3HT, but highly miscible with $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ due to the $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking between the core of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ and the benzene moiety of F-ADD. Due to this selective interaction with $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ , F-ADD can tune the surface energy of F-ADD and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ mixture and induce a gradient nanostructure alignment in the vertical direction. Later, Park and co-authors [81] further designed a solid additive, tetrabromothiophene (Br-ADD), which could selectively interact with PTB7 to increase the surface energy of PTB7 (from 25.04 to $3 0 . 1 6 \mathrm { m N m ^ { - 1 } }$ ), reaching values comparable to that of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ $3 6 . 3 6 \mathrm { m N m ^ { - 1 } }$ . As a result, Br-ADD not only delivered a smoother surface and well-mixed heterojunction but also changed the PTB7 and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ distribution in the vertical direction in the film.

The current non-fullerene acceptors are featured with an A-D-A structure consisting of a planar electron-donating backbone, two electron-withdrawing terminal groups, and alkyl chains. Due to the strong steric hindrance effect from the side chains, it is difficult for the electron-donating backbone to form intermolecular stacking for efficient $\pi$ -orbital overlaps; therefore, the electron transport mainly occurred between the terminal groups of two adjacent A-D-A molecules. On top of this principle, Hou group [82] designed a volatilizable solid additive SA-1 that can volatilize out of the active layer after TA. As shown in Figure 14.15, SA-1 possesses good miscibility and similar structure to the electron-withdrawing end groups of the A-D-A type IT-4F acceptor. Upon TA, the volatilization of SA-1 in the PBDB-TF:IT-4F blend film can induce the rearrangement of IT-4F to form strong intermolecular $\pi { - } \pi$ interaction, leading to enhanced charge transport and PCE. More importantly, compared to the conventional DIO additive which exhibits bad morphology stability as slow evaporation of the residual DIO in the film could induce large aggregation of IT-4F, SA-1 can volatilize out of the film and lead to superior morphology stability. Later, Hou and Ma group [83] have further investigated the effect of the volatilization of those solid additives on morphology optimization. As shown in Figure 14.15, they found that although both SA-4 and SA-7 could facilitate ordered molecular arrangements, their different volatilization leads to different morphology features and device performance. SA-4 possesses stronger volatility, which allows it to volatilize out from the active layer completely, however, SA-7 possesses inferior volatility; therefore, part of SA-7 could be trapped in the BHJ active layer and cast a negative effect on the morphology stability. Very recently, Cai et al. [84] designed three volatilizable additives with different degrees of fluorination. They found that although these additives can be evaporated upon moderate TA, more fluorine atoms on their chemical structures could lead to enhanced intermolecular $\pi { - } \pi$ stacking, encouraging the PCE increased from $1 5 . 2 \%$ to $1 6 . 5 \%$ in PM6:Y6 OSCs. With further molecular dynamic simulations, they revealed the attractive interaction between these additives and Y6.

# 14.3.6 Substrate Effect

During the film-forming process of a BHJ film, the substrate of the casting solution can also affect the morphology. This is associated with the physical and chemical interactions between the substrate and the solution, which could modulate molecular arrangement in the film. As early as 2007, Campoy-quiles et al. [44] observed that casting the $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ film on PEDOT:PSS or a hydrophobic substrate could induce different vertical segregation of P3HT and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ components in the BHJ layer. The result can be well explained by the different surface energy of P3HT, $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ as well as PEDOT:PSS and hydrophobic substrates. P3HT possesses lower surface energy than $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ , P3HT will be driven to the interface with air to lower the energy of the free surface when casting on PEDOT:PSS substrate. In contrast, when the $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 0 } B M }$ film was cast on the hydrophobic substrate, P3HT is more compatible with the hydrophobic substrate having high surface energy and preferentially attracted to the bottom surface. In addition to surface energy, Bjorstrom et al. [85] reported that the nature of the substrate could also affect the vertical composition distributions in the APFO- $3 { : } \mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ film. In their work, although silicon substrate exhibits similar surface energy to gold substrate, a $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ -rich phase can be found close to the bottom substrate when the blend film is cast on silicon, while the bottom interface is enriched with APFO-3 when the blend film is cast on gold. This is attributed to the chemical interactions between APFO-3 and gold, as the thiophene groups in the APFO-3 backbone could self-assembly on gold substrate and drive the polymer to the bottom surface.

In non-fullerene systems, the effect of substrates on the three-dimensional morphology and device performance has also been studied. As shown in Figure 14.16a,b, Wang group [86] has applied XPS with etching technique to characterize the PBDB-T:IT-M films cast on PEDOT:PSS and $\mathrm { T i O } _ { 2 }$ substrate with different TA conditions. They found that casting film on PEDOT:PSS or $\mathrm { T i O } _ { 2 }$ at room temperature or $8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ has a similar effect to the vertical separation of PBDB-T and IT-M in the BHJ film: a PBDB-T-rich layer can be clearly seen in the first $1 0 \mathrm { n m }$ of the top surface. However, when the active layers were thermally-annealed at high temperature $( 1 6 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ , this PBDB-T-rich surface layer remained on the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ substrate based film but disappeared on the PEDOT:PSS substrate-based film. This phenomenon can be explained by the interaction between PEDOT:PSS and PBDB-T. During the high TA process, PBDB-T can diffuse to the bottom surface and trapped by the existence of PEDOT:PSS.

In addition, the substrate effect on the film-forming process has also been demonstrated to affect the molecular order and aggregation of the donor and the acceptor in a BHJ active layer. For example, Chen and Yan group [87, 88] reported a high crystalline conjugated polymer electron-donor PffBT4T-2OD which exhibits a strong temperature-dependent aggregation behavior in solution. When the $\mathrm { P f f B 4 T - } 2 \mathrm { O D } { : } \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ blend film is cast on a substrate at relatively low temperature $( 9 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ , the strong aggregation of PffBT4T-2OD will make it form a face-on molecular orientation and result in facilitated hole mobility as well as enhanced PCE. In contrast, when the PffB4T-2OD: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 0 } \mathrm { B M }$ blend film is cast on a substrate with high temperature $( 1 3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ , the polymer chains of PffBT4T-2OD can be disaggregated during film formation, allowing the alky chains of PffBT4T-2D organize lamellar stacking in the out-of-plane and this converts the molecular order of PffBT4T-OD from face-on to edge-on. Very recently, Wang group [19, 56] also reported that casting film on a $1 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ hot substrate can inhibit the self-organization of several high crystalline non-fullerene acceptors during the film-forming process. As shown in Figure 14.16c-h, casting the PTB7-Th:CO,8DFIC film at room temperature makes ${ \mathrm { C O } } _ { i } { 8 \mathrm { D F I C } }$ has enough time to self-organize, allowing ${ \mathrm { C O } } _ { i } { 8 \mathrm { D F I C } }$ molecules to form large fibrils with edge-on and flat-on molecular orientations (More pronounced when solvent annealing is assisted to increase the crystallinity). Inversely, casting PTB7-Th:CO;8DFIC film on a $1 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ hot substrate could suppress the crystallization of ${ \mathrm { C O } } _ { i } { 8 \mathrm { D F I C } }$ effectively whilst convert ${ \mathrm { C O } } _ { i } { 8 \mathrm { D F I C } }$ lamellar crystallites into face-on-oriented $H$ and $J .$ - type aggregates, which not only improves the charge transport ability but also blue-shifts and red-shifts the ${ \mathrm { C O } } _ { i } { 8 \mathrm { D F I C } }$ absorbance simultaneously and therefore enhances the light absorption ability.

# 14.4 Conclusion

In this chapter, we have reviewed a wide range of morphological characterization methods covering microscopic, scattering, and spectroscopic techniques that are capable of investigating the domain size, phase separation, miscibility, domain purity, and depth profiles of the BHJ active layer from microscale to nanoscale. We have also summarized a range of morphological manipulation methods for both fullerene- and non-fullerene-based BHJ active layers. The principle of those morphological manipulation methods as well as their correlation with the morphology development and device performance were discussed in detail. This chapter has shown the significance of understanding and further optimizing the BHJ morphology for the eventual success of OSC technology.

As we discussed above, compared to the traditional balllike fullerene acceptors, the novel non-fullerene acceptors possess similar chemical structure to the electron donor. The use of nonfullerene acceptors not only reduces contrast for morphology characterization using such as TEM and GISAXS but also renders more complicated morphological metrics and photovoltaic processes in polymer:non-fullerene OSCs. This brings challenges as well as opportunities to manipulate the morphology and performance of non-fullerene OSCs.

With the rising of non-fullerene acceptors, OsCs have experienced rapid development in the last six years and have stepped into the door of commercialization. More studies on morphologies in OsCs should emphasis on the transition from laboratory based to industrially relevant processes. Designing environmentally friendly solution-processing techniques while achieving ideal morphology to realize efficient, thick-junction and large-area OsCs would emerge shortly as the top priority in the community.
