# 15.1 Introduction

Organic solar cells (OsCs) are an attractive alternative to traditional inorganic solar cells. The development of solution-processable OSCs has attracted great interest due to its low-cost non-vacuum process technology. The organic semiconductors also exhibit a remarkable flexibility in turning the material properties such as molecular weight, light absorption, energy bandgap for new device concepts. The organic photovoltaic technology creates a pathway to design new semiconductor materials that can be integrated with organic-organic and nanostructure-organic composites for novel applications. A variety of organic optoelectronic systems are being explored for application in organic light-emitting diode (OLED) displays and lighting [1], organic field effect transistors [2], organic photodetectors [3, 4], OsCs [5, 6], organic photonics in communication [7], all-polymeric opto-couplers [8-10], chemical sensing [11, 12], biosensing [13], refractometers [14], memory [15], organic optical sensors [16], and optical integrated systems [17].

Organic electronic technology is highly promising as it can produce higher profitability in advanced OLED-based flat panel displays, OLED solid-state lighting, and OSCs. For example, OSCs are a potentially attractive alternative to inorganic counterparts and the development of solution-processable OSCs has attracted great interests due to its low-cost non-vacuum process photovoltaic technology. Power conversion efficiency (PCE) of ${ > } 1 8 \%$ for both single junction and tandem OSCs [18, 19] has been reported due to the development of low bandgap photoactive organic semiconductors and improved device design [20, 21].

A broad range of distinct device technologies based on small organic molecules and polymeric photoactive materials are rapidly developing. Apart from the encouraging results in achieving high PCE for OSCs, realizing stabile performance of OsCs over a long operation lifetime also attracts a significant research effort. The commonly used bulk heterojunction (BHJ) OSCs, forming a regular configuration OsC, have a donor/acceptor blend sandwiched between a front transparent indium tin oxide (ITO) anode and a reflective rear metal cathode. In regular configuration OsCs, a hole-transporting buffer layer of poly(3,4-ethylene dioxythiophene):(polystyrene sulfuric acid) (PEDOT:PSS) is often deposited on an ITO surface to assist in hole transport and hole extraction at the ITO/organic interface. It has been shown that the use of acidic PEDOr:Pss hole-transporting layer is not the best choice for efficient operation of OsCs over a long period of time due to the deterioration in the contact property at the ITO/PEDOT:PSS interface [22]. The upper metallic cathode in regular configuration OSCs often undergoes a gradual oxidation resulting in a thermally unstable cathode/organic interface [23].

A comprehensive study on the degradation mechanisms of the regular configuration OSCs has been performed. The unbalanced charge mobility in the photoactive layer, due to oxygen-induced charge traps, is one of the degradation mechanisms [24]. In a previous work, two distinguishable degradation pathways in the regular configuration OSCs were identified [25]. One is associated with a localized failure related to the moisture encroachment in the charge generation area, inducing the charge recombination and thus eliminating the photocurrent. The other is dominated by an inevitable initial oxidation at the organic/cathode interface due to the presence of residual moisture and oxygen, leading to lowering PCE of OSCs. The degradation caused by the interfacial passivation can be avoided by the removal of the low work function cathode. This implies that the reverse configuration with a relatively environmental sensitive cathode/organic interface away from the top contact in the cell is preferred compared to the regular configuration OSCs.

Inverted or reverse configuration OsCs, having an organic functional photoactive layer sandwiched between a front transparent cathode and a rear anode, are preferable for efficient cell operation. In this device configuration, a PEDOT:PSS hole-transporting layer is nonexistent, avoiding the use of acidic PEDOT:PSS on ITO surface. In inverted OSCs, ITO surface is often modified with a suitable low work function electron extraction layer (EEL), for example, solution-processable ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ [5], $\mathrm { T i O } _ { 2 }$ [26] and ${ \mathrm { C s } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { C O } } _ { 3 }$ [27], low work function metals of Ca [28] and Al [29], and surface dipole-inducing materials [30].

In parallel to the development of new functional organic semiconductors, the detailed understanding of photo-generated exciton dynamics, charge transport, and recombination processes is another key to improving the performance of OSCs. The excited states in the photoactive organic films have been studied by the steady state photo-induced absorption using pump-probe technique [31]. For example, relaxation processes and dynamics of charge separation (from exciton) to charge transfer (CT) exciton at the donor (D)/acceptor (A) interface and the succeeding dissociation to free charges have been reported [32-34]. It has been shown that a significant amount of CT excitons can be recombined at the D/A interface before they are able to completely separate to form mobile charges [32, 34]. Various processes such as thermal annealing [33] or new syntheses route [35] can alter the morphology of the functional organic semiconductor layer and subsequently impact the relaxation dynamics and free charge yields. The recent progresses on electrode/organic interfacial engineering, interfacial exciton dissociation at the metal/organic interface, charge collection, and operational stability of solution-processed OsCs are discussed in the following sections.

# 15.2 Bimolecular Recombination in Organic Solar Cells

The emerging organic photovoltaic technology creates a pathway of manufacturing solar cells from conventional vacuum deposition methods to solution-processable techniques. Exciton dissociation at the donor/accepter interface governs the photocurrent generation and that at the organic/electrode interfaces are critical for charge collection in OsCs. Electronic properties at the metal/organic interface in OSCs have been investigated using in situ photoelectron spectroscopy. The rapid exciton dissociation at the metal/organic interface also has a profound effect on charge collection and a long-term stability of OsCs. However, it cannot be revealed using these approaches. It also is hardly observed in the measurement of current density-voltage $\left( J - V \right)$ characteristics under the steady state conditions, for example, measured under AM 1.5G illumination of $1 0 0 \mathrm { m W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . The intensity of the solar simulator used for the measurement of OsCs is usually calibrated using a silicon reference cell (with a KG-5 visible color filter) to minimize the spectral mismatch.

In this section, performance of BHJ OsCs made with the blend system of poly[[4,8-bis[(2-ethylhexyl)oxy]benzo[1,2 $. b ; 4 , 5 - b ^ { \prime }$ ]dithiophene-2,6-diyl][3-fluoro-2- [(2-ethylhexyl)carbonyl]thieno[3,4-b]thiophenediyl]](PTB7):[6,6]-phenyl-C71- butyric acid methyl ester $( \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } )$ is discussed. The charge recombination processes, the distribution of charge density under different operation conditions, and charge collection at the organic/electrode interfaces in $\mathrm { P T B 7 { : } P C _ { 7 1 } B N }$ I-based OSCs are studied systematically using a combination of theoretical calculation, transient photocurrent (TPC) measurements, morphology analyses, and device optimization. The charge transport and recombination properties in the BHJ OSCs are investigated using the photo-induced charge extraction by linearly increasing voltage (photo-CELIV) method. Combined with light intensity-dependent $J { - } V$ characteristic and external quantum efficiency (EQE), it is shown that the use of ZnO EEL has a profound effect on enhancing charge collection efficiency and thereby improving the overall performance of OsCs. The origin of the improvement in the cell performance is mainly associated with the improved charge collection efficiency. Light intensity-dependent $J { - } V$ characteristics and the photo-CELIV results suggest that the charge recombination at the organic/cathode interface can be effectively suppressed by inserting an ultrathin ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL, leading to a significant improvement in the charge collection efficiency.

# 15.2.1 Effect of Metal Oxide Interlayer on Cell Performance

Despite the rapid growth during the last decade, the performance of OsCs, associated with low charge mobility and unstable organic/electrode interfacial properties, have placed a limitation on practical applications. The diffusion length of the excitons is only within a few nanometers. Exciton dissociation at the D/A interface determines the photocurrent generation [36]. To facilitate efficient separation of photo-induced excitons, the BHJ is introduced to minimize the domain size on nanometer scale, thereby to facilitate the efficient exciton dissociation [37, 38]. However, the high interfacial area in BHJ could also lead to increasing recombination of the photo-excited carriers, which is one of the main loss mechanisms that limits the photocurrent generation in the cells [39]. The processes of charge collection and recombination in OsCs are critical factors influencing the short-circuit current density $( J _ { \mathrm { s c } } )$ and fill factor (FF), hence the PCE of OsCs [35, 40]. The interfacial properties at the organic/electrode interfaces have a profound impact on charge collection, efficiency, and operation stability of OsCs. To improve the performance of OSCs, it is important to understand charge recombination, transport, and collection processes in the cells, and the effects on the cell performance.

The loss of the photo-generated carriers due to recombination includes monomolecular and bimolecular recombination processes. Monomolecular recombination is considered as the first-order recombination process, where the charges in the excited states are still bounded due to the Coulomb interaction. It takes place between charges from the same excitons [39, 41, 42]. Monomolecular recombination process occurs in the OSCs that are operated typically in the voltage range between the short-circuit condition and maximum power point, due to the low carrier mobility and strong Coulomb interaction between the charges in the excited states in the organic BHJ blend.

The bimolecular recombination is the recombination process that occurs between the photo-generated electrons and holes before they are collected by the respective electrodes in the cells [40, 43]. Bimolecular recombination is one of the main losses affecting the charge transport in the BHJ and charge collection at the organic/electrode interface, resulting in inefficient charge extraction. Bimolecular recombination process has a strong impact on the FF. It is dominated in the OSCs operated at a relatively low effective potential across the active region, e.g. corresponding to the cells that are operated over the voltage range between the maximum power point and open-circuit condition.

Recombination of the charges prior to the charge collection at the organic/ electrode interface has been identified as one of the most critical factors limiting the device performance [36, 44]. Different charge extraction layers, including EEL and hole extraction layer (HEL), are used to engineer the organic/electrode interfaces to minimize the recombination loss and therefore to enhance the charge collection efficiency. The use of the appropriate charge extraction layer also helps to modify the surface of the electrodes forming a desired ohmic contact at the BHJ/electrode interface, avoiding the formation of unfavorable interface dipoles and carrier traps for efficient device operation [45-49]. An ultrathin ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL is one of the most commonly applied cathode interlayers, which can be prepared by the different solution fabrication processes [20, 50-52]. It has been reported that the morphology and surface properties of ZnO EEL have a great impact on the cell performance. The performance of the cells also is influenced by the process conditions of ZnO EEL, e.g. ZnO formulation [53], process condition [54], and post-deposition treatment [55].

The effect of ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL on charge recombination and collection process and thereby the performance reproducibility of the solution-processed OsCs are analyzed systematically using a combination of photo-CELIV, TPC, and light intensity-dependent $J { - } V$ characteristic measurements. In the study, a $3 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ -thick PEDOT:PSS (Baytron PVP AI4083) was first spin-coated onto the pre-cleaned ITO substrate and annealed at $1 4 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in air for 10 minutes. A $9 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ -thick PTB7: $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ layer was then formed on the surface of PEDOT:PSS by spin-coating the polymer blend solution at $2 0 0 0 \mathrm { r p m }$ for 120 seconds inside glove box. After drying at room temperature for ${ \sim } 1$ hour, a $2 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ -think ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL was spin-coated on the surface of the active layer. Finally, samples were transferred to an adjacent vacuum evaporator for the deposition of a $1 0 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ -thick Al top contact. OsCs thus made have a device structure of ITO/PEDOT:PSS $( 3 0 \ \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { P T B 7 { : } P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ $( 9 0 \mathrm { \ n m } ) / \mathrm { Z n O }$ $( 2 0 \ \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { A l }$ - $\cdot 1 0 0 \ \mathrm { n m } ,$ . A structurally identical control cell without the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL was made for comparison studies.

The $J { - } V$ characteristics of OsCs with a ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL and control cell measured under $\mathrm { A M } 1 . 5 \mathrm { G }$ illumination $\mathrm { ( 1 0 0 ~ m W ~ c m ^ { - 2 } }$ ) are plotted in Figure 15.1a. The cell parameters obtained for both types of cells are summarized in Table 15.1. It can be found in Figure 15.1 that an obvious improvement in FF is obtained when an ultrathin ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL is used, which is achieved without any compensation in $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and open-circuit voltage $( V _ { \mathrm { o c } } )$ as compared to that of the optimized control cell. The cell with a $2 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ -thick ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL produces a high FF of $7 2 . 9 4 \%$ as compared to that of the control cell $( 6 7 . 2 3 \% )$ . This leads to improving the PCE from $7 . 0 3 \%$ to $7 . 6 9 \%$ . As shown in Table 15.1, the OSC with a ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL also has a relatively lower series resistance $( R _ { \mathrm { S } } )$ and higher shunt resistance $( R _ { \mathrm { S H } } )$ compared to that of the control cell. $R _ { \mathrm { { S } } }$ and $R _ { \mathrm { S H } }$ seen in the OSC are associated with the charge transport and extraction at the organic/electrode interface, affecting FF of the cell. The results suggest that the use of a ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL improves the contact quality of the active layer/Al interface, leading to a significant reduction in the leakage current, seen in the dark $J { - } V$ characteristics in Figure 15.1b [24]. As a result, the use of the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL contributes to the enhanced charge extraction and collection capability in the cells.

# 15.2.2 Charge Recombination Processes in Organic Solar Cells

The charge mobility and recombination process are important factors determining the performance of OSCs. The effect of the ZnO EEL on bimolecular recombination coefficient and concentration of the photo-excited charges in the OsCs are studied using photo-CELIV measurements. Photo-CELIV is a powerful technique for analyzing the extracted density of carriers by varying the delay time, providing an efficient way to investigate both the carrier mobility and recombination dynamics [24, 56-60]. In the photo-CELIV measurement, a laser pulse is introduced to generate the photo-carriers. The photocurrent extracted under the linearly increasing voltage pulse can then be recorded using an oscilloscope. A reverse bias linearly increasing voltage pulse with a voltage rise speed $A = \mathrm { d } U / \mathrm { d } t$ is used in the measurement. The photo-generated charges can be extracted by adjusting the delay time between the laser pulse and the voltage pulse. The time taken to reach the extraction current maximum $( t _ { \operatorname* { m a x } } )$ and the maximum current due to photoexcitation $( \Delta j )$ can be estimated from the photo-CELIV transients. The charge mobility $\left( \mu \right)$ can be calculated using Eq. (15.1) as given below:

$$
\mu = \frac { 2 d ^ { 2 } } { 3 { A t _ { \operatorname* { m a x } } } ^ { 2 } \left[ 1 + 0 . 3 6 \frac { \Delta j } { j ( 0 ) } \right] }
$$

Equation (15.1) is corrected for the electric field re-distribution during the charge extraction process. By selecting the proper voltage rise speed $A$ and the forward offset voltage $U _ { \mathrm { o f f s e t } }$ in the photo-CELIV measurements, the photo-CELIV transients are recorded for OSCs with a thin ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL and the control cell over a delay time range from 5 to $1 0 0 0 \mu \mathrm { s }$ $U _ { \mathrm { o f f s e t } }$ is set to be $- 0 . 6 \mathrm { V } ,$ which is very close to the built-in potential in the cell.

Figure 15.2 presents the typical photo-CELIV transients measured for the OSCs using different delay times of 5 and $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { s }$ The carrier mobility results, calculated using Eq. (15.1), show that the effective carrier mobility $\mu$ in the device with a $\mathrm { Z n O } / \mathrm { A l }$ cathode is higher than that of the control cell. For example, with a delay time of $5 \mu \mathrm { s }$ used in the photo-CELIV measurement, the mobility for the carriers in the device with a $\mathrm { Z n O } / \mathrm { A l }$ contact is estimated to be $2 . 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 3 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \ \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ , which is higher than that of the control cell $( 9 . 7 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { V } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 } )$ . This reveals that the incorporation of a thin ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer promotes the efficient carrier transport in the cells.

![](images/05a0cd1b8cacb2da5e4818cb1ab2c34f422cb64cc1cd95504bdeb54a121dcebb.jpg)  
Figure 15.3 Double logarithmic plot of delay time-dependent (a) carrier concentration characteristics and (b) bimolecular recombination coefficients obtained for OSC with a $2 0 \cdot \mathsf { n m }$ -thick $z _ { \mathsf { n O } }$ interlayer and the control cell. Source: Weixia Lan.

Figure 15.3a exhibits the double logarithmic plot of delay time-dependent density of the carriers in the blend layer, obtained by integrating the photo-CELIV transients over time (dots) as well as the corresponding curve fitting data (solid lines). The carrier density includes the total number of the remaining photo-generated charges after the recombination. The number of the extracted carriers varies with the delay time used in the photo-CELIV measurements. Two distinguishable different delay time-dependent $n ( t )$ behaviors can be seen in Figure 15.3a. First, the density of total extracted charges decreases with the increase in the delay time for both devices. This behavior reflects that the longer the delay time is applied, the lesser the photo-generated carriers can be collected due to the recombination processes. Second, both types of devices exhibit different delay time-dependent carrier density characteristics. The fitting results suggest the power law dependence between the density of the carriers and the delay time for the control device. While for the OSC with a $2 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ -thick ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer, $n ( t )$ exhibits a much faster decay as the delay time increases. At a shorter delay time, the density of the carriers in OSC with a ZnO EEL is higher than that of the control cell, while it is much lower when delay time is in the order of several hundred $\mu \mathrm { s }$ , suggesting higher-order dependence between delay time and carrier density in OSC with a ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL [60].

The different delay time-dependent $n ( t )$ behaviors in OsCs having dissimilar contacts were observed in the transient absorption spectrum (TAS) experiments reported for a number of different polymer/PCBM systems [61, 62]. A multiple trapping model, involving free and localized holes, is used to explain the phenomena. For the fast decay phase, it is assigned to the bimolecular recombination due to the presence of a large population of free holes in the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOmO), which is usually observed more clearly with high carrier densities when the density of photo-generated charges exceeds the density of localized states. Conversely, the slower phase is due to the limited bimolecular recombination of dissociated charges due to the trap states. Furthermore, $n ( t )$ decay dynamics can also be influenced by the nonuniform charge distribution located at the organic/electrode interfaces. The modification of the contact properties is mainly responsible for the change in recombination processes observed for both types of the cells, as seen in Figure 15.3, since the fabrication process conditions of the cells are identical.

Based on the bimolecular recombination model, the delay time-dependent density of electrons $n ( t )$ , and density of holes $p ( t )$ , can be expressed by [56]:

$$
n ( t ) = p ( t ) = \frac { n ( 0 ) } { 1 + ( t / \tau _ { \mathrm { B } } ) ^ { \gamma } }
$$

where $n ( 0 )$ is the initial carrier density, $t$ is the delay time, $\tau _ { B }$ is the bimolecular recombination lifetime, and $\gamma$ $( 0 < \gamma \leq 1 )$ is the dispersion parameter. Solid curves in Figure 15.3a are the theoretical fitting using Eq. (15.2), indicating that $n ( t )$ derived by photo-CELIV measurements are in good agreement with the results obtained by the bimolecular recombination model. The fitted results of $n ( 0 )$ $\tau _ { \mathrm { B } }$ , and $\gamma$ for different cells are summarized in Table 15.2. The $\gamma$ values calculated for the control device and cell with a $2 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ -thick ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL are 0.26 and 0.98, respectively. The small y value derived from the photo-CELIV measurements implies that a highly dispersive recombination process dominates in the control cell, whereas a high $\gamma$ of 0.98 suggests that an almost nondispersive recombination (for $\gamma = 1 \mathrm { \ i }$ ) is anticipated in the OSCs with a thin ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL-modified cathode [56].

According to the delay time-dependent bimolecular recombination equation:

$$
{ \frac { \mathrm { d } n } { \mathrm { d } t } } = { \frac { \mathrm { d } p } { \mathrm { d } t } } = - \beta ( t ) n p
$$

The bimolecular recombination coefficient $\beta ( t )$ as a function of carrier density $n ( t )$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\beta ( t ) = - \frac { \mathrm { d } n ( t ) \big / \mathrm { d } t } { n ^ { 2 } ( t ) }
$$

Table 15.2 Values of bimolecular recombination lifetime $\tau _ { \mathsf { B } }$ and dispersion parameter $\gamma$ obtained for both types of the cells, acquired by the curve fitting using Eq. (15.2).   

<table><tr><td></td><td>n(0) (cm-3)</td><td></td><td>TB (s)</td></tr><tr><td>ZnO/Al</td><td>4.12  1015</td><td>0.98</td><td>21.41</td></tr><tr><td>Al</td><td>1.27  1015</td><td>0.26</td><td>0.01</td></tr></table>

Combining Eqs. (15.2) and (15.3), $\beta ( t )$ can also be expressed as:

$$
\beta ( t ) = a \gamma n _ { 0 } ^ { - 1 } ( a t ) ^ { \gamma - 1 }
$$

where $a = 1 / \tau _ { \mathrm { B } }$ and $\tau _ { \mathrm { B } }$ is defined as the "effective' bimolecular recombination lifetime $\begin{array} { r } { \left( \tau _ { \mathrm { B } } = \left\{ \frac { \gamma } { [ n ( 0 ) \beta _ { 0 } ] } \right\} ^ { 1 / \gamma } \right) } \end{array}$ The "effective"' bimolecular recombination lifetime $\tau _ { \mathrm { B } }$ in the OSC with a ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer is $2 . 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }$ second, obtained from the curve fitting using Eq. (15.5). This is 4 orders of magnitude higher than that of the control cell $( 9 . 6 \times 1 0 ^ { - 9 }$ second). One crucial factor for a high bimolecular recombination coefficient of an OsC is that the bimolecular recombination lifetime of the carriers should be higher than their transit time in the intrinsic electric field. The improved bimolecular recombination lifetime is beneficial for efficient carrier transport and collection, and thereby a higher bimolecular recombination coefficient of a solar cell.

The relationship between $\beta ( t )$ and $t$ can then be achieved by substituting the previously fitted parameters $n ( 0 )$ $\tau _ { \mathrm { B } }$ and $\gamma$ into Eq. (15.5), which is presented in Figure 15.3b. The results reveal different power law dependences between $\beta ( t )$ and delay time for two cells with different cathode structures. For OSC with a $2 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ -thick ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer, the bimolecular recombination coefficient is almost independent on the delay time, with a constant $\beta$ value of $\sim 1 . 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 1 1 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } \ \mathrm { s } ^ { - 1 }$ While for the control device, $\beta$ shows a significant dependence on the delay time. A decrease by 2 orders of magnitude in $\beta$ is observed for the control cell when the delay time in the photo-CELIV measurements increases from 5 to $1 0 0 \mu \mathrm { s }$ The similar delay time dependency on $\beta$ was also observed in the P3HT:PCBM and other blend systems, measured by TAS measurements [61]. The behavior of delay time-dependent bimolecular recombination coefficient in an OsC is closely associated with the trap-limited recombination processes. Therefore, compared to the power law dependency between the delay time and $n ( t )$ observed in the OSC with a ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer, the slower decay in $n ( t )$ seen in the control cell is predominantly due to the trap-limited recombination processes. While the faster decay in $n ( t )$ observed in the ZnO EEL-modified cell suggests that the pure bimolecular recombination is the major loss mechanism. As a result, it is seen clearly that the effect of the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer helps to suppress the trap-limited recombination leading to the improvement of the charge collection efficiency.

# 15.2.3 Bias-Dependent Charge Collection

The presence of a metal oxide interlayer between the active layer and the metal contact plays an important role in determining the cell performance. The charge transport, extraction properties, and the interfacial exciton dissociation at the electrode/organic interface in solution-processed OsCs are investigated using light intensity-dependent $J { - } V$ characteristic measurements.

The charge transport and recombination characteristics in OSCs can be analyzed using space charge limited current (SCLC) model. Figure 15.4a,b show the double logarithmic plot of $J _ { \mathrm { p h } } ( J _ { \mathrm { p h } } = J _ { \mathrm { l } } - J _ { \mathrm { d } }$ where $J _ { \mathrm { l } }$ and $J _ { \mathrm { d } }$ are the photocurrent density and dark current density) versus light intensity measured for two types of OSCs, showing the power law dependence of $J _ { \mathrm { p h } }$ on light intensity, $J _ { \mathrm { p h } } \propto I ^ { \alpha }$ [63]. The power exponent, $\alpha$ , of both OsCs are about 1 at a relatively high effective voltage $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } }$ $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } } = V _ { 0 } - V _ { \mathrm { b } }$ , where $V _ { 0 }$ is the built-in potential measured at $J _ { \mathrm { p h } } = 0$ , and $V _ { b }$ is the applied bias, suggesting that almost all of the charges are collected at the electrode at high $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } }$ The power exponents of $J _ { \mathrm { { p h } } }$ I characteristics measured for all cells approach to one at $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } } > 0 . 2 5 \mathrm { V } _ { \mathrm { : } }$ which is around the maximum output power point. This suggests that most photo-generated charges can be efficiently collected without charge accumulation in the cell at high $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } }$ As the charge mobility in organic materials is field-dependent, less efficient charge transport and collection in the OSCs would occur at the low $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } }$ , leading to the accumulation of space charges that gives rise to higher recombination, and thereby a lower power exponent in the $J _ { \mathrm { { p h } } }$ I characteristics. As shown in Figure 15.4, when $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } }$ decreases to a much lower value of 0.087 V, $\alpha$ drops to 0.67 for the control device, while higher exponent value of 0.85 can still be obtained for OSC with a ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer. The different value of $\alpha$ at low $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } }$ suggests the different strengths of recombination in the two types of devices, indicating stronger recombination in the control device, leading to the poor charge transport and collection efficiency.

saturated photocurrent, $J _ { \mathrm { s a t } }$ , also is shown in Figure 15.5. As $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } }$ decreases, charge recombination would increase and not all the photo-generated carriers are collected. Thus, under specific $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } }$ charge collection efficiency $( \eta _ { \mathrm { C C } } )$ can be expressed as [64]:

$$
\eta _ { \mathrm { C C } } ( I , V _ { \mathrm { e f f } } ) = J _ { \mathrm { p h } } ( I , V _ { \mathrm { e f f } } ) \big / J _ { \mathrm { p h , s a t } } ( I )
$$

At high $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } } \left( > 0 . 5 \mathrm { V } \right)$ $\eta _ { \mathrm { C C } }$ approaches unity and gives rise to almost $1 0 0 \%$ collection of the photo-generated charges. In this regime, recombination is negligible. The recombination becomes increasingly important at low $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } }$ $P$ decreases with $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } } .$ As shown in Figure 15.5, charge collection efficiency of the control cell decreases much faster than that of the OSC with a 20-nm-thick ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer at $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } } < 0 . 5 \ : \mathrm { V } .$ The loss in photocurrent due to recombination is obviously much lower in the OSCs with a ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer than that in the control cell, revealing improvement in charge collection efficiency. As OSCs with a $2 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ -thick ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL and the control cell have the identical anode/organic contact and blend system, the charge accumulation and recombination behaviors at the anode contact and in the active layer could be considered the same. Hence, the variation in exponent of $J _ { \mathrm { p h } } { - } I$ characteristics and the change in charge collection efficiency are attributed to the different charge accumulation behaviors at the organic/cathode interfaces in the devices. The difference in the $J _ { \mathrm { p h } } { - } I$ characteristics suggests that the charge accumulation and recombination loss at the organic/cathode interface in the control cell is much stronger than that in the OSCs with a ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer. The $J _ { \mathrm { p h } } { - } V _ { \mathrm { e f f } }$ results also indicate that the use of $2 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ -thick ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL apparently favors an efficient charge collection process. It shows that insertion of a ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer between the BHJ and metal contact helps to suppress the charge recombination.

# 15.3 Metal/Organic Interfacial Exciton Dissociation in Organic Solar Cells

Exciton dissociation at the D/A interface dominates the photocurrent generation in OsCs [65, 66]. The processes of exciton dissociation at the organic/electrode interface are critical for charge collection in OSCs. For regular OSCs with a typical configuration of ITO/PEDOT:PSS/organic photoactive layers $( 1 0 0 - 2 0 0 \mathrm { n m } )$ /metal cathode, the exciton dissociation at the organic/cathode interface is relatively less investigated as compared to that at the D/A and anode/organic interfaces [67, 68]. Electronic properties at the organic/electrode in OsCs have been investigated using in situ X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) [69]and ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPs) [7o]. The correlation between the charge transport/recombination and the cell performance parameters (lifetime, efficiency) have also been studied using SCLC [71] and photo-CELIV [24]. The exciton dissociation at the opaque metal/organic cathode interface in OsCs, however, cannot be elucidated fully using these approaches. TPC technique is used for measuring recombination kinetics of photo-generated carriers in OSCs [72, 73]. The photocurrent, generated due to interfacial exciton dissociation in the absence of internal built-in potential in the bulk is observed at ITO/organic interface. A clear understanding of the exciton dissociation at organic/cathode interface and its impact on the performance of OsCs are desired.

An Nd:YAG pulsed laser with pulse duration of 5 ns and the wavelength of $3 5 5 \mathrm { n m }$ was used to generate the transient signals in the TPC measurements. The TPC, taking the difference between the current $( I _ { \mathrm { L } } )$ excited by the laser and the dark current $( I _ { \mathrm { D } } )$ , for the devices at different biases can be expressed as:

$$
I _ { \mathrm { T P C } } = I _ { \mathrm { L } } - I _ { \mathrm { D } }
$$

where $I _ { \mathrm { T P C } }$ in Eq. (15.7) includes the sum of photo-induced current contributed by (i) the drift current formed under the internal electric field $( E _ { \mathrm { i n t } } )$ , and (ii) the exciton dissociations at $\mathrm { D } / \mathrm { A }$ and organic/electrode interfaces that are not dependent on $E _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ Assuming a uniform electric field crossing the stack of the functional active layers in OSCs, $E _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ can be expressed as:

$$
{ E _ { \mathrm { i n t } } = ( V _ { 0 } - V _ { \mathrm { b } } ) / d }
$$

where $V _ { 0 }$ in Eq. (15.8) is the intrinsic built-in potential in the OSCs, $V _ { \mathfrak { b } }$ is the applied external bias, and $d$ is the thickness of the stack of the functional layers. Usually, contributions to $I _ { \mathrm { T P C } }$ due to exciton dissociations at $\mathrm { D } / \mathrm { A }$ heterojunction and at organic/electrode cannot be easily distinguished or identified in the TPC measurements. In order to better understand the processes of exciton dissociation at the organic/electrode interface, the contribution in $I _ { \mathrm { T P C } }$ due to the drift current arising from $\mathrm { D } / \mathrm { A }$ interface under $E _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ can be offset by applying an opposite external bias on devices in the TPC measurements. This allows to exam the interfacial exciton dissociation in the absence of internal built-in potential. Therefore, the information of exciton dynamics and recombination kinetics of photo-generated carriers at organic/electrode interface can be obtained by measuring $I _ { \mathrm { T P C } }$ for samples at different biases.

# 15.3.1 Charge Collection in Regular Configuration Organic Solar Cells

Regular OSCs with a configuration of ITO/PEDOT:PSS $( 3 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { P T B 7 { : } P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ $( 9 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { A l }$ and reverse configuration OsCs with a structure of ITO/Al $( \sim 1 . 2 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { P T B 7 : P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } ( 9 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { M o O } _ { 3 } ( 2 . 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { A g } \ltimes$ vere made. The pre-patterned ITO substrates, with a sheet resistance of ${ \sim } 1 5 \Omega$ per square, were cleaned by ultrasonication sequentially with acetone, ethanol, deionized water, and isopropanol for 10 minutes, followed by an ex situ oxygen plasma prior to the cell fabrication. For reverse configuration OSCs, the surface of ITO/glass substrates was modified with ${ \sim } 1 . 2 – \mathrm { n m }$ -thick Al, deposited by thermal evaporation in vacuum with a base pressure of $< 1 . 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \mathrm { P }$ a at an evaporation rate of $0 . 1 \mathring \mathrm { A } \mathbf { s } ^ { - 1 }$ . The Al-modified ITO substrates were then transferred to an adjacent glove box with $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ levels below $0 . 1 \mathrm { p p m }$ , which is connected to the evaporator. A pre-prepared polymer blend of PTB7 (1 Material) and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ (NanoC) in a weight ratio of 1: 1.5, dissolved in chlorobenzene solution, was spin-coated on substrates. Different OsCs have an identical active area of $3 . 0 \mathrm { m m } \times 3 . 0 \mathrm { m m }$ . They are encapsulated with a glass lid in the glove box with both oxygen and moisture levels less than $0 . 1 \mathrm { p p m }$

In order to analyze the exciton dissociation at the organic/cathode interface, samples consisting of a $4 0 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ -thick acceptor layer in a regular cell configuration of ITO/PEDOT:PSS $( 3 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } ( 4 0 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { A l } ( 3 0 \mathrm { n m } )$ were prepared for the TPC measurements. The use of a thick photoactive layer, e.g. four times thicker than the actual active layer used in OSCs, is to suppress the influence of the drift current generated in the bulk. Samples with a ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer at the cathode/organic interface, e.g. ITO/PEDOT:PSS $( 3 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } ( 4 0 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { Z n O } ( 2 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { A l } ( 3 0 \mathrm { n m } )$ , were also made for comparison studies. A 20-nm-thick ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ thin layer was coated on $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ surface using solution process, following the procedure described in a previous work [74]. In the experiments, $I _ { \mathrm { T P C } }$ of the samples was measured using a small optical perturbation, provided by a pulsed Nd:YAG laser from the $3 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ thick semitransparent Al cathode side. Under this condition, very small amount of photons can be absorbed at the PEDOT:PSS/ $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ anode interface after they penetrate through the semitransparent Al cathode and a $4 0 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ -thick $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ layer. Therefore, the contribution to $I _ { \mathrm { T P C } }$ due to the exciton dissociation at the anode/organic interface can then be neglected, and the exciton dissociation at $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } / \mathrm { A l }$ interface in the devices can be seen clearly.

TPCs measured for the samples with a configuration of ITO/PEDOT:PSS/ $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ $( 4 0 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { A l } \left( 3 0 \mathrm { n m } \right)$ at different biases from 0.3 to $0 . 5 \mathrm { V }$ are plotted in Figure 15.6a. The positive $I _ { \mathrm { T P C } }$ measured for samples without the bias is always observed and is predominantly contributed by the drift current under optical perturbation, due to the difference in the work function between Al and ITO $\mathrm { \Delta } V _ { 0 }$ of $\sim 0 . 5 \mathrm { V } .$ . As the drift current dominates in the TPC measurement, the contribution to the $I _ { \mathrm { T P C } }$ due to the exciton dissociation at the $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } / \mathrm { A l }$ interface is hardly observed. When a positive bias was applied between the ITO anode and Al cathode, e.g. from 0.3 to $0 . 5 \mathrm { V } ,$ the strength of the built-in potential inside the device is offset and decreases gradually with increase in the external bias. Therefore, the fraction in $I _ { \mathrm { T P C } }$ arising from the drift current ( $\langle E _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ -dependent) decreases, while the contribution due to the exciton dissociation at the $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } / \mathrm { A l }$ interface (not $E _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ -dependent) increases.

Figure 15.6a illustrates clearly that the fast negative TPC is observed within a time frame of \~ns after the optical perturbation, a slower positive $I _ { \mathrm { T P C } }$ is then appeared after a longer period of several tens of ns. The change in the polarity of the TPC reflects the contribution of exciton dissociation at the $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } / \mathrm { A l }$ interface. The swift negative $I _ { \mathrm { T P C } }$ signal shown in Figure 15.6a originates from exciton dissociation at the $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } / \mathrm { A l }$ interface, which is very sensitive to the photoexcitation (within 1 ps), and the slower positive $I _ { \mathrm { T P C } }$ signal comes from the carriers that drift with $E _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ in the bulk and decrease with the increase in the positive bias. Figure 15.6a reveals clearly that the exciton dissociation at the $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } / \mathrm { A l }$ interface in regular OSCs produces an inherent adverse effect on electron collection. Photo-generated electrons, drifted with the internal electric field, must be compensated first by the electrons that flow in the opposite direction, due to unfavorable exciton dissociation at the $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } / \mathrm { A l }$ interface, before being collected by the cathode. The rapid negative TPC is apparently disadvantageous for electron collection in regular cells, but it is hardly observed in the measurement of photo-generated current under the steady state conditions, e.g. $J { - } V$ characteristics of OSCs.

Device with a configuration of ITO/PEDOT:PSS/ $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } / \mathrm { Z n O }$ $( 2 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { A l }$ $\left( 3 0 \mathrm { n m } \right)$ , with a built-in potential $V _ { 0 }$ of ${ \sim } 0 . 8 \mathrm { V } ,$ is used for the TPC measurements. TPCs measured for ITO/PEDOT:PSS $( 3 0 \mathrm { n m } )$ $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ $( 4 0 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { Z n O }$ (20 nm)/Al $\left( 3 0 \mathrm { n m } \right)$ are plotted in Figure 15.6b. It shows clearly that the rapid negative TPC signal is not perceived in $I _ { \mathrm { T P C } }$ measured for samples under different biases. Instead, a rapid positive TPC is observed at a bias $V _ { \mathrm { b } } = 0 . 9 \ : \mathrm { V }$ within a time frame of ${ \sim } \mathrm { n s }$ after the optical perturbation. A slower negative $I _ { \mathrm { T P C } }$ signal is observed, arising from the carriers drifted with $E _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ , e.g. $V _ { 0 } – 0 . 9 = - 0 . 1$ , in the bulk. This suggests that the direction of transient current, created by the exciton dissociation at the cathode contact of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } / \mathrm { Z n O } / \mathrm { A l } .$ is the same as that of the drift current in the bulk. TPC measurements reveal that the inevitable adverse interfacial exciton dissociation at organic/Al interface in regular OSCs, as shown in Figure 15.6a, can be eliminated by interposing a thin solution-processed ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer, revealing its impact on preventing the detrimental interfacial exciton dissociation, thereby improving the electron collection efficiency.

In an actual BHJ OSC, a $\mathrm { D } / \mathrm { A }$ blend layer is sandwiched between the anode and the cathode. The possible exciton dissociation at the contact between PTB7 and Al is also examined by the TPC measurements. The transient currents measured for samples consisting of a $4 0 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ -thick PTB7 donor layer in a regular configuration of ITO/PEDOT:PSS/PTB7 $( 4 0 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { A l }$ $\left( 3 0 \mathrm { n m } \right)$ and that recorded for ITO/PEDOT:PSS/PTB7 $( 4 0 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { Z n O ( 2 0 \mathrm { n m ) } / A l ( 3 0 \mathrm { n m } ) }$ at different biases were also studied. It is found that there is no rapid TPC observed in $I _ { T P C }$ measured for both types of samples, regardless of whether a ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer is present or not at the interface between PTB7 and Al contact. This suggests no exciton dissociation can be observed at PTB7/Al interface.

# 15.3.2 Charge Collection in Inverted Organic Solar Cells

TPCs measured for samples with a reverse configuration of ITO/Al $( 1 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ $( 4 0 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { M o O } _ { 3 }$ $( 2 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { A g }$ and ITO/Al $( 1 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { Z n O }$ (20 nm)/ $\mathrm { ^ { \prime } P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ $( 4 0 0 \mathrm { n m } ) /$ $\mathrm { M o O } _ { 3 } \left( 2 \mathrm { n m } \right) / \mathrm { A g }$ under different biases are shown in Figure 15.7. The rapid positive TPCs, observed for the reverse configuration samples at different biases, originate from the exciton dissociation at $\mathrm { A l / P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ (Figure 15.7a) and $\mathrm { Z n O / P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ (Figure 15.7b) interfaces, while the negative slower photocurrents are the drift current generated in the bulk of the samples under different internal electric fields, $E _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ . It is clear that unfavorable exciton dissociation that impedes the electron collection at $\mathrm { A l / P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ interface in regular OSCs, as shown in Figure 15.6a, does not occur in their reverse geometry cells. The inverse exciton dissociation at the $\mathrm { A l / P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ interface in regular and inverted OsCs comes from the difference of the contact properties, depending on the sequence of forming an organic photoactive layer on cathode contact or depositing metal (e.g. Al) cathode on organic layer. When an organic/metal interface is formed by depositing the organic layer on the cathode in the reverse configuration cells, a relatively clear metal/organic interface is expected. Organic/Al interface is often formed by depositing Al contact on organic layer. The incoming energetic metal atoms can easily interrupt the relatively weak van der Waals interaction between molecules in the organic layer. The penetration of energetic metal atoms into the underlying functional organic layer is primary responsible for the complex interfacial properties, forming interfacial defects that could result in adverse exciton dissociation at the organic/metal interface in regular OSCs. However, for the inverted OSCs, the organic/metal interfaces are formed by coating organic layers onto predeposited Al, resulting in a smooth contact without any risk of high-temperature damage or metal penetration.

![](images/08eccda71536f3f9245c76c262b25a1bbf950d6fc6e5852add000b15182bb2d7.jpg)  
Figure 15.7 Transient photocurrents measured for samples with a reverse configuration of (a) ITO/Al $( 1 0 \mathsf { n m } )$ $\mathsf { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathsf { B M }$ $( 4 0 0 \mathsf { n m } ) / \mathsf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ $( 2 \mathsf { n m } ) / \mathsf { A g }$ and (b) ITO/Al $( 1 0 \mathsf { n m } ) / 2 \mathsf { n O }$ $( 2 0 \mathsf { n m } ) /$ $\mathsf { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathsf { B M }$ $( 4 0 0 \mathsf { n m } ) / \mathsf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ $( 2 \mathsf { n m } ) / \mathsf { A g }$ at different biases. Source: Bo Wu.

Metal/organic material interfaces are crucial and play important roles in deter. mining both the charge collection property and stability of OsCs. Much work has been reported to investigate the interfacial properties at Al/fullerene or . $\mathrm { 4 l / P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ interfaces. An electron transfer from Al to fullerene due to Fermi level-pinning at the Al/fullerene interface was reported [75, 76]. The sublevel electronic states in the bandgap of organic layer, formed due to the interface defects, film roughness, and inhomogeneous contact, are some of the factors that can influence or dominate carrier flow into and out of OsCs. Schematic diagram illustrating the processes of exciton dissociation at $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } / \mathrm { A l }$ and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } / \mathrm { Z n O } / \mathrm { A l }$ interfaces is shown in Figure 15.8a,b.

Upon photon excitation, adverse exciton dissociation at the $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } / \mathrm { A l }$ interface results in an accumulation of holes at these sub-band levels. They are likely collected by Al generating a negative TPC as shown in Figure $1 5 . 7 \mathrm { a }$ . Photo-generated electrons, drifted with the internal electric field, are compensated partially by the electrons created by unfavorable interfacial exciton dissociation, leading to the poor electron collection at the $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } / \mathrm { A l }$ interface. The valance band maximum $( - 7 . 2 \mathrm { e V } )$ of ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ is much lower than HOMO of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ (6.1eV). When a ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer is present at the interface between $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and Al, the exciton dissociation takes place at the $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } / \mathrm { Z n O }$ interface, the possible flow of holes toward Al can be blocked effectively [77], as shown in Figure 15.8b. Therefore, the electrons that created by adverse exciton dissociation at $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } / \mathrm { A l }$ interface are suppressed at $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } / \mathrm { Z n O } / \mathrm { A l }$ contact generating a positive TPC as shown in Figure 15.6b. The above analyses, based on the TPC measurements, provide an insight on understanding the origin of inverse exciton dissociation at the metal/organic interface in inverted and regular OSCs.

The relevance of above analyses made with TPC measurements can be seen by measuring the performance of regular or inverted OsCs having different cathode contacts. For regular structure, it is demonstrated that the FF and PCE can be improved by insertion of a $2 0 \mathrm { - n m }$ -thick ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL between BHJ and cathode, as shown in Figure 15.6a. While for reverse configuration OSCs, the performance of the cells made with or without the ZnO EEL is almost the same, suggesting that the unfavorable electron collection observed in the regular configuration OsCs is not present in the inverted cells.

Figure 15.8Schematic diagram illustrating the processes of exciton dissociation at (a) $\mathsf { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathsf { B M / A l }$ and (b) $\mathsf { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathsf { B M } / \mathsf { Z n O } / \mathsf { A l }$ interfaces. Source: Bo Wu.

# 15.4 Improvement of Charge Collection and Performance Reproducibility

In the previous section, it shows that inverted OSCs are more favorable than corresponding regular configuration cells. ZnO is one of the commonly used EEL due to its low cost and simple solution-based preparation process. The morphology of the EEL, e.g. solution-processed oxide interlayer, plays an important role in determining the contact quality at the cathode/active layer interface in the cells. The effect of the surface morphology of the oxide interlayer on the morphology evolution of the organic functional active layer in the inverted OsCs is analyzed. It demonstrates that the inverted OsCs are favorable for forming smaller domains in the active layer as compared to that in the active layer of the cells having a regular configuration. The improvement in the performance of inverted devices associates with the reduced domain size, which could then be closer to the exciton diffusion length in the polymer blend, favoring efficient operation of the OSCs [78].

In addition to the surface morphology, the electronic properties of the ultrathin ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EEL are essential for the development of high-performance solution-processed inverted OSCs [79]. A thin film ZnO EEL interlayer, prepared by the sol-gel process at a sintering temperature of $2 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , has been used for application in inverted OsCs. Surface engineering of a sol-gel processed ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ with a thin conjugated polyelectrolyte interfacial layer has a significant impact on enhancing the cell performance, achieved due to an improved charge transport via suppressed bimolecular recombination [80]. A cross-linkable water/alcohol-soluble conjugated polymer interlayer was also adopted for tuning the surface work function of ZnO interlayer in high-efficiency ZnO-based inverted OSCs [81]. It has been reported that the associated fluctuation in morphological and surface electronic properties of ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ modified ITO cathode, e.g. changes due to the experimental conditions of ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ formulation [53], film fabrication [54], and post treatment [55], also place a practical challenge limiting the reproducibility of the performance of OSCs. However, the report on the effect of the sub-gap states, induced by the defects in the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer, on charge collection behavior and thereby the performance reproducibility of the solution-processed OsCs is rather rare. For commercialization of OsCs, there is a need to develop a robust and an effective ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ modification approach that can be easily repeatable for application in making high-performance OSCs via a solution-processable route.

# 15.4.1 Effect of Metal Oxide Interlayer on Cell Performance

The inverted OSCs made with Al-modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer have a device configuration of $\mathrm { I T O } / \mathrm { Z n O }$ $\mathrm { / Z n O ~ ( 2 0 \ n m ) / A l ~ ( 1 . 2 n m ) / P T B 7 { : } P C _ { 7 1 } B M ~ ( 9 0 \ n m ) / M o O _ { 3 } ~ ( }$ $( 2 . 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { A g }$ The structurally identical control OsCs with a single cathode interlayer of ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ $\left( 2 0 \mathrm { n m } \right)$ also were prepared for comparison. Pre-patterned ITO-coated glass substrates, with a sheet resistance of ${ \sim } 1 5 \Omega$ per square, were cleaned by ultrasonication sequentially with acetone, ethanol, deionized water, and isopropanol for 10 minutes each. The ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer is solution-prepared following the processes described in a previous work [74]. For OSCs with Al-modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer, ${ \sim } 1 . 2 – \mathrm { n m }$ -thick Al was deposited on $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O / I T O } } }$ surface by thermal evaporation in a vacuum chamber with a base pressure of $< 1 . 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 } \mathrm { P a }$ at an evaporation rate of $0 . 1 \mathring \mathrm { A } \mathbf { s } ^ { - 1 }$ . The Al-modified $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O / I T O } } }$ substrates were then transferred to an adjacent glove box connected to the evaporator with $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ levels below $0 . 1 \mathrm { p p m }$

The results show that the $R _ { \mathrm { { S } } }$ of the cells made with an Al-modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer and that of the control cell are similar. However, $R _ { \mathrm { S H } }$ of the control cell is much larger for the OsCs made with an Al-modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer. OsCs with an Al-modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer also exhibited an improved EQE in almost the whole spectrum region, demonstrating an enhancement in the charge collection at the interface between functional organic layer and Al-modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ as compared to that at organic/ $\mathrm { z n O }$ interface in the control cell. The device parameters obtained for two types of the inverted OSCs are summarized in Table 15.3.

It is known that the performance of the OsCs is also dependent on the surface morphology of the ZnO EEL [78]. In parallel to the analyses of the $J { - } V$ characteristics of the OSCs, the possible change in the surface morphology of ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ , caused by the modification of an ultrathin Al layer, was also examined by the scanning electron microscope (SEM) measurements. The SEM images measured for the surfaces of a pure ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ and an ultrathin Al $( 1 . 2 \mathrm { n m } )$ -modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ EELs, deposited on ITO/glass using the identical condition for cell fabrication, are shown in Figure 15.10. It is clear that there is no observable change in the surface morphology, revealing the enhancement in the PCE of the cells is originated primarily from the improved contact quality and the charge collection at the cathode/organic interface.

Therefore, under a large reverse bias, $J _ { \mathrm { { p h } } }$ is primarily determined by light absorption and the exciton dissociation rate in the photoactive layer, which is almost the same for both types of devices.

# 15.4.2 Suppression of ZnO Sub-Gap States

Figure 15.12a,b show the double logarithmic plot of $J _ { \mathrm { { p h } } }$ versus light intensity for both types of the devices as well as the corresponding linear fitting data, suggesting power law dependence between these two quantities. The ideal SCLC characteristics give rise to a power exponent $\alpha$ of 0.75 [83, 84]. However, the power exponent of both devices is about 1 at a high effective voltage $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } } = 1 . 8 \mathrm { V } ,$ indicating that almost all the photo-generated carriers are collected at the electrode without any space charge generation due to the balanced carrier transport. However, at lower $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } }$ the less efficient charge transport and collection lead to the build-up of space charges that gives rise to higher bimolecular recombination and lower power exponent.

![](images/49c5c9bcc352abc6645059e56b7a0b4f3d741c7778cb17e790287d932fa72f56.jpg)  
Figure 15.12 Double logarithmic plot of $J _ { \mathsf { p h } }$ as a function of the intensity of light, illustrating the change in the power law exponent $\alpha$ for (a) control cell with a pure $z _ { \mathsf { n O } }$ interlayer and (b) OSC with Al modified $z _ { \mathsf { I } \mathsf { I } } { \mathsf { O } }$ interlayer, measured under different $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } }$ . Solid lines are the linearly fitting results. Source: Bo Wu.

In Figure 15.12a, the exponent is 0.89 for the OSCs with Al-modified cathode interlayer, while for the control device, it decreases to 0.85 at the same $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } }$ of $0 . 1 \mathrm { V } ,$ as shown in Figure 15.12b, implying that more space charges are generated in the control cell. As the only difference between these two devices comes from the cathode interface, the results clearly reveal that the Al-modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer helps to suppress the generation of space charges and the sequential bimolecular charge recombination, which otherwise would occur at the $\mathrm { Z n O / P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ interface, leading to an enhancement in FF, as shown in Table 15.3.

The sublevel electronic states in the bandgap of ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer, induced by the defects in the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer, are crucial and play important role in determining both the charge collection at the organic/electrode interface and stability of OSCs. In this work, the interfacial properties at the organic/ $_ { z \mathrm { n O } }$ interfaces in the inverted OSCs were analyzed using photothermal deflection spectroscopy (PDS) and XPS measurements. In the PDS measurements, the Al-modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ and pure ZnO samples were immersed in an inert liquid (Fluorinert FC-72) with a high refractive index. A monochromatic pump light is incident on the ZnO sample. The heat generated in the sample, caused by the absorption and subsequent non-radiative relaxation process, produces a thermal gradient in the liquid near its surface. The layers of liquid near the sample surface are hotter, less dense than the upper liquid and have lower refractive indices. A probe light, using a laser beam with the wavelength of $6 3 2 \mathrm { n m }$ , parallel to the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ surface is refracted. By scanning the wavelength of the pump light, the correlation between the refraction angle of the probe light and the change in the refractive index of the liquid near the surface of the sample can then be obtained. The corresponding absorption coefficient of the samples at different photon energies, which provides the information of the excitation from the sub-band states in the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ , can then be measured. In this work, the PDS spectra of the specimens were obtained by measuring the refracted probe light using a position sensor and lock-in amplifier.

PDS is a high-sensitive absorption measurement technique, which can detect the change in the optical absorption due to the variation in sub-band gap states induced by the defects and energetic disorders [85, 86] in the specimens. Figure 15.13a plots the PDS spectra measured for the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ and Al-modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ layers. The absorption coefficient of both samples saturates at the photon energy ${ > } 3 . 3 7 \mathrm { e V } ,$ caused by the band-to-band absorption in the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ layer. The absorption of both samples drops rapidly when the photon energy is less than $3 . 4 \mathrm { e V } .$ The Urbach Energy, $E _ { \mathrm { u } }$ , can be extracted by the linear fitting of the cutoff edge in the PDS spectra, an important parameter that provides the information of sub-band gap states in the materials. When the photon energy, $E$ is less than bandgap $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ the relationship between the absorption coefficient $A$ and $E _ { \mathrm { u } }$ can be expressed by [85]:

$$
A = A _ { \mathrm { 0 } } ~ \mathrm { e x p } ( ( E - E _ { \mathrm { g } } ) / E _ { \mathrm { u } } )
$$

According to Eq. (15.9), the corresponding $E _ { \mathrm { u } }$ values calculated for the pure ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ and Al-modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ films are 59 and $5 3 \mathrm { m e V } _ { \mathrm { : } }$ respectively, implying that the sub-band states in the solution-processed ZnO layer can be suppressed effectively by modification of its surface with an ultrathin Al layer.

![](images/ae0c34459b98f6ae520ad6f22a9de16fa64f0f7a40f5940e76af147bca99aa06.jpg)  
Figure 15.13 (a) PDS spectra measured for the pure ZnO and Al-modified ZnO layers. (b) Dark $J - V$ characteristics measured for the inverted OSCs with the Al-modified ZnO and pure $z _ { \mathsf { n O } }$ interlayers. Source: Bo Wu.

As shown in Figure 15.13a, there is an obvious reduction in the absorption in the Al-modified ZnO layer as compared to the pure ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ layer over the sub-gap energy region from 2.7 and $3 . 4 \mathrm { e V } .$ The change in the PDS spectra suggests that the sub-gap states can be suppressed effectively in Al-modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer. The suppression of the sub-gap states in the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer benefits the charge collection at the organic/electrode interface, which otherwise would act as the shallow electron traps to give rise to the bimolecular charge recombination and hamper the charge transport and charge extraction.

The relevance of PDS analyses can be seen by measuring the dark $J { - } V$ characteristics of the inverted OsCs with the Al-modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ and pure ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayers. As shown in Figure 15.13b, the decrease in the leakage current is clearly observed in the inverted OSCs with an Al-modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer, demonstrating the effect of the suppression of the sub-gap states in the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ buffer layer on organic/electrode contact quality. The sub-band states in the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer provide additional sites to assist in charge injection, thereby an increase in the leakage current as seen in Figure 15.13b. The dark $J { - } V$ characteristics clearly illustrate the change in the contact properties at the organic. $_ { z \mathrm { n O } }$ and organic/Al-modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interfaces in the inverted OSCs. The leakage current can be reduced by suppressing the sub-gap states in ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer in the OsCs, as shown in Figure 15.13a.

In a related work, the vertical phase separation in the polymer BHJ, based on the $\mathrm { P T B 7 : P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ blend system, was studied by the XPS measurement, and its effect on the performance of the regular and inverted OsCs was examined [33]. The XPS results indicate that the segregation of donor/acceptor forming a $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ rich region at the bottom of the blend films can be moderated using solvent additive. The quantitative analyses show that the size of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ domains in the BHJ decreases from 67 to $3 8 \mathrm { n m }$ with the addition of the solvent additive. The use of the solvent additive helps to improve the homogeneous vertical phase separation in the $\mathrm { P T B 7 : P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ BHJ, and thereby favoring an enhanced exciton dissociation process for attaining high-performance OSCs.

The hole collection and electron extraction in the cells are closely correlated to the interfacial electronic properties at the electron donor (PTB7)/anode and cathode/acceptor $\mathrm { ( P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M ) }$ interfaces. As the OsCs with different cathodes of $Z _ { Ḋ } \mathrm { n O / I T O }$ and Al-modified $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O / I T O } } }$ have the identical anode of $\mathrm { M o O } _ { 3 } / \mathrm { A g }$ , the variation in charge collection of the cells can be associated with the modification in the contact property at the cathode/ $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ interface. A better understanding on electron collection behavior with respect to the interfacial electronic properties at the cathode/ $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ interface is important for achieving high-performance OsCs. Following our previous work of analyzing the interfacial exciton dissociation at the interface between the cathode and the surface of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ rich $\mathrm { P T B 7 { : } P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ blend layer in the OSCs [87], the interfacial electronic properties at the $\mathrm { Z n O / P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and Al-modified $\mathrm { Z n O / P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ contacts were investigated by XPS measurements in situ. In this work, a thin layer of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ was deposited using sublimation process stepwise onto the Al $( 1 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { Z n O }$ - $2 0 \mathrm { n m }$ /ITO sample.

For XPS characterizations, a ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ $( 2 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { I T O }$ substrate was loaded into an ultra-high vacuum (UHV) deposition chamber. A $1 . 2 { \cdot } \mathrm { n m }$ Al film was deposited onto the substrate. The sample was then transferred to the UHV analysis chamber for XPS measurements. The bottom dashed line in Figure 15.14a shows an XPS Al 2p core level spectrum of the Al $( 1 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { Z n O } ( 2 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { I T O }$ sample. The sharp Al 2p peak at $7 2 . 8 \mathrm { e V }$ can be attributed to metallic Al. Meanwhile, a broad peak emerges at $7 5 . 2 \mathrm { e V }$ indicating the evaporated Al was partially oxidized forming $\mathrm { A l O } _ { X }$ . Al 2p and C 1s XPS core level spectra of $\mathrm { P C _ { 7 1 } B M ( x n m ) / A l ( 1 n m ) / Z n O ( 2 0 n m ) / I T O } ,$ with $x$ of 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, and $1 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , are shown as solid lines in Figure 15.14a,b, respectively. No obvious change in the Al 2p peak is observed as the $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ coverage increases. On the other hand, a strong C 1s peak can be found at ${ \sim } 2 8 4 . 8 \mathsf { e V }$ corresponding to the C-C bond signal from $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ . It is interesting to note that a small C 1s peak emerges at $2 8 7 . 1 \mathrm { e V }$ during the initial coverage of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ . This C 1s peak later disappears when the coverage of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ reaches $5 . 0 \mathrm { n m }$ . The XPS results reveal an interfacial interaction between $\mathbf { A l O } _ { X }$ and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ during the initial deposition of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ $( 0 . 5 \mathrm { - } 2 . 0 \mathrm { n m } )$ , which provides a better contact and energy alignment of $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ and the interlayer, favoring the charge transport and collection at the cathode interface.

For device fabrication, the yield of high-performance OsCs is affected by fluctuation in morphology and surface electronic characteristics of the ZnO interlayer that vary due to many processing variables. There is thus a need to develop a robust and an effective interfacial modification approach that does not require any posttreatment for application in making high-performce OsCs via solution-processable route. The results of this work reveal clearly that the use of an Al-modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer improves the performance reproducibility of $\mathrm { P T B 7 { : } P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ -based inverted OsCs fabricated in different batches as shown in Figure 15.15. Performance parameters of OsCs made with the pure ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer and Al-modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer are summarized in Table 15.4. OSCs with different cathode interlayers of Al $( { \sim } 1 . 2 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { Z n O }$ $( 2 0 \mathrm { n m } )$ and ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ $( 2 0 \mathrm { n m } )$ , and different surface treatment conditions, e.g. with and without UV exposure prior to the cell fabrication, were made for comparison. It shows that pre-UV exposure of the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ $( 2 0 \mathrm { n m } ) / \mathrm { I T O }$ cathode has a substantial influence on the performance of the cells, resulting in a much-reduced PCE of $5 . 9 \%$ for cells made with UV treated $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O / I T O } } }$ cathode, as compared to $6 . 8 \%$ for the structurally identical OsCs fabricated with non-UV-treated $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O } / I T O } }$ cathode. However, there is almost no change in the performance of the set of OsCs made with Al-modified $Z _ { \mathrm { { n O / I T O } } }$ cathode with and without UV exposure.

The deviation in the performance of both types of OsCs is attributed to suppress of the sub-gap states in the ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer, arising from the significant decrease in the interfacial defects at the organic/electrode interface. For example, the reaction between Al and loosely bound oxygen atoms in ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ passivates the defects generated upon UV irradiation, which act as electron traps due to their deep energy level if they were not removed [88]. The density of such interfacial traps in the solution-processed ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer may vary according to the different film preparation conditions and post-deposition treatments, e.g. with different UV exposures and post-annealing temperatures, causing an undesired increase in the charge recombination at the cathode/organic interface.

The surface condition of the ultrathin Al-modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ is very stable, due to the formation of $\mathrm { A l O } _ { X }$ even in the UHV condition, as illustrated by the Al 2p high-resolution XPS core-level spectra in Figure 15.14a. It is found that the cells made with a freshly prepared Al $( \sim 1 . 2 \mathrm { n m } )$ -modified $Z _ { Ḋ } \mathrm { n O / I T O }$ cathode and the ones that were prepared with the same condition but kept overnight in the glove box, with $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ levels below $0 . 1 \mathrm { p p m }$ , remain essentially no observable change in the device performance. The Al-modified solution-processed ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ interlayer assists in creation of a more stable cathode/organic interface for attaining high-performance OSCs. The above analyses, based on the PDS, XPS, and light-intensity-dependent $J { - } V$ characteristic measurements, provide an insight on understanding the effect of suppression of ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ sub-gap states on charge collection and performance reproducibility in inverted OSCs. This suggests that ultrathin Al $( \sim 1 . 2 \mathrm { n m } )$ -modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ is a simple and effective cathode modification approach, revealing the robustness and the process condition independent characteristics of the cathode that is suitable for high-performance OsC fabrication in a consistent and repeatable way, a process that can be easily adopted for mass production.

# 15.5 Effect of Built-in Potential on Stability of Organic Solar Cells

Apart from the steady progresses made in the increase of PCE, further improvement in the operational stability of OsCs is desired for practical applications. The device stability is closely associated with choice of the materials, material processing, morphology of the functional layers, the change in the stratification of the donor and acceptor in the BHJ [89, 90], interfacial chemical reaction at the BHJ/contact interfaces [25], balanced charge mobility in photoactive layer [24], and retaining a high built-in potential across the OSCs [91, 92]. Much research effort is needed to improve the stability of the OsCs through improved understanding of the degradation mechanisms.

PEDOT:PSS layer is one of the widely used hole contact materials for application in solution-processed OSCs [93]. However, a PEDOT:PSS HEL is coated using a highly acidic aqueous suspension, which results in corrosion of the ITO electrode. Its high hydroscopic property also leads to the encroachment of the moisture in the active layer, accelerating the cell degradation [82, 94]. To address this issue, a variety of chemical stable and low-cost hole extraction materials have been proposed to substitute PEDOT:PSS for more stable and efficient OSCs. Transition metal oxide, including NiO, ${ \mathrm { W O } } _ { 3 }$ , and $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ , represents an alternative class of materials that could potentially combine all-important attributes of an ideal HEL for OSC applications [95, 96]. In particular, solution-processable $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ has been proved promising with excellent optical transparency and suitable high work function [97, 98]. However, the relatively high surface trap density and inferior charge transporting property of the pristine solution-processed $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ HEL often cause poor contact at the organic. $\mathbf { \Delta } \mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ interface, resulting in high leakage current and undesired charge recombination loss [99]. The impact of a $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 } ,$ /antimonene HEL on the stability of OSCs, e.g. prepared using a blend system of poly[(2,6-(4,8-bis(5-(2-ethylhexyl-3-fluoro)thiophen-2-yl)-benzo $[ 1 , 2 - b ; 4 , 5 - b ^ { \prime } ]$ dithiophene))-alt-(5,5- $_ { 1 ^ { \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime } }$ -di-2-thienyl- $. 5 ^ { \prime } , 7 ^ { \prime }$ -bis(2-ethylhexyl)benzo $[ 1 ^ { \prime } , 2 ^ { \prime } - c ; 4 ^ { \prime } , 5 ^ { \prime } - c ^ { \prime } ]$ dithiophene-4,8-dione)](PM6) and 3,9-bis(2-methylene-((3-(1,1-dicyanomethylene) -6,7-difluoro)-indanone))-5,5,11,11-tetrakis(4-hexylphenyl)-dithieno $[ 2 , 3 - d ; 2 ^ { \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime } - d ^ { \prime } ] .$ s-indaceno[1,2-b:5,6 $\cdot b ^ { \prime }$ Jdithiophene (IT-4F), has been examined. It shows that removal of the interfacial chemical reactions between PEDOT:PSS HEL and the 2-(3-oxo-2,3-dihydroinden-1-ylidene)malononitrile (INCN) moieties in nonfullerene acceptor (NFA)-based OSCs is one of the critical factors for enhancing the stability of the OSCs. The use of bilayer $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene HEL helps to eliminate the interfacial reaction between the PEDOT:PSS and INCN moieties in NFA, one of the recently found major degradation mechanisms in the NFA-based OSCs with a PEDOT:PSS HEL. The use of a bilayer $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 } ,$ /antimonene HEL also favors the stable operation of the OsCs through retaining a high built-in potential.

# 15.5.1 Interlayer Modification

The $J { - } V$ and EQE characteristics, measured for the OSCs with a $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ HEL, a bilayer $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 } ,$ /antimonene HEL and the control OSCs with a PEDOT:PSS HEL, are shown in Figure 15.16a,b. The OSCs with a $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene HEL have an obvious higher PCE as compared to that of the cell with a pristine $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ HEL, e.g. $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ of $1 8 . 0 1 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of $0 . 8 2 \mathrm { V } ,$ and FF of $6 6 . 9 2 \%$ . The combination of these improvements leads to a PCE of ${ \sim } 1 2 \%$ in OSCs with a $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene HEL, achieving ${ > } 1 7 \%$ increase in PCE as compared to that of the OSCs with a pristine $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ HEL $( 1 0 . 0 2 \% )$ . A device performance obtained for the PM6:IT-4F OSCs with a bilayer a $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 } ,$ /antimonene HEL is comparable to that of a control cell with a PEDOT:PSS HEL. The work function of the PEDOT:PSS and $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene layers was measured using the UPS. The corresponding UPS spectra measured for these films are presented in Figure 15.16c. The work function of $- 5 . 4 \mathrm { e V }$ is obtained for the bilayer $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene, which is slightly higher than that of a PEDOT:PSS layer $( - 5 . 2 \mathrm { e V } )$ . The corresponding schematic diagram illustrating the energy levels of the functional materials used in the OSCs is shown in Figure 15.16d. The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images measured for a solution-processed antimonene layer are shown in Figure 15.17. The antimonene layer has a lattice fringe of 0.21 nm, corresponding to a (110) plane of the crystalline Sb as shown in Figure 15.17b.
