It shows that the solution-processed bilayer $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene HEL is energetically more favorable for hole extraction as compared to that of the PEDOT:PSS HEL for use in OSCs.

$\eta _ { \mathrm { C C } }$ of the PM6:IT-4F OSCs with a bilayer $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene HEL and a control cell with a PEDOT:PSS HEL has been analyzed, the results are presented in Figure 15.18. The efficient charge extraction can be realized in OSCs operated under a high effective voltage, facilitating an efficient sweeping-out of the charge carriers under a relatively high effective internal electric field. The charge collection efficiency $\eta _ { \mathrm { C C } }$ of the OSCs reduces with the decrease of $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } } .$ . This is because of the low efficiency in sweeping out of the photo-generated charges, thereby a high charge recombination to take place in the cells. $\eta _ { \mathrm { C C } }$ at low $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } }$ also provides an insight revealing the charge collection capability of the cells. Apparently, a higher $\eta _ { \mathrm { C C } }$ at a low $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } }$ reflects the superior charge collection capability and reduced charge recombination loss in the OSCs. As shown in Figure 15.18, OSCs with a bilayer $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene HEL shows similar charge collection properties over the whole $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } }$ range, suggesting the favorable BHJ/HEL interfacial properties for assisting in charge extraction.

# 15.5.2 Built-in Potential in Organic Solar Cells

$E _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ in the BHJ OSCs plays a crucial role in charge transfer, as the photo-generated charge carriers drift with the $E _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ in the OSCs. A larger $E _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ is desired for assisting the efficient charge transfer, thereby suppressing the bimolecular recombination. The device performance difference observed between the PM6:IT-4F OSCs with a bilayer $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene HEL and ones with a PEDOT:PSS HEL is closely associated with the variation of the built-in potential $V _ { \mathrm { b i } }$ in these OSCs during the aging test. The $V _ { \mathrm { b i } }$ in the OSCs was analyzed using the TPC measurements. The TPC $( I _ { \mathrm { T P C } } )$ is a function of $E _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ in a cell. $I _ { \mathrm { T P C } }$ measured for the OSCs operated under different external biases are shown in Figure 15.19. A larger $E _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ in the OSCs helps for the efficient exciton dissociation and charge transfer, as the photo-generated charge carriers drift with the $E _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ . The relationship between the applied bias $( V _ { \mathrm { a } } )$ and $E _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ has been described in Section 15.3 Eq. (15.8). $V _ { \mathrm { b i } }$ can be determined by applying an opposite $V _ { \mathrm { a } }$ to compensate $V _ { \mathrm { b i } }$ for $I _ { \mathrm { T P C } }$ approaching zero. Since $d$ is the same for PM6:IT-4F OSCs with different HELs, $E _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ is proportional to $V _ { \mathrm { b i } }$ in the OSCs. As shown in Figure 15.19, $I _ { \mathrm { T P C } }$ decreases with increase in $V _ { \mathrm { a } }$ and reaches zero when $V _ { \mathrm { a } } = 0 . 8 4 \mathrm { V }$ for the control OSCs with a PEDOT:PSS HEL. $V _ { \mathrm { a } }$ of $0 . 8 1 \mathrm { V }$ was required for compensating $V _ { \mathrm { b i } }$ in the PM6:IT-4F OSCs with a $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 } .$ /antimonene HEL.

![](images/e238b710bd020412d6f9a85475c210a8c28bce476f07a9ecad12a709b4e6664d.jpg)  
Figure 15.19Transient photocurrents of the PM6:IT-4F-based OSCs with (a) a PEDOT:PSS HEL and (b) a ${ \mathsf { M o O } } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene HEL, measured under different reverse biases. Source: Weixia Lan.

The effect of the HELs on the stability of the PM6:IT-4F OSCs has been inves. tigated through examining the built-in potential in the OsCs using an aging test. $V _ { \mathrm { b i } }$ of the PM6:IT-4F OSCs with different HELs as a function of the aging time was investigated. Normalized $V _ { \mathrm { b i } }$ - aging time correlations measured for the PM6:IT-4F OSCs with a bilayer $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 } ,$ /antimonene HEL and a PEDOT:PSS HEL are shown in Figure 15.20. A $1 0 \%$ drop in $V _ { \mathrm { b i } }$ of the PM6:IT-4F OSCs with a $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene HEL was observed during the aging test over a period of 30 days. However, a $2 2 \%$ drop in $V _ { \mathrm { b i } }$ was observed for the control OSCs with a PEDOT:PSS HEL, dropping more than two times faster than the one observed in the PM6:IT-4F OSCs with a bilayer $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene HEL. A steady $V _ { \mathrm { b i } }$ or a constant large $E _ { \mathrm { i n t } }$ is a prerequisite for the efficient and stable operation of OsCs. TPC results reveal clearly that a gradual decrease in $V _ { \mathrm { b i } }$ across the BHJ, as shown in Figure 15.20, is one main reason responsible for the deterioration in the performance of the PM6:IT-4F OSCs with a PEDOT:PSS HEL.

# 15.5.3 Stability of Organic Solar Cells

The stability of the encapsulated PM6:IT-4F OSCs made with different HELs has been analyzed in air. The $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ , FF, and PCE of different PM6:IT-4F OSCs as a function of the aging time are shown in Figure 15.21. The results show that the PM6:IT-4F OSCs with a bilayer $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene HEL are more stable than the control cells with a PEDOT:PSS HEL. A $4 6 \%$ decrease in $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and a $2 5 \%$ drop in FF were observed for the control cells with a PEDOT:PSS HEL, leading to a $5 5 \%$ reduction in PCE after a 30-day aging test in air. In comparison, an $1 1 \%$ decrease in $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and a $1 3 \%$ drop in FF were observed in the PM6:IT-4F OSCs with a bilayer $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 } ,$ /antimonene HEL, having a $2 5 \%$ drop in PCE for the OSCs aged over the same stability test.

The normalized $\eta _ { \mathrm { C C } }$ obtained for the PM6:IT-4F OSCs with different HELs, operated at the maximum power point $( P _ { \mathrm { m a x } } )$ and near $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ conditions, as a function of the aging time are shown in Figure 15.22. It shows that the $\eta _ { \mathrm { C C } }$ , monitored for the OSCs with a bilayer $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene HEL operated at $P _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ $V _ { \mathrm { e f f } } = 0 . 2 3 \mathrm { V } ,$ , is more stable as compared to the one observed for the OSCs with a PEDOT:PSS HEL aged over the same aging period. The advantage of the bilayer $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene HEL for use in PM6:IT-4F OSCs is clearly manifested, as shown in Figure 15.22.

![](images/2b364f9149ea60b49649503a4e6626b747fca8d973f68960bbbec959b805cd2f.jpg)  
Figure 15.22 Normalized $\eta _ { \mathsf { C C } }$ as a function of the aging time, measured for the different NFA-based OSCs operated at (a) $P _ { \mathrm { { m a x } } }$ $( V _ { \mathrm { e f f } } = 0 . 2 3 \ : \forall )$ and (b) near $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ $( V _ { \mathrm { e f f } } = 0 . 1 3 \vee )$ conditions. Source: Weixia Lan.

The possible interfacial reaction between HEL and BHJ photoactive layer was analyzed to reveal the degradation mechanism in the PM6:IT-4F OSCs. It is known that photostability of the polymer donors and NFAs used in OSCs are sensitive to the surrounding environment. The change in the absorption spectra of the functional organic semiconductors is associated with the deterioration in their functions, caused by the possible material degradation or imperfection. The absorption spectra measured for the PM6 layers, formed on the PEDOT:PSS and $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene surfaces and exposed to the one sun illumination over an exposure period from zero to four hours, are shown in Figure 15.23a,b. There is no observable change found in the absorption spectra measured for the PM6 layer deposited on either a PEDOT:PSS HEL or a $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 } ,$ antimonene HEL, suggesting that there is no observable interfacial reaction between the PM6 donor and HELs. However, an obvious variation was observed in the absorption spectra measured for the IT-4F layers deposited on different HELs, as shown in Figure 15.23c,d. A much faster reduction was observed in the absorption spectra measured for the IT-4F layer formed on the PEDOT:PSS HEL as compared to the ones measured for the IT-4F layer deposited on the bilayer $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 } ,$ /antimonene HEL over the wavelength range from 600 to $8 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$

The significant change in the absorption behavior observed for the IT-4F layer formed on the PEDOT:PSS HEL is associated closely with the interfacial chemical reaction between the PEDOT structures and INCN moieties in IT-4F acceptor [91, 92], accompanied by free radical reaction during the photo-oxidation process. The concentration of free radicals in the NFA layer increases with the illumination time. IT-4F is an acceptor-donor-acceptor-type molecule, as shown in the inset in Figure 15.23c. The free radicals, generated by the INCN moieties under light illumination, would diffuse through to disturb conjugated bonds in the IT-4F molecules. The interaction between the free radicals on adjacent backbones and side chains induces a decrease in absorption due to the cross-linking of the polymer film.

![](images/f3b8e050b20b1d521e689a8a7392b7403269b4f1027ca4001d4aa7543e30989d.jpg)  
Figure 15.23 Absorption spectra measured for the (a) ${ \mathsf { M o O } } _ { 3 } .$ /antimonene/PM6 layer, (b) PEDOT:PSS/PM6 layer, (c) ${ \mathsf { M o O } } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene/IT-4F layer, and (d) /PEDOT:PSS/IT-4F layer exposed to $1 0 0 \mathsf { m w c m ^ { - 2 } }$ illumination over a light-soaking period from zero to four hours. Source: Weixia Lan.

The absorption peak at $\sim 7 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ is related to the $\pi { - } \pi ^ { * }$ transition and intramolecular charge transfer between the donor and accepter moieties in the IT-4F molecules. The change in the absorption spectra measured for the IT-4F layer formed on the PEDOT:PSS HEL reveals a disruption of the intramolecular charge transfer between the donor and accepter moieties in the IT-4F molecules, caused by the interfacial reaction between the INCN moieties in the IT-4F molecules and the PEDOT quinoidal nanostructures in the PEDOT:PSS HEL. It shows the deterioration of the electron-withdrawing end moieties in NFA molecules, caused by the interfacial reaction between the INCN moieties in the IT-4F and the PEDOT quinoidal nanostructures in PEDOT:PSS [91, 92]. The fast decrease in the absorption measured for the IT-4F layer on PEDOT:PSS HEL, as shown in Figure 15.23d, is due to the interfacial interaction between the IT-4F acceptor and the PEDOT:PSS HEL, resulting in an undesired weakening in the $\pi { - } \pi ^ { * }$ transition and intramolecular charge transfer between the donor and accepter moieties in the IT-4F. The inevitable interfacial reaction between the IT-4F acceptor and the PEDOT:PSS HEL gives rise to a persistent decrease in $V _ { \mathrm { b i } }$ , and hence a continuing drop in $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and FF in the PM6:IT-4F OSCs with a PEDOT:PSS HEL. The continuous deterioration in the IT-4F molecules, introduced by the inevitable interfacial reaction between IT-4F and PEDOT:PSS molecules, is apparently not favorable for the stable operation of PM6:IT-4F OSCs with a PEDOT:PSS HEL. This problem can be resolved by replacing a solution-processable NFA inert $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene HEL for PEDOT:PSS HEL. A stable and high $V _ { \mathrm { b i } }$ in the PM6:IT-4F OSCs with a $\mathbf { M o O } _ { 3 }$ /antimonene HEL is clearly demonstrated, offering an encouraging option for making efficient and durable OSCs.

# 15.6 Summary

This chapter highlights the understanding of the organic/electrode interfacial exciton dissociation, charge recombination processes, and charge collection, which underpin the optimum device design and performance. The charge transport and recombination properties in the BHJ OSCs are investigated systematically using a combination of theoretical calculation, TPC measurements, morphology analyses, and device optimization. It is found that the dissociation of excitons at the organic/metal interface in regular geometry OSCs hampers the electron collection. The origin of unfavorable electron collection is mainly due to the trap-limited bimolecular recombination, resulting in the compensation of drifted photo-generated electrons at the organic/cathode interface. The undesired charge collection can be eliminated by inserting a thin metal oxide interlayer between the organic layer and electrode. It clearly reveals that the removal of the unfavorable interfacial exciton dissociation is a perquisite for a significant enhancement in overall performance of OsCs. Suppression of the metal oxide sub-gap states significantly improves the charge extraction and performance reproducibility. An enhanced stability of the OsCs can be realized through interfacial modification of the interlayer for retaining a high built-in potential. The use of a NFA inert HEL benefits the efficient operation of NFA-based OSCs through suppression of interfacial reaction between the HEL and the INCN moieties in NFA, which otherwise would occur in IT-4F-based NFA-based OSCs with a PEDOT:PSS HEL. The improved understanding on the organic/electrode interfacial modification and retaining a high built-in potential in OSCs provide a comprehensive insight for applications in efficient and stable operation of OSCs.

# Voltage Losses and Charge Transfer States in Donor-Acceptor Organic Solar Cells

Hongbo Wu, Mengyang Li, Zaifei Ma, and Zheng Tang

Donghua University, College of Materials Science and Engineering, Center for Advanced Low-dimension Materials, State Key Laboratory for Modification of Chemical Fibers and Polymer Materials, North Renmin road 2999, Songjiang District, Shanghai 201620, PR. China

# 16.1 The Origin of $\pmb { V _ { \mathrm { o c } } }$ of Solar Cells

# 16.1.1 Voltage Loss in an Ideal Solar Celland the Upper Limit for $\pmb { V _ { \mathrm { o c } } }$

Performance of organic solar cells is improving rapidly, owing to the development of highly efficient photo-active material systems. Short-circuit current density $( J _ { \mathrm { s c } } )$ and fill factor (FF) of state-of-the-art organic solar cells are already comparable to those of inorganic or organic/inorganic hybrid perovskite solar cells [1-15]. However, $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of organic solar cells is quite low, compared to that of the inorganic or perovskite solar cells, when active materials are with similar bandgap energy $( E _ { \mathrm { g } } )$ [16, 17]. This is the main reason that performance of organic solar cells is still worse than that of inorganic or perovskite solar cells. In other words, a large $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ , defined as the difference between $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and $E _ { \mathrm { g } } / q$ , limits the power conversion efficiency (PCE) of organic solar cells [18-25].

To understand the reason for the high $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ in organic solar cells, we first study the origin of $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ in an ideal solar cell. This was first derived by Shockley and Queisser, using the detailed balanced theory [26]. Assuming that for the ideal solar cell, the photo-absorbing active layer is a semiconductor with two energy levels for the ground state and the excited state. This gives rise to a clearly defined energy of bandgap $( E _ { \mathrm { g } } )$ . Thus, photons with energy higher than $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ can be absorbed by the active layer of the ideal solar cell, resulting in generation of electron-hole pairs. Meanwhile, the photo-generated electrons and holes can also recombine. Assuming that the photons are absorbed at a rate, $N _ { \mathrm { a b s } }$ , and the charge carriers recombine at a rate, $N _ { \mathrm { r e c } }$ , then, the rate for extracting the photo-generated charge carriers $( N _ { \mathrm { e x t } } )$ can be defined by the difference between $N _ { \mathrm { a b s } }$ and $N _ { \mathrm { r e c } }$

$$
N _ { \mathrm { e x t } } = N _ { \mathrm { a b s } } - N _ { \mathrm { r e c } }
$$

According to the detailed balance theory [26], a lower limit for $N _ { \mathrm { r e c } }$ is when charge carriers recombine radiatively. Therefore, for the ideal solar cell, charge carriers can only recombine radiatively. Thus, $N _ { \mathrm { r e c } }$ is equal to the photon emission rate $( N _ { \mathrm { e m i } } )$ of the active material in the solar cell. According to Wurfel's generalized Planck law [27], $N _ { \mathrm { e m i } }$ is related to the blackbody radiation spectrum $( B B ( E )$ Figure 16.1) and the absorption spectrum $( A ( E ) )$ of the photo-active layer, characterized by a step-like function, i.e. $1 0 0 \%$ absorbing for photons with energy larger than $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ and non-absorbing for photons with energy smaller than $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ (Figure 16.1); thus,

![](images/61aaadd2c8501a44711c77db651073cbb604e11653c71c8a041163063428d697.jpg)  
Figure 16.1  Blackbody radiation spectrum at $T = 3 0 0 \mathsf { K }$ absorption spectrum of the ideal solar cell, represented by a step-like function, and absorption spectrum of a hypothetic solar cell. Source: Mengyang Li.

$$
N _ { \mathrm { r e c } } = N _ { \mathrm { e m i } } = \int _ { E _ { \mathrm { g } } } ^ { + \infty } B B ( E ) \mathrm { d } E
$$

$B B ( E )$ can be expressed as

$$
B B ( E ) = { \frac { 2 \pi E ^ { 2 } } { c ^ { 2 } h ^ { 3 } \left[ \mathrm { e } ^ { \left( { \frac { E - q V } { k T } } \right) } - 1 \right] } }
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } & { } & { N _ { \mathrm { r e c } } = N _ { \mathrm { e m i } } = \displaystyle \int _ { E _ { \mathrm { g } } } ^ { + \infty } \frac { 2 \pi E ^ { 2 } } { c ^ { 2 } h ^ { 3 } \left[ \mathrm { e } ^ { \left( \frac { E - q V } { k T } \right) } - 1 \right] } \mathrm { d } E } \\ & { } & { \approx \displaystyle \frac { 2 \pi E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { 2 } k T } { c ^ { 2 } h ^ { 3 } } \mathrm { e } ^ { \left( - \frac { E _ { \mathrm { g } } } { k T } \right) } \left[ \mathrm { e } ^ { \left( \frac { q V } { k T } \right) } - 1 \right] } \end{array}
$$

where $q$ is the elementary charge, $c$ is the light speed, $h$ is the Planck's constant, $k$ is the Boltzmann constant, $E$ is the photon energy, and $V$ is the potential voltage over the solar cell.

Assuming that the origin of dark current in the ideal solar cell is a recombination of charge carriers, thus, Eq. (16.4) can be rewritten as

$$
J _ { \mathrm { d a r k } } = J _ { 0 , \mathrm { s q } } \left[ \mathbf { e } ^ { \left( \frac { q V } { k T } \right) } - 1 \right]
$$

![](images/bd1a1faa3279deb88791c1839ad03c7c1e14b6745907de0b9683fd00e5253151.jpg)  
Figure 16.2 (a) $V _ { \mathrm { o c } , \mathsf { S } \mathsf { q } }$ and (b) $\Delta V _ { \ r }$ as a function of $E _ { \mathfrak { g } }$ for an ideal solar cell, derived using the Shockley-Quessier theory. Source: Mengyang Li.

where $J _ { \mathrm { d a r k } }$ is the dark current density, as a function of applied voltage, for the ideal solar cell, and ${ { J } _ { 0 , \mathrm { { s q } } } }$ is often referred to as the dark saturation current density of the ideal Shockley-Quessier solar cell, related to a prefactor $( J _ { 0 0 } )$ and an exponential term dependent on Eg:

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { J _ { 0 , \mathrm { s q } } = J _ { 0 0 } \exp \left( - { \displaystyle { \frac { E _ { \mathrm { g } } } { k T } } } \right) } } \\ { { J _ { 0 0 } = q \displaystyle { \frac { 2 \pi E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { 2 } k T } { c ^ { 2 } h ^ { 3 } } } } } \end{array}
$$

Thus, the characteristic current density $\left( J - V \right)$ curve of the ideal solar cell under illumination is formulated:

$$
J = J _ { \mathrm { p h } } - J _ { \mathrm { d a r k } } = J _ { \mathrm { p h } } - J _ { 0 , \mathrm { s q } } \left[ \mathrm { e } ^ { \left( \frac { q V } { k T } \right) } - 1 \right]
$$

where the photocurrent density $( J _ { \mathrm { p h } } )$ generated by the solar cell is related to $N _ { \mathrm { a b s } }$ via

$$
J _ { \mathrm { p h } } = q \int _ { E _ { \mathrm { g } } } ^ { + \infty } N _ { \mathrm { a b s } } ( E ) \mathrm { d } E
$$

Under an open-circuit condition, the total current density $J$ is equal to zero,

$$
J _ { \mathrm { p h } } = J _ { 0 , \mathrm { s q } } \left[ \mathrm { e } ^ { \left( \frac { q V _ { \mathrm { 0 c } } } { k T } \right) } - 1 \right]
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { V _ { \mathrm { o c } } \approx \frac { k T } { q } \ln \left( \frac { J _ { \mathrm { p h } } } { J _ { 0 , \mathrm { s q } } } \right) } \\ & { \approx \frac { E _ { \mathrm { g } } } { q } + \frac { k T } { q } \ln \left( \frac { c ^ { 2 } h ^ { 3 } J _ { \mathrm { p h } } } { q 2 \pi E _ { \mathrm { g } } ^ { 2 } k T } \right) } \end{array}
$$

From the Eq. (16.12), it can be seen that $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the solar cell increases with increas$\operatorname { i n g } E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ (Figure 16.2a). The second term on the right side of the Eq. (16.12) is a negative value. Thus, Eq. (16.12) shows that energy of the photons absorbed by the solar cell is not preserved, and $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the ideal solar cell is always smaller than $E _ { \mathrm { g } } / q$

Two different mechanisms can be deduced for the loss of photon energy in the ideal solar cell. The first type of energy loss is associated with rapid relaxations of the excited charge carriers, from higher energy states to the edge of the conduction band, releasing heat. The relaxation or thermalization loss of charge carriers can be reduced using multiply active materials with different $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ to construct multijunction solar cells [28-33]; however, for a single junction solar cell, the thermalization energy loss is high.

The second type of energy loss is related to the second term on the right-hand side of Eq. (16.12), which is mainly determined by the characteristics of the recombination current; thus, this loss is related to the rate of photon emission from the ideal solar cell, $N _ { \mathrm { e m i } }$ , or in other words, the rate of radiative recombination of charge carriers. The relationship between charge carrier recombination and $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ or $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ can be intuitively understood: under an open-circuit condition, charge carriers must recombine; therefore, concentration of charge carriers in the solar cell is limited under steady state. This reduces the degree of quasi-Fermi level splitting in the active layer, thus, limits $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ [34, 35]. Because the second term on the right-hand side of Eq. (16.12) is related to radiative recombination of charge carriers in the ideal solar cell, it is often referred to as the radiative recombination loss $( \Delta V _ { \mathrm { r } } )$ term, and it is inevitable in all solar cells. According to Eq. (16.12), it can be deduced that $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { r } }$ increases with increasing $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ (Figure 16.2b).

# 16.1.2 $\pmb { V _ { \mathrm { o c } } }$ and Voltage Loss in Non-ideal Solar Cells

In reality, the active layer of a solar cell is not a perfect absorber and absorption spectrum of the active layer is far from being a step-like function. Therefore, a useful equation, more general than the Wurfel's generalized Planck law, was derived by Rau [36], which relates the emission rate and the dark current to the photovoltaic action of the solar cell:

$$
J _ { \mathrm { d a r k } } = q \int B B ( E ) E Q E _ { P V } ( E ) \mathrm { d } E \left[ \mathrm { e } ^ { \left( \frac { q V } { k T } \right) } - 1 \right]
$$

where $E Q E _ { P V } ( E )$ represents the photovoltaic external quantum efficiency of the solar cell, as a function of photon energy $E$ . Note that $E Q E _ { P V } ( E )$ is equivalent to absorption in the active layer $( A ( E ) )$ , assuming that the ratio between the rate of extracted charge carriers and the rate of absorbed photons, i.e. the internal quantum efficiency (IQE), is $1 0 0 \%$ for the solar cell. Thus, ${ { J } _ { 0 , \mathrm { { s q } } } }$ in Eq. (16.11) is replaced by Jo,rad expressed as

$$
J _ { \mathrm { 0 , r a d } } = q \int B B ( E ) E Q E _ { P V } ( E ) \mathrm { d } E
$$

for the derivation of $J { - } V$ characteristics of the non-ideal solar cell. We now have:

$$
V _ { \mathrm { o c } } \approx \frac { k T } { q } \ln \left( \frac { J _ { \mathrm { p h } } } { J _ { \mathrm { 0 , r a d } } } \right)
$$

Because $B B ( E )$ rapidly reduces with increasing photon energy, ${ \cal J } _ { 0 , \mathrm { r a d } }$ , related to the integral of the product of $E Q E _ { P V }$ and $B B ( E )$ , is primarily determined by the low energy absorption tail of the solar cell (Eq. (16.14)). Therefore, both $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { r } }$ are expected to be strongly dependent on the spectral shape of the absorption onset of the active layer.

For a real solar cell with an absorption spectrum that differs from a step-like function, ${ \cal J } _ { 0 , \mathrm { r a d } }$ is always higher compared to ${ { J } _ { 0 , \mathrm { { s q } } } }$ for a given $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ (determination of $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ for a real-world organic semiconductor will be discussed later in this chapter). Thus, the radiative recombination voltage loss is always higher than that predicted by the Shockley-Quessier theory. Furthermore, charge carriers can also recombine nonradiatively in a real-world solar cell, leading to additional voltage losses. To analyze the additional voltage losses, the total recombination rate $( N _ { \mathrm { r e c } } )$ in Eq. (16.2) for deriving realistic $J { - } V$ characteristics of the solar cell should be rewritten as a function of both radiative $( N _ { \mathrm { e m i } } )$ and non-radiative recombination rate $( N _ { \mathrm { n r } } )$ of charge carriers:

$$
N _ { \mathrm { r e c } } = N _ { \mathrm { e m i } } + N _ { \mathrm { n r } }
$$

Because $N _ { \mathrm { e m i } }$ and $N _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ are related to the electroluminescence external quantum efficiency $( E Q E _ { E L } )$ of the solar cell,

$$
E Q E _ { E L } = \frac { N _ { \mathrm { e m i } } } { N _ { \mathrm { e m i } } + N _ { \mathrm { n r } } }
$$

Equation (16.16) is modified to

$$
N _ { \mathrm { r e c } } = \frac { N _ { \mathrm { e m i } } } { E Q E _ { E L } }
$$

Compared to Eq. (16.2), $N _ { \mathrm { r e c } }$ is not only determined by $N _ { \mathrm { e m i } }$ but also by $E Q E _ { E L }$

The dark saturation current for a real-world solar cell $\left( { { J } _ { 0 } } \right)$ with both radiative and non-radiative recombination decay paths is then

$$
J _ { 0 } = \frac { 1 } { E Q E _ { E L } } J _ { 0 , \mathrm { r a d } }
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle V _ { \mathrm { o c } } \approx \frac { k T } { q } \ln \left( \frac { J _ { \mathrm { p h } } } { J _ { 0 } } \right) } } \\ { { \displaystyle \approx V _ { \mathrm { o c , r a d } } + \frac { k T } { q } \ln ( E Q E _ { E L } ) } } \end{array}
$$

where

$$
V _ { \mathrm { o c , r a d } } \approx \frac { k T } { q } \ln \left( \frac { J _ { \mathrm { p h } } } { J _ { \mathrm { 0 , r a d } } } \right)
$$

Now we have a complete formula (Eq. (16.21) for the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ of a real-world solar cell, in which both radiative and non-radiative recombination of charge carriers can occur. In this formula, the non-radiative recombination voltage loss, represented by the second term, can be quantified by the measurement of $E Q E _ { E L }$ of the solar cell. When $E Q E _ { E L }$ is $1 0 0 \%$ , there is no non-radiative recombination voltage loss in the solar cell, thus Eq. (16.20) is reduced to Eq. (16.15). When the absorption spectrum of the active layer is engineered into a perfect step-like function described by Shockley and Quessier, this equation is further reduced to Eq. (16.11). Now we define $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of a solar cell with $1 0 0 \% E Q E _ { E L }$ as $V _ { \mathrm { o c , r a d } }$ , in addition, we define $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of a solar cell with

![](images/b9325111530aa96ee275c4b9b17ff5e5fbf55222a4da7d3b7b4dd5e7187ffb76.jpg)  
Figure 16.3 Definition of different voltage losses in a real-world solar cell. $E _ { \mathfrak { g } }$ is the optical bandgap energy of the active layer used in the solar cell; $V _ { \mathrm { o c } , \mathsf { S } \mathsf { q } }$ stands for the upper $V _ { \mathsf { o c } }$ Limit derived from the Shockley-Quessier theory; $V _ { \mathrm { o c , r a d } }$ is the radiative recombination Limit for $V _ { \mathrm { o c } } ; \Delta V _ { \mathrm { r , 5 q } }$ $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { r , a d d } }$ , and $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ are the inevitable radiative recombination loss, the radiative recombination loss due to broadening of the absorption tail of the active layer, and the non-radiative recombination loss, respectively. $1 0 0 \% ~ E Q E _ { E L }$ and a step-function absorption spectrum as $V _ { \mathrm { o c , s q } }$ . Then, all voltage loss terms, and their relation to $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ and $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ , as well as the total voltage loss $( V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } )$ due to charge carrier recombination, can be illustrated in one chart, as shown in Figure 16.3. From Figure 16.3, it is clear that in order to increase $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and reduce $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ , we need to reduce both the non-radiative recombination loss $( \Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } } )$ and the additional part of the radiative recombination loss $( \Delta V _ { \mathrm { r , a d d } } )$

# 16.2 $\pmb { V _ { \mathrm { o c } } }$ of Organic Solar Cells

# 16.2.1 Charge Transfer States in Organic Solar Cells

In contrast to inorganic or perovskite solar cells in which free charge carriers are directly generated upon photon excitation, light absorption in organic solar cells results in generation of Frenkel excitons [37-43]. At room temperature, the excitons are tightly bound electron-hole pairs, thus additional energy is needed for the excitons to dissociate into free charge carriers.

In organic solar cells based on the bulk-heterojunction (BHJ) concept [44-47], the active layer is a mixture of an electron donor and an electron acceptor material (Figure 16.4a). At the interface between the donor and the acceptor material, a new ground state often, referred to as the charge transfer (CT) complex, is formed [48-51]. Upon excitation of the new ground state, a new excited state, CT state, is created (Figure 16.4b).

![](images/7fdcf01baecf43b95a43c7a25eba5b2669a7fb8901de5249f7a37327ca366178.jpg)  
Figure 16.4 (a) A schematic picture for the device architecture of an organic solar cell based on the concept of BHJ. The photo-active layer is based on a blend of an electron donor and an electron acceptor material, sandwiched in between two electrodes. One of the electrodes is transparent to allow for light in-coupling. (b) Energetics of excited states and ground state in an organic BHJ solar cell; $E _ { \mathsf { A } ^ { \ast } }$ and $E _ { \mathsf { D } ^ { \star } }$ represent the energies of the local excited states of the acceptor and the donor, respectively. $E _ { \sigma }$ represents the energy of charge transfer state formed at the interface between the donor and the acceptor. $E _ { \mathsf { F C } }$ is the energy for free charge carriers in the solar cell. Source: Mengyang Li.

Optical transitions between the ground state and the CT state are possible to detect using highly sensitive absorption or emission measurement techniques (Figure 16.5) [52-55], and the energy of CT state $( E _ { \mathrm { C T } } )$ is related to the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) levels of the donor and the acceptor materials in the blend. Because $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ is generally lower than that of the local excited (LE) states in the pristine phases, an energetic offset defined as driving energy $( \Delta E _ { \mathrm { { C T } } } )$ or driving force exists, $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } } = E _ { \mathrm { g } } - E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ [56]. Excitons generated in the pristine phases and diffused to the donor-acceptor interface can dissociate into free charge carriers via the intermediate CT state, as illustrated by the schematic picture shown in Figure 16.5c. Thus, the CT states play a crucial role in determining the performance of the solar cell. In this chapter, we mainly focus on the impact of the property of CT state on $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ in organic solar cells.

# 16.2.2 Relation Between CT State and $\pmb { V _ { \mathrm { o c } } }$ of Organic Solar Cells

CT state is the lowest energy state for a BHJ solar cell [49, 51, 57-61]. Therefore, CT state absorption determines the lower energy part, i.e. the tail of the absorption spectrum of the solar cell. Because $B B ( E )$ spectrum decreases rapidly with increasing photon energy, the integral of the product of $B B ( E )$ and $E Q E _ { P V } ( E )$ spectra in Eq. (16.14), determining ${ \cal J } _ { 0 , \mathrm { r a d } }$ for an organic solar cell, is primarily determined by the CT state absorption properties.

Vandewal et al. showed that CT state absorption is a Gaussian function by performing highly sensitivity $E Q E _ { P V }$ measurements [62] and reported that the absorption feature and $E Q E _ { P V }$ of CT state can be well explained in the framework

![](images/a3b2cc4229281b2721d3315a1da3ddb868755e07c8f0b9aaaefdbc9d6ea5cacd.jpg)  
Figure 16.5 (a) Electroluminescence spectra of an organic solar cell based on PBDB-T as the donor material and ITIC as the acceptor material. The emission spectrum is red shifted compared to the emission of either PBDB-T or ITIC, suggesting that there is a new lower emissive energy state formed in the blend active layer of the solar cell, which is assigned to CT state. (b) Sensitive $E Q E _ { P V }$ spectra of the solar cell based on PBDB-T and ITIC, an absorption band, red-shifted compared to that of the neat materials can be resolved in the lower energy part of the spectrum, corresponding to CT absorption. The CT absorption region can be fitted using Eq. (16.23), derived in the framework of Marcus theory. (c) A schematic picture illustrating the formation of local excited state, CT state, and generation of free charge carriers in an organic donor-acceptor blend. Source: Mengyang Li.

of Marcus theory [63],

$$
E Q E _ { P V } ( E ) = { \frac { f E } { \sqrt { 4 \pi \lambda k T } } } \exp \left( { \frac { - ( E _ { C T } + \lambda - E ) ^ { 2 } } { 4 \lambda k T } } \right)
$$

where $k$ is the Boltzmann constant, $T$ is the temperature, $\lambda$ is the reorganization energy, and $f$ is a prefactor mainly determined by the density of the donor and acceptor interfaces $( N _ { \mathrm { C T C } } )$ that allows for the formation of CT states and the oscillator strength $( f _ { \mathrm { o s c } } )$ for the transition from the ground state to the CT state.

Equation (16.18) can now be expanded for an analytical determination of ${ \mathrm { ~  ~ \cal ~ J ~ } } _ { 0 }$ , using CT state-related molecular parameters.

$$
J _ { 0 } \approx \frac { q } { E Q E _ { E L } } f \frac { 2 \pi } { h ^ { 3 } c ^ { 2 } } ( E _ { C T } - \lambda ) \exp \left( - \frac { E _ { C T } } { k T } \right)
$$

By combining Eqs. (16.20) and (16.24), $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of an organic solar cell is expressed as a function of a number of parameters related CT state properties.

$$
V _ { \mathrm { o c } } = { \frac { E _ { C T } } { q } } + { \frac { k T } { q } } \ln \left( { \frac { J _ { s c } h ^ { 3 } c ^ { 2 } } { f q 2 \pi ( E _ { C T } - \lambda ) } } \right) + { \frac { k T } { q } } \ln ( E Q E _ { E L } )
$$

Equation (16.25) shows that $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of a BHJ solar cell depends linearly on $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ . Moreover, the radiative recombination voltage loss $( \Delta V _ { \mathrm { r } } )$ , which is the second term on the right-hand side of the equation, is determined mainly by the prefactor $f$ , related to $N _ { \mathrm { C T C } } \mathrm { a n d } f _ { \mathrm { o s c } }$ of CT state transition. Another important implication from Eq. (16.25) is that for BHJ solar cells, it is the rate of CT state decay instead of free charge carrier recombination determining $J _ { 0 }$ and thus $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ . In addition, $E Q E _ { E L }$ , determining non-radiative recombination voltage loss, represented by the third term on the right-hand side of the Eq. (16.25), is defined by the ratio between the radiative decay rate and the total decay rate of CT state. This was verified by Vandewal et al. by measuring $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ as a function of temperature [62]: extrapolations of $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ to $_ { 0 \mathrm { K } }$ were shown to match the value of $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ determined by a fitting to the $E Q E _ { P V }$ tail using Eq. (16.23).

The fact that $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of an organic solar cell is determined by the CT state properties is also observed in a simple three-state model [58, 64, 65]. As shown in Figure 16.6, in this model, free charge carriers can only be generated and recombined via CT state. Assuming that in steady state, free charge carriers are generated by dissociation of CT state with a density $N _ { \mathrm { { C T C } } } ^ { * }$ and a rate constant $K _ { \mathrm { d i s s } }$ . Under an open-circuit condition, this process needs to be balanced with the disappearing of free charge carriers via formation of CT states with a rate constant $K _ { \mathrm { f c } }$ . Therefore, the following equation must be valid to balance the loss and the creation of free charge carriers:

$$
K _ { \mathrm { f c } } n p = K _ { \mathrm { d i s s } } N _ { \mathrm { C T C } } ^ { \ast }
$$

where $n$ and $p$ represent the density of free electrons and the density of free holes, respectively. Furthermore, generation of CT states via dissociation of the LE states in the pure phases (at a rate $G _ { \mathrm { C T } } \mathrm { . }$ ) and via encounter of free charge carriers (at a rate $K _ { \mathrm { f c } } n p $ ) must be balanced with the disappearing rate of the CT state via CT state dissociation (at a rate $K _ { \mathrm { d i s s } } N _ { \mathrm { C T C } } ^ { * } )$ and via CT state recombination (at a rate $K _ { \mathrm { r e c } } N _ { \mathrm { C T C } } ^ { * } )$ Therefore, we have

$$
G _ { \mathrm { C T } } + K _ { \mathrm { f c } } n p = K _ { \mathrm { d i s s } } N _ { \mathrm { C T C } } ^ { * } + K _ { \mathrm { r e c } } N _ { \mathrm { C T C } } ^ { * }
$$

Combining Eqs. (16.26) and (16.27) gives

$$
G _ { \mathrm { C T } } = K _ { \mathrm { r e c } } N _ { \mathrm { C T C } } ^ { * }
$$

Using Boltzmann statistics, generation of CT states $( N _ { \mathrm { C T C } } ^ { * } )$ and free charge carriers $( n p )$ via thermal excitation depend mainly on $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ and the energy for free charge carrier state $( E _ { \mathrm { f c } } )$ , respectively.

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { N _ { \mathrm { { C T C } } } ^ { * } = N _ { \mathrm { { C T C } } } \exp \left( - \frac { E _ { \mathrm { { C T } } } } { k T } \right) } } \\ { { n p = N _ { A } N _ { D } \exp \left( - \frac { E _ { \mathrm { { f c } } } } { k T } \right) } } \end{array}
$$

where $N _ { \mathrm { A } }$ and $N _ { \mathrm { D } }$ are the effective density of state for the donor and the acceptor material, respectively. Combining Eqs. (16.26), (16.29), and (16.30) gives:

$$
E _ { \mathrm { f c } } = E _ { \mathrm { C T } } - k T \ln \left( \frac { N _ { \mathrm { C T C } } } { N _ { \mathrm { A } } N _ { \mathrm { D } } } \frac { K _ { \mathrm { d i s s } } } { K _ { \mathrm { f c } } } \right)
$$

![](images/5bc5603dfbb09cd1146a968ceb1151aa56f1f9e860c0deb53220110a77716c4d.jpg)  
Figure 16.6 A three-state model illustrating the competition between CT state dissociation and recombination. LE $( \mathsf { S } _ { 1 } )$ represents the local excited state in the donor or the acceptor phase. $\mathsf { S } _ { 0 }$ represents the ground state. $G _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ is the rate for the transition from $\mathsf { S } _ { 1 }$ to CT state; $K _ { \mathrm { d i s s } }$ and $K _ { \mathrm { f c } }$ are the rates for the transitions between CT and free charge carrier (FC) states. $K _ { \mathrm { { r e c } } }$ is the decay rate of CT state. Source: Mengyang Li.

Because the expression for $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ , derived in classic semiconductor physics [19, 66], should also be valid for the organic solar cells, we can derive:

$$
V _ { \mathrm { o c } } = { \frac { E _ { \mathrm { f c } } } { q } } + { \frac { k T } { q } } \ln \left( { \frac { n p } { N _ { \mathrm { A } } N _ { \mathrm { D } } } } \right)
$$

Now, using Eqs. (16.26) and (16.31), the above Eq. (16.32) is reformulated as

$$
V _ { \mathrm { o c } } = \frac { E _ { \mathrm { C T } } } { q } + \frac { k T } { q } \ln \left( \frac { N _ { \mathrm { C T C } } ^ { * } } { N _ { \mathrm { C T C } } } \right)
$$

Using Eq. (16.28), we have

$$
V _ { \mathrm { o c } } = \frac { E _ { \mathrm { C T } } } { q } + \frac { k T } { q } \ln { \left( \frac { G _ { \mathrm { C T } } } { K _ { \mathrm { r e c } } N _ { \mathrm { C T C } } } \right) }
$$

and Eq. (16.34) can be further modified as

$$
V _ { \mathrm { o c } } = { \frac { E _ { C T } } { q } } + { \frac { k T } { q } } \ln \left( { \frac { G _ { C T } } { K _ { \mathrm { r } } N _ { C T C } } } \right) + { \frac { k T } { q } } \ln ( E Q E _ { E L } )
$$

where $K _ { \mathrm { r } }$ is the radiative decay rate constant of CT state, and $E Q E _ { E L }$ is determined by the ratio between $K _ { \mathrm { r } }$ and $K _ { \mathrm { r e c } }$

The expression for the $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of an organic solar cell derived by Vandewal et al. using the simple three-state model is similar to that derived using the detailed balance theory (Eq. (16.25). They both predict that $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ depends linearly on $E _ { \mathrm { C T } } ( \mathrm { n o t } E _ { \mathrm { g } } )$ of the active materials. Thus, the energetic offset, $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ , is a limiting term for $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ . In addition, $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ is logarithmically dependent on $E Q E _ { E L }$ , and there is a radiative recombination loss term related to the radiative decay rate of CT state and the density of CT complex.

# 16.2.3 Determining Factors of $\pmb { K } _ { \mathsf { r } }$ and $\pmb { K } _ { \mathfrak { n } \mathfrak { r } }$ for Organic Solar Cells

From the above analyses, it is clear that the mechanism and the rate of CT state decay are critically important in determining $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ and $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ in organic solar cells. To reduce $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } , K _ { \mathrm { r } }$ should be minimized and $K _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ should be eliminated.

In the framework of Marcus theory, $K _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ is expressed as [67]:

$$
K _ { \mathrm { n r } } = { \frac { 2 \pi } { h } } V _ { \mathrm { c } } ^ { 2 } { \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 4 \pi \lambda k T } } } \exp { \left( - { \frac { ( \lambda - E _ { \mathrm { C T } } ) ^ { 2 } } { 4 k T \lambda } } \right) }
$$

where $V _ { \mathrm { c } }$ is related to the electronic coupling between CT state and ground state, and reorganization energy () is related to the electron-vibration coupling. Considering the quantum nature of electron vibration, $\lambda$ should be divided into two parts, one for the classical low-frequency vibrations and the other for the quantum mechanical high-frequency vibrations [68]. Accordingly, using Born-Oppenheimer approximation, $K _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ is related additionally to the Franck-Condon weighted density of states (FCWD) for a consideration of transitions from the lowest vibrational CT states to the ground states.

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { F C W D ( g ) = ( 4 \pi \lambda _ { s } k T ) ^ { - 0 . 5 } \displaystyle \sum _ { j = 0 } ^ { \infty } \frac { \mathrm { e } ^ { - S } S ^ { j } } { j ! } \exp \left[ - \frac { ( g - j h \overline { { \nu } } _ { \mathrm { v } } - \lambda _ { s } ) ^ { 2 } } { 4 \lambda _ { s } k T } \right] } } \\ { { K _ { \mathrm { n r } } \propto V _ { \mathrm { c } } ^ { 2 } F C W D ( g = E _ { C T } ) } } \end{array}
$$

where $\overline { { \nu } } _ { \mathrm { v } }$ is the mean frequency of the high-frequency vibration modes, $S = \lambda _ { \nu } / h \overline { { \nu } } _ { \mathrm { v } }$ is the Huang Rhys factor, and $\lambda _ { s }$ and $\lambda _ { \nu }$ are the high- and the low-frequency reorganization energies, respectively. Accordingly, the expression for $K _ { \mathrm { r } }$ is also a function FCWD, similar to that of $K _ { \mathrm { n r } }$

$$
\frac { K _ { \mathrm { r } } ( \nu ) } { \nu } \propto V _ { \mathrm { c } } ^ { 2 } \Delta \mu ^ { 2 } F C W D ( g = E _ { C T } - h \nu )
$$

where $\Delta \mu$ is the difference between the static dipole moment of CT state and ground state.

Thus, both $K _ { \mathrm { r } }$ and $K _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ are proportional to ${ V _ { \mathrm { { c } } } } ^ { 2 }$ , and the non-radiative voltage loss $( \Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } } )$ is strongly dependent on $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ and the reorganization energies. Assuming $\lambda _ { s }$ and $\Delta \mu$ do not vary, Vandewal et al. showed that $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ defined by the ratio between $K _ { \mathrm { r } }$ and $K _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ can be expressed as

$$
\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } } \propto A - B \frac { E _ { \mathrm { C T } } - \lambda _ { s } } { h \bar { \nu } _ { \mathrm { v } } }
$$

These results suggest that $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ is very high for systems with low $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ . An intuitive understanding of the dependence of $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ on $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ can be obtained from the diagram of potential energies of the CT and the ground state, as shown in Figure 16.7: the transition rate from the lowest vibrational state in the CT state to the higher vibrational ground state is expected to be significantly higher in the systems with a lower $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ compared to that with a higher $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ , due to a higher degree of overlapping between the vibrational wavefunctions in the CT and the ground states for the lower $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ system.

![](images/6b36564246017baab3605eef7799b5a673cc8f9024eb3258524c3784b66f85bd.jpg)  
Figure 16.7 Potential energy diagram for the excited CT state and the ground state for (a) a high and (b) a low $E _ { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { C T } }$ system. The sublevels indicate the vibrational states and their wavefunctions, and $K _ { \mathfrak { r } }$ and $K _ { \mathfrak { n } \mathfrak { r } }$ are indicated as $k _ { \mathrm { r } }$ and $k _ { \mathfrak { n } \mathfrak { r } }$ in these graphs. The green areas represent the overlap of the wavefunctions between the lowest vibrational state in CT state and a higher vibrational state in the ground state. The degree of wavefunction overlapping determines the non-radiative transition rate from the CT state to the ground state. Source: Mengyang Li.

Considering the surrounding molecular environment in the organic BHJ active layer and its impact on CT state, Azzouzi et al. evaluated additional factors affecting $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ [69]. In their work, FCwD was expressed for all transitions possible between CT and ground states,

$$
\begin{array} { l l r } {  { F C W D ( h \nu ) = \frac { 1 } { \sqrt { 4 \pi \lambda _ { s } k T } } { \sum _ { w = 0 } ^ { \infty } { \sum _ { t = 0 } ^ { \infty } { \frac { \mathrm { e } ^ { - S } S ^ { w - t } } { w ! } } { \big [ } L _ { t } ^ { w - t } ( S ) { \big ] } ^ { 2 } } } } } \\ & { } & { \mathrm { e } ^ { - \{ [ h \nu - \Delta G _ { 0 } + \lambda _ { s } + ( w - t ) * h \bar { \nu } _ { \mathrm { v } } ] ^ { 2 } / 4 \lambda _ { s } k T \} } \mathrm { e } ^ { - t h \bar { \nu } _ { \mathrm { v } } / k T } } \end{array}
$$

where $L$ is the generalized Laguerre polynomial, $w$ and $t$ are the quantum numbers of the vibrational levels in the ground and CT state, respectively, and $\Delta G _ { 0 }$ is the Gibbs-free energy between the initial and the final states, equivalent to $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ , thus,

$$
K _ { \mathrm { n r } } = \frac { 4 \pi ^ { 2 } } { h } V _ { \mathrm { c } } ^ { 2 } F C W D ( 0 )
$$

For deriving the radiative recombination rate constant $K _ { \mathrm { r } }$ , a dipole approximation was used. The recombination rate for a transition resulting in emission of photon energy $h \nu$ $k _ { \mathrm { r } } ( h \nu )$ was expressed as

$$
k _ { \mathrm { r } } ( h \nu ) = \frac { 1 6 \pi ^ { 3 } } { 3 \varepsilon _ { 0 } h ^ { 4 } } \left( \frac { h \nu } { c } \right) ^ { 3 } M ^ { 2 } \mathrm { F C W D } ( h \nu )
$$

where $\varepsilon _ { 0 }$ is the permittivity of free space and $M$ is the transition dipole moment, proportional to the square root of the oscillator strength $f _ { \mathrm { o s c } }$ . Then, the net radiative recombination rate $K _ { \mathrm { r } }$ could be calculated by integrating $k _ { \mathrm { r } } ( h \nu )$ over all the photon energies,

$$
K _ { \mathrm { r } } = \int k _ { \mathrm { r } } ( h \nu ) \mathrm { d } h \nu
$$

The electronic coupling $V _ { \mathrm { c } }$ and transition dipole moment $M$ were related to each other using the generalized Mulliken-Hush (GMH) method.

$$
V _ { \mathrm { c } } = { \frac { M E _ { \mathrm { C T } } } { \sqrt { \Delta \mu ^ { 2 } + 4 M ^ { 2 } } } }
$$

In addition, the expression for $E Q E _ { \mathrm { E L } }$ was modified by the probability of the reabsorption of the emitted photons, expressed as [70]

$$
p _ { e } = \frac { \int A ( E ) B B ( E ) \mathrm { d } E } { 4 d \int n ^ { 2 } \alpha ( E ) B B ( E ) \mathrm { d } E }
$$

where $d$ is the thickness of the active layer, n is the refractive index, $A ( E )$ is the absorption of photons in the active layer, and $\alpha ( E )$ is the absorption coefficient, which can be reproduced theoretically based on calculation of Einstein coefficient [69] and photon-absorption rate.

As a result, Azzouzi et al. showed that oc,rad for an organic solar cell could be modeled using Eq. (16.15), when CT state parameters needed by the FCwD were provided. In addition, $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ could be calculated as

$$
\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } } = - k T \ln \left( p _ { e } \frac { 4 \pi } { 3 \varepsilon _ { 0 } h ^ { 3 } } \frac { \left( \Delta \mu ^ { 2 } + \frac { 3 h ^ { 2 } } { 2 \pi ^ { 2 } h v _ { \mathrm { a g p } } m _ { \mathrm { e } } } f _ { o s c } \right) \int F C W D ( h v ) ( h v ) ^ { 3 } \mathrm { d } h \nu } { F C W D ( 0 ) E _ { C T } ^ { 2 } } \right)
$$

where $m _ { \mathrm { e } }$ is the electron mass and $\nu _ { \mathrm { a v g } }$ is the average frequency of emitted photons. This equation predicts that $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ depends also on the additional molecular parameters, including reorganization energies, $\Delta \mu ^ { 2 }$ , etc. Both the high and the low-frequency reorganization energies could play very important role in determining $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ , especially for organic BHJ systems with higher $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ . For blend systems with smaller $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ is more dominantly determined by the low-frequency reorganization energy. Furthermore, absorption oscillator strength is also important in determining $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ of the solar cells with lower $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$

The method proposed by Azzouzi et al. to analytically reproduce the absorption spectrum of the organic blends, allowing for the determination of $V _ { \mathrm { o c , r a d } }$ , also enabled computational studies on the entangled impact of these additional CT state parameters on both the $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { r } }$ (leading to reduced $V _ { \mathrm { o c , r a d } } )$ and the $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ of organic solar cells. An important result can be derived, i.e. a reduced $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ does not always lead to reduced $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ , as $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { r } }$ could increase as a result of the reduced $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ . Furthermore, it can be seen that to reduce $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ for a selected material system with a fixed $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ the more effective methods are increasing $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ and reducing the high-frequency reorganization energy, $\lambda _ { \nu }$ . In addition, reducing $N _ { \mathrm { { C T C } } }$ and reducing the low-frequency reorganization energy, $\lambda _ { s }$ , or increasing the difference between static dipole moment of the CT and the ground state can also lead to reduced $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ However, increasing $f _ { \mathrm { o s c } }$ is found to be least effective in reducing $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$

![](images/5e8ff105bc757886d6adbcc5fbc871f229a1333ed00fdc1ec6d053e333700e35.jpg)  
Figure 16.8 (a) Determination of CT state-related parameters for an organic solar cell from a fit based on the use of Eq. (16.23), derived in the framework of Marcus theory. The fitting gives the value for $E _ { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { C T } } , f _ { \scriptscriptstyle \mathrm { i } }$ and reorganization energy. Moreover, using the reciprocal relation between absorption and emission allows for a conversion of the CT state $E Q E _ { P V }$ spectrum to the emission spectrum. (b) Reconstructing the tail of the $E Q E _ { P V }$ spectrum from a measured EL spectrum, using the reciprocal relation, for a solar cell with a low $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { { C T } } }$ . The reconstructed $E Q E _ { P V }$ values span for over 10 orders of magnitudes, enabling CT fitting for organic solar cells with small $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { { C T } } }$ . Source: Mengyang Li.

# 16.2.4 Experimental Determination of CT State-Related Parameters

Experimental evaluation on the relationship between $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ and the CT state parameters in organic solar cells requires accurate determination of the different loss values, as well as the CT state-related parameters. A commonly used method is based on sensitive $E Q E _ { P V }$ measurements for a determination of the characteristics of the CT state absorption. Equation (16.23) is used to fit the CT state-related lower energy part of $E Q E _ { P V }$ spectra. The fitting allows for a quantitative determination of $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ and total reorganization energy. In addition, the prefactor $f$ related to the product of $N _ { \mathrm { { C T C } } }$ and $f _ { \mathrm { o s c } }$ can also be determined, as illustrated in Figure 16.8a.

For a series of non-fullerene acceptor-based BHJ blends, CT state absorption is difficult to detect, due to a small energetic offset $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ leading to overlapping between the CT absorption and the LE state absorption [67, 71-73]. To solve this problem, electroluminescence spectroscopic measurements [74-76] are often employed, since the dominant contribution to the EL spectrum of a BHJ solar cell is from CT emission, as discussed before in Figure 16.8a. The measured EL spectrum can be used to reconstruct the lower energy part of the $E Q E _ { P V }$ spectra (Figure 16.8b), using a reciprocal relation [36], extending the tail of the $E Q E _ { P V }$ spectrum for a better determination of CT state absorption properties. However, a recent study pointed out that optical cavity effect in the solar cell device could lead to a distorted CT state EL spectrum, especially for solar cells with very thick active layers. Thus, the accuracy of the method of using EL to determine CT state parameters needs to be further evaluated [77].

The energetic offset between LE and CT state leads to reduced $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ , thus it is a voltage loss term. Determination of the energetic offset $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ requires the determination of $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ For organic materials, the physical definition of $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ is the energetic difference between the vibrationally relaxed excited state and ground states (Figure 16.9) [56]. Optical transitions from the relaxed ground state to high energy vibrational excited states lead to absorption of photon energy larger than $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ and the transitions from the relaxed excited state to higher vibrational ground states lead to emission of photon energy smaller than $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ . Using harmonic oscillators to represent the vibrations in organic molecules, absorption $\left( A ( E ) \right)$ and emission $\left( N ( E ) \right)$ can be expressed as

![](images/fb8dbdeb1619bddd676958e2d4385029c29463dd54eb752e5b201ec81b190c8b.jpg)  
Figure 16.9 Definition of $E _ { \mathfrak { g } }$ for organic semiconductors. (a) A schematic picture showing the excited and the ground state of an organic material. Excitation and recombination occur between the vibrational states in the excited and the ground state. $E _ { \mathfrak { g } }$ is defined as the energy difference between the lowest vibrational states in the excited state and the ground state. (b) Reduced and normalized emission and absorption spectra of a hypothetic organic semiconductor material. The crossing point between the emission and the absorption spectrum gives the value for $E _ { \mathfrak { g } }$ . Source: Mengyang Li.

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { A ( E ) \sim E \exp \left( - \frac { ( E - E _ { \mathrm { g } } - \lambda ) ^ { 2 } } { 4 \lambda _ { L } k T } \right) } } \\ { { N ( E ) \sim E ^ { 3 } \exp \left( - \frac { ( E - E _ { \mathrm { g } } + \lambda ) ^ { 2 } } { 4 \lambda k T } \right) } } \end{array}
$$

These equations indicate that when absorption and emission spectrum are reduced, i.e. divided by $E$ for $A ( E )$ and divided by $E ^ { 3 }$ for $N ( E )$ , the crossing point of the reduced spectra gives the exact value for $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ [56].

A quantitative determination of $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ can then be realized, which is the difference between $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ and $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ . Meanwhile, the measurement used for characterizing CT state $E Q E _ { P V }$ spectrum enables calculation of ${ \cal J } _ { 0 , \mathrm { r a d } }$ , using Eq. (16.14). Note that in Eq. (16.14), the blackbody spectral flux reduces rapidly with increasing photon energy $E$ ; thus, as discussed before, the integral of the product between $E Q E _ { P V } ( E )$ and $B B ( E )$ is primarily determined by the CT absorption related low energy part of the $E Q E _ { P V }$ spectra. Consequently, for an accurate determination of ${ \cal J } _ { 0 , \mathrm { r a d } }$ , a sensitive $E Q E _ { P V }$ measurement for a complete spectral coverage of CT absorption is critical. Accordingly, $V _ { \mathrm { o c , r a d } }$ can be calculated using Eq. (16.15), and $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { r } }$ defined as the difference between $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ and $V _ { \mathrm { o c , r a d } }$ can be quantified. Using $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ as the effective $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ in the Shockley-Queisser limit, we can additionally calculate the upper limit for $V _ { \mathrm { o c , s q } } ( E _ { \mathrm { C T } } )$ of BHJ solar cells then the difference between $V _ { \mathrm { o c , s q } } ( E _ { \mathrm { C T } } )$ and $V _ { \mathrm { o c , r a d } }$ represent the additional radiative recombination voltage losses $( \Delta V _ { \mathrm { r , a d d } } )$ due to CT state absorption spectrum being a non-step-like function, as shown in Figure 16.3. This shows how much can $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ be increased by reducing $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { r } }$ in organic solar cells. Nonradiative voltage losses $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ can also be quantified, when $V _ { \mathrm { o c , r a d } }$ is known, since $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ equals to the difference between $V _ { \mathrm { o c , r a d } }$ and $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of the solar cell measured under solar illumination. In addition, $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ can be quantified by direct measurements of $E Q E _ { E L }$ (Eq. (16.21).

# 16.3 Strategies to Reduce $\pmb { V _ { \mathrm { n r } } }$ and $\boldsymbol { v } _ { \mathrm { { r } } }$ in Organic Solar Cells

In reference [68], it was shown that $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ reduced with increasing $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ , agreeing well with that predicted by Eq. (16.40). More importantly, via investigating a wide range of different organic materials systems, a common mechanism for the high-frequency vibrations in organic blends, being responsible for the large non-radiative recombination voltage losses in organic solar cells, was proposed. According the authors, this mechanism could be assigned to the vibration of carbon-carbon bonds.

To further demonstrate the possibility to achieve low non-radiative voltage loss in BHJ organic photovoltaic devices, Vandewal and coworkers employed organic materials with very high $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ to construct organic solar cells [78]. Because of the high energy of CT state in these blends, solar cells based on these materials exhibited very high $E Q E _ { E L }$ , thus very low $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ . This was a clear evidence proving that the vibronic coupling between the excited and the ground CT state in BHJ could be efficiently reduced using materials combinations with large $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ . It was also observed that transport of charge carriers, thus the IQE and the fill factor (FF), could be problematic in the solar cells based on high $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ materials systems, due to strong binding energies of CT state excitons. However, this problem was resolved using a better suited combination of materials with more desired microstructures. This implied that the electronic property of the highly emissive blend system with high $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ was not an intrinsic limit for achieving good photovoltaic characteristics in organic solar cells. In fact, a major limit for the method of using high $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ system is related to the poor optical property of the blend: to achieve high $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ , active materials with high $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ must be used; thus, the spectral coverage of the photons to be absorbed in the active layer of the solar cell is limited, which leads to low $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$

Maximizing $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ of a BHJ system with a given $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ , or in other words, reducing the energetic difference between $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ and $E _ { \mathrm { C T } } \left( \Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } } \right)$ is a more appropriate strategy to achieve low $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ in organic solar cells with a desired spectral coverage for high photocurrent generation [65, 79-82]. For fullerene organic solar cells, this was observed in the isoindigo:PCBM systems [83]. Compared to an isoindigo-based polymer donor P3TI with three thiophene groups in the repeating unit, another isoindigo-based polymer PTI-1 with only one thiophene had deeper laying LUMO and HOMO levels. Therefore, $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ of the blend based on PTI-1 and PCBM was higher compared to that of the P3TI:PCBM blend, despite that $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ of PTI-1 and P3TI was found very similar. As a result, the energetic offset between the donor and the acceptor in the PTI-1:PCBM blend was found extremely low, approaching $0 \mathrm { e V , }$ which could be assigned as the primary reason for the considerably higher $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ achieved in the PTI-1:PCBM-based solar cell, compared to that in P3TI:PCBM. More importantly, it was found that $E Q E _ { E L }$ of the solar cell based on PTI-1:PCBM was much higher, over an order of magnitude higher than that in P3TI:PCBM, indicating a $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ -dependent $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$

To evaluate that $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ is indeed dependent on $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ , two additional isoindigo-based polymer donors, P5TI and P6TI, were synthesized [84]. More thiophenes were added to the polymer backbones, and $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ of the isoindigo materials was found to be unaffected by the change of the number of thiophenes in the polymer backbone unit. However, it was noted that both the LUMO and the HOMO levels were shifted upward with the increasing number of the thiophenes , leading to reduced $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ and larger $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ . A clear dependence of $E Q E _ { E L }$ on $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ was found, confirming that low $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ could lead to lower $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$

Despite the low $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ achieved using small $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ systems, IQE of the fullerene solar cells were found to be limited when $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ was very small. A possible reason for the low IQE was assigned to inefficient dissociation of CT state excitons into free charge carriers [85-87]. Thus, it was strongly debated whether the method of using the materials combinations with small $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ to achieve lower $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ was effective in improving the overall performance of organic solar cells, until the development of high efficiency non-fullerene organic solar cells.

For non-fullerene acceptor-based organic solar cells, $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ was also found to reduce with smaller $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ . This was first observed using P3TEA as the donor and SF-PD12 as the acceptor: the electroluminescence spectrum of the solar cell based on the blend of P3TEA and SF-PDI2 was found to be identical to that of the device based on pure donor [79], suggesting that $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ of the blend active layer was very close to $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ of the donor material, and $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ was negligible. The small $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ could also be seen from the fact that $V _ { \mathrm { o c , r a d } }$ of the organic solar cell was similar to that predicted by the Shockley-Quessier theory. More importantly, $E Q E _ { P V }$ achieved using this materials system was comparable to that of typical organic solar cells with large $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ suggesting that dissociation of CT excitons was not necessarily prohibited by a low $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ . The benefit of using the low $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ system was clear, and the $E Q E _ { E L }$ of the non-fullerene solar cell based on P3TEA and SF-PDI2 was over $1 0 ^ { - 5 }$ , allowing to achieve $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ as low as $0 . 2 6 \mathrm { V } ,$ approaching that of perovskite solar cells operating without CT states. A comparative study was carried out, and it revealed that the use of a different donor material for a larger $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ resulted in reduced $E Q E _ { E L }$ and increased $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ , suggesting that $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ reducing with $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ was a general trend for organic BHJ solar cells, regardless of the type of the acceptor, fullerene, or non-fullerene, used.

Similarly, high $E Q E _ { P V }$ with low $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ was also achieved using several other non-fullerene materials combinations with small $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ by other groups [88]. To understand the mechanism for the reduced $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ in organic solar cells with small $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ Qian et al. studied a low $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ system, PTB7-Th:IEICO with high $E Q E _ { E L }$ and low $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ [65]. They employed a three-state model in which the electronic coupling for the transition rates between CT and LE state was considered for the determination of the CT state decay dynamics (Figure 16.10).

![](images/90847c827d5a85bed110291a7680dbdd6ea079769757cefc8f0430e372d03c6e.jpg)  
Figure 16.10 A schematic picture of a three-state model used to show the impact of LE excitation on CT state properties in organic solar cells with low $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { { C T } } }$ . Source: Mengyang Li.

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were used to derive the parameters needed in Marcus theory for a determination of the transition rates of the possible transitions between the different states. As a result, a rapid back transfer from CT to LE state with a transition rate order of magnitudes higher than that of the CT to ground state was predicted for the BHJ systems with very small $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ . Thus, two mechanisms for the increased $E Q E _ { \mathrm { E L } }$ and reduced $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ in systems with small $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ were proposed: (i) a hybridization between the CT and the highly emissive LE state, allowing emission probability of CT state to increase through an intensity borrowing mechanism [89, 90]; (ii) the opening of an additional pathway for CT state to decay through the more emissive LE state. Similar conclusion was draw in reference [91].

The intensity borrowing mechanism for organic solar cells with small $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ was explained by Eisner et al. using a similar three-state model [72]. In their work, the interactions between the wave functions of LE state and CT state were allowed for deriving a mathematic expression for the transition dipole moment $( M )$ of the CT to ground state transition. This gave rise to an effective CT to ground state oscillator strength $( f _ { \mathrm { S } _ { 0 } , \mathrm { C T } } ^ { * } )$ , related to the LE to ground state $( f _ { \mathrm { S } _ { 1 } , \mathrm { S } _ { 0 } } )$ , the LE to CT state $( f _ { \mathrm { S _ { 1 } , C T } } )$ and the CT to ground state transition oscillator strength $( f _ { \mathrm { S } _ { 0 } , \mathrm { C T } } )$ derived without considering the hybridization of the states,

$$
f _ { \mathrm { S } _ { 0 } , \mathrm { C T } } ^ { * } = f _ { \mathrm { S } _ { 0 } , \mathrm { C T } } + \frac { f _ { \mathrm { S } _ { 1 } , \mathrm { S } _ { 0 } } V _ { \mathrm { S } _ { 1 } , \mathrm { C T } } ^ { 2 } } { \Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } } ^ { 2 } } + 2 \frac { f _ { \mathrm { S } _ { 1 } , \mathrm { S } _ { 0 } } ^ { 1 / 2 } f _ { \mathrm { S } _ { 0 } , \mathrm { C T } } ^ { 1 / 2 } V _ { \mathrm { S } _ { 1 } , \mathrm { C T } } } { \Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } } }
$$

where $V _ { \mathrm { S } _ { 1 } , \mathrm { C T } }$ represents the electronic coupling between the LE and the CT state.

An important observation from Eq. (16.50) was that the ratio between $f _ { \mathrm { S } _ { 0 } , \mathrm { C T } } ^ { * }$ and $f _ { \mathrm { C T } , \mathrm { S } _ { 0 } }$ increased drastically with a reducing $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ , suggesting that the effective oscillator strength determining CT state decay rate was significantly higher in a low $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ system with hybridized states than that in the high $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ system. Furthermore, from Eq. (16.50), the dependence of $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ on $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ and on $V _ { \mathrm { o c , r a d } }$ can be observed. For the systems in which LE state and CT state were hybridized, $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ was predicted to decrease with decreasing $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ , and it decreased much quicker when $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ was close to $0 \mathrm { e V . }$ Nevertheless, it was noted that the reduced $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ did not always lead to reduced $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ for the hybridized system because $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { r } }$ increased due to the increased effective oscillator strength $f _ { \mathrm { S } _ { 0 } , \mathrm { C T } } ^ { * }$ . Further calculations revealed that $K _ { \mathrm { r } }$ did increase with decreasing $\Delta E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$

The reduced $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ , associated with increased $K _ { \mathrm { r } }$ leading to increased $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { r } }$ , was also observed experimentally in solar cells constructed using a solvent vapor annealing (SVA) method. Using different processing conditions [69], Azzouzi et al. showed that by varying the time used for the SVA treatment, $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ of the solar cells based on a series of BIT oligomer donors could be easily tuned: $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { r } }$ increased and $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ reduced with the reducing SVA time, leading to a rather constant $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ . Because the energetics of the active layer and $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ remained unaffected by the SVA treatment, the most likely reason for the increased $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { r } }$ and reduced $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ was thus assigned to increased $f _ { \mathrm { o s c } }$ , which was also confirmed by using the theoretical model proposed in that work [69]. Thus, increasing $f _ { \mathrm { o s c } }$ would not always be an effective method to reduce $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ in organic solar cells.

The impact of the density of charge transfer complex $( N _ { \mathrm { C T C } } )$ on $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ was also found to be strong. Vandewal et al. studied a series of $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ -based vacuum deposited small molecule solar cells in which the concentration of the donor component (TAPC or MeO-TPD) in the active layer was varied from $1 \%$ to $1 0 \%$ [92]. Despite that the donor concentrations in these active layers were low and $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ was the main absorber, high $E Q E _ { P V }$ were obtained from the solar cells with a low donor content. More importantly, the $E Q E _ { P V }$ measurements revealed that $N _ { \mathrm { { C T C } } }$ reduced with the decreasing concentration of the donor in the active layer, while $E _ { \mathrm { C T } }$ remained constant. Thus, the impact of $N _ { \mathrm { { C T C } } }$ on $V _ { \mathrm { o c , r a d } }$ could be evaluated: $V _ { \mathrm { o c , r a d } }$ was found to increase with the reducing $N _ { \mathrm { C T C } }$ , a result of reduced $K _ { \mathrm { r } }$ , and the increased $V _ { \mathrm { o c , r a d } }$ could fully explain the increase in $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ achieved in the solar cells with a lower donor concentration. Therefore, it was suggested that the reduced $N _ { \mathrm { { C T C } } }$ leading to reduced $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { r } }$ could in turn lead to reduced $V _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$ . Moreover, the impact of $N _ { \mathrm { { C T C } } }$ on $\Delta V _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ was expected to be weak because the change of $N _ { \mathrm { { C T C } } }$ should equally influence both $K _ { \mathrm { r } }$ and $K _ { \mathrm { n r } }$ . Indeed, transient photovoltage decay measurement revealed that the charge carrier life time (inversely proportional to recombination rate) increased with reducing Ncrc.

# 16.4 Summary

Organic solar cells are highly promising as an alternative technology to inorganic solar cells. PCE of state-of-the-art organic solar cells are already over $1 8 \%$ , and further improvement in the solar cell performance will rely heavily on the elimination of unnecessary voltage losses. In this chapter, we discussed the origin of voltage losses in both ideal and nonideal solar cells using theoretical methods and demonstrated the importance of CT state properties in determining $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ of organic solar cells. The dependences of both radiative and non-radiative recombination voltage losses on the radiative and non-radiative decay rates of CT state were discussed, and the determining factors for the decay rates of CT state were analyzed. Furthermore, experimental methods for evaluating the CT state-related properties and determining different types of voltage losses were introduced. Finally, the strategies used to reduce voltage losses in organic solar cells were reviewed.
