# 17.1 Introduction

Owing to the unique properties, such as low production cost, lightweight, and ease of continuous manufacturing on a large scale, organic photovoltaics (OPVs) technology is considered one of the most attractive renewable energy sources for off-grid power supply [1, 2]. Substantial efforts have been devoted to improving the performance of organic solar cells (OsCs) over the last two decades. Encouragingly, innovations in both material design and device engineering have recently driven the power conversion efficiency (PCE) of OSCs over $1 8 \%$ [3], approaching the benchmark efficiency of $2 0 \%$ [4, 5]. while the performance of OsCs has been continuously developed to reach the market readiness, the relatively poor stability (or short operational lifetime) of OsCs compared to other conventional photovoltaic technologies needs to be fully investigated. Today's OPV modules are targeting lifetimes of ${ > } 5$ years for flexible products and ${ > } 1 0$ years for glass-based products. Further increasing the lifetimes of OPV devices will directly contribute to the reduction of the levelized cost of energy (LCOE) and to broaden their applicability in various scenarios, for instance, the building- and mobile-integrated applications. Although OSCs with impressive device stability under various conditions have been reported in the literature, the stability of most state-of-the-art high-performing OPV systems is not very encouraging. As the stability of OsCs is one of the main obstacles toward their commercialization and industrial applications, it is imperative to investigate and understand the degradation mechanisms of OsCs under various conditions. In the following sections, we will discuss the major factors that are limiting the stability of OsCs, including extrinsic stresses and intrinsic ones. The evaluation protocols of device stability suggested by international commission and organizations are summarized and demonstrated. We will then review the recent progress on developing stable OSCs, specially focusing on the OPV material systems with stable microstructures and strategies to effectively enhance the morphological stability of OSCs.

# 17.2 Factors Limiting the Stability of Organic Solar Cells

In order to continuously develop the OPV technology with high efficiency and stability, it is very useful to ascertain the origin of degradation mechanisms. Is the degradation of OsCs fundamentally related to the organic materials or to the processing parameters? Is it possible to address or suppress the degradation of OSCs during operation? It has been found that many factors, including external stresses and intrinsic factors, can limit the stability of OsCs in a simulated environment or in the real operational conditions. For instance, a poor extrinsic stability could be caused by forming crack or delamination, whereas a poor intrinsic stability could be linked to an interface or phase separation inside a well-operating solar cell. In this section, we focus on the limiting factors behind the instability from the perspective of external stresses and intrinsic factors.

# 17.2.1 Extrinsic Stresses

OSCs with a multilayer structure suffer from external stresses under operation conditions, including irradiation, heating, oxidation, mechanical stress, etc. Here we will discuss the mechanisms of major external stresses as mentioned in the literature.

# 17.2.1.1 Light Effect

Light effect, also known as light-induced degradation or photo-degradation, is one of the well-known degradation mechanisms for OSCs, including photo-physical and photochemical degradations [6, 7]. The photo-physical degradation is a main pathway for photo-degradation of OsCs, which was found to be more sensitive to the ultraviolet (UV) light [7, 8]. On the one hand, UV light could induce decomposition of light-sensitive additives remained in the photoactive layer (e.g. 1,8-diiodooctane (DIO), which creates more electron traps to reduce the device performance [9]. On the other hand, the solar irradiation could also increase the temperature of OSCs, resulting in the change of microscopic morphology of the photoactive layer as well as device performance [10].

Additionally, the photochemical degradation is another pathway for photodegradation of OsCs, which is caused by the photo-oxidation of the active layer and interface layers in most of the cases. Both the donor and acceptor materials could face photo-oxidation process under illumination, which changes their molecular structures [11], and as a result, leads to reduced light absorption, charge generation, and mismatched energy level alignment [12-14]. In addition, the photo-oxidation process could generate sub-bandgap states, which induce traps and energetic disorders in the active layer and accelerate the non-radiative recombination, and thus attenuate device performance [12, 15, 16]. Besides, other photochemical processes such as the photo-oligomerization of fullerene acceptors are also responsible for the photochemical degradation in OsCs [17, 18]. Apart from the photo-physical degradation and photochemical degradation of active layer materials, stability of interfacial materials also plays a critical role in the photo-degradation process. Moreover, the interface property is also one of the most important factors that contribute to the photo-degradation behaviors of OSCs.

# 17.2.1.2Thermal Effect

Most of high-performance OsCs suffer from the thermal instability issues in the real world [19-21], which is related to the physical degradation to a large extent [22, 23]. It is known that the optimal blend morphology is generally away from its thermodynamic equilibrium state and could slowly evolve to the equilibrium case without extrinsic factors [24], even at a low temperature [25]. Of particular note is that the working temperature of solar cells could be relatively high due to continuous illumination $( > 6 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ , which may significantly accelerate the evolution of blend microstructure morphology, for instance, the thermal-induced aggregation and crystallization of fullerene and non-fullerene acceptors (NFAs) in the active layer [23, 26-28]. The changes of blend morphology in terms of obvious phase separation in the active layer can reduce the interface area between the donor and acceptor materials, which can sharply decrease the performance of OsCs resulting from inefficient exciton separation and charge transfer by decreased D/A interfaces [23]. Moreover, heating-induced degradation can also occur at the interface between active layer and interface layers [29, 30] and between the interface layers and electrodes [7], normally leading to the increased energy barriers for hole and/or electron extraction [29-31].

# 17.2.1.3 Environmental Effect

Air instability is another important issue for OSCs, which is generally detrimental to the device performance [32]. Ambient water and oxygen can diffuse throughout the whole device and result in severe physical and chemical degradation in the active layers, interface layers as well as electrodes [33-35]. It has been reported that oxygen and water could take part in the photo-oxidation process of photovoltaic materials, which changes their molecular structures, optoelectronic properties, and charge transport mobilities [12, 14, 36, 37]. In addition, the permeation of water and oxygen could also cause the morphology changes of photoactive layers, leading to reduced open-circuit voltage $( V _ { \mathrm { o c } } )$ and fill factor (FF). Besides, water and oxygen permeation can also cause oxidation in interface layers and at the interfaces [38], as well as low work function metal electrodes such as calcium and aluminum [39-41], which generally act as pinholes or electrically insulating layer to inhibit charge transport and extraction properties. Notably, water and oxygen always simultaneously lead to device degradation [42, 43].

# 17.2.1.4Mechanical Stress Effect

Degradation induced by mechanical stress, which occurs in the fabrication, transportation, installation, and application, is generally unavoidable in OSCs [44-46]. Moreover, factors in real external conditions such as hail, wind, and rain can also cause mechanical stress to devices [47]. Thus, the mechanical robustness is one of the most crucial requirements for ensuring the long-term device stability. There are several types of degradation that can occur in OSCs under mechanical stress.

First, mechanical stress could cause delamination of the blend morphology resulting in the poor charge transport and extraction properties in devices [48]. Second, the linear mechanical tension can create strains of OPV materials which changes the blend morphology leading to the loss of device performance [49]. Third, the lateral mechanical strain can also cause degradation in the relative brittle layers (e.g. indium tin oxide [ITO] electrode and active layer), which further degrades the device performance [50, 51]. Fourth, mechanical stress can result in cracks and punctures in the functional layers of OsCs. These defects may facilitate the ingress of water and oxygen in the devices and thus accelerate the degradation of device performance [52]. Therefore, mechanical stress could induce degradation in photoactive layer, interface layers and electrodes. This is even critical when replacing the rigid glass substrates with flexible substrates for large-scale roll-to-roll production of OSCs.

# 17.2.2 Intrinsic Factors

OSCs with a multilayer stacked architecture show uncontrollable stability even without extrinsic degradation factors. It is known that the morphology changes in the active layer and the diffusion of interfacial and electrode materials into the photoactive layer are two main reasons for the inherent device instability [33, 34].

As aforementioned, the optimum morphology, which delivers the best performance, is usually away from its thermodynamic equilibrium. Even though the optimum bulk-heterojunction (BHJ) morphology is optimized for achieving high device performance, it will slowly evolve toward the equilibrium state and cause more or less microstructure changes in the active layer, or at the interfaces between the active layer and interfacial layers [24, 25]. Due to the different interfacial surface energy and high diffusion constant of donor and acceptor photovoltaic materials [24, 25], and sometimes the structural incompatibilities between donor and acceptor materials [22, 28, 53], the donor/acceptor phase separation is the main result of the inherent morphology evolution. Moreover, it has also been demonstrated that the high stability of BHJ photovoltaic systems can result from its ideal miscibility of donor and acceptor materials that the initially optimized morphology is located at the thermodynamic equilibrium [26, 54, 55].

Similar to the OPV materials, the interface materials and metal electrodes of OSCs also exhibit diffusivity. For instance, the commonly used hole transport layer PEDOT:PSS (poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrenesulfonate)) could diffuse into the active layer [39]. Of note is that PEDOT:PSS layer possesses the hygroscopicity, acidity, and anisotropic charge injection properties, which could result in device instability. With respect to the commonly used electrodes, e.g., Ag and ITO, Ag and In atoms could diffuse into the functional semiconducting layers even without extrinsic factors [56-58]. The diffusion of electrodes can cause traps in the active layer and tune the relevant energy levels [11]. As a result, all of these intrinsic factors can accelerate the non-radiative charge recombination and lead to the inherent device instability.

It is worthwhile to mention that most of "degradation profiles" of OsCs can be divided into two regimes, which include an initial sharp drop in performance (also called as "burn-in' degradation) followed by a slow linear performance degradation trend [59]. Researchers speculated possible reasons for the origin of burn-in losses, including the increased trap mediated charge recombination, the broad polydispersity of polymer materials, the fullerene dimerization, the organic or inorganic impurities in the film, which have to be in-depth analyzed for given material systems [60-63]. In addition, many recent studies also revealed that the morphological change of photoactive layer is the reason for the initial sharp performance degradation of OSCs [23, 24, 64]. Notably, both intrinsic and extrinsic factors can cause morphology changes and accelerate the morphology evolution which present as a fast degradation at the initial stage. The rate of morphology evolution could be slowed down when the microstructure morphology is close to the equilibrium state, thus exhibiting the slow linear degradation behavior. As expected, the stability issues caused by the interface materials and electrodes could be effectively overcome by developing advanced functional materials. However, for efficient and stable OsCs, the control of the subtle nanometer-scale morphology is of the utmost importance, since efficient photo-to-electricity conversion processes depend crucially on the microstructure of the photoactive layer.

# 17.3 Stability Evaluation Protocols

Apart from cost and efficiency, the reliability assessment is regarded as a critical prerequisite for pre-commercial photovoltaic concepts. The lifetime for photovoltaic modules is expected to be around 20 years or longer for possible commercial applications. Thus, international committees have been developing standardized qualification test. In particular, a suite of standard documents were designed by International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC, Genf, Switzerland), including three most applied standards: terrestrial photovoltaic (PV) modules - design qualification and type approval (IEC 61215); thin-film terrestrial photovoltaic (PV) modules - design qualification and type approval (IEC 61646); and concentrator photovoltaic (CPV) modules and assemblies - design qualification and type approval (IEC 62108). These tests, however, are more applicable for the well-understood degradation modes generally related to the terrestrial thin film at the module level, which are not intended to interpret degradation pathways and identify the relative mechanism limiting the device lifetime. Thus, this must be considered when applying it directly to the emerging technologies such as OSCs, dye-sensitized solar cells (DssCs), and perovskite solar cells (PSCs) because of their different material properties, various unapprehended failure modes, and immature product development for commercialization. In 2010, the International Summits on Organic PV Stability (IsOs) held in Roskilde, Denmark, discussed and established the standardized aging experiments (so-called IsOs protocols). These are summarized in a publication entitled "Consensus stability testing protocols for OPV materials and devices' in 2011 [65], offering a consensus in the OPV field on investigating and reporting degradation research in a controllable, comparable, and reproducible way, subsequently, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of device degradation that is not fully elucidated or appreciated by IEC standards. Briefly, IEC standards (such as IEC technical specification [TS] 62876-2-2:2018) and IsOS stability protocols both describe the typical stress conditions including radiation, temperature, humidity, atmosphere, load, etc., but differing in some specific parameters. For example, IEC 61646 provides some extreme external stress conditions, like UV precondition, mechanical load, hail, or high external voltage. Further tests include bypass diode and hot spot endurance, and these tests intend to confirm device safety and qualify the device for commercial products.

Table 17.1 displays the newest existing ISOS protocols and suggests additional protocols that are discussed in the 11th International Summit on Organic and Hybrid Photovoltaics Stability. Generally, the ISOS protocols are grouped in terms of the applied stresses into seven categories, dark storage testing, outdoor testing, light soaking testing, thermal cycling testing, solar-humidity-thermal cycling testing, light-dark cycling and electrical bias in the dark testing, as well as three levels of execution with increasing complexity and requirement on equipment and accuracy, namely basic, intermediate, and advanced. In addition to these measurement conditions, many discussions regarding the light source used for artificial illumination, correct interpretation for stability data, and operational lifetimes are also discussed. Overall, these two frameworks outlined the hierarchy in stability analysis for module level (IEC) and cell level (IsOs), allowing the requirement of standardized testing conditions for industrial and scientific community [67].

# 17.4  Progress in Developing Stable Organic Solar Cells

# 17.4.1 Development of Organic Photovoltaic Materials with Stable Microstructure Morphology

The revolution and development of OPV materials with new molecule structures have greatly contributed to the rapid development of OPV technology [68, 69]. On the early stage of development of OsCs, some representative materials like polymer donor poly[2-methoxy-5-(2-ethylhexyloxy)-1,4-phenylenevinylene] (MEH-PPV), poly(3-hexylthiphene-2,5-diyl) (P3HT) and $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 }$ derivative [6,6]-phenyl $C _ { 6 1 }$ butyricacid methyl ester $( \mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M } )$ ,and its corresponding $\mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ derivative [6,6]-phenyl- $\mathrm { \cdot } \mathrm { C } _ { 7 1 }$ -butyric acid methyl ester $\mathrm { ( P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M ) }$ dominated the highperformance active layer materials, delivering a PCE of $4 \% - 5 \%$ thus attracting worldwide interests in OPV. Many more high-performance polymers have been developed subsequently. In 2009, Yu and coworkers developed a low bandgap polymer donor material PTB1 [70] and these serials PTBn $\mathit { \Delta } n = 1 { - } 7 \mathit { \Delta }$ boosted efficiency up to $7 . 4 \%$ . Following this work, PCEs of more than $1 0 \%$ were frequently reported for fullerene-based OSCs with new materials [71]. On

the other side, NFAs, including both polymeric and small molecular organic acceptors, attracted increasing attention in recent years. A breakthrough was made in 2015 by Zhan and coworkers, who reported an electron acceptor material (3,9-bis (2-methylene-(3-(1,1-dicyanomethylene) - indanone))-5,5,11,11- tetrakis(4- hexylphenyl)-dithieno $[ 2 , 3 \mathrm { - } \mathrm { d } ; 2 ^ { \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime } \mathrm { - } \mathrm { d } ^ { \prime } ]$ -s-indaceno[1,2-b:5,6-b']dithiophene[ITIC]) [72] showing a superior PCE to $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ in OSCs. This type of fused-ring electron acceptors (FREAs) remarkably boosted PCEs of OSCs to $1 5 \%$ [73]. Recently, high PCEs of $1 5 \% - 1 8 \%$ attained for brand-new Y-series acceptors significantly prompted OSCs research [3, 74, 75] which in turn eagerly appeal for the improvement of stability and reducing synthetic costs.

# 17.4.1.1 Organic Solar Cells Based on Fullerene Acceptors

The previous investigation on improvement of PCE via subtle molecular structure design and modulation endows us with a new perceive into the interrelation among structure, morphology, and stability, which also attracted increasing researchers' attention and was typically used as a supplementary section in the article along with discussion about molecular design guidelines. In most cases of fullerenes-based devices, the initial loss up to $2 0 \% - 5 0 \%$ of PCE (referred to as "burn-in loss") in the time period from a few hours to days imposes restrictions on industrialization. Tremendous studies revealed that such reported burn-in losses not barely stem from one single factor. The multiple degradation pathways occur and interact according to various environmental stresses, such as photo-induced dimerization [76], micro-phase separation caused by spinodal donor-acceptor demixing [24], fullerene diffusion induced formation of crystals via Ostwald ripening under thermal stress [77], and photochemical reaction with DIO [78, 79]. With these insights, the investigation of modification on molecular structure has been made to enhance the stability of fullerene-based OsCs. In addition, engineering of donor materials is one of the important research fields. McGehee and coworkers found that molecule size and crystallinity of active layer affected the initial exponential burn-in process. Heat- and light-induced burn-in was retarded by larger molecules and active layer morphology with higher crystallinity [80]. A similar result was demonstrated by Brabec and coworkers, as shown in Figure 17.1a [18]. With the enhancement of donor polymer crystallinity, leading to the formation of pure fullerene domains, fullerene dimers are more likely to be produced in the blend film during light soaking. By increasing fullerene ordering crystallinity, enhanced photo-stability against photo-induced dimerization was observed compared to the amorphous one. Briefly, these findings strongly suggested that phase morphology of OPV films, especially in terms of crystallization, has a strong impact on photo-stability. Thus, the knowledge of the effects of structural device stability is a prerequisite for superior stability by the rational structure design of donor materials. Also, it is now recognized that the stability of OsCs is influenced by the side chains of donor materials. Yang and coworkers synthesized three polymers, P1, P2, and P3 (as shown in Figure 17.1b) [81], containing different conjugated lengths of side chains on the same backbone and found that the longest side chain polymer, alkyl-thieno[3,2-b]thiophene (TT)-substituted P3, offered improved morphological stability relative to other two counterparts. The outstanding morphological stability of P3 blend could be ascribed to continuous networks of polymer whiskers served as frames to "lock" the nanoscale PCBM domains, greatly reducing the nucleation rate of PCBM and impeding its further aggregations. As a result, P3-based devices exhibited the most stable performances and presented a slight PCE loss (Figure 17.1c). Furthermore, alkyl chain length and side chain placement could impact the thermal stability as well [83]. Besides, a number of researchers have reported that significant phase separation induced by PCBM dimerization/aggregation is responsible for performance deterioration due to the driven of thermodynamic non-equilibrium state. Thus some efforts have been devoted to the substitution of fullerene with modified derivatives [84]. Brabec and coworkers found that miscibility between donor and acceptor is also an essential parameter for the stability evaluation. Accordingly, two fullerene derivatives, pyrrolidinofullerene (PyF5) and methanofullerene (FAP1), showing improved miscibility with PTB7-Th than PCBM, exhibited excellent device thermal stability (Figure 17.1d) [82].

# 17.4.1.2 Organic Solar Cells Based on Non-fullerene Acceptors

Burn-in loss free has been reported for NFA-based OSCs, yielding excellent lightand thermal-stability [85, 86]. Therefore, the replacement of fullerene derivatives with NFAs in OPV has been recently proven to be useful to enhance stability. Furthermore, the diversity of the NFAs structure by rational design provides us with more options regarding prolonged intrinsic stability. Some valid strategies like altering the planarity and rigidity with the enhancement in crystallinity [87], incorporating the antioxidant additive [12], the substitution of unstable molecular side chains [88], and increasing the molecular weight [53] have been developed to significantly suppress the initial rapid attenuation. Recently, we investigated a group of ITIC derivatives and found that end-group and side-chain engineering of the NFAs strongly influenced the photo-stability of OSCs (Figure 17.2a) [88]. The energetic traps were raised with the breaking of conjugation during photo-aging. More specifically, fluorination of the end-group stabilized molecules against light soaking, while the addition of methyl groups showed an opposite trend, and side-chain modification can significantly influence the morphological stability, disclosing molecular orientation transformation from more face-on to edge-on after illumination in the case of ITIC (Figure 17.2b). Later, based on this observation, further investigations on the photo-stability of poly[(2,6-(4,8-bis(5-(2-ethylhexyl)thiophen-2-yl)benzo[1,2-b: $4 , 5 \cdot 6 ^ { \prime }$ |dithiophene)-co-(1, 3-di(5-thiophene-2-yl)-5,7-bis(2-ethylhexyl)-benzo[1, 2-c: $ 4 , 5 \mathrm { - c ^ { \prime } }$ |dithiophene-4,8-dione))] (PBDB-T) derivatives (PBDB-T-2F or PM6) incorporating IT-4F (also named as ITIC-2F) were discussed. We revealed that the initial morphology as to the ordering of both polymer and aggregated IT-4F domains significantly influenced degradation rate (Figure 17.2c).

Notably, a deeper insight demonstrated the formation of small-scale isolated NFA domains as a result of polymer reorganization and low diffusion coefficient of IT-4F (Figure 17.2d), which contributes to the morphological traps for electron transport and causes long-term FF degradation [89]. Moreover, the subtle changes in molecular structure, especially in the linkage difference, have been demonstrated to provide decent longevity under the external stress. Song and coworkers designed and synthesized a NFA i-IEICO-2F, an isomer of IEICO-2F [90]. The electron-withdrawing portion of i-IEICO-2F is connected at the 4-position of the alkoxythiophene unit, instead of the previously reported 5-position, leading to a more twisted main chain configuration and a significant blue shift of absorption peak by $1 3 2 \mathrm { n m }$ . In return, this tiny structure variation with more twisted main chain has increased the intramolecular steric hindrance, maintained a consistent morphology and molecular orientation regardless of the continuous thermal stress, which decreased aggregation and phase separation. On the contrary, a higher-order packing and agglomeration of IEICO-4F and i-IEICO-4F generated excessive phase separation, resulting in poor charge transport, and eventually a rapid deterioration in $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ and FF.

In summary, these continuous efforts provide insights into the effect of molecular structure, orientation, and morphology of the blended films on device stability; the more thorough understanding of molecular structure dependence of intrinsic material stability, materials compatibility between donor and acceptor, and morphology evolutions under environmental stresses should be emphasized in the following investigation.

# 17.4.1.3 Organic Solar Cells Based on Polymeric Acceptors

Another promising strategy for enhancing device stability was focused on the polymerization of small molecule acceptors or polymer acceptors. Many studies have shown that all-polymer solar cells possess unique characteristics, such as superior thermal stability, mechanical stability, and photo-stability in comparison to fullerene and small-molecule acceptor materials [91]. A direct comparison between all-polymers and polymer-fullerene-based OsCs was performed by Kim and coworkers [92]. The thermal-driven diffusion of PCBM and observable phase separation deteriorated the performance for fullerene-based OsCs. In contrast, an unchanged morphology under the same aging conditions was observed for all-polymer OsCs due to the low diffusion kinetics of the polymer acceptors (Figure 17.3a). Moreover, further exploration by Ma and coworkers disclosed that all-polymer photovoltaic devices displayed a stronger resistance against moisture over their polymer:PCBM counterparts [93]. They speculated that diffusion of water through the PCBM domains into the blend film changes the electrical properties, and further induces the aggregation of fullerene. Consequently, all-polymer devices almost remained the initial efficiency under ambient condition ${ ( { \approx } 2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } }$ relative humidity: $2 0 \%$ ), while polymer-fullerene device exhibited only $6 7 \%$ of its initial performance (Figure 17.3b). Other merits of all-polymer OSCs have also been proposed in recent years including excellent photo-stability and mechanical property [76, 94]. Under these scenarios, all-polymer systems are expected to be a promising candidate for further enhancing the long-term stability of OsCs under the real operational condition.

# 17.4.2  Strategies to Enhance the Morphological Stability of Organic Solar Cells

So far, most of the studies on stability of organic solar cells have been done with fullerene-based material systems. In recent years, dramatic progress was evidenced in NFA-based systems. Readers are referred to the recent review articles on this topic [95-97]. Here, we focus on the strategies specifically for improving morphological stability in both fullerene acceptor (FA) and NFA material systems.

For FA-based material systems, the main obstacles for stable morphology are phase separation between donor and FA acceptors and/or crystallization under thermal or illumination stress. For example, $\mu \mathrm { m }$ sized PCBM crystals could form in P3HT:PCBM blends under thermal stress [98]. Strong demixing of donor and acceptor materials even under dark storage could lead to severe $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ burn-in losses [24]. Over the past decades, significant efforts have been devoted to tackling these issues. Phase separation normally occurs in the amorphous donor/acceptor mixed region [24]. In general, increasing crystallinity, miscibility and/or compatibility between the components, and glass transition temperature of the polymer component could enhance the microstructure stability as well as the device stability [99]. Other strategies for stabilizing morphology are summarized in the following categories: (i) molecular level engineering of photo-active materials including side-chain variations for introducing non-covalent interactions, or covalently linking donor and acceptor materials as a single-component active layer. (ii) Introducing cross-linking concept either by adding crosslinking groups in donor or acceptor side chains or adding extra crosslinkers. (ii) Adding solid additives to form extra bonding or as phase compatibilizers. (iv) Improving initial morphology by processing in terms of solvents, thermal annealing, solvent additives, etc. (v) Using ternary or multinary photo-active semiconductor components. (vi) Synthesizing organic nanoparticles to lock the nano-morphology. (vii) Novel processing methods for morphology control such as layer by layer sequential processing or bilayer heterojunction structures. We separately discuss the strategies with representative examples in the following.

# 17.4.2.1 Introducing Hydrogen Bonding in the Photo-Active Materials

In 2012, Watkins and coworkers reported the cooperative self-assembly of functionalized fullerenes and all-conjugated block copolymers (BCPs) containing polythiophene derivatives in both segments to yield solar cells with well-defined nanostructures and enhanced morphological stability [1oo]. The hydrogen bond interactions between bis-[6,6]-phenyl-C61-butyric acid (bis-PCBA) and P3TODT (Figure 17.4a) segments further suppressed crystallization and macro-phase separation of the fullerenes, even under harsh annealing conditions $\mathrm { ~ \ } 1 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 12 hours). Similarly, in 2013, Qin and coworkers reported a polythiophene diblock copolymer selectively functionalized with 1-n-hexylisoorotic acid moieties (P4) and a 2,6-diaminopyridine tethered fullerene derivative (phenyl-C61-butyric acid 4-( $4 ^ { \prime }$ -pyridinyl)-butyl ester [PCBP]) (Figure 17.4b) [101]. Self-assembly between P4 and PCBP through "three-point' complementary hydrogen bonding interactions was utilized to control and stabilize blend morphologies. Compared to P3HT:PCBM, the thermal stability of devices was improved when annealed at $1 1 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 120 hours in nitrogen atmosphere. In 2020, Liu et al. reported hydroxyl-functionalized NFAs, i.e. IT-OH with one hydroxyl and IT-DOH with two hydroxyls (Figure 17.4c), which could tune the molecular packing and crystallinity assisted by strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds [102]. The solar cells based on IT-DOH showed improved storage and light stabilities compared to those based on ITIC as acceptors, indicating that introducing hydroxyl groups is a promising strategy to tune the molecular packing and crystallinity to design NFAs in order to improve both device efficiency and stability.

# 17.4.2.2 Chemically Linked Donor and Acceptor as a Single-Component Photoactive Layer

An early strategy is to covalently link the donors and acceptors to prevent large-scale phase separation in fullerene-based systems. In 2012, Tajima and coworkers developed oligo $p$ -phenylenevinylene)- $\mathrm { \cdot C } _ { 7 0 }$ dyad, which showed a thermally stable morphology compared to its BHJ counterpart (Figure 17.5a) [103]. In 2017, Woo and coworkers reported BDTRh-PCBM comprising three covalently linked blocks with a PCE of $2 . 4 \%$ showing no degradation at $8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 100 hours (Figure 17.5b) [104]. In 2019, single-component solar cells based on a double-cable polymer, SCP3, were reported to be super stable under thermal and illumination conditions (Figure 17.5c) [105]. The double-cable polymer was designed by covalently linking a diketopyrrolopyrrole (DPP)-based polymer backbone and pendant perylene bisimide (PBI) as electron acceptor with flexible alkyl side chains [107]. Solar cells based on this single-component active layer achieved a PCE of $2 . 7 \%$ and showed no performance losses under white light emitting diode (LED) illumination with $9 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ thermal stress after 300 hours. In a long time, the single-component solar cells have suffered from low performance despite of the promising morphological stability. Very recently, Li and coworkers demonstrated single-component solar cells based on PBDBPBI-S with a PCE of $6 . 3 2 \%$ after film annealed at $2 3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 10 minutes, demonstrating high potential for further simultaneous improvement of performance and morphological stability using this concept (Figure 17.5d) [106].

# 17.4.2.3 Cross-Linking

The idea behind crosslinking is to fix the nanoscale morphology of the active layer. Crosslinking has been explored in different ways including introducing cross linkable groups in the side-chains of donors and/or acceptors, and adding crosslinker in the BHJ blends [108-110]. The crosslinking can be initiated by external stresses like UV illumination and thermal annealing or by photo initiators [108]. Here we highlight some early and recent examples. In 2009, Frechet and coworkers synthesized a series of bromine-functionalized poly(3-hexylthiophenes-2,5-diyl) copolymers (P3HT-Br) containing various amounts of UV crosslinkable brominated unit [111]. Solar cells based on the copolymer with $1 0 \%$ Br content showed comparable PCE with the reference cells without Br, but significantly improved thermal stability at $1 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (Figure 17.6a). The crosslinkable polymer was also used in P3HT/PCBM bilayer devices with a PCE of $2 . 2 \%$ [111]. As a similar approach, in 2019, Park and coworkers synthesized P2FBTT-Br by random copolymerization using an asymmetric monomer with bromine-functionalized alkyl chains on one side and extended branching alkyl chains on the other (Figure 17.6b) [112]. A fast and highly efficient crosslinking can be triggered upon UV light irradiation through radical cleavage between bromine and carbon. This cross-linkable polymer was added into PTB7-Th:IEICO-4F or PTB7-Th:PCBM-based solar cells and effectively enhanced the device thermal and photo-stability (Figure 17.6b). It is noted that the UV-induced crosslinking might also cause photo-degradation of the photoactive materials. While the side-chains are used as crosslinking sites, the conjugated backbone has to be stable against UV irradiation [114]. For instance, several co-polymers (PPDT2FBT-Vx) based on PPDT2FBT and analogues with terminal vinyl-appended side chains for crosslinking showed excellent UV-stability (Figure 17.6c) [113]. The crosslinking concept has also been applied to double-cable single-component photoactive layers [115] and all-polymers solar cells [116] with significantly enhanced morphological stability.

# 17.4.2.4 Solid Additives

Many types of solid additives have been investigated to enhance the morphological stability of OPV materials. The mechanisms include formation of noncovalent chemical bonding (hydrogen and F--S bonding), compatibilizer with similar chemical structures [117], heat resistant insulating resins forming matrix to restrain the migration of molecular chain and freeze morphology [118] etc. Introducing solid additives which form hydrogen bonding between donor and PCBM can act as phase stabilizers. A classic example is 1,4-Piperazine (Figures 17.7a-d), which effectively suppresses demixing in P3HT:PCBM, PTB7-Th:PCBM, [119] and PCE11:PCBM systems [1o]. Impressively, it is possible to rationally screen molecular phase stabilizers according to their interaction parameters/miscibility with the donor and acceptor materials [10]. In 2016, Zhan and coworkers demonstrated $^ { 4 , 4 ^ { \prime } }$ -Biphenol (BPO), a common and cheap chemical, could be employed as a "molecular lock" in blends of fluorine-containing polymers or small molecule donors and fullerene acceptors to lock donors via hydrogen bond formed between the donor and BPO (Figure 17.7e) [120]. The molecular lock is a versatile strategy to enhance the efficiency and stability of OSCs simultaneously. PTB7-Th:ITIC systems with $1 0 \%$ coumarin 7 (C7) as a photoactive component also showed improved morphology stability due to the formed hydrogen bonding between C7 and ITIC [121].

# 17.4.2.5 Solvent Additives

Solvent additives are widely used for tuning nanoscale morphology of the BHJ blends, such as crystallinity, phase purity, and domain spacing, which are vital for both device performance and stability [122]. However, despite the positive effect on optimizing microstructure and the resulting morphological stability [89], the residual of high boiling point solvent additives in the active layer films was found to be detrimental for photochemical- [79, 123] and thermal-stability [124]. It is thus essential to completely remove the solvent additives after film formation. Several methods such as vacuum treatment [125], solvent washing [126], and thermal annealing [79] have been explored. In this regard, solvent additives with low boiling point which can be easily removed from the active layers are favorable [125, 127]. Volatile solid additives which can tune the nanostructure morphology during film drying process and can be easily removed afterwards are also toward the same direction for improving both PCE and stability [128]. The elimination of using any solvent additives in many material systems also looks promising [129].

# 17.4.2.6 Ternary and Multiple Composites

The ternary strategy has been very successful in both FA and NFA systems to enhance the device performance [130-132]. The third and multicomponent composites in the host semiconductors might be able to increase the entropy and hence the operational stability [133]. Here we highlight some recent achievements by employing the ternary concept to simultaneously increase device performance and morphological stability in Figure 17.8. Kim and coworkers developed a new acceptor-donor-acceptor (A-D-A) triad-type small molecule, 5TRh-PCBM, consisting of an oligothiophene segment as the central core and fullerene derivatives as the end groups [117]. This small molecule as a third component in various material systems showed multiple beneficial effects and enhanced the thermal stability and mechanical properties of efficient OSCs while increasing their PCEs (Figure 17.8a,b). By introducing a small amount of fullerene ( $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M } )$ into a narrow bandgap NFA-based BHJ nanocomposite (PTB7-Th:IEICO-4F), both efficiency and photo-stability were simultaneously enhanced (Figure 17.8c) [134]. Adding a small amount of polymer donor PZ1 significantly improved the thermal stability of PM6 and BTTT-2Cl, showing no degradation after annealing at $1 1 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 800 hours (Figure 17.8d) [135]. Using $( ( 5 \mathrm { Z } , 5 ^ { \prime } \mathrm { Z } )  – 5 , 5 ^ { \prime }$ $( 7 , 7 ^ { \prime }$ -(4,4,9,9-tetraoctyl-4,9-dihydros-indaceno $1 , 2 \cdot \mathbf { b } { : } 5 , 6 \cdot \mathbf { b } ^ { \prime } .$ |dithiophene-2,7-diyl)bis(benzo[c][1,2,5]thiadiazole-7,4- diyl)bis(methanylylidene))bis(3-ethyl-2-thioxothiazolidin-4-one)) (O-IDTBR) as a third component, the stability of PM6:Y6-based solar cells could be enhanced under full solar spectrum illumination for 200 hours (Figure 17.8e) [136].

# 17.4.2.7 Organic Nanoparticles

The research on organic nanoparticles with embedded mixed donor and acceptor or separate donor/acceptor nanoparticles is largely driven by eco-friendly processing with water or alcohol-based solvents [137]. The synthesis routes include mini-emulsion technique [138, 139], surfactant-free precipitation method [140], or surfactant assisted nanoprecipitation [141]. It should be noted that the related approach also has the potential to freeze nanostructure and hence enhance morphological stability. Xie et al. demonstrated solar cells based on P3HT:IDTBR nanoparticles dispersed in water showing promising device efficiency and photo-stability [141]. It is noted that most of the research focused on synthesizing nanoparticles especially with stable dispersions as well as processing techniques to get the PCE on par with conventional aromatic solvent processed OSCs; investigation about microstructure stability is still limited and requires further research efforts.

# 17.4.2.8 Stratified Photoactive Layer Structure

From processing point of view, sequentially depositing donor and acceptor layers has the potential to better control the morphology than one-step coating of mixed donor and acceptor inks. In 2009, Schwartz and coworkers questioned the need for BHJ in polymer-fullerene photovoltaics by showing that P3HT/PCBM bilayer sequentially processed from orthogonal solvents can have the similar performance [142]. Later in 2011, Burn and coworkers studied morphology of sequentially solution processed P3HT/PCBM layers and concluded that intermixed region formed initially and can be completed by thermal annealing. The origin for the initially intermixed domains is speculated to be the swelling of P3HT by PCBM solvent (dichloromethane) which allows PCBM interdiffusion without decreasing the P3HT crystalline domains [143]. In the past few years, several research groups have further investigated the sequential layer deposition to control morphology with successful results [144-152]. Among them, improved photo- and thermal stability compared to BHJ has been demonstrated. In 2019, Huang and coworkers demonstrated PffBT4T-2OD/ $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 }$ BM-based bilayer devices with comparable PCE to BHJ devices and slightly improved photo-stability (Figure 17.9a) [145]. This bilayer structure outperformed the BHJ blend when processed with non-halogenated solvent. In 2019, Min and coworkers showed layer-by-layer (LbL) processed OSCs based on J71 and ITC6-IC outperformed BHJ control device in terms of light, thermal, and mechanical stability (Figure 17.9b) [146]. Of note is that this processing technique has also been applied successfully for fabrication of high-performance solar modules [153].

# 17.5 Recent Progress on Developing Organic Solar Cells with Excellent Stability

In 2011, McGehee and coworkers firstly reported polymer solar cells with seven years of $\mathrm { T } _ { 8 0 }$ lifetime based on poly[[9-(1-octylnonyl)-9H-carbazole-2,7-diyl]- 2,5-thiophenediyl-2,1,3-benzothiadiazole-4,7-diyl-2,5-thiophenediyl] (PCDTBT): PCBM with a PCE of ${ \sim } 5 . 5 \%$ (Figure 17.10a) [154]. Since 2017, the community evidenced several material systems with excellent device stability. Long-term stability under illumination is essential for solar cell operation. In many cases, UV part is filtered to mimic the employment of UV filters for real applications. Under UV-free simulated white light LED, P3HT:EH-IDTBR system with PCE of $6 \%$ survived 2o00hours illumination with only $5 \%$ losses (Figure 17.10b) [86]. For PBDB-T:ITIC-2F or ITIC-Th (PCE ${ \sim } 8 \%$ , devices were relatively stable within 1700 hours illumination after $1 0 \%$ burn-in losses in the first hundreds hours [88]. A linear extrapolation of stability data showed a $\mathrm { T } _ { 8 0 }$ lifetime over $1 1 0 0 0$ hours for PBDB-T:ITIC-2F (Figure 17.10c), which would lead to an impressive operational lifetime over 10years considering an average of 3.33 sun hours per day for south Germany according to the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) database. With $\mathrm { C } _ { 6 0 } { \cdot } \mathrm { S A M }$ modified ${ \mathrm { Z n O } }$ as electron transport layer (ETL), the extrapolated $\mathrm { T } _ { 8 0 }$ lifetime of inverted solar cells based on PTB7-Th:IEICO-4F operating under one sun illumination equivalent reached 34000hours (Figure 17.10d) [155]. Based on an estimation of solar irradiance of $1 5 0 0 \mathrm { k W h } \mathrm { m } ^ { - 2 } \mathrm { y r } ^ { - 1 }$ for China, this would be equivalent to a potential of 22years. For PffBT4T-2OD:EH-IDTBR with a PCE of $9 . 5 \%$ no degradation was observed under 60hours white LED illumination (Figure 17.10e) [85]. In 2021, Min and coworkers reported all polymer solar cells based on PM6:poly[ $( 2 , 2 ^ { \prime }$ ((2Z,2'Z)-(12,13-bis(2-octyldodecyl)-3,9-diundecyl-12,13-dihydro[1,2,5]thiadiazolo [3,4e]thieno] $2 ^ { \prime \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime \prime } { : } 4 ^ { \prime } , 5 ^ { \prime } ]$ thieno| $^ { 2 ^ { \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime } : 4 , 5 ] }$ pyrrolo[3,2-g]thieno $[ 2 ^ { \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime } { : } 4 , 5 ]$ thieno[3,2- b]-indole-2,10-diyl)bis (methanylylidene))bis (3-oxo-2,3-dihydro-1H-indene-2,1- diylidene))dimalononitrile-alt-2,5-thiophene)] (PYT):PY2F-T achieved a PCE of

In 2019, Forrest group demonstrated extremely stable evaporated solar cells based on tetraphenyldibenzoperiflanthene $( \mathrm { D B P } ) { : } \mathrm { C } _ { 7 0 }$ with a PCE of $6 \%$ (Figure 17.11) [157]. Impressively, the devices measured under 20 suns of UV illumination showed no losses with dose equivalent to 9.3years when accumulated outdoors, demonstrating that OPV materials could be super-photostable. The accelerated aging test under 37 suns (solar cells surface temperature went to $1 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ ) even showed an extrapolated $\mathrm { T } _ { 8 0 }$ operational lifetime extending to more than 27 o00 years. Although being different with solution-processed OsCs in terms of material purity, crystallinity, and morphology, this work is an outstanding demonstration of intrinsic stability of the OSCs being reliable for long-term application [157].

# 17.6 Summary and Outlook

In this chapter, we reviewed the recent progress on developing stable OSCs based on fullerene derivatives and NFAs. The efficiency of OSCs has reached an impressively high level, which surpasses the benchmark value for commercialization and industrial applications. However, the operational lifetime of mature PV technologies based on Si and III-V semiconductors is generally more than 25years, which is much longer than that of state-of-the-art OPV devices. Nevertheless, it is not required for OsCs to reach such a lifetime value, as they are anyway targeting at applications in different scenarios, such as building- and vehicle-integrated applications, portable flexible energy suppliers, etc. Therefore, it is generally accepted that OSCs should demonstrate at least 10years lifetime in order to meet the requirements for the real-world applications. This is still very challenging for state-of-the-art high-performing OSCs, as the stability of OSCs is strongly influenced by many extrinsic and intrinsic factors, as discussed in this chapter. Although the extrinsic stresses could be minimized by performing excellent device encapsulation to improve the device operational stability, the intrinsic factors such as material stability and microstructure stability do play a decisive role in determining the operational lifetime of OsCs. It has to be mentioned that most OSCs that exhibit promising device stability are generally fabricated and evaluated in $\Nu _ { 2 }$ atmosphere, which is much different from the PV products operating in the real world. For large-scale roll-to-roll production, OSCs are processed using green solvents, in a fully printable device architecture (with printed interfacial layers and electrodes) and under ambient conditions. The achieved microstructure, interface properties as well as defect density are expected to be different from that of optimized small-scale devices reported in the literature. Therefore, intensive research efforts are required in order to continuously develop OPV products with promising device efficiency and stability. It is hoped that this chapter could trigger more research interests and efforts to successfully address the stability issues of OPV devices, not only for lab-scale small area devices but also for large-scale flexible organic solar modules.

# Potential Applications of Organic Solar Cells

Chengyi Xiao and Weiwei Li

Beijing University of Chemical Technology, Beijing Advanced Innovation Center for Soft Matter Science and Engineering, State Key Laboratory of Organic-Inorganic Composites, North Third Ring East Road 15, Beijing, 100029, P.R. China

# 18.1 Introduction

Solar energy is regarded as promising renewable energy in the future and is expected to occupy an important place in future energy systems [1]. In its latest available World Energy Outlook, the International Energy Agency predicted that "the increasing competitiveness of solar photovoltaic pushes its installed capacity beyond that of wind before 2025, past hydropower around 2030 and past coal before $2 0 4 0 ^ { \circ }$ [2]. Organic solar cells (OsCs), with the ability to directly converting sunlight to electricity, are regarded as a promising pathway to solve energy shocks and global warming [3]. In recent years, OsCs have made tremendous development with power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) beyond $1 7 \%$ by developing conjugated materials as electron donor/acceptor materials [4-10], controlling microphase separation in bulk-heterojunction (BHJ) photoactive layers [11, 12], and selecting suitable inorganic/organic materials as the interfacial layer to realize efficient charge transportation [13-15]. In particular, Lin et al. reported the fused-ring non-fullerene acceptor 3,9-bis(2-methylene-(3(1,1-dicyanomethylene) indanone))-5,5,11,11-tetrakis(4-hexylphenyl)-dithieno $[ 2 , 3 - d ; 2 ^ { \prime } , 3 ^ { \prime } - d ^ { \prime } ]$ -s-indaceno $[ 1 , 2 - b ; 5 , 6 - b ^ { \prime } ]$ |dithiophene (ITIC) in 2015 that showed a PCE of $6 . 8 \%$ [16], and in 2019, Yuan et al. developed the non-fullerene electron acceptors Y6 that boosted PCEs up to $1 5 . 7 \%$ [17]. Since then, a record PCE of $1 8 . 2 2 \%$ by Liu et al. was rapidly realized in the state-of-the-art OsCs [4], making non-fullerene acceptors-based solar cells the most promising OsCs [4, 8, 9, 18-25].

Compared with the inorganic semiconductors, the versatility to design and synthesize of organic semiconductors enables a large-range tunability in chemical structures, absorption, and frontier orbital levels [26]. More importantly, organic semiconductors have the advantages of inherent flexibility and stretchability compared with the rigid inorganic counterparts [27-29]. Thus, flexible OSCs are lighter and have the compatibility of different surfaces, which make them have a much broader scope of applications [30-32]. Such as researchers of Merck Chemicals represented a ${ > } 2 5 0 \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ flexible power system reaching an average performance of ${ \sim } 4 \%$ PCE named "solar trees" [33]. In the viewpoint of manufacturing technologies, most of the organic semiconductors can be processed by solution-based roll-to-roll (R2R) coating or printing technologies, such as slot-die coating, spray coating, blade coating, inkjet printing, and screen printing, etc. which make the manufacturing more inexpensive, energy saving, and higher throughput [34, 35]. Most recently, researchers have demonstrated that OSC modules possessed operational stability for two years through monitoring of a pilot OSC (organic photovoltaics) solar park [36]. These advantages allow OSCs to be applied in many low-energy-consumption and maintenance-free scenarios. Considering their superiority, OsCs have been recognized as energy-harvesting systems for third-generation electronics.

Accompanied by the rapidly increased PCEs and established coating technique, the OsC modules are believed to be very close to commercialization. The application of OSCs will be a great complement to the existing photovoltaic market and expand the border of the photovoltaics industry. As we mentioned above, the performance and stability of the OsCs have been raised to a sufficient height through materials updates and processing optimizations. However, different targeted applications would result in distinct demands for performance, stability, and mechanical parameters, etc. For example, for a skin-wearable application, devices should possess a stretchability of at least $3 0 \%$ to be conformable with human skin [37]. Thus, one should consider a specific targeted application to make the relevant parameters straightforward before designing and constructing OsC devices, such as the demands in output power/voltage/current, encapsulation, and nontoxicity, etc.

Here, we discuss the numerous attempts on exploiting the possibility of OSCs for emerging unique industrialization. OSCs can be regarded as power solutions to several important fields, covering self-powered wearable sensors, electronic textiles, implantable/biological electronics, internet of things (IoTs), and potential indoor applications (Figure 18.1). Therefore, this chapter describes examples of where OSC technology can act as an energy source, potentially enabling larger deployment of low-power, low-maintenance, and environmentally friendly hardware solutions, aiming to find the most appropriate ways to realize their commercialization. Notably, many companies such as infinity PV, Merck Chemicals, BELECTRIC OSC, and ARMOR have devoted numerous efforts to the actual products of OSCs.

# 18.2 Building-Integrated OSCs

The combination of global warming and energy shortage is expected to put significant stress on renewable energy systems. Among the clean powers, solar energy is supposed to take an important place in the energy systems [1]. Compared with perovskite solar cells and (poly- or mono-) crystalline silicon (Si)-based solar cells, the photoactive layers of OsCs have the superior advantages of low-temperature and solution-processing manufacturing. Owing to the large-range tunability of organic semiconductors in chemical structures, absorption, and frontier orbital levels, OSC devices can be tuned to create a wide range of choices in colors, transparency, and indoor efficiency [26, 38]. This allows OsCs to achieve semitransparency and meet many functional and esthetic demands in building-integrated OSCs (building-integrated organic solar cells [BIOsCs], Figure 18.2) [39, 40].

Uniform and large-scale printing technologies are another core issues for the commercialization of OsCs. Most of the photoactive materials exhibit impressive solubility in organic solvents, which enable cost-effective and eco-friendly R2R manufacturing compared to the typical evaporation or sputtering manufacturing process [3]. Therefore, OSCs are more suitable for large-scale, high-throughput, and uniform R2R process, and more promising than rigid cells in terms of cost and productivity [34, 41]. The thin, flexible and laminates features are other superiorities for OSCs. The state-of-the-art thin OSCs on plastic foil substrates have been demonstrated to be less than $2 \mu \mathrm { m }$ thick, with equal PCEs to their glass-based counterparts [42, 43]. This feature enables ease of large-scale fabrication over arbitrary substrates and building materials, which are highly expected to offer functions of power supplying elements in the future BIOSCs products. Besides, utilizing OSCs in BIOSCs in greenhouses for agricultural applications have more obvious advantages over the traditional Si-based module due to the versatility of spectrum control [44]. Furthermore, OsC systems have been demonstrated their long-term stability in outdoor conditions [36] and even in space [45]. Here, we will elaborate on four promising applications of BIOSCs including solar panels as house energy suppliers, semitransparent windows, solar trees, and greenhouse integrated OSCs.

# 18.2.1  Solar Parks

Household installation of solar panels as energy suppliers is the common commercial product for Si-based solar cells. This application type is considered to reduce both global warming and urban heat island while generating electricity for human life [46, 47]. Organic semiconductors have the inherent advantages of flexibility and high mass-specific power in comparison with their inorganic counterparts. While OSCs showed both comparative PCE, long-term stability [48], and fast processing [34, 49] at the lab level, the OSC panels are supposed to be installed in building facades or roofs.

In order to compare different energy technologies, an analysis method named life cycle analysis (LCA), which defined in the ISO14040 series [50], was introduced by Krebs et al. to evaluate how efficient the given technology is in converting the source energy into the form of energy that we would like to use [41]. The LCA is a complex method that can give parameters such as energy pay-back time (EPBT), embodied energy, and global warming potential (GwP). As shown in Table 18.1, it is clear that the OSC technology exhibits faster EPBT, larger embodied energy, and producing less $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ in the whole manufacturing process than other competitors.

A solar park based on polymer solar panels was installed and operated by Krebs et al. in Denmark and southern Spain (Figure 18.3) [41]. The installation and de-installation rate were above $1 0 0 \mathrm { { m m i n ^ { - 1 } } }$ , and considering the present performance and web width, the whole installation was of ${ > } 2 0 0 \mathrm { W } \operatorname* { m i n } ^ { - 1 }$ , which was much faster than any other photovoltaic technology. In terms of performance, the solar panels exhibited PCE of ${ > } 2 \%$ for a large active area of over $1 4 . 7 \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ (with six lanes of $_ { 1 0 0 \mathrm { m } }$ stretches of solar cell foil in a web width of $3 0 5 \mathrm { m m }$ ). And the solar panels stabilized relatively constant PCEs of $1 . 6 \% { - } 1 . 8 \%$ in the long-time operation (277 days in Denmark and 180days in southern Spain). When the six lanes connected in parallel (the active area ${ > } 8 8 . 2 \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } .$ ), the PCEs of the solar panels dropped to $1 . 5 3 \%$ ascribed to the loss in fill factors (FFs) and open circuit voltages $\left( V _ { \mathrm { { O C } } } \mathbf { s } \right)$ . Without any additional washing or cleaning procedure, they conjectured the initial drop in PCEs could be ascribed to shades by bird droppings. An LCA procedure was carried out by inputting the manufacturing and installation data, which revealed that the EPBT was 0.49 years in a southern European setting. For the GwP, the emissions of $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ in the installation of the solar panels include all the manufacturing process was $1 2 9 2 2 \mathrm { k g } \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 \mathrm { e q } }$ which implied $4 2 0 \mathrm { g } \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ per kW h in Denmark and the carbon footprint was $0 . 1 1 2 \mathrm { k g } \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ per kW h. Similarly, the carbon footprint was $0 . 0 7 2 \mathrm { k g } \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ per kW h in southern Spain.

From an OsC targeted costing perspective, Chatzisideris et al. demonstrated that OSC-battery systems (OSC integrated with battery storage) would offer the most cost-effective solution compared to OSC-only systems [64]. Eventually, they identified the OsC cost thresholds of $0 . 9 \ : \mathrm { { \sf t / W p } }$ for Denmark and $1 . 6 \ : \mathrm { { ‰} }$ for Greece. Furthermore, they built up an economic analysis model to demonstrate the environmental impacts of electricity self-consumption from OSC systems in

Denmark and Greece. The model proved that OSC systems tended to be associated with lower environmental impacts than other electricity sources.

# 18.2.2 Smart Windows

Compared with the traditional inorganic semiconductors, the organic semiconductor materials often have lower carrier mobility, which results in thin BHJ active layers with a thickness less than $2 0 0 \mathrm { n m }$ [65] and brings to the optical semitransparency of the thin organic layer [66]. In another viewpoint, due to the large-range tunability of organic semiconductors in chemical structures, absorptions, and bandgaps, the active layers in OsCs can be designed effectively to weaken the absorption in the visible light range $( 3 7 0 - 7 4 0 \mathrm { n m } )$ and result in a whole semitransparent device. These features of OsCs are generally used to achieve many functional and esthetic demands.

Smart windows (Figure 18.4) were demonstrated by Yao et al., which integrated both power-generation functions and color adjustment in a high-performance semitransparent organic solar cells (ST-OSCs) [67]. The smart windows were realized by introducing a gasochromic tungsten trioxide/platinum $\mathrm { ( W O } _ { 3 } / \mathrm { P t ) }$ as a back-reflector layer. The ${ \mathrm { W O } } _ { 3 } / { \mathrm { P t } }$ film was switchable between colored and bleached states during hydrogen exposure [68, 69], thus dynamic and reversible adjustments in the colors of ST-OSCs could be achieved. Moreover, ultra-thin gasochromic ${ \tt W O } _ { 3 } / { \tt P t }$ film in the colored state could significantly increase the absorptions from the visible region to the near-infrared (NIR) region [70] and further improved the PCEs of ST-OSCs. As a result, the ST-OSCs integrated with the gasochromic ${ \mathrm { W O } } _ { 3 } / { \mathrm { P t } }$ film exhibited a PCE of $1 0 . 2 \%$ at the colored state and $9 . 1 \%$ at bleached states, as well as the corresponding average visible-light transmittance (AVT) of $2 5 . 4 \%$ and $3 3 . 8 \%$ (Eq. (18.1)), respectively. The novel design concept of gasochromic materials integrated to the ST-OSCs has broadened the functions of OsCs as smart windows and sunroof of hydrogen fuel cell automobile.

![](images/17b5cbc763eca6b7cf4636c368507959bbac0f13544dca935691b2a1e028e89b.jpg)  
Figure 18.4  A color and transparency-switchable ST-OSC. (a) Illustration of the structure of an ST-OSC device. PFN, poly[(9,9-bis( $3 ^ { \prime }$ -(N,N-dimethylamino)propyl)-2,7-fluorene)- alt-2,7-(9,9-dioctylfluorene)]. (b) Schematic diagram of the gasochromic ${ \sf W O } _ { 3 } / { \sf P t }$ layer. (c) Absorption spectra of $\mathsf { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathsf { B M }$ , PTB7-Th, and acceptor as a thin film. Source: Yao et al. [67]/Reproduced with permission of Elsevier.

In general, AVT is measured in the visible wavelength range $( 3 7 0 - 7 4 0 \mathrm { n m }$ ) and defined as follows [40]:

$$
\mathrm { A V T } = \frac { \int T _ { \mathrm { t r a n s } } ( \lambda ) P _ { \mathrm { r } } ( \lambda ) S _ { \mathrm { A M 1 . 5 G } } ( \lambda ) \mathrm { d } ( \lambda ) } { \int P _ { \mathrm { r } } ( \lambda ) S _ { \mathrm { A M 1 . 5 G } } ( \lambda ) \mathrm { d } ( \lambda ) }
$$

where $T _ { \mathrm { t r a n s } }$ is the transmittance, $P _ { \mathrm { r } }$ is the photopic response (determined by the spectral sensitivity of the human eye), and $S _ { \mathrm { A M 1 . 5 G } }$ is the solar photon flux under air mass (AM) 1.5G for window applications, $\lambda$ is the wavelength.

# 18.2.3 Solar Trees

Researchers of Merck Chemicals and BELECTRIC OSC represented a paradigm shift for semitransparent $( \mathrm { A V T } \approx 2 0 \% )$ OSCs modules by preparing large-area OSC products named "solar trees" and installing them at the German pavilion, Universal Exhibition Milan 2015 (Figure 18.5) [33]. This attempt have addressed many of the current technical challenges and provided definite standards for OsCs using in building-integrated photovoltaics. Such as: the conjugated polymer active materials should have a good balance of PCE, solubility, acceptor miscibility, viscosity and coating uniformity, and better being entirely halogen-free. To approach the lab-to-manufacturing translation, all the fabrication processes, including ink formulations and device optimizations, should operate in a printing or R2R technique instead of the lab-level spin-coating.

In this case, all the layers of the devices were fabricated by doctor-blade coating technique under ambient conditions at lab-scale except the poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:Pss) hole transporting layer (HTL), which was spin-coated onto the stacked devices. The manufacturing-scale OSCs were fabricated by a typical R2R process. Benefiting from the principles, the device transferred from lab-scale $( 0 . 0 4 \mathsf { c m } ^ { 2 } )$ to manufacturing-scale $( 2 5 0 \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } )$ without additional optimization. Eventually, hexagonal "leaves" modules of the solar trees were obtained by connecting six groups in parallel, and each group had nine serially connected cells. With the areas growing larger, the PCEs of the devices decreased in sequence from $8 . 5 \%$ $( 0 . 0 4 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } )$ to $7 . 2 \%$ $( 1 . 0 0 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } ) $ $4 . 3 \%$ $( 1 1 4 . 5 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } )$ and $4 \%$ $( 2 5 0 \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } )$

They also tried to quantify the stability standards for OsCs integrating into the building-integrated photovoltaics. After heating two hours at $1 2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in the lamination process, the overall performance of a single cell showed no significant change. And after operating under 1 sun illumination for over 100 hours, there was not any significant decrease in PCEs. The results indicated that the whole cells had excellent thermal- and photo-stabilities. The solar trees appearing at the Universal EXPO 2015 in Milan clearly demonstrated the possibility of large-scale solution-processable OSC systems.

# 18.2.4 Greenhouse and Photosynthesis

The greenhouse can provide a suitable environment for crops growing regardless of the outdoor environment, which greatly improves agricultural land-use efficiency. However, due to functions such as temperature regulation, they need to consume more energy than conventional farming. ST-OSCs with specific spectral absorption can be one of the approaches to relieve this problem.

ST-OSCs were employed on greenhouses to achieve net-zero energy greenhouses in warm and moderate climates by O'Connor and coworkers (Figure 18.6) through an elaborated dynamic energy fluxes balance model [71]. Two ST-OSCs with varying spectral absorption characteristics were employed. Also, both the generated solar power and the greenhouse energy load changes were considered in this model. Furthermore, distinct climates in different locations, including Phoenix (hot-dry), Raleigh (mixed-humid), and Antigo (cold), were selected in their work. The research revealed that the ST-OSCs-integrated greenhouse could afford sufficient energy in managing the thermal load of the system throughout the year in hot and mixed-humid climates. Despite the generated OsC power that cannot meet the energy load of greenhouse in a cold climate, the energy generated by the ST-OSCs would contribute to significant energy savings.

Another important issue of the research is related to the low-radiation nature of the ITO (indium tin oxide) electrodes and optical coating. This characteristic would avoid overheating at daylight by reducing IR (infrared ray) transmittance from sunlight while retaining the thermal energy at night through increasing IR reflectance from the thermal radiation of the greenhouse. It was found that the cooling demand of the conventional and OsC-greenhouses were almost the same, which was attributed to the transmittance of the ST-OSC. Overall, this modeling demonstrated that solar power can afford most of the energy needs of the greenhouse in warm and moderate climates by analyzing the realistic solar cell performance metrics and greenhouse energy demands. And there are significant opportunities for achieving net-zero energy OsC-greenhouse operation through reasonable energy fluxes for OSC-greenhouse.

Photosynthesis processes for plant growth generally absorb light irradiations in the visible light region $( 3 7 0 - 7 4 0 \mathrm { n m } )$ because of the dominant status of chlorophyll a and b pigments [72]. And the photomorphogenesis process for plants also needs lights located at specific regions. For example, light irradiations with short-wavelength would facilitate vegetative leaf growth and with long-wavelength would accelerate for flowering. Thus, the semitransparent OsCs with tuned spectrum can be integrated into the greenhouse to provide additional electrical energy while transmitting enough sunlight for plant growth, or controlling the photomorphogenesis process.

Greenhouses for agricultural applications have been studied in many inorganic systems [73-76]. Recently, Song et al. exploited the feasibility of adopting foldable-flexible OSCs for photosynthesis on the lab-scale [77]. The ST-OSCs were fabricated with modified PEDOT:PSS as electrodes and PBDB-T-2F:Y6 as a photoac. tive layer to ensure enough transmittance in the visible region (Figure 18.7a). The modified PEDOT:PSS/PET (polyethylene terephthalate) exhibited low reflectance $( < 1 5 \% )$ across the wavelength region of $3 0 0 { - } 8 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ and overall AVT of ${ \approx } 8 0 \%$ across $3 5 0 \mathrm { - } 8 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ , while PBDB-T-2F:Y6 blend had the main absorptions located in the NIR region. The overall semitransparent foldable-flexible OSCs yielded

(c) Optical photograph of mung bean leaves changing in nine days under direct sunlight (L), direct sunlight with ST-OSCs roof (S), and dark (D). Source: Song et al. PCEs of ${ > } 1 0 \%$ and $T _ { \mathrm { t r a n s } }$ of $2 1 \%$ in the visible region. Excellent mechanical stability was proven through the bending and folding test. Furtherly, the semitransparent foldable-flexible OSCs were integrated as part of roofs into the simulated greenhouse (Figure 18.7b). The plants showed comparable growth rates under semitransparent foldable-flexible OsCs with those grown under sunlight after monitoring for nine days (Figure 18.7c). The researchers also prospected that additional power can be used for future multifunctional self-powered greenhouse, although they did not provide or store the output power.

# 18.3 Wearable-Integrated OSCs

The IoTs involve all aspects of the national economy and human life and are the third information technology revolution after computer and Internet [78, 79]. As the underlying hardware base of IoTs, billions of wireless sensors will be installed in human life within the next decade. In the IoTs landscape, wearable electronics are attracting a lot of attention for their potential applications in human health monitoring and smart healthcare. A recent report by McKinsey Global Institute summarized the potential commercial impact of IoTs and concluded that the IoTs market is expected to increase as much as 11 trillion dollars by 2025 [80].

Flexible IoT sensors generally consist of three parts: sensors, control circuits (CC), and energy supply modules [81]. Relevant researches at home and abroad mainly focus on independent sensor unit and free-standing power supply modules. Achieving wearable IoTs sensors requires independent and fewer power modules, which are generally rechargeable and replaceable lithium batteries. However, the range and frequency of data transmission can reduce battery life, thus limiting the use of conventional batteries. In addition, the battery replacement and charging process will incur higher operating and maintenance costs. As an emerging energy source, OSCs have the advantages of high quality-specific energy (over $1 0 \mathrm { W } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ ) [82], flexibility, and large-area preparation, etc., which are very suitable for being the energy module of the IoTs system and provide a reliable and continuous energy source for low-power wireless sensor network.

# 18.3.1 Portable Device Photovoltaics

In 2016, O'Connor et al. reported the fabrication of ultra-flexible and wearable OSCs [83]. In these ultra-flexible OSCs, the thin PI (polyimide) films $( 1 3 \mu \mathrm { m } )$ adhesive substrates were spin-coated with PEDOT:PSS, polyethylenimine (PEI), and P3HpT (P3HT): $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ in sequence. Another PEDOT:PSS layer was then transferred on top of the overall device using thermal release tape, and silver paint was then applied to make the front electrode. An encapsulation layer ( $_ { \mathrm { 1 - \mu \mathrm { m } } }$ barrier of parylene C) was deposited on the whole devices by vacuum vapor evaporation before attaching them to the skin to increase the stability of the devices for outdoor applications.

The ultra-flexible and wearable OSCs have been adhered to human skin, exhibiting stable operational performance when compressively strained by about $7 5 \%$

The usefulness of the wearable solar cells was to exploit their potential applications by directly powering an LED (light-emitting diode) and a digital watch under $9 8 0 \mathrm { W } \mathrm { m } ^ { - 2 }$ of natural sunlight after carrying the deliberate selection of materials based on mechanical properties rather than just efficiency for wearable electronics (Figure 18.8) [83]. The OSCs were wired in series to fulfill the required voltages $( 2 . 1 8 \mathrm { V } )$ to power watch and 15 cells were wired in series to produce a $V _ { \mathfrak { p p } }$ (voltage peak to peak) of $4 . 6 6 \mathrm { V }$ and an $I _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ (maximum discharge current) of $2 0 1 \mathrm { m A }$ to charge the portable battery. Differently, two substrates and eight cells were connected in parallel to light up the LED (which needs $0 . 4 \mathrm { V }$ and ${ \sim } 1 \mathrm { m A }$ . These results demonstrated the possible use as the primary cells for OSCs devices.

# 18.3.2 Implantable and Wearable Self-Powered Sensors

Someya and coworkers at The University of Tokyo make a significant effort on the ultrathin and ultra-flexibility OSCs [42, 84, 85]. In 2012, they demonstrated ultrathin OSCs based on $1 . 4 \ – \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thickness PET substrate (which is commercially available Mylar 1.4 Cwo2) could be fabricated in a total $< 2 \mu \mathrm { m }$ thickness device while exhibited comparative efficiency with ITO/glass-based counterparts [42]. The overall ultrathin OSCs yielded PCEs of $4 . 2 \%$ and an excellent specific weight value of $1 0 \mathrm { W } \mathrm { g } ^ { - 1 }$ . Also, high flexibility was measured by adhering the flexible device to a pre-stretched elastomer. The OSCs could survive quasi-linear compression to below $7 0 \%$ and cyclic compression and stretching to $5 0 \%$ , over more than 20 full cycles.

Further in 2018, they proved the possibility of OsCs integrating into organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) and thus the self-powered cardiac sensors were achieved (Figure 18.9) [82]. The cardiac sensors were proven to have high transconductance $( 0 . 8 \mathrm { m S } )$ , high responsivity $( 1 0 ^ { 5 } )$ , high-speed responses $\left( 0 . 5 8 \mathrm { - } 0 . 6 2 \mathrm { m s } \right)$ , and compatible with the frequency ranges of human biological signals (approximately $2 0 0 \mathrm { H z } ,$ benefiting from the application of OECTs. The flexible OSC module in the system was demonstrated to have an enormous contribution to the signal-to-noise ratio $( S / N )$ as it exhibited the lowest noise currents of $0 . 0 2 \mu \mathrm { A }$ compared with that of the source meter $( 0 . 5 8 \mu \mathrm { A } )$ and commercial battery $( 0 . 0 8 \mu \mathrm { A } )$ . The self-powered sensors were attached to the fingertip and the exposed surface of a rat heart with $S / N$ of 25.9 and 40.02 dB, respectively.
