NIR light is generally appropriate for skin-interfaced health monitoring, such as photoplethysmogram [87], because NIR is not harmful to humans and has a long propagation distance $\left( > 4 \thinspace \mathrm { m m } \right)$ within the tissue [88]. Thus, F-SOCs with narrow-bandgap active layer can be applied to NIR organic photodetectors. Park et al. fabricated an ultra-flexible OSCs-structured NIR skin-conformal photoplethys. mogram sensor based on a narrow-bandgap regioregular polyindacenodithiophenepyridyl[2,1,3]thiadiazole-cyclopentadithiophene (PIPCP) and $\mathrm { P C } _ { 6 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ photovoltaic active layer (Figure 18.10) [86]. The ultrathin ( $3 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ thick) OSCs-structured NIR photodetector exhibited mechanical stability at bending radius of $r < 3 \mu \mathrm { m }$ for 1000 bending cycles. Also, the fabricated sensors exhibited outstanding cut-off response frequency over $1 \mathrm { k H z }$ at $- 3 \mathrm { d B }$ and better sensitivity than a normal rigid glass-based device. Therefore, OSCs would be capable as a human-compatible, wireless power source emerged in the next-generation electronics due to their high conformability and biocompatibility.

# 18.3.3 OSC Textile Toward Smart Clothing

Self-powered smart clothes integrated with multifunctional electronic devices have attracted much attention in the IoTs. For electronic wearable devices, it is essential to possess features of environmental stability, sufficient energy efficiency, and mechanical robustness. Textile-based wearable OsCs, which produce power from the surrounding environment and even the indoor circumstances, are promising to smart clothes. There are two strategies to realize smart clothes: the planar stacked structured OsCs based on textile substrate and the textile weaved by 1D (one-dimension) shaped OSCs.

In the planar stacked structured OsCs based on the textile substrate, there are many difficulties as the susceptibility of the traditional flexible OsC architecture and active layers to the surrounding moisture and oxygen. To address this problem, thin-film encapsulation barriers were utilized [89, 90]. Jinno et al. reported the single-/double-side-coated passivation layer, prepared by coating $5 0 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick acrylic elastomers (3M VHB Y-4905J), was used to improve the operational stability of OSCs (Figure 18.11) [89]. The textile-based OSCs showed excellent washability with only a $5 . 4 \%$ decrease of PCEs after immersing in water for 120 minutes.

(c) Chemical structure of PNTz4T. (d) Schematic of the double-side-coated OSCs. (e) Schematic diagrams of the optoelectronic module and organic light-emitting diode (OLED) structure and the picture of the operating module during the washable test with the inset image indicating the module being dipped in water after washing. NPB, $\mathsf { N } , \mathsf { N } ^ { \prime }$ -Bis(naphthalen-1-yl) $\cdot \mathsf { N } , \mathsf { N } ^ { \prime }$ -bis(phenyl)benzidine. Source: Jinno et al. [89]/with permission of Springer Nature, Jeong et al. [90]/Reproduced with permission of The Royal Society of Chemistry.

Furthermore, due to the elastomeric state of the passivation layer, PCEs of the OSCs remained at $8 0 \%$ of the initial values even after $5 2 \%$ mechanical compression for 20 cycles with 100 minutes of water exposure. Jeong et al. [90] incorporated the $\mathrm { S i O } _ { 2 }$ (silicon dioxide)-polymer composite capping layer to encapsulate the OsCs. The textile-based washable OSCs exhibited water resistance with only $2 \%$ degradation after washing 20 times for 10 minutes and mechanical stability when operating at a low curvature radius $r = 3 \mathrm { m m }$

Compared with the stacked planar structure, the 1D structured OSCs possess many promising advantages, such as miniaturization, adaptability, and wearability, which make it more attractive for smart clothes [91-94]. The 1D structured OSCs consist of coaxial structure [95] and twisted structure [96]. Zhang et al. reported the coaxial structured flexible organic solar cell (F-OSC) textiles by dip-coated with the $\mathrm { P 3 H T { : } P C _ { 6 1 } B M }$ photoactive layer, PEDOT:PSS HTL, and carbon nanotube-based transparent electrode on a metal textile electrode (Figure 18.12a) [95]. The flexible OSC device based on the coaxial structured textiles exhibited a PCE of $1 . 0 8 \%$ at every side and maintained ${ > } 9 7 \%$ efficiencies after bending for ${ } > 2 0 0$ cycles. Also, the flexible textiles showed an excellent areal density of $5 . 9 \mathrm { m g } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . The twisted structured textiles are regarded as lighter and more flexible than the coaxial structure textiles.

In 2009, Lee et al. demonstrated the twisted structured textiles by incorporating a second wire to the solar power wires [96]. The phase-separated photovoltaic layer was coated onto a thin stainless-steel wire. While the second stainless-steel wire, coated with a silver film and serving as the counter electrode, was wrapped around the first wire. The two wires were added by a transparent polymer. The PCE values of the solar power wires ranged from $2 . 7 9 \%$ to $3 . 2 7 \%$ . The stretchable structure is usually achieved by intertwining two wires around an elastic substrate, which can enhance the stretchability of the textiles. In 2014, Zhang et al. have proven the twisted structured OsCs by incorporating a Ti (titanium) wire and an aligned multiwalled carbon nanotube (MwCNT) fiber as cathode and anode, respectively [98]. The as-prepared wire-shaped OSCs, with a maximum PCE of $1 . 7 8 \%$ , could be easily woven into various flexible structures without the necessity for sealing. Further in 2018, the ZnO (zinc oxide) electron transporting layer (ETL) was imported to the wire-shaped OSCs through immersing the Ti wire into a sol-gel precursor solution of zinc acetate dehydrates and the following thermal annealing process (Figure 18.12b) [97]. To demonstrate the practicality of the flexible textile as a power source for applications in fields such as wearable electronics, a piece of this photovoltaic textile was woven and used to drive an electronic device (Figure 18.12c).

The novel OsC textiles showed lightweight, thin, and flexible while high running stability, and revealed the possibility of OsCs attached or wove to daily clothes affording certain power. Considering these features, the OSC textiles will play an important part in many emerging new application fields, such as smart clothing, biomedical electronics, and facilitates the OsCs commercialization.

# 18.4 OSCs-Integrated Energy Storage System

The BIOsCs and wearable-integrated OSCs have partly demonstrated the possible applications for OsCs devices. Moreover, according to previous cost forecast [36, 64, 99], the costs of OSC modules could be cut down to $0 . 0 5 \ : \mathrm { \notin / W p }$ due to the low-cost materials and the high-throughput R2R printing, while that of Si-based PV modules were $0 . 5 { - } 0 . 6 \notin / \mathrm { W p }$ in Europe. The colossal competitive advantage in price makes OSC-generated electricity more attractive than the Si-based PV modules. However, the performance of OsCs is sensitive to light intensity and incident angles, which means that the OsC modules are not a stable and constant energy source.

To address this issue, OSC-integrated energy storage systems (ESSs, Figure 18.13), such as photocharging (or named self-rechargeable) devices composed of OSCs and flexible supercapacitors [100, 101] or lithium battery [102] as energy storage units were reported. Also, Chatzisideristhe et al. [64] proved the economic costs and gains, and life cycle environmental impacts of the OSCs-integrated ESSs, which can offer a more cost-effective solution compared to OsC-only systems. Normally, there are two kinds of OSC structure integrated to combine ESS: a planar stacked OSCs-integrated ESS (Figures 18.13 and 18.14) and fiber-based OSCs-integrated ESS (Figure 18.15) [104].

To evaluate the performance of the whole OsCs-integrated ESS, there are various parameters in this system that need to be studied. The PCE of the OSC device represents the converted efficiency from solar energy into electric energy, which was calculated from the equation:

$$
\mathrm { P C E } = { \frac { P _ { \mathrm { m a x } } } { P _ { \mathrm { i n } } } } = { \frac { J _ { \mathrm { s c } } \times V _ { \mathrm { o c } } \times \mathrm { F F } } { P _ { \mathrm { i n } } } } \times 1 0 0 \%
$$

![](images/5763dff83a581b6d50a187fc77fe713871e4fbdf13f2b0db1eb9a4d90e791167.jpg)  
Figure 18.13 Schematic illustration of a photovoltaicsintegrated energy storage system. Source: Chengyi Xiao.

where $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ , FF, $P _ { \mathrm { m a x } }$ , and $P _ { \mathrm { i n } }$ represent the open-circuit voltage, short-circuit current densities, fill factor, maximum power output, and input light density $( \mathrm { m } \mathrm { W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } ) ,$ , respectively.

The total efficiency of the OSCs-integrated EsS was calculated by dividing the total input energy from light by the stored energy in the battery or supercapacitor during the photocharging process; for total solar-to-PCE $( \eta _ { \mathrm { S T P } } )$ at a specific time with a discharging test, $E _ { \mathrm { A } }$ (energy density) was calculated from the discharging curve:

$$
\eta _ { \mathrm { S T P } } = ( E _ { \mathrm { A } } \times S _ { 1 } ) / ( P _ { \mathrm { i n } } \times t _ { 2 } \times S _ { 2 } )
$$

where $P _ { \mathrm { i n } }$ is the illuminated light density $\left( \mathbf { m } \mathbf { W } \thinspace \mathbf { c m } ^ { - 2 } \right.$ $t _ { 2 }$ is the photocharging time, and $S _ { 1 }$ and $S _ { 2 }$ are the effective area of the batteries/supercapacitors and OsC device, respectively.

# 18.4.1  Planar Stacked OsCs-Integrated ESS

The photocharging system can provide an independent power supply for next-generation wearable electronics or biomedical devices. A solid-state MwCNTPEDOT:PSS-based supercapacitor with the PVA (polyvinyl alcohol) $\mathrm { { ^ { \prime } H _ { 2 } S O _ { 4 } } }$ (sulfuric acid) as gel electrolyte on the PET substrate was applied in the planar stacked OSCs-integrated ESS [io0]. To balance the trade-off between performance and thickness, they demonstrated that the $5 0 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick flexible photocharging capacitor showed a total efficiency $( \eta _ { \mathrm { S T P } } )$ of $5 . 9 2 \%$ (Eqs. (18.3), (18.4), (18.5)) by integrating $3 \mathrm { - } \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick OSCs on $4 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ -thick carbon nanotube/polymer-based supercapacitors with a $\mathrm { P V A } / \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ gel electrolyte (Figure 18.14). The flexible photocharging capacitor was achieved by stacking the OSCs and the supercapacitor. The systems also exhibited superior operational stability $( > 9 6 \%$ efficiency retention after 100 charge/discharge cycles for one week) and mechanical robustness $( 9 4 . 6 6 \%$ efficiency retention after 5000 bending cycles at a $r \approx 2 \mathrm { m m }$ ). However, the systems suffered the issues of undercharging or unbalanced charge storage of the supercapacitor arrays in practical application due to the instability of OSCs.

The energy density $( E _ { \mathrm { A } } )$ was calculated using the equation:

$$
E _ { \mathrm { A } } = 0 . 5 \times C _ { \mathrm { A } } \times V ^ { 2 }
$$

The areal capacitances $( C _ { \mathrm { A } } )$ of the solid-state electrochemical supercapacitor with a $\mathrm { P V A } / \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ gel electrolyte were calculated from the galvanostatic charge-discharge curves at different current densities using the following formula:

$$
C _ { A } = I \times t _ { 1 } / S _ { 1 } \times V
$$

where $I$ is the constant current, $t _ { 1 }$ is the discharge time, $S _ { 1 }$ is the area of the supercapacitor, and $V$ is the operating voltage window obtained from the discharge curves excluding the voltage drop for a full discharge.

Flexible and stretchable power sources were demonstrated by combing flexible silver-zinc batteries and rigid OSCs [105]. This approach adopted specialized device layouts, such as helical springs and serpentines, to achieve enhanced mechanical property for current collectors used as structural support and backbone for all battery components. The wire-shaped batteries exhibited robust deformability while retaining electrochemical performance over 17 000 flexure cycles at a $0 . 5 \mathrm { c m }$ bending radius. An ITO/glass-based OSC was integrated with the wire-shaped batteries to construct an ESS. Also, varied light intensities (sunlight, LED, and compact fluorescent light) were employed to measure the performance of the ESS, and the resulting highest $\eta$ is $2 . 7 \%$

Thostenson et al. [101] further incorporated a conversion and CC between OSCs and supercapacitors through the three dimension (3D)-printing technique, demonstrating its possiblity to solve the problems. The application of CC achieved more energy harvesting from the OsCs and stored in the supercapacitor bank. The photo-active layers in the OSCs absorbed light and generated electron-hole pairs. The electron-hole pairs were separated under a built-in electrical field and transferred to a corresponding electrode with electrons to the anode of the supercapacitor to attract the positive ions and holes to the cathode to attract the negative ions in the electrolyte. The charging of the supercapacitor via the OSC was realized by such a photo-charge generation and transfer process under continuous light illumination until the voltage on the supercapacitor approached the open-circuit voltage of the OSC.

# 18.4.2 Fiber-Based OsCs-Integrated ESS

Compared with the planar stacked OSCs-integrated ESS, the fiber-based OSCsintegrated ESS possesses many promising advantages, such as miniaturization, adaptability, and weavability [91-94].

In 2014, Zhang et al. combined fiber-based OsCs and fiber-based supercapacitors on the same treated Ti fiber substrate via electrochemical anodization to develop a novel, all-solid-state, flexible "energy fiber' [106]. For the OsCs part, perpendicularly aligned $\mathrm { T i O } _ { 2 }$ nanotubes array was grown on the Ti wire (back electrode) by electrochemical anodization, and the modified wire was dipped into a chlorobenzene solution of the active layer $\mathrm { ( P 3 H T : P C _ { 6 1 } B M ) }$ . The PEDOT:PSS layer was further coated on the active layer, following by wrapped with MwCNT to produce the OSC part as a front electrode. The PCEs of the fiber-like OSCs showed obvious lengths (ranging from $6 5 0 \mathrm { n m }$ to $4 \mu \mathrm { m }$ ) dependence and the optimized PCE was $1 . 0 1 \%$ for the device length of $1 . 8 \mu \mathrm { m }$ . For the supercapacitor part, the $\mathrm { P V A } / \mathrm { H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 }$ (phosphoric acid) gel electrolyte and MwCNT were coated on the $\mathrm { T i O } _ { 2 }$ nanotubes treated Ti fiber in sequence. The supercapacitor part exhibited a discharge rate from 0.1 to $5 \mu \mathrm { A }$ and the scan rate from 100 to $5 0 0 0 \mathrm { m V s ^ { - 1 } }$ . Finally, the "energy fiber' achieved an overall $\eta _ { \mathrm { S T P } }$ of $0 . 8 2 \%$

In 2013, Lee et al. proposed mixed OSCs-integrated ESS, in which the textile battery and the planar flexible OSC were integrated (Figure 18.15) [103]. Polymer solar cells were fabricated on ITO-coated polyethylene naphthalate (PEN) substrates.

The PEDOT:PSS layer, PCDTBT $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ active layer, and $\mathrm { T i O } _ { x }$ (titanium oxide) were coated on the ITO-PEN substrate layer-by-layer and Al (aluminum) was deposited through a shadow mask by thermal evaporation on the devices. The overall flexible OSC showed a PCE of $5 . 4 9 \%$ on the PEN substrate. For the textile battery, nickel (Ni)-coated polyester yarn was adopted as a current collector to release stress; polyurethane (PU) binder was employed for strong adhesion of active materials. The wearable textile battery was embedded in clothes and watchstraps and exhibited comparable electrochemical performance to those of conventional metal foil-based cells even under severe bending conditions.

# 18.5 Other Applications

# 18.5.1 OSCs-Driven Water Splitting

Solution-processable OSCs have been well established as electric power for many integrating applications as we described above. Different from these applications, OSCs-driven water splitting, which converting solar energy to chemical energy (hydrogen, $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 }$ , oxygen, $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } .$ , has attracted very little attention recently. Owing to the diurnal and annual variations of irradiation, meteorological phenomena, and the nonuniformity through different regions, energy storage technology is needed to collect the OSC-generated power. Similar to the OSC-integrated battery or supercapacitor storage system, OsCs-driven water-splitting technology is another way to transfer and store the solar energy to renewable chemical energy [107-109]. In the OSCs-driven water splitting system, the solar-to-hydrogen conversion efficiency $( \eta _ { \mathrm { S T H } } )$ is defined as Eq. (18.6):

$$
\eta _ { \mathrm { S T H } } = ( J _ { \mathrm { O P } } \times 1 . 2 3 \times \eta _ { \mathrm { F } } ) / ( P _ { \mathrm { s o l a r } } )
$$

where $J _ { \mathrm { O P } }$ is the operating current density $\mathrm { \ t m { A } } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 } ,$ , the $\eta _ { \mathrm { F } }$ is assumed to be $1 0 0 \%$ and $P _ { \mathrm { s o l a r } }$ is the irradiance intensity of $1 0 0 \mathrm { m W } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$

The mechanism of OSC-driven water splitting is shown in Figure 18.16 [107]. The system consists of an OSC device wired with an electrolysis cell filling with an aqueous electrolyte. The anode performs the oxygen evolution process (OER), while the cathode executes the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in the OSC-driven water splitting system. The photogenerated holes of the OSC are collected and transported to the anode, whereas the photogenerated electrons of the OsC are collected and transported to the cathode, and thus produce a photo potential. The OsC generated potentials are then acting as the potentials of electrolysis cell to perform the OER and HER reactions, and the electrochemical reactions are mediated by the OER and HER catalysts. Finally, a membrane separates the evolved $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ gasses.

Lin et al. reported a low-cost overall OsC-driven water splitting system combining a novel tandem OSC device and metal-organic framework (MOFs) derived bimetallic nanohybrids based flexible electrocatalysts [110]. The MOF-precursor Prussian blue analogs (PBAs) were used to synthesize the coupled electrocatalysts: nitrogen-doped carbon encased iron-cobalt bimetallic phosphides (CF@FeCoP/ NC, an electrocatalyst for HER) and sulfides (CF@FeCoS/NC, an electrocatalyst for

![](images/940270671f4d6b13cb5dbc4a343075a4ca8a902b475f1d2e1319ceed54d4a46c.jpg)  
Figure 18.16 (a) Schematic representation for OSC-biased water splitting using a double BHJ junction tandem cell wired to an electrolysis cell. (b) The energy level diagram of a double BHJ junction tandem OSC device and the operation of water splitting reactions. Source: Yao et al. [107]/Reproduced with permission of John Wiley & Sons.

OER). The electrolyzer consisted of the electrode exhibited excellent catalysis property. A novel tandem OSC (ITO/ZnO/active layer/PEDOT/ZnO/PCE-10:IEIC-O-4F/ $\mathrm { V } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 5 } / \mathrm { A l } )$ was developed to power this electrolyzer, which showed the $J _ { \mathrm { s c } }$ $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ FF, and PCE of $1 0 . 8 4 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ $1 . 7 6 \mathrm { V } ,$ $6 7 \%$ , and $1 2 . 7 6 \%$ , respectively. The performance of the tandem OSCs illustrated that one device was sufficient to power the electrolyzer for overall water splitting. Eventually, the resulting OSC-driven water splitting system was proved to realize a current density of $1 0 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ at a low cell voltage of $1 . 6 0 \mathrm { V } ,$ while maintaining rather stable in a long-time durability test in alkaline media. The overall OSC-driven water splitting system yielded a high water-splitting current density of $7 . 5 \mathrm { m A c m } ^ { - 2 }$ with a $\eta _ { \mathrm { S T H } }$ of $9 . 2 \%$

In 2016, Esiner et al. investigated theoretical limits and experimental approach for $\eta _ { \mathrm { S T H } }$ in series-connected OSCs-driven electrochemical water splitting [111]. In the theoretical modeling, the electrochemical water splitting potential was assumed to be $1 . 5 0 \mathrm { V }$ and the external quantum efficiency (EQE) and FF are both supposed as 0.65 of the polymer solar cell. Considering the realistic value of the polymer solar cells, the minimum photon energy loss $( E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } } )$ which was determined by the energy difference between the optical band gap $( E _ { \mathrm { g } } )$ and $V _ { \mathrm { o c } }$ was set to $0 . 8 \mathrm { e V } .$ With these assumptions in the modeling, the two series-connected single-junction cells with $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ of $1 . 7 3 \mathrm { e V }$ and three series-connected cells with $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ of $1 . 4 4 \mathrm { e V }$ were both expected to give a resulting $\eta _ { \mathrm { S T H } }$ of $6 . 9 \%$ , which slightly decreased to $6 . 2 \%$ for four series-connected cells at an optimal $E _ { \mathrm { g } } = 1 . 3 3 \mathrm { e V } .$ In the experimental approach, PTPTIBDT-OD $( E _ { \mathrm { g } } = 1 . 8 9 \mathrm { e V } )$ , PTB7-Th $( E _ { \mathrm { g } } = 1 . 5 6 \mathrm { e V } )$ , and PDPP5T-2 $( E _ { \mathrm { g } } = 1 . 4 4 \mathrm { e V } )$ were blended with $\mathrm { P C } _ { 7 1 } \mathrm { B M }$ as BHJ active layer for two, three, and four series-connected OSC devices, respectively, giving the $\eta _ { \mathrm { S T H } }$ values of $4 . 1 \%$ $6 . 1 \%$ , and $4 . 9 \%$ . The deviations between the theoretical limits and experimental approach were ascribed to the differences in $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ and $E _ { \mathrm { l o s s } }$

The OsC devices fabricated by a large-scale slot-die printing method also have been employed in the OsCs-driven water splitting system. In 2019, Wu et al. demonstrated a high-performance non-fullerene OsC fabricating by a slot-die printing technology based on PBDB-T-SF:IT-4F photovoltaic blends [112]. The OSC showed a PCE of $1 2 . 2 7 \%$ for normal structure and $1 2 . 9 0 \%$ for inverted architecture after a detailed balancing of the flowing rate and coating speed combinations. Moreover, flexible OSCs based on a PET substrate were proved to a PCE of ${ > } 1 2 \%$ while a large-area OsC module with $0 . 4 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ yielded a PCE of $1 2 . 1 2 \%$ for two series-connected flexible OsC devices. When the large-scale printed solar module was integrated into an existing water splitting system, $\eta _ { \mathrm { S T H } }$ of $6 . 1 5 \%$ was achieved. In this system, the commercial platinum $\mathrm { ( P t ) }$ and Ni foam as OER and HER reaction electrodes were used.

# 18.5.2 OSCs-Integrated Glasses

In 2017, Landerer et al. integrated solution-processed ST-OsCs into smart sun glasses which were named solar glasses (Figure 18.17) [113]. The inverted ST-OSCs adopted the structure as glass/ITO/ZnO/active layer/PEDOT:PSS (transparent electrode), in which the ternary active layer was PBTZT-stat-benzo[1,2-b:4,5-b'] dithiophene (BDTT) $\mathrm { \cdot 8 { : } P C _ { 6 1 } B M { : } P C _ { 7 1 } B M }$ (seen in Figure 18.17). The larger substrates $( 1 7 . 8 \mathsf { c m } ^ { 2 } )$ were shaped to fit the lens frames, thereby increasing the photoactive area to $1 5 . 5 \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ , using about $9 0 \%$ of the substrate area for energy harvesting. The ST-OSCs were sandwiched between the shaped substrate and an epoxy encapsulation layer to achieve the solar glasses. In the solar glasses, the ST-OSC had been used to power a small signal processing sensor, providing constant information about the ambient temperature and the solar illumination intensity on two displays. All of the units, including power-supply ST-OSCs, signal processing sensors, and the displays were integrated into the model of the solar glasses. Moreover, the ST-OSCs unit was the only energy source for self-powered solar glasses. This system was designed to work under both low-light conditions (indoors) and high-light conditions (in the bright sun), and also under oblique light incidence and indirect or diffuse light.

# 18.6 Conclusion and Outlook

Owing to the speedy updates of the photoactive semiconductor materials and the innovation and optimization of the large-scale R2R techniques, the performance of the OsCs has been quickly prompted from $1 0 \%$ to over $1 7 \%$ in the past fiveyears. Aiming to realize the actual commercial applications of OSCs, researchers have devoted many efforts to locate and extend their most appropriate application scenarios. As mentioned above, OsCs were integrated into building facades, smart clothes, batteries, water-splitting systems, sunglasses, etc., enabling solar-to-electricity or solar-to-hydrogen conversion. In all of the application fields, OSCs exhibited bright prospects due to its inherent features like flexibility, low-cost, high mass-specific power, etc. However, different targeted applications would result in distinct demands for performance, stability, and mechanical parameters. For example, for a skin-wearable application, devices should possess a stretchability of at least $3 0 \%$ to be conformable with human skin [27]. Thus, one should consider a specific targeted application to make the relevant parameters straightforward before designing and constructing OSC devices and modules. Hence, we discuss the numerous attempts on exploiting the possibility of OsCs for emerging unique industrialization.

![](images/1912322817588d7890dd9e36e7acf8b838c7df786d013574e28b8404753f339d.jpg)  
Figure 18.17  (a) Illustration of the solar glasses assembly with the organic solar cells sandwiched between glass substrates and encapsulation glass. (b) The solar glasses in operation. (c) The output power of a typical lens-fitted solar cell measured under different illumination spectra and intensities: an $\mathsf { A M 1 . 5 G }$ spectrum to represent outdoor illumination and a white-light LED spectrum to simulate artificial indoor lighting. (d) Representative transmission spectrum and photo of a lens-fitted solar cell. Source: Landerer et al. [113]/Reproduced with permission of John Wiley & Sons.

Wide attempts have been devoted to the practical use of OsCs, including building-integrated photovoltaics, portable electric chargers, smart clothing, and implantable/biological electronics. Among these applications, the solar parks and solar trees require a little comparable performance while strict operational and long-term stability were needed. The attended mode between devices in solar modules is also very important to reduce resistance or eliminate device failures. While for the OsCs used in smart windows and greenhouse, the photoactive layer of the device should be chosen based on their absorption, and frontier orbital levels to achieve the demand colors, transparency, and also the efficiency. The wearable OSCs demand ultra-flexibility, stretchability, and biocompatibility for implantable self-powered sensors while certain flexibility and excellent waterproofness. And as for the OsCs-integrated ESS, stable and efficient power charging is the chief issue. Besides, the innovative segment in OSCs varies in different applications. For example, a waterproof textile substrate and encapsulation are essential in washable electronics. Therefore, specific targeting applications should be fixed to make the relevant parameters straightforward before designing and constructing OSC devices.

However, most application attempts of OsCs are in a primary stage and just focus on a prototype device as shown in this section. Only very few researches have emphasized the importance of technical achievements, economic, and environmental performances for the application of OsCs. Thus, more efforts should be devoted to further extend the potential application of OsCs while taking technical craft, economic benefit, environmental issues into consideration, promoting the acceptance of OSCs by the end-consumer. The OSCs will be an important asset for other mobile and consumer electronics and occupy a major position in the future energy industry.
